agents.name: Lead Analyst
agents.role: Leads the investment research team: sets the scope and research plan, briefs the six analysts and the Red Team, writes the thesis, scoring and executive summary, runs QA, and is the only bot that talks to the user.

agents.name: Company Analyst
agents.role: Researches and writes the report's company overview (legal entities, timeline, cap table) and team sections from filings, registries and public records.

agents.name: Product Analyst
agents.role: Researches and writes the report's technology and product and development strategy sections from papers, patents, regulators' databases and product evidence.

agents.name: Market Analyst
agents.role: Researches and writes the report's market and industry and competitive landscape sections, product by product and region by region.

agents.name: Fundamentals Analyst
agents.role: Researches and writes the report's business model and financial analysis sections from SEC filings, their notes and unit economics.

agents.name: Valuation Analyst
agents.role: Researches and writes the report's funding history and valuation and exit strategy sections from prices, peer multiples, rounds and precedent exits.

agents.name: Regulatory Analyst
agents.role: Researches regulators' and courts' records and policy for the whole report, writes its ESG section and files user data requests for records behind a login.

agents.name: Red Team Analyst
agents.role: Attacks the thesis before review: researches the case against it, writes the report's risk assessment and the red-team review.

agents.name: IC Reviewer
agents.role: Reviews each report version like a skeptical investment committee partner, in the skill's five passes, and approves it or returns Critical and Important items to each section's owner.

Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation
CONFIDENTIAL: shared under NDA with Meridian Capital Ventures. Do not distribute, forward or disclose any figures in this document.

1. Orrin Fieldworks at a glance
-  Autonomous strawberry-picking robots, rented to growers by the season (Robots-as-a-Service).
-  Orrin Fieldworks, Inc.: a Delaware corporation headquartered in Salinas, California, founded in September 2021.
-  38 employees, 22 in engineering; field teams in California and Florida; assembly in Guadalajara, Mexico.
-  14 pilot farms to date; 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026; a fleet of 64 robots.
-  Annual recurring revenue: $3.2M (company definition, slide 10); FY2025 revenue $1.9M.
-  Raising $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money valuation (slide 14).
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 1 of 15

--- p.2 ---
2. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at
peak harvest. Harvest labor is the largest single cost line for most growers.
-  Strawberries are picked by hand every three to four days through a season of up to seven months; a picker covers roughly a quarter of an acre a
day (company estimate).
-  Growers tell us their crews are smaller and older each year, while wages and worker housing keep getting more expensive (grower interviews, 2025).
-  Fruit left unpicked rots on the plant and spreads mold to the next pass, so a short crew costs more than the berries it leaves behind.
-  Harvest aids such as carts and conveyors make pickers faster, but still need a full crew.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 2 of 15

--- p.3 ---
3. Our product: the Orrin Picker
-  An autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives the furrows at night and day, finds ripe berries with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and
picks them with a soft three-finger gripper.
-  Pick rate: 94% of ripe fruit on the rows tested in our 2025 pilots (company measurement; definition on slide 4).
-  Throughput: one robot covers roughly 1.5 acres per 24 hours.
-  Two picking arms place berries straight into the grower's retail clamshells on board, so fruit is handled once.
-  Runs about 20 hours a day on swappable battery packs; one field technician supervises up to 8 robots, on site or remotely.
-  Sold as Robots-as-a-Service: growers pay per robot per season; we own, maintain and insure the fleet.
-  Current model: Orrin Picker v3, released to the field in March 2026. The v4, designed for lower cost, is planned for the 2027 season.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 3 of 15

--- p.4 ---
4. Technology and field performance
Metric (2025 pilots, company measurement) Result
Pick rate: ripe berries picked / ripe berries detected 94%
Rows tested 212 rows at 9 of the 14 pilot farms
Berries bruised or punctured in picking 3.8%
Unripe berries picked by mistake 2.1%
Picking speed 5.6 seconds a berry, per arm
Uptime in scheduled hours 86%
Average time between operator interventions 3.4 hours
-  Perception: two stereo camera pairs per arm, with LED lighting for night work. The ripeness model was trained on 1.9 million labelled berry images
from the Calder University lab and our pilots.
-  Gripper: three silicone fingers with slip sensing; the stem is cut, not pulled.
-  Navigation: furrow following without GPS, so robots keep working in coastal fog and at night.
Definitions: "ripe berries detected" are the berries the vision system classified as ripe. Test rows were chosen by Orrin's field team; rows under plastic
tunnels, with standing water or on slopes over 4% were excluded.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 4 of 15

-  $42B global fresh-produce harvesting labor market.

-  Bottom-up: about 50,000 US strawberry acres need about 14,300 robots at one robot per 3.5 acres. At the 2027 list price of $16,500 a robot-season
that is about $236M a year from strawberries alone, before raspberries, blackberries and blueberries.
-  Adoption assumed in our plan: 2% of US strawberry acreage by 2028 and 15% by 2031.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: report_strategy_playbook.md > Choose the Analysis Spine

## Choose the Analysis Spine

Select 1-3 primary spines and make them visible in the report.

| Company type | Primary spine | Must answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public equity / listed company | earnings quality, competitive position, valuation, catalysts, downside risk | Is the market mispricing future cash flow or risk? |
| Early-stage startup | team, problem urgency, product proof, market timing, fundraising path | Is there enough evidence to underwrite team and learning speed? |
| Growth-stage startup | unit economics, GTM repeatability, retention, margin, financing need | Can growth scale without destroying economics? |
| Deep tech / hard tech | technical feasibility, validation evidence, manufacturing, capex, regulation | What has been proven, under what conditions, and what remains unproven? |
| Biotech / medtech | mechanism, clinical data, regulatory path, reimbursement, IP, pipeline optionality | Is the clinical/regulatory risk priced correctly? |
| Industrial / hardware | BOM, supply chain, quality, installation/service economics, utilization | Can the company produce and support at scale? |
| Marketplace / platform | liquidity, network effects, take rate, cohort behavior, subsidy reliance | Is the marketplace becoming more efficient with scale? |
| Consumer / brand | customer insight, repeat behavior, channel economics, brand defensibility | Is demand durable or promotion-driven? |
| Infrastructure / tools | workflow lock-in, switching cost, integration depth, developer/operator adoption | Is this a must-have system of record/workflow or a feature? |
| Geographic / market-system-sensitive | home market, customer market, supplier ecosystem, GTM, pricing, foreign comparables, capital market, exit venue | Which geography or market system actually drives demand, economics, valuation, and exit? |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: decision_framework.md

# Decision Framework

Use this file before drafting the executive briefing, investment thesis, recommendation, scoring, or final decision. Do not force precision when evidence does not support it.

## Contents

- Consensus / Non-Consensus View
- Scenario Analysis
- Key Assumptions
- Historical Analogs
- Capital Efficiency
- Position Sizing / Deal Sizing
- The One Question
- Three Takeaways

## Consensus / Non-Consensus View

State what the market, comparable investors, or the company's own pitch appears to assume. Then state whether the report has a differentiated view.

If there is no non-consensus insight, say the thesis is consensus and explain what that means for return expectations, valuation discipline, or margin of safety. Do not invent a variant perception for appearance.

## Scenario Analysis

Use bull/base/bear cases with explicit drivers and approximate probabilities.

- For public equities and growth companies, scenarios may use revenue, margin, multiple, cash flow, valuation, catalyst timing, or downside drawdown.
- For early-stage, biotech, hard-tech, and data-poor cases, use milestone scenarios such as product-market fit, regulatory readout, manufacturing yield, customer conversion, financing survival, or exit path.

Each scenario should include:

- Specific driver or failure mode.
- Evidence that makes it plausible.
- Financial or milestone implication.
- Investor implication.

For public equities, build scenarios from explicit financial drivers where data allows: revenue growth, segment mix, gross/operating margin, tax, share count, capex, working capital, free cash flow, net cash/debt, and valuation multiple. Include current share price context before stating upside/downside.

## Key Assumptions

Rank the 3-5 assumptions that most affect the decision. For each, state:

- Confidence.
- What would disprove it.
- Impact if wrong.
- Early warning sign.

This is often more useful than adding more facts.

## Historical Analogs

Use historical analogs only when they are close enough to teach a decision rule. A good analog matches on business model, market structure, stage, regulation, customer behavior, or capital intensity.

If no close analog exists, say so.

## Capital Efficiency

Use a capital efficiency scorecard when the company has raised material capital and data exists. Useful metrics include burn multiple, revenue per dollar raised, runway, revenue per employee, capex to next milestone, and dilution efficiency.

If data is unavailable, state which missing data would be required.

For public equities, capital efficiency should use reported financials where available: ROIC, ROE, ROA, asset turnover, incremental margins, reinvestment rate, FCF conversion, dividend/buyback yield, dilution, and M&A returns. Tie these to management capital allocation quality.

## Position Sizing / Deal Sizing

Use position sizing for public equities, liquid secondaries, or explicit portfolio-allocation requests.

For public equities, position size must reflect valuation upside/downside, balance-sheet resilience, liquidity, accounting quality, catalyst timing, volatility, evidence confidence, and whether the downside is mark-to-market volatility or permanent capital impairment.

For primary-market deals, translate this into check size, valuation discipline, downside loss, reserve strategy, and conditions for follow-on investment.

## The One Question

Before finalizing, identify the single diligence question whose truthful answer would most change the investment decision. It must be specific, answerable in principle, and decision-changing.

## Three Takeaways

End with the three things the reader should remember. These should be decision statements, not generic summaries."}],"isError":false}

## Mandatory Evidence Gate

Do not draft the final report until every material section has an evidence packet in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`. Evidence may include public web sources, user-provided files, filings, databases, industry reports, patents, job posts, media interviews, customer/procurement records, or clearly labelled analyst estimates.

Minimum evidence packet per section:

| Required item | Minimum standard |
| --- | --- |
| Search work | 3-6 targeted queries unless user-provided materials are sufficient. |
| Sources opened | At least 2 independent sources; 3+ for market, competition, team, funding, financials, and risk when public data exists. |
| Source IDs | At least 2 distinct source IDs per section in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`; the final HTML should usually show 3+ distinct source IDs per major section. |
| Primary/source-of-truth check | At least 1 primary or near-primary source where available: filing, company page, registry, patent, investor announcement, regulatory record, official report, customer/procurement record. |
| Mechanism | Explain how the evidence changes economics, adoption, pricing power, risk, financing need, valuation, or exit probability. A fact without mechanism is not analysis. |
| Public-equity source-of-truth | For listed companies, use primary filings or company IR for financial statements and record market data timestamp, exchange, currency, latest price, market cap, and enterprise value if available. |
| Public-equity financial analysis | For listed companies, analyze income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, notes/accounting quality, valuation, peer comparison, and stock-price context before making a recommendation. |
| Company-claim verification | Mark material pitch-deck claims as verified, partially verified, unverified, contradicted, or not publicly disclosed. |
| Quantification | At least 2 numbers, ranges, or proxies for measurable sections; if unavailable, state what evidence is missing. |
| Comparison | At least 1 competitor, benchmark, base rate, industry norm, or historical comparable. |
| Counter-evidence | At least 1 contradicting source, weakness, adverse case, or reason the thesis may fail. |
| Investor implication | A decision-relevant conclusion: invest, pass, wait, lower valuation, add condition, or request diligence. |

The `_work/evidence_matrix.md` table is a hard gate. Each section's `Deep Evidence Table` must contain source IDs, source type, finding/fact, mechanism, benchmark or peer context, weakening evidence, investor implication, confidence, and follow-up. Do not mark a section complete by checking boxes unless those cells contain section-specific content.

Evidence gate failure rules:

- If a section has only company-provided material, write it as low-confidence and do not make a strong positive claim.
- If no independent source can verify a claim, explicitly say `未独立验证`.
- If a section lacks counter-evidence, add a red-team paragraph with the most plausible failure mode.
- If a section lacks quantification, state which metric is missing and how it affects investment confidence.
- If a section lacks peer/benchmark context, do not score it above 7/10.
- For a public-equity report, do not issue Buy/Add/Sell/Reduce before analyzing latest price/valuation, income statement quality, margin drivers, cash flow conversion, working capital, capex, balance-sheet health, accounting notes, debt/liquidity, capital allocation, and downside risk. If financial statements or price data cannot be obtained, make that the central limitation and use Watchlist/Hold off unless the user only asked for a preliminary screen.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: company_deep_dive_playbook.md > The Granularity Benchmark

## The Granularity Benchmark

Professional investment analysis is defined by **specificity**, not length. A 200-page report that uses vague language is worse than a 50-page report where every claim has a number attached. The following standards are non-negotiable:

### Numbers Must Be Precise
- ❌ "approximately 45%" → ✅ "43.1373%" or "43.1%" (state source and confidence)
- ❌ "hundreds of patents" → ✅ "69 granted patents + 12 pending across US/CN/EP"
- ❌ "founded in 2023" → ✅ "2023年10月15日" or "2023年10月"
- ❌ "raised several hundred million" → ✅ "$75M Series B at $450M pre-money (2025-03-15)"
- ❌ "large facility" → ✅ "16,000平方米，含二类/三类有源医疗器械GMP厂房"

### People Must Be Traceable
- ❌ "毕业于知名大学" → ✅ "本科 中国科学技术大学 机械电子工程；硕士 香港理工大学 软件工程"
- ❌ "曾在多家公司工作" → ✅ each role: company + title + dates + specific achievements
- ❌ "行业资深人士" → ✅ "69篇同行评审论文；曾任职于Neuralink担任临床合作负责人"
- Every founder bio must trace from undergraduate through highest degree
- Every key hire must have: institution + degree + year + prior employer + role + achievements

### Events Must Be Dated
- ❌ "recently completed funding" → ✅ "2026年6月26日，超级工厂一期竣工投运"
- ❌ "has partnerships with hospitals" → ✅ "与上海华山医院、上海市精神卫生中心、华西医院共建联合实验室"
- ❌ "attended by investors" → ✅ "华映资本季薇、清松资本张松、戈壁创投唐啟波、傅利叶顾捷出席剪彩"

### If Data Is Unavailable
- State EXACTLY what is missing (e.g., "注册资本未公开" not "信息不足")
- Explain how material the gap is to the investment decision
- List what source would resolve it (e.g., "需查阅工商登记档案")
- NEVER fill the gap with vague language that sounds informative but conveys no data

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: analysis_core.md > Section Writing Contract

## Section Writing Contract

Each final section must cover the full analytical logic, but it should read like an investment memo, not a compliance checklist. Use judgement, evidence, mechanism, comparison, counter-evidence, investor implication, confidence, and diligence questions as the internal reasoning scaffold. Do not force every section to show the same subheadings such as `判断 / 证据 / 机制 / 对标 / 反证 / 投资含义 / 待验证问题`.

The final report should not become pure black text on a white background. Use visual hierarchy and compact evidence displays to make dense analysis readable, while avoiding repetitive card stacks.

Internal workflow language must not appear in the final report. Never write sentences that explain how the section should be written, such as `本节要把证据等级...放在同一条逻辑链`, `不能被写成`, `而不是把材料拆成孤立事实`, or `source ID只用于锁定证据来源`. The final report should analyze the company, not describe the report-writing rubric.

Preferred section shape:

1. Start with a short thesis sentence that states the section-level judgement.
2. Explain the evidence in narrative paragraphs, weaving in source confidence, dates, and specific numbers.
3. Show why the evidence matters economically or strategically.
4. Compare with peers, substitutes, base rates, or historical analogs where it changes the decision.
5. Bring the main weakness or contrary evidence into the same discussion rather than isolating it mechanically.
6. End with the investor implication and the most decision-relevant open questions.

Use tables, KPI strips, risk matrices, scenario tables, or short callout cards when they improve scanability. Use explicit micro-headings only when they fit the section's content, not as a repeated template. Good micro-headings are content-specific, for example `现金流质量比利润表弱`, `监管路径是估值折扣的来源`, or `客户验证仍停留在试点阶段`.

Recommended readable section pattern:

- 1 short opening judgement paragraph.
- 2-4 analytical paragraphs, each with a clear point and evidence.
- 1 compact visual element when useful: KPI dashboard, mini table, risk matrix, timeline, scenario table, or source/confidence callout.
- 1 short closing sentence or small callout for investor implication/open question.

Use visual components selectively:

- Use a KPI/dashboard strip for numbers that need comparison.
- Use a table for peers, financial trends, milestone gates, or scenario assumptions.
- Use warning/danger callouts for decision-changing risks, not every weakness.
- Use source/confidence tags inline or at paragraph ends to preserve credibility without interrupting flow.
- Use bullets only for short lists; avoid long bullet walls.

Avoid rigid writing patterns:

- Do not write `{section name}判断`, `{section name}的机制`, `{section name}的benchmark`, `{section name}原件优先级`, `{section name}决策门槛`, or `{section name}决策清单`.
- Do not repeat the same seven labels in every section.
- Do not make each section a stack of independent bullet cards.
- Do not replace structured cards with unbroken long paragraphs.
- Do not put evidence in one box and interpretation in another when a paragraph would read better.
- Do not add a token "对标" or "反证" sentence just to satisfy the form; integrate comparison and counter-evidence into the argument.
- Do not hide the recommendation until the end of a long fact list.
- Do not append the same `投资人读法`, `来源/Source`, `数字锚点`, `仍需确认`, or generic transaction-structure paragraph to every section. If a reader would recognize the paragraph from another section, rewrite it as section-specific analysis or delete it.
- Put full citations in one `数据来源与引用 / Source Appendix` module. Inline source/confidence tags should support the most important claims, not repeat the same source list in every paragraph.

Avoid shallow claims unless evidence-backed:

- "Market space is large."
- "Team background is strong."
- "Technology has barriers."
- "Business model is scalable."
- "Competition is intense."
- "Risks are controllable."

Rewrite them into concrete questions: which market segment, which team achievement, which moat type, which scaling constraint, which competitor, and which risk-mitigation milestone.

Investor perspective is a US venture fund, so the underwriting currency is USD and the exit venue is a US/European strategic or IPO path.
arguments.hypothesis: The customer pain is real and independently documented, but at the deck's own numbers the current unit economics do not work: a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over the stated 4 seasons is $12,000 a season against $3,900 of 2026 gross profit per robot-season, so every paid 2026 robot-season is cash-negative before any fleet-level overhead. The thesis therefore turns entirely on the unbuilt v4 BOM ($31,000-$33,000) and a 74% price increase to $16,500, neither of which has a signed contract behind it. Pick-rate evidence is company-measured on self-selected rows with material exclusions, one pilot has already been lost to bruising, and the technical core sits in a university licence that goes non-exclusive below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 (Orrin plans 360). At $72M pre-money for $1.9M FY2025 revenue and $2.6M FY2026E, we are inclined to wait for milestone — a third-party-verified 2027 season of 150+ robots at unit cost below $36,000 with renewals at the $12,700 price — rather than lead at this price, unless the diligence establishes the v4 cost path and customer concentration is cured.
arguments.industry_map: Value chain: strawberry genetics and nursery stock (e.g. UC Davis and proprietary breeder programmes) -> growers (California and Florida, top-20 growers farm over half of California acreage per the deck) -> harvest execution (hand crews, farm-labour contractors, H-2A crews) and harvest aids (conveyor platforms, carts) -> robotic picking hardware, perception software and fleet service -> cooling/pack (clamshells, pallet) -> retail and foodservice. Decisive bottleneck: the peak-harvest labour window. Berries must be picked every three to four days for up to seven months, the crop is perishable and mould spreads from unharvested fruit, so a crew shortfall costs more than the fruit lost; that is what a robot must be priced against. Second bottleneck: capital and service intensity — the robot earns only within a roughly seven-month California season and a four-month Florida season against a $48,000 build, so utilisation across geographies and seasons, not pick rate alone, determines the return. Orrin's place: it is not a grower or a labour contractor but an equipment OEM plus a service operator — Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. holds the patents and the Calder University licence, Orrin Fleet Services LLC owns the fleet, signs the grower contracts and carries the Kestrel debt, so the capital intensity sits one layer below the parent that raises the equity. It competes for the grower's harvest budget against hand crews and $10,000-$30,000 harvest-aid platforms, not only against other robots.

spines.must_answer: What has actually been proven about the Orrin Picker under field conditions, and what remains unproven? Specifically: whether a 94% pick rate measured on 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, chosen by the company, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%, transfers to commercial blocks; whether 3.8% bruising is inside the retail tolerance that one lost pilot already tested; whether the IP is enforceable given that every claim of the lead gripper application was rejected in a first office action and the two core perception families are licensed, not owned, on a 100-robot exclusivity test due 2027-12-31.

Can Orrin build, deploy and service 360 robots for the 2027 season at a cost that earns a return? The test is the v4 BOM ($31,000 target, $33,000 assumed in the use-of-funds budget, $36,000 milestone ceiling against a $48,000 v3 build), the $16,500 2027 list price against $9,500 on signed 2025-2026 contracts, service cost of $3,100 plus $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables per robot-season, 86% uptime and one technician per 8 robots at fleet scale — and whether a 7-month California plus 4-month Florida year can keep a fleet utilised.

Is there enough evidence to underwrite this team and its learning speed at a $72M pre-money? The test is whether a first-time CEO with a robotics PhD and a harvest-operations COO can convert 14 pilots into paid renewals (2 converted in 2025, 5 paying growers in 2026, one Florida pilot lost to bruising), hire a CTO after the co-founder CTO left in 2023-08, and reach the 2027 milestones (360 robots, $8M ARR on a definition that includes letters of intent and an engineering contract, unit cost below $36,000) on the $18M raise that carries 9 months of runway at $410,000 monthly net burn.

# Geographic Market Context Lens

Use this file when the company, customers, suppliers, competitors, capital markets, or exit paths span different countries or regions. The goal is to avoid applying one market's logic to another market.

This is broader than competition. Geography and jurisdiction can change the entire investment thesis.

## Core Principle

Before analyzing market, competition, business model, valuation, risk, or exit, identify which market system you are talking about.

Separate:

- **Company home base**: incorporation, headquarters, R&D, manufacturing, data, licenses.
- **Current revenue market**: where customers actually pay today.
- **Target expansion market**: where the company claims it can grow.
- **Supplier and infrastructure market**: chips, cloud, components, instruments, manufacturing, talent, IP, data.
- **Comparable company market**: where benchmarks and valuation comps operate.
- **Capital market**: where investors, financing, listing, liquidity, and valuation multiples come from.
- **Exit market**: likely acquirers, IPO venue, strategic buyers, regulatory review.
- **Reader / investor perspective**: domestic investor, international investor, strategic buyer, public-market investor, or primary-market investor.

Do not collapse these into one generic "global market."

## Analysis Dimensions

Answer the dimensions that are material:

1. **Demand and budget**: Are customer pain, budget owner, procurement cycle, payment reliability, and willingness to pay similar across regions?
2. **Go-to-market and distribution**: Does the company need local sales, service, channel partners, hospital access, developer ecosystem, government qualification, or after-sales support?
3. **Pricing and unit economics**: Are ASP, gross margin, labor cost, logistics, tariffs, cloud cost, reimbursement, or subsidy economics different by geography?
4. **Product localization**: Are language, workflow, standards, certification, integration, data residency, safety, or support requirements market-specific?
5. **Competition and substitutes**: Who competes in the same buyer process today? Who is only a foreign comparable, future entrant, substitute, or valuation benchmark?
6. **Supply chain and ecosystem**: Does the company depend on region-specific suppliers, talent, manufacturing clusters, research networks, standards bodies, or platform ecosystems?
7. **Policy and regulation**: Which jurisdictions affect licenses, procurement, subsidies, export controls, sanctions, data, antitrust, reimbursement, or safety approval? Use `policy_geopolitics_lens.md` if material.
8. **Capital and valuation**: Are comps from the same market system? Adjust for liquidity, disclosure, governance, growth quality, country risk, listing venue, and exit optionality.
9. **Exit path**: Are likely acquirers domestic or international? Are foreign buyer limits, national-security review, sector approval, or listing restrictions relevant?
10. **Macro and currency**: Do FX, rates, inflation, fiscal budgets, trade cycles, or geopolitical shocks affect revenue, cost, financing, or valuation?

## Competitor / Comparable Classification

When foreign or adjacent companies appear in research, classify them:

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Direct competitor | Competes for the same buyer, budget, use case, geography, and procurement path today. |
| Local substitute | Solves the same pain through a different product, channel, or service model in the same market. |
| International competitor | Competes elsewhere and could enter if barriers are solved. |
| Strategic comparable | Useful for margins, valuation, technology route, or exit logic, but not a current competitor. |
| Future entrant | Could become a competitor in 12-36 months. |
| Non-comparable | Similar label/category, but different customer, market access, regulation, or business model. |

## Report Integration

Do not add a generic geography essay. Integrate the lens into:

- Executive briefing: state which geography/perspective drives the conclusion.
- Market: separate global TAM, serviceable geography, and realistically obtainable market.
- Product/GTM: explain localization, channel, support, certification, and customer-access constraints.
- Business model/financials: adjust pricing, margin, sales cycle, payment risk, labor/capex, and supply-chain assumptions by region.
- Competition: separate direct competitors from foreign comparables, substitutes, future entrants, and non-comparables.
- Valuation: avoid using foreign comps without adjustment; explain why the comp is relevant or only directional.
- Risk: include market-entry, localization, supply-chain, FX, macro, regulation, policy, and exit-market risks when material.
- Exit: test whether likely acquirers/listing venues exist in the same market system.

If the lens is not material, state briefly: `地理/市场体系因素：未发现对投资结论有重大影响的跨区域差异。`"}],"isError":false}

## Mandatory Evidence Gate

Do not draft the final report until every material section has an evidence packet in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`. Evidence may include public web sources, user-provided files, filings, databases, industry reports, patents, job posts, media interviews, customer/procurement records, or clearly labelled analyst estimates.

Minimum evidence packet per section:

| Required item | Minimum standard |
| --- | --- |
| Search work | 3-6 targeted queries unless user-provided materials are sufficient. |
| Sources opened | At least 2 independent sources; 3+ for market, competition, team, funding, financials, and risk when public data exists. |
| Source IDs | At least 2 distinct source IDs per section in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`; the final HTML should usually show 3+ distinct source IDs per major section. |
| Primary/source-of-truth check | At least 1 primary or near-primary source where available: filing, company page, registry, patent, investor announcement, regulatory record, official report, customer/procurement record. |
| Mechanism | Explain how the evidence changes economics, adoption, pricing power, risk, financing need, valuation, or exit probability. A fact without mechanism is not analysis. |
| Public-equity source-of-truth | For listed companies, use primary filings or company IR for financial statements and record market data timestamp, exchange, currency, latest price, market cap, and enterprise value if available. |
| Public-equity financial analysis | For listed companies, analyze income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, notes/accounting quality, valuation, peer comparison, and stock-price context before making a recommendation. |
| Company-claim verification | Mark material pitch-deck claims as verified, partially verified, unverified, contradicted, or not publicly disclosed. |
| Quantification | At least 2 numbers, ranges, or proxies for measurable sections; if unavailable, state what evidence is missing. |
| Comparison | At least 1 competitor, benchmark, base rate, industry norm, or historical comparable. |
| Counter-evidence | At least 1 contradicting source, weakness, adverse case, or reason the thesis may fail. |
| Investor implication | A decision-relevant conclusion: invest, pass, wait, lower valuation, add condition, or request diligence. |

The `_work/evidence_matrix.md` table is a hard gate. Each section's `Deep Evidence Table` must contain source IDs, source type, finding/fact, mechanism, benchmark or peer context, weakening evidence, investor implication, confidence, and follow-up. Do not mark a section complete by checking boxes unless those cells contain section-specific content.

Evidence gate failure rules:

- If a section has only company-provided material, write it as low-confidence and do not make a strong positive claim.
- If no independent source can verify a claim, explicitly say `未独立验证`.
- If a section lacks counter-evidence, add a red-team paragraph with the most plausible failure mode.
- If a section lacks quantification, state which metric is missing and how it affects investment confidence.
- If a section lacks peer/benchmark context, do not score it above 7/10.
- For a public-equity report, do not issue Buy/Add/Sell/Reduce before analyzing latest price/valuation, income statement quality, margin drivers, cash flow conversion, working capital, capex, balance-sheet health, accounting notes, debt/liquidity, capital allocation, and downside risk. If financial statements or price data cannot be obtained, make that the central limitation and use Watchlist/Hold off unless the user only asked for a preliminary screen.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: company_deep_dive_playbook.md > Section 6: Competition — Per-Product Forensic Mapping

## Section 6: Competition — Per-Product Forensic Mapping

**CRITICAL: Competition is per-product, NOT per-company. A company with 4 products faces 4 DIFFERENT competitive landscapes.** Lumping all competitors into one table under "the company competes with Medtronic and Abbott" is analytically useless — Medtronic's DBS for Parkinson's does NOT compete with a non-invasive tibial nerve stimulator for OAB. The analyst MUST build a separate competitive landscape for EACH product.

### 6.0 Pre-Draft Gate: Per-Product Competitor Identification

Before writing the competition section, the analyst must:

1. List every product the company has (commercial, clinical, preclinical, R&D)
2. For EACH product, search: "[product category] competitors", "[specific indication] treatment options", "[product type] FDA approved", "[product type] NMPA approved"
3. Search PubMed/ClinicalTrials.gov: "[indication] [technology type]" to find ALL clinical-stage competitors
4. Search government procurement databases for the specific product category
5. Search patent databases for competitive filings in the specific technology area
6. Do NOT combine competitors across products — build separate competitor maps

### 6.1 Per-Product Competitor Database Template

For EACH product, build this table:

```
### Product: [Product Name] — [Indication]

#### Direct Competitors (Same Indication, Same Technology Route)

| Competitor | Product Name | Technology | Regulatory Status | Efficacy Data | Price | Market Share | Strengths vs Us | Weaknesses vs Us |
|-----------|-------------|-----------|-------------------|---------------|-------|-------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| [A] | [X] | [Approach] | FDA/NMPA [status] | [Key clinical result] | $[X] | [X]% | [Why they win] | [Where we win] |

#### Indirect Competitors (Same Indication, Different Technology)

| Competitor | Product/Approach | Technology Route | Why Customers Choose This Instead |
|-----------|-----------------|-----------------|----------------------------------|
| [Current Standard of Care] | [Drug/Surgery/Device] | [Pharma/Surgical/Behavioral] | [Reason for preference] |

#### Pipeline Competitors (Same Indication, Clinical/Preclinical Stage)

| Company | Product | Stage | Key Differentiator | Expected Launch | Threat Level |
|---------|---------|-------|-------------------|----------------|-------------|
| [Name] | [X] | Phase [I/II/III] | [Advantage] | [Year] | [High/Med/Low] |

#### Status Quo / "Do Nothing" Competitor

- What patients currently do: [describe current standard of care, including "just live with it" for untreated conditions]
- Why they don't adopt existing solutions: [cost, invasiveness, side effects, lack of access]
- What would make them switch: [our product's specific advantage]
```

### 6.2 Example: 复远数科 Per-Product Competition (Illustrative)

**Product 1: CSNS (SCI Cervical Stimulation)**
- Direct competitors: ARCEX (ONWARD Medical, Swiss), ExaStim (GTX Medical, Netherlands), TESCoN device (various academic)
- NOT competitors: Medtronic Intellis SCS (different approach—invasive, different indication—pain, different patient segment—lumbar)
- Pipeline: NCT07361627 (Montreal), NCT07423949 (UBC), NCT07334977 (France)

**Product 2: 胫享™ TNS (OAB Tibial Nerve Stimulation)**
- Direct competitors: Urgent PC (Laborie, percutaneous PTNS), eCoin (Valencia Technologies, implantable), RENOVA (Stimwave, implantable), TENSmini (academic wearable)
- NOT competitors: Medtronic InterStim (sacral, not tibial; invasive, not transcutaneous), Axonics (sacral, implantable)
- Indirect: Anticholinergics (tolterodine, solifenacin), β3-agonists (mirabegron), Botox injections

**Product 3: PNS (VTE Neuromuscular Stimulation)**
- Direct competitors: geko (Firstkind, UK), VenaPulse (various), traditional IPC devices (Covidien, Cardinal Health)
- NOT competitors: Eliquis/Xarelto (anticoagulant drugs — different mechanism, complementary not competing)

**Product 4: OSA Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulator (R&D)**
- Direct competitors: Inspire (Inspire Medical Systems, FDA approved), Genio (Nyxoah, CE mark), aura6000 (LivaNova, clinical)
- NOT competitors: CPAP machines (ResMed, Philips — different technology route, first-line not surgical)

### 6.3 Competitive Positioning Map (Per Product)

For EACH product, create a separate positioning map:

| | Market Leader | Strong Challenger | Niche Player | Emerging Threat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Product 1: [Name]** | [Company/Product] | [Company/Product] | [Company/Product] | [Company/Product] |
| **Product 2: [Name]** | [DIFFERENT Company] | [DIFFERENT Company] | — | [DIFFERENT Company] |

**Do not fill the same companies into every product row. If they appear in multiple rows, justify why.**

### 6.4 Source Authority Requirements for Competition Analysis

For each competitor identified, the analyst MUST cite at least ONE authoritative source:
- Company's own website/IR page (product description, indications, regulatory status)

## The Granularity Benchmark

Professional investment analysis is defined by **specificity**, not length. A 200-page report that uses vague language is worse than a 50-page report where every claim has a number attached. The following standards are non-negotiable:

### Numbers Must Be Precise
- ❌ "approximately 45%" → ✅ "43.1373%" or "43.1%" (state source and confidence)
- ❌ "hundreds of patents" → ✅ "69 granted patents + 12 pending across US/CN/EP"
- ❌ "founded in 2023" → ✅ "2023年10月15日" or "2023年10月"
- ❌ "raised several hundred million" → ✅ "$75M Series B at $450M pre-money (2025-03-15)"
- ❌ "large facility" → ✅ "16,000平方米，含二类/三类有源医疗器械GMP厂房"

### People Must Be Traceable
- ❌ "毕业于知名大学" → ✅ "本科 中国科学技术大学 机械电子工程；硕士 香港理工大学 软件工程"
- ❌ "曾在多家公司工作" → ✅ each role: company + title + dates + specific achievements
- ❌ "行业资深人士" → ✅ "69篇同行评审论文；曾任职于Neuralink担任临床合作负责人"
- Every founder bio must trace from undergraduate through highest degree
- Every key hire must have: institution + degree + year + prior employer + role + achievements

### Events Must Be Dated
- ❌ "recently completed funding" → ✅ "2026年6月26日，超级工厂一期竣工投运"
- ❌ "has partnerships with hospitals" → ✅ "与上海华山医院、上海市精神卫生中心、华西医院共建联合实验室"
- ❌ "attended by investors" → ✅ "华映资本季薇、清松资本张松、戈壁创投唐啟波、傅利叶顾捷出席剪彩"

### If Data Is Unavailable
- State EXACTLY what is missing (e.g., "注册资本未公开" not "信息不足")
- Explain how material the gap is to the investment decision
- List what source would resolve it (e.g., "需查阅工商登记档案")
- NEVER fill the gap with vague language that sounds informative but conveys no data

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: analysis_core.md > Section Writing Contract

## Section Writing Contract

Each final section must cover the full analytical logic, but it should read like an investment memo, not a compliance checklist. Use judgement, evidence, mechanism, comparison, counter-evidence, investor implication, confidence, and diligence questions as the internal reasoning scaffold. Do not force every section to show the same subheadings such as `判断 / 证据 / 机制 / 对标 / 反证 / 投资含义 / 待验证问题`.

The final report should not become pure black text on a white background. Use visual hierarchy and compact evidence displays to make dense analysis readable, while avoiding repetitive card stacks.

Internal workflow language must not appear in the final report. Never write sentences that explain how the section should be written, such as `本节要把证据等级...放在同一条逻辑链`, `不能被写成`, `而不是把材料拆成孤立事实`, or `source ID只用于锁定证据来源`. The final report should analyze the company, not describe the report-writing rubric.

Preferred section shape:

1. Start with a short thesis sentence that states the section-level judgement.
2. Explain the evidence in narrative paragraphs, weaving in source confidence, dates, and specific numbers.
3. Show why the evidence matters economically or strategically.
4. Compare with peers, substitutes, base rates, or historical analogs where it changes the decision.
5. Bring the main weakness or contrary evidence into the same discussion rather than isolating it mechanically.
6. End with the investor implication and the most decision-relevant open questions.

Use tables, KPI strips, risk matrices, scenario tables, or short callout cards when they improve scanability. Use explicit micro-headings only when they fit the section's content, not as a repeated template. Good micro-headings are content-specific, for example `现金流质量比利润表弱`, `监管路径是估值折扣的来源`, or `客户验证仍停留在试点阶段`.

Recommended readable section pattern:

- 1 short opening judgement paragraph.
- 2-4 analytical paragraphs, each with a clear point and evidence.
- 1 compact visual element when useful: KPI dashboard, mini table, risk matrix, timeline, scenario table, or source/confidence callout.
- 1 short closing sentence or small callout for investor implication/open question.

Use visual components selectively:

- Use a KPI/dashboard strip for numbers that need comparison.
- Use a table for peers, financial trends, milestone gates, or scenario assumptions.
- Use warning/danger callouts for decision-changing risks, not every weakness.
- Use source/confidence tags inline or at paragraph ends to preserve credibility without interrupting flow.
- Use bullets only for short lists; avoid long bullet walls.

Avoid rigid writing patterns:

- Do not write `{section name}判断`, `{section name}的机制`, `{section name}的benchmark`, `{section name}原件优先级`, `{section name}决策门槛`, or `{section name}决策清单`.
- Do not repeat the same seven labels in every section.
- Do not make each section a stack of independent bullet cards.
- Do not replace structured cards with unbroken long paragraphs.
- Do not put evidence in one box and interpretation in another when a paragraph would read better.
- Do not add a token "对标" or "反证" sentence just to satisfy the form; integrate comparison and counter-evidence into the argument.
- Do not hide the recommendation until the end of a long fact list.
- Do not append the same `投资人读法`, `来源/Source`, `数字锚点`, `仍需确认`, or generic transaction-structure paragraph to every section. If a reader would recognize the paragraph from another section, rewrite it as section-specific analysis or delete it.
- Put full citations in one `数据来源与引用 / Source Appendix` module. Inline source/confidence tags should support the most important claims, not repeat the same source list in every paragraph.

Avoid shallow claims unless evidence-backed:

- "Market space is large."
- "Team background is strong."
- "Technology has barriers."
- "Business model is scalable."
- "Competition is intense."
- "Risks are controllable."

Rewrite them into concrete questions: which market segment, which team achievement, which moat type, which scaling constraint, which competitor, and which risk-mitigation milestone.

### 7.1 Income Statement Deep-Dive

Go beyond top-line revenue:

- Revenue by product line / segment / geography (in percentages and absolute)
- Revenue by customer type (enterprise vs. SMB, hospital vs. clinic, etc.)

- Stock-based compensation: as % of revenue, dilution rate
- Customer acquisition cost (CAC) trend
- Customer lifetime value (LTV)
- Payback period on CAC

### 7.2 Detailed Unit Economics

Break down the economics of a single transaction/customer:

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: public_equity_financials_lens.md > Professional Financial Statement Analysis

## Professional Financial Statement Analysis

Analyze trends over at least 3 years when available, plus the latest interim/quarterly period.

Read the three statements and notes together. The analysis should explain economic reality, not only reproduce line items. Use common-size analysis, year-over-year and multi-year CAGR/trend analysis, peer comparison, and ratio analysis where data supports it.

Income statement:

- Separate volume, price, mix, FX, acquisition/disposal, one-off, and accounting effects where possible.
- Check gross margin and operating margin drivers rather than only reporting changes.
- Flag stock-based compensation, capitalization of expenses, fair-value gains, subsidies, asset sales, impairment reversals, and other non-operating items.
- Compare reported net income, adjusted/non-GAAP profit, operating profit, EBITDA, EPS, and tax rate; explain which profit measure is most decision-relevant and why.
- For segment disclosures, identify which segment creates value, which consumes capital, and whether mix shift improves or weakens quality.

Cash flow:

- Compare net income to operating cash flow and free cash flow.
- Identify working-capital pulls: receivables, inventory, payables, contract assets/liabilities, prepayments.
- For capex-heavy companies, distinguish maintenance capex from growth capex when possible.
- Treat earnings growth with weak cash conversion as lower quality unless there is a clear temporary reason.
- Reconcile CFO, capex, acquisitions/disposals, financing cash flows, dividends, buybacks, issuance, and debt repayment to the change in cash.
- Check whether free cash flow is structurally positive, cyclical, temporarily depressed, or dependent on working-capital release.

Balance sheet:

- Assess net cash/debt, debt maturity, interest coverage, refinancing risk, pledged assets, guarantees, off-balance-sheet commitments, lease liabilities, and contingent liabilities where disclosed.
- Assess asset quality: goodwill/intangibles, capitalized R&D, inventory age, receivable concentration/aging, related-party balances, investment property/fair value assets, restricted cash.
- Compare leverage and liquidity with peer norms and cyclicality.
- State whether assets and liabilities are healthy, stretched, or fragile under the bear case.
- Analyze equity quality: retained earnings, accumulated losses, minority interests, treasury shares, accumulated other comprehensive income, and dilution from options/convertibles.
- For banks/insurers/financials, replace industrial leverage metrics with capital adequacy, asset quality, NPL/credit cost, reserve coverage, duration/ALM, solvency, and regulatory capital metrics.

Notes and disclosures:

- Read accounting policies and key estimates before judging quality.
- Check revenue recognition, lease accounting, impairment testing, fair-value hierarchy, provisions, tax contingencies, related-party transactions, guarantees, pledges, restricted cash, commitments, and post-balance-sheet events.
- Flag auditor qualifications, emphasis of matter, material weakness, internal-control issues, delayed filings, restatements, regulator inquiries, or enforcement actions.

Return and efficiency:

- Calculate or discuss ROE, ROA, ROIC, asset turnover, working-capital turnover, inventory days, receivable days, payable days, cash conversion cycle, and incremental margins when relevant.
- Compare returns with cost of capital and peer ranges. A company that grows below its cost of capital may destroy value even if revenue grows.

Capital allocation:

- Review dividends, buybacks, issuance, M&A, related-party transactions, insider ownership, management incentives, and historical ROIC.
- Ask whether management compounds capital or dilutes/allocates poorly.

Forecast bridge:

- Build a compact bridge from historical results to bull/base/bear scenarios: revenue growth, margin, tax, capex, working capital, FCF, share count, and terminal/multiple assumption.
- Tie every forecast driver to evidence: backlog/order book, pricing, utilization, capacity, regulation, end-market demand, management guidance, consensus, or peer base rates.

arguments.hypothesis: The customer pain is real and independently documented, but at the deck's own numbers the current unit economics do not work: a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over the stated four seasons is $12,000 a season against $3,900 of 2026 gross profit per robot-season, so each paid 2026 robot-season is cash-negative before any fleet-level overhead and before the 11.5% equipment debt. The thesis therefore turns on the unbuilt v4 bill of materials ($31,000-$33,000) and a 74% price increase to $16,500, neither of which has a signed contract behind it. Pick-rate evidence is company-measured on self-selected rows with material exclusions, one pilot has already been lost to bruising, and the technical core sits in a university licence that goes non-exclusive below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 against a plan of 360. At $72M pre-money for $1.9M FY2025 revenue and $2.6M FY2026E, the initial inclination is to wait for milestone — a third-party-verified 2027 season of 150+ robots at unit cost below $36,000 with renewals at the $12,700 price — rather than lead at this price, unless diligence establishes the v4 cost path and cures the customer concentration.
arguments.industry_map: Value chain: strawberry genetics and nursery stock -> growers (California and Florida; the top 20 growers farm over half of California acreage per the deck) -> harvest execution (hand crews, farm-labour contractors, H-2A crews) and harvest aids (conveyor platforms, carts) -> robotic picking hardware, perception software and fleet service -> cooling and pack (clamshells, pallets) -> retail and foodservice. Decisive bottleneck: the peak-harvest labour window. Berries must be picked every three to four days for up to seven months, the crop is perishable and mould spreads from unharvested fruit, so a crew shortfall costs more than the fruit lost; that is what a robot must be priced against. Second bottleneck: capital and service intensity — the robot earns only within a roughly seven-month California season and a four-month Florida season against a $48,000 build, so utilisation across geographies and seasons, not pick rate alone, determines the return. Orrin's place: not a grower or a labour contractor but an equipment OEM plus service operator. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. holds the patent applications and the university licence; Orrin Fleet Services LLC owns the fleet, signs the grower contracts and carries the equipment debt, so the capital intensity sits one layer below the entity raising equity. It competes for the grower's harvest budget against hand crews and harvest-aid platforms, not only against other robots.

Also relevant: university technology-transfer policy, because the two core patent families are licensed on a milestone-linked exclusivity, and patent-office procedure, because the lead gripper application has had every claim rejected once. The policy channel is mostly indirect but decision-relevant: any expansion of the legal guest-worker supply lowers the grower's cost of hand labour and therefore the robot's price ceiling, while tighter labour enforcement raises it.

## Mandatory Evidence Gate

Do not draft the final report until every material section has an evidence packet in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`. Evidence may include public web sources, user-provided files, filings, databases, industry reports, patents, job posts, media interviews, customer/procurement records, or clearly labelled analyst estimates.

Minimum evidence packet per section:

| Required item | Minimum standard |
| --- | --- |
| Search work | 3-6 targeted queries unless user-provided materials are sufficient. |
| Sources opened | At least 2 independent sources; 3+ for market, competition, team, funding, financials, and risk when public data exists. |
| Source IDs | At least 2 distinct source IDs per section in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`; the final HTML should usually show 3+ distinct source IDs per major section. |
| Primary/source-of-truth check | At least 1 primary or near-primary source where available: filing, company page, registry, patent, investor announcement, regulatory record, official report, customer/procurement record. |
| Mechanism | Explain how the evidence changes economics, adoption, pricing power, risk, financing need, valuation, or exit probability. A fact without mechanism is not analysis. |
| Public-equity source-of-truth | For listed companies, use primary filings or company IR for financial statements and record market data timestamp, exchange, currency, latest price, market cap, and enterprise value if available. |
| Public-equity financial analysis | For listed companies, analyze income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, notes/accounting quality, valuation, peer comparison, and stock-price context before making a recommendation. |
| Company-claim verification | Mark material pitch-deck claims as verified, partially verified, unverified, contradicted, or not publicly disclosed. |
| Quantification | At least 2 numbers, ranges, or proxies for measurable sections; if unavailable, state what evidence is missing. |
| Comparison | At least 1 competitor, benchmark, base rate, industry norm, or historical comparable. |
| Counter-evidence | At least 1 contradicting source, weakness, adverse case, or reason the thesis may fail. |
| Investor implication | A decision-relevant conclusion: invest, pass, wait, lower valuation, add condition, or request diligence. |

The `_work/evidence_matrix.md` table is a hard gate. Each section's `Deep Evidence Table` must contain source IDs, source type, finding/fact, mechanism, benchmark or peer context, weakening evidence, investor implication, confidence, and follow-up. Do not mark a section complete by checking boxes unless those cells contain section-specific content.

Evidence gate failure rules:

- If a section has only company-provided material, write it as low-confidence and do not make a strong positive claim.
- If no independent source can verify a claim, explicitly say `未独立验证`.
- If a section lacks counter-evidence, add a red-team paragraph with the most plausible failure mode.
- If a section lacks quantification, state which metric is missing and how it affects investment confidence.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: company_deep_dive_playbook.md > The Granularity Benchmark

## The Granularity Benchmark

Professional investment analysis is defined by **specificity**, not length. A 200-page report that uses vague language is worse than a 50-page report where every claim has a number attached. The following standards are non-negotiable:

### Numbers Must Be Precise
- ❌ "approximately 45%" → ✅ "43.1373%" or "43.1%" (state source and confidence)
- ❌ "hundreds of patents" → ✅ "69 granted patents + 12 pending across US/CN/EP"
- ❌ "founded in 2023" → ✅ "2023年10月15日" or "2023年10月"
- ❌ "raised several hundred million" → ✅ "$75M Series B at $450M pre-money (2025-03-15)"
- ❌ "large facility" → ✅ "16,000平方米，含二类/三类有源医疗器械GMP厂房"

### People Must Be Traceable
- ❌ "毕业于知名大学" → ✅ "本科 中国科学技术大学 机械电子工程；硕士 香港理工大学 软件工程"
- ❌ "曾在多家公司工作" → ✅ each role: company + title + dates + specific achievements
- ❌ "行业资深人士" → ✅ "69篇同行评审论文；曾任职于Neuralink担任临床合作负责人"
- Every founder bio must trace from undergraduate through highest degree
- Every key hire must have: institution + degree + year + prior employer + role + achievements

### Events Must Be Dated
- ❌ "recently completed funding" → ✅ "2026年6月26日，超级工厂一期竣工投运"
- ❌ "has partnerships with hospitals" → ✅ "与上海华山医院、上海市精神卫生中心、华西医院共建联合实验室"
- ❌ "attended by investors" → ✅ "华映资本季薇、清松资本张松、戈壁创投唐啟波、傅利叶顾捷出席剪彩"

### If Data Is Unavailable
- State EXACTLY what is missing (e.g., "注册资本未公开" not "信息不足")
- Explain how material the gap is to the investment decision
- List what source would resolve it (e.g., "需查阅工商登记档案")
- NEVER fill the gap with vague language that sounds informative but conveys no data

## Integration into the Analysis Workflow

### When to Trigger This Lens

Trigger when the company belongs to:
- Biotech/medtech/pharma → NMPA/CDE/NHSA databases
- SOE or SOE supply chain → SASAC/procurement databases
- Semiconductor/advanced manufacturing → MIIT/CNIPA databases
- AI/internet/platform → CAC algorithm registry
- Aerospace/satellite → CAAC/国防科工局 databases
- Fintech/payment → PBOC/NFRA license databases
- Energy/nuclear → NEA/NNSA databases
- Any company → gsxt.gov.cn (business registration) + wenshu.court.gov.cn (litigation check) as baseline

### Workflow Steps

1. **Before research:** Identify the company's industry → map to regulatory databases using the tables above.
2. **During web search:** Include 2-3 targeted searches against each relevant public registry.
3. **If account-gated:** Emit a User Data Request using the template.
4. **If information cannot be obtained:** Explicitly note in the report: "未能从 [数据库名] 获取 [信息类型]，该数据对 [投资判断维度] 具有 [重要性等级] 的重要性。建议在尽调中要求公司提供。"
5. **When user provides files:** Treat them as primary-source evidence (confidence: high), cite by filename and issuing agency.

### Data Hierarchy

Regulatory data ranks at the top of the evidence hierarchy:

```
1. Court judgments / regulatory filings (源之根源) ← HIGHEST CONFIDENCE
2. Government-issued licenses / certificates
3. Procurement contract awards (ccgp.gov.cn)
4. Patent office records (CNIPA/USPTO)
5. Public company filings (年报/招股书 via 巨潮)
   --- "hard evidence" line ---
6. Company-provided materials (pitch decks, internal reports)
7. Media reports / industry analysis
8. OCR-derived text from scanned documents ← LOWEST CONFIDENCE
```

Anything below the "hard evidence" line should be cross-verified against something above it whenever possible.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: policy_geopolitics_lens.md

# Policy and Geopolitics Lens

Use this file when policy, national strategy, international relations, regulation, government procurement, export controls, sanctions, data security, strategic industries, or cross-border supply chains can materially affect market size, competition, valuation, risk, or exit.

Do not impose one country's policy logic on every company. First identify the relevant jurisdictions and the report's investment perspective.

## Trigger Conditions

Read this lens when any of these are true:

- The company operates in a regulated or license-dependent market.
- The industry is strategic: aerospace, defense, semiconductors, AI, energy, biotech, medtech, telecom, cybersecurity, data infrastructure, finance, transportation, agriculture, critical minerals, or advanced manufacturing.
- Customers, revenue, subsidies, procurement, or approvals depend on government budgets or policy continuity.
- The product is dual-use, export-controlled, sanction-sensitive, or dependent on foreign components, cloud, models, chips, instruments, materials, data, or IP.
- Overseas expansion, listing, M&A, financing, supply chain, or exit depends on international market access.

## Jurisdiction and Perspective Setup

Before analysis, map:

- **Company base**: incorporation, headquarters, R&D, manufacturing, data hosting, operating licenses.
- **Revenue markets**: current customers, target customers, government or enterprise budget owners.
- **Supply chain**: critical suppliers, components, cloud/models/chips, instruments, IP, and data flows.
- **Capital and exit path**: investor jurisdiction, listing venue, likely acquirers, foreign-investment review exposure.
- **Reader perspective**: domestic investor, international investor, strategic buyer, public-market investor, or primary-market investor.

Then choose the lens:

| Situation | Primary policy lens |
| --- | --- |
| China company serving China market | central policy, local implementation, procurement, industrial catalogs, subsidies, data/security reviews, domestic substitution, local-government payment risk |
| China company going global | China outbound rules plus target-market access, sanctions/export controls, tariffs, foreign-investment review, overseas compliance, brand/geopolitical perception |
| US company | federal/state regulation, procurement, export controls, CFIUS, antitrust, IRA/CHIPS/health/defense/data rules as relevant, international sales restrictions |
| European company | EU-level regulation, member-state implementation, GDPR/data, CE/MDR/EMA/energy/AI Act as relevant, state aid, procurement, trade and supply-chain rules |
| Cross-border supply chain | home market + supplier market + customer market + financing/listing market + likely acquirer market |
| Global category leader | compare US/EU/China policy regimes and ask which regime creates advantage, compliance cost, or market-access constraint |

If the company location is uncertain, state the uncertainty and analyze the jurisdictions that could materially change the conclusion.

## Analysis Questions

Answer only the questions that matter for the company:

1. **National / regional strategy fit**: Is the company aligned with national, regional, state, EU-level, or international policy priorities? Is policy support structural demand or temporary subsidy?
2. **Regulatory path**: What licenses, approvals, certifications, safety reviews, reimbursement rules, data rules, or procurement qualifications are required?
3. **Government customer / budget**: Who controls the budget, how long is procurement, how reliable is payment, and can policy changes delay revenue?
4. **International exposure**: What export controls, sanctions, tariffs, foreign investment reviews, data-transfer rules, or market-access barriers matter?
5. **Supply-chain sovereignty**: Which components, chips, instruments, materials, software, cloud services, or IP create choke points?
6. **Standards and certification**: Does the company benefit from or depend on technical standards, industry certifications, safety regimes, or international bodies?
7. **Policy upside vs. policy trap**: Does policy create a moat/catalyst, or does it inflate TAM, invite crowded competition, and reduce pricing power?
8. **Investment implication**: How should policy change valuation, timeline, probability of milestones, required diligence, downside case, and exit route?

## Evidence Sources

Prefer primary or near-primary sources:

- Laws, regulations, regulatory drafts, enforcement actions, licenses, procurement notices, official budgets, government plans, industry catalogs, standards bodies, export-control lists, sanctions lists, customs/tariff rules, official statistical releases, and stock-exchange filings.
- For China-related analysis, check central policy, provincial/local implementation, procurement catalogs, subsidies, standards, industrial parks, data/security review, and domestic-substitution rules separately. Local support is not the same as national demand.
- For US-related analysis, separate federal and state rules; check agency guidance, procurement, export controls, sanctions, CFIUS, antitrust, sector regulators, and subsidy/industrial-policy programs when relevant.
- For Europe-related analysis, separate EU-level regulation from member-state implementation; check GDPR/data transfer, product certification, sector regulators, state aid, procurement, and EU trade/supply-chain rules when relevant.
- For international exposure, compare the rules in the company's home market, target market, supplier market, financing/listing market, and likely acquirer market.

## Report Integration

Do not write a generic policy essay. Integrate findings into:

- Market and industry: TAM/SAM/SOM, adoption timing, subsidy dependence, government budget, replacement cycle.
- Competition: protected incumbents, national champions, local-content rules, foreign competitors blocked or advantaged.
- Product and technology: certification, safety, dual-use constraints, standards, export-control sensitivity.
- Business model and financials: procurement cycle, payment risk, margin pressure from policy pricing, capex/subsidy dependency.
- Risk: policy reversal, compliance breach, sanctions, data-security review, local-government payment delay, supply-chain interruption.
- Valuation and exit: policy-driven discount/premium, IPO/M&A restrictions, foreign buyer limits, lock-up or national-security review.

If the lens is not material, state briefly: `政策/地缘因素：未发现对投资结论有重大影响的政策或跨境约束。`"}],"isError":false}

2. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at

{"url":"https://calag.ucdavis.edu/reports/2026-06-18-strawberry-market-report.html","title":"June 2026 California Strawberry Market Report","text":"The 2026 Season: A Heavy, Early Crop After a Winter Spike
 Wholesale prices for California strawberries have swung widely in 2026, and in mid-June they were running above the same weeks of the prior two years. According to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS), which reports prices in 11 large US wholesale (terminal) markets, a flat of California strawberries sold for an average of about $23.05 over roughly the first 24 weeks of 2026 (using the midpoint of each reported price range), close to $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024. However, that season average hides the recent rise: over the six weeks from early May to mid-June, a flat of California fruit averaged about $27.02, well above the same weeks of 2025 ($18.28) and 2024 ($14.99).
 Prices moved in three phases this season. In February (weeks 5 to 8), terminal prices opened high, at about $25 to $29 per flat. Grower prices were also high: FreshFruitPortal (April 21, 2026) reported them up about 32% in January, after heavy rain in late 2025 cut California shipments in the fourth quarter by about 27%. A late-February hailstorm also delayed the Santa Maria Valley harvest by two to three weeks (KEYT, February 25, 2026). Prices then fell to a low near $15.63 per flat in late March (week 13) as the large, early crop arrived. They climbed again to about $31 per flat in early May (week 19) as early growing districts such as Oxnard wound down, and by mid-June had eased to about $23.
 Growers are harvesting a large crop this season. The California Strawberry Commission, the state's grower-funded commodity board, projects 2026 acreage up about 2% to 43,726 total acres, the first increase after several years of decline, and projects fresh production above the 2025 crop, with weekly volumes of 7 to 8 million trays through August (Ag Alert, May 6, 2026; FreshFruitPortal, April 23, 2026). A warm, dry winter pulled the season forward two to three weeks: Monterey County (Watsonville-Salinas) reached 2.9 million crates by early April versus 230,000 at the same point in 2024, more than 12 times as much (Ag Alert, May 6, 2026).

 What This Report Covers
 In this report, we compare the 2026 California strawberry season with 2024 and 2025: what growers' fruit is selling for at wholesale and at retail, where the strawberries sold in US terminal markets come from through the year, and how California's exports and the 2026 trade case against Mexican winter strawberries affect California growers.

 Key Observations

 By mid-June, California strawberry wholesale prices were well above prior years: about $27.02 per flat from early May to mid-June, versus $18.28 in the same weeks of 2025, even though the season average is close to last year (USDA AMS Terminal Fruit).
 Prices swung widely: they fell to about $15.63 per flat in late March as a large, early crop arrived, then climbed to about $31 in early May as early districts finished (USDA AMS Terminal Fruit).
 Supply is growing: California acreage is projected up about 2% in 2026, the first increase after several years of decline (Ag Alert, May 6, 2026).

 How Terminal-Market Prices Are Measured
 USDA Agricultural Marketing Service publishes daily wholesale-price ranges for fruit moving through large US terminal markets. The strawberry series here pools 11 markets: Asheville, Atlanta, Baltimore, Bronx, Chicago, Columbia, Detroit, Everett, Los Angeles, Miami, and Philadelphia, with 22,759 price quotes through June 12, 2026. For each origin and package, AMS reporters publish a low-to-high price range; we take the midpoint of that range and average it across all quotes, so markets that report more quotes, mainly the large Eastern markets, carry more weight. These are wholesale prices (what terminal wholesalers charge their buyers), not retail shelf prices. Because most produce now moves directly to retailers' distribution centers rather than through terminal markets, these prices are a sample of the wholesale market, not the whole of it, so the comparison across seasons is more informative than the price level in any one week.

 California Strawberry Terminal Wholesale Price, Year-Over-Year
 Weekly mid-price (mean of low and high) for California-origin strawberries, pooled across the 11 USDA AMS Terminal Fruit markets. The 2026 line opened high in winter, dipped to about $15.63 in late March as the large crop arrived, then climbed to about $31 in early May as early districts finished, running above 2024 and 2025 through late spring. Season-to-date, 2026 averages about $23.05 per flat versus $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024.

 Source: USDA AMS Market News, Terminal Fruit reports (Asheville, Atlanta, Baltimore, Bronx, Chicago, Columbia, Detroit, Everett, Los Angeles, Miami, Philadelphia), weekly averages of mid-price, California-origin strawberries.

 Grower Prices and the Wholesale-Retail Divergence
 Grower prices and terminal wholesale prices both rose in winter. According to FreshFruitPortal (April 21, 2026), grower prices were up about 32% in January 2026, after late-2025 rain in California cut fourth-quarter shipments by about 27%. Terminal prices then dipped as the large 2026 crop arrived, before rising again in May to about $31 per flat as early districts wound down. Whether prices hold through the summer depends on volume. The Commission projects weekly volumes of 7 to 8 million trays through August, and if that fruit arrives on schedule, the added supply would push prices down from their mid-June level (California Strawberry Commission, via Ag Alert, May 6, 2026; FreshFruitPortal).
 Over the season as a whole, advertised retail prices are slightly higher than last year, while the average wholesale price is slightly lower. According to the USDA AMS National Retail Report, which averages grocery ad prices nationwide, strawberries were advertised at about $4.69 per unit on average through May 30, 2026, versus $4.48 in 2025 and $4.44 in 2024. Grocery ad prices tend to follow wholesale prices with a delay, and they also reflect which weeks stores choose to run promotions, so the advertised price can rise in a season when the average wholesale price falls.

 National Retail Ad Price, Year-Over-Year
 Weekly national weighted-average advertised retail price for strawberries. The 2026 line runs at or above 2024 and 2025 across most weeks, with the season-to-date average about $4.69 versus $4.48 in 2025. Retail ad pricing lags wholesale and reflects promotion decisions, so it can diverge from the terminal wholesale series above.

 Source: USDA AMS Market News, National Retail Report (Specialty Crops), weekly weighted-average advertised retail price, all package types.

 Where the Fruit Comes From
 California supplies most US terminal strawberry quotes, with Mexico and Florida filling the winter and early-spring windows. Across the pooled USDA AMS Terminal Fruit quotes, the origin mix is California about 62%, Mexico about 20%, Florida about 16%, and South and North Carolina about 1% each. Because California strawberries ship nationwide, their share of quotes is a reasonable guide to their place in these markets, although it is a share of price reports, not of production. USDA AMS shipment (movement) reports show the seasons: California fruit ships mostly in spring and summer, Mexican fruit from January through April, and Florida fruit in late winter (chart below).
 The 2026 California crop is heavy and early. The California Strawberry Commission projects acreage up about 2% to 43,726 total acres (32,412 fall-planted for winter, spring, and summer production, plus 11,314 summer-planted for fall), the first increase after several years of decline, with nearly half of plantings in proprietary varieties (varieties owned and licensed by private breeding companies) (Ag Alert, May 6, 2026; FreshFruitPortal, April 23, 2026). A warm, dry winter pulled the season forward two to three weeks (UC Cooperative Extension adviser Mark Bolda, via Ag Alert, May 6, 2026).

| [Subsidiary 1] | [Location] | [Type] | R&D center | X% | — |
