{"url":"https://migration.ucdavis.edu/rmn/blog/post/?id=2668","title":"Rural Migration Blog","text":"Strawberries: Growth and Labor

 Click here to download this blog post as a PDF file
 November 19, 2021
 The retail value of fresh berries sold in the US was $8 billion in 2021, accounting for 20 percent of supermarket produce sales. Strawberries (47 percent) represented almost half of the value of retail berry sales, followed by blueberries, 25 percent, raspberries, 15 percent, and blackberries, 10 percent.

US Berry Sales, 52 weeks ending 8/8/21

Major reasons for increased fresh berry sales include the taste and flavor of berries, convenient packaging that allows them to be consumed as snacks or at meals, and their health benefits.

California. California is the leading producer of raspberries and strawberries, and has a fast-growing blueberry industry. California had 36,500 acres of strawberries in 2021, almost all in three coastal areas, Oxnard in the south, Santa Maria in the central coast, and Salinas-Watsonville in the north. The Santa Maria area has the longest growing season and surpassed Salinas-Watsonville in acreage of both conventional and organic strawberries in 2019.

Santa Maria has more strawberry acreage than Oxnard and Salinas/Watsonville

California produces over 90 percent of US-grown strawberries, and ships berries year-round. US production peaks in May-June at almost 70 million pounds and reaches a low of 20 million pounds in November-December. About 10 percent of US-grown strawberries are organic.

US strawberry production peaks in May-June

Strawberries are sold in flats that have eight one-pound clamshells or 12 pints. Grower prices for conventional strawberries in 2020 ranged from $6 to $17 a flat, with the lowest prices in May-June when production peaks and the highest prices in November-December when production is lowest. Grower prices for organic strawberries are about 50 percent higher than for conventional strawberries. The organic premium varies over the year, reaching up to 80 percent during November-December when there is little production.

Grower prices are $9-$10 per flat during the May-June peak production period

The strawberry share of the US berry market has been shrinking, while the share of fresh blueberries increases. The volume of berries sold rose almost 50 percent between 2010 and 2020, a period during which the share of strawberries dropped from three-fourths to two-thirds of berry volume. The volume of organic strawberries tripled between 2010 and 2020 and grower prices rose.

Berry shipments to US consumers rose almost 50% between 2010 and 2020, as organic strawberry shipments tripled

Labor. Strawberries are the most labor-intensive crop grown in California, involving about 1.5 workers per acre and 50,000 to 60,000 workers to harvest strawberry fields twice a week during the peak season. Labor is the major cost of growing strawberries, representing 50 to 60 percent of variable production costs.

California strawberries are harvested year-round, beginning in the southern part of the state in winter and moving north in spring and summer. During the winter and spring, Florida also produces fresh strawberries, competing with fresh strawberries that are imported from Mexico. Most strawberry growers are specialized, producing only strawberries.

A strawberry field may be picked 40 to 50 times during the harvest season. Workers push a light wheelbarrow containing the plastic clamshells in which strawberries are sold between two adjacent elevated rows, picking from both rows. Full trays are taken to a checker at the end of the row to receive credit for the tray. Strawberries must be at least two-thirds red to be picked and packed; non-salable berries are discarded in a bucket attached to the picking cart or on the ground. Some workers literally run with full trays to the checker and back to their carts to maximize their piece rate earnings.

Strawberry harvesters wheel a cart with clamshells between elevated rows

Most workers are paid piece rate wages of $1.75 to $2.25 per flat of 12-12 once pints or eight one-pound clamshells, and guaranteed at least the California minimum wage ($14 an hour in 2021). Some growers offer workers an hourly wage of $5 an hour and a piece rate of $1.25 to $1.50 for each flat, while others guarantee the minimum wage and offer $0.50 to $0.75 per tray after eight trays an hour. Workers typically pick eight to 12 flats an hour, enabling most to achieve piece rate earnings that exceed the minimum wage by at least $2 an hour.

Worker productivity and earnings vary with individual skill, the size and yield of the berries, and time of day, with workers often picking slower at the end of the day. Some growers place slow-moving conveyor belts in front of harvesters, allowing them to place full flats of berries on the belt rather than carry them to the end of the row, which gives workers more time to pick and raises their productivity. Piece rates are lower in fields with conveyor belts because workers can pick faster.

Conveyor belts reduce walking and enable harvesters to pick faster

Many of the workers who harvest strawberries are non- or limited-Spanish speakers from southern Mexican states such as Oaxaca and Chiapas. There are often several members of a family and their relatives in a crew, so that strawberry crews are more diverse than the solo male work crews that dominate the harvest of tree fruits. This means that there is more variance in productivity among strawberry harvesters than in other crops that pay harvest workers piece rate wages, such as crews that pick apples or oranges.

Most strawberry harvesters are hired directly by farmers rather than brought to farms by contractors. Some farmers keep older and slower workers on their payrolls in order to retain their younger and faster relatives.

Strawberry workers are more diverse than tree fruit workers

The strawberry labor market is “fluid,” with workers often changing employers. Some workers monitor yields to determine where they are most likely to maximize their piece-rate earnings, and change employers to pick in the fields with the most berries to harvest. In the past, some growers refused to rehire workers who quit during the season and went elsewhere. However, the slowdown in unauthorized Mexico-US migration after the 2008-09 recession has ended most no-rehire-during-the-season policies.

Strawberry harvesting crews typically include 30 to 60 workers. The key figure is the crew supervisor, who ensures that crews have 80 to 90 percent of their expected workers and helps to monitor the quantity and quality of berries that are picked.

H-2A. Many growers use the H-2A program to obtain berry workers. Berries were the most common type of job filled by H-2A workers in FY19, accounting for 10 percent of the 258,000 US jobs certified to be filled with guest workers, the last year for which DOL reported H-2A jobs by commodity.

The number of jobs certified to be filled by H-2A workers tripled between FY13 and FY21, from less than 100,000 to almost 318,000. H-2A workers harvest half or more US apples and oranges, and are harvesting an ever higher share of fresh berries.

The number of jobs certified for H-2A workers tripled between FY13 and FY21

References

With the assumption of 9,000 trays per acre at a unit price of $11, the report estimates cultural costs at $22,264 per acre and harvest costs at $79,288 per acre. With the inclusion of 9% interest on operating capital, the total operating costs per acre are estimated at $105,809.

With the addition of overhead, the total costs per acre totaled $112,694 per acre.

The report stresses that strawberry production is a high risk endeavor. While the report can’t fully represent all of the elements that can affect the economics and profitability of fresh strawberries, it does its best to provide this information based on the real-world practices of a typical strawberry farm found in the central coastal regions of the state.

There are many factors that can heavily influence fluctuations in these estimates. These specific regions alone have varying land rents and taxes, and farm-specific practices and input costs can move overall production costs in either direction.

For example, the study assumed flat land and fumigation land preparation that includes discing six times, subsoiling twice, chiseling twice, followed by a half acre-inch of water prior to fumigating with a combination of chloropicrin and 1,3-dichloropropene. With the inclusion of the permit, this is estimated at $5,028 for solid, tarped fumigation.

Plants were planted at 17,424 plants to the acre with 5% — or 870 plants — built into the cost estimates as a buffer for plants that would need to be replanted in the following weeks for a variety of possible reasons.

Labor rates included overhead of 48%, putting rates at $24.42 and $29.60 per hour for field labor and machine operators, respectively. This included not only basic hourly wages, but payroll taxes, workers compensation, and other factors. Use of the federal H-2A program would also affect these costs.

This study provides growers with a baseline to estimate their own costs, which can help when applying for production loans, projecting labor costs, securing market arrangements, or understanding costs associated with water and nutrient management and regulatory programs,” said Brittney Goodrich, UC Cooperative Extension specialist and study co-author.

1. Orrin Fieldworks at a glance

2. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at
peak harvest. Harvest labor is the largest single cost line for most growers.
-  Strawberries are picked by hand every three to four days through a season of up to seven months; a picker covers roughly a quarter of an acre a
day (company estimate).
-  Growers tell us their crews are smaller and older each year, while wages and worker housing keep getting more expensive (grower interviews, 2025).
-  Fruit left unpicked rots on the plant and spreads mold to the next pass, so a short crew costs more than the berries it leaves behind.
-  Harvest aids such as carts and conveyors make pickers faster, but still need a full crew.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 2 of 15

--- p.3 ---
3. Our product: the Orrin Picker
-  An autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives the furrows at night and day, finds ripe berries with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and
picks them with a soft three-finger gripper.
-  Pick rate: 94% of ripe fruit on the rows tested in our 2025 pilots (company measurement; definition on slide 4).
-  Throughput: one robot covers roughly 1.5 acres per 24 hours.
-  Two picking arms place berries straight into the grower's retail clamshells on board, so fruit is handled once.
-  Runs about 20 hours a day on swappable battery packs; one field technician supervises up to 8 robots, on site or remotely.
-  Sold as Robots-as-a-Service: growers pay per robot per season; we own, maintain and insure the fleet.
-  Current model: Orrin Picker v3, released to the field in March 2026. The v4, designed for lower cost, is planned for the 2027 season.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 3 of 15

The Department of Labor published updated Adverse Effect Wage Rates for H-2A farmworkers on August 3, 2026, and the new rates take effect the same day they hit the Federal Register. The notice, issued by the Employment and Training Administration at 91 FR 48946, also resets the national average AEWR used to size surety bonds for H-2A Labor Contractors to $15.96 per hour, down from the $17.74 in place since January 1, 2025. That is a cut of $1.78 an hour, roughly 10 percent, in one update.

The AEWR is not a suggestion. It is the floor an H-2A employer must offer in the job order, advertise during domestic recruitment, and actually pay to both H-2A workers and any U.S. workers in corresponding employment. Under 20 CFR 655.120 and 655.122(l), employers in non-range occupations must pay at least the highest of the AEWR, the applicable prevailing wage, the collective bargaining rate, the federal minimum wage, or the state minimum wage.

There are two effective dates, not one. The rates apply nationally on August 3, 2026. For employers and states covered by the court order in Kansas et al. v. U.S. Department of Labor, 749 F. Supp. 3d 1363 (S.D. Ga. 2024), the same rates instead take effect on August 17, 2026. That two week gap has become a standing feature of AEWR notices since the Southern District of Georgia enjoined the 2024 Farmworker Protection Rule in 17 plaintiff states.

DOL set new H-2A adverse effect wage rates effective August 3, 2026, with the average AEWR for surety bonds falling to $15.96 an hour.

Those 17 states are Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia. Several are among the heaviest users of the H-2A program, so the later date covers a large share of certified positions.

The notice itself prints no state table. DOL directs employers to a searchable spreadsheet at flag.dol.gov/wage-data/adverse-effect-wage-rates, where rates can be looked up by state or territory and by Standard Occupational Classification code. Brian Pasternak, Administrator of the Office of Foreign Labor Certification, is listed as the contact. Marek Laco, Acting Assistant Secretary for Employment and Training, signed the three-page notice.

The numbers come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics survey, not the Department of Agriculture Farm Labor Survey that set AEWRs for decades. DOL made that switch in an interim final rule published October 2, 2025 at 90 FR 47914. This August notice is the first full annual refresh under that methodology, and it uses the OEWS release of May 15, 2026, which carries May 2025 wage estimates.

Two Skill Levels, One Housing Deduction

Job orders filed on or after August 3, 2026 use the new rates. Employers and states covered by the Kansas v. DOL order get until August 17, 2026.

The OEWS methodology splits every state into two rates instead of one. A Skill Level I AEWR applies to entry-level job opportunities where workers need no formal education or specialized training credentials. A Skill Level II AEWR applies where the employer requires qualifications typical of experienced or fully proficient workers. DOL computes Skill Level I at the equivalent of the 17th percentile of the occupational wage distribution, the same convention used for skill-based prevailing wages in other visa programs.

Most H-2A jobs still fall inside the field and livestock workers (combined) category, which aggregates five SOC codes: 45-2041, 45-2091, 45-2092, 45-2093 and 53-7064. Where OEWS reports no statewide figure at a given skill level, the national average for that level applies instead.

The notice also updates the statewide downward compensation adjustments allowed under 20 CFR 655.120(b)(3). Those deductions apply only to H-2A workers who receive housing at no cost, and they can shave another dollar or more off the hourly rate. A federal court in California just ordered the US Department of Labor (DOL) to quickly come up with a new methodology for calculating the Adverse Effect Wage Rate (AEWR) for H-2A job orders, just weeks after the agency released long-awaited new H-2A farmworker rates. Those rates had been calculated under a framework established in an interim final rule, which the DOL issued in 2025 and the United Farm Workers challenged. The district court issued an order on August 26 largely siding with the UFW and finding the IFR to be unlawful, though it stopped short of vacating the rule entirely. Even still, the potential for a backpay order covering the difference in wages between the current AEWR methodology and DOL’s future methodology creates tremendous uncertainty for farms, FLCs, workers, and consumers. What does this mean for agricultural employers and H-2A wage rates?
Quick Background
The DOL issued an interim final rule (IFR) in October 2025 that dramatically reshaped the H-2A program’s minimum wage policy. Under this framework, the DOL calculates the AEWR for H-2A job orders using a new skill-based and occupation specific wage structure. The United Farm Workers filed suit to challenge the rule, and in May the court denied the UFW’s request to temporarily block the rule while the litigation plays out.
In the meantime, the DOL published the new AEWRs on August 3, which took effect immediately for most states. (A slightly later effective date of August 17 applied to states covered by a 2024 court ruling related to the Farmworker Protection Rule, including Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia.)
What’s the Latest?
A district court in California handed the UFW a major win on August 26 by ruling that the DOL’s October 2025 IFR is unlawful and ordering the agency to promptly produce and publish a new methodology for calculating AEWRs for H-2A workers. Specifically, the court held that:

each of the challenged components of the IFR – including the tier system, the housing adjustment, the use of the Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics survey, and the “greater than 50%” rule – are arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA); and
the DOL did not have “good cause” to issue the IFR on an emergency basis and bypass the APA’s usual procedural requirements for rulemaking.

The August 26 order applies nationwide – it is not limited to the UFW or a specific jurisdiction. The good news is that the court did not immediately vacate the rule but instead ordered the DOL to create a new one.
What Was the Court’s Reasoning?

The court found that the use of wage “tiers” based on experience “is not inherently unreasonable,” but the use of the 17thpercentile and 50thpercentile was “arbitrary and capricious” where the DOL estimated that 92% of jobs would be assigned to the lower-tier wage rate. This leaves the door open to a different wage-tiering mechanism in DOL’s next AEWR rule. 
The court also found the “housing adjustment” in the IFR to be unlawful, based on the separate requirement in the DOL’s H-2A rules that employers provide housing to H-2A workers “at no cost” to them. The DOL proposed removing that regulatory requirement in the IFR, and when they created the H-2A program, Congress required only that employers “shall furnish housing in accordance with regulations,” but not that it be “at no cost.” Because it perceived a conflict within the existing DOL rules, the court found the housing adjustment to be unlawful.
Third, the court faulted the DOL for using the OEWS without specifically considering alternatives, since the OEWS surveys farm labor contractors but specifically excludes farms from the survey. The DOL may reframe the OEWS to include farms in future surveys. 
Lastly, the court found unlawful the “greater than 50%” or “primary duties” rule for assigning a wage to a job with duties that span different occupations. The court suggested that the DOL should have considered other alternatives, like requiring employers to pay different wage rates for different hours of the day to reflect work with different wage rates (the example given was an H-2A worker spending 49% driving heavy trucks and 51% on ranch work – the court suggested that the DOL require the truck-driver wage for hours spent driving and the livestock wage for the rest of the week).

What’s Next? Key Takeaways for Agricultural Employers
The DOL now has seven days to notify state workforce agencies, employers, and the public that employers may be required for make wage adjustment payments to qualifying H-2A workers and US farmworkers in corresponding employment who worked during the “backpay period” (the period between when the DOL sends the notice and when it issues a new AEWR methodology). This signals that a court might order employers to pay the difference between the current AEWRs paid during the backpay period and the new AEWRs that the DOL ultimately issues. The court declined to rule on the issue of “back pay” yet but ordered DOL to put employers on notice of the possibility of such an order in the future.
How soon the DOL issues the new AEWR methodology remains to be seen, but Wednesday’s order requires the agency to submit an initial status report in two weeks to detail steps it has taken and its anticipated timeline. It’s also unclear whether the DOL will have to issue notice of proposed rulemaking, a new interim final rule, or something else. After DOL issues the new AEWR methodology, the court will re-open briefing regarding backpay issue flagged in the notice.

2. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at
peak harvest. Harvest labor is the largest single cost line for most growers.
-  Strawberries are picked by hand every three to four days through a season of up to seven months; a picker covers roughly a quarter of an acre a
day (company estimate).
-  Growers tell us their crews are smaller and older each year, while wages and worker housing keep getting more expensive (grower interviews, 2025).
-  Fruit left unpicked rots on the plant and spreads mold to the next pass, so a short crew costs more than the berries it leaves behind.
-  Harvest aids such as carts and conveyors make pickers faster, but still need a full crew.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 2 of 15

--- p.3 ---
3. Our product: the Orrin Picker
-  An autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives the furrows at night and day, finds ripe berries with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and
picks them with a soft three-finger gripper.
-  Pick rate: 94% of ripe fruit on the rows tested in our 2025 pilots (company measurement; definition on slide 4).
-  Throughput: one robot covers roughly 1.5 acres per 24 hours.
-  Two picking arms place berries straight into the grower's retail clamshells on board, so fruit is handled once.
-  Runs about 20 hours a day on swappable battery packs; one field technician supervises up to 8 robots, on site or remotely.
-  Sold as Robots-as-a-Service: growers pay per robot per season; we own, maintain and insure the fleet.
-  Current model: Orrin Picker v3, released to the field in March 2026. The v4, designed for lower cost, is planned for the 2027 season.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 3 of 15

The 2026 Tariff Landscape: What Actually Changed
If you’re relying on tariff information from even three months ago, you’re likely working with outdated numbers. Three distinct regimes now operate simultaneously, each with different triggers, exemptions, and implications depending on where goods originate, where they’re processed, and where they’re ultimately sold.
What tariff applies to Mexican imports entering the United States?
This changed on February 20, 2026, when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Learning Resources v. Trump that the use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose broad import tariffs exceeded presidential authority. The 25% IEEPA tariff that had applied to Mexican imports since March 4, 2025 was struck down.
The administration responded by invoking Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, imposing a 10% surcharge on imports from Mexico (and Canada) effective February 24, 2026. The administration announced an increase to 15% (the statutory maximum), but as of March 2026, no formal proclamation has been issued. Section 122 has a statutory limit: the tariff expires after 150 days unless Congress acts, placing the expiration date at approximately July 24, 2026.
The critical continuity for manufacturers: USMCA-qualifying goods remain exempt under Section 122, just as they were under IEEPA. Products that meet USMCA rules of origin enter the United States duty-free or at normal MFN rates. Non-qualifying goods in covered product categories now face a 10% surcharge rather than the previous 25%, with a potential increase to 15% pending. The proclamation excludes goods already subject to Section 232 duties, approximately 1,100 HTS codes listed in Annex II (covering pharmaceuticals, certain electronics, aerospace products, critical minerals, and energy products), and other specified categories.
The IEEPA period is not completely behind us. On March 4, 2026, the Court of International Trade ordered CBP to refund all IEEPA duties collected between March 4, 2025 and February 24, 2026. CBP disclosed it collected approximately $166 billion in IEEPA tariffs from roughly 330,000 importers across 53 million entries. CBP is building a new automated refund system called CAPE (Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries), a dedicated module within the existing ACE platform. As of the March 19 status hearing, the CAPE claim portal is 73% complete and mass processing is 45% complete. No firm refund start date has been committed. The court suspended its immediate-compliance directive to give CBP time to build the system, with the next status hearing scheduled for March 31, 2026. CAPE will not initially cover certain entry types, including those subject to antidumping or countervailing duty proceedings. For manufacturers who paid significant IEEPA duties over the past year, this refund represents a potential cash recovery, but the timeline remains uncertain.

What about Mexico’s own tariff changes?
Mexico’s December 29, 2025 decree, published in the Diario Oficial de la Federación, expanded import duties on 1,463 tariff lines covering automotive parts, textiles, steel, aluminum, plastics, electronics, furniture, footwear, glass, and toys. Tariff rates range from 10% to 50% ad valorem. These duties apply exclusively to imports from countries with which Mexico does not maintain a free trade agreement, primarily China, India, South Korea, Thailand, and Turkey. Imports from the United States and Canada under USMCA are unaffected.
And the tariff structure on Chinese goods?
Through layered Section 301 tariffs, Section 232 duties, and the Section 122 global baseline tariff, the effective tariff rate on Chinese goods reached 33.9% by the end of 2025, according to the Penn Wharton Budget Model. That figure was calculated before the Supreme Court’s February 2026 ruling replaced IEEPA tariffs with Section 122, though the Treasury Department has stated that the combination of Section 122, Section 301, and Section 232 results in “virtually unchanged” tariff revenue for 2026. Product-specific rates run significantly higher: lithium-ion batteries at 25%, steel and aluminum products above 50%, and some categories that spiked to announced rates of 145% during the April 2025 tariff escalation before being partially rolled back.

{"url":"https://fruitgrowersnews.com/news/uc-strawberry-study-looks-at-growing-costs-returns/","title":"UC strawberry study looks at growing costs, returns - Fruit Growers News","text":"A new study can help estimate costs and potential returns for growing strawberries on California’s Central Coast.

The University of California (UC) Agriculture and Natural Resources, UC Cooperative Extension (UCCE) and the UC-Davis Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics released the study, “2024 Sample Costs to Produce and Harvest Strawberries.”

“This study provides growers with a baseline to estimate their own costs, which can help when applying for production loans, projecting labor costs, securing market arrangements, or understanding costs associated with water and nutrient management and regulatory programs,” Brittney Goodrich, UCCE specialist and study co-author.

The cost study models a management scenario for a 50-acre farm, 45 acres of which are planted to strawberries, in Santa Cruz, Monterey or San Benito counties. The remaining acres are for the irrigation system, roads and buildings. The study describes the cultural practices used in strawberry production and harvest, including land preparation, soil fertility and pest management, irrigation and labor needs.

File photos courtesy of University of California-Davis

The 19-page study shows costs for each operation, material inputs and costs, and cash and non-cash overhead costs in a variety of formats for one production and harvest cycle. A ranging analysis is also included and shows potential profits or losses over a range of prices and yields.

The UC-Davis Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics website has dozens of cost and return studies for specialty crops.

For a detailed explanation of the assumptions and calculations used to estimate the costs and potential returns for each crop, readers can refer to the narrative portion of each study.

For more information, email Mark Bolda, UCCE farm advisor, at [email protected], or Jeremy Murdock in the Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics at [email protected].","truncated":false}

arguments.title: Harvest CROO Robotics: press release, commercial viability of automated strawberry harvest (Duette, FL)
arguments.claims: Harvest CROO (Tampa, FL) reported that its B8 autonomous strawberry harvester reached performance rates on par with human harvesting in a commercial picking operation at Duette, Florida, at the end of the 2025 Florida season; it cites 13 patents and a 200x jump in vision processing with NVIDIA chips; co-founder Gary Wishnatzki owns Wish Farms; CEO Joe McGee.
arguments.claims_weakened: Company press release: no pick rate, bruising rate, throughput per hectare, price or number of paying growers is disclosed; 'on par with human harvesting' is undefined and not independently verified.

arguments.title: Sacramento Business Journal: Robotic fruit-picker maker Advanced Farm ceases operations
arguments.claims: Advanced Farm Technologies Inc., a Davis, California developer of robotic fruit-picking machines with commercial strawberry growers, quietly closed down earlier in 2025.
arguments.claims_weakened: Paywalled trade report; the reason for closure and the disposal of its IP are not established by this source.

arguments.title: Future Farming: Oishii acquires Tortuga AgTech to scale robotic strawberry harvesting
arguments.claims: Vertical-farming company Oishii acquired the key IP, assets and engineering team of Tortuga AgTech, a Colorado robotic strawberry and table-grape harvest company, in 2025.
arguments.claims_weakened: No price or fleet-size disclosure; the acquisition moves Tortuga's technology into protected vertical farming rather than open-field strawberry harvest.

arguments.title: Tevel: Flying Autonomous Robots for Fruit Harvesting (company website)
arguments.claims: Tevel's tethered flying robots harvest apples, peaches, apricots, nectarines, plums and pears in orchards; named customers are Rivoira Group (Italy), HMC Farms (Kingsburg, California) and Unifrutti (Chile); no strawberry product or customer is listed.
arguments.claims_weakened: Company site describes capability, not sold volume or performance; absence of strawberries is evidence of scope, not proof Tevel will never enter.

arguments.title: The Robot Report: Abundant Robotics shuts down fruit harvesting business
arguments.claims: Abundant Robotics (Hayward, CA, founded 2016) shut down in 2021; a memo on its liquidation said it 'was unable to develop the market traction necessary to support its business during the pandemic' and it put its IP and assets up for sale on 2021-06-29; its competitors then included FFRobotics, Ripe Robotics and Tevel.
arguments.claims_weakened: Trade-press account; the relative weight of technical, unit-economics and financing causes is not separated.

arguments.title: HortiDaily: Root AI acquired by AppHarvest for $60 million
arguments.claims: Root AI, developer of the Virgo harvesting robot for indoor farms, was acquired by AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021, the same period in which Abundant Robotics shut down.
arguments.claims_weakened: Root AI was an indoor/vertical-farm picker, not an open-field strawberry competitor; AppHarvest itself later failed, which limits the exit as a success benchmark.

arguments.title: The Henry Ford: Contradictory Impacts — Mechanizing California's Tomato Harvest
arguments.claims: Mechanical tomato harvesters went from 25 machines picking about 0.5% of California's processing tomato crop in 1961 to 512 machines and 70% of the crop in 1966, after the University of California developed a machine-harvestable tomato variety and growers redesigned the crop system.
arguments.claims_weakened: Processing tomatoes are a once-over, industrial-input crop; the fresh-market strawberry is picked 40-50 times and sold on appearance, so the tomato base rate is an upper bound, not a forecast.

arguments.title: UC Davis (Geisseler): Production of Processing Tomatoes in California
arguments.claims: Widespread adoption of the mechanical tomato harvester required a systems approach: new crop management and tomato varieties bred for mechanical harvest, not only a machine.
arguments.claims_weakened: Historical agronomic account; does not measure current mechanisation share or labour displacement.

arguments.title: VisaVerge: New H-2A AEWR wage rates take effect August 2026
arguments.claims: Under the OEWS-based methodology, 2026-27 AEWRs took effect 2026-08-03 (2026-08-17 in 17 states under the Kansas v. DOL order); the average AEWR used for H-2A surety bonds fell to $15.96/hour from $17.74, about 10%, and entry-level rates fell as much as 35.3% in Louisiana.
arguments.claims_weakened: Trade-law commentary, not the DOL rate table; other summaries report average entry-level rates rising about 3.7% with declines in 13 states, so the direction and size of the change by state are disputed. The DOL AEWR page returned HTTP 503 on 2026-10-30.

arguments.title: New H-2A AEWR Wage Rates Take Effect August 3, 2026 (reporting DOL notice at 91 FR 48946)
arguments.claims: AEWRs effective 2026-08-03 (2026-08-17 for the 17 Kansas v. DOL states including Florida). California non-range AEWR fell from the last Farm Labor Survey rate of $19.97/hr to Skill Level I $16.45 and Skill Level II $18.71 (-17.6% at Level I); Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 (Level I) and $15.06 (Level II) (-23.2% at Level I). National average AEWR for H-2A labor contractor surety bonds fell to $15.96/hr from $17.74 (~-10%). California allows a housing-related downward adjustment of up to $3.00/hr. Skill Level I is set at roughly the 17th percentile of the OEWS wage distribution; rates come from BLS OEWS May 2026 release, not the USDA Farm Labor Survey.
arguments.claims_weakened: Secondary trade publication, not the Federal Register notice itself; rates are shown before the housing deduction and may be revised by the pending AEWR litigation. DOL's own state table is published only as a spreadsheet at flag.dol.gov.

arguments.title: Federal Register: Adverse Effect Wage Rate Methodology for H-2A Nonimmigrants in Non-Range Occupations, interim final rule (90 FR 47914)
arguments.claims: DOL issued an interim final rule on 2025-10-02 amending the methodology for setting hourly AEWRs for non-range H-2A occupations, replacing the USDA Farm Labor Survey basis with BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, split by skill level; comment period closed 2025-12-01.
arguments.claims_weakened: Issued without notice-and-comment; a district court later held the rule unlawful, so the wage floor it produced is provisional.

arguments.claims: A federal district court in California ruled on 2026-08-26, in litigation brought by the United Farm Workers, that the October 2025 AEWR interim final rule is unlawful: each challenged component (skill tiers, housing adjustment, OEWS survey use, greater-than-50% primary-duty rule) was arbitrary and capricious under the APA, and DOL lacked good cause to skip notice and comment. The order applies nationwide, declined to vacate the rule, ordered DOL to publish a new AEWR methodology promptly, and required DOL to notify employers that back wage adjustments may be ordered for the period before a new methodology issues.

{"url":"https://agfundernews.com/breaking-exclusive-john-deere-acquires-see-spray-robotics-startup-blue-river-technology-305m","title":"John Deere Acquires ‘See & Spray’ Robotics Startup Blue River Technology for $305m","text":"Editor’s Note: Deere & Company has acquired ag robotics startup Blue River Technology, according to an agreement announced at close of trading today. The tractor giant is acquiring the Sunnyvale, California-based Blue River for $305 million. (AgFunder Research can reveal that’s a roughly four times increase on the $87 million post-money valuation the company fetched at its last round of funding.)
Blue River has developed a farm robotics technology using computer vision that can see, diagnose, and execute actions such as deciding to spray a weed with herbicide – avoiding the crop – or to thin the crop. Just this summer the company released its “See & Spray” weed control machine. The company claims it can reduce agrochemical use by 90% with this technology.
Blue River last raised funding at Series B stage in a $17 million round led by Pontifax AgTech, joined by Monsanto Growth Ventures (MGV), Syngenta Ventures, and existing investors Khosla Ventures, Data Collective Venture Capital, and Eric Schmidt’s Innovation Endeavors.
“Robotics stands to solve some key issues in agriculture including sustainability concerns, such as reducing chemical loads, labor shortages, and the use of data to allow for the more precise and efficient production of crops,” said Phil Erlanger of Pontifax AgTech. “John Deere is acquiring a best-in-class robotics company in Blue River; they are unambiguously the best technical team in the sector.  They have created a compelling and disruptive technology that can truly change the face of crop production.”
“This is the start of the next chapter in agriculture,” says Kiersten Stead from MGV.
Below Stead offers more thoughts on Blue River’s key attributes and why it’s an attractive investment for John Deere.  

While the agtech market is awash in companies selling capabilities in remote sensing and providing advice on this information — which is no doubt needed — Blue River is the first integrated technology that can see-diagnose-and-execute at full speed, and in real time. We (MGV) initially invested in Blue River Technology when the company was prototyping lettuce thinning machines. They did so by precisely spraying nitrogenous fertilizer on lettuce seedlings, leaving only lettuce rosettes that were computationally determined to maximize lettuce head development and yield. While the company was thinning lettuce fields and helping farmers cope with the critical labor shortages that have received much press, Blue River was also quietly learning, and hiring wisely. Although not without some growing pains, the company got busy combining Silicon Valley AI and engineering with real-world agronomists and ag industry veterans. Today, Blue River Technology’s robotic implements are weeding in cotton fields using contact herbicides with high accuracy, and over a 90% reduction in chemistry applications. “See and spray” will clearly be another tool for farmers who need to cope with weed suppression of yield and herbicide resistance. We can now see a legitimate path to a utopian time-not-too-far-away, where “see and spray” fungicides, microbes, and, of course, weeding combinations of selective and non-selective herbicides, can be used to tend each plant individually.
Blue River is still a young company and its full effects are years from the general market, nevertheless there were a few important reasons the company has been successful up to this point:
1.  Emerging ML/AI science capabilities in a poorly digitized vertical. The interplay between these sectors is just beginning take shape. In a world dominated by AI talent flocking to solve problems for the Googles, the Ubers, and the Amazons, less digitized sectors like the life sciences and production agriculture, are left simply dabbling. For this reason, MGV is supporting other disruptive technologies of this ilk like Resson andUnderstory Weather. As I imagine, this is just the beginning.
2.  A focus on building value in a hard technology, not necessarily driving revenue or acquiring customers. While the tradeoff is a difficult decision to make in real-life, when your livelihoods feel at stake, Blue River got behind the idea that they needed to demonstrate value by getting fully functional machines out into the wild. The team embraced the idea that anything outside their core expertise could be done with others, later. Getting the machines into production fields revealed to the company a cascade of product concepts, technical issues, and efficiencies that they may not have seen otherwise. 
3.  Talent. Fundamentally, this was a bet on founder Jorge Heraud and his team. Investing in agriculture is made more challenging by the fact that less than 2% of the US population is involved in agriculture today. This means that the talent pool of people who have asymmetric information in agriculture and who can start companies is lower than other industries. Jorge is an entrepreneur with prior experience at Trimble Navigation, and so was likely to understand what a commercial ready-agriculture implement needed to embody. Moreover, Blue River retained AI/engineering talent amidst the constant pressure of other AI talent siphons. Attracting and retaining this breadth and depth of talent early in their trajectory is a hallmark of many successful early stage companies.
4.  Working openly with strategic partners. Blue River took advantage of working with the best-established chemistry and agronomic partners to find the first practical agricultural problem to go and solve, first in vegetables and soon-after in row crops. Finding great dedicated partners is highly enabling, as they provide access to both foundational test cases and product concept candidates, as well as deep expertise and resources. Blue River consciously pursued this strategy, understanding that their first use-case in row crops needed to work. The hardware business, like biotechnology, leaves little equity capital wiggle-room for retrenching.
As is evident in the details of this deal, Blue River delivered an attractive return on our investment. Having raised just over $30 million of equity capital in seed to Series B funding, the payment of $305 million represents a nice multiple.
Why would MGV invest in a company reducing herbicide applications?
This might be a question of some of your minds. From the beginning, Blue River’s objectives, if met, looked like a fulfillment of many of Monsanto’s key objectives for precision agriculture and integrated solutions. More than anyone, Monsanto knows growers will receive the full benefit of its technologies when they work optimally together. {"url":"https://techcrunch.com/2024/07/22/monarch-tractor-ceo-says-133m-raise-will-help-it-escape-quite-a-challenging-time/","title":"Monarch Tractor CEO says $133M raise will help it escape ‘quite a challenging time’","text":"Monarch Tractor was in a tricky spot late last year as the autonomous electric tractor startup juggled growth and an uncertain fundraising environment. Now, with $133 million in new funds, CEO Praveen Penmetsa tells TechCrunch that the startup is plowing ahead into greener pastures. 

The $133 million Series C funding round was co-led by agri-food tech impact firm Astanor and HH-CTBC Partnership L.P., an affiliate fund of Foxconn. The new round values the startup at more than $500 million. Monarch has raised $220 million to date.

Monarch has integrated technology into electric tractors that offer customers a variety of automated driving features. The company has about 400 tractors in the field right now being used by customers, according to Penmetsa, who said the fresh funding round will help Monarch start “producing more tractors, supporting our customers through our sales and service side of things as well, and then continuing to expand into more states.”

That expansion is coming with some changes. The company recently laid off some workers, TechCrunch has learned. Penmetsa said the cuts were “less than” 15% of Monarch’s 250- to 300-person workforce and were part of a necessary reshuffling as the young company looks to support its growth — especially on the after sales and service side.

Penmetsa said part of Monarch’s business wasn’t really keeping up with the number of tractors it put out into the world. Monarch’s output grew in 2023 alongside its geographic footprint as the startup shifted away from its initial market of vineyards and fruit farms in California and started working with dairy farms, airports and other customers across the country.

“We didn’t have enough coverage in those areas in the early days,” he admitted.

Those struggles, combined with delays in the fundraising process — thanks in part to a much weaker overall investment cadence in agtech overall, according to data from PitchBook — made the back half of 2023 “quite a challenging time for Monarch,” Penmetsa said.

But Penmetsa believes that has turned around. Earlier this year, Monarch rebuilt its service and support teams.

“Our customers are saying your service and support now in these six months is better than the [prior] six months,” Penmetsa said. That increased support has helped lead to 15% of Monarch’s customers coming back to the startup to buy more tractors — a number Penmetsa says is above the company’s initial expectations.

“Don’t get me wrong, it’s a number that I wish was higher, like any CEO, and I think as we continue this fundraise will really help us invest into sales,” he said. “This fundraise is going to allow us to really give confidence to our dealers that we are here for the long term, and that, you know, we are here to support our products, and that they should also join the movement in getting these tractors out to farmers.”

“The value we see in Advanced Farm’s technology lies in its ability to address labor shortages and enhance the efficiency and resilience of the agricultural industry,” said a CNH spokesperson. “By integrating Advanced Farm’s technologies into our broader innovation strategy, we aim to further advance robotic harvesting solutions. CNH was an early investor in Advanced Farms Technologies Inc., supporting the Davis, Calif.-based company‘s vision of developing a novel apple and strawberry-picking robotic solution. According to sources, CNH plans to continue commercializing the platform.
The Advanced Farm team introduced their robot at a demo site during FIRA 2024. | Credit: The Robot Report

arguments.claims: California legislative activity in August 2026: a draft trailer bill would allow unpiloted (autonomous) farm machines to work alongside farmworkers; labour groups, including unions, opposed it on job-loss and safety grounds (published 2026-08-25).
arguments.title: Politico: Unions sound alarm on last-minute push for robot farm equipment
arguments.claims_weakened: The article body returned HTTP 403 on fetch; only the headline and standfirst were readable, so the bill number, author, hearing date and the identity of the opposing unions are not established here. Paywalled or blocked content means this fact needs confirmation from the California Legislative Information record.

arguments.claims: 21 CFR 112.123 (Produce Safety Rule, Subpart L) requires that all food-contact surfaces of equipment and tools used in harvesting, packing and holding be inspected, maintained, cleaned and sanitized as necessary to protect against contamination of covered produce, that food-contact surfaces be smooth and cleanable, and that non-food-contact surfaces be cleaned as frequently as reasonably necessary. 21 CFR Part 112's equipment definition expressly includes mechanical harvesters and food-packing material.
arguments.title: eCFR: 21 CFR 112.123 — general requirements for equipment and tools under the FSMA Produce Safety Rule
arguments.claims_weakened: Sets design and cleaning duties on the equipment, not a certification; the rule does not prescribe a specific validation for robotic harvesters, so no certificate exists to obtain.

arguments.claims: 35 U.S.C. 204 provides that no small business firm or nonprofit organization that receives title to a federally funded subject invention, and no assignee of such a firm or organization, may grant to any person the exclusive right to use or sell the subject invention in the United States unless that person agrees that products embodying the invention will be manufactured substantially in the United States; the requirement may be waived in individual cases by the federal funding agency (e.g. on a showing that reasonable but unsuccessful efforts were made to grant licences on similar terms to potential licensees that would be likely to manufacture substantially in the US).
arguments.title: 35 U.S.C. §204 — Preference for United States industry (Bayh-Dole Act, Chapter 18)
arguments.claims_weakened: Applies only if the licensed university patent families were made with federal funding and the exclusive grant covers the US right; whether a robot assembled in Mexico is "manufactured substantially in the United States" is a fact-specific test not disclosed.

arguments.claims: Standard structure of university exclusive licences: a grant of exclusive rights balanced by diligence milestones and termination-for-failure-to-commercialise remedies, escalating milestone schedules, and step-in or conversion remedies; non-exclusive licences generally drop the milestone schedule and rely on an annual minimum royalty or maintenance fee. Licensors often prefer non-exclusive licensing or separate patent filings where exclusivity would block other licensees.
arguments.title: CASRAI guide: Diligence milestones and termination-for-failure-to-commercialize clauses in university exclusive licences
arguments.claims_weakened: Practitioner guidance rather than a survey statistic; it describes market practice in kind, not the frequency of conversion clauses, and gives no royalty-rate benchmark.

Now, before drafting, I need to build the evidence blocks. But first, let me verify a couple of key numbers and fill gaps:

1. CNH filing keyword search for Advanced Farm.
2. Maybe Deere 10-K item 1 for competition/technology? Not necessary.

Also I want a source for California strawberry value. Could search a teammate's source? None.

Let me think about the market-size arithmetic more rigorously, because this is the core.

Top-down:
- US strawberry acreage: CA 43,726 (2026 projection), FL ~10% of production. Total US likely 50,000-55,000.
- Harvest labor cost per acre: UC 2024 harvest cost $79,288/acre (includes labor, packing, harvest overhead). If purely labor at $24.42/hr fully loaded, and 1.5 workers/acre, a worker picking 8-12 flats/hour at $2/flat earns $16-24/hr. 9,000 trays/acre ÷ 10 trays/hour = 900 hours/acre; × $24.42 = $21,978/acre. Hmm, that's much less than $79,288. Wait — 9,000 trays at 8 lb = 72,000 lbs/acre, which is high; at 10 trays/hr, 900 hours. $22k labor. Plus packing materials: 9,000 trays × maybe $2 = $18k. Plus cooling/transport. $79k seems too high. Unless harvest is 40-50 passes and workers are slower.

Let me reconsider: a picker covers ~0.25 acre/day (deck). 1.5 workers/acre means each acre needs 4 worker-days per pass. At 40 passes = 160 worker-days/acre/season. At 8 hours/day × $24.42 = $31,258/acre. Plus piece-rate premium. That's in the $25-35k range. Still not $79k.

Hmm, maybe the UC study's 9,000 trays/acre is per season across multiple harvests, and harvest cost includes 9,000 trays × $2.50 packaging = $22.5k, labor $40k, harvest aids, supervisors, cooling, hauling = $79k. Plausible.

So I should be careful: the $79,288 is "harvest costs", not "hand-pick labour". The robot competes with the whole harvest budget but only displaces the picking labor portion. UC Davis says labor is 50-60% of variable production costs (total variable costs maybe $60k? then labor $30-36k/acre). That's consistent with my $25-35k estimate. So hand-pick labor is roughly $25,000-35,000/acre, and $79,288 is the full harvest cost including packing. Good — I can present both: full harvest cost $79,288 [S10]; labor 50-60% of variable costs [S12]; implied pick labor ~$25-35k/acre.

Then robot price per acre $4,714 vs hand-pick labor $25-35k = 13-19% of pick labor cost. That's still a strong value proposition on paper — but only if it replaces a large share of the crew and matches throughput. If a robot covers 3.5 acres and costs $16,500, and hand-pick labor is $25-35k/acre, the grower saves $87k-122k per robot-season in labor for $16.5k — implausibly good, which suggests the robot doesn't fully replace crew labor (it picks only some passes, at lower speed, or the 3.5 acres is a partial share). Indeed, Orrin charges only $16,500, which is ~5-19% of the labor bill; they'd be leaving enormous value on the table if full substitution. That's a pricing-power point: if the robot performs, Orrin could price at 30-50% of displaced labor, i.e., $40-60k/robot-season; instead it prices $12.7-16.5k, implying either the robot covers a small fraction of passes or the grower's willingness to pay is capped by imperfections. Interesting mechanism: current pricing implies the robot displaces ~$16.5k-33k of labor (at 50-100% capture), i.e., 0.5-1.3 acres of hand-pick labor, not 3.5 acres. Or adoption is subsidized to win logos.

That's a genuinely good analytical insight: unit price reveals the company's own implicit estimate of displaced labor. At $16,500 and assuming the grower captures 50% of savings, displaced labor = $33,000 ≈ 1.1-1.3 acres at $25-30k/acre. So the "one robot per 3.5 acres" claim is inconsistent with its price unless penetration per acre is partial.

Let me also compute the $310M impossibility: at $16,500, $310M = 18,788 robots. At 3.5 acres = 65,758 acres > 50,000 claimed US acres. If instead all 50,000 acres = 14,286 robots = $235.7M. So max strawberry RaaS revenue at list price is $236M, and $310M requires other crops or higher prices. Meanwhile 15% adoption = 2,143 robots = $35.4M, and 2028's 2% = 286 robots = $4.7M vs their FY2028 RaaS plan $12.9M. Wait: 2% in 2028 = 1,000 acres / 3.5 = 286 robots × $16,500 = $4.7M, but their plan says $12.9M RaaS in 2028 — that implies 782 robots at $16,500 or 1,358 at $9,500, i.e., 5.5% of acreage by 2028, not 2%. Another internal inconsistency! Great.

Let me check: FY2027P RaaS $4.6M, with 360 robots planned in 2027. $4.6M/360 = $12,778 average — matches "2027 renewals average $12,700". Good. FY2028P $12.9M at $16,500 = 782 robots; acres = 2,737 = 5.5% of 50,000. But plan says 2% by 2028. Contradiction. Unless price mix is lower ($12,700 → 1,016 robots = 3,556 acres = 7.1%). Either way >2%.

This is excellent: the financial plan implies 5.5-7% acreage penetration by 2028, not 2%. So either the plan's adoption statement is conservative marketing or the revenue plan is unsupported.

Also 15% by 2031 = 7,500 acres = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M, far below $310M. To hit $310M at 15% share, the "serviceable market" would need to be $2.07B, not $3.1B. Or 15% of $3.1B = $465M, not $310M. Wait, deck says $310M = 10% of $3.1B. And adoption 15% by 2031. So 15% adoption should yield $465M if adoption share = revenue share. Inconsistent by 1.5x. Unless price declines.

Great material.

Now let me also test "one robot per 3.5 acres" against robot throughput: 1.5 acres/24h × 20h/24h? They say one robot covers 1.5 acres per 24 hours, running 20h/day. Season 7 months = 210 days → 315 acre-days. If each acre needs a pass every 3-4 days (deck) = 52-70 passes/season → 4.5-6.1 acres/robot. So 3.5 acres/robot is conservative by 30-75% — meaning the robot count (14,300) may be overstated and revenue per robot lower utilization. OR the 1.5 acres/day is an optimistic peak. Either way, the two claims are in tension: at 1.5 acres/day and 3-4 day picking intervals, one robot can serve 4.5-6 acres; if it only serves 3.5, either uptime (86%) and weather cut it, or throughput is lower in practice. Good mechanism.

Now market growth/CAGR. What CAGR? US strawberry acreage has been declining (2021 36,500 → 2024 ~42,300? Actually 2025 42,885, 2026 43,726 — rising). Hmm, 2021 36,500 vs 2025 42,885 — that's growth. Wait, the UC blog said CA had 36,500 acres in 2021; 2025 42,885. That's +4.1% CAGR over 4 years. But the CalAg report says "first increase after several years of decline" in 2026 — contradictory with 2024→2025 +1.3%. Hmm, CSC acreage includes summer plantings. Anyway, acreage roughly flat-to-up.

Market value growth: prices $24.67 (2024) → $24.75 (2025) → $23.05 (2026 season avg), roughly flat. So the strawberry market itself is not growing much; the robot market grows by penetration, not by crop growth. That's an important finding: the TAM is a replacement/labor-substitution market, not a growth market. Its growth depends on wage inflation and adoption, not berry demand.

CAGR for harvest labor spend: if AEWR falls in 2026, labor spend growth could slow. H-2A positions grew 3.4% in FY2025 (398,258 vs 384,900). Wage rates: AEWR average $17.74 → $15.96 (-10%) per VisaVerge. If both, H-2A wage bill growth could be negative in 2026-27. That's the single biggest swing factor and it cuts against the thesis. Strong counter-evidence.

But careful: VisaVerge is low confidence and conflicts with Seso. I'll present as "trade summaries conflict; the DOL rate table could not be retrieved (HTTP 503), so the 2026-27 wage floor is a material unresolved variable" and model both: at +3.7%, labor cost rises ~4%; at -10%, the robot payback lengthens ~10%. That's honest and decision-relevant.

Now, the market section needs a regional table with regions, market size (year), growth, company position, barriers, competitors, source. Rows: California; Florida; Mexico; Europe; Australia. Market size figures:
- California: 43,726 acres (2026), ~90% of US production; harvest labor spend? Could compute 43,726 × $25-35k = $1.1-1.5B. Hmm, derived. Or use full harvest cost $79,288 × 43,726 = $3.47B. That's close to the $3.1B claim! Interesting: 43,726 × $79,288 = $3.47B. So the $3.1B "serviceable market" is approximately California's total harvest cost. That validates $3.1B as a harvest-cost pool, but not as a robot revenue pool (robot captures only the labor share and only at its price). Good insight.

Let me compute precisely: 43,726 × 79,288 = 3,466,000,000 ≈ $3.47B. If using 2025 acreage 42,885 × 79,288 = $3.40B. So $3.1B is roughly 90% of that or based on slightly lower per-acre cost. This strongly suggests the $3.1B is California strawberry harvest cost (or US at lower per-acre). So "serviceable market" is the harvest-cost pool, and a robot priced at $4,714/acre captures 5.9% of it. 10% of $3.1B = $310M would be 10% of the harvest-cost pool — but Orrin captures only 5.9% of the pool even at 100% acreage. Therefore $310M requires ~50% acreage penetration at list price, not 10%. Precisely: $310M / ($4,714/acre) = 65,758 acres = 150% of CA acreage / 132% of 50k. Yes.

Wait, actually: revenue per acre at 3.5 acres/robot = $4,714. $310M/$4,714 = 65,758 acres. At 15% of 50,000 = 7,500 acres → $35.4M. So $310M is 8.8x the 15%-adoption revenue. To hit $310M you'd need 132% of US acreage. Decisive.

Alternatively if price rises to $40k/robot (value-based), then 15% adoption = 7,500/3.5=2,143 robots × $40k = $85.7M. Still not $310M. At $145k/robot it works — implausible.

So the SOM is contradicted by the company's own unit economics. That's the central market judgement: the harvest-labour need is real and large ($3.1-3.5B pool), but the obtainable revenue at the stated adoption curve is ~$35M by 2031, not $310M; the $310M figure is a pool-size, not a revenue forecast. Investment implication: at $72M pre-money with $12.9M 2028 revenue and $35M 2031 revenue, the valuation implies ~2x 2031 revenue at 100% success — actually $72M/$35M = 2.1x, which isn't crazy for a hardware/RaaS business with 60% margins if it gets there. Hmm, but risk of failure is high. Let me not stray into valuation (that's the Valuation Analyst's section), but I can note the implication for the adoption curve.

Competition section judgement: Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO claims human parity in open-field Florida (April 2025); the two most credible US peers (Advanced Farm, Tortuga) exited or were absorbed in 2025, which both validates the difficulty and removes near-term price competition. The dangerous competitor is Harvest CROO (same geography, grower-backed, 13 patents, RaaS). But its claim is unverified. The bigger threat is the status quo plus harvest-aid platforms (Agrobot 30-40% labor savings at near-zero running cost) and equipment makers (CNH reportedly holds Advanced Farm IP; Tallis is Orrin's own contract manufacturer and noteholder with a board observer seat). Pricing power: if a competitor proves parity, the RaaS price falls toward the value of displaced labor; Orrin's $9,500→$16,500 increase (+74%) is untested and already produced a 2026 churn.

Also: Grower E ended pilot over bruising — direct evidence that the 3.8% bruising rate is not universally acceptable; in fresh strawberries, bruising >2-3% may be unacceptable for premium retail. And Orrin's 94% pick rate is on selected rows (excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes >4%), so the effective field performance is lower.

Competition classification:
- Direct: Harvest CROO (open-field FL), Advanced Farm (exited 2025), Tortuga (absorbed by Oishii 2025).
- Local substitute: hand crews at piece rate; harvest-aid platforms/conveyors (UC Davis notes conveyors raise productivity); Agrobot solar platform.
- International competitor: Agrobot (Spain, tabletop/open-field?), maybe Octinion (Belgium; not verified).
- Strategic comparable: Tevel (orchard, flying robots), FFRobotics (apple), Metomotion (greenhouse tomato) — non-comparable for strawberries but valuation/technology benchmarks.
- Future entrant: CNH/Deere/equipment OEMs adding picking arms; Tallis (contract manufacturer, noteholder, observer) — conflict.
- Status quo: hand crews, 50-60% of variable cost.

Positioning table: Product (open-field strawberry harvest) | Leader: Harvest CROO (claim) | Challenger: Orrin | Niche: Agrobot (harvest aid) | Emerging threat: CNH/Tallis equipment integration.

arguments.claims: The US Supreme Court struck down the 25% IEEPA tariff on Mexican imports on 2026-02-20 (Learning Resources v. Trump). A 10% Section 122 surcharge on Mexico/Canada took effect 2026-02-24, exempting USMCA-qualifying goods, and expired around 2026-07-24 under the 150-day statutory limit, replaced by a Section 301 action per the publication's September 2026 update. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico continued to enter at 0% duty, and USMCA utilization reached 85% in January 2026; the USMCA joint review took place on 2026-07-01.

arguments.claims: USMCA-compliant goods from Mexico enter the US at 0% duty; goods that fail origin face standard MFN rates plus a 10% tariff on non-USMCA Mexican goods. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper (50%) apply even to USMCA-qualifying goods. USMCA rules of origin are met by tariff shift or by a regional value content threshold of 60% for most goods (75% for autos/parts), and require a valid certificate of origin. Industrial machinery of Mexican USMCA origin is shown at 0% duty.

AGCO Corporation (NYSE: AGCO), a worldwide manufacturer and distributor of agricultural machinery and Precision Ag technology, announced it has entered into a Joint Venture (JV) with Trimble (Nasdaq: TRMB), where AGCO will acquire an 85% interest in Trimble’s portfolio of Ag assets and technologies for cash consideration of $2.0 billion and the contribution of JCA Technologies.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20230927470614/en/

The JV creates a global leading mixed-fleet Precision Ag platform that will be the exclusive provider of Trimble Ag’s comprehensive technology offering, supporting the future development and distribution of next-generation Ag technologies. Trimble Ag offers a wide variety of user-friendly technologies compatible across brands, equipment models and farm types. Its hardware, software solutions and cloud-based applications span all aspects of the crop cycle, from land preparation to planting and seeding to harvest.

“This landmark transaction creates a JV that becomes the premier mixed-fleet Precision Ag business in the world and accelerates AGCO’s strategic transformation,” said Eric Hansotia, AGCO’s Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer. “This deal significantly enhances AGCO’s technology stack with disruptive technologies that cover every aspect of the crop cycle, which ultimately helps us better serve farmers no matter what brand they use.”

The JV will complement and enhance AGCO’s existing Precision Ag portfolio to deliver even more industry leading solutions across the crop cycle while supporting over 10,000 equipment models. By combining these two Precision Ag portfolios and leveraging multi-channel access across Trimble Ag, AGCO OEM & Aftermarket, other OEMs, and Precision Planting dealers, the JV will be positioned to drive outsized growth and better provide next-generation technologies to even more farmers around the world.

Hansotia continued, “The exclusive access to Trimble Ag products, combined with AGCO’s existing Precision Ag offerings also accelerates AGCO’s growth ambitions around autonomy, precision spraying, connected farming, data management and sustainability. All of these touchpoints will result in us being even more farmer focused."

Commercial synergies resulting from direct access to AGCO’s global OEM, aftermarket, other OEM, and retrofit channels, in addition to modest run-rate cost synergies are expected to approximately double the JV’s EBITDA by year 5 post closing.

"Farmers today are looking for mixed fleet solutions across their tractors and the implements that they use to most efficiently and sustainably feed the world," said Rob Painter, CEO of Trimble. "We believe a joint venture with AGCO, complemented by the successful mixed fleet approach that they have developed with their Precision Planting business model, can help us better serve farmers and OEMs together.”

The $2.0 billion purchase price for AGCO’s 85% ownership in the Trimble Ag business represents an implied enterprise value of approximately $2.35 billion and implies a transaction multiple of approximately 13.8x based on 2023E EBITDA of approximately $170 million. Inclusive of estimated revenue and run-rate cost synergies of $100 million by year 3 and the net present value of tax attributes in excess of $50 million, the synergized multiple is approximately 8.5x on a 2023E basis.

The transaction is not subject to a financing condition. AGCO has secured $2.0 billion in fully committed bridge financing from Morgan Stanley Senior Funding, Inc. The purchase price of $2.0 billion is expected to be funded by a combination of existing liquidity, free cash flow generation and new debt. AGCO remains committed to maintaining its solid investment grade credit rating.

Closing is expected in the first half of 2024, subject to the satisfaction of regulatory approval and customary closing conditions.

AGCO has also announced that the Grain & Protein business will be placed under strategic review as part of AGCO’s broader portfolio transformation. Under this review, AGCO will assess all strategic options to ensure the Grain & Protein customers are serviced in the best way possible, and that the business is best positioned to maximize its full potential.

Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC is acting as exclusive financial advisor to AGCO. Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP is acting as legal advisor to AGCO, and Troutman Pepper Hamilton Sanders LLP is acting as its financing counsel.

Centerview Partners LLC is acting as exclusive financial advisor to Trimble, and Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP is acting as its legal advisor.

rows.finding: California strawberry acreage is 43,726 in the 2026 Commission projection (32,412 fall-planted + 11,314 summer-planted) after 42,885 in 2025, and California supplies about 90% of US production; Florida is the only other significant state at about 10%.
rows.mechanism: Acreage is the denominator of every bottom-up robot count; if the US base is larger than the company's 50,000 acres, the 14,300-robot figure is understated, not overstated.
rows.benchmark: Company plan assumes about 50,000 US strawberry acres; California alone is 43,726, i.e. 87% of that base before Florida and other states.
rows.weakens: Florida acreage and the 2019-2023 NASS series were not retrieved in this run, so the 50,000-acre total cannot be reconciled exactly; the California Commission figure is a projection, not a harvested-acre census.
rows.implication: Use 50,000 acres as a floor. The market is big enough to matter, but its ceiling is set by acreage, not by the $42B global figure.
rows.confidence: high on California; medium on the national total
rows.follow_up: What are Florida planted and harvested strawberry acres for 2019-2025 in USDA NASS Quick Stats, and does the state total exceed 50,000?

rows.finding: The 2024 UC Central Coast sample budget puts harvest cost at $79,288 per acre against $22,264 of cultural costs and $112,694 of total cost per acre on 9,000 trays at $11; UC Davis puts labour at 50-60% of variable production cost and piece rates at $1.75-2.25 per flat with 8-12 flats picked per hour.
rows.mechanism: The robot competes for the harvest line, not the whole farm budget. Hand-pick labour is roughly $25,000-35,000 per acre (author calculation from the 50-60% labour share), so a robot priced at $4,714 per acre (one per 3.5 acres at $16,500) costs 13-19% of the wage bill it targets.
rows.benchmark: Robot rental of $4,714 per acre per season versus $79,288 of harvest cost and $25,000-35,000 of hand-pick labour per acre.
rows.weakens: The $79,288 harvest line bundles packing, cooling and supervision, so it overstates displaceable wages; the UC budget is one Central Coast scenario with a 48% labour overhead, and Florida costs are lower.
rows.implication: The value proposition is real on paper: even a 10% harvest-cost saving is worth about $7,929 per acre. The open question is what share of the wage bill the robot actually removes.
rows.confidence: medium: strong university source, but a sample budget summarised by trade press
rows.follow_up: What is the pure hand-pick wage line per acre (excluding trays, cooling and hauling) in the 2024 UC study, and what is the equivalent Florida budget?

rows.finding: The company's obtainable-market figure does not survive its own unit economics: $310M at $16,500 per robot-season requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, which is 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M.
rows.mechanism: Revenue = acres / 3.5 x price. At the list price the entire US strawberry acreage is worth $236M a year, so a $310M obtainable market cannot come from US strawberries at the stated density and price.
rows.benchmark: Company's own $236M full-penetration figure and its 15% 2031 adoption assumption.
rows.weakens: The $310M could include other soft fruit or higher value-based pricing, but the deck presents it as 10% of a $3.1B serviceable market and separately values strawberries alone at $236M.
rows.implication: Treat $310M as a harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast. The 2031 revenue case is closer to $35M at 15% adoption, which changes what the $72M pre-money is paying for.
rows.confidence: high: arithmetic from company figures
rows.follow_up: Which crops and what price per robot-season are inside the $310M, and what revenue does the company actually underwrite for 2031?

rows.finding: The financial plan is ahead of the adoption statement: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of 50,000 acres, not the 2% the market slide assumes; at the $12,700 renewal price it implies 7.1%.
rows.mechanism: Either the adoption curve on the market slide understates the plan the company is actually selling, or the revenue plan has no acreage basis.
rows.benchmark: Company's 2% by 2028 assumption versus its FY2028P revenue of $12.9M.
rows.weakens: Mixed pricing ($9,500 legacy, $12,700 renewal, $16,500 list) and pilot revenue make the implied robot count a range, not a point.
rows.implication: Ask management to reconcile the market slide with the financial plan before accepting either the adoption curve or the revenue build.
rows.confidence: medium: relies on company projections and a price mix
rows.follow_up: Provide the 2028 robot count and average price behind the $12.9M RaaS line.

rows.finding: The robot-density assumption is internally conservative: at 1.5 acres per 24 hours over a 210-day California season a robot covers 315 acre-passes, which at the 40-50 picks per season documented by UC Davis serves 6.3-7.9 acres, not 3.5; one robot per 3.5 acres implies about 90 passes a season.
rows.mechanism: Utilisation sets revenue per robot. If throughput is real, the fleet needed for a given acreage is smaller (about 6,300-7,900 robots for 50,000 acres), which lowers the TAM in robot units or implies the 3.5-acre figure already discounts uptime, weather and partial-row work.
rows.benchmark: Company's 1.5 acres/24h, 86% uptime and one robot per 3.5 acres versus UC Davis' 40-50 harvest passes.
rows.weakens: The 1.5 acres per 24 hours is a company measurement on selected rows; field uptime, fog, mud and row ends will lower it.
rows.implication: The robot count is not the constraint; the constraint is how many passes a robot can do at commercial quality. Underwrite revenue per robot, not acres per robot.
rows.confidence: medium: company throughput against university harvest frequency
rows.follow_up: What is the measured acres-per-24-hours on unselected commercial rows, and how many passes per season does Orrin actually contract for?

rows.finding: The labour shortage is acute but the policy tailwind is turning: H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025 (+13,358, +3.5%) with Florida above 14% of the national total, while the October 2025 interim final rule replaced the USDA Farm Labor Survey basis for the AEWR with BLS OEWS data and is under litigation; trade summaries conflict, one showing the average AEWR falling to $15.96 from $17.74 and another showing entry-level rates up about 3.7% with declines in 13 states.
rows.mechanism: The AEWR sets the grower's legal alternative wage, so a lower wage floor lengthens robot payback exactly when the technology is trying to scale; a higher floor shortens it.
rows.benchmark: FY2019 berries were 10% of 258,000 certified H-2A jobs; FY2025 total is 398,258. June 2025 Ventura County enforcement left up to 70% of workers absent.
rows.weakens: The structural-shortage story is supported by the 2025 enforcement shock but not by the guest-worker programme, which has kept expanding; the direction of the 2026-27 wage floor is unresolved and the DOL rate table returned HTTP 503 on 2026-10-30.
rows.implication: Policy is the biggest single swing factor in willingness to pay. Model both a 4% wage increase and a 10% cut; do not underwrite the deck's 10-15% crop-loss premise as permanent.
rows.confidence: high on H-2A counts and the rule change; low on the 2026-27 rate level
rows.follow_up: What are the final 2026-27 AEWRs for California and Florida, and what hourly rate do Santa Maria and Plant City growers actually pay hand pickers?

rows.finding: The only comparable mechanisation succeeded through crop redesign, not a drop-in machine: California processing tomatoes went from 25 machines and 0.5% of the crop in 1961 to 512 machines and 70% in 1966, after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers switched to once-over harvest.
rows.mechanism: Mechanisation is a system change: uniform ripening, one pass and an industrial end use. Fresh-market strawberries are picked 40-50 times and graded on appearance, so the tomato curve is an upper bound on speed.
rows.benchmark: 0.5% to 70% in five years for processing tomatoes versus 0% of US fresh strawberry acres harvested commercially by robot in 2025 and the plan's 2% by 2028 / 15% by 2031.
rows.weakens: The tomato case proves adoption can be fast when genetics, agronomy and the buyer all change together, which is the scenario Orrin would need; it also shows a machine alone was not enough.
rows.implication: Use 2-5% specialty-crop robotic harvest penetration as the base case for 2028 and treat 15% by 2031 as the upside case that requires a variety and buyer reset.
rows.confidence: high on the history; medium on the analogy
rows.follow_up: Has any US retailer or shipper committed to a robot-picked fresh strawberry programme, and do the varieties in Orrin's pilot farms ripen uniformly enough for night-only passes?

plan.decision_question: Is the US strawberry harvest-labour pool large and urgent enough to support 2% acreage adoption by 2028 and 15% by 2031, and is the $310M obtainable market arithmetically reachable at the company's own price and robot density?
plan.thesis_sentence: The harvest-labour pool is real — roughly $3.1-3.5B a year of US strawberry harvest cost, with hand-pick labour around $25,000-35,000 an acre — but at the company's own $16,500 price and one-robot-per-3.5-acres density, 100% of US strawberry acreage is worth only about $236M a year, so the $310M obtainable market is the size of the cost pool rather than a revenue forecast, and the investment case depends on adoption speed and pricing power, not on market size.
plan.why_different: This section sizes the prize and tests the adoption arithmetic; the competition section tests who else can take the same harvest budget, and the financial section tests whether Orrin can deliver at its cost structure.
plan.mechanism: Revenue = strawberry acres x penetration / acres per robot x price per robot-season. The grower's willingness to pay is bounded by the hand-pick wage bill the robot displaces (roughly $25,000-35,000 an acre), which the AEWR sets at the margin; the plan's $310M requires 132% of US strawberry acreage at the stated density and price.
plan.comparison_set: Processing-tomato mechanisation (0.5% to 70% in five years after a varietal and system redesign), current robotic harvest of fresh strawberries (no commercial scale identified in 2025), and H-2A growth (398,258 certified positions in FY2025, +3.5%).
plan.counter_evidence: The 2025 immigration enforcement shock (up to 70% of workers absent in Ventura County) makes the shortage urgent, and a lower 2026-27 AEWR would weaken the grower's willingness to pay; a Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising; tabletop and tunnel acres are excluded from the addressable set; and hand crews remain the default for small growers.
plan.visual: A market-size table with TAM, SAM and SOM built top-down and bottom-up, plus a regional table separating California, Florida, Mexico and the non-US competitor geographies.
plan.prohibited: huge market, large and growing, strong demand, clear runway, tailwinds, well positioned, fierce competition, risks are manageable, about 5
