Also the executed licence: exclusivity field, the 100-robot test wording, cure rights, the royalty and minimum, and any federal-agency waiver under 35 U.S.C. 204.
arguments.why: Three things turn on these documents. First, whether the licence's US rights are exclusive at all, which is the moat the $72M pre-money is priced on. Second, whether 35 U.S.C. 204's US manufacturing preference binds, because the company assembles grippers and harnesses in Guadalajara. The licensor cannot be searched by name, so only the data room or the patent record settles this.

{"url":"https://agfundernews.com/oishii-acquires-tortuga-agtechs-ip-assets-and-engineering-team-to-supercharge-its-vertical-farms","title":"Oishii acquires Tortuga AgTech’s IP, assets, and engineering team to ‘supercharge’ its vertical farms","text":"Tortuga AgTech's harvesting robots picking strawberries on a farm.
Image credit: Tortuga AgTech

 Vertical farming company Oishii, best known for its premium strawberries and tomatoes, has acquired the “key IP and assets” of harvest robotics startup Tortuga AgTech. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
Colorado-based Tortuga AgTech is best known for its robots that harvest strawberries, table grapes, and berries, in addition to collecting data from plants and performing a few other tasks such as trimming and treating plants with UV-C light.
“We have had our eye on Tortuga AgTech’s growth over the years and watched as they successfully deployed $50 million in capital over eight years to develop industry leading technology,” Oishii cofounder and COO Brendan Somerville told AgFunderNews.
He noted that the primary decision behind the acquisition was “the importance of staying at the forefront of agricultural innovation, building stronger infrastructure, and constantly striving to advance in our field.”

“We have known the Oishii team for years, but began partnering this past fall to apply our technology in Oishii’s farm units,” Tortuga AgTech CEO and cofounder Eric Adamson told AgFunderNews.
“With the downturn in agritech venture capital, we realized that the ethos and team at Oishii offered the best fit for creating the most immediate and valuable opportunities for all parties involved. Oishii also stands out as an innovator that has uniquely gotten real products to market.”

Oishii is no stranger to automation, having built in-house automation capabilities since the company’s inception, he adds. “This acquisition will continue to further that growth. The combination of what Tortuga AgTech has built since its founding in 2016, married with our state-of-the-art technology allows us to scale automated harvesting more quickly and efficiently while ultimately decreasing net costs.”

The company currently uses robotics in its vertical farms to detect ripeness in each strawberry before picking it. The Amatelas Farm—Oishii’s main facility—currently uses around 50 ‘bots, which can also capture data that’s used over time to adjust environmental variables like light, temperature and wind speed.

The Tortuga AgTech ‘bot working between rows of strawberries. Image credit: Tortuga AgTech

Robots can ‘surpass human farmers in the picking of strawberries’
Tortuga AgTech’s commercial harvesting fleet is currently 150 robots strong and was originally built for strawberry picking.
Oishii will acquire Tortuga AgTech’s advanced robotics technologies including its AI models, frontier robotics software and custom hardware. These technologies will be integrated into Oishii’s robotic system, which it has developed in partnership with Yaskawa Robotics.
Oishii claims that these additions will enable the robots to “surpass human farmers in the picking” of strawberries and reduce harvest expenses by 50%.
That’s no small claim, considering the fact that harvest is widely seen as the most difficult task on the farm to automate and/or roboticize, largely due to engineering challenges.
In addition to Tortuga AgTech’s IP and assets, its team was  a major draw for Oishii, said Somerville.
“Specifically, Oishii has welcomed key members of Tortuga AgTech’s world-leading engineering team to join forces with our own,” he said. “These individuals bring invaluable expertise that will contribute significantly to our ongoing innovation and development efforts.”
The majority of Tortuga’s team has been immediately integrated, and the teams are already actively working together, he added.
Oishii is one of just a handful of vertical farming companies that are currently thriving at a time when many more have either declared bankruptcy or closed up shop completely. The company, which raised $134 million in 2024, has been slowly but steadily expanding availability of its strawberries from the Northeast US to other parts of the country including D.C., Chicago, Virginia, Texas, and Wisconsin.
For the Tortuga AgTech team and tech, the deal presents “a promising future,” Tortuga’s Adamson told AgFunderNews.
“Oishii’s strong vision, industry leadership, and great success in fundraising from many types of investors gives Tortuga’s technology and vision the best chance of industry-changing success, while directly impacting Oishii’s bottom line.”
Adamson said the company will for the time being focus on integrating its technologies into Oishii’s existing production facilities and technical roadmap. He hinted at future innovations for harvesting robots but noted that the team is “not ready to share plans yet.”
“Along with a sharp sense of the economic and commercial requirements for success, acceleration is key her,” he added. “Tortuga supercharges the strong engineering foundation Oishii has already built and we’re excited about seeing the expansion of our robotics expertise as a team.”","truncated":false}

rows.benchmark: Orrin's full autonomy at $16,500 per robot-season versus a harvest-aid platform sold or leased at an undisclosed price.
rows.weakens: Company promotional claim with no independent trial data, price, units sold or named growers.

 Vertical farming company Oishii, best known for its premium strawberries and tomatoes, has acquired the “key IP and assets” of harvest robotics startup Tortuga AgTech. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
Colorado-based Tortuga AgTech is best known for its robots that harvest strawberries, table grapes, and berries, in addition to collecting data from plants and performing a few other tasks such as trimming and treating plants with UV-C light.

He noted that the primary decision behind the acquisition was “the importance of staying at the forefront of agricultural innovation, building stronger infrastructure, and constantly striving to advance in our field.”

“We have known the Oishii team for years, but began partnering this past fall to apply our technology in Oishii’s farm units,” Tortuga AgTech CEO and cofounder Eric Adamson told AgFunderNews.

The company currently uses robotics in its vertical farms to detect ripeness in each strawberry before picking it. The Amatelas Farm—Oishii’s main facility—currently uses around 50 ‘bots, which can also capture data that’s used over time to adjust environmental variables like light, temperature and wind speed.

The Tortuga AgTech ‘bot working between rows of strawberries. Image credit: Tortuga AgTech

Robots can ‘surpass human farmers in the picking of strawberries’

Oishii claims that these additions will enable the robots to “surpass human farmers in the picking” of strawberries and reduce harvest expenses by 50%.
That’s no small claim, considering the fact that harvest is widely seen as the most difficult task on the farm to automate and/or roboticize, largely due to engineering challenges.
In addition to Tortuga AgTech’s IP and assets, its team was  a major draw for Oishii, said Somerville.
“Specifically, Oishii has welcomed key members of Tortuga AgTech’s world-leading engineering team to join forces with our own,” he said. “These individuals bring invaluable expertise that will contribute significantly to our ongoing innovation and development efforts.”
The majority of Tortuga’s team has been immediately integrated, and the teams are already actively working together, he added.
Oishii is one of just a handful of vertical farming companies that are currently thriving at a time when many more have either declared bankruptcy or closed up shop completely. {"url":"https://modern-ag.net/new-report-estimates-strawberry-growing-costs-in-coastal-california/","title":"New report estimates strawberry growing costs in coastal California - Modern Ag Media","text":"University of California (UC) Agriculture and Natural Resources Cooperative Extension and UC Davis Dept. of Agricultural and Resource Economics released a new 19-page report that looks at strawberry production costs along the Central Coast in California. The study, titled Sample Costs to Produce and Harvest Strawberries, assumed 45 acres of strawberries on 50 acres of rented land in a vegetable rotation in its model, and provided sample costs for everything from labor to materials to repairs.

With the assumption of 9,000 trays per acre at a unit price of $11, the report estimates cultural costs at $22,264 per acre and harvest costs at $79,288 per acre. With the inclusion of 9% interest on operating capital, the total operating costs per acre are estimated at $105,809.

With the addition of overhead, the total costs per acre totaled $112,694 per acre.

The report stresses that strawberry production is a high risk endeavor. While the report can’t fully represent all of the elements that can affect the economics and profitability of fresh strawberries, it does its best to provide this information based on the real-world practices of a typical strawberry farm found in the central coastal regions of the state.

There are many factors that can heavily influence fluctuations in these estimates. These specific regions alone have varying land rents and taxes, and farm-specific practices and input costs can move overall production costs in either direction.

For example, the study assumed flat land and fumigation land preparation that includes discing six times, subsoiling twice, chiseling twice, followed by a half acre-inch of water prior to fumigating with a combination of chloropicrin and 1,3-dichloropropene. With the inclusion of the permit, this is estimated at $5,028 for solid, tarped fumigation.

Plants were planted at 17,424 plants to the acre with 5% — or 870 plants — built into the cost estimates as a buffer for plants that would need to be replanted in the following weeks for a variety of possible reasons.

Post-plant irrigation also has a wider range of cost variability due to soil types, water districts and fees, weather conditions and other factors. Effective rainfall was not considered in the study, and irrigation water cost is estimated at $360 per acre-foot ($30 per acre-inch).

Labor rates included overhead of 48%, putting rates at $24.42 and $29.60 per hour for field labor and machine operators, respectively. This included not only basic hourly wages, but payroll taxes, workers compensation, and other factors. Use of the federal H-2A program would also affect these costs.

This study provides growers with a baseline to estimate their own costs, which can help when applying for production loans, projecting labor costs, securing market arrangements, or understanding costs associated with water and nutrient management and regulatory programs,” said Brittney Goodrich, UC Cooperative Extension specialist and study co-author.

The 2022 report (Sample Costs to Produce and Harvest Organic Strawberries) is available for organic strawberry production, which makes up about 13% of the market.","truncated":false}

The robot at $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres is $2,714 an acre, 7.5%-13% of that; at the 2027 list price of $16,500 it is $4,714 an acre, 13%-22%.", "source_ids": "S1, S80, S82", "source_type": "company-provided (deck) combined with primary wage data; the arithmetic is mine", "mechanism": "A grower buys the robot out of the hand-labour budget, so the ceiling on price is hand cost avoided less quality losses plus overtime premiums avoided. The robot is priced an order of magnitude below the labour it displaces, which means price is not the constraint on adoption and the 74% price increase from $9,500 to $16,500 is not the risk it looks like in the financials.", "benchmark": "No company disclosure of grower payback or of a hand-harvest cost per acre. The UC Davis 2024 Central Coast strawberry cost study is the reference benchmark and its harvest-labour figures were not obtained.", "weakens": "Depends on a company estimate of picker productivity and on an assumed number of passes; a robot that completes fewer passes earns less of that avoided cost than the comparison implies.", "implication": "The adoption constraint is quality and uptime, not price. A valuation case that leans on the 2027 list price increase should be discounted until bruising is below the hand-picked benchmark.", "follow_up": "How many harvest passes does a California strawberry field take in a season, and what does the UC 2024 study put harvest labour at per acre and per tray?", "confidence": "medium; the wage figures are solid, the pass count is assumed"}, {"finding": "The $3.52 an hour cut in the California Level I rate removes about $4,224 of hand-harvest cost per acre over a 40-pass season (160 picker-days at $131.60 falling to $105.20). That is 1.6 times the robot's $2,714 an acre-season price, so one court ruling is worth more to the grower per acre than a season of Orrin's service.", "source_ids": "S80, S1", "source_type": "primary wage data plus company-provided pricing; the arithmetic is mine", "mechanism": "When the policy input is larger than the product's price, the product's value proposition is partly a function of litigation the company does not control. This cuts both ways: reinstatement of a higher floor would add value equal to 1.6 robot-seasons an acre.", "benchmark": "Against a 17.6% cut in the wage floor and a $2,714 an acre robot price.", "weakens": "Assumes the robot covers the acres and passes it is priced for; if it works a fraction of the season, the comparison overstates the stake.", "implication": "The 2027 pricing environment is set by a docket, not by the company's sales execution. That argues for a milestone-linked tranche rather than a single close.", "follow_up": "Will growers build their 2027 labour budget on the OEWS rate, the old Farm Labor Survey rate, or wait for the new methodology?", "confidence": "medium"}, {"finding": "USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, but a non-qualifying robot pays about 10% on customs value: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, equal to 26% of the $12,700 2027 renewal price and 85% of the 2026 gross profit of $3,900 a robot-season. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper (50%) apply even to USMCA goods. On 2026-10-28 a Section 232 robotics proclamation found that imports threaten national security, imposed no tariff, and set a first joint Commerce-USTR update within 180 days, about 2027-04-26, with tariffs, quotas and fees explicitly left open.", "source_ids": "S89, S90, S88, S87, S91", "source_type": "primary (Federal Register notice) plus independent advisers", "mechanism": "Orrin owns the fleet, so an import duty is levied on its own capital cost, not passed to the grower. It lands on the $9.9M robot budget and on the Kestrel facility secured on those robots, which requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times.", "benchmark": "MFN duty on agricultural machinery is effectively zero, and USMCA utilization nationally reached 85% in January 2026, so the entire exposure is policy-created rather than tariff-schedule-created.", "weakens": "Whether the robot meets USMCA rules of origin is not disclosed; 10% is the non-qualifying case, and the metals exposure depends on an undisclosed material content. The 180-day clock may end in a negotiated outcome with no duty.", "implication": "Stress the 2027 build at +10% landed cost ($990,000 on $9.9M) and at a 25% Section 232 outcome ($2.48M, which would consume the round). Make a USMCA certificate of origin a condition precedent.", "follow_up": "Does Orrin hold a USMCA certificate of origin for v3 and v4, and what share of the bill of materials is steel, aluminium or copper?", "confidence": "high on the architecture of the rules; medium on the exposure size"}, {"finding": "The university licence pays 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 a year minimum; the minimum binds in FY2026 (2.5% of $0.71M is $17,750, so the floor is 5.6% of RaaS revenue), and it becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet in 2026. If the licensed inventions were federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to agree that products embodying the invention are manufactured substantially in the United States, while grippers and wiring harnesses are assembled in Guadalajara.", "source_ids": "S1, S85, S86", "source_type": "company-provided (deck) plus primary statute and independent practice guidance", "mechanism": "Exclusivity on the two families is the legal bar to a better-funded entrant buying the same rights from the university. Conversion to non-exclusive removes that bar at a fixed date, and the licensor holds no equity, so it has no upside to trade away in exchange for an extension. Section 204 separately conditions the exclusive US right on domestic manufacture.", "benchmark": "University practice is a schedule of escalating diligence milestones with cure periods and step-in rights; a single binary test at a fixed date with no cure is harsher than the norm.", "weakens": "The 360-robot 2027 plan clears the threshold comfortably, so conversion requires a slippage of about 72% rather than a miss of a stretch target. Whether the two families were federally funded is not disclosed, so Section 204 may not bind.", "implication": "Treat exclusivity as conditional until 2028-01-01 and reprice the moat accordingly; require a representation that the licence is in good standing and that the robot count is measured on the company's own definition.", "follow_up": "Is the 100-robot test measured on robots in service on 2027-12-31 or cumulatively, is there a cure period, and were the two university families federally funded?", "confidence": "high on the licence terms; medium on the Section 204 conclusion"}, {"finding": "Strawberries are covered produce under 21 CFR Part 112; the rule names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 21 CFR 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable, inspected and cleaned and sanitised as necessary to protect against contamination. Picking directly into the retail clamshell makes the interior of the machine a food-contact and food-packing surface. No harvester-specific federal certification exists and none is disclosed.", "source_ids": "S83", "source_type": "primary (eCFR)", "mechanism": "The legal duty sits on the grower as the farm, but the equipment design sets the contamination risk, and a clamshell packed in the field reaches the consumer without a further wash step. Retailer audit standards, not the FDA, are the practical gate, and a recall traced to machine contact is a delisting rather than a fine.", "benchmark": "Hand crews meet the same rule through worker hygiene and container sanitation; machine surfaces can be validated and documented in a way hand labour cannot, which is an unexploited advantage.", "weakens": "No FDA warning letter, recall or enforcement action against machine-harvested berries was found; the risk is prospective.", "implication": "A sanitary-design and cleaning validation for the v4 is a cheap condition that removes a retailer objection and a diligence discount.", "follow_up": "Does the company hold a cleaning and sanitation protocol or validation for the clamshell path, and has a retailer or third-party auditor reviewed it?", "confidence": "high on the rule; low on current compliance, which is undisclosed"}, {"finding": "ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles, verification and information-for-use requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery. No US federal approval or certification requirement for autonomous field machinery was identified, and the company discloses no ISO 18497 assessment.", "source_ids": "S92, S84", "source_type": "primary (ISO) plus independent press, article body blocked", "mechanism": "The unit economics assume one technician supervises up to eight robots, on site or remotely, and a $3,100 a robot-season field-service line. An operating rule requiring a human spotter within sight of each machine converts 1:8 into 1:1 and multiplies that line by roughly eight.", "benchmark": "Road-vehicle autonomy is regulated through exemptions and permits; agricultural autonomy has no equivalent US regime, so the rule is being written now and the standard is voluntary.", "weakens": "The bill number, text and status could not be read because the article body returned HTTP 403, so neither the timing nor the content of any rule is established.", "implication": "Model the field-service line at a 1:4 supervision ratio as a downside case; at 1:1 gross margin on the $9,500 price turns negative.", "follow_up": "What supervision ratio would the California proposals require, and what ratio does the fleet insurer require?", "confidence": "medium"}, {"finding": "The United Farm Workers is the plaintiff that overturned the AEWR methodology in district court on 2026-08-26, and labour groups opposed the California trailer bill on unpiloted machines. On quality, 3.8% of berries were bruised or punctured in the 2025 pilots, Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026.", "source_ids": "S81, S84, "source_type": "independent litigation reporting plus company-provided deck", "mechanism": "Labour substitution sells a robot only where labour supply is the binding constraint. Where quality is the constraint it does not, and a union with a recent court win has both the motive and the standing to shape the operating rule that decides whether a machine can run beside a crew.", "benchmark": "The company's own targets are a pick rate above 95% and, by implication, bruising below the 3.8% pilot level; no retailer standard specific to machine-harvested berries was identified.", "weakens": "No boycott, campaign, shareholder resolution or retailer sourcing policy aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was found, so the social liability is potential rather than actual.", "implication": "Do not credit an ESG premium, and do not let an ESG discount drive the decision either: the material social metric here is bruising and pick rate, which belongs in the product and risk sections.", "follow_up": "Has any retailer or buyer requested a labour-impact or food-safety statement, and what are the bruising rates at the two largest customers?", "confidence": "medium"}, {"finding": "USAspending returns zero federal awards to a recipient named Orrin Fieldworks, against a deck claim of a $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award over 2024-2026 and grant revenue of $0.80M across FY2023-FY2026E - more than the stated award.", "source_ids": "S91, S1", "source_type": "primary (USAspending) plus company-provided deck", "mechanism": "A grant line that cannot be traced to an award is either a subaward, a different legal entity or not federal money. It is non-recurring and vanishes from the FY2027 plan, so it does not change enterprise value, but a checkable fact that does not check bears on disclosure quality, which is a governance input to the valuation.", "benchmark": "A federal prime award to a named small business is normally visible in USAspending within the reporting lag.", "weakens": "A zero result does not prove absence: awards can be recorded under another legal name or as subawards, and part of the $0.80M may be state money.", "implication": "Treat the grant line as zero in the model and ask for the award notice before the round closes.", "follow_up": "What is the award number, agency and period, and is any of the $0.80M state rather than federal?", "confidence": "high on the search result; medium on the conclusion"}], "gate_done": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9], "plan": {"decision_question": "Which policy and regulatory facts change the grower's alternative cost of hand labour, the company's cost of goods, or its right to operate - and do they raise or lower what Meridian should pay for a $12M Series A at $72M pre-money?", "thesis_sentence": "Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case are being decided by other people before the 2027 season - a wage floor a court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff decision due by about 2027-04-26, a university exclusivity test on 2027-12-31 and a California rule on unpiloted machines - and on the evidence available the balance of them is mildly negative for the 2027 season and positive thereafter, which is a reason to price and stage the round rather than a reason to pass.", "why_different": "The other sections treat policy as background or as a risk category. This one converts each policy into a dollar per acre, per robot or per season so the market, financials and risk sections can carry a number instead of an adjective. It is also the only section that owns the registries where these decisions land.", "mechanism": "The AEWR is a legal wage floor paid to H-2A and corresponding US workers, so it sets the grower's hand-labour cost per acre and therefore the ceiling on what a robot-season can be sold for. USMCA rules of origin and Section 232 duties set the landed cost of a Mexico-assembled robot, which Orrin bears because it owns the fleet rather than selling equipment. The licence's 100-robot test decides whether a competitor can buy the same two patent families from the same university. The California operating rule would set the technician-to-robot ratio behind the $3,100 field-service line, and 21 CFR 112 makes the robot a piece of food-contact equipment whose cleaning regime the grower must be able to document.", "comparison_set": "Hand crews at the 2026 AEWR against the pre-October-2025 Farm Labor Survey rate; the robot's $2,714 an acre-season against a derived $21,000-$36,000 an acre of hand harvest; $12,700 renewal against $16,500 list; a US-manufactured build against the Guadalajara build for the Bayh-Dole question; and university-licence practice - a milestone schedule with cure and step-in - against a single binary test with no cure.", "counter_evidence": "The strongest case against the judgement is that the wage-floor cut is the least durable of the four factors: a district court has already held the rule unlawful, ordered a replacement methodology and required a back-wage notice, so the grower's alternative cost is more likely to rise than fall before the 2027 season, which restores the robot's value case. Second, the company may already satisfy USMCA origin and may never be caught by a robotics tariff, in which case the cost-of-goods exposure is zero. Third, no regulator, retailer or union has yet acted against machine-harvested berries, so the food-safety and social liabilities are potential rather than actual, and an ESG discount would be as unearned as an ESG premium.", "visual": "Three tables: the ESG issues table (issue, why material, evidence, rating impact), the regulatory record table (regulator, record, date, status) and the policy impact matrix (factor, exposure, probability, impact, mitigant). The matrix carries the section's judgement because it puts a date and a dollar figure on each policy.", "prohibited": "No 'ESG premium', 'regulatory moat', 'tailwind', 'headwind', 'responsible AI', 'sustainable agriculture' or 'well positioned' as unearned labels; no 'recently', 'soon' or 'going forward' without an absolute date; no claim that a policy is supportive or adverse without a dollar figure attached; no reference to how the section was researched, to review items, or to internal records."}}

arguments.title: The Robot Report: Carbon Robotics raises $70M Series D
arguments.claims: Carbon Robotics raised a $70M Series D in October 2024, bringing total funding to $157M since 2018, to scale its LaserWeeder weeding robot; the round was led by BOND.
arguments.claims_weakened: The valuation was not disclosed, so it cannot be used as a priced mark; Carbon is a weeding, not harvesting, robot.

arguments.title: Global AgInvesting: Tevel raises $20M Series B for flying fruit-picking robots
arguments.claims: Tevel raised a $20M Series B for its flying fruit-picking robots; Kubota participated in the round.
arguments.claims_weakened: The valuation was not disclosed; Tracxn puts total funding at $31.5M including a $2.5M Israeli grant.

arguments.title: AgFunderNews: farm robotics funding falls 36% Q2 to Q3 2025
arguments.claims: Venture capital funding for agrifood robotics and mechanization fell 36% from $168M in Q2 2025 to $108M in Q3 2025, a 57% year-over-year decline versus Q3 2024.
arguments.claims_weakened: Quarterly VC totals are volatile and can understate strategic or project finance; the series is a funding-flow indicator, not a valuation index.

arguments.title: iGrow Network: ag robotics and automation 2025 funding, M&A and patents
arguments.claims: Ag robotics and automation recorded $668M of funding, 14 acquisitions and 3,987 patents in 2025, according to the report summary.
arguments.claims_weakened: The article is paywalled and the underlying deal list is not visible, so the count of $100M+ exits cannot be verified from it alone; treat as a sector activity indicator.

arguments.title: Sacramento Business Journal: robotic fruit-picker maker Advanced Farm ceases operations
arguments.claims: Advanced Farm Technologies, a Davis, California ag-tech startup, ceased operations in July 2025 due to lack of funding; CNH Industrial acquired its intellectual property.
arguments.claims_weakened: The article is a trade/media report; the CNH asset price is undisclosed, so the recovery to equity is unknown.

arguments.title: Theia/Dealroom: Monarch Tractor layoffs and headquarters closure
arguments.claims: Monarch Tractor vacated its Livermore headquarters and laid off almost all employees after raising around $220-242M, including a $133M Series C in July 2024; it was shifting from hardware manufacturing to software licensing.
arguments.claims_weakened: The report is secondary and the company's current status is not confirmed in a filing; it is used only to show that a >$500M ag-robotics mark did not hold.

arguments.title: PrivateMarketView: Harvest CROO funding rounds

arguments.title: PR Newswire: Monarch Tractor announces $133M Series C

The US strawberry harvest is a real $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool, and hand-pick labour alone is worth roughly $25,000-35,000 an acre, but the company's $310M obtainable market is the size of that pool rather than of its revenue: at its own $16,500 robot-season price and one robot per 3.5 acres, 100% of US strawberry acreage is worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The opportunity is large enough to build a company on and too small to support the headline number, which moves the investment question from market size to adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps once competitors arrive [S1].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** At $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year; 15% adoption is worth $35.4M, and the $310M figure requires 132% of the US acreage base. Source: S1.
:::

| Measure | Top-down | Bottom-up | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global fresh-produce harvest labour | $42B (2025), company estimate, not independently verified | — | S1 |
| SAM — US strawberry harvest cost | $3.1B company figure vs $3.47B author calculation (43,726 California acres × $79,288 harvest cost/acre) | 50,000 acres × $62,000-79,000 harvest cost/acre = $3.1-3.9B | S1, S9, S10 |
| SOM — company claim, 2031 | $310M, presented as 10% of $3.1B | 18,788 robots × $16,500 = $310M, requiring 65,758 acres = 132% of the 50,000-acre base | S1 |
| SOM — tested, 2031 at 15% adoption | — | 7,500 acres ÷ 3.5 = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M | S1, author calculation |
| Near-term obtainable revenue, FY2028 | $12.9M RaaS plan | 782 robots at $16,500 = 2,737 acres = 5.5% of 50,000 acres | S1 |

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up roughly 2% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces 90% of the US crop; Florida is the only other significant producer at 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% annual decline, while the California Strawberry Commission projects 7-8 million trays a week through August 2026. A robot that saves labour therefore sells into a crop growing at 2% a year in volume and shrinking in unit value, so its own growth has to come from penetration, not from the crop [S9, S8].

### The wage bill sets the price ceiling
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. The 2024 UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural costs and $112,694 of total cost, on 9,000 trays at $11; UC Davis puts labour at 50-60% of variable production cost, with pickers paid $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour. That implies hand-pick labour of roughly $25,000-35,000 an acre. At $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $4,714 an acre, 13-19% of the wage bill it targets, and a 10% harvest-cost saving would be worth $7,929 an acre to the grower. The gap between value and price is the most decision-relevant number in the market case: either the robot removes only part of the crew's work, or Orrin is pricing for adoption and has room to raise price later [S10, S12].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic
The $310M figure requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, which is 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; the entire US strawberry acreage at the same density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is also ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not the 2% the market page assumes, and at the $12,700 renewal price it implies 7.1%. Robot density is internally conservative in the other direction: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over a 210-day California season is 315 acre-passes, which at the 40-50 passes a season UC Davis documents serves 6.3-7.9 acres, not 3.5 — one robot per 3.5 acres implies about 90 passes. Either throughput is a peak measurement or the fleet count is inflated; both change revenue per robot [S1, S12].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs roughly seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet that works both calendars is utilised for eleven months and a fleet that works one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop production under high tunnels is being tried on a limited scale in Santa Maria with no published acreage, so the addressable set is open-field acres with slopes under 4%, no standing water and rows wide enough for a track — the same exclusions Orrin applied to its own test rows. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies roughly 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia, where Orrin has no sales or service [S9, S13, S14].

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024, with Florida above 14% of the national total; the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost changed on 2025-10-02, when the Department of Labor replaced the USDA Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate with BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics data; the rule is under litigation and trade summaries disagree on the outcome, one showing the average rate falling to $15.96 an hour from $17.74 and another showing entry-level rates up about 3.7% with declines in 13 states. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure is episodic rather than annual: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes went from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966, but only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%, and ask for the pure hand-pick wage line in the 2024 UC budget, the final 2026-27 adverse effect wage rates for California and Florida, and the acres and passes behind the 3.5-acre robot density [S15, S18, S33].

plan.decision_question: Which policy and regulatory facts change the grower's alternative cost of hand labour, the company's cost of goods, or its right to operate - and do they raise or lower what Meridian should pay for a $12M Series A at $72M pre-money?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case are being decided by other people before the 2027 season - a wage floor a court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff decision due by about 2027-04-26, a university exclusivity test on 2027-12-31 and a California rule on unpiloted machines - and on the evidence available the balance of them is mildly negative for the 2027 season and positive thereafter, which is a reason to price and stage the round rather than a reason to pass.
plan.why_different: The other sections treat policy as background or as a risk category. This one converts each policy into a dollar per acre, per robot or per season so the market, financials and risk sections can carry a number instead of an adjective. It is also the only section that owns the registries where these decisions land.
plan.mechanism: The AEWR is a legal wage floor paid to H-2A and corresponding US workers, so it sets the grower's hand-labour cost per acre and therefore the ceiling on what a robot-season can be sold for. USMCA rules of origin and Section 232 duties set the landed cost of a Mexico-assembled robot, which Orrin bears because it owns the fleet rather than selling equipment. The licence's 100-robot test decides whether a competitor can buy the same two patent families from the same university. A California operating rule would set the technician-to-robot ratio behind the $3,100 field-service line, and 21 CFR 112 makes the robot a piece of food-contact equipment whose cleaning regime the grower must be able to document.
plan.comparison_set: Hand crews at the 2026 AEWR against the pre-October-2025 Farm Labor Survey rate; the robot's $2,714 an acre-season against a derived $21,000-$36,000 an acre of hand harvest; $12,700 renewal against $16,500 list; a US-manufactured build against the Guadalajara build for the Bayh-Dole question; and university-licence practice - a milestone schedule with cure and step-in - against a single binary test with no cure.
plan.counter_evidence: The strongest case against the judgement is that the wage-floor cut is the least durable of the four factors: a district court has already held the rule unlawful, ordered a replacement methodology and required a back-wage notice, so the grower's alternative cost is more likely to rise than fall before the 2027 season, which restores the robot's value case. Second, the company may already satisfy USMCA origin and may never be caught by a robotics tariff, in which case the cost-of-goods exposure is zero. Third, no regulator, retailer or union has yet acted against machine-harvested berries, so the food-safety and social liabilities are potential rather than actual, and an ESG discount would be as unearned as an ESG premium.
plan.visual: Three tables: the ESG issues table (issue, why material, evidence, rating impact), the regulatory record table (regulator, record, date, status) and the policy impact matrix (factor, exposure, probability, impact, mitigant). The matrix carries the section's judgement because it puts a date and a dollar figure on each policy.
plan.prohibited: No 'ESG premium', 'regulatory moat', 'tailwind', 'headwind', 'responsible AI', 'sustainable agriculture' or 'well positioned' as unearned labels; no 'recently', 'soon' or 'going forward' without an absolute date; no claim that a policy is supportive or adverse without a dollar figure attached; no reference to how the section was researched, to review items, or to internal records.

rows.finding: The 2026 H-2A wage floor for California fell from $19.97/hr (the last Farm Labor Survey rate, in force to 2025-10-01) to $16.45/hr at Skill Level I and $18.71/hr at Skill Level II, a 17.6% cut at Level I; Florida fell from $16.23/hr to $12.47/hr and $15.06/hr, a 23.2% cut at Level I. Rates took effect 2026-08-03, and 2026-08-17 in the 17 states covered by Kansas v. DOL, which include Florida.
rows.source_type: primary (DOL notice 91 FR 48946) as reported by independent trade press; the DOL state table itself returned HTTP 503
rows.mechanism: The AEWR is a legal floor paid both to H-2A workers and to US workers in corresponding employment, so it sets the marginal cost of an hour of hand picking and therefore the maximum a grower will pay to avoid that hour. A 17.6% cut in the floor cuts hand-harvest cost per acre by 17.6% with no change in the robot's price or cost.
rows.benchmark: Prior Farm Labor Survey basis: California $19.97, Florida $16.23. National average AEWR used for H-2A labour contractor surety bonds fell to $15.96 from $17.74, about -10%.
rows.weakens: Provisional: on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the interim final rule unlawful on all four challenged components, ordered a new methodology and required DOL to warn employers of possible back wage adjustments.
rows.implication: The grower's alternative cost fell faster than the robot's price in 2026. Do not underwrite 2027 renewals at $12,700 as if the labour shortage had deepened; model the wage floor as a litigated variable.
rows.follow_up: What will DOL's replacement methodology set for California Skill Level I before the 2027 season, and does a back-wage order reach 2026-season growers?
rows.confidence: high on the rates (two independent reports of the same notice); medium on durability, because the rule is in litigation

rows.finding: On the deck's own productivity figure (one picker covers about 0.25 acre a day) and the 2026 California floor, a single pass over one acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II, at 8 paid hours. A 40-pass season is $21,053-$23,948 an acre; a 60-pass season is $31,580-$35,922. The robot at $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres is $2,714 an acre, 7.5%-13% of that; at the 2027 list price of $16,500 it is $4,714 an acre, 13%-22%.
rows.source_type: company-provided (deck) combined with primary wage data; the arithmetic is mine
rows.mechanism: A grower buys the robot out of the hand-labour budget, so the ceiling on price is hand cost avoided less quality losses and overtime premiums avoided. The robot is priced an order of magnitude below the labour it displaces, so price is not the constraint on adoption and the 74% price increase from $9,500 to $16,500 is not the risk it looks like in the financials.
rows.benchmark: No company disclosure of grower payback or of a hand-harvest cost per acre. The UC Davis 2024 Central Coast strawberry cost study is the reference benchmark and its harvest-labour figures were not obtained.
rows.weakens: Depends on a company estimate of picker productivity and on an assumed number of passes; a robot that completes fewer passes earns less of that avoided cost than the comparison implies.
rows.implication: The adoption constraint is quality and uptime, not price. A valuation case that leans on the 2027 list price increase should be discounted until bruising is below the hand-picked benchmark.
rows.follow_up: How many harvest passes does a California strawberry field take in a season, and what does the UC 2024 study put harvest labour at per acre and per tray?
rows.confidence: medium; the wage figures are solid, the pass count is assumed

rows.finding: The $3.52 an hour cut in the California Level I rate removes about $4,224 of hand-harvest cost per acre over a 40-pass season (160 picker-days at $131.60 falling to $105.20). That is 1.6 times the robot's $2,714 an acre-season price, so one court ruling is worth more to the grower per acre than a season of Orrin's service.
rows.source_type: primary wage data plus company-provided pricing; the arithmetic is mine
rows.mechanism: When the policy input is larger than the product's price, the value proposition is partly a function of litigation the company does not control. It cuts both ways: reinstating a higher floor would add value equal to 1.6 robot-seasons an acre.
rows.benchmark: Against a 17.6% cut in the wage floor and a $2,714 an acre robot price.
rows.weakens: Assumes the robot covers the acres and passes it is priced for; if it works a fraction of the season the comparison overstates the stake.
rows.implication: The 2027 pricing environment is set by a docket, not by sales execution, which argues for a milestone-linked tranche rather than a single close.
rows.follow_up: Will growers build their 2027 labour budget on the OEWS rate, the old Farm Labor Survey rate, or wait for the new methodology?
rows.confidence: medium

rows.finding: USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, but a non-qualifying robot pays about 10% on customs value: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, equal to 26% of the $12,700 2027 renewal price and 85% of the 2026 gross profit of $3,900 a robot-season. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper (50%) apply even to USMCA goods. rows.source_type: primary (Federal Register notice) plus independent advisers
rows.mechanism: Orrin owns the fleet, so an import duty is levied on its own capital cost rather than passed to the grower. It lands on the $9.9M robot budget and on the Kestrel facility secured on those robots, which requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times.

rows.source_type: company-provided (deck) plus primary statute and independent practice guidance
rows.finding: The university licence pays 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 a year minimum; the minimum binds in FY2026 (2.5% of $0.71M is $17,750, so the floor is 5.6% of RaaS revenue), and the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet in 2026. If the licensed inventions were federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to agree that products embodying the invention are manufactured substantially in the United States, while grippers and wiring harnesses are assembled in Guadalajara.
rows.mechanism: Exclusivity on the two families is the legal bar to a better-funded entrant buying the same rights from the university. Conversion to non-exclusive removes that bar at a fixed date, and the licensor holds no equity, so it has no upside to trade away for an extension. Section 204 separately conditions the exclusive US right on domestic manufacture.
rows.benchmark: University practice is a schedule of escalating diligence milestones with cure periods and step-in rights; a single binary test at a fixed date with no cure is harsher than the norm.
rows.weakens: The 360-robot 2027 plan clears the threshold comfortably, so conversion requires a slippage of about 72% rather than a miss of a stretch target. Whether the two families were federally funded is not disclosed, so Section 204 may not bind.
rows.implication: Treat exclusivity as conditional until 2028-01-01 and reprice the moat; require a representation that the licence is in good standing and that the robot count is measured on the company's own definition.

rows.confidence: high on the licence terms; medium on the Section 204 conclusion

rows.finding: Strawberries are covered produce under 21 CFR Part 112; the rule names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 21 CFR 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable, inspected and cleaned and sanitised as necessary to protect against contamination. Picking directly into the retail clamshell makes the interior of the machine a food-contact and food-packing surface. No harvester-specific federal certification exists and none is disclosed.
rows.mechanism: The legal duty sits on the grower as the farm, but the equipment design sets the contamination risk, and a clamshell packed in the field reaches the consumer without a further wash step. Retailer audit standards rather than the FDA are the practical gate, and a recall traced to machine contact is a delisting rather than a fine.
rows.benchmark: Hand crews meet the same rule through worker hygiene and container sanitation; machine surfaces can be validated and documented in a way hand labour cannot, which is an unexploited advantage.
rows.weakens: No FDA warning letter, recall or enforcement action against machine-harvested berries was found; the risk is prospective.
rows.implication: A sanitary-design and cleaning validation for the v4 is a cheap condition that removes a retailer objection and a diligence discount.
rows.follow_up: Does the company hold a cleaning and sanitation protocol or validation for the clamshell path, and has a retailer or third-party auditor reviewed it?
rows.confidence: high on the rule; low on current compliance, which is undisclosed

rows.finding: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles, verification and information-for-use requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery. In August 2026 California was considering a trailer bill to allow unpiloted machines to work alongside farmworkers, which labour groups opposed. No US federal approval or certification requirement for autonomous field machinery was identified, and the company discloses no ISO 18497 assessment.

rows.benchmark: Road-vehicle autonomy is regulated through exemptions and permits; agricultural autonomy has no equivalent US regime, so the rule is being written now and the standard is voluntary.
rows.weakens: The bill number, text and status could not be read because the article body returned HTTP 403, so neither the timing nor the content of any rule is established.
rows.implication: Model the field-service line at a 1:4 supervision ratio as a downside case; at 1:1 gross margin on the $9,500 price turns negative.
rows.follow_up: What supervision ratio would the California proposals require, and what ratio does the fleet insurer require?
rows.confidence: medium

rows.finding: The United Farm Workers is the plaintiff that overturned the AEWR methodology in district court on 2026-08-26, and labour groups opposed the California trailer bill on unpiloted machines. On quality, 3.8% of berries were bruised or punctured in the 2025 pilots, Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026.

rows.weakens: No boycott, campaign, shareholder resolution or retailer sourcing policy aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was found, so the social liability is potential rather than actual.
rows.implication: Credit neither an ESG premium nor an ESG discount: the material social metric here is bruising and pick rate, which belongs in the product and risk sections.
rows.follow_up: Has any retailer or buyer requested a labour-impact or food-safety statement, and what are the bruising rates at the two largest customers?
rows.confidence: medium

The Department of Labor's skill-based wage floor, effective 2026-08-03, put California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour, down from the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced-worker level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06 [S80]. The average rate behind H-2A contractor surety bonds fell from $17.74 to $15.96.

On the deck's own productivity figure of a quarter-acre a picker-day, one pass over an acre now costs $526 of hand labour in California at Level I and $599 at Level II; a 40-pass season is $21,053-$23,948 an acre, a 60-pass season $31,580-$35,922. The robot, at $9,500 a season over 3.5 acres, is $2,714 an acre — 7.5% to 13% of that — and $4,714 at the 2027 list price. Two consequences follow. First, price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14 while Grower E left over bruising, which is a quality signal, not a price signal. Second, the 2026 repricing removed about $4,224 an acre of hand cost over a 40-pass season, 1.6 times the robot's annual price per acre. One rule change is worth more to the grower than a season of the service.

### The cut is provisional

On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the Department of Labor's October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds, ordered a replacement methodology and required the department to warn employers of possible back-wage adjustments [S81]. I put a 60-70% probability on a higher California entry-level rate applying to the 2027 season; that would restore most of the $4,224 an acre and lift the price ceiling the company sells against. The practical effect for the round is that Orrin's 2027 renewal price of $12,700 sits against a moving floor, and the company's own plan does not discuss it.

### Who is organised, and against what

The union that won that case is the one most likely to shape the operating rule. In August 2026 California was drafting a trailer bill to let unpiloted machines work alongside farmworkers, and labour groups opposed it on job-loss and safety grounds [S84]. That is the single highest-leverage rule for the unit economics: one technician supervising eight robots supports the $3,100 a robot-season field-service line, and a requirement for a human spotter within sight of each machine would take that line to roughly $24,800 and turn the 41% gross margin negative. California overtime — time and a half after eight hours or forty in a week since 2022-01-01 — works the other way, raising the hand-crew cost the robot displaces [S82].

Florida is different in kind: the state's hand crews are the part of the market most exposed to immigration enforcement, which is why the deck's one exit happened there. No Florida enforcement record against the company was found.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics, a Tampa company co-founded by Wish Farms owner Gary Wishnatzki, announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester reached performance rates on par with human harvesting in a commercial picking operation at Duette, Florida — a direct public claim to open-field strawberry picking that the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. That claim is company-issued and unverified, but it removes the "only player" premise from the investment case. What disciplines Orrin's price is less the rival robot than the hand crew it must beat, the harvest-aid platform that takes part of the saving at a fraction of the capital, and the 2025 exits that show how hard it is to keep a harvest-robotics company funded [S27, S28].

::: evidence
**The direct competitive field is thinner than the technology narrative implies, and it is not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in July 2025; Tortuga's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in 2025. The surviving direct comparison is a Florida grower-backed platform against Orrin's 75 paid robot-seasons. Source: S27, S28, S34.
:::

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Status (2026) | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Tampa, FL) | B8 strawberry harvester | Row-following platform, AI vision, LIDAR, robotics-as-a-service | Commercial field trials, Duette FL, April 2025 | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified); no pick rate or bruising data published | Not disclosed | No fleet count disclosed; Florida trials only | 13 patents; grower-backed (Wish Farms); Florida presence; earlier commercial claim | Florida-only, December-March season; no California service; no independent metrics | S27, S78 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies (Davis, CA) | Robotic strawberry picker | Vision and robotic arm on a mobile platform | Ceased operations July 2025 | Had reached named commercial strawberry growers | Not disclosed | Exited; share now zero | Had California commercial relationships | Ran out of funding; no service network at scale | S28, S79 |
| Tortuga AgTech (US) | Model F/G strawberry and table-grape harvester | Dual-arm picking and direct packing | IP, assets and engineering team acquired by Oishii in 2025 | Commercial fleet before the sale | Not disclosed | Exited open-field market | Commercial deployment experience; direct packing | Buyer was an indoor-farming company; open-field business not continued | S34 |
| Agrobot (Spain) | Solar harvest-aid platform | Self-steering solar platform carrying pickers | Commercial platform | 30-40% labour saving (company claim, unverified) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Low capital cost; no fruit-quality risk; near-zero running cost | Still needs a full crew; no autonomy | S77 |
| Hand crews (status quo) | Piece-rate picking crew | Human pickers, carts and conveyors | Universal | 8-12 flats per hour at $1.75-2.25 a flat; 40-50 passes a season | $1.75-2.25 a flat | Nearly all US strawberry acres | Proven quality, no capex, flexible across varieties and fields | Availability shock in 2025; rising wage floor; housing and supervision cost | S12 |
| Tevel; FFRobotics; Metomotion | Orchard and greenhouse harvesters | Flying robots (Tevel); apple and greenhouse tomato systems | Commercial in orchards (Tevel: Italy, California, Chile) | Named orchard customers; no strawberry product listed | Not disclosed | Not applicable to strawberries | Capital, perception engineering and commercial deployments | No strawberry end-effector or row system; different crop and buyer | S30 |

The direct field consolidated in 2025 rather than expanded. Advanced Farm Technologies, which had reached named commercial strawberry growers in California, ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and engineering team to the vertical-farming company Oishii. No public market shares exist for strawberry robots; the best available proxy is paid robot-seasons, where Orrin reports 75 in 2026 against Harvest CROO's undisclosed trial fleet. Orrin's share of open-field robot-picked acres is therefore best described as the largest disclosed paid base, not a leading market share [S27, S34].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
The cautionary base rate is direct. Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after years of commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo said it "was unable to develop the market traction necessary to support its business", and it put its IP and assets up for sale on 2021-06-29. Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, was sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021 rather than scale independently. The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against a $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30. The RaaS model shifts capital to Orrin's balance sheet and removes the grower's capex objection, but it does not remove the constraint that killed the first cohort; it concentrates it [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour, and conveyor belts placed in front of pickers already raise productivity by cutting walking; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform adds a further partial step: it carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost, a company claim that is unverified but directionally relevant because it captures part of the saving with none of the autonomy risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: the reported transfer of Advanced Farm's IP to CNH Industrial is unverified, but the logic is plain — a picking arm bolted onto a harvest-aid platform that already sells, services and finances equipment is a cheaper route to the same grower than a new autonomous fleet. Orrin must beat a crew at $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour, and it charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but so is the risk that a $10,000-20,000 platform captures the easy half of it [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field row architecture, same robotics-as-a-service model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim already in the market. Its weaknesses are that the Florida season runs only December-March, it publishes no pick rate, bruising or throughput data, and it has no California service network — which is exactly where Orrin's 14 pilots and 4 paying growers sit. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct packing into the grower's clamshells so fruit is handled once, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows, and the COO's California grower relationships. The wedge is real but narrow: it is a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly [S30, S1].

| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest | Harvest CROO (Florida commercial claim; unverified) | Orrin Fieldworks (75 paid robot-seasons, California and Florida) | Agrobot (harvest-aid platform) | Equipment makers integrating picking arms; Tallis as contract manufacturer and noteholder | S27, S1, S77 |

### The price is the tell
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025 and 2026 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase, with renewals averaging $12,700. That is a large increase to test on a customer base that has not yet renewed at list, and the company's own disclosure contains the counter-evidence: Grower E in Plant City ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers. The offsetting evidence is that four growers contracted 110 robots for 2027 (Marisol Ridge 40, Pajaro Bluff 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20), so some buyers accept the quality at the renewal price. If Harvest CROO's parity claim proves true in Florida, Orrin's price converges on displaced labour and the $16,500 list is at risk; if Orrin's 3.8% bruising holds across retail specifications, it can keep pricing up. The single diligence question that matters most is whether the bruising rate is measured against a retailer's specification or only against Orrin's own test rows, followed by the terms of the Tallis relationship: Tallis is Orrin's contract manufacturer, a $2.5M noteholder, a board observer and a $1M investor in this round, and it could build the competing platform [S1, S28].

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Night operation doubles usable hours; direct-to-clamshell handling limits fruit touches; 94% pick rate and 3.8% bruising on 212 selected rows; 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026; California grower relationships through the COO | S1 |
| Weaknesses | Florida pilot lost to bruising; 53% of 2026 robot-seasons with two growers; no independent performance data; $48,000 unit cost and 41% gross margin; single product and single crop | S1 |
| Opportunities | Advanced Farm closed and Tortuga was absorbed, thinning the direct field; 2025 enforcement shock and 398,258 H-2A certifications keep labour at the top of the grower's agenda; 110 robots contracted for 2027 | S28, S34, S15, S1 |
| Threats | Harvest CROO claims human parity in Florida; Agrobot sells a 30-40% labour saving at low capital cost; equipment makers could integrate picking arms; a lower OEWS-based wage floor lengthens payback | S27, S77, S79, S18 |

arguments.markdown:
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case are being decided by other people before the 2027 season: a wage floor a California court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff decision due by about 2027-04-26, a university exclusivity test on 2027-12-31 and a California rule on unpiloted machines. On the evidence available the balance is mildly negative for the 2027 season and positive after it, which argues for staging and pricing the round rather than for passing on it.

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour, against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced-worker level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06, and the national average behind H-2A contractor surety bonds fell to $15.96 from $17.74 [S80, S1].

On the deck's own figure of a quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre now costs $526 of hand labour in California at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,053–$23,948 an acre over a 40-pass season, $31,580–$35,922 over 60 passes. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 7.5%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price. Price therefore is not what stops adoption — Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14 while Grower E left over bruising, which is a quality signal, not a price signal. The 2026 repricing removed about $4,224 an acre of hand cost over a 40-pass season, 1.6 times the robot's annual price per acre: one rule change is worth more to the grower than a season of the service.

### The cut is provisional

On 2026-08-26 a California district court held that the October 2025 methodology was unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing adjustment, the wage survey used, and the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and required the Department of Labor to warn employers of possible back-wage adjustments. I put a 60%–70% probability on a higher California entry-level rate applying to the 2027 season (analyst estimate), which would restore most of that per-acre saving and lift the ceiling Orrin prices against. The company's 2027 plan assumes neither outcome; a $12,700 renewal price sits against a floor that is being relitigated.

### Who is organised, and against what

The union that won that case is the one most likely to shape the operating rule. In August 2026 California was drafting a trailer bill to let unpiloted machines work alongside farmworkers, and labour groups opposed it on job-loss and safety grounds. That is the highest-leverage rule in the file: one technician to eight robots supports the $3,100 a robot-season field-service line, and a human-spotter requirement would take that line to roughly $24,800 and turn the 41% gross margin negative [S84, S82, S1]. California overtime runs the other way, adding to the hand-crew cost the robot displaces: time and a half after eight hours or forty in a week since 2022-01-01. Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement rather than wage rules, and the single pilot the company has lost is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so import duty lands on its own capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at about 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper at 50% apply even to USMCA goods and fall on an undisclosed metal content. The larger tail is new: the Section 232 proclamation of 2026-10-28 on robotics and industrial machinery found that imports threaten national security, imposed no duty, and set a first joint Commerce–USTR update within 180 days, with tariffs, quotas and fees left explicitly open [S88, S89]. At 25% on $33,000 that is $8,250 a robot, 65% of the renewal price, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin at all is not disclosed.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The university licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A single binary test with no cure is harsher than standard practice, where exclusive licences carry escalating diligence milestones, cure periods and step-in rights. The 360-robot 2027 plan clears the threshold, so the cliff needs a 72% slippage rather than a missed stretch goal; I put conversion risk at 20%–25% (analyst estimate). Separately, if the two licensed families were federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to agree that products embodying the invention are manufactured substantially in the United States — and the plant in Guadalajara assembles the grippers. That is a waiver, a US pilot line, or a limit on US exclusivity, and it is unverified.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the retail clamshell on board makes the interior of the machine a packing surface, and fruit packed in the field reaches the consumer with no further wash. No federal certificate for robotic harvesters exists to obtain, and no FDA action, recall or warning letter against machine-harvested berries was found; the practical gate is a retailer audit, and a recall is a delisting rather than a fine. On machine safety, ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery and is voluntary, and the company discloses no assessment against it.

### The social case is a product metric

For growers, labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds; where quality binds it is not, and the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate on selected rows, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime. The pilot exclusions — plastic tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4% — say how narrow the evidence is. No retailer standard, boycott or sourcing policy aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified, so an ESG discount would be as unearned as a premium. Governance carries more weight than the environment column: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, quoted contract manufacturer and investor in this round; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and the ARR figure includes signed letters of intent and a contract that ends on 2027-06-30. A USAspending search returns no federal award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91].

### What could not be checked

Four records sit outside reach and are requested with this report: the Office of Foreign Labor Certification's H-2A disclosure files and official wage table (the department's wage page returned an error on 2026-10-30), the SBIR award record, the USPTO assignment chain and the licence itself, and the text of the California trailer bill. Each is material — the first sets the labour pool, the second the revenue quality, the third the exclusivity and Section 204 question, the fourth the supervision ratio — and until they arrive the section carries medium confidence on the tariff and licence exposures and low confidence on food-safety compliance.

Now Orrin's price per acre: one robot per 3.5 acres (deck p.7) at $9,500 = $2,714/acre; at $16,500 = $4,714/acre. Against $79,288/acre harvest cost, that's 3.4%-5.9% of harvest cost. So the robot is priced at a tiny fraction of the harvest cost it addresses. But wait — what share of harvest does it do? 94% pick rate of ripe fruit; if the robot replaces 94% of hand picking, the value is enormous ($74k/acre) vs $2.7k price. That seems too good — suggesting either the deck's "one robot per 3.5 acres" is understated (i.e., a robot can serve far more acres, so price per acre could be higher) or the robot is not actually replacing the crew (throughput 1.5 acres/24h vs a picker 0.25 acre/day = 6 picker-equivalents; a crew of 6 per 3.5 acres at 3-4 day cycles...). Let's sanity check: hand crew of 6 pickers covers 1.5 acres/day; for 3.5 acres every 3.5 days that's 1 acre/day — so actually 4 pickers would suffice at 0.25 acre/day each = 1 acre/day. So the robot at 1.5 acres/day equals ~6 pickers. Harvest labour cost per acre $79,288; 3.5 acres = $277,508 of harvest labour. Six pickers over a 7-month season at $24.42/hr, 8h/day, 210 days = 6 × 24.42 × 8 × 210 = $246,153. Consistent! So the robot (1.5 acres/day, ~6 picker-equivalents) addresses ~$250k of seasonal harvest labour per 3.5 acres, and is priced at $9,500-$16,500 — i.e. 4-7% of the labour cost. That implies a massive value gap, which in turn says either (a) the robot is wildly underpriced (why raise at $72M?), or (b) the robot cannot actually deliver the 1.5 acres/day at 94% pick rate in commercial conditions, or (c) the grower's willingness to pay is limited by the robot's effective throughput/quality. This is an important analytical point: at the deck's own productivity claim, the price is 4-7% of the harvest labour cost it displaces, so price is not the binding constraint — reliability is. That supports the Lead's hypothesis but from a different angle.

Let me compute exactly:
- 1 robot at 1.5 acres/24h; 7-month CA season. If it runs 20h/day at 86% uptime over 213 days: 213 × 0.86 = 183.2 operating days × 1.5 acres = 274.7 acres per robot-season. That's 78x the 3.5 acres it is assigned. So "one robot per 3.5 acres" is a density assumption tied to the pick cycle (3.5 acres / 1.5 acres per day = 2.3 days per pass), not a capacity limit. If a robot can cover 3.5 acres every 2.3 days at 94% pick rate, then it is doing the work of a 6-person crew. At $24.42/hr loaded and 8-hour days over the season, per-acre harvest cost $79,288 — the robot's price of $2,714-$4,714/acre is 3.4%-5.9%. That's excellent business-model analysis: price is not the constraint; proof is. And it means the price increase to $16,500 is only 5.9% of harvest cost, still trivially cheap — so a rational grower should pay it if the robot works, but the signed contracts at $9,500 reflect either pilot pricing or the grower's option value.

But also: the bruising issue. 3.8% bruised/punctured. Retail tolerance? Lost pilot (Grower E) over bruising. And 2.1% unripe picked. Quality penalties can exceed the robot's price. At $11/tray and 9,000 trays/acre, a 1% bruise loss = $990/acre — vs robot cost $2,714-4,714/acre. So 5% bruising could cost $4,950/acre, more than the robot's price. That's a crucial mechanism: quality losses are 1.8x the robot price per acre. Let me compute: 9,000 trays × $11 = $99,000/acre revenue. 3.8% bruising = $3,762/acre. At 4.714k/acre (list price), the bruise loss is 80% of the robot fee; at $2,714, it's 139%. So the quality risk can consume the entire value of the robot. Excellent. Though not all bruised fruit is unsaleable — "bruised or punctured" may be culled or discounted. But it's a reasonable sensitivity: each 1 percentage point of fruit loss costs ~$990/acre, i.e. 21-36% of the robot's per-acre fee. That's a strong unit-economics insight and ties to the lost Florida pilot.

Now, this is business model gold. Let me also think about pricing per season vs per acre: deck prices per robot per season, not per acre. If a robot covers 3.5 acres in CA but 3.5 in FL too, the grower pays $9,500 per robot-season.

Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics, co-founded by Wish Farms owner Gary Wishnatzki, announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester reached performance rates on par with human harvesting in a commercial picking operation at Duette, Florida — a direct open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. :::
