arguments.markdown:
$18M funds the 360-robot plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the $12M minimum the plan is about a third short, the cash covenant binds during 2027, and most of the $3.2M ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023 to FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement, no segment note and no auditor; its head of finance is part-time. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% in FY2026E to 51.8% in FY2027P before rising to 60.6% in FY2028P - the "60%+ at scale" claim is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base that the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified), calc |

| Cash / drawn debt | - | - | - | 3.7 / 1.6 | - | - | S1 (unverified) |

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone is arithmetically reached only by adding 360 robots at the full $16,500 list, the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots - three of those four are not signed recurring revenue at that level [S1].

| Current season signed | 0.71 | 75 robots x $9,500 | 22.3% of the headline | S1 (unverified), calc |

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The company's nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but it must keep $1.5M unrestricted at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency. That date falls before the April 2027 season starts, when no 2027 rental revenue has been collected, and it moves with the round's closing date rather than with the operating plan. A close delayed by one quarter does not shorten the runway by three months - it lands after the covenant has already been breached, which makes the closing date itself a condition of the investment rather than a scheduling detail.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands about five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is about $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is about $6.1M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

Three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4 ($9.77M), so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, essentially the renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and about $13.9M of capex nowhere in the plan [S1].

### Margins are flattered by where depreciation sits

The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of about $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into about -$0.3M, or -5.7%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while the 52% and 61% equal the company-wide margin, so the series changes definition between years. Returns cannot be computed at all without a balance sheet: ROE, ROIC, receivable days, inventory days and the cash conversion cycle are not disclosed, interest cover is -29.3x on FY2026E EBIT of -$5.4M, and net cash of $2.1M includes $1.5M the company must keep. Cumulative losses of $32.0M compare with $20.5M raised, $320,313 of capital per robot in service, and $68,421 of revenue per employee against Deere's $625,000 [S1, S21, S37].

### The matrix is the decision

The matrix below shows that only the top-right corner - list price with a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling - produces positive contribution; the base case sits in the negative middle, the downside is worse, and even the upside leaves the company loss-making because fleet contribution is small against operating expenses. Price realisation is the bigger swing between the renewal and list cases, but build cost is the gate to structural viability: no price makes the current v3 economics work.

### What an audit would settle

None of this can be audited from the deck: there is no auditor, no balance sheet and no cash flow, 50% of FY2025 revenue comes from a related party that is simultaneously the largest creditor, a board observer, the v4 manufacturer and a new investor, and $310,000 was paid in 2025 and 2026 to the COO's wholly owned haulage and night-shift company - at half the period that is 67% of the 2026 field-service line. A public search on 2026-10-30 found no SBIR, USAspending or press record for the company; the only "Orrin Fieldworks" registration is a Massachusetts grounds-maintenance LLC, a namesake with no established relation. The data room would settle revenue recognition on the engineering contract, whether grower payments are in arrears, the loan's amortisation and covenant test, and whether the v3 fleet is impaired by the v4 launch; until then the revenue and cash figures are company-reported and unverified [S1, S37].

The investment implication is that $18M is the minimum credible size and still leaves a Series B need in the first half of 2028, while the $12M minimum is a different, unfunded plan. The conditions that would change the answer are an audited 2026-09-30 balance sheet and cash flow, executed 2027 contracts at the list price, a covenant waiver or bridge for a delayed close, and a 2028 plan that shows the capex behind its revenue.

arguments.markdown:
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while the harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.8x — enough to return capital, not enough to carry a venture fund. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Each buyer is buying a different asset. Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would be buying the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend its See & Spray and autonomy stack into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would be buying a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would be buying fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but less need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would be buying harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet — they can manufacture — so the fleet is a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security, grower data, supply chain; no public robotics M&A found (not publicly disclosed) | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga in 2024; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93 |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | Growth capital; requires scale, float and profitability; no comparable IPO in the set (not publicly disclosed) | 2030+ | Very low | S95 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag was bought for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven, a public precision-ag company at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI was acquired by AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii for undisclosed terms. No harvesting-robot company in the set has been sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | What the target had | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River | 2017 | $305M | 3.5x the $87M post-money; revenue n/a | See & Spray, $30M+ raised | S98 |
| Deere / Bear Flag | 2021 | $250M | 31.6x the $7.9M seed; revenue n/a | Autonomous tractor retrofit, founded 2017 | S96, S118 |
| CNH / Raven | 2021 | $2.1B EV | n/a; 33.6% premium | Public precision-ag company | S99 |
| AGCO / Trimble Ag (85%) | 2023-24 | $2.35B EV | 13.8x 2023E EBITDA | Precision-ag portfolio, $170M EBITDA | S101 |
| Kubota / AgJunction | 2021 | $73M | n/a | Guidance and auto-steer | S104 |
| CNH / Advanced Farm assets | 2025 | Undisclosed | n/a | Strawberry and apple picking IP and team | S97, S28 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2024 | Undisclosed | n/a | $50M deployed, 150 robots | S93 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | n/a | Tomato harvesting robot | S32 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none reached $100M+, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. The 2025 market recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money, a $100M exit returns 1.1x before dilution, a $250M exit 2.8x and a $40M exit 1.0x because of the 1x preference. With illustrative probabilities of 40% at $40M, 35% at $100M, 20% at $250M and 5% at $500M, the expected MOIC is 1.6x before dilution and 1.4x after a 20% Series B — below the 3x a venture fund needs. The counter-case is that Deere or CNH pays $250-305M for the team and perception model, as they did for Blue River and Bear Flag; if Orrin proves 95% pick rates at 360 robots, a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 base rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

| Outcome | Count | Share | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ag-robotics companies in the comparison set | 8 | 100% | S98, S96, S105, S102, S93, S109, S94, S107 |
| Reached a $100M+ exit | 2 (Blue River, Bear Flag) | 25% | S98, S96 |
| Harvesting-robot companies in the set | 5 (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin) | 100% | S105, S102, S93, S107, S95 |
| Harvesting-robot companies at $100M+ | 0 | 0% | S105, S102, S93, S107, S95 |
| Ag-robotics acquisitions in 2025 | 14 | n/a | S108 |

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue, the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; a round above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is: $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Metric | 2027 plan | 2028 plan | Test for a Series B above $72M pre | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $5.6M | $13.2M | $13.2M at 7x forward, or $18M at 5x | S95 (unverified) |
| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |
| Renewal | 110 contracted 2027 seasons | n/a | 80% or more of 2026 paying growers renew | S95 (unverified) |
| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to US, European and Japanese strategics: Deere and AGCO are US-listed, CNH is Dutch/Italian and Kubota is Japanese, and all have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, the Calder license and the grower data, and the Mexico assembly adds tariff and supply-chain diligence. An IPO is not a realistic exit before 2030: $1.9M of revenue, a $5.2M net loss in FY2025 and no comparable ag-robotics IPO in the set; a listing would need scale and audited growth the company does not have. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes the exit to 2030-2032. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.0x at $90M, 1.1x at $100M, 1.7x at $150M, 2.8x at $250M and 5.6x at $500M; a 20% Series B dilution cuts those to 1.0x, 1.0x, 1.4x, 2.2x and 4.4x. The IRR is 0% at $90M, 10.8% at $150M and 22.7% at $250M over five years. A 20-30% lower entry price, or a 1.5x preference, would make the same exits work; at $72M pre-money the lead is buying an option that needs a $250M+ bid. The implication is to pass at $72M pre-money, or invest only at a 20-30% lower price with a 1.5x preference and a milestone tranche. Diligence should confirm the Advanced Farm and Tortuga prices, the ownership of the grower contracts (Orrin Fieldworks or Orrin Fleet Services), the Calder license's change-of-control terms and the customer concentration — 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons sit with two named growers. [S95, S97, S93]

arguments.markdown:
$18M funds the 360-robot plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the $12M minimum the plan is about a third short, the cash covenant binds during 2027, and most of the $3.2M ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023 to FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement, no segment note and no auditor; its head of finance is part-time. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% in FY2026E to 51.8% in FY2027P before rising to 60.6% in FY2028P - the "60%+ at scale" claim is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

| $M, year to 31 December | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cost of revenue | 0.1 | 0.1 | 0.9 | 1.1 | 2.7 | 5.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S1 (unverified) |
| Net loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S1 (unverified) |
| Total gross margin | 0% | 75.0% | 52.6% | 57.7% | 51.8% | 60.6% | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Reported gross margin line | n/a | n/a | 22% | 41% | 52% | 61% | S1 (unverified) |
| Cash / drawn debt | - | - | - | 3.7 / 1.6 | - | - | S1 (unverified) |

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone is reached only by adding 360 robots at the full $16,500 list, the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots - three of those four are not signed recurring revenue at that level [S1].

| ARR component, 2026-09-30 | $M | What it is | Treatment | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contracted 2027 robot-seasons | 1.4 | 110 robots x $12,700 | Contracted, not yet earned | S1 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 1.2 | Fixed term to 2027-06-30, related party | Remove: expires mid-2027 | S1 (unverified) |
| Letters of intent | 0.6 | 50 robots, non-binding | Remove: not contracted | S1 (unverified) |
| Like-for-like recurring | 1.4 | 43.8% of the $3.2M headline |  | S1 (unverified), calc |

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The company's nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but it must keep $1.5M unrestricted at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts, when no 2027 rental revenue has been collected. That date moves with the round's closing date rather than with the operating plan. A close delayed by one quarter does not shorten the runway by three months - it lands after the covenant has already been breached, which makes the closing date a condition of the investment rather than a scheduling detail.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands about five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is about $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is about $6.1M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

Three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4 ($9.77M), so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, essentially the renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and about $13.9M of capex nowhere in the plan. The only capex-free reading is 360 robots each doing two seasons at $17,900, which requires a Florida business that does not yet exist at scale [S1].

| Reconciliation test | Calculation | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2027 robot budget | 300 x $33,000 | $9.9M | S1 (unverified) |
| 360 in service | 64 v3 + 296 v4 at $33,000 | $9.77M | S1 (unverified), calc |
| 2027 implied price | $4.6M / 360 robots | $12,778 = renewal average | S1 (unverified), calc |
| 2028 implied fleet at $16,500 | $12.9M / $16,500 | 782 robots, 422 more, $13.9M capex | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Undrawn fleet facility | $2.5M - $1.6M | $0.9M = 27 robots | S1 (unverified), calc |

### Margins are flattered by where depreciation sits

The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of about $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into about -$0.3M, or -5.7%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while the 52% and 61% equal the company-wide margin, so the series changes definition between years. Returns cannot be computed at all without a balance sheet: ROE, ROIC, receivable days, inventory days and the cash conversion cycle are not disclosed, interest cover is -29.3x on FY2026E EBIT of -$5.4M, and net cash of $2.1M includes $1.5M the company must keep. Cumulative losses of $32.0M compare with $20.5M raised, $320,313 of capital per robot in service, and $68,421 of revenue per employee against Deere's $625,000 [S1, S21, S37].

| Returns and working capital | Value | Source / status |
|---|---|---|
| ROE, ROIC, asset turnover | Not computable | No balance sheet |
| Interest cover | -29.3x (FY2026E EBIT -$5.4M / $184,000 interest) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Net cash | $2.1M, of which $1.5M must stay unrestricted | S1 (unverified) |
| Receivable, inventory, payable days | Not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |
| Goodwill / stock-based compensation | None disclosed / not disclosed; options 13.0% of fully diluted pre-round | S1 (unverified) |
| Cumulative net loss vs capital raised | $32.0M vs $20.5M | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Capital per robot in service | $320,313 ($20.5M / 64) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Revenue per employee | $68,421 vs Deere $625,000 | S1, S37 |

### The matrix is the decision

The matrix below shows that only the top-right corner - list price with a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling - produces positive contribution; the base case sits in the negative middle, the downside is worse, and even the upside leaves the company loss-making because fleet contribution is small against operating expenses. Price realisation is the bigger swing between the renewal and list cases, but build cost is the gate to structural viability: no price makes the current v3 economics work.

| Contribution after depreciation, $ per robot-season | $31,000 build | $33,000 build | $36,000 build | $48,000 build |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price $9,500 | (3,850) | (4,350) | (5,100) | (8,100) |
| Price $12,700 | (650) | (1,150) | (1,900) | (4,900) |
| Price $16,500 | 3,150 | 2,650 | 1,900 | (1,100) |
| Source | S1 (unverified), calc | S1 (unverified), calc | S1 (unverified), calc | S1 (unverified), calc |

### What an audit would settle

None of this can be audited from the deck: there is no auditor, no balance sheet and no cash flow, 50% of FY2025 revenue comes from a related party that is simultaneously the largest creditor, a board observer, the v4 manufacturer and a new investor, and $310,000 was paid in 2025 and 2026 to the COO's wholly owned haulage and night-shift company - at half the period that is 67% of the 2026 field-service line. A public search on 2026-10-30 found no SBIR, USAspending or press record for the company; the only "Orrin Fieldworks" registration is a Massachusetts grounds-maintenance LLC, a namesake with no established relation. The data room would settle revenue recognition on the engineering contract, whether grower payments are in arrears, the loan's amortisation and covenant test, and whether the v3 fleet is impaired by the v4 launch; until then the revenue and cash figures are company-reported and unverified [S1, S37].

The implication is that $18M is the minimum credible size and still leaves a Series B need in the first half of 2028, while the $12M minimum is a different, unfunded plan. What would change the answer: an audited 2026-09-30 balance sheet and cash flow, executed 2027 contracts at the list price, a covenant waiver or bridge for a delayed close, and a 2028 plan that shows the capex behind its revenue.

plan.comparison_set: Capital-heavy ag robotics peers and their exits: Monarch (133M Series C, layoffs, Caterpillar asset purchase 2026-04), Advanced Farm (25M Series B, ceased operations 2025-07, IP to CNH), Tortuga (IP and team to Oishii 2025-03), Abundant Robotics (shut down 2021), FarmWise (service to dealer-sale pivot), Carbon Robotics (machines sold outright, 70M Series D). Base rate: of six, one is still selling machines; four ended in asset sales or shutdowns; one pivoted from service to dealer sales.
plan.counter_evidence: If the 360-robot season lands, the 2027 list price and the v4 cost-down turn gross margin from 41 to 52 percent, and 100+ robots in service preserves the licence, the plan looks self-funding and a Series B at a higher price is credible. The outsourced build also keeps fixed costs low, which is exactly what the peer failures lacked.
plan.decision_question: Can 64 robots become 360 in one season on an outsourced build and a price 74 percent above signed contracts?
plan.mechanism: RaaS puts the asset on Orrin's balance sheet: each robot-season sold at $16,500 against a $48,000 build over four seasons and $5,600 of current service cost loses about $1,100, so growth consumes cash precisely where the plan assumes it generates gross profit; and a $33,000 v4 build only breaks even on the $12,700 renewal price if the build comes in under $28,400.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong pipeline', no 'well positioned', no market-size restatement, no adopting the company's ARR definition as revenue, no describing LOIs as contracted.
plan.thesis_sentence: The plan does not add up on its own numbers: at the current $48,000 build even the 2027 list price leaves each robot-season about $1,100 short over a four-season life, the v4 must come in below $28,400 to earn its keep on a $12,700 renewal, and a 5.6-times fleet increase by April 2027 depends on a single outsourced build quote and a $14M gap in a round that has not closed.
plan.visual: Milestone table with target date, status and what it proves, then the partner table showing Tallis's five simultaneous roles.
plan.why_different: Section 9 tests whether the resources match the plan and what must be true in twelve months; the business model section prices the unit economics as reported, the technology section tests the picker. Only here is the sequence of capital, season calendar and supplier dependence judged against the peer base rate.

rows.finding: The 2.1-season payback claim uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, omitting $3,850 of current per-robot-season cost; on the reported $5,600 service cost the payback is 2.8 seasons at $31,000 and 4.4 seasons at today's $48,000 build, longer than the four-season life the same page assumes.
rows.follow_up: Which cost lines are inside the $1,750 target and what evidence supports the 69 percent reduction?
rows.implication: Treat payback as roughly double the company figure and require a per-robot-season cost bridge before the next round.
rows.mechanism: Payback is build cost divided by price minus the cost of keeping the robot running; leaving out two thirds of the running cost cuts the payback in half.
rows.weakens: Transport and insurance are partly distance-driven and may fall with denser grower clusters; the deck gives no cluster economics.

rows.benchmark: Carbon Robotics (machines sold, $70M Series D 2024); Advanced Farm ($25M Series B 2021, ceased operations 2025-07, IP to CNH); Tortuga (IP and team to Oishii 2025-03); Monarch ($133M Series C 2024, layoffs, assets to Caterpillar 2026-04); Abundant Robotics (shut 2021); FarmWise (Titan service to Vulcan dealer sales).
rows.confidence: high on the events, medium on the inference from five cases.
rows.finding: Five of the six comparable capital-heavy ag-robot companies ended in an asset sale, a shutdown or a pivot from service to selling machines; the one that scaled, Carbon Robotics, sells equipment and reached nine-figure revenue, while the four that carried the asset or the service model did not survive independently.
rows.follow_up: What did CNH and Caterpillar pay per dollar raised, and what did the RaaS contracts convert to in the asset sale?
rows.implication: A $72M pre-money on a RaaS model prices the option that five of six peers failed to hold; the credible exit is an incumbent buying the fleet data and grower contracts, at a price set by the buyer.
rows.mechanism: RaaS converts working capital into a fleet the company must finance, insure and service through a seven-month season with no revenue in the other five months, while a machine sale converts the grower's balance sheet into the company's cash.
rows.weakens: Survivorship cuts both ways: the failures were orchard and apple harvesters and a tractor, not strawberry pickers, and Orrin's per-season rental matches the crop calendar better than a year-round tractor subscription.

rows.benchmark: FY2025 revenue $1.9M of which $0.95M engineering services and $0.30M grants; FY2026E $2.6M with $1.20M services and $0.35M grants.
rows.confidence: high: the concentration is disclosed and the contract end date is dated.
rows.finding: Tallis Agricultural Machinery is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, the $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer (50 percent of FY2025 revenue), the quoted contract manufacturer for the v4, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round; the services contract ends 2027-06-30, so 46 percent of FY2026 estimated revenue disappears within two quarters of the season the round funds.
rows.follow_up: What is the arm's-length evidence for the v4 bill of materials quote, and who else priced it?
rows.implication: Require a second and third build quote and a related-party committee sign-off before any capital is released against the 300-robot order; the supplier is also the customer and a creditor.
rows.mechanism: When one counterparty sets the build cost, buys the engineering hours and holds debt, the bill of materials is not a market price and the cost-down the plan needs cannot be tested.
rows.weakens: A single supplier with a board seat may genuinely be the fastest route to a 2027 season, and the deck discloses every role.

rows.benchmark: Cash $3.7M at 2026-09-30, monthly net burn $410,000, 9 months of runway; the equipment facility requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, so usable cash is about $2.2M, or five months.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, high on the dates.
rows.finding: The 2027 season needs 360 robots by April 2027, of which 300 are to be built with $9.9M of this round; the round is $14M short of its lead as of 2026-10-30 with a 2026-12-15 target close, leaving about three and a half months from cash to a build that must be finished before the California season opens.
rows.follow_up: What is the build slot lead time with the contract manufacturer, and what deposits are due before the season?
rows.implication: The round is not growth capital, it is the season's working capital: a close after January 2027 makes 360 robots arithmetically impossible, which in turn puts the 100-robot licence test at risk.
rows.mechanism: Hardware ramps are set by supplier slot bookings and deposits months before revenue; a five-times fleet increase inside one season leaves no slack for a late close or a re-quote.
rows.weakens: The $1.5M minimum is a covenant test, not a spend restriction, and the company could raise a bridge.

rows.benchmark: USMCA-qualifying goods enter the US at 0 percent; non-qualifying Mexican goods face 10 percent; a Section 232 investigation into robotics and industrial machinery was opened in 2025-09 with a proclamation on 2026-10-28.
rows.confidence: medium: the tariff regime is moving and the bill of materials content is not disclosed.
rows.finding: The v4 is to be assembled in Guadalajara by a supplier that is also an investor, into a market where the US opened a Section 232 investigation into imported robotics and industrial machinery in 2025-09-26 and issued a related proclamation on 2026-10-28; the deck's $33,000 unit cost carries no tariff line.
rows.follow_up: What share of the v4 bill of materials is US content, and does it qualify under USMCA rules of origin?
rows.implication: Model a 10 percent tariff on the build as a base case: it adds $3,300 a robot, which alone exceeds the $28,400 break-even headroom on renewals.
rows.mechanism: An outsourced build moves cost risk to a border; a duty applies to the landed value and cannot be designed out in one season, and the cost-down roadmap assumed a stable landed cost.
rows.weakens: USMCA qualification at 0 percent is plausible if regional value content is met, and the Section 232 outcome is not yet a duty.

arguments.markdown:
$18M funds the 360-robot plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the $12M minimum the plan is about a third short, the cash covenant binds during 2027, and most of the $3.2M ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023 to FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor; its head of finance is part-time. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cost of revenue | 0.1 | 0.1 | 0.9 | 1.1 | 2.7 | 5.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S1 (unverified) |
| Net loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S1 (unverified) |
| Total gross margin | 0% | 75.0% | 52.6% | 57.7% | 51.8% | 60.6% | S1 (unverified), calc |

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone is reached only by adding 360 robots at the full $16,500 list, the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots - three of those four are not signed recurring revenue at that level [S1].

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contracted 2027 robot-seasons | 1.4 | 110 robots x $12,700 | Contracted, not yet earned | S1 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 1.2 | Fixed term to 2027-06-30, related party | Remove: expires mid-2027 | S1 (unverified) |
| Letters of intent | 0.6 | 50 robots, non-binding | Remove: not contracted | S1 (unverified) |
| Like-for-like recurring | 1.4 | 43.8% of the $3.2M headline |  | S1 (unverified), calc |

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep $1.5M unrestricted at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts, when no 2027 rental revenue has been collected. That date moves with the closing date rather than the operating plan: a close delayed one quarter does not shorten the runway by three months, it lands after the covenant has already been breached, which makes the closing date a condition of the investment rather than a scheduling detail.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is about $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is about $6.1M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

Three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4, so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, essentially the renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and about $13.9M of capex nowhere in the plan. Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at

arguments.markdown:
$18M funds the 360-robot plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the $12M minimum the plan is about a third short, the cash covenant binds during 2027, and most of the $3.2M ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023 to FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time head of finance. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

| $M, year to 31 December | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cost of revenue | 0.1 | 0.1 | 0.9 | 1.1 | 2.7 | 5.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S1 (unverified) |
| Net loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S1 (unverified) |
| Total gross margin | 0% | 75.0% | 52.6% | 57.7% | 51.8% | 60.6% | S1 (unverified), calc |

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level [S1].

| ARR component, 2026-09-30 | $M | What it is | Treatment | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contracted 2027 robot-seasons | 1.4 | 110 robots x $12,700 | Contracted, not yet earned | S1 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 1.2 | Fixed term to 2027-06-30, related party | Remove: expires mid-2027 | S1 (unverified) |
| Letters of intent | 0.6 | 50 robots, non-binding | Remove: not contracted | S1 (unverified) |
| Like-for-like recurring | 1.4 | 43.8% of the $3.2M headline |  | S1 (unverified), calc |

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep $1.5M unrestricted at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts, when no 2027 rental revenue has been collected. It moves with the closing date: a quarter's delay does not shorten the runway by three months, it lands after the covenant is breached, making the closing date a condition of the investment.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is about $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is about $6.1M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

Three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4, so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, essentially the renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and about $13.9M of capex nowhere in the plan. The only capex-free reading is 360 robots each doing two seasons at $17,900, requiring a Florida business that does not exist at scale [S1].

| Reconciliation test | Calculation | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2027 robot budget | 300 x $33,000 | $9.9M | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027 implied price | $4.6M / 360 robots | $12,778 = renewal average | S1 (unverified), calc |
| 2028 implied fleet at $16,500 | $12.9M / $16,500 | 782 robots, 422 more, $13.9M capex | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Undrawn fleet facility | $2.5M - $1.6M | $0.9M = 27 robots | S1 (unverified), calc |

### Margins are flattered by where depreciation sits

The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of about $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into about -$0.3M, or -5.7%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while the 52% and 61% equal the company-wide margin, so the series changes definition between years. Returns cannot be computed without a balance sheet: ROE, ROIC and working-capital days are not disclosed, interest cover is -29.3x on FY2026E EBIT of -$5.4M, and net cash of $2.1M includes $1.5M the company must keep. Cumulative losses of $32.0M compare with $20.5M raised, $320,313 of capital per robot in service, and $68,421 of revenue per employee against Deere's $625,000 [S1, S21, S37].

| ROE, ROIC, asset turnover, working-capital days | Not computable, not disclosed | No balance sheet |
| Interest cover | -29.3x (FY2026E EBIT -$5.4M / $184,000 interest) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Net cash | $2.1M, of which $1.5M must stay unrestricted | S1 (unverified) |
| Goodwill / SBC | None disclosed / not disclosed; options 13.0% of fully diluted pre-round | S1 (unverified) |
| Cumulative net loss vs capital raised | $32.0M vs $20.5M | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Capital per robot in service | $320,313 ($20.5M / 64) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Revenue per employee | $68,421 vs Deere $625,000 | S1, S37 |

### The matrix is the decision

Only the top-right corner - list price with a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling - produces positive contribution; the base case sits in the negative middle, the downside is worse, and even the upside leaves the company loss-making because fleet contribution is small against operating expenses. Price realisation is the bigger swing between the renewal and list cases, but build cost is the gate to structural viability: no price makes the current v3 economics work.

| Contribution after depreciation, $ per robot-season | $31,000 build | $33,000 build | $36,000 build | $48,000 build |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price $9,500 | (3,850) | (4,350) | (5,100) | (8,100) |
| Price $12,700 | (650) | (1,150) | (1,900) | (4,900) |
| Price $16,500 | 3,150 | 2,650 | 1,900 | (1,100) |
| Source | S1 | S1 | S1 | S1 |

### What an audit would settle

None of this can be audited from the deck: no auditor, no balance sheet, no cash flow, 50% of FY2025 revenue from a related party that is also the largest creditor, a board observer, the v4 manufacturer and a new investor, and $310,000 paid in 2025 and 2026 to the COO's wholly owned haulage and night-shift company - at half the period that is 67% of the 2026 field-service line. A public search on 2026-10-30 found no SBIR, USAspending or press record for the company. The data room would settle revenue recognition on the engineering contract, whether grower payments are in arrears, the loan's amortisation and covenant test, and whether the v3 fleet is impaired by the v4 launch; until then the revenue and cash figures are company-reported and unverified [S1, S37].

The implication is that $18M is the minimum credible size and still leaves a Series B need in the first half of 2028, while the $12M minimum is a different, unfunded plan. arguments.markdown:
The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising already spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position consists of a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. To pick 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; conversely, holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which only reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure at the top of the density range, not a picked-acre figure [S1, S27].

Harvest CROO's published configuration cross-checks the arithmetic rather than the claim: 16 picking units and 8 acres a day is what 16 arms at Orrin's own cycle time produce at about the same berry density. The two companies agree on arm speed and disagree eight-fold on machinery per acre, which means coverage is a function of capital per machine, not of a better algorithm.

| Metric | Company claim | Independent benchmark | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Berries per 24 h | not disclosed | 22,114 derived; 205,714 for 16 arms | 2 arms, 5.6 s/berry, 20 h, 86% uptime | S1, S27 |
| Acres per 24 h | 1.5 | 1.0-1.2 | derived above, 21,800 ripe berries/acre-pass | S1, S119 |
| Pick rate | 94% of ripe berries detected | no peer-reviewed open-field rate above 95% found | 212 company-chosen rows, 9 of 14 farms | S1, S27 |
| Bruised or punctured | 3.8% | 5% serious damage, 10% total defects, 2% decay | company measurement, definition not disclosed | S1, S120 |
| Unripe picked | 2.1% | not applicable | company measurement | S1 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not disclosed | company log | S1 |
| Operator interventions | every 3.4 h = 5.9 per robot-day | 47 per technician-day at 8 robots each | derived | S1 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | Harvest CROO implies comparable per-arm speed | company measurement | S1, S27 |

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it is the one that decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the entire defect budget, before field rots, handling and the two to five days in which a bruise actually expresses itself at the cooler. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a 10 percent lot allowance that the grower also spends on everything else. This is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and it is why a 94 percent pick rate can coexist with a grower who does not renew [S1, S120].

::: evidence
**The picker's economics turn on damage, not on pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling.**

Packers work to a lot-level standard, not a per-machine one: 10 percent total defects, 5 percent serious damage, 2 percent decay for U.S. No. 1, and a bruise that appears after seven days is still the grower's loss [S120]. The company's own pilot record shows the consequence — one of six named growers left over fruit bruising after a season [S1].
:::

### What is defensible is the data and the service, not the patents

| Technique | Orrin Picker v3 | Harvest CROO B8 | Tortuga F/G | Advanced Farm | Benchmark |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picking units | 2 arms | 16 units | dual arm | ceased 2025-07 | — |
| Coverage | 1.5 acres/24 h claimed, 1.0-1.2 derived | 8 acres/day, vendor-stated | not disclosed | not disclosed | night work doubles hours |
| Field | open field, day and night | open field | tabletop and greenhouse | open field | 4% slope limit excludes hilly blocks |
| Model | RaaS per robot-season | not disclosed | per-kilogram RaaS | machine sale | Carbon Robotics sells machines |
| Status 2026 | 64 robots, 5 paying growers | commercial in Florida | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025-03 | IP bought by CNH | two of five peers failed |
| Source | S1 | S27, S78 | S93 | S28, S97 | S109 |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet perception data | 6 | 1.9 million labelled berry images and 75 paid robot-seasons; labels compound only with deployed hours | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Gripper mechanics | 3 | three silicone fingers with slip sensing; the literature on soft fruit grippers is public and the claims were rejected | 1 year | S1, S4 |
| Licence and freedom to operate | 4 | exclusive but lapsable, and it is the licensor's patent, not the company's | not applicable | S1, S86 |
| Service density | 5 | one technician per 8 robots within driving distance of two California clusters | 2 years | S1 |
| Safety certification | 3 | ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the autonomy framework; no certification or field audit is disclosed | 1-2 years | S92 |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | | **minimum 2 years** | |

The replication test is unkind. A funded team of 50 with the published patents would need about a year for a gripper, because the mechanism — cut the stem, hold with compliant fingers, sense slip — is standard soft-robotics practice, and about two to three years for the perception stack, because the training data comes from fields the team cannot buy. What it could not buy in that time is 75 robot-seasons of grower trust in two valleys where the top 20 growers hold over half the acreage, which is the actual barrier and is a sales barrier, not a technical one.

| Patent or application | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper with slip sensing | US | 2022-09-02 | published 2024-03; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | the one mechanical claim set; unprotected while rejected | S1 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night-time stereo detection of hidden fruit | US | 2024-05-06 | published 2025-11, awaiting examination | overlaps the licensed perception family | S1 |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following track platform | WIPO | 2025-04-29 | national phase due 2026-10-30, not decided | Europe, Mexico, Australia; EPO and Australia allow 31 months | S1 |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 compliant fingers | US | 2026-07-08 | unpublished | second attempt at the same mechanism | S1 |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling across growers | US | 2026-04-17 | provisional, must convert by 2027-04-17 | the only filing aimed at the service model | S1 |
| CU-2017-031 | Stereo ripeness model | US | granted 2020 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core perception; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |
| CU-2019-114 | Berry-stem localisation | US | granted 2022 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core manipulation; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |

Nothing in that table is a wall. The gripper is a rejected application; the v4 filing is unpublished and untested; the PCT decision falls due today; and the two families that actually read on the product belong to a university whose licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A public-index search on 2026-10-30 returned no record of US 17/902,118, so prosecution status rests entirely on the company's account [S1, S86].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker v3 | commercial | 2026-03 | $0.71M FY2026E RaaS | 41% gross | 360 in service, April 2027 | S1 |
| Picker v4 | design | 2027 season | none | target 52% | $33,000 build, 300 units | S1 |
| Paid pilots | service | 2024 | $0.34M FY2026E | not disclosed | convert 2 letters of intent, 50 robots | S1 |
| Engineering services | contract | 2025-03 | $1.20M FY2026E | not disclosed | ends 2027-06-30 | S1 |
| SBIR grant | grant | 2024-09 | $0.35M FY2026E | not applicable | not visible in federal award data | S1, S91 |

Two gaps bound the confidence. The company does not publish the detection recall that sits under the 94 percent, so the true field pick rate is 94 percent times an unknown recall; and USAspending returns no federal award to the company, which contradicts the SBIR revenue line and should be settled before the grant is treated as recurring-adjacent income [S91]. The diligence questions that would move this section are exact: what ripe-fruit density and pick interval the 212 rows saw, what the damage rate is after seven days at one degree Celsius, how many of the 3.4-hourly interventions need a person in the field, and whether the Calder licence counts robots deployed or robots paid for.

arguments.markdown:
The full round funds the 360-robot plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the minimum close the plan is not funded, the cash covenant binds during 2027, and most of the reported ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023 to FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time head of finance. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

| $M, year to 31 December | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cost of revenue | 0.1 | 0.1 | 0.9 | 1.1 | 2.7 | 5.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S1 (unverified) |
| Net loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S1 (unverified) |
| Total gross margin | 0% | 75.0% | 52.6% | 57.7% | 51.8% | 60.6% | S1 (unverified), calc |

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The company-reported, unaudited $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level [S1].

| ARR component, 2026-09-30 | $M | What it is | Treatment | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contracted 2027 robot-seasons | 1.4 | 110 robots x $12,700 | Contracted, not yet earned | S1 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 1.2 | Fixed term to 2027-06-30, related party | Remove: expires mid-2027 | S1 (unverified) |
| Letters of intent | 0.6 | 50 robots, non-binding | Remove: not contracted | S1 (unverified) |
| Like-for-like recurring | 1.4 | 43.8% of the $3.2M headline |  | S1 (unverified), calc |

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep a minimum unrestricted balance at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts. It moves with the closing date: a quarter's delay does not shorten the runway by three months, it lands after the covenant is breached, making the closing date a condition of the investment.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 (company-reported, unaudited) less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is $6.085M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

On the company-reported, unaudited plan, three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4, so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, $78 above the $12,700 renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and $13.93M of capex nowhere in the plan. The only capex-free reading is 360 robots each doing two seasons at $17,900, requiring a Florida business that does not exist at scale [S1].

| Reconciliation test | Calculation | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2027 robot budget | 300 x $33,000 | $9.9M | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027 implied price | $4.6M / 360 robots | $12,778 = renewal average + $78 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| 2028 implied fleet at $16,500 | $12.9M / $16,500 | 782 robots, 422 more, $13.93M capex | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Undrawn fleet facility | $2.5M - $1.6M | $0.9M = 27 robots | S1 (unverified), calc |

### Margins are flattered by where depreciation sits

The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into -$0.31M, or -5.5%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while the 52% and 61% equal the company-wide margin, so the series changes definition between years. Returns cannot be computed without a balance sheet: ROE, ROIC and working-capital days are not disclosed, interest cover is -29.3x on FY2026E EBIT of -$5.4M, and net cash of $2.1M includes $1.5M the company must keep. Cumulative losses of $32.0M compare with $20.5M raised, $320,313 of capital per robot in service, and $68,421 of revenue per employee against Deere's $625,000 [S1, S21, S37].

| ROE, ROIC, asset turnover, working-capital days | Not computable, not disclosed | No balance sheet |
| Interest cover | -29.3x (FY2026E EBIT -$5.4M / $184,000 interest) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Net cash | $2.1M, of which $1.5M must stay unrestricted | S1 (unverified) |
| Goodwill / SBC | None disclosed / not disclosed; options 13.0% of fully diluted pre-round | S1 (unverified) |
| Cumulative net loss vs capital raised | $32.0M vs $20.5M | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Capital per robot in service | $320,313 ($20.5M / 64) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Revenue per employee | $68,421 vs Deere $625,000 | S1, S37 |
| Fee per acre vs harvest cost | $2,714-$4,714 vs $79,288 (3.4%-5.9%) | S1, S10 |

### The matrix is the decision

Only the top-right corner - list price with a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling - produces positive contribution; the base case sits in the negative middle, the downside is worse, and even the upside leaves the company loss-making. Price realisation is the bigger swing between the renewal and list cases, but build cost is the gate to structural viability: no price makes the current v3 economics work.

| Contribution after depreciation, $ per robot-season | $31,000 build | $33,000 build | $36,000 build | $48,000 build | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price $9,500 | (3,850) | (4,350) | (5,100) | (8,100) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Price $12,700 | (650) | (1,150) | (1,900) | (4,900) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Price $16,500 | 3,150 | 2,650 | 1,900 | (1,100) | S1 (unverified), calc |

### What an audit would settle

None of this can be audited from the deck: no auditor, no balance sheet, no cash flow, 50% of FY2025 revenue from a related party that is also the largest creditor, a board observer, the v4 manufacturer and a new investor, and $310,000 paid in 2025 and 2026 to the COO's wholly owned haulage and night-shift company - at half the period that is 67% of the 2026 field-service line. A public search on 2026-10-30 found no SBIR, USAspending or press record for the company. The data room would settle revenue recognition on the engineering contract, whether grower payments are in arrears, the loan's amortisation and covenant test, and whether the v3 fleet is impaired by the v4 launch; until then the revenue and cash figures are company-reported and unverified [S1, S37].

arguments.markdown:
The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position is a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure at the top of the density range, not a picked-acre figure [S1, S27].

Harvest CROO's published configuration cross-checks the arithmetic rather than the claim: 16 picking units and 8 acres a day is what 16 arms at Orrin's own cycle time produce at about the same berry density. The two companies agree on arm speed and differ eight-fold on machinery per acre, so coverage is a function of capital per machine, not of a better algorithm.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Berries per 24 h | not disclosed | 22,114 derived; 205,714 for 16 arms | 2 arms, 5.6 s/berry, 20 h, 86% uptime | S1, S27 |
| Acres per 24 h | 1.5 | 1.0-1.2 | derived above, 21,800 ripe berries/acre-pass | S1, S119 |
| Pick rate | 94% of ripe berries detected | no peer-reviewed open-field rate above 95% found | 212 company-chosen rows, 9 of 14 farms | S1, S27 |
| Bruised or punctured | 3.8% | 5% serious damage, 10% total defects, 2% decay | company measurement, definition not disclosed | S1, S120 |
| Unripe picked | 2.1% | not applicable | company measurement | S1 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not disclosed | company log | S1 |
| Operator interventions | every 3.4 h = 5.9 per robot-day | 47 per technician-day at 8 robots each | derived | S1 |

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the two to five days in which a bruise expresses itself at the cooler. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

::: evidence
**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling.**

Packers work to a lot-level standard, not a per-machine one: 10 percent total defects, 5 percent serious damage, 2 percent decay for U.S. No. 1, and a bruise that appears after seven days is still the grower's loss [S120].
:::

### What is defensible is the data and the service, not the patents

| Picking units | 2 arms | 16 units | dual arm | ceased 2025-07 | — |

| Field | open field, day and night | open field | tabletop and greenhouse | open field | 4% slope limit excludes hilly blocks |
| Model | RaaS per robot-season | not disclosed | per-kilogram RaaS | machine sale | Carbon Robotics sells machines |

| Fleet perception data | 6 | 1.9 million labelled berry images, 75 paid robot-seasons; labels compound only with deployed hours | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Gripper mechanics | 3 | silicone fingers with slip sensing; soft-fruit gripper work is public and the claims were rejected | 1 year | S1, S4 |
| Licence and freedom to operate | 4 | exclusive but lapsable, and it is the licensor's patent, not the company's | not applicable | S1, S86 |
| Service density | 5 | one technician per 8 robots within reach of two California clusters | 2 years | S1 |
| Safety certification | 3 | ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the framework; no certification or field audit disclosed | 1-2 years | S92 |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | | **minimum 2 years** | |

The replication test is unkind. A funded team of 50 with the published patents needs about a year for a gripper, because cutting the stem, holding with compliant fingers and sensing slip is standard practice, and two to three years for the perception stack, because the training fields cannot be bought. What it cannot buy in that time is 75 robot-seasons of grower trust in two valleys where the top 20 growers hold over half the acreage — the real barrier, and a sales barrier rather than a technical one.

| CU-2019-114 | Berry-stem localisation | US | granted 2022 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core manipulation; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |

Nothing there is a wall. The gripper is a rejected application, the v4 filing is unpublished and untested, the PCT falls due today, and the two families that read on the product belong to a university whose licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A public-index search on 2026-10-30 returned no record of US 17/902,118, so prosecution status rests on the company's account alone [S1, S86].

Two gaps bound the confidence. Detection recall sits under the 94 percent and is not published, so the true field pick rate is 94 percent times an unknown; and USAspending returns no federal award to the company, contradicting the SBIR revenue line, which should be settled before grant income is treated as recurring-adjacent [S91]. The questions that would move this section are exact: the ripe-fruit density and pick interval the 212 rows saw, the damage rate after seven days at one degree Celsius, how many of the 3.4-hourly interventions need a person in the field, and whether the Calder licence counts robots deployed or robots paid for.
