arguments.markdown:
The full round funds the 360-robot plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the minimum close the plan is not funded, the cash covenant binds during 2027, and most of the reported ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023 to FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time head of finance. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

| $M, year to 31 December | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cost of revenue | 0.1 | 0.1 | 0.9 | 1.1 | 2.7 | 5.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S1 (unverified) |
| Net loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S1 (unverified) |
| Total gross margin | 0% | 75.0% | 52.6% | 57.7% | 51.8% | 60.6% | S1 (unverified), calc |

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The company-reported, unaudited $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level [S1].

| ARR component, 2026-09-30 | $M | What it is | Treatment | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contracted 2027 robot-seasons | 1.4 | 110 robots x $12,700 | Contracted, not yet earned | S1 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 1.2 | Fixed term to 2027-06-30, related party | Remove: expires mid-2027 | S1 (unverified) |
| Letters of intent | 0.6 | 50 robots, non-binding | Remove: not contracted | S1 (unverified) |
| Like-for-like recurring | 1.4 | 43.8% of the $3.2M headline |  | S1 (unverified), calc |

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep a minimum unrestricted balance at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts. It moves with the closing date: a quarter's delay does not shorten the runway by three months, it lands after the covenant is breached, making the closing date a condition of the investment.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 (company-reported, unaudited) less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is $6.085M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

On the company-reported, unaudited plan, three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4, so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, $78 above the $12,700 renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and $13.93M of capex nowhere in the plan. The only capex-free reading is 360 robots each doing two seasons at $17,900, requiring a Florida business that does not exist at scale [S1].

| Reconciliation test | Calculation | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2027 robot budget | 300 x $33,000 | $9.9M | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027 implied price | $4.6M / 360 robots | $12,778 = renewal average + $78 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| 2028 implied fleet at $16,500 | $12.9M / $16,500 | 782 robots, 422 more, $13.93M capex | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Undrawn fleet facility | $2.5M - $1.6M | $0.9M = 27 robots | S1 (unverified), calc |

### Margins are flattered by where depreciation sits

The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into -$0.31M, or -5.5%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while the 52% and 61% equal the company-wide margin, so the series changes definition between years. Returns cannot be computed without a balance sheet: ROE, ROIC and working-capital days are not disclosed, interest cover is -29.3x on FY2026E EBIT of -$5.4M, and net cash of $2.1M includes $1.5M the company must keep. Cumulative losses of $32.0M compare with $20.5M raised, $320,313 of capital per robot in service, and $68,421 of revenue per employee against Deere's $625,000 [S1, S21, S37].

|---|---|---|
| ROE, ROIC, asset turnover, working-capital days | Not computable, not disclosed | No balance sheet |
| Interest cover | -29.3x (FY2026E EBIT -$5.4M / $184,000 interest) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Net cash | $2.1M, of which $1.5M must stay unrestricted | S1 (unverified) |
| Goodwill / SBC | None disclosed / not disclosed; options 13.0% of fully diluted pre-round | S1 (unverified) |
| Cumulative net loss vs capital raised | $32.0M vs $20.5M | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Capital per robot in service | $320,313 ($20.5M / 64) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Revenue per employee | $68,421 vs Deere $625,000 | S1, S37 |
| Fee per acre vs harvest cost | $2,714-$4,714 vs $79,288 (3.4%-5.9%) | S1, S10 |

### The matrix is the decision

Only the top-right corner - list price with a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling - produces positive contribution; the base case sits in the negative middle, the downside is worse, and even the upside leaves the company loss-making. Price realisation is the bigger swing between the renewal and list cases, but build cost is the gate to structural viability: no price makes the current v3 economics work.

| Contribution after depreciation, $ per robot-season | $31,000 build | $33,000 build | $36,000 build | $48,000 build | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price $9,500 | (3,850) | (4,350) | (5,100) | (8,100) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Price $12,700 | (650) | (1,150) | (1,900) | (4,900) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Price $16,500 | 3,150 | 2,650 | 1,900 | (1,100) | S1 (unverified), calc |

### What an audit would settle

None of this can be audited from the deck: no auditor, no balance sheet, no cash flow, 50% of FY2025 revenue from a related party that is also the largest creditor, a board observer, the v4 manufacturer and a new investor, and $310,000 paid in 2025 and 2026 to the COO's wholly owned haulage and night-shift company - at half the period that is 67% of the 2026 field-service line. A public search on 2026-10-30 found no SBIR, USAspending or press record for the company. The data room would settle revenue recognition on the engineering contract, whether grower payments are in arrears, the loan's amortisation and covenant test, and whether the v3 fleet is impaired by the v4 launch; until then the revenue and cash figures are company-reported and unverified [S1, S37].

The implication is that $18M is the minimum credible size and still leaves a Series B need in the first half of 2028, while the minimum close is unfunded. What would change it: audited accounts, signed 2027 contracts at list, and a funded 2028 capex plan.

arguments.markdown:
The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position is a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure at the top of the density range, not a picked-acre figure [S1, S27].

Harvest CROO's configuration cross-checks the arithmetic rather than the claim: 16 picking units and 8 acres a day is what 16 arms at Orrin's own cycle time produce at about the same berry density. Coverage is a function of capital per machine, not of a better algorithm.

| Metric | Company claim | Independent benchmark | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Berries per 24 h | not disclosed | 22,114 derived; 205,714 for 16 arms | 2 arms, 5.6 s/berry, 20 h, 86% uptime | S1, S27 |
| Acres per 24 h | 1.5 | 1.0-1.2 | derived above, 21,800 ripe berries/acre-pass | S1, S119 |
| Pick rate | 94% of ripe berries detected | no peer-reviewed open-field rate above 95% found | 212 company-chosen rows, 9 of 14 farms | S1, S27 |
| Bruised or punctured | 3.8% | 5% serious damage, 10% total defects, 2% decay | company measurement, definition not disclosed | S1, S120 |
| Unripe picked | 2.1% | not applicable | company measurement | S1 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not disclosed | company log | S1 |
| Operator interventions | every 3.4 h = 5.9 per robot-day | 47 per technician-day at 8 robots each | derived | S1 |

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the two to five days in which a bruise expresses itself at the cooler. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

::: evidence
**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling.**

Packers work to a lot-level standard, not a per-machine one: 10 percent total defects, 5 percent serious damage, 2 percent decay for U.S. No. 1, and a bruise that appears after seven days is still the grower's loss [S120].
:::

### What is defensible is the data and the service, not the patents

| Technique | Orrin Picker v3 | Harvest CROO B8 | Tortuga F/G | Advanced Farm | Benchmark |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picking units | 2 arms | 16 units | dual arm | ceased 2025-07 | — |
| Coverage | 1.5 acres/24 h claimed, 1.0-1.2 derived | 8 acres/day, vendor-stated | not disclosed | not disclosed | night work doubles hours |
| Field | open field, day and night | open field | tabletop and greenhouse | open field | 4% slope limit excludes hilly blocks |
| Model | RaaS per robot-season | not disclosed | per-kilogram RaaS | machine sale | Carbon Robotics sells machines |
| Status 2026 | 64 robots, 5 paying growers | commercial in Florida | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025-03 | IP bought by CNH | two of five peers failed |
| Source | S1 | S27, S78 | S93 | S28, S97 | S109 |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet perception data | 6 | 1.9 million labelled berry images, 75 paid robot-seasons; labels compound only with deployed hours | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Gripper mechanics | 3 | silicone fingers with slip sensing; soft-fruit gripper work is public and the claims were rejected | 1 year | S1, S4 |
| Licence and freedom to operate | 4 | exclusive but lapsable, and it is the licensor's patent, not the company's | not applicable | S1, S86 |
| Service density | 5 | one technician per 8 robots within reach of two California clusters | 2 years | S1 |
| Safety certification | 3 | ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the framework; no certification or field audit disclosed | 1-2 years | S92 |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | | **minimum 2 years** | |

The replication test is unkind. A funded team of 50 with the published patents needs about a year for a gripper, because cutting the stem, holding with compliant fingers and sensing slip is standard practice, and two to three years for the perception stack, because its training fields cannot be bought. What it cannot buy in that time is 75 robot-seasons of grower trust in two valleys, which is the real barrier and a sales one.

| Patent or application | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper with slip sensing | US | 2022-09-02 | published 2024-03; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | the one mechanical claim set | S1 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night-time stereo detection of hidden fruit | US | 2024-05-06 | published 2025-11, awaiting examination | overlaps the licensed family | S1 |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following track platform | WIPO | 2025-04-29 | national phase due 2026-10-30, undecided | Europe, Mexico, Australia; EPO and Australia allow 31 months | S1 |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 compliant fingers | US | 2026-07-08 | unpublished | second attempt at the same mechanism | S1 |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling across growers | US | 2026-04-17 | provisional, converts by 2027-04-17 | the only filing aimed at the service model | S1 |
| CU-2017-031 | Stereo ripeness model | US | granted 2020 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core perception; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |
| CU-2019-114 | Berry-stem localisation | US | granted 2022 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core manipulation; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |

Nothing there is a wall. The gripper is a rejected application, the v4 filing is unpublished and untested, the PCT falls due today, and the two families that read on the product belong to a university whose licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A public-index search on 2026-10-30 returned no record of US 17/902,118, so prosecution status rests on the company's account alone [S1, S86].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker v3 | commercial | 2026-03 | $0.71M FY2026E RaaS | 41% gross | 360 in service, April 2027 | S1 |
| Picker v4 | design | 2027 season | none | target 52% | $33,000 build, 300 units | S1 |
| Engineering services | contract | 2025-03 | $1.20M FY2026E | not disclosed | ends 2027-06-30 | S1 |
| SBIR grant | grant | 2024-09 | $0.35M FY2026E | not applicable | not visible in federal award data | S1, S91 |

Two gaps bound the confidence: detection recall sits under the 94 percent and is unpublished, so the true field pick rate is 94 percent times an unknown; and USAspending returns no federal award to the company, contradicting the SBIR line, which should be settled before grant income counts as recurring-adjacent [S91]. The questions that would move this section are exact: the ripe-fruit density and pick interval the 212 rows saw, the damage rate after seven days at one degree Celsius, how many 3.4-hourly interventions need a person in the field, and whether the Calder licence counts robots deployed or robots paid for.

arguments.markdown:
The full round funds the fleet plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the minimum close the plan is not funded, the cash covenant binds before the season starts, and most of the reported ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023 to FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time head of finance. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cost of revenue | 0.1 | 0.1 | 0.9 | 1.1 | 2.7 | 5.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S1 (unverified) |
| Net loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S1 (unverified) |
| Total gross margin | 0% | 75.0% | 52.6% | 57.7% | 51.8% | 60.6% | S1 (unverified), calc |

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The company-reported, unaudited $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level [S1].

| ARR component, 2026-09-30 | $M | What it is | Treatment | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contracted 2027 robot-seasons | 1.4 | 110 robots x $12,700 | Contracted, not yet earned | S1 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 1.2 | Fixed term to 2027-06-30, related party | Remove: expires mid-2027 | S1 (unverified) |
| Letters of intent | 0.6 | 50 robots, non-binding | Remove: not contracted | S1 (unverified) |
| Like-for-like recurring | 1.4 | 43.8% of the $3.2M headline |  | S1 (unverified), calc |

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep a minimum unrestricted balance at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts. It moves with the closing date: a quarter's delay does not shorten the runway by three months, it lands after the covenant is breached, making the closing date a condition of the investment.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 (company-reported, unaudited) less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is $6.085M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

On the company-reported, unaudited plan, three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4, so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, $78 above the $12,700 renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and $13.93M of capex nowhere in the plan. The only capex-free reading is 360 robots each doing two seasons at $17,900, requiring a Florida business that does not exist at scale [S1].

| Undrawn fleet facility | $2.5M - $1.6M | $0.9M = 27 robots | S1 (unverified), calc |

### Margins are flattered by where depreciation sits

The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into -$0.31M, or -5.5%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while the 52% and 61% equal the company-wide margin, so the series changes definition between years. Cumulative losses of $32.0M compare with $20.5M raised, $320,313 of capital per robot in service, and $68,421 of revenue per employee against Deere's $625,000 [S1, S21, S37].

### The matrix is the decision

Only the top-right corner - list price with a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling - produces positive contribution; the base case sits in the negative middle, the downside is worse, and even the upside leaves the company loss-making. Price realisation is the bigger swing between the renewal and list cases, but build cost is the gate to structural viability: no price makes the current v3 economics work.

| Price $12,700 | (650) | (1,150) | (1,900) | (4,900) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Price $16,500 | 3,150 | 2,650 | 1,900 | (1,100) | S1 (unverified), calc |

### What an audit would settle

None of this can be audited from the deck: no auditor, no balance sheet, no cash flow, 50% of FY2025 revenue from a related party that is also the largest creditor, a board observer, the v4 manufacturer and a new investor, and $310,000 paid in 2025 and 2026 to the COO's wholly owned haulage and night-shift company - at half the period that is 67% of the 2026 field-service line. A public search on 2026-10-30 found no SBIR, USAspending or press record for the company. The data room would settle revenue recognition on the engineering contract, whether grower payments are in arrears, the loan's amortisation and covenant test, and whether the v3 fleet is impaired by the v4 launch; until then the revenue and cash figures are company-reported and unverified [S1, S37].

The implication is that the full round is the minimum credible size and still leaves a Series B need before the plan's final year can be delivered, while the minimum close is unfunded. What would change it: audited accounts, signed contracts at the list price, and a funded capex plan for the later fleet.

arguments.markdown:
The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position is a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure at the top of the density range, not a picked-acre figure. Harvest CROO's advertisement cross-checks the arithmetic rather than the claim: its sixteen units at Orrin's cycle time produce its advertised eight acres, so coverage follows capital per machine, not a better algorithm [S1, S27].

| Metric | Company claim | Benchmark | Method and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Berries per 24 h | not disclosed | 22,114 derived; 205,714 at 16 arms | arithmetic from company inputs | S1, S27 |
| Acres per 24 h | 1.5 | 1.0-1.2 | derived; company claim unverified | S1, S119 |
| Pick rate | 94% of ripe berries detected | no peer-reviewed open-field rate above 95% found | 212 company-chosen rows, unverified | S1, S27 |
| Bruised or punctured | 3.8% | 5% serious damage, 10% total defects, 2% decay | company measurement, definition undisclosed, unverified | S1, S120 |
| Unripe picked | 2.1% | not applicable | company measurement, unverified | S1 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not disclosed | company log, unverified | S1 |
| Operator interventions | every 3.4 h = 5.9 per robot-day | 47 per technician-day at 8 robots each | derived from company figures, unverified | S1 |

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the two to five days in which a bruise expresses itself at the cooler. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

::: evidence
**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling. [S1, S120]**

Packers work to a lot-level standard, not a per-machine one: 10 percent total defects, 5 percent serious damage, 2 percent decay for U.S. No. 1, and a bruise that appears after seven days is still the grower's loss.
:::

### What is defensible is the data and the service, not the patents

| Dimension | Orrin Picker v3 | Harvest CROO B8 | Tortuga F/G | Advanced Farm | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picking units | 2 arms | 16 units | dual arm | ceased 2025-07 | — | S1, S27, S28 |
| Coverage | 1.5 acres/24 h claimed, 1.0-1.2 derived | 8 acres/day, vendor-stated | not disclosed | not disclosed | night work doubles hours | S1, S27, S78 |
| Model | RaaS per robot-season | not disclosed | per-kilogram RaaS | machine sale | Carbon Robotics sells machines | S1, S93, S109 |
| Status 2026 | 64 robots, 5 paying growers | commercial in Florida | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025-03 | IP bought by CNH | two of five peers failed | S1, S27, S97 |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet perception data | 6 | 1.9 million labelled images and 75 paid robot-seasons, company-stated and unaudited; labels compound only with deployed hours | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Gripper mechanics | 3 | silicone fingers with slip sensing; soft-fruit gripper work is public and the claims were rejected | 1 year | S1, S4 |
| Licence and freedom to operate | 4 | exclusive but lapsable, and it is the licensor's patent, not the company's | not applicable | S1, S86 |
| Service density | 5 | one technician per 8 robots within reach of two California clusters | 2 years | S1 |
| Safety certification | 3 | ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the framework; no certification or field audit disclosed | 1-2 years | S92 |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | | **minimum 2 years** | |

The replication test is unkind. A funded team of 50 with the published patents needs about a year for a gripper, because cutting the stem, holding with compliant fingers and sensing slip is standard practice, and two to three years for the perception stack, because its training fields cannot be bought. What it cannot buy in that time is 75 robot-seasons of grower trust in two valleys, which is the real barrier and a sales one.

| Patent / Application No. | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper with slip sensing | US | 2022-09-02 | published 2024-03; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | the one mechanical claim set | S1 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night-time stereo detection of hidden fruit | US | 2024-05-06 | published 2025-11, awaiting examination | overlaps the licensed family | S1 |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following track platform | WIPO | 2025-04-29 | national phase due 2026-10-30, undecided | Europe, Mexico, Australia; EPO and Australia allow 31 months | S1 |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 compliant fingers | US | 2026-07-08 | unpublished | second attempt at the same mechanism | S1 |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling across growers | US | 2026-04-17 | provisional, converts by 2027-04-17 | the only filing aimed at the service model | S1 |
| CU-2017-031 | Stereo ripeness model | US | granted 2020 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core perception; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |
| CU-2019-114 | Berry-stem localisation | US | granted 2022 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core manipulation; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |

Nothing there is a wall. The gripper is a rejected application on US 17/902,118, the v4 filing is unpublished and untested, the PCT falls due today, and the two families that read on the product belong to a university whose licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A public-index search on 2026-10-30 returned no record of the application, so prosecution status rests on the company's account alone [S1, S86].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker v3 | commercial | 2026-03 | $0.71M FY2026E RaaS | 41% gross | 360 in service, April 2027 | S1 |
| Picker v4 | design | 2027 season | none | target 52% | $33,000 build, 300 units | S1 |
| Engineering services | contract | 2025-03 | $1.20M FY2026E | not disclosed | ends 2027-06-30 | S1 |
| SBIR grant | grant | 2024-09 | $0.35M FY2026E | not applicable | not visible in federal award data | S1, S91 |

Two gaps bound the confidence: the detection recall behind the pick rate is unpublished, so the true field rate is the headline times an unknown; and the federal award data returns no grant to the company, contradicting the SBIR line, which should be settled before grant income counts as recurring-adjacent [S91]. The questions that would move this section are exact: the ripe-fruit density and pick interval the 212 rows saw, the damage rate after seven days at one degree Celsius, how many 3.4-hourly interventions need a person in the field, and whether the Calder licence counts robots deployed or robots paid for.

rows.weakens: A 12% pool is defensible if the 2027 plan genuinely needs 40+ hires; the deck names no hiring plan to justify it.
rows.confidence: High on the arithmetic; medium on whether 12% is the negotiated number or a placeholder.
rows.follow_up: What hiring plan supports 12% post-money, and how much of it is for the missing CTO and manufacturing roles?

rows.finding: The 2025 notes convert at 80% of the Series A price ($3.7716), giving 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares or 10.8% of the post-money, against 1,648,000 shares at the full price. The 20% discount is worth about $1.95M, of which the founders bear roughly $0.6M and the seed investors about $0.3M.
rows.mechanism: A conversion discount inside the pre-money moves value from earlier holders to noteholders and raises the effective price the new investor pays per unit of ownership.
rows.benchmark: Note discounts typically run 15-25%; 20% is market. What is not market is that $2.5M of the $7.77M converting is held by a counterparty that is simultaneously a customer, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round.
rows.implication: The discount itself is acceptable; the counterparty mix is not. Require the note conversion mechanics and any side letters to be disclosed, and confirm no noteholder holds a most-favoured-nation or additional discount.
rows.weakens: The noteholders took real risk in 2025-02 when the company had $0.4M of FY2024 revenue, so the discount is earned rather than extracted.
rows.confidence: High on the arithmetic; medium on the allocation between Granary ($3.5M), Tallis ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M), which is inferred from the 2025-02-10 principal amounts plus accrued interest.
rows.follow_up: What is the accrued interest and the exact conversion formula, and are there side letters?

rows.finding: The 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed (about $11.0M on the 2023 round size, which the deck does not state), a stack of about $36.8M or 40.9% of the $90.0M post-money. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit, where 46.5% as-converted equals the preference.
rows.mechanism: A preference stack sets a floor below which common is worthless and a crossover above which the preferred converts; between the two the new investor is effectively a 1x lender with equity upside.
rows.benchmark: 1x non-participating and broad-based weighted average are the founder-friendly end of market terms; the risk here is size, not structure, because the stack equals 41% of the post-money.
rows.implication: At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at a $79M sale and needs about a $180M exit for 2x. The $72.0M pre-money should be underwritten as an option struck at $79M, not as a mark on the common.
rows.weakens: If the seed preference is materially below $11.0M (for example if the SAFEs converted at a cap inside the seed), the stack is smaller and the crossover moves down.
rows.confidence: Medium-high: the maths is exact but the seed preference amount is assumed from the round size, not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: What is the Series Seed liquidation preference and price per share, and do the SAFEs carry a separate preference?

rows.finding: Revenue-generating assets sit below the issuer. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (Delaware) holds the five US patent filings and the Calder University licence; Orrin Fleet Services LLC (California, 2023-11-02) owns the fleet, signs the grower contracts and is the Kestrel borrower; Orrin Fieldworks Mexico S. de R.L. de C.V. (Jalisco, 2024-07-19) does gripper and harness assembly with 7 staff and is 1% owned by the California fleet LLC.
rows.mechanism: A holdco/opco split lets the lender take a security interest in the revenue contracts while the equity investor buys the parent; the investor's claim on the cash flow is therefore indirect and conditional on intercompany funding and lender consent.
rows.benchmark: Standard for asset-backed equipment finance; unusual only in that a pre-revenue-hardware company has put its entire commercial contracting layer into the borrower.
rows.implication: Conditions before closing: Calder's consent to operation and sublicense by the fleet subsidiary; Kestrel's consent to the round and confirmation of which entity and which balance the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant is tested against; a parent-level guarantee or a restriction on moving assets out of the borrower.
rows.weakens: There is no evidence in the deck of an actual lien conflict or consent failure; the structure works perfectly well if the intercompany arrangements are documented.
rows.confidence: Medium: entity roles are stated in the deck, but the licence's sublicense terms, the loan agreement and the intercompany agreements are not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Does the Calder licence permit sublicensing or operation by an affiliate, and is the Kestrel covenant tested at parent or borrower level?

rows.finding: The $1.5M minimum unrestricted cash covenant is met with $2.2M of headroom at 2026-09-30 cash of $3.7M against $410,000 monthly net burn, which runs out around 2027-03. Runway to zero is about 2027-06, three months before the 2027 season ships, while $9.9M of hardware must be spent before April 2027.
rows.mechanism: A covenant struck on a cash balance falls before the equity does; it converts a slow fundraising process into an event of default at the worst point in the season calendar.
rows.benchmark: An 18-24 month post-Series-A runway is the norm; this round buys about 9 months of the current burn even at the full $18M, so the Series B is a 2027 event, not a 2028 option.
rows.implication: The round must close by 2026-12-15 to build the 2027 fleet at all. A $12M lead plus the $4.0M committed leaves about $7.3M at season start against a planned FY2027 net loss of $7.9M, so the minimum close is under-funded before the first robot ships.
rows.weakens: If the $12M lead is only the first tranche of a larger close and the $2.0M gap is filled, the arithmetic improves by $2M but does not change the 2027 funding requirement.
rows.confidence: High: arithmetic from stated cash, burn, covenant and use of funds.
rows.follow_up: At which entity is the covenant tested, and will Kestrel waive it through the 2027 build?

rows.finding: Five roles sit in one counterparty: Tallis Agricultural Machinery is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer (37.5% of stated $3.2M ARR, ending 2027-06-30), the quoted manufacturer whose $33,000 v4 unit cost underpins the $9.9M robot budget, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round. The COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services LLC was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date, and the COO's 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer.
rows.mechanism: Related-party revenue and related-party cost estimates are not arm's length, so both the revenue multiple and the unit-cost path in the plan are set by parties with an interest in the outcome.
rows.benchmark: Two of the deck's own five paying 2026 growers are named, and they are 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons; neither is labelled a related party although one is the COO's former employer.
rows.implication: Conditions: a second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials, a fairness review of the Vashti contract, the Tallis observer seat limited to non-confidential sessions, and the valuation tested on revenue excluding related parties.
rows.weakens: Tallis funding its own customer and manufacturing its product may be genuine strategic alignment, and the deck does disclose the roles, which is more than most decks do.
rows.confidence: High on the roles (deck p.12); medium on how much of Tallis's revenue is at non-market prices, which the deck does not say.
rows.follow_up: What are the Vashti contract's rates against local market, and what does an independent quote put the v4 robot at?

plan.decision_question: Is the legal and ownership structure clean enough to wire $12M into, and does the $72M pre-money survive its own cap table?
plan.thesis_sentence: The structure is wire-ready only with conditions: the $72.0M pre-money is arithmetically coherent at a $90.0M post-money but is struck on a share count 27% larger than the deck's headline, it sits $7M below the level at which the preference stack stops absorbing all common proceeds, and the grower contracts, the fleet and the equipment debt all sit in a subsidiary the Series A does not buy.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that can disqualify the wire rather than the business: it tests who the issuer is, what it actually owns, who else holds claims on the cash flow, and how the round's own arithmetic moves value between holders. Technology, market and unit economics are tested elsewhere and are irrelevant if the entity is wrong.
plan.mechanism: Value transfer through share-count and preference conventions: the pool shuffle, the 80% note conversion and a $36.8M equal-rank preference determine how much of any given exit reaches the founders and the new investor, independently of the operating story.
plan.comparison_set: Standard Series A conventions (pre-money fully diluted including pool and note conversion; 1x non-participating; 10-15% post-money pool) and the company's own prior rounds: $2.5M pre-seed SAFEs 2022-04, $11.0M Series Seed 2023-03, $7.0M convertible notes 2025-02, $2.5M equipment facility 2025-06.
plan.counter_evidence: The terms the deck does state are founder-friendly: 1x non-participating rather than participating preferred, broad-based weighted average rather than full ratchet, equal ranking rather than a senior stack, and a 20% note discount that is market. Disclosed related parties can be a strength when a manufacturer funds its own customer. No lien conflict, entity lapse or litigation is evidenced anywhere in the deck.
plan.visual: kpi table of six decision metrics, plus the rebuilt post-round cap table and the legal entity map
plan.prohibited: clean structure, solid structure, huge market, strong team, well positioned, about five, many

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,908 characters)
At the price Orrin has actually signed, one robot-season does not cover the depreciation on the robot, so the rental business loses money on every unit today; the case rests on an unbuilt v4 and a price increase no grower has signed.

### The revenue is mostly not rental

The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season (company-reported, unaudited): about seven months in California (April-October) and four in Florida (December-March), one season at a time, with Orrin owning, maintaining and insuring the fleet. No multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M divides into robot rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E is little better, with rental at $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%). The engineering customer is also a $2.5M noteholder, a board observer, the quoted manufacturer of the v4 and a $1.0M committed investor in this round, so half of FY2025 revenue is related-party and 80% is one-off, grant-funded or related-party. What the company has proven is that five growers will rent 75 robot-seasons at $9,500; the rest of the revenue line is an engineering contract and a grant, and its own strategy assumes both disappear by 2028 [S1].

### One robot-season loses $8,100 before any overhead

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company, unaudited) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Interest-only debt service ($1.6M x 11.5% / 75 seasons) | (2,453) | 25.8 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Cash contribution after interest-only debt service | 1,447 | 15.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Cash contribution after amortising debt service | (3,051) | (32.1) | S1 (unverified), calc |

The company-reported 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: fleet depreciation sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue. Charging the $48,000 v3 over its four-season life puts $12,000 against each season, more than the $9,500 the grower pays before a single technician is paid. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and should not be added; the economic measure is the negative $8,100 contribution, while the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only and -$3,051 if it amortises over the robot's four-season life. The benchmark: United Rentals earned a gross margin of 38.0% on equipment rentals in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue. Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at the $16,500 list price with the v3, and only reaches +19.1% with both the list price and a $31,000 v4 [S21].

### The 2.1-season payback is the best case of three unproven inputs

The claimed 2.1 seasons is $31,000 divided by ($16,500 list price less $1,750 target service), which drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely. Putting it back gives 2.53 seasons on the company's own target cost and price. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet actually ran in 2026, against a four-season asset life. Even at the $31,000 target build and the signed price the payback is 7.95 seasons; at the list price and the current build it is 4.40 seasons, longer than the asset lasts. Of the four inputs that decide payback, build cost is unbuilt, price unsigned, service cost unreconciled to the technician ratio and transport omitted from the slide. All of these are company-reported, unaudited figures [S1].

### Utilisation cannot repair a per-season capital charge

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two (the California and Florida seasons cover eleven months). At the signed price the fleet needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 seasons, 85% of the maximum; at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles its revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads fixed overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital hurdle. Service cost is no more forgiving. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 loaded field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour, over 213 days, costs $41,611 per technician-season, or $5,201 per robot-season; at the $29.60 machine-operator rate it is $6,305. The deck reports $3,100, which implies a technician costs $24,800 for seven months before a vehicle, tools or travel. At 360 robots the same ratio needs 45 technicians and $1.12M at the reported rate, so the cost is linear in robots, not diluted by scale; on the $6,305 figure, gross profit at the signed price falls to $695, or 7.3%, before depreciation [S1, S10].

### Price is not the constraint; proof and quality are

At one robot per 3.5 acres the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the 2027 list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre - 3.4% to 5.9% of the labour bill the robot targets. At 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray, each percentage point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21% to 36% of the robot fee; the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee and 80% of the list fee. That asymmetry explains why price has not moved to list and why one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising: a grower is buying an option on a harvest, not a proven substitute for a crew. The risk is not that growers cannot afford the robot but that the robot, at 94% of detected ripe fruit and 86% uptime, cannot yet promise the bruising and reliability a retail supply chain requires [S10].

| Offer | $ per robot-season | vs signed | $ per acre (3.5 acres/robot) | % of $79,288/acre harvest cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 3.4% | S1 (unverified), S10 |
| 2027 renewal average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 4.6% | S1 (unverified), S10 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 5.9% | S1 (unverified), S10 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 6.3% | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 4.8% | S1 (unverified), calc |

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at a small fraction of the harvest cost it addresses, so a working unit could charge several times more; the answer is that two peers with more capital and more robots did not get there. Tortuga and FarmWise both owned fleets and rented or serviced them before retreating, and Orrin's capital intensity per robot is essentially the same as Tortuga's.

|---|---|---|---|
| Tortuga AgTech | 150 harvesting robots; about $50M deployed over eight years | IP, assets and team sold to Oishii, 2025-03 | S93 |
| FarmWise | $45M Series B in 2022; $65M equity in total | Titan run as a service, then Vulcan sold through dealer RDO Equipment; wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms, 2025-04 | S100, S116 |

### What would have to be true

The unit turns positive only if both conditions hold at once: a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling and a price at or above the breakeven in the table, with the v4 in service. The investment should therefore be conditioned on signed 2027 contracts at the list price with deposits, a verified v4 bill of materials from a manufacturer independent of the largest revenue customer, an audited service-cost build reconciled to the 1:8 technician ratio, and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on the company's own figures; the service-cost cross-check and the bruise-to-revenue link are medium confidence, and the open questions are the loan amortisation schedule, the Florida season price and the share of bruised fruit actually culled.

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unaudited) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures alone produce the negative contribution, the 12.31-season payback at the signed price and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven [S1].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 财务分析 Financial Analysis (financials, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,974 characters)
The full round funds the fleet plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the minimum close the plan is not funded, the cash covenant binds before the season starts, and most of the reported ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023-FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time head of finance. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

| $M, year to 31 December | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cost of revenue | 0.1 | 0.1 | 0.9 | 1.1 | 2.7 | 5.2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S1 (unverified) |
| Net loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S1 (unverified) |
| Total gross margin | 0% | 75.0% | 52.6% | 57.7% | 51.8% | 60.6% | S1 (unverified), calc |

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The company-reported, unaudited $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level [S1].

| ARR component, 2026-09-30 | $M | What it is | Treatment | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contracted 2027 robot-seasons | 1.4 | 110 robots x $12,700 | Contracted, not yet earned | S1 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 1.2 | Fixed term to 2027-06-30, related party | Remove: expires mid-2027 | S1 (unverified) |
| Letters of intent | 0.6 | 50 robots, non-binding | Remove: not contracted | S1 (unverified) |
| Like-for-like recurring | 1.4 | 43.8% of the $3.2M headline |  | S1 (unverified), calc |

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep a minimum unrestricted balance at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts. It moves with the closing date: a quarter's delay does not shorten the runway by three months, it lands after the covenant is breached, making the closing date a condition of the investment.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 (company-reported, unaudited) less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is $6.085M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

On the company-reported, unaudited plan, three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4, so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, $78 above the $12,700 renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and $13.93M of capex nowhere in the plan. The only capex-free reading is 360 robots each doing two seasons at $17,900, requiring a Florida business that does not exist at scale [S1].

| Reconciliation test | Calculation | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2027 robot budget | 300 x $33,000 | $9.9M | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027 implied price | $4.6M / 360 robots | $12,778 = renewal average + $78 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| 2028 implied fleet at $16,500 | $12.9M / $16,500 | 782 robots, 422 more, $13.93M capex | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Undrawn fleet facility | $2.5M - $1.6M | $0.9M = 27 robots | S1 (unverified), calc |

### Margins are flattered by where depreciation sits

The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into -$0.31M, or -5.5%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while the 52% and 61% equal the company-wide margin, so the series changes definition between years. Returns cannot be computed without a balance sheet: ROE, ROIC and working-capital days are not disclosed, interest cover is -29.3x on FY2026E EBIT of -$5.4M, and net cash of $2.1M includes $1.5M the company must keep. Cumulative losses of $32.0M compare with $20.5M raised, $320,313 of capital per robot in service, and $68,421 of revenue per employee against Deere's $625,000 [S1, S21, S37].

| Returns and working capital | Value | Source / status |
|---|---|---|
| ROE, ROIC, asset turnover, working-capital days | Not computable, not disclosed | No balance sheet |
| Interest cover | -29.3x (FY2026E EBIT -$5.4M / $184,000 interest) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Net cash | $2.1M, of which $1.5M must stay unrestricted | S1 (unverified) |
| Goodwill / SBC | None disclosed / not disclosed; options 13.0% of fully diluted pre-round | S1 (unverified) |
| Cumulative net loss vs capital raised | $32.0M vs $20.5M | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Capital per robot in service | $320,313 ($20.5M / 64) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Revenue per employee | $68,421 vs Deere $625,000 | S1, S37 |
| Fee per acre vs harvest cost | $2,714-$4,714 vs $79,288 (3.4%-5.9%) | S1, S10 |

### The matrix is the decision

arguments.markdown:
The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position is a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure at the top of the density range, not a picked-acre figure. Harvest CROO's advertisement cross-checks the arithmetic rather than the claim: its sixteen units at Orrin's cycle time produce its advertised eight acres, so coverage follows capital per machine, not a better algorithm [S1, S27].

| Metric | Company claim | Benchmark | Method and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Berries per 24 h | not disclosed | 22,114 derived; 205,714 at 16 arms | arithmetic from company inputs | S1, S27 |
| Acres per 24 h | 1.5 | 1.0-1.2 | derived; company claim unverified | S1, S119 |
| Pick rate | 94% of ripe berries detected | no peer-reviewed open-field rate above 95% found | 212 company-chosen rows, unverified | S1, S27 |
| Bruised or punctured | 3.8% | 5% serious damage, 10% total defects, 2% decay | company measurement, definition undisclosed, unverified | S1, S120 |
| Unripe picked | 2.1% | not applicable | company measurement, unverified | S1 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not disclosed | company log, unverified | S1 |
| Operator interventions | every 3.4 h = 5.9 per robot-day | 47 per technician-day at 8 robots each | derived from company figures, unverified | S1 |

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the two to five days in which a bruise expresses itself at the cooler. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

::: evidence
**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling. [S1, S120]**

Packers work to a lot-level allowance for total defects, serious damage and decay rather than a per-machine one, and a bruise that appears after a week in the cooler is still the grower's loss.
:::

### What is defensible is the data and the service, not the patents

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picking units | 2 arms | 16 units | dual arm | ceased 2025-07 | — | S1, S27, S28 |
| Coverage | 1.5 acres/24 h claimed, 1.0-1.2 derived | 8 acres/day, vendor-stated | not disclosed | not disclosed | night work doubles hours | S1, S27, S78 |
| Model | RaaS per robot-season | not disclosed | per-kilogram RaaS | machine sale | Carbon Robotics sells machines | S1, S93, S109 |
| Status 2026 | 64 robots, 5 paying growers | commercial in Florida | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025-03 | IP bought by CNH | two of five peers failed | S1, S27, S97 |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |

| Gripper mechanics | 3 | silicone fingers with slip sensing; soft-fruit gripper work is public and the claims were rejected | 1 year | S1, S4 |
| Licence and freedom to operate | 4 | exclusive but lapsable; it is the licensor's patent, not the company's | not applicable | S1, S86 |
| Service density | 5 | one technician per 8 robots near two California clusters, company-stated and unaudited | 2 years | S1 |
| Safety certification | 3 | ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the framework; no certification or field audit disclosed | 1-2 years | S92 |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | | **minimum 2 years** | S1, S4, S86, S92 |

The replication test is unkind. A funded team of fifty with the published patents needs about a year for a gripper, because cutting the stem, holding with compliant fingers and sensing slip is standard practice, and two to three years for the perception stack, because its training fields cannot be bought. What it cannot buy in that time is the seventy-five robot-seasons of grower trust built in two valleys, which is the real barrier and a sales one [S1, S4].

| Patent Number | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper with slip sensing | US | 2022-09-02 | published 2024-03, every claim rejected, response 2026-05 — company-stated | the one mechanical claim set | S1 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night-time stereo detection of hidden fruit | US | 2024-05-06 | published 2025-11, awaiting examination — company-stated | overlaps the licensed family | S1 |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following track platform | WIPO | 2025-04-29 | national phase due 2026-10-30, undecided — company-stated | Europe, Mexico, Australia; EPO and Australia allow 31 months | S1 |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 compliant fingers | US | 2026-07-08 | unpublished — company-stated | second attempt at the same mechanism | S1 |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling across growers | US | 2026-04-17 | provisional, converts by 2027-04-17 — company-stated | the only filing aimed at the service model | S1 |
| CU-2017-031 | Stereo ripeness model | US | granted 2020 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core perception; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |
| CU-2019-114 | Berry-stem localisation | US | granted 2022 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core manipulation; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |

Nothing there is a wall. The gripper is a rejected application on US Patent 17/902,118, the v4 filing is unpublished and untested, the PCT falls due today, and the two families that read on the product belong to a university whose licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A public-index search on 2026-10-30 returned no record of the application, so prosecution status rests on the company's account alone [S1, S86].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker v3 | commercial | 2026-03 | $0.71M FY2026E RaaS | 41% gross | 360 in service, April 2027 | S1 |
| Picker v4 | design | 2027 season | none | target 52% | $33,000 build, 300 units | S1 |
| Engineering services | contract | 2025-03 | $1.20M FY2026E | not disclosed | ends 2027-06-30 | S1 |
| SBIR grant | grant | 2024-09 | $0.35M FY2026E | not applicable | not visible in federal award data | S1, S91 |

Two gaps bound the confidence: the detection recall behind the pick rate is unpublished, so the true field rate is the headline times an unknown; and the federal award data returns no grant to the company, contradicting the SBIR line, which should be settled before grant income counts as recurring-adjacent [S91]. The questions that would move this section are exact: the ripe-fruit density and pick interval the test rows saw, the damage rate after a week at one degree Celsius, how many of the hourly interventions need a person in the field, and whether the Calder licence counts robots deployed or robots paid for.

arguments.markdown:
The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position is a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure, not a picked-acre figure. Harvest CROO's advertisement cross-checks the arithmetic rather than the claim: its sixteen units at Orrin's cycle time produce its advertised eight acres, so coverage follows capital per machine, not a better algorithm [S1, S27].

| Metric | Company claim | Benchmark | Method and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Berries per 24 h | not disclosed | 22,114 derived; 205,714 at 16 arms | arithmetic from company inputs | S1, S27 |
| Acres per 24 h | 1.5 | 1.0-1.2 | derived; company claim unverified | S1, S119 |
| Pick rate | 94% of ripe berries detected | no peer-reviewed open-field rate above 95% found | 212 company-chosen rows, unverified | S1, S27 |
| Bruised or punctured | 3.8% | 5% serious damage, 10% total defects, 2% decay | company measurement, definition undisclosed, unverified | S1, S120 |
| Unripe picked | 2.1% | not applicable | company measurement, unverified | S1 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not disclosed | company log, unverified | S1 |
| Operator interventions | every 3.4 h = 5.9 per robot-day | 47 per technician-day at 8 robots each | derived from company figures, unverified | S1 |

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the week in which a bruise expresses itself. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

::: evidence
**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling. [S1, S120]**

Packers work to a lot-level allowance for total defects, serious damage and decay rather than a per-machine one, and a bruise that appears after a week in the cooler is still the grower's loss.
:::

### What is defensible is the data and the service, not the patents

| Technical Dimension | Orrin Picker v3 | Harvest CROO B8 | Tortuga F/G | Advanced Farm | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picking units | 2 arms | 16 units | dual arm | ceased 2025-07 | — | S1, S27, S28 |
| Coverage | 1.5 acres/24 h claimed, 1.0-1.2 derived | 8 acres/day, vendor-stated | not disclosed | not disclosed | night work doubles hours | S1, S27, S78 |
| Model | RaaS per robot-season | not disclosed | per-kilogram RaaS | machine sale | Carbon Robotics sells machines | S1, S93, S109 |
| Status 2026 | 64 robots, 5 paying growers | commercial in Florida | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025-03 | IP bought by CNH | two of five peers failed | S1, S27, S97 |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet perception data | 6 | 1.9 million labelled images and 75 paid robot-seasons, company-stated and unaudited; labels compound only with deployed hours | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Gripper mechanics | 3 | silicone fingers with slip sensing; soft-fruit gripper work is public and the claims were rejected | 1 year | S1, S4 |
| Licence and freedom to operate | 4 | exclusive but lapsable; it is the licensor's patent, not the company's | not applicable | S1, S86 |
| Service density | 5 | one technician per 8 robots near two California clusters, company-stated and unaudited | 2 years | S1 |
| Safety certification | 3 | ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the framework; no certification or field audit disclosed | 1-2 years | S92 |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | | **minimum 2 years** | S1, S4, S86, S92 |

The replication test is unkind. A funded team of fifty with the published patents needs about a year for a gripper, because cutting the stem, holding with compliant fingers and sensing slip is standard practice, and two to three years for the perception stack, because its training fields cannot be bought. What it cannot buy in that time is the seventy-five robot-seasons of grower trust built in two valleys, which is the real barrier and a sales one [S1, S4].

| Patent Number | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper with slip sensing | US | 2022-09-02 | published 2024-03, every claim rejected, response 2026-05 — company-stated | the one mechanical claim set | S1 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night-time stereo detection of hidden fruit | US | 2024-05-06 | published 2025-11, awaiting examination — company-stated | overlaps the licensed family | S1 |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following track platform | WIPO | 2025-04-29 | national phase due 2026-10-30, undecided — company-stated | Europe, Mexico, Australia; EPO and Australia allow 31 months | S1 |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 compliant fingers | US | 2026-07-08 | unpublished — company-stated | second attempt at the same mechanism | S1 |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling across growers | US | 2026-04-17 | provisional, converts by 2027-04-17 — company-stated | the only filing aimed at the service model | S1 |
| CU-2017-031 | Stereo ripeness model | US | granted 2020 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core perception; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |
| CU-2019-114 | Berry-stem localisation | US | granted 2022 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core manipulation; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |

Nothing there is a wall. The gripper is a rejected application on US Patent 17/902,118, the v4 filing is unpublished and untested, the PCT falls due today, and the two families that read on the product belong to a university whose licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A public-index search on 2026-10-30 found no record of the application, so prosecution status rests on the company's account alone [S1, S86].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker v3 | commercial | 2026-03 | $0.71M FY2026E RaaS | 41% gross | 360 in service, April 2027 | S1 |
| Picker v4 | design | 2027 season | none | target 52% | $33,000 build, 300 units | S1 |
| Engineering services | contract | 2025-03 | $1.20M FY2026E | not disclosed | ends 2027-06-30 | S1 |
| SBIR grant | grant | 2024-09 | $0.35M FY2026E | not applicable | not visible in federal award data | S1, S91 |

Two gaps bound the confidence: the detection recall behind the pick rate is unpublished, so the true field rate is the headline times an unknown; and the federal award data returns no grant to the company, contradicting the SBIR line, which should be settled before grant income counts as recurring-adjacent [S91]. The questions that would move this section are exact: the ripe-fruit density and pick interval the test rows saw, the damage rate after a week at one degree Celsius, how many of the hourly interventions need a person in the field, and whether the Calder licence counts robots deployed or robots paid for.

rows.finding: The $4.7145 price is $72.0M divided by 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares, a count that already includes the $7.77M note conversion and the option pool at 12% of post-money. The line printed as fully diluted total is 12,000,000, and twelve million shares at $4.7145 come to $56.6M, not $72.0M.
