arguments.markdown:
The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position is a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure, not a picked-acre figure. Compared with Harvest CROO, the unit arithmetic is identical and the acreage eight times higher, so coverage follows capital per machine, not a better algorithm [S1, S27].

| Metric | Company claim | Benchmark | Method and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Berries per 24 h | not disclosed | 22,114 derived; 205,714 at 16 arms | arithmetic from company inputs | S1, S27 |
| Acres per 24 h | 1.5 | 1.0-1.2 | derived; company claim unverified | S1, S119 |
| Pick rate | 94% of ripe berries detected | no peer-reviewed open-field rate above 95% found | 212 company-chosen rows, unverified | S1, S27 |
| Bruised or punctured | 3.8% | 5% serious damage, 10% total defects, 2% decay | company measurement, definition undisclosed, unverified | S1, S120 |
| Unripe picked | 2.1% | not applicable | company measurement, unverified | S1 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not disclosed | company log, unverified | S1 |
| Operator interventions | every 3.4 h = 5.9 per robot-day | 47 per technician-day at 8 robots each | derived from company figures, unverified | S1 |

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the week in which a bruise expresses itself. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

::: evidence
**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling. [S1, S120]**

Packers work to a lot-level allowance for total defects, serious damage and decay rather than a per-machine one, and a bruise that appears after a week in the cooler is still the grower's loss.
:::

### What is defensible is the data and the service, not the patents

| Technical Dimension | Orrin Picker v3 | Harvest CROO B8 | Tortuga F/G | Advanced Farm | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picking units | 2 arms | 16 units | dual arm | ceased 2025-07 | — | S1, S27, S28 |
| Coverage | 1.5 acres/24 h claimed, 1.0-1.2 derived | 8 acres/day, vendor-stated | not disclosed | not disclosed | night work doubles hours | S1, S27, S78 |
| Model | RaaS per robot-season | not disclosed | per-kilogram RaaS | machine sale | Carbon Robotics sells machines | S1, S93, S109 |
| Status 2026 | 64 robots, 5 paying growers | commercial in Florida | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025-03 | IP bought by CNH | two of five peers failed | S1, S27, S97 |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet perception data | 6 | 1.9 million labelled images and 75 paid robot-seasons, unverified; labels compound only with deployed hours | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Gripper mechanics | 3 | silicone fingers with slip sensing; soft-fruit gripper work is public and the claims were rejected | 1 year | S1, S4 |
| Licence and freedom to operate | 4 | exclusive but lapsable; it is the licensor's patent, not the company's | not applicable | S1, S86 |
| Service density | 5 | one technician per 8 robots near two California clusters, unverified | 2 years | S1 |
| Safety certification | 3 | ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the framework; no certification or field audit disclosed | 1-2 years | S92 |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | | **minimum 2 years** | S1, S4, S86, S92 |

The replication test is unkind. A funded team of fifty with the published patents needs about a year for a gripper, because cutting the stem, holding with compliant fingers and sensing slip is standard practice, and two to three years for the perception stack, because its training fields cannot be bought. What it cannot buy in that time is the seventy-five robot-seasons of grower trust built in two valleys, which is the real barrier and a sales one.

| Patent Number | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper with slip sensing | US | 2022-09-02 | published 2024-03, every claim rejected, response 2026-05 — unverified | the one mechanical claim set | S1 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night-time stereo detection of hidden fruit | US | 2024-05-06 | published 2025-11, awaiting examination — unverified | overlaps the licensed family | S1 |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following track platform | WIPO | 2025-04-29 | national phase due 2026-10-30, undecided — unverified | Europe, Mexico, Australia; EPO and Australia allow 31 months | S1 |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 compliant fingers | US | 2026-07-08 | unpublished — unverified | second attempt at the same mechanism | S1 |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling across growers | US | 2026-04-17 | provisional, converts by 2027-04-17 — unverified | the only filing aimed at the service model | S1 |
| CU-2017-031 | Stereo ripeness model | US | granted 2020 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core perception; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |
| CU-2019-114 | Berry-stem localisation | US | granted 2022 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core manipulation; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |

Nothing there is a wall. The gripper is a rejected application on US Patent 17/902,118, the v4 filing is unpublished and untested, the PCT falls due today, and the two families that read on the product belong to a university whose licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A public-index search on 2026-10-30 found no record of the application, so prosecution status rests on the company's account alone [S1, S86].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker v3 | commercial | 2026-03 | $0.71M FY2026E RaaS | 41% gross | 360 in service, April 2027 | S1 |
| Picker v4 | design | 2027 season | none | target 52% | $33,000 build, 300 units | S1 |
| Engineering services | contract | 2025-03 | $1.20M FY2026E | not disclosed | ends 2027-06-30 | S1 |
| SBIR grant | grant | 2024-09 | $0.35M FY2026E | not applicable | not visible in federal award data | S1, S91 |

Two gaps bound the confidence: the detection recall behind the pick rate is unpublished, so the true field rate is the headline times an unknown; and the federal award data returns no grant to the company, contradicting the SBIR line, which should be settled before grant income counts as recurring-adjacent [S91]. The questions that would move this section are exact: the ripe-fruit density and pick interval the test rows saw, the damage rate after a week at one degree Celsius, how many of the hourly interventions need a person in the field, and whether the Calder licence counts robots deployed or robots paid for.

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure, not a picked-acre figure. Compared with Harvest CROO, the unit arithmetic is identical and the acreage eight times higher, so coverage follows capital per machine, not a better algorithm [S1, S27].

| Metric | Company claim | Benchmark | Method and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Berries per 24 h | not disclosed | 22,114 derived; 205,714 at 16 arms | arithmetic from company inputs | S1, S27 |
| Acres per 24 h | 1.5 | 1.0-1.2 | derived; company claim unverified | S1, S119 |
| Pick rate | 94% of ripe berries detected | no peer-reviewed open-field rate above 95% found | 212 company-chosen rows, unverified | S1, S27 |
| Bruised or punctured | 3.8% | 5% serious damage, 10% total defects, 2% decay | company measurement, definition undisclosed, unverified | S1, S120 |
| Unripe picked | 2.1% | not applicable | company measurement, unverified | S1 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not disclosed | company log, unverified | S1 |
| Operator interventions | every 3.4 h = 5.9 per robot-day | 47 per technician-day at 8 robots each | derived from company figures, unverified | S1 |

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the week in which a bruise expresses itself. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

::: evidence
**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling. [S1, S120]**

Packers work to a lot-level allowance for total defects, serious damage and decay rather than a per-machine one, and a bruise that appears after a week in the cooler is still the grower's loss.
:::

### What is defensible is the data and the service, not the patents

| Technical Dimension | Orrin Picker v3 | Harvest CROO B8 | Tortuga F/G | Advanced Farm | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picking units | 2 arms | 16 units | dual arm | ceased 2025-07 | — | S1, S27, S28 |
| Coverage | 1.5 acres/24 h claimed, 1.0-1.2 derived | 8 acres/day, vendor-stated | not disclosed | not disclosed | night work doubles hours | S1, S27, S78 |
| Model | RaaS per robot-season | not disclosed | per-kilogram RaaS | machine sale | Carbon Robotics sells machines | S1, S93, S109 |
| Status 2026 | 64 robots, 5 paying growers | commercial in Florida | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025-03 | IP bought by CNH | two of five peers failed | S1, S27, S97 |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet perception data | 6 | 1.9 million labelled images and 75 paid robot-seasons, unverified; labels compound only with deployed hours | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Gripper mechanics | 3 | silicone fingers with slip sensing; soft-fruit gripper work is public and the claims were rejected | 1 year | S1, S4 |
| Licence and freedom to operate | 4 | exclusive but lapsable; it is the licensor's patent, not the company's | not applicable | S1, S86 |
| Service density | 5 | one technician per 8 robots near two California clusters, unverified | 2 years | S1 |
| Safety certification | 3 | ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the framework; no certification or field audit disclosed | 1-2 years | S92 |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | | **minimum 2 years** | S1, S4, S86, S92 |

The replication test is unkind. A funded team of fifty with the published patents needs about a year for a gripper, because cutting the stem, holding with compliant fingers and sensing slip is standard practice, and two to three years for the perception stack, because its training fields cannot be bought. What it cannot buy in that time is the seventy-five robot-seasons of grower trust built in two valleys, which is the real barrier and a sales one.

| Patent Number | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper with slip sensing | US | 2022-09-02 | published 2024-03, every claim rejected, response 2026-05 — unverified | the one mechanical claim set | S1 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night-time stereo detection of hidden fruit | US | 2024-05-06 | published 2025-11, awaiting examination — unverified | overlaps the licensed family | S1 |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following track platform | WIPO | 2025-04-29 | national phase due 2026-10-30, undecided — unverified | Europe, Mexico, Australia; EPO and Australia allow 31 months | S1 |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 compliant fingers | US | 2026-07-08 | unpublished — unverified | second attempt at the same mechanism | S1 |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling across growers | US | 2026-04-17 | provisional, converts by 2027-04-17 — unverified | the only filing aimed at the service model | S1 |
| CU-2017-031 | Stereo ripeness model | US | granted 2020 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core perception; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |
| CU-2019-114 | Berry-stem localisation | US | granted 2022 | licensed exclusively since 2022-01-20 | core manipulation; licensed, not owned | S1, S86 |

Nothing there is a wall. The gripper is a rejected application on US Patent 17/902,118, the v4 filing is unpublished and untested, the PCT falls due today, and the two families that read on the product belong to a university whose licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A public-index search on 2026-10-30 found no record of the application, so prosecution status rests on the company's account alone [S1, S86].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker v3 | commercial, unverified | 2026-03 | $0.71M FY2026E RaaS | 41% gross | 360 in service, April 2027 | S1 |
| Picker v4 | design, unverified | 2027 season | none | target 52% | $33,000 build, 300 units | S1 |
| Engineering services | contract, unverified | 2025-03 | $1.20M FY2026E | not disclosed | ends 2027-06-30 | S1 |
| SBIR grant | grant, unverified | 2024-09 | $0.35M FY2026E | not applicable | not visible in federal award data | S1, S91 |

Two gaps bound the confidence: the detection recall behind the pick rate is unpublished, so the true field rate is the headline times an unknown; and the federal award data returns no grant to the company, contradicting the SBIR line, which should be settled before grant income counts as recurring-adjacent [S91]. The questions that would move this section are exact: the ripe-fruit density and pick interval the test rows saw, the damage rate after a week at one degree Celsius, how many of the hourly interventions need a person in the field, and whether the Calder licence counts robots deployed or robots paid for.

plan.comparison_set: What the first three years of the closest harvesting-robotics founding teams produced could not be sourced in this review, so the comparison is stated as an open test rather than a finding; the firm comparison used instead is the company's own progression (14 pilots, 2 paying conversions in 2025, 5 paying growers in 2026, 1 pilot lost) against the 2027 plan and against a 360-unit build capability.
plan.counter_evidence: Castellano's lab work produced the licensed IP and eleven filings, which is real technical depth; Vashti converted his own former employer into a 40-robot 2027 contract, which is real commercial proof; the company shipped three hardware generations in four years with no CTO, which is execution the CVs do not capture and a real argument that the vacancy matters less than it looks.
plan.decision_question: Does this team have the specific capability to take a hand-built pilot fleet to 360 robots in one season?
plan.mechanism: Founder-market fit is a match between a person's prior role and the company's current binding constraint. Orrin's constraint moved from perception research (2019-2023) to manufacturing and service scale (2026-2027), and the executive team did not move with it: the CTO seat has been empty for 26 months and no one holds volume manufacturing, supply chain or quality.
plan.prohibited: strong team, experienced team, world-class, about five, many patents, seasoned
plan.thesis_sentence: Castellano and Vashti are a credible perception researcher and a credible harvest operator, but the specific capability the 2027 plan needs, building and servicing 360 robots at a 35% lower unit cost, is held by nobody on the executive team: the co-founder CTO who owned it left on 2023-08-31, the seat is still open, and the two people now carrying it have never run a volume build.
plan.visual: team assessment matrix across the four named executives, plus the education and career chronology tables
plan.why_different: Every other section prices what the company has, this one prices who can build what it does not yet have. The product claims and the market map are only as good as the organisation's ability to ship 360 units and service them in a seven-month season.

queries: Deck pages 11 to 13 read line by line for role, date, education and prior employer of each of the five named executives
Deck page 5 read for inventorship and the licensed university patent families, then cross-read against the departure date on page 13
Deck page 6 read for customer concentration against the COO's stated employment history
Checked every claimed credential against a retrievable public record: no education, employer, patent, award or press record could be retrieved for any named executive
Attempted the patent office assignment and prosecution records to test inventorship on the licensed families: not reachable from this environment
Tested the 2027 commercial plan against the contracted book: 110 contracted robots against a 360-robot target with one sales vice president 16 months into the role

rows.benchmark: A 300-unit hardware build with a 35% unit-cost reduction normally has a VP Operations or manufacturing leader and a full-time CFO in place before the Series A, not after it.
rows.confidence: High on the role structure; medium on whether an unstated hire is already in progress.
rows.finding: Of the four executives plus the departed co-founder, none has manufacturing, supply chain or quality experience. The chief financial role is part-time and fractional (since 2024-09), the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, and 22 of 38 employees are engineers who report through a VP Engineering hired in 2024-02.
rows.follow_up: Who signs the 300-unit purchase orders and the quality plan, and will the lead require a VP Manufacturing and a full-time CFO as closing conditions?
rows.implication: Treat the two missing executive hires as conditions or accept that the $9.9M hardware budget is being spent by people doing the job for the first time. The hiring plan behind the pool increase should be published before the pool is agreed.
rows.mechanism: A company's binding constraint shifts as it scales, and the organisation has to shift with it. Orrin's moved from perception research to manufacturing engineering, and the executive bench did not follow: no one on the team has taken a hardware product past a few dozen units.
rows.weakens: A small team can rent manufacturing capability from a contract manufacturer, which is exactly what the Tallis quote implies; the absence of a manufacturing executive matters less if the contract manufacturer owns the process.

rows.benchmark: Enterprise hardware companies typically enter a Series A with a sales leader who has carried a quota at scale in the category; here the vice president has twenty years in crop inputs and sixteen months in robotics.
rows.confidence: High on the concentration; medium on whether the two named customers were introduced by the COO, which the deck implies but does not state.
rows.finding: Sales run through the co-founder's own grower relationships. Five paying growers in 2026, two of them named, and those two are 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons. One of the two is the company where the COO was director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021.
rows.follow_up: How many of the five 2026 customers came through the COO, and what is the pipeline outside his network?
rows.implication: Value the book as founder-led revenue, not as a repeatable sales motion, and test whether the two named accounts pay the same price as the three unsigned ones. The 2027 plan needs roughly 250 more robots sold in a four-month window.
rows.mechanism: Founder network sales convert fast up to the size of the network and stop. With about 15 remaining large California growers named as the addressable top tier, the network exhausts around the point the plan needs to quadruple the fleet.
rows.weakens: Founder-led selling is normal at this stage and the relationships are the company's single biggest commercial asset; a 40-robot contract from a former employer is a real endorsement, not a favour.

rows.benchmark: A 26-month vacancy in the role that owns the technical roadmap is unusual at any stage; the plan it leaves behind (a 35% unit-cost cut and a 5.6x fleet increase) is the hardest technical programme the company has attempted.
rows.confidence: High on the vacancy and the dates; low on the circumstances, which only a reference check can settle.
rows.finding: The co-founder and CTO left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. He retains 720,000 vested common shares, 6.0% today and 3.8% after the round, and whether he is a named inventor on the two licensed university families is not stated in the deck and could not be checked at the patent office. No public footprint or new venture could be retrieved for him.
rows.follow_up: What did the departure agreement say about IP assignment, non-solicit and share repurchase, and where is he now?
rows.implication: Before closing: confirm every invention assignment from him to the company and to the university, confirm the company holds no repurchase right it has failed to exercise, and check whether he now works for a competitor or a customer; a 3.8% holder with unrestricted vested shares and the core technology in his head is a hireable asset for anyone else.
rows.mechanism: A departed technical founder is a permanent option held by third parties: his shares are vested so there is no forfeiture leverage, his knowledge sits in the licensed families, and California does not let the company restrain where he works.
rows.weakens: The company shipped three hardware generations after he left, so the organisation clearly no longer depends on him day to day; the vacancy may reflect a deliberate decision to run engineering through the VP rather than a failure to hire.

rows.benchmark: Eleven years at one robotics company is a strong retention signal and a narrow one: it means one employer's processes, not a range of builds.
rows.confidence: Medium-high: dates and employer are from the deck; the scope of her role there is not.
rows.finding: The VP Engineering joined in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at a single robotics company, progressing from manipulation engineer to engineering manager for grippers. That is a direct match for the bruising and pick-rate problem, and no match at all for the cost-down and fleet-reliability problem that decides 2027.
rows.follow_up: What did her gripper programme ship, at what unit cost and volume, and why did she leave after eleven years?
rows.implication: The person carrying the 2027 milestone is one level below the executive team with no CTO above her, which concentrates retention risk in an untested equity package: budget a CTO-level hire and a retention grant for her before the round closes.
rows.mechanism: The engineering leader's prior scale becomes the company's ceiling. A gripper programme inside a larger robotics company is a subsystem budget; a 360-robot build with a 35% cost target is a full product and supply-chain programme.
rows.weakens: She has now shipped the v3 into the field in 2026-03 within two years of joining, which is evidence of delivery beyond her prior job title.

rows.benchmark: A 360-robot season needs roughly three times the contracted book signed within about four months, sold by one vice president and two founder-sellers.
rows.confidence: High: share counts and contract quantities are stated; the sales capacity judgement is mine.
rows.finding: 110 robots are contracted for the 2027 season plus 50 under letters of intent, against a 360-robot plan: 31% of the target is signed or nearly signed five months before the season, and the letters of intent are not binding and are excluded from revenue.
rows.follow_up: What is the conversion rate on letters of intent to date, and what happens to the 2027 plan if only the contracted 110 robots are built?
rows.implication: Size the 2027 build to the contracted book rather than the plan. At 110 robots the unit cost stays near the $48,000 v3 build, the $31,000 target is not reached at that volume, and the payback case does not close without the 500-unit pricing.
rows.mechanism: Unit cost and volume are the same variable: the v4 cost target is quoted at 500 units, the plan builds 300, and the contracted book supports 110, so the cost curve depends on selling ahead of building.
rows.weakens: Seasonal orders in this industry land late, and the two named growers have already increased their commitment every year since 2024.

rows.benchmark: A Series A team normally shows at least one prior build, exit or scale event across the executive bench; this one shows none, and none of the five degree claims could be verified.
rows.confidence: High that nothing was verifiable from this environment; the underlying credentials may well be genuine.
rows.finding: Every credential in the team table (three degrees for the chief executive, four other degrees, five prior employers and eleven patent filings) rests on the deck alone. No education record, employer page, patent record or press mention could be retrieved for any named executive, and no prior company, exit or board seat outside this company is claimed for anyone.
rows.follow_up: Run degree verification through the institutions' registrars and a patent-inventor check before the reference calls.
rows.implication: Treat the team section as unverified until the registries and the patent office confirm it. That is not a reason to decline, but it is a reason not to let the biographies into an investment committee memo as established fact.
rows.mechanism: In a private deal the deck is the only evidence the company controls, so every credential is simultaneously the claim and the proof; independent records are the only way to separate them.
rows.weakens: Nothing in the deck contradicts itself on education or dates, and the career chronology is internally consistent from degree year to employer to founding date.

arguments.markdown:
The plan does not add up on its own numbers. At the current $48,000 build even the 2027 list price leaves each robot-season about $1,100 short over a four-season life, the v4 must land below $28,400 to earn its keep at the $12,700 renewal price, the company's own FY2027 revenue projection implies an average price of $12,778 rather than the $16,500 list, and a 5.6-times fleet increase by April 2027 rests on one outsourced build quote and a $14M gap in a round that has not closed [S1].

### The price rise is a solvency requirement, not a margin story

At $5,600 a season of reported field service, transport, insurance and consumables, a robot priced at the $12,700 renewal average can cost at most $28,400 and still repay itself over four seasons; the v4 budget is $33,000. Priced at the $16,500 list it can cost $43,600 and still repay, which the $48,000 v3 does not. The gap is not theoretical: on the reported costs each robot-season at the renewal price loses $4,900, so a 360-robot fleet at the 2027 revenue line of $4.6M loses about $1.76M a season before a dollar of overhead, and even the $33,000 v4 turns positive only if service cost also falls to the $1,750 target. Depreciation sits in operating expenses rather than cost of revenue, so the reported 52 percent gross margin for 2027 excludes roughly $9,000 a robot-season of hardware consumption — on a $4.6M revenue line that is $3.24M of depreciation and $2.02M of service cost against a gross profit of $2.9M [S1].

The payback figure that carries the story uses the best case at every input. At a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, 2.1 seasons is right; at the $5,600 the company actually reports for 2026, payback stretches to 2.8 seasons at that build and 4.4 seasons at today's $48,000 — longer than the four-season life the same page assumes. The gap between $1,750 and $5,600 is $3,850 a robot-season, $1.39M across 360 robots, and no cost bridge is disclosed for it [S1].

### A price that is too low to be replacing a hand crew

The pricing question runs the other way from the usual one. At $9,500 for the 3.5 acres a robot serves, a grower pays $2,714 an acre a season; the 2027 list is $4,714 an acre. The California Strawberry Commission puts the cost to cultivate and harvest strawberries at an average $87,000 an acre, $15.34 a tray, rising to $17.73 a tray in 2023, so Orrin's asking price is between 3 and 5 percent of the total cost of the crop [S121]. A machine that replaced the hand crew over 3.5 acres would be worth several times that, and five growers buying 75 robot-seasons would not have left it on the table. Either the robot is harvesting a small fraction of the fruit on the acres it drives, or the price has been set to buy pilots and the 2027 increase is the first real test of willingness to pay. Grower B cutting from 22 robots to 14 and Grower E exiting over bruising say the test is live; the two letters of intent for 50 robots are not contracts [S1].

### Peers that carried the asset did not survive it

RaaS makes Orrin the lessor: at 64 robots it carries about $3.1M of fleet on its balance sheet, at 360 about $17.3M at the v3 build or $11.9M at the v4 budget, funded by $18M of equity and a $2.5M secured facility. Carbon Robotics, which sells machines and raised a $70M Series D, is the exception [S28, S93, S97, S109, S116, S122].

The same arithmetic that makes RaaS hard for Orrin is why growers like it, and the base rate says the model is only financeable if the fleet turns fast: 75 paid robot-seasons from 5 growers in 2026, 360 planned in 2027, with 53 percent of 2026 seasons in two named customers and one of them the chief operating officer's former employer.

At $5,600 a season of reported, unverified field service, transport, insurance and consumables, a robot priced at the $12,700 renewal average can cost at most $28,400 and still repay itself over four seasons; the v4 budget is $33,000. The pricing question runs the other way from the usual one. At $9,500 for the 3.5 acres a robot serves, a grower pays $2,714 an acre a season; the 2027 list is $4,714 an acre. Priced at the $16,500 list it can cost $43,600 and still repay, which the $48,000 v3 does not. The gap is not theoretical: on the reported costs each robot-season at the renewal price loses $4,900, so a 360-robot fleet at the 2027 revenue line of $4.6M loses $1.76M a season before a dollar of overhead, and even the $33,000 v4 turns positive only if service cost also falls to the $1,750 target. Depreciation sits in operating expenses rather than cost of revenue, so the reported 52 percent gross margin for 2027 excludes $3.24M of hardware consumption on a $4.6M revenue line, alongside $2.02M of service cost, against total gross profit of $2.9M. The payback figure that carries the story uses the best case at every input: at a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, 2.1 seasons is right, but at the $5,600 the company reports, unverified, for 2026, payback stretches to 2.8 seasons at that build and 4.4 seasons at today's $48,000, longer than the four-season life the same page assumes. The gap between $1,750 and $5,600 is $3,850 a robot-season, $1.386M across 360 robots, and no cost bridge is disclosed for it [S1].

### A price that is too low to be replacing a hand crew

The pricing question runs the other way from the usual one. At $9,500 for the 3.5 acres a robot serves, a grower pays $2,714 an acre a season; the 2027 list is $4,714 an acre. The California Strawberry Commission puts the cost to cultivate and harvest strawberries at an average $87,000 an acre, $15.34 a tray, rising to $17.73 a tray in 2023, so Orrin's asking price is between 3 and 5 percent of the total cost of the crop [S1, S121]. A machine that replaced the hand crew over 3.5 acres would be worth several times that, and five growers buying 75 robot-seasons would not have left it on the table. Either the robot harvests a small fraction of the fruit on the acres it drives, or the price was set to buy pilots and the 2027 increase is the first real test of willingness to pay. Grower B cutting from 22 robots to 14 and Grower E exiting over bruising say the test is live; the two letters of intent for 50 robots are not contracts.

### Peers that carried the asset did not survive it

RaaS makes Orrin the lessor: at 64 robots it carries $3.07M of fleet on its balance sheet, at 360 $17.28M at the v3 build or $11.88M at the v4 budget, funded by $18M of equity and a $2.5M secured facility. Five of six comparable companies did not hold that position. Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP to CNH; Tortuga moved to a per-kilogram service and sold its IP and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025; Monarch raised a $133M Series C at a reported valuation above $500M in 2024, cut staff, and had its assets bought by Caterpillar in April 2026 after failing to pivot to software services; Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021; FarmWise moved from a per-acre Titan service to selling through Vulcan dealers. Carbon Robotics, which sells machines and raised a $70M Series D, is the exception. Three things. The round closes by 2026-12-15 so that build slots and deposits are in place for an April 2027 season; the v4 reaches $33,000 or less on a second and third quote, because at $48,000 the fleet consumes its own gross profit; and at least one grower renews at or near the $16,500 list after a season with an independently measured pick rate and damage rate. The signposts are dated and checkable: a signed 2027 contract at list price, a second contract-manufacturing quote, the v4 first-article build date, and whether the 100-robot licence test is met by robots in commercial service rather than robots built. Against $3.7M of cash, $410,000 of monthly net burn and a $1.5M minimum-cash covenant, usable runway is 5.4 months; a close in January 2027 makes 360 robots impossible and puts the licence cliff at risk [S1, S91].

Two limitations bound this judgement. The v4 unit cost is a single unverified quote and the service-cost target has no disclosed bridge from the reported figure, so the margin case cannot be tested from outside; and the public record returns no federal award to the company, which contradicts the SBIR revenue line in the plan.

No registry record was retrievable: the Delaware and California searches were unreachable, so incorporation, good standing, the agent for service, the foreign qualification and any UCC-1 over the fleet are unverified and rest on the company's own pages. The name also returned no press, grant or patent trace — either a business with no public footprint or a failed retrieval, and the certificates are what separate the two. Confidence below is capped accordingly.

### Three entities, and the investor buys the one without the contracts

The 80% note conversion yields 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares against 1,648,000 at full price, moving about $1.95M to noteholders, roughly $0.6M of it from the founders. Voting percentages assume one vote per share and no voting agreement, which the deck does not disclose — material, because two common seats of five is all that keeps the founders off a board they do not control [S1].

### The $72M sits below its own preference stack

The 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed (about $11.0M on the 2023 round size, which the deck does not state): a $36.8M stack, 40.9% of the $90.0M post-money. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit, where 46.5% as-converted equals the preference. At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at a $79M sale and needs about a $180M exit for 2x, so the pre-money is best underwritten as an option struck at $79M, not a mark on the common. The structure is founder-friendly; the size of the stack decides whether a modest success reaches the common at all.

Orrin sells a robot-season, not a robot. The customer is a strawberry grower, the user is the crew the robot displaces, and the budget owner holds the harvest-labour line — in practice the owner or head of harvest at a business farming hundreds of acres. Growth comes from converting pilots into paid seasonal rentals and renewing them: 14 pilot farms since 2024, two conversions in 2025, five paying growers in 2026, 110 robots contracted for 2027 plus 50 under letters of intent. The chief operating officer's wholly owned services company took $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date under a contract approved by a board he sits on, with no independent director, and his 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer. Conditions before closing:

- An independent director at signing, agreed by the lead, chairing audit and compensation.
- Observer rights limited to non-confidential sessions, with no sight of the lead's diligence.
- A second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials, reviewed by the lead's engineer.
- Kestrel consent and a covenant waiver through the 2027 build, naming the entity tested.
- Calder consent to affiliate operation and sublicensing, with the licence and side letters.
- Founder reverse-vesting and a full-time chief financial officer by closing.

Assembly sits in Guadalajara into a market where a Section 232 investigation into imported robotics and industrial machinery opened in September 2025 and a related proclamation followed on 2026-10-28; USMCA-qualifying goods enter at zero and non-qualifying at 10 percent, which on a $33,000 robot is $3,300 a unit, $990,000 across 300 units and 72 percent of the $4,600 of unit headroom between the v4 budget and break-even [S1, S87, S88, S89].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tallis Agricultural Machinery | v4 contract manufacturer, engineering services, $2.5M note, board observer, $1.0M investor | 2025-02-10 note; 2025-03 services | unverified; services to 2027-06-30, sole build quote | S1 |
| Kestrel Equipment Finance | $2.5M facility at 11.5%, secured on the fleet | 2025-06-16 | unverified; $1.6M drawn, $1.5M cash covenant | S1 |
| Calder University | exclusive harvesting licence, 2.5% royalty, $40,000 minimum | 2022-01-20 | exclusive only while 100 robots are in commercial service at 2027-12-31 | S1, S86 |
| Granary Ventures | seed lead, $3.0M pro rata in this round | 2023-03-08 | unverified; committed | S1 |
| Vashti Harvest Services | robot relocation and night supervision, $310,000 paid | not disclosed | unverified; related party, board approved | S1 |

### Peers that carried the asset did not survive it

RaaS makes Orrin the lessor: at 64 robots it carries $3.07M of fleet on its balance sheet, at 360 $17.28M at the v3 build or $11.88M at the v4 budget, funded by $18M of equity and a $2.5M secured facility. Five of six comparable companies did not hold that position. Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP to CNH; Tortuga moved to a per-kilogram service and sold its IP and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025; Monarch raised a $133M Series C at a reported valuation above $500M in 2024, cut staff, and had its assets bought by Caterpillar in April 2026 after failing to pivot to software services; Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021; FarmWise moved from a per-acre Titan service to selling through Vulcan dealers. Carbon Robotics, which sells machines and raised a $70M Series D, is the exception. The same arithmetic that makes RaaS hard for Orrin is why growers like it, and the base rate says the model is financeable only if the fleet turns fast: 75 paid robot-seasons from 5 growers in 2026 against 360 planned in 2027, with 53 percent of 2026 seasons in two named customers, one of them the chief operating officer's former employer [S1, S28, S93, S97, S109, S116, S122].

### What must be true in twelve months

Three things. The round closes by 2026-12-15 so that build slots and deposits are in place for an April 2027 season; the v4 reaches $33,000 or less on a second and third quote, because at $48,000 the fleet consumes its own gross profit; and at least one grower renews at or near the $16,500 list after a season with an independently measured pick rate and damage rate. The signposts are dated and checkable: a signed 2027 contract at list price, a second contract-manufacturing quote, the v4 first-article build date, and whether the 100-robot licence test is met by robots in commercial service rather than robots built. Against $3.7M of cash, $410,000 of monthly net burn and a $1.5M cash covenant, usable runway is 5.4 months; a close in January 2027 makes 360 robots impossible and puts the licence cliff at risk [S1, S91].

Two limitations bound this judgement. The v4 unit cost is a single unverified quote and the service-cost target has no disclosed bridge from the reported figure, so the margin case cannot be tested from outside; and the public record returns no federal award to the company, which contradicts the SBIR revenue line in the plan.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks is a real operating company: Delaware-incorporated on 2021-09-14, 38 staff, three hardware generations shipped by 2026-03, $1.9M FY2025 revenue and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026. It is not yet safe to wire $12M into, because the entity signing the grower contracts, owning the fleet and carrying the equipment debt is a subsidiary the Series A does not buy. The $72.0M pre-money is internally coherent — $72.0M ÷ 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares = $4.7145, and $18.0M buys 3,818,008 shares, 20.0% of a $90.0M post — but 15,272,108 is not the "12,000,000 fully diluted total" printed beside it, which at $4.7145 is $56.6M. The priced count absorbs the $7.77M note conversion and the pool at 12% of post-money, so every derived figure must be rebuilt before a term sheet [S1].

No registry record was retrievable: the Delaware and California searches were unreachable, so incorporation, good standing, the agent for service, the foreign qualification and any UCC-1 over the fleet are unverified and rest on the company's own pages. The name returned no press, grant or patent trace either — a business with no public footprint or a failed retrieval, which the certificates would separate. Confidence below is capped accordingly.

### Three entities, and the investor buys the one without the contracts

::: entity
| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Salinas, CA | Corporation | Series A issuer; US staff; 5 filings and the Calder licence | Shareholders, below | S1 |
| Orrin Fleet Services LLC | California, 2023-11-02 | LLC | Fleet; grower contracts; Kestrel borrower | 100% parent | S1 |
| Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. | Jalisco, 2024-07-19 | S. de R.L. de C.V. | Gripper and harness assembly; 7 staff | 99% parent / 1% fleet LLC | S1 |
:::

The parent holds five US patent filings and an exclusive Calder University licence from 2022-01-20 for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum. The California LLC holds the fleet, the grower contracts and the Kestrel facility: $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 2025-06-16, 11.5%, secured on the fleet, with a $1.5M minimum cash covenant. The Mexican company assembles components with seven staff on a 99/1 split, the 1% with the California LLC, giving the Mexican company its second partner. Three questions follow, none answerable from the deck: whether the licence permits operation or sublicensing by an affiliate; whether Kestrel has consented to new equity and at which entity the covenant is tested; and whether the 99/1 split sits in a registered deed and the foreign-investment registry [S1].

### The $72M sits below its own preference stack

The 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed (about $11.0M on the 2023 round size, which the deck does not state): a $36.8M stack, 40.9% of the $90.0M post-money. The chief operating officer's wholly owned services company took $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date under a contract approved by a board he sits on, with no independent director, and his 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer. Conditions before closing:

- An independent director at signing, agreed by the lead, chairing audit and compensation.
- Observer rights limited to non-confidential sessions, no sight of diligence.
- A second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials.
- Kestrel consent and a covenant waiver through the 2027 build, naming the entity tested.

The priced count absorbs the $7.77M note conversion and the pool at 12% of post-money, so every derived figure must be rebuilt before a term sheet [S1].

::: entity
| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Salinas, CA | Corporation | Series A issuer; US staff; 5 filings and the Calder licence | Shareholders, below | S1 |
| Orrin Fleet Services LLC | California, 2023-11-02 | LLC | Fleet; grower contracts; Kestrel borrower | 100% parent | S1 |
| Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. | Jalisco, 2024-07-19 | S. de R.L. de C.V. | Gripper and harness assembly; 7 staff | 99% parent / 1% fleet LLC | S1 |
:::

The parent holds five US patent filings and an exclusive Calder University licence from 2022-01-20 for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum. The pool rises from 1,080,000 unallocated shares to 2,290,805, up 112%, costing existing holders $5.71M at the round price, 7.9% of the pre-money. After closing the board is five seats — two common, one seed, one Series A, one independent agreed by both — and the independent seat is vacant, so the tie-breaker is unfilled and the chair is the chief executive. - An independent director at signing, agreed by the lead, chairing audit and compensation.
- Observer rights limited to non-confidential sessions.
- A second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials.
- Kestrel consent and a covenant waiver through the 2027 build, naming the entity tested.
- Calder consent to affiliate operation and sublicensing, with the licence and side letters.
- Founder reverse-vesting and a full-time chief financial officer by closing.

arguments.markdown:
The team is built for the problem Orrin had in 2021, not the one it has in 2027. Dr. Imani Castellano, chief executive and board chair, is a perception researcher with a robotics PhD who spent five years in a university field-robotics lab and is named on eleven patent filings; Teodor Vashti, chief operating officer, ran harvest operations for two large berry growers across twenty years. Neither has built hardware at volume: nobody on the five-person executive group has taken a product past a few dozen units, none has founded or sold a company, and the co-founder who owned the technical roadmap left on 2023-08-31. All of this is company-reported and unverified; no education, employer, patent or press record could be retrieved for any named person [S1].

### The pairing fits two problems and misses the third

The combination matches the first two problems a picking robot has to solve — seeing ripe fruit, and being allowed onto a farm — and not the third, making 360 of them. Castellano invents and raises: the licensed university patent families come out of her lab, the company holds five filings of its own, and she is the face of the raise. Vashti sells and operates, and the commercial book shows it: five paying growers in 2026, the two named ones taking 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons, and the largest of those two is the farm where he was director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021, now contracted for 40 robots in 2027. That is genuine commercial proof and also the limit of it: the funnel is one man's twenty-year network, and the 2027 plan requires roughly 250 more robots sold in a four-month window before the season opens.

### A CTO seat empty for 26 months

The co-founder and CTO, Dr. Soren Abernathy, left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. He keeps 720,000 vested common shares — 6.0% before the round, 3.8% after — which is enough to make him a permanent party to the cap table and too little to give him any reason to protect the company. Whether he is a named inventor on the two licensed university families is not stated in the deck and could not be checked at the patent office; the deck attributes the licensed work to Castellano's lab, which is not the same as confirming he is outside it. No public footprint or new venture could be retrieved for him either. A 3.8% holder with unrestricted vested shares and the core perception work in his head is a hireable asset for any competitor or customer, and California does not let the company restrain where he works.

### The technical bet sits one level below the executive team

Dr. Mei Hollander joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at a single robotics company, moving from manipulation engineer to engineering manager for grippers. That is a direct match for the bruising problem — 3.8% of berries damaged in the 2025 pilots, and the reason one Florida grower ended its pilot in 2026-06 — and no match at all for the problem that decides 2027, which is cutting unit cost from $48,000 to a $33,000 build average while multiplying the fleet by 5.6. With no CTO above her, the hardest programme the company has attempted is owned by one vice president hired 32 months ago, on an equity package the deck does not describe; that is where retention risk concentrates [S1].

### Selling 360 robots with one new sales leader

Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales and Customer Success in 2025-06 after twenty years at a crop-inputs company, ending as regional sales director for the West. She has sixteen months in robotics. The contracted book for 2027 is 110 robots plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, against a 360-robot plan — 31% signed five months before the season, with two founder-sellers and one vice president to close the gap. The commercial risk is not that growers dislike the product; it is that this industry buys late, the season starts in April in California and December in Florida, and a 360-unit build has to be committed to before the orders exist. Nothing in the deck shows a sales pipeline by stage, so the 250-robot gap cannot be assessed from the materials at all.

### What would settle it

Three records would turn this from biography into evidence. Degree verification through each institution's registrar, because three of the five degrees sit at institutions whose names appear nowhere else in the file; patent-inventor records, because eleven filings at the university and five at the company are checkable and the departed CTO's inventorship is not stated; and reference calls at the four prior employers, most urgently the farm where the chief operating officer worked for seven years before founding the company. The comparison that matters is what Harvest CROO Robotics, Agrobot, Advanced Farm Technologies and Tortuga AgTech each had built by their third year — the test being whether any of them reached a contracted fleet of this size that fast; that comparison could not be sourced here and is not asserted. What can be said is that this team's own three years produced 14 pilot farms, two paying conversions and one lost pilot [S1].

arguments.markdown:
The team is built for the problem Orrin had in 2021, not the one it has in 2027. Dr. Imani Castellano, chief executive and board chair, is a perception researcher with a robotics PhD who spent five years in a university field-robotics lab and is named on eleven patent filings; Teodor Vashti, chief operating officer, ran harvest operations for two large berry growers across twenty years. Neither has built hardware at volume: nobody on the five-person executive group has taken a product past a few dozen units, none has founded or sold a company, and the co-founder who owned the technical roadmap left on 2023-08-31. All of this is company-reported and unverified; no education, employer, patent or press record could be retrieved for any named person [S1].

### The pairing fits two problems and misses the third

The combination matches the first two problems a picking robot has to solve — seeing ripe fruit, and being allowed onto a farm — and not the third, making 360 of them. Castellano invents and raises: the licensed university families come out of her lab, the company holds five filings of its own, and she is the face of the raise. Vashti sells and operates, and the book shows it: five paying growers in 2026, the two named ones taking 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons, and the largest of those two is the farm where he was director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021, contracted for 40 robots in 2027. That is commercial proof and also its limit: the funnel is one man's twenty-year network, and the plan needs 250 more robots sold in a four-month window [S1].

### A CTO seat empty for 26 months

The co-founder and CTO, Dr. Soren Abernathy, left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. He keeps 720,000 vested common shares — 6.0% before the round, 3.8% after — which makes him a permanent party to the cap table without giving him a reason to protect it. Whether he is a named inventor on the two licensed university families is not stated in the deck and could not be checked at the patent office; the deck attributes the licensed work to Castellano's lab, which is not the same as placing him outside it. No public footprint or new venture could be retrieved for him. A 3.8% holder with unrestricted vested shares and the core perception work in his head is a hireable asset for any competitor or customer, and California does not let the company restrain where he works [S1].

### The technical bet sits one level below the executive team

Dr. Mei Hollander joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at one robotics company, moving from manipulation engineer to engineering manager for grippers — company-reported and unverified. That is a direct match for the bruising problem, 3.8% of berries damaged in the 2025 pilots and the reason one Florida grower ended its pilot in 2026-06, and no match for the problem that decides 2027: cutting the build from $48,000 to a $33,000 average while multiplying the fleet by 5.6. With no CTO above her, the hardest programme the company has attempted is owned by one vice president hired 32 months ago, on an equity package the deck does not describe, which is where retention risk concentrates [S1].

### Selling 360 robots with one new sales leader

Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales and Customer Success in 2025-06 after twenty years at a crop-inputs company, ending as regional sales director for the West: sixteen months in robotics, unverified. The contracted book for 2027 is 110 robots plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, 31% of the 360-robot plan five months before the season, with two founder-sellers and one vice president to close the gap. The risk is not that growers dislike the product; it is that this industry buys late, the season opens in April in California and December in Florida, and a 360-unit build must be committed before the orders exist. The deck shows no pipeline by stage, so the 250-robot gap cannot be assessed from these materials at all [S1].

### What would settle it

Three records would turn this from biography into evidence: degree verification through each institution's registrar, because three of the five degrees sit at institutions named nowhere else in the file; patent-inventor records, because eleven university filings and five company filings are checkable and the departed CTO's inventorship is not stated; and reference calls at the four prior employers, most urgently the farm where the chief operating officer worked for seven years. Against the closest comparison available, the company's own history, the fleet went from 12 robots in 2024 to 64 in 2026, a 5.3x in two seasons, while the plan asks for 5.6x in one season and a one-third cost cut. The peer comparison the decision needs — what Harvest CROO Robotics, Agrobot, Advanced Farm Technologies and Tortuga AgTech had built by their third year — could not be sourced and is not asserted. For the lead, the implication is that people risk is priceable and should be priced: a CTO-level hire, a manufacturing leader and a retention grant for the VP Engineering as closing conditions, not intentions [S1].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 创始人与核心团队 Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 3 by Company Analyst, 8,626 characters)
The team is built for the problem Orrin had in 2021, not the one it has in 2027. Dr. Imani Castellano, chief executive and board chair, is a perception researcher with a robotics PhD who spent five years in a university field-robotics lab and is named on eleven patent filings; Teodor Vashti, chief operating officer, ran harvest operations for two large berry growers across twenty years. Neither has built hardware at volume: nobody on the five-person executive group has taken a product past a few dozen units, none has founded or sold a company, and the co-founder who owned the technical roadmap left on 2023-08-31. All of this is company-reported and unverified; no education, employer, patent or press record could be retrieved for any named person [S1].

### The pairing fits two problems and misses the third

The combination matches the first two problems a picking robot has to solve — seeing ripe fruit, and being allowed onto a farm — and not the third, making 360 of them. Castellano invents and raises: the licensed university families come out of her lab, the company holds five filings of its own, and she is the face of the raise. Vashti sells and operates, and the book shows it: five paying growers in 2026, the two named ones taking 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons, and the largest of those two is the farm where he was director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021, contracted for 40 robots in 2027. That is company-reported commercial proof and also its limit: the funnel is one man's twenty-year network, and the plan needs 250 more robots sold in a four-month window [S1].

### A CTO seat empty for 26 months

The co-founder and CTO, Dr. Soren Abernathy, left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. On the company's unverified account he keeps 720,000 vested common shares — 6.0% before the round, 3.8% after — which makes him a permanent party to the cap table without giving him a reason to protect it. Whether he is a named inventor on the two licensed university families is not stated in the deck and could not be checked at the patent office; the deck attributes the licensed work to Castellano's lab, which is not the same as placing him outside it. No public footprint or new venture could be retrieved for him. A 3.8% holder with unrestricted vested shares and the core perception work in his head is a hireable asset for any competitor or customer, and California does not let the company restrain where he works [S1].

### The technical bet sits one level below the executive team

Dr. Mei Hollander joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at one robotics company, moving from manipulation engineer to engineering manager for grippers — company-reported and unverified. That is a direct match for the bruising problem, 3.8% of berries damaged in the 2025 pilots and the reason one Florida grower ended its pilot in 2026-06, and no match for the problem that decides 2027: cutting the build from $48,000 to a $33,000 average while multiplying the fleet by 5.6. With no CTO above her, the hardest programme the company has attempted is owned by one vice president hired 32 months ago, on an equity package the deck does not describe, which is where retention risk concentrates [S1].

### Selling 360 robots with one new sales leader

Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales and Customer Success in 2025-06 after twenty years at a crop-inputs company, ending as regional sales director for the West: sixteen months in robotics, unverified. The contracted book for 2027 is 110 robots plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, 31% of the 360-robot plan five months before the season, with two founder-sellers and one vice president to close the gap. The risk is not that growers dislike the product; it is that this industry buys late, the season opens in April in California and December in Florida, and a 360-unit build must be committed before the orders exist. The deck shows no pipeline by stage, so the 250-robot gap cannot be assessed from these materials at all [S1].

### What would settle it

Three records would turn this from biography into evidence, all of them unverified now: degree checks through each institution's registrar, because three of the five degrees sit at institutions named nowhere else in the file; patent-inventor records, because eleven university filings and five company filings are checkable and the departed CTO's inventorship is not stated; and reference calls at the four prior employers, most urgently the farm where the chief operating officer worked for seven years. Against the closest comparison available, the company's own history, the fleet went from 12 robots in 2024 to 64 in 2026, a 5.3x in two seasons, while the plan asks for 5.6x in one season and a one-third cost cut. The peer comparison the decision needs — what Harvest CROO Robotics, Agrobot, Advanced Farm Technologies and Tortuga AgTech had built by their third year — could not be sourced and is not asserted. For the lead, the implication is that people risk is priceable and should be priced: a CTO-level hire, a manufacturing leader and a retention grant for the VP Engineering as closing conditions, not intentions [S1].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 技术与产品 Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,898 characters)
The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position is a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure, not a picked-acre figure. Compared with Harvest CROO, the unit arithmetic is identical and the acreage eight times higher, so coverage follows capital per machine, not a better algorithm [S1, S27].

| Pick rate | 94% of ripe berries detected | no peer-reviewed open-field rate above 95% found | 212 company-chosen rows, unverified | S1, S27 |
| Bruised or punctured | 3.8% | 5% serious damage, 10% total defects, 2% decay | company measurement, definition undisclosed, unverified | S1, S120 |
| Unripe picked | 2.1% | not applicable | company measurement, unverified | S1 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not disclosed | company log, unverified | S1 |
| Operator interventions | every 3.4 h = 5.9 per robot-day | 47 per technician-day at 8 robots each | derived from company figures, unverified | S1 |

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the week in which a bruise expresses itself. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

::: evidence
**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling. [S1, S120]**

Packers work to a lot-level allowance for total defects, serious damage and decay rather than a per-machine one, and a bruise that appears after a week in the cooler is still the grower's loss.
:::

### What is defensible is the data and the service, not the patents

What it cannot buy in that time is the seventy-five robot-seasons of grower trust built in two valleys, which is the real barrier and a sales one.

The questions that would move this section are exact: the ripe-fruit density and pick interval the test rows saw, the damage rate after a week at one degree Celsius, how many of the hourly interventions need a person in the field, and whether the Calder licence counts robots deployed or robots paid for."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,451 characters)
The plan does not add up on its own numbers, which are company-stated and unverified. At the current $48,000 build even the 2027 list price leaves each robot-season $1,100 short over a four-season life, the v4 must land below $28,400 to earn its keep at the $12,700 renewal price, the company's own FY2027 revenue projection implies an average price of $12,778 rather than the $16,500 list, and a 5.6-times fleet increase by April 2027 rests on one outsourced build quote and a $14M gap in a round that has not closed [S1].

### The price rise is a solvency requirement, not a margin story

At $5,600 a season of reported, unverified field service, transport, insurance and consumables, a robot priced at the $12,700 renewal average can cost at most $28,400 and still repay itself over four seasons; the v4 budget is $33,000. Priced at the $16,500 list it can cost $43,600 and still repay, which the $48,000 v3 does not. The gap is not theoretical: on the reported costs each robot-season at the renewal price loses $4,900, so a 360-robot fleet at the 2027 revenue line of $4.6M loses $1.76M a season before a dollar of overhead, and even the $33,000 v4 turns positive only if service cost also falls to the $1,750 target. Depreciation sits in operating expenses rather than cost of revenue, so the reported 52 percent gross margin for 2027 excludes $3.24M of hardware consumption on a $4.6M revenue line, alongside $2.02M of service cost, against total gross profit of $2.9M. The payback figure that carries the story uses the best case at every input: at a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, 2.1 seasons is right, but at the $5,600 the company reports, unverified, for 2026, payback stretches to 2.8 seasons at that build and 4.4 seasons at today's $48,000, longer than the four-season life the same page assumes. The gap between $1,750 and $5,600 is $3,850 a robot-season, $1.386M across 360 robots, and no cost bridge is disclosed for it [S1].

### A price that is too low to be replacing a hand crew

The pricing question runs the other way from the usual one. At $9,500 for the 3.5 acres a robot serves, a grower pays $2,714 an acre a season; the 2027 list is $4,714 an acre. The California Strawberry Commission puts the cost to cultivate and harvest strawberries at an average $87,000 an acre, $15.34 a tray, rising to $17.73 a tray in 2023, so Orrin's asking price is between 3 and 5 percent of the total cost of the crop [S1, S121]. A machine that replaced the hand crew over 3.5 acres would be worth several times that, and five growers buying 75 robot-seasons would not have left it on the table. Either the robot harvests a small fraction of the fruit on the acres it drives, or the price was set to buy pilots and the 2027 increase is the first real test of willingness to pay. Grower B cutting from 22 robots to 14 and Grower E exiting over bruising say the test is live; the two letters of intent for 50 robots are not contracts.

### Manufacturing risk sits with one supplier that is also a customer, a creditor and an investor

The build plan is 300 robots for $9.9M, 55 percent of the round, at an average $33,000 on a design that has never been manufactured. That is a 31 percent cut from the $48,000 v3 on a single quote from Tallis Agricultural Machinery dated 2026-08, a counterparty that is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, the $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer, the quoted contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round. Assembly sits in Guadalajara into a market where a Section 232 investigation into imported robotics and industrial machinery opened in September 2025 and a related proclamation followed on 2026-10-28; USMCA-qualifying goods enter at zero and non-qualifying at 10 percent, which on a $33,000 robot is $3,300 a unit, $990,000 across 300 units and 72 percent of the $4,600 of unit headroom between the v4 budget and break-even [S1, S87, S88, S89].

| Calder University | exclusive harvesting licence, 2.5% royalty, $40,000 minimum | 2022-01-20 | exclusive only while 100 robots are in commercial service at 2027-12-31 | S1, S86 |

| Vashti Harvest Services | robot relocation and night supervision, $310,000 paid | not disclosed | unverified; related party, board approved | S1 |

### Peers that carried the asset did not survive it

RaaS makes Orrin the lessor: at 64 robots it carries $3.07M of fleet on its balance sheet, at 360 $17.28M at the v3 build or $11.88M at the v4 budget, funded by $18M of equity and a $2.5M secured facility. Five of six comparable companies did not hold that position. Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP to CNH; Tortuga moved to a per-kilogram service and sold its IP and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025; Monarch raised a $133M Series C at a reported valuation above $500M in 2024, cut staff, and had its assets bought by Caterpillar in April 2026 after failing to pivot to software services; Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021; FarmWise moved from a per-acre Titan service to selling through Vulcan dealers. Carbon Robotics, which sells machines and raised a $70M Series D, is the exception. The same arithmetic that makes RaaS hard for Orrin is why growers like it, and the base rate says the model is financeable only if the fleet turns fast: 75 paid robot-seasons from 5 growers in 2026 against 360 planned in 2027, with 53 percent of 2026 seasons in two named customers, one of them the chief operating officer's former employer [S1, S28, S93, S97, S109, S116, S122].

### What must be true in twelve months

Three things. The round closes by 2026-12-15 so that build slots and deposits are in place for an April 2027 season; the v4 reaches $33,000 or less on a second and third quote, because at $48,000 the fleet consumes its own gross profit; and at least one grower renews at or near the $16,500 list after a season with an independently measured pick rate and damage rate. The signposts are dated and checkable: a signed 2027 contract at list price, a second contract-manufacturing quote, the v4 first-article build date, and whether the 100-robot licence test is met by robots in commercial service rather than robots built. Against $3.7M of cash, $410,000 of monthly net burn and a $1.5M cash covenant, usable runway is 5.4 months; a close in January 2027 makes 360 robots impossible and puts the licence cliff at risk [S1, S91].

Two limitations bound this judgement. The v4 unit cost is a single unverified quote and the service-cost target has no disclosed bridge from the reported figure, so the margin case cannot be tested from outside; and the public record returns no federal award to the company, which contradicts the SBIR revenue line in the plan."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 5 by Market Analyst, 8,890 characters)
The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool, and hand-pick labour alone is worth $25,000-35,000 an acre, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at its own $16,500 robot-season price and one robot per 3.5 acres, 100% of US strawberry acreage is worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The opportunity is large enough to build a company on and too small to support the headline number, which moves the investment question from market size to adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps once competitors arrive [S1].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** The $310M and $16,500 inputs are company figures, unverified; at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year and 15% adoption is worth $35.4M, while $310M requires 132% of the US acreage base. Source: S1.
