The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces 90% of the US crop; Florida is the only other significant producer at 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline, while the California Strawberry Commission projects 7-8 million trays a week through August 2026. A robot that saves labour therefore sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so its own growth has to come from penetration, not from the crop [S9, S8].

### The wage bill sets the price ceiling
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. The 2024 UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural costs and $112,694 of total cost, on 9,000 trays at $11; UC Davis puts labour at 50-60% of variable production cost, with pickers paid $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour. That implies hand-pick labour of $25,000-35,000 an acre. At $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $4,714 an acre, 13-19% of the wage bill it targets, and a 10% harvest-cost saving would be worth $7,929 an acre to the grower. The gap between value and price is the most decision-relevant number in the market case: either the robot removes only part of the crew's work, or Orrin is pricing for adoption and has room to raise price later [S10, S12].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, which is 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; the entire US strawberry acreage at the same density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is also ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not the 2% the market page assumes, and at the $12,700 renewal price it implies 7.1%. Robot density is internally conservative in the other direction: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over a 210-day California season is 315 acre-passes, which at the 40-50 passes a season UC Davis documents serves 6.3-7.9 acres, not 3.5 — one robot per 3.5 acres implies 90 passes. Either throughput is a peak measurement or the fleet count is inflated; both change revenue per robot [S1, S12].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet that works both calendars is utilised for eleven months and a fleet that works one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop production under high tunnels is being tried on a limited scale in Santa Maria with no published acreage, so the addressable set is open-field acres with slopes under 4%, no standing water and rows wide enough for a track — the same exclusions Orrin applied to its own test rows. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia, where Orrin has no sales or service [S9, S13, S14].

| California | 43,726 acres (2026); $3.47B harvest cost (author calculation) | +2.0% acres 2025-26; terminal price -3.3% CAGR 2024-26 | Entered: 14 pilots since 2024, 4 paying growers | 7-month season; slopes over 4% and standing water excluded; retailer bruising specifications | Hand crews, harvest-aid platforms, Harvest CROO (Florida) | S9, S10, S1 |
| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed, USDA NASS state series would settle it | Not disclosed; NASS series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over fruit bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation for a rented fleet | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems; competes with US fruit on price | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |
| Europe (Spain, Netherlands) | Not sized; Agrobot capability is a company claim, unverified | Not disclosed | Not entered | CE marking, distance, no service network | Agrobot harvest-aid platforms | S77 |
| Australia | Not sized; patent national-phase entry due 2026-10-30 is a company statement, unverified | Not disclosed | Patent entry only, no revenue | No presence, no service | None identified | S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024, with Florida above 14% of the national total; the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost changed on 2025-10-02, when the Department of Labor replaced the USDA Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate with BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics data; the rule is under litigation and trade summaries disagree on the outcome, one showing the average rate falling to $15.96 an hour from $17.74 and another showing entry-level rates up 3.7% with declines in 13 states. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic rather than annual: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The risk cuts both ways: a lower OEWS-based wage floor lengthens robot payback by roughly the same percentage, while a court overturning the rule restores the higher Farm Labor Survey rate and shortens it. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes went from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966, but only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: what is the pure hand-pick wage line per acre in the 2024 UC budget? What are the final 2026-27 adverse effect wage rates for California and Florida? How many passes and acres sit behind the 3.5-acre robot density [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117]?"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,944 characters)
Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics, co-founded by Wish Farms owner Gary Wishnatzki, announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester reached performance rates on par with human harvesting in a commercial picking operation at Duette, Florida — a direct open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but it removes the "only player" premise. What disciplines Orrin's price is less the rival robot than the hand crew it must beat, the harvest-aid platform that takes part of the saving at a fraction of the capital, and the 2025 exits that show how hard harvest robotics is to fund [S27, S28].

::: evidence
**The field is thinner than the technology narrative implies, and it is not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in 2025. Source: S27, S28, S34.
:::

The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm Technologies, which had reached named commercial growers in California, ceased operations in 2025, reported on 2025-07-08; Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and team to vertical-farming company Oishii. No public market shares exist; the best proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre US base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S27, S34].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo said it "was unable to develop the market traction necessary to support its business", and it put its IP and assets up for sale on 2021-06-29. Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, was sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021. The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against a $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30. RaaS shifts capital to Orrin's balance sheet and removes the grower's capex objection, but it concentrates the constraint rather than removing it [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour, and conveyors already raise productivity by cutting walking; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform adds a partial step: it carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost, a company claim that is unverified but captures part of the saving with none of the autonomy risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: the reported transfer of Advanced Farm's IP to CNH Industrial is unverified, but a picking arm on a harvest-aid platform that already sells and services equipment is a cheaper route to the grower than a new autonomous fleet. Orrin must beat a crew costing $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour and charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field row architecture, same RaaS model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim already in the market. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published pick rate or bruising data, and no California service network — where Orrin's 14 pilots and 4 paying growers sit. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct packing into the grower's clamshells so fruit is handled once, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows, and the COO's California grower relationships. It is a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly [S30, S1].

### The price is the tell
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025 and 2026 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase, with renewals averaging $12,700. It is a large increase on a base not yet renewed at list, and the company's own disclosure contains the counter-evidence: Grower E in Plant City ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers. Offsetting it, four growers contracted 110 robots for 2027 (Marisol Ridge 40, Pajaro Bluff 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20), so some buyers accept the quality at the renewal price. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,908 characters)
At the price Orrin has actually signed, one robot-season does not cover the depreciation on the robot, so the rental business loses money on every unit today; the case rests on an unbuilt v4 and a price increase no grower has signed.

### The revenue is mostly not rental

The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season (company-reported, unaudited): about seven months in California (April-October) and four in Florida (December-March), one season at a time, with Orrin owning, maintaining and insuring the fleet. No multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M divides into robot rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E is little better, with rental at $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%). The engineering customer is also a $2.5M noteholder, a board observer, the quoted manufacturer of the v4 and a $1.0M committed investor in this round, so half of FY2025 revenue is related-party and 80% is one-off, grant-funded or related-party. What the company has proven is that five growers will rent 75 robot-seasons at $9,500; the rest of the revenue line is an engineering contract and a grant, and its own strategy assumes both disappear by 2028 [S1].

### One robot-season loses $8,100 before any overhead

|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Interest-only debt service ($1.6M x 11.5% / 75 seasons) | (2,453) | 25.8 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Cash contribution after interest-only debt service | 1,447 | 15.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Cash contribution after amortising debt service | (3,051) | (32.1) | S1 (unverified), calc |

The company-reported 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: fleet depreciation sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue. Charging the $48,000 v3 over its four-season life puts $12,000 against each season, more than the $9,500 the grower pays before a single technician is paid. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and should not be added; the economic measure is the negative $8,100 contribution, while the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only and -$3,051 if it amortises over the robot's four-season life. The benchmark: United Rentals earned a gross margin of 38.0% on equipment rentals in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue. Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at the $16,500 list price with the v3, and only reaches +19.1% with both the list price and a $31,000 v4 [S21].

### The 2.1-season payback is the best case of three unproven inputs

The claimed 2.1 seasons is $31,000 divided by ($16,500 list price less $1,750 target service), which drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely. Putting it back gives 2.53 seasons on the company's own target cost and price. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet actually ran in 2026, against a four-season asset life. Even at the $31,000 target build and the signed price the payback is 7.95 seasons; at the list price and the current build it is 4.40 seasons, longer than the asset lasts. Of the four inputs that decide payback, build cost is unbuilt, price unsigned, service cost unreconciled to the technician ratio and transport omitted from the slide. All of these are company-reported, unaudited figures [S1].

### Utilisation cannot repair a per-season capital charge

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two (the California and Florida seasons cover eleven months). At the signed price the fleet needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 seasons, 85% of the maximum; at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles its revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads fixed overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital hurdle. Service cost is no more forgiving. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 loaded field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour, over 213 days, costs $41,611 per technician-season, or $5,201 per robot-season; at the $29.60 machine-operator rate it is $6,305. The deck reports $3,100, which implies a technician costs $24,800 for seven months before a vehicle, tools or travel. At 360 robots the same ratio needs 45 technicians and $1.12M at the reported rate, so the cost is linear in robots, not diluted by scale; on the $6,305 figure, gross profit at the signed price falls to $695, or 7.3%, before depreciation [S1, S10].

### Price is not the constraint; proof and quality are

At one robot per 3.5 acres the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the 2027 list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre - 3.4% to 5.9% of the labour bill the robot targets. At 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray, each percentage point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21% to 36% of the robot fee; the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee and 80% of the list fee. That asymmetry explains why price has not moved to list and why one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising: a grower is buying an option on a harvest, not a proven substitute for a crew. The risk is not that growers cannot afford the robot but that the robot, at 94% of detected ripe fruit and 86% uptime, cannot yet promise the bruising and reliability a retail supply chain requires [S10].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 3.4% | S1 (unverified), S10 |
| 2027 renewal average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 4.6% | S1 (unverified), S10 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 5.9% | S1 (unverified), S10 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 6.3% | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 4.8% | S1 (unverified), calc |

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at a small fraction of the harvest cost it addresses, so a working unit could charge several times more; the answer is that two peers with more capital and more robots did not get there. Tortuga and FarmWise both owned fleets and rented or serviced them before retreating, and Orrin's capital intensity per robot is essentially the same as Tortuga's.

|---|---|---|---|
| Tortuga AgTech | 150 harvesting robots; about $50M deployed over eight years | IP, assets and team sold to Oishii, 2025-03 | S93 |
| FarmWise | $45M Series B in 2022; $65M equity in total | Titan run as a service, then Vulcan sold through dealer RDO Equipment; wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms, 2025-04 | S100, S116 |

### What would have to be true

The unit turns positive only if both conditions hold at once: a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling and a price at or above the breakeven in the table, with the v4 in service. The investment should therefore be conditioned on signed 2027 contracts at the list price with deposits, a verified v4 bill of materials from a manufacturer independent of the largest revenue customer, an audited service-cost build reconciled to the 1:8 technician ratio, and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on the company's own figures; the service-cost cross-check and the bruise-to-revenue link are medium confidence, and the open questions are the loan amortisation schedule, the Florida season price and the share of bruised fruit actually culled.

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unaudited) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures alone produce the negative contribution, the 12.31-season payback at the signed price and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven [S1].
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 财务分析 Financial Analysis (financials, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,974 characters)
The full round funds the fleet plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the minimum close the plan is not funded, the cash covenant binds before the season starts, and most of the reported ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023-FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time head of finance. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The company-reported, unaudited $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level [S1].

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep a minimum unrestricted balance at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts. It moves with the closing date: a quarter's delay does not shorten the runway by three months, it lands after the covenant is breached, making the closing date a condition of the investment.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 (company-reported, unaudited) less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is $6.085M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

On the company-reported, unaudited plan, three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4, so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, $78 above the $12,700 renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and $13.93M of capex nowhere in the plan. The only capex-free reading is 360 robots each doing two seasons at $17,900, requiring a Florida business that does not exist at scale [S1].

### Margins are flattered by where depreciation sits

The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into -$0.31M, or -5.5%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while the 52% and 61% equal the company-wide margin, so the series changes definition between years. Only the top-right corner - list price with a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling - produces positive contribution; the base case sits in the negative middle, the downside is worse, and even the upside leaves the company loss-making. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 退出策略分析 Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 4 by Valuation Analyst, 8,947 characters)
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while the harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.8x — enough to return capital, not enough to carry a venture fund. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Each buyer is buying a different asset. Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would be buying the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend its See & Spray and autonomy stack into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would be buying a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would be buying fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but less need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would be buying harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet — they can manufacture — so the fleet is a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security, grower data, supply chain; no public robotics M&A found (not publicly disclosed) | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 |

| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | Growth capital; requires scale, float and profitability; no comparable IPO in the set (not publicly disclosed) | 2030+ | Very low | S95 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag was bought for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven, a public precision-ag company at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI was acquired by AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii for undisclosed terms. No harvesting-robot company in the set has been sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none reached $100M+, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. The 2025 market recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money, a $100M exit returns 1.1x before dilution, a $250M exit 2.8x and a $40M exit 1.0x because of the 1x preference. With illustrative probabilities of 40% at $40M, 35% at $100M, 20% at $250M and 5% at $500M, the expected MOIC is 1.6x before dilution and 1.4x after a 20% Series B — below the 3x a venture fund needs. The counter-case is that Deere or CNH pays $250-305M for the team and perception model, as they did for Blue River and Bear Flag; if Orrin proves 95% pick rates at 360 robots, a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 base rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue, the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; a round above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is: $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Revenue | $5.6M | $13.2M | $13.2M at 7x forward, or $18M at 5x | S95 (unverified) |
| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |
| Renewal | 110 contracted 2027 seasons | n/a | 80% or more of 2026 paying growers renew | S95 (unverified) |
| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to US, European and Japanese strategics: Deere and AGCO are US-listed, CNH is Dutch/Italian and Kubota is Japanese, and all have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, the Calder license and the grower data, and the Mexico assembly adds tariff and supply-chain diligence. An IPO is not a realistic exit before 2030: $1.9M of revenue, a $5.2M net loss in FY2025 and no comparable ag-robotics IPO in the set; a listing would need scale and audited growth the company does not have. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes the exit to 2030-2032. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.0x at $90M, 1.1x at $100M, 1.7x at $150M, 2.8x at $250M and 5.6x at $500M; a 20% Series B dilution cuts those to 1.0x, 1.0x, 1.4x, 2.2x and 4.4x. The IRR is 0% at $90M, 10.8% at $150M and 22.7% at $250M over five years. A 20-30% lower entry price, or a 1.5x preference, would make the same exits work; at $72M pre-money the lead is buying an option that needs a $250M+ bid. The implication is to pass at $72M pre-money, or invest only at a 20-30% lower price with a 1.5x preference and a milestone tranche. Diligence should confirm the Advanced Farm and Tortuga prices, the ownership of the grower contracts (Orrin Fieldworks or Orrin Fleet Services), the Calder license's change-of-control terms and the customer concentration — 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons sit with two named growers. Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case are being decided by other people before the 2027 season: a wage floor a California court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff decision due by 2027-04-26, a university exclusivity test on 2027-12-31 and a California rule on unpiloted machines. The balance is mildly negative for 2027 and positive after it, which argues for staging the round rather than passing on it.

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's figure of a quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14 while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost over 40 passes, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre [S80, S1].

### The cut is provisional

On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing adjustment, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and required the Department of Labor to warn employers of possible back-wage adjustments. My judgement is that a higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, which would restore most of that saving and lift the ceiling Orrin prices against.

### Who is organised, and against what

The union that won that case is most likely to shape the operating rule. In August 2026 California was drafting a trailer bill to let unpiloted machines work alongside farmworkers, and labour groups opposed it. That rule decides the unit economics: one technician to eight robots supports the $3,100 field-service line, and a human-spotter requirement would take it to $24,800 and turn the 41% gross margin negative [S84, S82, S1]. California overtime adds to the hand cost the robot displaces. Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement rather than wage rules, and the one pilot the company has lost is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its own capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper at 50% apply even under USMCA. The new tail: the Section 232 proclamation of 2026-10-28 on robotics and industrial machinery found that imports threaten national security, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days, with tariffs, quotas and fees left open [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The university licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A single binary test with no cure is harsher than standard practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones, cure periods and step-in rights. The 2027 plan clears the threshold, so the cliff needs 72% slippage; conversion risk 20%–25% (analyst estimate). If the licensed families were federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to agree that products embodying the invention are manufactured substantially in the United States, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the retail clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and fruit packed in the field reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists to obtain and no FDA action against machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds; where quality binds it is not, and the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, quoted contract manufacturer and investor in this round; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no federal award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91].

Four records are requested with this report — the H-2A disclosure files and wage table (the department's page returned an error on 2026-10-30), the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the California bill text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. Taken together, the four factors change what a season is worth rather than whether Orrin can sell one: the cheapest protection is to price the 2027 tranche against the wage-floor outcome and to make the USMCA certificate and the licence warranty conditions of closing.

rows.belief: The pain is real and countable: $79,288 an acre of harvest cost on California's Central Coast against $22,264 of cultural cost, with labour at 50-60% of variable production cost. But the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026 — the skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 cut California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate to $16.45 an hour from $19.97 (-17.6%) and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23 (-23.2%) — so urgency is weaker than the deck assumes.

rows.belief: The picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its deck: 94% pick rate on 212 company-chosen rows across 9 of 14 farms is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator, but 5.6 seconds a berry x 2 arms x 20 hours x 86% uptime is 22,114 berries, about 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable advantage is 75 paid robot-seasons of labelled fleet data and service density in two California valleys; the patents are not the moat.
rows.evidence: Pick rate, bruising 3.8%, unripe 2.1%, uptime 86% and the 1.5-acre claim [S1]; the coverage arithmetic against 9,000 trays an acre and a 3-5 day pick interval [S119, S1]; Harvest CROO's identical per-arm arithmetic at 8 times the acreage shows coverage follows capital per machine [S27].

rows.change: A published adoption base rate for fresh-market berry harvesting, or a retailer programme requiring machine-harvested fruit, would move the curve.

The full round funds the fleet plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the minimum close the plan is not funded, the cash covenant binds before the season starts, and most of the reported ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023-FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time head of finance. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The company-reported, unaudited $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level [S1].

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep a minimum unrestricted balance at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts. It moves with the closing date: a quarter's delay does not shorten the runway by three months, it lands after the covenant is breached, making the closing date a condition of the investment.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 (company-reported, unaudited) less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is $6.085M. [S1]
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG评估 ESG Assessment (esg, revision 3 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,971 characters)
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case are being decided by other people before the 2027 season: a wage floor a California court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff decision due by 2027-04-26, a university exclusivity test on 2027-12-31 and a California rule on unpiloted machines. The balance is mildly negative for 2027 and positive after it, which argues for staging the round rather than passing on it.

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's figure of a quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14 while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost over 40 passes, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre [S80, S1].

### The cut is provisional

On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing adjustment, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and required the Department of Labor to warn employers of possible back-wage adjustments. My judgement is that a higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, which would restore most of that saving and lift the ceiling Orrin prices against.

### Who is organised, and against what

The union that won that case is most likely to shape the operating rule. In August 2026 California was drafting a trailer bill to let unpiloted machines work alongside farmworkers, and labour groups opposed it. That rule decides the unit economics: one technician to eight robots supports the $3,100 field-service line, and a human-spotter requirement would take it to $24,800 and turn the 41% gross margin negative [S84, S82, S1]. California overtime adds to the hand cost the robot displaces. Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement rather than wage rules, and the one pilot the company has lost is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its own capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper at 50% apply even under USMCA. The new tail: the Section 232 proclamation of 2026-10-28 on robotics and industrial machinery found that imports threaten national security, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days, with tariffs, quotas and fees left open [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The university licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A single binary test with no cure is harsher than standard practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones, cure periods and step-in rights. The 2027 plan clears the threshold, so the cliff needs 72% slippage; conversion risk 20%–25% (analyst estimate). If the licensed families were federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to agree that products embodying the invention are manufactured substantially in the United States, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the retail clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and fruit packed in the field reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists to obtain and no FDA action against machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds; where quality binds it is not, and the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, quoted contract manufacturer and investor in this round; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no federal award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91].

Four records are requested with this report — the H-2A disclosure files and wage table (the department's page returned an error on 2026-10-30), the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the California bill text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. Taken together, the four factors change what a season is worth rather than whether Orrin can sell one: the cheapest protection is to price the 2027 tranche against the wage-floor outcome and to make the USMCA certificate and the licence warranty conditions of closing.

Orrin Fieldworks is a real operating company: Delaware-incorporated on 2021-09-14, 38 staff, three hardware generations shipped by 2026-03, $1.9M FY2025 revenue and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 — all company-reported and unverified. It is not yet safe to wire $12M into, because the entity signing the grower contracts, owning the fleet and carrying the equipment debt is a subsidiary the Series A does not buy. The $72.0M pre-money is internally coherent — $72.0M ÷ 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares = $4.7145, and $18.0M buys 3,818,008 shares, 20.0% of a $90.0M post — but 15,272,108 is not the "12,000,000 fully diluted total" printed beside it, which at $4.7145 is $56.6M. No registry record was retrievable: the Delaware and California searches were unreachable, so incorporation, good standing, the agent for service, the foreign qualification and any UCC-1 over the fleet rest on the company's own pages. The name returned no press, grant or patent trace either — no footprint, or a failed retrieval. Confidence below is capped accordingly.

### Three entities, and the investor buys the one without the contracts

| Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Salinas, CA | Corporation | Series A issuer; US staff; 5 filings and the Calder licence | Shareholders, below | S1, unverified |
| Orrin Fleet Services LLC | California, 2023-11-02 | LLC | Fleet; grower contracts; Kestrel borrower | 100% parent | S1, unverified |
| Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. | Jalisco, 2024-07-19 | S. de R.L. de C.V. | Gripper and harness assembly; 7 staff | 99% parent / 1% fleet LLC | S1, unverified |

The parent holds five US patent filings and an exclusive Calder University licence from 2022-01-20 for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum. The California LLC holds the fleet, the grower contracts and the Kestrel facility: $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 2025-06-16, 11.5%, secured on the fleet, with a $1.5M minimum cash covenant. The Mexican company assembles components with seven staff on a 99/1 split, the 1% with the California LLC. On the company's unverified cap table, the pool rises from 1,080,000 unallocated shares to 2,290,805, up 112%, costing existing holders $5.71M at the round price, 7.9% of the pre-money. Founders fall from 47.0% to 29.5%; 2.0 points is the pool, and the former CTO keeps 3.3% of the combined founder block. The 80% note conversion yields 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares against 1,648,000 at full price, moving $1.95M to noteholders and an estimated $0.6M from the founders. Voting percentages assume one vote per share and no voting agreement, which the deck does not disclose — material, because two common seats of five is all that keeps the founders off a board they do not control [S1].

### The $72M sits below its own preference stack

On the company's figures, unverified, the 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M assumed from the 2023 round size, which the deck does not state): a $36.8M stack, 40.9% of the $90.0M post-money. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit, where 46.5% as-converted equals the preference. At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at a $79M sale and needs a $180M exit for 2x, so the pre-money is best underwritten as an option struck at $79M, not a mark on the common. The structure is founder-friendly; the size of the stack decides whether a modest success reaches the common at all [S1].

### What it sells, and to whom

Orrin sells a robot-season, not a robot. The customer is a strawberry grower, the user is the crew the robot displaces, and the budget owner holds the harvest-labour line. Growth comes from converting pilots into paid seasonal rentals and renewing them: 14 pilot farms since 2024, two conversions in 2025, five paying growers in 2026, 110 robots contracted for 2027 plus 50 under letters of intent. Revenue quality is thinner than the $3.2M ARR headline: $1.4M is contracted robot-seasons at the $12,700 renewal price, $1.2M is engineering services ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M is non-binding letters of intent. ### Governance: five roles in one counterparty and an empty chair

After closing the board is five seats — two common, one seed, one Series A, one independent agreed by both — and the independent seat is vacant, so the tie-breaker is unfilled and the chair is the chief executive. Tallis Agricultural Machinery is at once a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer at 37.5% of stated ARR, the quoted manufacturer whose $33,000 unit cost underpins the $9.9M robot budget, a board observer and a $1.0M investor; it also employed the chief executive in 2010-2011. The chief operating officer's wholly owned services company took $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date under a contract approved by a board he sits on, with no independent director, and his 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer [S1]. Conditions before closing:

- An independent director at signing, agreed by the lead, chairing audit and compensation.
- Observer rights limited to non-confidential sessions.
- A second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials.
- Kestrel consent, a covenant waiver through the 2027 build, and Calder consent to affiliate operation and sublicensing.
- Founder reverse-vesting and a full-time chief financial officer by closing.

{"url":"https://www.1752.vc/learn/down-round","title":"Down Round Explained: Triggers, Terms, and 2026 Rates","text":"A down round is a financing in which a company sells shares at a lower price per share than in its previous round. Anti-dilution protection often shifts part of the cost onto common holders, and the new investor usually arrives with leverage to reset terms. Down rounds made up 11.4 percent of rounds in Carta's Q1 2026 data and 12.1 percent of Cooley's Q2 2026 deals.
Definition: A down round is an equity financing priced below the company's prior round: the new price per share is lower, and the new pre-money valuation is below the previous round's post-money valuation.
A down round is rarely where the problem starts. It's where the problem gets a price.
Illustrative worked example: A company raised a $5M Series A at $2.00 per share, a $25M post-money valuation on 12,500,000 fully diluted shares. Growth stalls, and a new investor offers $4M at $1.00 per share, a $12.5M pre-money valuation. Under a broad-based weighted average anti-dilution clause, the Series A conversion price falls from $2.00 to about $1.76, so the 2,500,000 preferred shares now convert into roughly 2,845,000 common shares. The other 10,000,000 shares, mostly founders and employees, fall from 80 percent to about 59.4 percent: 60.6 percent from the 4,000,000 new shares alone, and the rest from the roughly 345,000 extra shares issued to the Series A. Under full ratchet, the same holders would drop to about 52.6 percent.What triggers a down roundA round is "down" if the price per share falls, even when the headline valuation looks similar. Carta's guide lists internal problems (missed revenue targets, lawsuits, competition), market downturns, and sector-specific investor scrutiny as common causes. We group them into four patterns:

A missed plan. The company raised on a forecast and delivered half of it.
A market reset. The company grew, but valuation multiples fell faster, so a price set in a hotter market is hard to match.
An over-priced prior round. The last round was arguably the mistake, and the down round is the correction. Our guide to seed valuations and venture return math shows how to choose a price you can grow into, and our take on the $100M pre-seed problem covers what too much money too early can do to discipline.
A distressed insider round. No outside lead exists, and insiders reprice to fund a turnaround.
How common down rounds are in 2026Down rounds peaked after the 2021 boom and have been falling since. Carta's State of Private Markets report for Q1 2026 put the down-round rate at 11.4 percent, back in line with 2019 and 2020 levels, after a peak of 22 percent in 2023. In Q4 2025 Carta counted fewer than 14 percent, then the lowest rate in three years.
Cooley's Q2 2026 Venture Financing Report, covering 166 deals, shows 83.6 percent up rounds, 4.3 percent flat, and 12.1 percent down, compared with 10.9 percent down in Q1 2026. For context, Carta's down round guide puts the average from Q1 2015 to Q3 2022 at 10.6 percent. Today's rate is close to the long-run norm.
Two related terms from Cooley's Q2 2026 data: pay-to-play provisions appeared in 8.4 percent of deals, up from about 7 percent in Q1, and recapitalizations in 1.8 percent.Preferred investors with anti-dilution protection. Their conversion price drops, so they receive more common shares on conversion. The broad-based weighted average version produces a moderate adjustment; full ratchet resets the price entirely. The guide to the anti-dilution provision walks through the formula.
Founders and employees. They absorb the new shares and the adjustment, as the worked example shows.
The new investor. Buys at the lower price and may ask for richer terms, such as a senior or multiple liquidation preference, a larger option pool, board changes, or a pay-to-play provision.
Existing funds. Cooley GO notes that venture funds report to their limited partners based on portfolio value, so existing investors may have to write down their holdings after a down round. That's one reason insiders resist a lower price even when it is fair.Down round effects on employee options and the 409AA down round hits employees twice: dilution, and options that may now be underwater. Carta's guide warns that options priced above the current share price can become worthless if the price does not recover.

Get a new 409A valuation. Carta's 409A guide lists closing a new financing round as a material event that calls for a fresh valuation, and a 409A is valid for at most 12 months in any case. New grants should use the new fair market value.
Consider a repricing. Cooley GO explains that a simple repricing lowers the exercise price and leaves other terms unchanged, and that the new price for US taxpayers must be at least the fair market value on the repricing date. Board approval is required; stockholder approval depends on the plan.
Watch the ISO rules. Per Cooley GO, repricing an ISO counts as a new grant, which restarts the holding periods and retests the $100,000 annual limit, so some options may become nonqualified.
Mind the tender offer rules. If other terms change too, Cooley GO notes the offer may need to follow tender offer rules, including staying open at least 20 business days.
How an investor might evaluate a down roundFor the new investor:

Confirm the trigger: real traction with a stale price, or a broken model?
Model the fully diluted post-round table with every anti-dilution adjustment applied, and ask existing investors whether they will waive or reduce theirs. Cooley GO lists negotiating such waivers as one way to soften a down round.
Check the preference stack. If total preferences exceed any realistic exit value, common is worth little and the team has less reason to stay.
Budget for a pool refresh or option repricing so the team is re-motivated at the new price.
Price honestly. A down round that is still too high can produce another one.

For existing investors:

Decide whether to participate before the terms arrive, since pay-to-play can penalize waiting.
Weigh the waiver. Enforcing full anti-dilution on a team diluted to indifference can end up protecting a percentage of a company that stops growing. We'd rather own a bit less of something alive.
Read senior preferences ahead of yours for what they do to your recovery in a modest exit.
Consider a bridge round instead if a milestone is genuinely close.
Alternatives to a down roundCooley GO lists a bridge financing on convertible notes and other investor-friendly terms (a liquidation preference, dividends, or warrant coverage) as ways to avoid or soften a lower price, and Carta's guide adds tranched financing tied to milestones and venture debt. Tranches are common in life sciences: Cooley's Q2 2026 report found them in 29.6 percent of life sciences deals. A recapitalization that resets the cap table is the heavier option, and it remains rare (1.8 percent of Cooley's Q2 2026 deals).
Each has a cost. The new lead will likely also renegotiate the protective provisions."Shouldn't you avoid a down round at almost any cost?"That's the instinct in most boardrooms. A lower price stings, it can spook employees and future investors, and a flat round with some extra structure keeps the headline number intact. Nobody wants the word "down" in the press release.
But Structure that hides a down round often costs common holders more than an honest price would have. A flat round with a 2x participating preference can leave common worse off than a modest down round with clean terms. The headline survives. The founders' and employees' payout doesn't. In our view, a clean reset the team can grow out of usually beats a flattering price with a trapdoor under it.

A close on 2027-02-15 arrives with about $1.9M of cash against a $1.5M floor: three weeks of headroom, a waiver request to the secured lender in January, and the only likely bridge from the counterparty already owed $2.5M. The build compounds it: 300 units of an unbuilt design ordered in February cannot reach an April season on any lead time the deck discloses, so 2027 runs on 64 v3 robots plus a partial build, revenue lands at $0.8-1.8M against $4.6M, the 2027-12-31 licence test fails below 100 robots in commercial service, and the 2028 raise happens without exclusivity. ### One counterparty, five roles

Tallis Agricultural Machinery holds $2.5M of the $7.77M notes (32.2%), commits $1.0M to this round, buys $1.2M a year of engineering (46% of FY2026E revenue), sits as board observer, supplies the $33,000 v4 quote behind 300 units and $9.9M of purchase orders, and employed the chief executive in 2010-2011. arguments.markdown:
Orrin has a real cost pool and a broken price: every robot-season it has sold returns -$8,100 after depreciation at the $9,500 growers signed, the $33,000 v4 that would fix it is quoted by a counterparty that is also customer, noteholder and investor, and the California standard governing the fleet requires a human driver. The risk is that the $12M is subordinated before it is at risk. [S1, S95]

### The 1.0x floor sits at $40M, not $25M

The $36.77M preference is stated in the deck, not the documents, and ranks behind $1.6M of secured fleet debt. Net of debt and 8% costs the $12M is whole only at a $41.6M enterprise value — $39.4M at the likely $16M close, where the stack is $34.77M — and at $25M it returns 0.59x.

| Exit enterprise value | Equal-rank 1x (deck terms) | Notes senior at 2x | $10M senior 2028 round | Pay-to-play, lead does not follow | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $40M | 0.96x | 0.68x | 0.69x | 0.30x | S95, calc |
| $25M | 0.59x | 0.21x | 0.31x | 0.05x | S95, calc |
| $12M | 0.26x | 0.00x | 0.00x | 0.00x | S95, calc |

Down rounds were 11.4% of Carta's Q1 2026 rounds and 12.1% of Cooley's Q2 2026 deals, and new money asks for seniority or pay-to-play; the lead then funds pro rata or converts. With 82 of the plan's own probability points missing the 2027 plan, a 2028 down round is more likely than not at 45-55%, with 30-40% on senior or pay-to-play terms. A $15M purchase of patents, licence and team — the CNH and Oishii structure — pays $13.2M after costs and returns 0.36x; through the lender's collateral, nothing. [S95, S123]

### The base case multiplies three numbers the deck does not have

FY2027 revenue of $4.6M is 360 robots at $12,778, but 110 are contracted ($1.4M) and 250 must be signed in four months by two founders and one vice president hired in June 2025. At 250 robots revenue is $3.18M, and depreciation on 64 v3 and 186 v4 units is $2.30M against $1.78M of gross profit before it: -$0.53M, worse than the plan's -$0.31M, since field service does not shrink with the fleet. The 51.8% FY2027 margin excludes $3.21M of depreciation; with it the year is -5.5%, and the 2026 41% is rental-only, so the series changes definition. The 2028 plan needs 782 robots and $13.93M of capex absent from the use of funds. [S1]

### A late close is a different company, not a slower start

A close on 2027-02-15 arrives with $1.9M against a $1.5M floor: three weeks of headroom, a January waiver request, and the only likely bridge from the counterparty already owed $2.5M. Bridge money prices senior or converts at a discount, so the position becomes uninvestable at the first waiver request, not the first missed number. The build compounds it: 300 units of an unbuilt design ordered in February cannot reach an April season on any lead time the deck discloses, so 2027 runs on 64 v3 robots and a partial build, revenue lands at $0.8-1.8M against $4.6M, the licence test fails below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the 2028 raise happens without exclusivity. A six-month delay does not slow this model; it ends the 2027 season. [S1, S95]

### One counterparty, five roles

Tallis Agricultural Machinery holds $2.5M of the $7.77M notes (32.2%), commits $1.0M to this round, buys $1.2M a year of engineering (46% of FY2026E revenue), sits as board observer, and supplies the $33,000 quote behind 300 units and $9.9M of orders. One counterparty touches $14.6M of the round and supplies the number that decides viability. A 10% error is $3,300 a unit and $825 a season of depreciation, taking contribution at $12,700 from -$1,150 to -$1,975; at $44,000 the $16,500 list price stops covering depreciation. The chief operating officer's own services company took $310,000 in 2025-2026, about two-thirds of the season's field-service line, on a contract approved by a board he sits on; at a 25% premium the leakage is $62,000, small in dollars, telling on how related-party prices are set. With the independent seat vacant the board is two common, one seed and the lead, so Meridian cannot carry a related-party resolution. The quote is an offer, not evidence: $50-58M with two independent quotes, not $72M. [S1, S95]

### The rule that actually breaks the model

California is the only state that prohibits autonomous agricultural equipment, through Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces; the fix died when AB 187 passed on 2026-08-31, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01, so no rule can change before the 2027 season. Both readings are fatal: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season; if the fleet sits outside it, one citation ends a season that is all of the 2026 revenue. I put 20-25% on a material restriction or enforcement action in 2027, with -70% to -90% of equity value.

| Policy clock | Decision date | Probability | Impact on Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Section 232 duty on robotics | Report due 2027-04-26 | 30-35% at 25% or more | $8,250 a robot; $2.48M of capex | S88 |
| Non-USMCA origin at 10% | Each import | 40% origin undocumented | $3,300 a robot, 85% of gross profit | S89 |
| Bayh-Dole US manufacture | At licence exercise | 30-40% | $1,500-3,000 a robot to reshore | S85 |

The tariff is the likeliest material cost shock and the least fatal: the 2026-10-28 proclamation found a threat, imposed nothing and set a Commerce-USTR report within 180 days, six days before the season opens. The wage floor runs in Orrin's favour at 60-70% odds but cannot fix bruising.

### Absence is a finding, not proof

No registry entry, no federal award against the grant the deck describes, no granted patent and no auditor's opinion: the inference is not misrepresentation but that every fact the decision turns on is management representation. Absence proves less than it seems: registries sit behind paywalls, applications stay unpublished for eighteen months, subawards appear on no federal site. It proves enough — the money would be wired on unverified facts, a condition-precedent problem before a price problem.

::: info danger
**The model-breaker is the California equipment prohibition, not the tariff.** California alone bars autonomous agricultural equipment, the fix died in AB 187 on 2026-08-31, and the advisory committee does not sit until 2026-12-01. arguments.markdown:
Orrin has a real cost pool and a broken price: every robot-season it has sold loses $8,100 after depreciation at the $9,500 growers signed, the $33,000 v4 that would fix it is quoted by a counterparty that is also customer, noteholder and investor, and the California standard governing the fleet requires a human driver. The mechanism is a lessor whose build cost exceeds the value of its price: equity is consumed on every unit and the preference decides who absorbs it. The risk is that the $12M is subordinated before it is at risk. Company figures are unverified. [S1, S95]

### The 1.0x floor sits at $40M, not $25M

| Exit enterprise value | Equal-rank 1x (deck terms) | Notes senior at 2x | $10M senior 2028 round | Pay-to-play, lead does not follow | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $40M | 0.96x | 0.68x | 0.69x | 0.30x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $25M | 0.59x | 0.21x | 0.31x | 0.05x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $12M | 0.26x | 0.00x | 0.00x | 0.00x | S95 (unverified), calc |

The $36.77M preference is described in the deck, not the documents, and ranks behind $1.6M of secured fleet debt; net of debt and 8% costs the $12M is whole only at a $41.6M enterprise value — $39.4M at the likely $16M close, where the stack is $34.77M — and at $25M it returns 0.59x, which means the bear case must be priced off net proceeds. Down rounds were 11.4% of Carta's Q1 2026 rounds and 12.1% of Cooley's Q2 2026 deals, and new money asks for seniority or pay-to-play; the lead then funds pro rata or converts. With 82 of the plan's own probability points missing the 2027 plan, a 2028 down round is more likely than not at 45-55%, with 30-40% on senior or pay-to-play terms. A $15M purchase of patents, licence and team — the CNH and Oishii structure — pays $13.2M after costs and returns 0.36x; through the lender's collateral, nil. [S95, S123]

### The plan multiplies three numbers the deck does not have

The v4 misses $36,000 with a 55% probability, and FY2027 revenue of $4.6M is 360 robots at $12,778, but 110 are contracted ($1.4M, company-reported) and 250 must be signed in four months by two founders and one vice president hired in June 2025. At 250 robots revenue is $3.18M, and depreciation on 64 v3 and 186 v4 units is $2.30M against $1.78M of gross profit before it: -$0.53M, worse than the plan's -$0.31M, because field service does not shrink with the fleet. The 51.8% FY2027 margin excludes $3.21M of depreciation; with it the year is -5.5%, and the 2026 41% is rental-only. The 2028 plan needs 782 robots and $13.93M of unplanned capex. A close on 2027-02-15 arrives with $1.9M against a $1.5M floor: three weeks of headroom, a January waiver request and the only likely bridge from the counterparty already owed $2.5M — so the position becomes uninvestable at the first waiver request, not the first missed number. The build compounds it: 300 units of an unbuilt design ordered in February cannot reach an April season, so 2027 runs on 64 v3 robots and a partial build, revenue lands at $0.8-1.8M, the licence test fails below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the 2028 raise happens without exclusivity. A six-month delay does not slow this model; it ends the 2027 season. [S1]

### One counterparty, five roles

Tallis Agricultural Machinery holds $2.5M of the $7.77M notes (32.2%), commits $1.0M to this round, buys $1.2M a year of engineering (46% of FY2026E revenue), sits as board observer, and supplies the $33,000 quote behind 300 units and $9.9M of orders (company-reported). One counterparty touches $14.6M of the round and supplies the number that decides viability. A 10% error is $3,300 a unit and $825 a season of depreciation, taking contribution at $12,700 from -$1,150 to -$1,975; at $44,000 the $16,500 list price stops covering depreciation. The chief operating officer's own services company took $310,000 in 2025-2026, about two-thirds of the season's field-service line, on a contract approved by a board he sits on; at a 25% premium the leakage is $62,000. With the independent seat vacant, Meridian cannot carry a related-party resolution alone. The quote is an offer, not evidence: $50-58M with two independent quotes, not $72M. [S1, S95]

### The rule that actually breaks the model

California alone prohibits autonomous agricultural equipment, through Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces; the fix died when AB 187 passed on 2026-08-31, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01, so no rule can change before the 2027 season. Both readings are fatal: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season; if the fleet sits outside it, one citation ends a season that is all of the 2026 revenue. The probability of a material restriction or enforcement action in 2027 is 20% to 25%, with -70% to -90% of equity value. The tariff is likelier and less fatal: the 2026-10-28 proclamation found a threat, imposed nothing and set a Commerce-USTR report within 180 days — 2027-04-26, six days before the season — and a 25% duty is $8,250 a robot, $2.48M on 300 and a 75-robot smaller fleet at 30-35%. Non-USMCA origin at 10% costs $3,300 a robot, 85% of gross profit, with origin undocumented at 40%; Bayh-Dole US manufacture would cost $1,500-3,000 a robot to reshore if a licensed family was federally funded, at 30-40%. The wage floor helps at 60-70% odds but cannot fix bruising. [S126, S124, S88, S89, S85]

### Absence is a finding, not proof

No registry entry, no federal award against the grant the deck describes, no granted patent and no auditor's opinion: the inference is not misrepresentation but that every fact the decision turns on is management representation. Absence proves less than it seems: registries sit behind paywalls, applications stay unpublished for eighteen months, subawards appear on no federal site. It proves enough — the money would be wired on unverified facts, a condition-precedent problem before a price problem.

::: info danger
**The model-breaker is the California equipment prohibition, not the tariff.** California alone bars autonomous agricultural equipment, the fix died on 2026-08-31, and the committee does not sit until 2026-12-01. Both readings end the investment: one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season, and a citation stops the only revenue line. [S126, S124]
:::

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v4 above $36,000 on one interested-party quote | 55% | -30% to -60% of value | critical | 2027-01 to 2027-04 | A second quote above $36,000; first-article slip | Two quotes; $6M tranche on proof | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| California bars autonomous equipment; legal basis undisclosed | 20-25% | -70% to -90% of value | critical | 2027 season; 2026-12-01 committee | Citation, insurer refusal, indemnity demand | Counsel's opinion; revenue outside California | S126, S124 |
| Close slips past 2027-02 and a bridge prices senior | 35% | 0.05-0.40x | critical | 2027-01 to 2027-03 | Waiver request; cash under $2.5M | Close by 2026-12-15; Kestrel consent | S1 (unverified) |
| Preference not equal-rank (notes senior or 2x) | 30% | -$3.8M at a $25M exit | high | At exit | Note purchase agreement; seed charter | Pari passu warranty; MFN | S95 (unverified) |
| 2028 down round with senior preference or pay-to-play | 45-55% | -$4M to -$9M | high | 2028 H1 | Fleet under 250; ARR under $4M | Anti-dilution; pay-to-play veto; reserve | S123, S95 |
| Kestrel forecloses the fleet | 10%, or 40% if the close slips | Equity nil | high | 2027-03-10 | Cash under $1.5M; waiver refused | Standstill; covenant reset | S1 (unverified) |
| A second grower leaves over bruising | 45% | -20% to -25% of revenue | high | 2027 season | Packer rejection; 7-day 1°C test above 3% | Independent trial; rebate clause | S1, S120 |
| Section 232 duty of 25% or more | 30-35% | $2.48M of capex; 75 fewer robots | high | 2027-04-26 | Commerce-USTR notice; HTS change | USMCA certificate; US assembly option | S88, S89 |
| Calder licence falls non-exclusive | 25% | -20% of value; moat removed | medium | 2027-12-31 | Under 100 robots in paid service at Q3 2027 | Renegotiate before the test | S1, S86 |
| No audit, registry, grant or patent record | 100% absence | Unverifiable; 10-15% of price | medium | Now | No auditor; no USAspending award | Quality-of-earnings review | S91, S1 |
:::

On the plan's own probabilities the position returns about its capital over five years once the bear case is repriced to these structures — preservation at best, negative after fees and time. No price makes this a venture return while the v4 is unbuilt and contribution is negative at every signed price; the fix is evidence, and only a staged term sheet with two quotes, the licence warranty, the lender's consent and a higher preference buys it.

The mechanism is a lessor whose build cost exceeds the value of its price: equity is consumed on every unit and the preference decides who absorbs it. The risk is that the $12M is subordinated before it is at risk. Company figures are unverified. [S1, S95]

### The 1.0x floor sits at $40M, not $25M
