{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,908 characters)
At the price Orrin has actually signed, one robot-season does not cover the depreciation on the robot, so the rental business loses money on every unit today; the case rests on an unbuilt v4 and a price increase no grower has signed.

### The revenue is mostly not rental

The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season (company-reported, unaudited): about seven months in California (April-October) and four in Florida (December-March), one season at a time, with Orrin owning, maintaining and insuring the fleet. No multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M divides into robot rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E is little better, with rental at $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%). The engineering customer is also a $2.5M noteholder, a board observer, the quoted manufacturer of the v4 and a $1.0M committed investor in this round, so half of FY2025 revenue is related-party and 80% is one-off, grant-funded or related-party. What the company has proven is that five growers will rent 75 robot-seasons at $9,500; the rest of the revenue line is an engineering contract and a grant, and its own strategy assumes both disappear by 2028 [S1].

### One robot-season loses $8,100 before any overhead

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company, unaudited) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Interest-only debt service ($1.6M x 11.5% / 75 seasons) | (2,453) | 25.8 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Cash contribution after interest-only debt service | 1,447 | 15.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Cash contribution after amortising debt service | (3,051) | (32.1) | S1 (unverified), calc |

The company-reported 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: fleet depreciation sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue. Charging the $48,000 v3 over its four-season life puts $12,000 against each season, more than the $9,500 the grower pays before a single technician is paid. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and should not be added; the economic measure is the negative $8,100 contribution, while the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only and -$3,051 if it amortises over the robot's four-season life. The benchmark: United Rentals earned a gross margin of 38.0% on equipment rentals in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue. Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at the $16,500 list price with the v3, and only reaches +19.1% with both the list price and a $31,000 v4 [S21].

### The 2.1-season payback is the best case of three unproven inputs

The claimed 2.1 seasons is $31,000 divided by ($16,500 list price less $1,750 target service), which drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely. Putting it back gives 2.53 seasons on the company's own target cost and price. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet actually ran in 2026, against a four-season asset life. Even at the $31,000 target build and the signed price the payback is 7.95 seasons; at the list price and the current build it is 4.40 seasons, longer than the asset lasts. Of the four inputs that decide payback, build cost is unbuilt, price unsigned, service cost unreconciled to the technician ratio and transport omitted from the slide. All of these are company-reported, unaudited figures [S1].

### Utilisation cannot repair a per-season capital charge

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two (the California and Florida seasons cover eleven months). At the signed price the fleet needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 seasons, 85% of the maximum; at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles its revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads fixed overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital hurdle. Service cost is no more forgiving. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 loaded field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour, over 213 days, costs $41,611 per technician-season, or $5,201 per robot-season; at the $29.60 machine-operator rate it is $6,305. The deck reports $3,100, which implies a technician costs $24,800 for seven months before a vehicle, tools or travel. At 360 robots the same ratio needs 45 technicians and $1.12M at the reported rate, so the cost is linear in robots, not diluted by scale; on the $6,305 figure, gross profit at the signed price falls to $695, or 7.3%, before depreciation [S1, S10].

### Price is not the constraint; proof and quality are

At one robot per 3.5 acres the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the 2027 list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre - 3.4% to 5.9% of the labour bill the robot targets. At 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray, each percentage point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21% to 36% of the robot fee; the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee and 80% of the list fee. That asymmetry explains why price has not moved to list and why one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising: a grower is buying an option on a harvest, not a proven substitute for a crew. The risk is not that growers cannot afford the robot but that the robot, at 94% of detected ripe fruit and 86% uptime, cannot yet promise the bruising and reliability a retail supply chain requires [S10].

| Offer | $ per robot-season | vs signed | $ per acre (3.5 acres/robot) | % of $79,288/acre harvest cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 3.4% | S1 (unverified), S10 |
| 2027 renewal average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 4.6% | S1 (unverified), S10 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 5.9% | S1 (unverified), S10 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 6.3% | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 4.8% | S1 (unverified), calc |

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at a small fraction of the harvest cost it addresses, so a working unit could charge several times more; the answer is that two peers with more capital and more robots did not get there. Tortuga and FarmWise both owned fleets and rented or serviced them before retreating, and Orrin's capital intensity per robot is essentially the same as Tortuga's.

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023-FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time head of finance. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep a minimum unrestricted balance at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts. ### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

On the company-reported, unaudited plan, three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4, so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 4 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,993 characters)
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, the largest controllable line in the grower's P&L and the one a machine can attack. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, trivial against the harvest bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026, when the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23; the deck's urgency is a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category. The seller measured it on rows the seller chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two core perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus, visible in $4.0M of insider commitments at the mark, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the 52-61% margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but that we price the lease book on the cash it produces at the price growers signed, $9,500, and on a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, roughly four times the $87M post-money of its last private round, and it bought a perception platform that fitted an existing sprayer line, not a fleet of leased harvesters. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. Agtech venture funding fell from $53bn in 2021 to $7bn in 2025; 18 companies shut down that year, and Q2 2026 raised $1bn against $2bn a year earlier. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x to this lead: above the sector's best recorded outcome and dependent on a 2028 round the market must supply. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

### The distribution, not the mean, decides it

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG评估 ESG Assessment (esg, revision 3 by Regulatory Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,971 characters)
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case are being decided by other people before the 2027 season: a wage floor a California court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff decision due by 2027-04-26, a university exclusivity test on 2027-12-31 and a California rule on unpiloted machines. The balance is mildly negative for 2027 and positive after it, which argues for staging the round rather than passing on it.

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's figure of a quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14 while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost over 40 passes, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre [S80, S1].

### The cut is provisional

On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing adjustment, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and required the Department of Labor to warn employers of possible back-wage adjustments. My judgement is that a higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, which would restore most of that saving and lift the ceiling Orrin prices against.

### Who is organised, and against what

The union that won that case is most likely to shape the operating rule. In August 2026 California was drafting a trailer bill to let unpiloted machines work alongside farmworkers, and labour groups opposed it. That rule decides the unit economics: one technician to eight robots supports the $3,100 field-service line, and a human-spotter requirement would take it to $24,800 and turn the 41% gross margin negative [S84, S82, S1]. California overtime adds to the hand cost the robot displaces. Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement rather than wage rules, and the one pilot the company has lost is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its own capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper at 50% apply even under USMCA. The new tail: the Section 232 proclamation of 2026-10-28 on robotics and industrial machinery found that imports threaten national security, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days, with tariffs, quotas and fees left open [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The university licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A single binary test with no cure is harsher than standard practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones, cure periods and step-in rights. The 2027 plan clears the threshold, so the cliff needs 72% slippage; conversion risk 20%–25% (analyst estimate). If the licensed families were federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to agree that products embodying the invention are manufactured substantially in the United States, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the retail clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and fruit packed in the field reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists to obtain and no FDA action against machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds; where quality binds it is not, and the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, quoted contract manufacturer and investor in this round; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no federal award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91].

Four records are requested with this report — the H-2A disclosure files and wage table (the department's page returned an error on 2026-10-30), the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the California bill text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. Taken together, the four factors change what a season is worth rather than whether Orrin can sell one: the cheapest protection is to price the 2027 tranche against the wage-floor outcome and to make the USMCA certificate and the licence warranty conditions of closing.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 退出策略分析 Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 4 by Valuation Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,947 characters)
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while the harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.8x — enough to return capital, not enough to carry a venture fund. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Each buyer is buying a different asset. Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would be buying the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend its See & Spray and autonomy stack into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would be buying a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would be buying fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but less need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would be buying harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet — they can manufacture — so the fleet is a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security, grower data, supply chain; no public robotics M&A found (not publicly disclosed) | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga in 2024; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93 |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | Growth capital; requires scale, float and profitability; no comparable IPO in the set (not publicly disclosed) | 2030+ | Very low | S95 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag was bought for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven, a public precision-ag company at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI was acquired by AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii for undisclosed terms. No harvesting-robot company in the set has been sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | What the target had | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River | 2017 | $305M | 3.5x the $87M post-money; revenue n/a | See & Spray, $30M+ raised | S98 |
| Deere / Bear Flag | 2021 | $250M | 31.6x the $7.9M seed; revenue n/a | Autonomous tractor retrofit, founded 2017 | S96, S118 |
| CNH / Raven | 2021 | $2.1B EV | n/a; 33.6% premium | Public precision-ag company | S99 |
| AGCO / Trimble Ag (85%) | 2023-24 | $2.35B EV | 13.8x 2023E EBITDA | Precision-ag portfolio, $170M EBITDA | S101 |
| Kubota / AgJunction | 2021 | $73M | n/a | Guidance and auto-steer | S104 |
| CNH / Advanced Farm assets | 2025 | Undisclosed | n/a | Strawberry and apple picking IP and team | S97, S28 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2024 | Undisclosed | n/a | $50M deployed, 150 robots | S93 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | n/a | Tomato harvesting robot | S32 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none reached $100M+, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. The 2025 market recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money, a $100M exit returns 1.1x before dilution, a $250M exit 2.8x and a $40M exit 1.0x because of the 1x preference. With illustrative probabilities of 40% at $40M, 35% at $100M, 20% at $250M and 5% at $500M, the expected MOIC is 1.6x before dilution and 1.4x after a 20% Series B — below the 3x a venture fund needs. The counter-case is that Deere or CNH pays $250-305M for the team and perception model, as they did for Blue River and Bear Flag; if Orrin proves 95% pick rates at 360 robots, a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 base rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

| Outcome | Count | Share | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ag-robotics companies in the comparison set | 8 | 100% | S98, S96, S105, S102, S93, S109, S94, S107 |
| Reached a $100M+ exit | 2 (Blue River, Bear Flag) | 25% | S98, S96 |
| Harvesting-robot companies in the set | 5 (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin) | 100% | S105, S102, S93, S107, S95 |
| Harvesting-robot companies at $100M+ | 0 | 0% | S105, S102, S93, S107, S95 |
| Ag-robotics acquisitions in 2025 | 14 | n/a | S108 |

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue, the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; a round above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is: $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Metric | 2027 plan | 2028 plan | Test for a Series B above $72M pre | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $5.6M | $13.2M | $13.2M at 7x forward, or $18M at 5x | S95 (unverified) |
| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |
| Renewal | 110 contracted 2027 seasons | n/a | 80% or more of 2026 paying growers renew | S95 (unverified) |
| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to US, European and Japanese strategics: Deere and AGCO are US-listed, CNH is Dutch/Italian and Kubota is Japanese, and all have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, the Calder license and the grower data, and the Mexico assembly adds tariff and supply-chain diligence. An IPO is not a realistic exit before 2030: $1.9M of revenue, a $5.2M net loss in FY2025 and no comparable ag-robotics IPO in the set; a listing would need scale and audited growth the company does not have. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes the exit to 2030-2032. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.0x at $90M, 1.1x at $100M, 1.7x at $150M, 2.8x at $250M and 5.6x at $500M; a 20% Series B dilution cuts those to 1.0x, 1.0x, 1.4x, 2.2x and 4.4x. The IRR is 0% at $90M, 10.8% at $150M and 22.7% at $250M over five years. A 20-30% lower entry price, or a 1.5x preference, would make the same exits work; at $72M pre-money the lead is buying an option that needs a $250M+ bid. The implication is to pass at $72M pre-money, or invest only at a 20-30% lower price with a 1.5x preference and a milestone tranche. Diligence should confirm the Advanced Farm and Tortuga prices, the ownership of the grower contracts (Orrin Fieldworks or Orrin Fleet Services), the Calder license's change-of-control terms and the customer concentration — 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons sit with two named growers. [S95, S97, S93]"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,451 characters)
The plan does not add up on its own numbers, which are company-stated and unverified. At the current $48,000 build even the 2027 list price leaves each robot-season $1,100 short over a four-season life, the v4 must land below $28,400 to earn its keep at the $12,700 renewal price, the company's own FY2027 revenue projection implies an average price of $12,778 rather than the $16,500 list, and a 5.6-times fleet increase by April 2027 rests on one outsourced build quote and a $14M gap in a round that has not closed [S1].

### The price rise is a solvency requirement, not a margin story

At $5,600 a season of reported, unverified field service, transport, insurance and consumables, a robot priced at the $12,700 renewal average can cost at most $28,400 and still repay itself over four seasons; the v4 budget is $33,000. Priced at the $16,500 list it can cost $43,600 and still repay, which the $48,000 v3 does not. The gap is not theoretical: on the reported costs each robot-season at the renewal price loses $4,900, so a 360-robot fleet at the 2027 revenue line of $4.6M loses $1.76M a season before a dollar of overhead, and even the $33,000 v4 turns positive only if service cost also falls to the $1,750 target. Depreciation sits in operating expenses rather than cost of revenue, so the reported 52 percent gross margin for 2027 excludes $3.24M of hardware consumption on a $4.6M revenue line, alongside $2.02M of service cost, against total gross profit of $2.9M. The payback figure that carries the story uses the best case at every input: at a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, 2.1 seasons is right, but at the $5,600 the company reports, unverified, for 2026, payback stretches to 2.8 seasons at that build and 4.4 seasons at today's $48,000, longer than the four-season life the same page assumes. The gap between $1,750 and $5,600 is $3,850 a robot-season, $1.386M across 360 robots, and no cost bridge is disclosed for it [S1].

### A price that is too low to be replacing a hand crew

The pricing question runs the other way from the usual one. At $9,500 for the 3.5 acres a robot serves, a grower pays $2,714 an acre a season; the 2027 list is $4,714 an acre. The California Strawberry Commission puts the cost to cultivate and harvest strawberries at an average $87,000 an acre, $15.34 a tray, rising to $17.73 a tray in 2023, so Orrin's asking price is between 3 and 5 percent of the total cost of the crop [S1, S121]. A machine that replaced the hand crew over 3.5 acres would be worth several times that, and five growers buying 75 robot-seasons would not have left it on the table. Either the robot harvests a small fraction of the fruit on the acres it drives, or the price was set to buy pilots and the 2027 increase is the first real test of willingness to pay. Grower B cutting from 22 robots to 14 and Grower E exiting over bruising say the test is live; the two letters of intent for 50 robots are not contracts.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Series A closed | 2026-12-15 | unverified; $14M of the lead unsought, $4.0M committed | whether the build is funded | S1 |
| 300 v4 robots built at $33,000 | 2027-01 to 2027-03 | unverified; design unbuilt, one bill-of-materials quote | whether a 5.6-times ramp holds cost | S1 |
| 360 robots in service | 2027-04 | unverified; 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 | whether supply and field service scale | S1 |
| Pick rate at or above 95% at 3 farms | 2027 season | unverified; 94% on company-chosen rows | whether the 74% price rise is defensible | S1 |
| Unit cost below $36,000 | 2027 | unverified; $48,000 today | whether gross margin reaches 52% | S1 |
| ARR of $8M on the company definition | 2027 | unverified; $3.2M today, including $1.2M services and $0.6M of letters of intent | whether recurring revenue is real | S1 |
| 100 robots in commercial service | 2027-12-31 | unverified; 64 today | whether licence exclusivity survives | S1 |
| Series B | 2028 | not started, unverified | whether the model is financeable | S1 |

### Manufacturing risk sits with one supplier that is also a customer, a creditor and an investor

The build plan is 300 robots for $9.9M, 55 percent of the round, at an average $33,000 on a design that has never been manufactured. That is a 31 percent cut from the $48,000 v3 on a single quote from Tallis Agricultural Machinery dated 2026-08, a counterparty that is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, the $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer, the quoted contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round. Assembly sits in Guadalajara into a market where a Section 232 investigation into imported robotics and industrial machinery opened in September 2025 and a related proclamation followed on 2026-10-28; USMCA-qualifying goods enter at zero and non-qualifying at 10 percent, which on a $33,000 robot is $3,300 a unit, $990,000 across 300 units and 72 percent of the $4,600 of unit headroom between the v4 budget and break-even [S1, S87, S88, S89].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tallis Agricultural Machinery | v4 contract manufacturer, engineering services, $2.5M note, board observer, $1.0M investor | 2025-02-10 note; 2025-03 services | unverified; services to 2027-06-30, sole build quote | S1 |
| Kestrel Equipment Finance | $2.5M facility at 11.5%, secured on the fleet | 2025-06-16 | unverified; $1.6M drawn, $1.5M cash covenant | S1 |
| Calder University | exclusive harvesting licence, 2.5% royalty, $40,000 minimum | 2022-01-20 | exclusive only while 100 robots are in commercial service at 2027-12-31 | S1, S86 |
| Granary Ventures | seed lead, $3.0M pro rata in this round | 2023-03-08 | unverified; committed | S1 |
| Vashti Harvest Services | robot relocation and night supervision, $310,000 paid | not disclosed | unverified; related party, board approved | S1 |

### Peers that carried the asset did not survive it

RaaS makes Orrin the lessor: at 64 robots it carries $3.07M of fleet on its balance sheet, at 360 $17.28M at the v3 build or $11.88M at the v4 budget, funded by $18M of equity and a $2.5M secured facility. Five of six comparable companies did not hold that position. Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP to CNH; Tortuga moved to a per-kilogram service and sold its IP and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025; Monarch raised a $133M Series C at a reported valuation above $500M in 2024, cut staff, and had its assets bought by Caterpillar in April 2026 after failing to pivot to software services; Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021; FarmWise moved from a per-acre Titan service to selling through Vulcan dealers. Carbon Robotics, which sells machines and raised a $70M Series D, is the exception. The same arithmetic that makes RaaS hard for Orrin is why growers like it, and the base rate says the model is financeable only if the fleet turns fast: 75 paid robot-seasons from 5 growers in 2026 against 360 planned in 2027, with 53 percent of 2026 seasons in two named customers, one of them the chief operating officer's former employer [S1, S28, S93, S97, S109, S116, S122].

### What must be true in twelve months

Three things. The round closes by 2026-12-15 so that build slots and deposits are in place for an April 2027 season; the v4 reaches $33,000 or less on a second and third quote, because at $48,000 the fleet consumes its own gross profit; and at least one grower renews at or near the $16,500 list after a season with an independently measured pick rate and damage rate. The signposts are dated and checkable: a signed 2027 contract at list price, a second contract-manufacturing quote, the v4 first-article build date, and whether the 100-robot licence test is met by robots in commercial service rather than robots built. Against $3.7M of cash, $410,000 of monthly net burn and a $1.5M cash covenant, usable runway is 5.4 months; a close in January 2027 makes 360 robots impossible and puts the licence cliff at risk [S1, S91].

Two limitations bound this judgement. The v4 unit cost is a single unverified quote and the service-cost target has no disclosed bridge from the reported figure, so the margin case cannot be tested from outside; and the public record returns no federal award to the company, which contradicts the SBIR revenue line in the plan."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"- U1 (esg, Regulatory Analyst): SBIR.gov award database (and the USDA NIFA SBIR Phase II award record): Award(s) to Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (Salinas, California; also check Orrin Fleet Services LLC): award number, agency and programme (USDA SBIR Phase II), obligation and total amount, period of performance, and the project title. The deck cites a $650,000 Phase II award over 2024-2026 and grant revenue of $0.80M cumulatively across FY2023-FY2026E.. Why: A USAspending recipient-name search returned zero federal awards on 2026-10-30, so either the award sits under another legal name, is a subaward, or the grant revenue line is not federal money. Grant revenue is 13% of FY2026E revenue and disappears from FY2027P onward, and any federal funding also triggers Bayh-Dole obligations on the licensed university patents, including the US manufacturing preference. Verification changes both the revenue quality and the IP risk. How: Search awards at sbir.gov/awards by firm name and by state; cross-check the USDA NIFA SBIR Phase II award list. A screenshot or export of the award record is sufficient.
- U2 (esg, Regulatory Analyst): US DOL Office of Foreign Labor Certification — H-2A disclosure data and AEWR state table (flag.dol.gov): Certified H-2A positions and employers by state (California, Florida) and SOC code 45-2092 (farmworkers and labourers, crops) for programme years 2019-2026, plus the official AEWR state table published with 91 FR 48946 (California and Florida, Skill Level I and II, before and after the housing adjustment).. Why: This is the size and price of the labour pool the robot competes against. The certified-position count tells us whether H-2A is a binding constraint for California and Florida berry growers (which supports adoption) or whether growers can simply certify more workers (which caps the robot's price). The official wage table is the single input to the grower's hand-harvest cost per acre; the DOL wage page returned HTTP 503 on 2026-10-30 and the rates used in the report are taken from a secondary report of the notice. How: Download the quarterly H-2A disclosure files at flag.dol.gov/performance-data/performance-data-downloads (no login, but the site was unreachable from here) and the AEWR spreadsheet linked from flag.dol.gov/wage-data/adverse-effect-wage-rates. A CSV export of the two states and SOC code is enough.
- U3 (esg, Regulatory Analyst): USPTO Patent Assignment Search and Patent Center; the university licence agreement in the data room: Chain of title for the two licensed patent families (stereo ripeness model, docket CU-2017-031, US patent granted 2020; berry-stem localisation, docket CU-2019-114, US patent granted 2022): patent numbers, recorded assignments from the university to Orrin Fieldworks, Inc., and whether the underlying inventions were made with federal funding. Also the executed licence: exclusivity field, the 100-robot test wording, cure rights, the royalty and minimum, and any federal-agency waiver under 35 U.S.C. 204.. Why: Three things turn on these documents. First, whether the licence's US rights are exclusive at all, which is the moat the $72M pre-money is priced on. Second, whether 35 U.S.C. 204's US manufacturing preference binds, because the company assembles grippers and harnesses in Guadalajara. Third, whether the 2027-12-31 robot-count test has a cure period; on the deck's own plan the company is at 75 paid robot-seasons against a 100-robot threshold. The licensor cannot be searched by name, so only the data room or the patent record settles this. How: USPTO Patent Assignment Search (assignment.uspto.gov) by assignee and by patent number; Patent Center for the two patents' prosecution and government-interest statements (the "Government Support" clause on the face of the patent). From the company: the licence agreement and any agency waiver letter.
- U4 (esg, Regulatory Analyst): California Legislative Information (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) — 2026 trailer bill on autonomous farm equipment: The bill number, author, committee and status of the 2026 draft trailer bill reported on 2026-08-25 as allowing unpiloted farm machines to work alongside farmworkers, and the text of any labour-relations or safety conditions it would impose (spacing, human oversight, notification, liability).. Why: This is the only identified state-level rule that would govern whether the robot may run unattended beside a crew, which is the operating model the unit economics assume (one technician per eight robots, remote supervision). If the bill fails or is amended to require a human spotter per machine, the field-service line of $3,100 a robot-season roughly doubles and the 41% gross margin goes with it. The news article body was blocked, so the bill itself must be read. How: Search leginfo.legislature.ca.gov for 2026 bills by subject (food and agriculture, labour) or by keyword "autonomous" or "unpiloted"; the Assembly and Senate agriculture and labour committee agendas for August 2026 will name it.
- U5 (financials, Fundamentals Analyst): SBIR.gov award database and USAspending.gov: Federal awards to Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (Salinas, California; Delaware corporation formed 2021-09-14): the USDA SBIR Phase II award of $650,000 said to run 2024-2026, its award number, obligation dates and whether the recipient is the parent or Orrin Fleet Services LLC; any other federal grant or contract since 2021.. Why: Grant revenue is $0.30M of FY2025 revenue (15.8%) and $0.35M of FY2026E; cumulative disclosed grant revenue of $0.80M exceeds the single $650,000 award, and a public search on 2026-10-30 found no federal record for the company. If the grant cannot be verified, 16% of FY2025 revenue and 13% of FY2026E revenue rest on an unaudited company claim, which lowers confidence in the revenue base and in the non-dilutive funding assumption in the plan. How: Search SBIR.gov's award database by firm name and by the USDA agency, and USAspending.gov's recipient search by legal name and UEI; export the award summary page with award number, amount, period of performance and recipient address. A screenshot or PDF of the award record is enough.
- U6 (financials, Fundamentals Analyst): California Secretary of State UCC filings; Delaware Division of Corporations; California Secretary of State business search: UCC-1 financing statements naming Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. or Orrin Fleet Services LLC as debtor (secured party Kestrel Equipment Finance), including collateral description, filing date and continuation; the Delaware corporate record for Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (file number, status, officers) and the California LLC record for Orrin Fleet Services LLC (entity number, status, manager, statement of information).. Why: The $1.6M drawn equipment facility at 11.5% is secured on the fleet, carries a $1.5M unrestricted-cash covenant and sits at a subsidiary that holds the grower contracts and revenue; the parent raises the equity. Whether the debt is guaranteed by the parent, what exactly is pledged and whether the loan restricts cash upstreaming determines whether the $18M is effectively subordinated and whether the covenant binds the parent's cash. The registry record also confirms the entities exist as described. How: California Secretary of State UCC search (bizfileonline.sos.ca.gov) by debtor name returns the UCC-1 image; the California business search returns the LLC statement of information; the Delaware Division of Corporations entity search returns the corporate file number and status. Pass 4: product/market fit. One Important item + notes with the five questions.

The item: sales cycle / CAC / lost-deal alternatives / budget owner. Sections: business_model, competition. Owner Fundamentals (business_model) + Market (competition).

Notes: answer the five questions as the report stands — the hardest thing about selling is quality/damage not price; budget owner is the harvest-labour line and the buyer is the grower; sales cycle not documented; adoption pace explained; lost deals: Grower E (bruising) and Grower B (22→14), but the alternative chosen is not stated.

Also: the 250-robot four-month gap. And that the report says "the deck shows no pipeline by stage".

items.action: Add a short funnel table to section 6 (pilots, paid seasons, renewals, deposits, days from pilot start to signature where known) and state what is missing: contract length, cancellation terms, whether a deposit is taken, the cost of running a pilot, and which alternative each lost account chose. Where a figure is not in the materials, write not disclosed and name the data-room document that carries it (U7, U9). Give the answer to 'why not faster' as one worked number: 250 robots in four months at the observed 14-pilots-in-three-seasons conversion rate.
items.evidence_request: What did Grower E and the two robots Grower B gave up go to instead - a hand crew, Harvest CROO, or no purchase - and what does a pilot cost Orrin to run? Plus the executed 2027 contracts with deposit, term and cancellation terms (U7, U9).
items.issue: The section establishes that price is not the obstacle (the fee is 3-6% of the harvest cost it attacks) and that quality is, which is the right answer to why adoption is slow. Three sales facts are missing. Sales cycle and cost of acquisition are nowhere: the section counts 14 pilots since 2024, two conversions in 2025 and five paying growers in 2026 - a conversion rate of about one in seven - but never turns that into a cycle length, a pilot cost or a cost per paid season, which is the number that decides whether the 250-robot gap can be bought with 20% of the round. Lost deals: one Florida grower (Grower E) left over bruising and Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14; neither section says what they did instead, so the substitute the customer actually chose is unidentified. Budget owner: the report says the budget owner holds the harvest-labour line, which is a company claim, and never asks whether a seasonal rental is signed by the grower-owner, a farm manager or a shipper, or whether it needs capex approval - which decides the cycle length.

arguments.notes: The five questions answered as the report stands. Hardest thing about selling: not price - the fee is 3.4-5.9% of a $79,288-an-acre harvest cost - but fruit quality and reliability, which is the mechanism behind the single documented loss (Grower E, Plant City, 2026-06, bruising) and behind Grower B cutting 22 robots to 14. Budget owner: the grower's harvest-labour line; the report asserts it and does not evidence it, and the buyer-versus-user split (the crew the robot displaces) is drawn well. Sales cycle: undocumented; the only data points are 14 pilots since 2024, 2 conversions in 2025, 5 paying growers in 2026, and a 2027 book of 110 contracted plus 50 letters of intent against a 360-robot plan, 31% five months before the season. Why adoption is not faster: well answered at the product level (3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA serious-damage allowance; 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5) and at the market level (the OEWS wage-floor cut lowered the grower's alternative cost by 17.6-23% in 2026). Lost deals: one loss documented, the alternative chosen not stated - this is the gap the item addresses. Strongest PMF evidence in the report: five growers paying, a renewal average of $12,700 (+33.7%) and four growers contracting 110 robots for 2027, one of them 40 robots at the COO's former employer. Weakest: 53% of 2026 paid seasons in two named growers, one of them an insider relationship, which the report states plainly.

- Critical: exit 1.6x vs 0.94x probability sets (exit, thesis, scoring).
- Critical: $28,400 breakeven build mispaired with $17,600 (executive_summary, scoring; business_model/strategy use $28,400 correctly at $12,700).

- Important: 2027 year-end cash $0.085M bridge not reproducible (financials, executive_summary).
- Minor: competition 262 acres / 0.5% share uses robot-seasons as robots (64 × 3.5 = 224 acres).
- Minor: per-acre harvest labour cost spread across sections.

Notes: stress-test arithmetic for other key numbers — the 30%-worse test. Let me include: 
- build cost +30% ($48,000 → $62,400): contribution at signed price worsens from -8,100 to -11,700; thesis still fails (Pass holds).
- price -30% ($9,500 → $6,650): contribution -14,850... note breakeven price is $17,600.
- Throughput -30% (1.0 → 0.7 acres/24h): robots per acre rises to 5.0 from 3.5, revenue per robot unchanged but acreage served falls 30% → requires 43% more robots per acre... Actually if 1 robot covers 3.5 acres and actually covers 2.45, then to serve 262 acres you need 107 robots not 75 — the $8M ARR needs 360 robots at 2.45 = 882 acres.
- The 30%-worse test on the $25M exit: 0.59x→0.41x; on the $100M exit: 1.1x→0.77x. Thesis survives either way (Pass).
- Verify pool: 12% post-money vs 9% pre; founders 47→29.5.
- Verify the 0.94x: 0.18×2.2 + 0.40×1.0 + 0.42×0.35 = 0.943 ✓. Kelly negative ✓.
- Verify 0.59x at $25M: lead's share = 12/36.77 = 32.6% of net proceeds (25 − 1.6 debt = 23.4, × 0.92 after 8% costs = 21.5) = $7.02M = 0.59x ✓ — so the risk table is internally consistent; the thesis table's 0.35x row is the outlier.
- Verify 0.96x at $40M: 38.4×0.92×0.326 = 11.5 = 0.96x ✓.
- $28,400 = 4 × (12,700 − 5,600); at $9,500 it is 4 × (9,500 − 5,600) = $15,600. And $43,600 = 4 × (16,500−5,600) ✓ consistent with "at $44,000 the list stops covering depreciation".
- 262 acres = 75 × 3.5 ✓ but as robot-seasons.

Include in notes.

items.action: Use one probability set across sections 11, 12 and 14 - the 18/40/42 at 2.2x/1.0x/0.35x set - and present section 12's $40M/$100M/$250M/$500M outcomes as the conditional sale case (given a sale happens) rather than a second expected return. Recompute the 12's expected MOIC on that set or delete it; label both with the same basis and dilution assumption.
items.issue: Section 12 reports an expected MOIC of 1.6x before dilution (1.4x after) from illustrative probabilities of 40% at $40M, 35% at $100M, 20% at $250M and 5% at $500M. Sections 11 and 14 report 0.94x from 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x and 42% at 0.35x. The two sets cannot both be true: section 12 assigns zero probability to an outcome below 1.0x, while section 10 assigns 42% weight to one. The Pass recommendation and the zero position size rest on 0.94x, and a reader can lift 1.6x from the exit section as the report's expected return.

items.action: Correct both to the signed-price breakeven build, $15,600 ($3,900 of gross profit per season × four seasons), and keep $28,400 only where the $12,700 renewal price is the input, as sections 6 and 9 already do. State the two breakeven pairs adjacently so the price assumed in each is unambiguous.

At $9,500 the breakeven build is $15,600. The pairing overstates the permissible build cost at the signed price by $12,800 a robot, $3,200 a season.

items.action: Recompute the four rows on a single stated structure (stack, proceeds net of debt and transaction costs, lead's 32.6% share of the A class) and label each row with the preference multiple and exit value it assumes, so section 11 matches the 0.59x/0.96x/0.26x series in section 10.
items.issue: The 'where the price turns' table gives a $25M exit at 0.35x under a 1.5x preference and a $100M exit at 1.0x under the same terms. On the waterfall used in section 10, a 1.5x pari passu preference returns about 0.49x at $25M (A class 18 of a 44.16 stack × net proceeds of 21.5, lead at two thirds of the class) and about 1.1x at $100M (the same exit section 11 scores at 1.1x on deck terms). The 0.35x figure is the blended bear central case, not the 1.5x structure, and the two recommendation-changing rows are the ones a reader will use to justify re-engaging.

items.action: Add the 2027 cash bridge (opening cash, EBITDA, working capital, capex, facility draw, debt service, closing cash) as a table row, or restate the closing figure to what the stated line items produce. The conclusion that the minimum close is unfunded survives either way; the arithmetic has to.
items.issue: Section 7 states that with $12M, 2027 year-end cash is $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor. That does not reconcile with the plan's own line items: $3.7M opening cash plus $12M, less a $7.9M net loss and $9.9M of robot capex, leaves about -$2M before the $0.9M undrawn facility, and an EBITDA-based bridge (loss plus $3.2M of depreciation) leaves about +$2M. Three different answers, one of them printed, and the underlying claim - that $12M funds about 200 robots and a 2028 down round is the base case - is one the committee will test.

items.action: Use 64 robots (224 acres) for the acreage-share statement, or state the proxy explicitly as robot-seasons and give the acre-pass equivalent.
items.issue: Section 5 converts 75 paid robot-seasons into 262 acres and a 0.5% share of the US base. Robot-seasons are not robots: the fleet is 64 machines and the same acres are served twice by 11 of them, so the acreage footprint is about 224 acres, 0.45%. The overstatement is small but the measure is the one used to call Orrin the largest disclosed paid base.

items.action: Reconcile the estimates in one table row in section 6 and state that the conclusion is unaffected: the fee is 3-6% of harvest cost on every estimate, so the price is not the obstacle under any of them.
items.issue: Four per-acre harvest-labour figures appear: $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour implies $12,000-18,000 an acre; section 13 derives $21,056-23,949 over 40 passes; section 4 uses $25,000-35,000; the UC budget line is $79,288. They measure different scopes (pick wages versus the full harvest cost including hauling, supervision and containers) but the report never says which line of the budget $79,288 covers.

arguments.notes: Stress arithmetic checked. (1) The section 10 waterfall is internally consistent: lead's share of net proceeds is 12/36.77 = 32.6% (two thirds of an A class taking its pro rata of a 36.77 stack), so $40M gives (40 - 1.6) × 0.92 × 0.326 = 0.96x, $25M gives 0.59x, $12M gives 0.26x, and the 1.0x floor sits at 41.6/39.4 - all reproduced. (2) Expected return reproduced: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35 = 0.94x, and Kelly is negative on b = 1.2/0.65 with p = 0.18. (3) 30%-worse tests: build at $62,400 takes contribution at the signed price from -$8,100 to -$11,700 and makes the licence test irrelevant; a 30% throughput miss (0.7 rather than 1.0 acres per 24 hours) needs 107 robots where 75 are sold and 882 acres for the $8M ARR the 360-robot plan claims, which is the most damaging single miss because it hits revenue per capital unit and the licence test together; a 30% lower exit takes $100M to 0.77x and $25M to 0.41x. None of these reverses Pass, which is why the rating survives. (4) Other figures spot-checked and correct: 36.8x on $69.9M/$1.9M, 49.9x on $1.4M, 132% of US acreage for the $310M SOM, 21,800 ripe berries an acre at 60 passes, 12.31-season payback, 3.08 seasons needed to cover depreciation at the signed price, 9,000 trays × $11 = $990 an acre per point of cull, 2-of-8 base rate, and the $5.71M pool cost. (5) Figures given as single-source and accepted because the section labels them: the $33,000 v4 quote, the $3,100 field-service line, the 86% uptime and the 2.5%-of-revenue licence royalty. (6) Not tested for lack of a public data point: whether the Kestrel interest is 11.5% fixed and whether the amortisation is straight-line over four seasons; both are stated as company figures with the alternative cash view given.

Meridian should pass at the $72M pre-money. Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the field and a real harvest cost pool to sell into, but at the $9,500 a robot-season growers signed and the $48,000 build the company can evidence (company-reported, unverified), every unit loses $8,100 before debt service, and the round prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund: the $12M cheque returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities and 2x only at a $180M exit. [S1, S95]

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pass | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; re-engage at $50-58M with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged | 4.5 | Medium | 12-24 months, to the 2027 season and the licence test | S95 (unverified), S1 (unverified) |
:::

### What is good, and what decides it

The pain is real and independently measured: the UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is cheap against that bill. The picker has the only labelled field dataset in the category — 94% pick rate on 212 rows, 75 paid robot-seasons, 110 robots contracted for 2027 at a $12,700 renewal price — and the two things that usually kill hardware start-ups, no customer and no evidence, are not the problem here. Four facts outweigh that. One robot-season loses $8,100 at the signed price, and the $33,000 build that would fix it is a single quote from a counterparty that is also noteholder, customer, board observer and investor. Bruising at 3.8% has already cost one grower and spends most of the USDA allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. [S119, S1, S95, S86]

|---|---|---|

| What is being bought | 64 robots in service, 110 contracted for 2027 of a 360-robot plan, a labelled field dataset and two valleys of grower relationships; no granted patent | S1 (unverified), S86 |
| Unit economics | -$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the signed price and build cost; breakeven at $17,600 a season or a $28,400 build | S1 (unverified) |

| The round | $18M target, $4.0M committed, $12M minimum; at $12M the plan funds about 200 robots and a 2028 down round becomes the base case | S95 (unverified) |
| Cash | $3.7M at 2026-09-30, $410,000 monthly net burn, a $1.5M covenant reached near 2027-03-10 | S1 (unverified) |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 4 by Lead Analyst, 8,993 characters)
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. ### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, the largest controllable line in the grower's P&L and the one a machine can attack. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, trivial against the harvest bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026, when the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23; the deck's urgency is a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category. The seller measured it on rows the seller chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two core perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

The consensus, visible in $4.0M of insider commitments at the mark, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 风险评估 Risk Assessment (risk, revision 3 by Red Team Analyst, 8,997 characters)
Orrin has a real cost pool and a broken price: every robot-season it has sold loses $8,100 after depreciation at the $9,500 growers signed, the $33,000 v4 that would fix it is quoted by a counterparty that is also customer, noteholder and investor, and the California standard governing the fleet requires a human driver. The mechanism is a lessor whose build cost exceeds the value of its price: equity is consumed on every unit and the preference decides who absorbs it. The risk is that the $12M is subordinated before it is at risk. Company figures are unverified. [S1, S95]

### The 1.0x floor sits at $40M, not $25M

| Exit enterprise value | Equal-rank 1x (deck terms) | Notes senior at 2x | $10M senior 2028 round | Pay-to-play, lead does not follow | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $40M | 0.96x | 0.68x | 0.69x | 0.30x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $25M | 0.59x | 0.21x | 0.31x | 0.05x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $12M | 0.26x | 0.00x | 0.00x | 0.00x | S95 (unverified), calc |

The $36.77M preference is described in the deck, not the documents, and ranks behind $1.6M of secured fleet debt; net of debt and 8% costs the $12M is whole only at a $41.6M enterprise value — $39.4M at the likely $16M close, where the stack is $34.77M — and at $25M it returns 0.59x, which means the bear case must be priced off net proceeds. Down rounds were 11.4% of Carta's Q1 2026 rounds and 12.1% of Cooley's Q2 2026 deals, and new money asks for seniority or pay-to-play; the lead then funds pro rata or converts. With 82 of the plan's own probability points missing the 2027 plan, a 2028 down round is more likely than not at 45-55%, with 30-40% on senior or pay-to-play terms. A $15M purchase of patents, licence and team — the CNH and Oishii structure — pays $13.2M after costs and returns 0.36x; through the lender's collateral, nil. [S95, S123]

### The plan multiplies three numbers the deck does not have

The v4 misses $36,000 with a 55% probability, and FY2027 revenue of $4.6M is 360 robots at $12,778, but 110 are contracted ($1.4M, company-reported) and 250 must be signed in four months by two founders and one vice president hired in June 2025. At 250 robots revenue is $3.18M, and depreciation on 64 v3 and 186 v4 units is $2.30M against $1.78M of gross profit before it: -$0.53M, worse than the plan's -$0.31M, because field service does not shrink with the fleet. The 51.8% FY2027 margin excludes $3.21M of depreciation; with it the year is -5.5%, and the 2026 41% is rental-only. The 2028 plan needs 782 robots and $13.93M of unplanned capex. A close on 2027-02-15 arrives with $1.9M against a $1.5M floor: three weeks of headroom, a January waiver request and the only likely bridge from the counterparty already owed $2.5M — so the position becomes uninvestable at the first waiver request, not the first missed number. The build compounds it: 300 units of an unbuilt design ordered in February cannot reach an April season, so 2027 runs on 64 v3 robots and a partial build, revenue lands at $0.8-1.8M, the licence test fails below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the 2028 raise happens without exclusivity. A six-month delay does not slow this model; it ends the 2027 season. [S1]

### One counterparty, five roles

Tallis Agricultural Machinery holds $2.5M of the $7.77M notes (32.2%), commits $1.0M to this round, buys $1.2M a year of engineering (46% of FY2026E revenue), sits as board observer, and supplies the $33,000 quote behind 300 units and $9.9M of orders (company-reported). One counterparty touches $14.6M of the round and supplies the number that decides viability. A 10% error is $3,300 a unit and $825 a season of depreciation, taking contribution at $12,700 from -$1,150 to -$1,975; at $44,000 the $16,500 list price stops covering depreciation. The chief operating officer's own services company took $310,000 in 2025-2026, about two-thirds of the season's field-service line, on a contract approved by a board he sits on; at a 25% premium the leakage is $62,000. With the independent seat vacant, Meridian cannot carry a related-party resolution alone. The quote is an offer, not evidence: $50-58M with two independent quotes, not $72M. [S1, S95]

### The rule that actually breaks the model

California alone prohibits autonomous agricultural equipment, through Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces; the fix died when AB 187 passed on 2026-08-31, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01, so no rule can change before the 2027 season. Both readings are fatal: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season; if the fleet sits outside it, one citation ends a season that is all of the 2026 revenue. The probability of a material restriction or enforcement action in 2027 is 20% to 25%, with -70% to -90% of equity value. The tariff is likelier and less fatal: the 2026-10-28 proclamation found a threat, imposed nothing and set a Commerce-USTR report within 180 days — 2027-04-26, six days before the season — and a 25% duty is $8,250 a robot, $2.48M on 300 and a 75-robot smaller fleet at 30-35%. Non-USMCA origin at 10% costs $3,300 a robot, 85% of gross profit, with origin undocumented at 40%; Bayh-Dole US manufacture would cost $1,500-3,000 a robot to reshore if a licensed family was federally funded, at 30-40%. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG评估 ESG Assessment (esg, revision 3 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,971 characters)
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case are being decided by other people before the 2027 season: a wage floor a California court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff decision due by 2027-04-26, a university exclusivity test on 2027-12-31 and a California rule on unpiloted machines. The balance is mildly negative for 2027 and positive after it, which argues for staging the round rather than passing on it.

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's figure of a quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14 while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost over 40 passes, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre [S80, S1].

### The cut is provisional

On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing adjustment, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and required the Department of Labor to warn employers of possible back-wage adjustments. My judgement is that a higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, which would restore most of that saving and lift the ceiling Orrin prices against.

### Who is organised, and against what

The union that won that case is most likely to shape the operating rule. In August 2026 California was drafting a trailer bill to let unpiloted machines work alongside farmworkers, and labour groups opposed it. That rule decides the unit economics: one technician to eight robots supports the $3,100 field-service line, and a human-spotter requirement would take it to $24,800 and turn the 41% gross margin negative [S84, S82, S1]. California overtime adds to the hand cost the robot displaces. Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement rather than wage rules, and the one pilot the company has lost is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its own capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper at 50% apply even under USMCA. The new tail: the Section 232 proclamation of 2026-10-28 on robotics and industrial machinery found that imports threaten national security, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days, with tariffs, quotas and fees left open [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The university licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A single binary test with no cure is harsher than standard practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones, cure periods and step-in rights. The 2027 plan clears the threshold, so the cliff needs 72% slippage; conversion risk 20%–25% (analyst estimate). If the licensed families were federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to agree that products embodying the invention are manufactured substantially in the United States, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the retail clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and fruit packed in the field reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists to obtain and no FDA action against machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds; where quality binds it is not, and the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, quoted contract manufacturer and investor in this round; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no federal award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91].

Four records are requested with this report — the H-2A disclosure files and wage table (the department's page returned an error on 2026-10-30), the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the California bill text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. Taken together, the four factors change what a season is worth rather than whether Orrin can sell one: the cheapest protection is to price the 2027 tranche against the wage-floor outcome and to make the USMCA certificate and the licence warranty conditions of closing.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 融资历程与估值 Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 4 by Valuation Analyst, 8,883 characters)
The $72M pre-money buys a $69.9M enterprise — $72M of equity plus $1.6M of drawn fleet debt less $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 — with $1.9M of FY2025 revenue at 36.8x EV/sales and $1.4M of contracted 2027-season revenue at 49.9x; the price already capitalizes the 2028 plan and leaves the $12M lead with a 1.0x return at any exit up to $90M. The deck's figures are company-provided and unverified; no audited statements, 409A or third-party valuation were supplied, though the cap-table arithmetic is internally consistent. [S95]

### The round reconciles on 15.27M shares, not 12M

The $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money and $90M post-money issues 3,818,008 Series A shares at $4.71449, taking the fully diluted count to 19,090,116 (company-provided, unverified). The $72M reconciles to 15,272,108 pre-money shares: 12,000,000 outstanding today, 2,061,303 shares from the 2025 notes and 1,210,805 new option-pool shares. The 12,000,000 shares today are not the pre-money count: 12,000,000 × $4.7145 is $56.6M, because the note conversion and pool top-up sit inside the $72M. The $7.77M of notes convert at 80% of the round price into shares worth $9.72M at $4.71449, a $1.95M uplift; the cash-equivalent pre-money is $70.05M and the cash-equivalent enterprise value is $67.95M. The last priced round was the March 2023 Series Seed at an implied $3.67/share (the $11.0M round divided by 3,000,000 seed shares), so the Series A is a 28.6% step-up, not a markup to a disclosed 2023 valuation; the February 2025 notes were not a priced round. The option pool rises from 9.0% to 12.0% of post-money, 1,210,805 new shares worth $5.71M at the round price; as a pre-money item it falls on existing holders — founders from 35.57% to 33.32%, seed from 16.78% to 15.71%, noteholders from 11.53% to 10.80% — while the new Series A owns 20.0%. ### The price is 9-22x the listed peer median

### The disclosed private marks sit below $72M

Harvest CROO has raised between $10M and $28.5M depending on the aggregator, with no disclosed valuation; Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in September 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M over eight years and 150 robots, then sold its IP and team to Oishii in 2024 for undisclosed terms; Tevel raised $20M in 2021 and carries a reported $63M secondary value. Carbon Robotics raised $70M in October 2024 with no disclosed valuation, and Monarch raised $133M at more than $500M in July 2024 before laying off almost all staff. The only disclosed $100M+ ag-robotics exits are Deere's purchases of Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), both autonomy platforms. Orrin's $90M post is above every disclosed harvesting-robot mark and near Blue River's 2015 $87M post-money — eleven years earlier. [S105, S28, S94]

### A $12M close improves the price and weakens the plan, while the preference delays the upside

The $18M target has only $4.0M committed and a $12M minimum (company-provided, unverified). At $12M the post-money is $84M, the lead owns 14.29% and the preference stack falls to $30.77M; the 2027 plan spends $9.9M of the $18M on 300 robots at a $33,000 average, so $12M funds about 200 robots, the 360-robot and $8M ARR milestones slip and a 2028 down round becomes the base case. At $16M — the lead's $12M plus the $4.0M committed — the post-money is $88M and the lead owns 13.64%. The company has $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly burn, nine months of runway to June 2027, so the close must land in Q1 2027 to order robots for the 2027 season. On the full round, the 1x preference returns the $12M in full at a $40M, $60M or $90M exit; only above $90M does the lead participate: $12.0M at $40M (1.0x), $12.0M at $60M (1.0x), $12.0M at $90M (1.0x), $20.0M at $150M (1.7x) and $33.3M at $250M (2.8x), while common shareholders receive $3.2M at $40M, $23.2M at $60M and $48.1M at $90M. To return 3x in five years the company must be worth $270M at exit, which at a 3-5x revenue multiple requires $54-90M of revenue — four to seven times the 2028 plan. The price is defensible only if the 2027 milestones are met and a strategic buyer pays above the listed peer multiples; the diligence questions are the note schedule and seed charter, the 2027 order book and deposits, the option-pool refresh policy, and the source of the $6M of unfilled Series A.
