{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 退出策略分析 Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 4 by Valuation Analyst, 8,947 characters)
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while the harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.8x — enough to return capital, not enough to carry a venture fund. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Each buyer is buying a different asset. Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would be buying the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend its See & Spray and autonomy stack into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would be buying a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would be buying fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but less need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would be buying harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet — they can manufacture — so the fleet is a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security, grower data, supply chain; no public robotics M&A found (not publicly disclosed) | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga in 2024; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93 |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | Growth capital; requires scale, float and profitability; no comparable IPO in the set (not publicly disclosed) | 2030+ | Very low | S95 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag was bought for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven, a public precision-ag company at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI was acquired by AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii for undisclosed terms. No harvesting-robot company in the set has been sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

| CNH / Raven | 2021 | $2.1B EV | n/a; 33.6% premium | Public precision-ag company | S99 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none reached $100M+, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. The 2025 market recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money, a $100M exit returns 1.1x before dilution, a $250M exit 2.8x and a $40M exit 1.0x because of the 1x preference. With illustrative probabilities of 40% at $40M, 35% at $100M, 20% at $250M and 5% at $500M, the expected MOIC is 1.6x before dilution and 1.4x after a 20% Series B — below the 3x a venture fund needs. The counter-case is that Deere or CNH pays $250-305M for the team and perception model, as they did for Blue River and Bear Flag; if Orrin proves 95% pick rates at 360 robots, a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 base rate is a small, survivor-biased set. ### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue, the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; a round above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is: $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |
| Renewal | 110 contracted 2027 seasons | n/a | 80% or more of 2026 paying growers renew | S95 (unverified) |
| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to US, European and Japanese strategics: Deere and AGCO are US-listed, CNH is Dutch/Italian and Kubota is Japanese, and all have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, the Calder license and the grower data, and the Mexico assembly adds tariff and supply-chain diligence. An IPO is not a realistic exit before 2030: $1.9M of revenue, a $5.2M net loss in FY2025 and no comparable ag-robotics IPO in the set; a listing would need scale and audited growth the company does not have. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes the exit to 2030-2032. Review of version 1 is back: revise. Your sections carry one Important item.

competition and market — Important. The direct field is well covered and passed, but four gaps remain and each changes the price ceiling or the addressable set:

1. Geographic: no Japanese or Chinese harvester appears. Japan has commercially deployed horticultural harvesters and China builds protected-culture picking machines; a machine at half Orrin's price point sets a lower ceiling on the $16,500 list. Search for Japanese strawberry and soft-fruit harvesters in commercial deployment and for Chinese protected-culture and open-field picking machines, and name a product only after the search confirms its status and price point. If the price point is not public, say so rather than estimating.
2. Academic: the section argues the perception stack cannot be bought, but names no university group working the same perception problem. Those groups are also what erodes the licensed families' value if exclusivity lapses on 2027-12-31. Add the groups you can confirm.
3. Substitutes that shrink the addressable acres rather than compete for them: tabletop and high-tunnel production currently appears only as an exclusion; and no berry marketer's machine-harvest breeding programme is examined, although a variety bred for a single destructive pass is what took processing tomatoes from about 0.5% to 70%. Treat both as a threat to the 50,000-acre base, not just a filter on it.
4. Adjacent: put Tallis in the competitor table as a potential builder — the report already says it could build the competing platform from the same bill of materials and it is the source of the unit-cost quote.

Add these to section 5 with the standard columns, and carry the acreage effect into section 4 if it changes the base. Search with generic terms only; no client-document names. Reply when both are saved.

Review of version 1 is back: revise. Your sections carry two Important items.

1. business_model and financials — the commercial mechanics are missing. Add: the sales cycle from first field trial to a signed robot-season (months, and who signs — owner, VP of growing, procurement); the cost of running a pilot and who bears it; what the accounts that did not renew or did not sign chose instead (hand crews, a competitor, a smaller robot count, or nothing); and the contract term and cancellation rights embedded in the $9,500 and $12,700 prices. This is what turns the contracted count of 110 into evidence about demand rather than a number.

2. financials — the $0.085M 2027 cash figure does not reconcile. A $12M close that starts from $3.7M at 2026-09-30, carries $410,000 a month of net burn to the close, then funds roughly 200 robots and a season cannot end 2027 at $85,000 without an assumption the section does not state. Either show the monthly path that produces it — opening cash, close proceeds, capex, season working capital, debt service, covenant floor — or replace it with the balance the path supports and say which line changed. State the same path for the $18M case ($6.085M) so the two are comparable.

Everything else passed and stays: the -$8,100 contribution, the 12.31-season payback, the $1.4M recurring revenue rebuild, the 52%/61% margins before $3.21M/$6.45M of depreciation, the United Rentals gross-margin and revenue-per-employee benchmarks. Do not restate the ARR definition.

Keep the section under the 9,000-character ceiling; if the additions do not fit, cut the narrative and keep the tables. Reply when both are saved.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 公司概览 Company Overview (company_overview, revision 3 by Company Analyst, 8,790 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks is a real operating company: Delaware-incorporated on 2021-09-14, 38 staff, three hardware generations shipped by 2026-03, $1.9M FY2025 revenue and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 — all company-reported and unverified. It is not yet safe to wire $12M into, because the entity signing the grower contracts, owning the fleet and carrying the equipment debt is a subsidiary the Series A does not buy. The $72.0M pre-money is internally coherent — $72.0M ÷ 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares = $4.7145, and $18.0M buys 3,818,008 shares, 20.0% of a $90.0M post — but 15,272,108 is not the "12,000,000 fully diluted total" printed beside it, which at $4.7145 is $56.6M. The priced count absorbs the $7.77M note conversion and the pool at 12% of post-money, so every derived figure must be rebuilt before a term sheet [S1].

No registry record was retrievable: the Delaware and California searches were unreachable, so incorporation, good standing, the agent for service, the foreign qualification and any UCC-1 over the fleet rest on the company's own pages. The name returned no press, grant or patent trace either — no footprint, or a failed retrieval. Confidence below is capped accordingly.

### Three entities, and the investor buys the one without the contracts

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Salinas, CA | Corporation | Series A issuer; US staff; 5 filings and the Calder licence | Shareholders, below | S1, unverified |
| Orrin Fleet Services LLC | California, 2023-11-02 | LLC | Fleet; grower contracts; Kestrel borrower | 100% parent | S1, unverified |
| Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. | Jalisco, 2024-07-19 | S. de R.L. de C.V. | Gripper and harness assembly; 7 staff | 99% parent / 1% fleet LLC | S1, unverified |

The parent holds five US patent filings and an exclusive Calder University licence from 2022-01-20 for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum. The California LLC holds the fleet, the grower contracts and the Kestrel facility: $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 2025-06-16, 11.5%, secured on the fleet, with a $1.5M minimum cash covenant. The Mexican company assembles components with seven staff on a 99/1 split, the 1% with the California LLC. Three questions follow, none answerable from the deck: whether the licence permits operation or sublicensing by an affiliate; whether Kestrel has consented to new equity and where the covenant is tested; and whether the 99/1 split is in a registered deed and the foreign-investment registry [S1].

### The cap table clears; the headline does not

| Shareholder | Class | % post-round | % votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dr. Imani Castellano | Common | 18.23% | 18.23% | S1, unverified |
| Teodor Vashti | Common | 11.31% | 11.31% | S1, unverified |
| Dr. Soren Abernathy, former CTO | Common, vested | 3.77% | 3.77% | S1, unverified |
| Granary Ventures | Series Seed | 9.43% | 9.43% | S1, unverified |
| Furrowline Angels and other seed | Series Seed | 6.29% | 6.29% | S1, unverified |
| 2025 noteholders, converted | Series A-1 | 10.80% | 10.80% | S1, unverified |
| New Series A money, $18.0M | Series A | 20.00% | 20.00% | S1, unverified |
| Options granted | Common | 8.17% | 8.17% | S1, unverified |
| Unallocated pool | Common, reserved | 12.00% | 0.00% | S1, unverified |

On the company's unverified cap table, the pool rises from 1,080,000 unallocated shares to 2,290,805, up 112%, costing existing holders $5.71M at the round price, 7.9% of the pre-money. Founders fall from 47.0% to 29.5%; 2.0 points is the pool, and the former CTO keeps 3.3% of the combined founder block. The 80% note conversion yields 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares against 1,648,000 at full price, moving $1.95M to noteholders and an estimated $0.6M from the founders. Voting percentages assume one vote per share and no voting agreement, which the deck does not disclose — material, because two common seats of five is all that keeps the founders off a board they do not control [S1].

### The $72M sits below its own preference stack

On the company's figures, unverified, the 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M assumed from the 2023 round size, which the deck does not state): a $36.8M stack, 40.9% of the $90.0M post-money. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit, where 46.5% as-converted equals the preference. At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at a $79M sale and needs a $180M exit for 2x, so the pre-money is best underwritten as an option struck at $79M, not a mark on the common. The structure is founder-friendly; the size of the stack decides whether a modest success reaches the common at all [S1].

### What it sells, and to whom

Orrin sells a robot-season, not a robot. The customer is a strawberry grower, the user is the crew the robot displaces, and the budget owner holds the harvest-labour line. Growth comes from converting pilots into paid seasonal rentals and renewing them: 14 pilot farms since 2024, two conversions in 2025, five paying growers in 2026, 110 robots contracted for 2027 plus 50 under letters of intent. Revenue quality is thinner than the $3.2M ARR headline: $1.4M is contracted robot-seasons at the $12,700 renewal price, $1.2M is engineering services ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M is non-binding letters of intent. The $8M ARR milestone cannot be met by the fleet being funded: 360 robots at $12,700 is $4.6M, at the $16,500 list price $5.9M [S1].

### Governance: five roles in one counterparty and an empty chair

After closing the board is five seats — two common, one seed, one Series A, one independent agreed by both — and the independent seat is vacant, so the tie-breaker is unfilled and the chair is the chief executive. Tallis Agricultural Machinery is at once a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer at 37.5% of stated ARR, the quoted manufacturer whose $33,000 unit cost underpins the $9.9M robot budget, a board observer and a $1.0M investor; it also employed the chief executive in 2010-2011. The chief operating officer's wholly owned services company took $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date under a contract approved by a board he sits on, with no independent director, and his 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer [S1]. Conditions before closing:

- An independent director at signing, agreed by the lead, chairing audit and compensation.
- Observer rights limited to non-confidential sessions.
- A second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials.
- Kestrel consent, a covenant waiver through the 2027 build, and Calder consent to affiliate operation and sublicensing.
- Founder reverse-vesting and a full-time chief financial officer by closing.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 创始人与核心团队 Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 3 by Company Analyst, 8,626 characters)
The team is built for the problem Orrin had in 2021, not the one it has in 2027. Dr. Imani Castellano, chief executive and board chair, is a perception researcher with a robotics PhD who spent five years in a university field-robotics lab and is named on eleven patent filings; Teodor Vashti, chief operating officer, ran harvest operations for two large berry growers across twenty years. Neither has built hardware at volume: nobody on the five-person executive group has taken a product past a few dozen units, none has founded or sold a company, and the co-founder who owned the technical roadmap left on 2023-08-31. All of this is company-reported and unverified; no education, employer, patent or press record could be retrieved for any named person [S1].

### The pairing fits two problems and misses the third

The combination matches the first two problems a picking robot has to solve — seeing ripe fruit, and being allowed onto a farm — and not the third, making 360 of them. Castellano invents and raises: the licensed university families come out of her lab, the company holds five filings of its own, and she is the face of the raise. Vashti sells and operates, and the book shows it: five paying growers in 2026, the two named ones taking 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons, and the largest of those two is the farm where he was director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021, contracted for 40 robots in 2027. That is company-reported commercial proof and also its limit: the funnel is one man's twenty-year network, and the plan needs 250 more robots sold in a four-month window [S1].

### A CTO seat empty for 26 months

The co-founder and CTO, Dr. Soren Abernathy, left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. On the company's unverified account he keeps 720,000 vested common shares — 6.0% before the round, 3.8% after — which makes him a permanent party to the cap table without giving him a reason to protect it. Whether he is a named inventor on the two licensed university families is not stated in the deck and could not be checked at the patent office; the deck attributes the licensed work to Castellano's lab, which is not the same as placing him outside it. No public footprint or new venture could be retrieved for him. A 3.8% holder with unrestricted vested shares and the core perception work in his head is a hireable asset for any competitor or customer, and California does not let the company restrain where he works [S1].

### The technical bet sits one level below the executive team

Dr. Mei Hollander joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at one robotics company, moving from manipulation engineer to engineering manager for grippers — company-reported and unverified. That is a direct match for the bruising problem, 3.8% of berries damaged in the 2025 pilots and the reason one Florida grower ended its pilot in 2026-06, and no match for the problem that decides 2027: cutting the build from $48,000 to a $33,000 average while multiplying the fleet by 5.6. With no CTO above her, the hardest programme the company has attempted is owned by one vice president hired 32 months ago, on an equity package the deck does not describe, which is where retention risk concentrates [S1].

### Selling 360 robots with one new sales leader

Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales and Customer Success in 2025-06 after twenty years at a crop-inputs company, ending as regional sales director for the West: sixteen months in robotics, unverified. The contracted book for 2027 is 110 robots plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, 31% of the 360-robot plan five months before the season, with two founder-sellers and one vice president to close the gap. The risk is not that growers dislike the product; it is that this industry buys late, the season opens in April in California and December in Florida, and a 360-unit build must be committed before the orders exist. The deck shows no pipeline by stage, so the 250-robot gap cannot be assessed from these materials at all [S1].

### What would settle it

Three records would turn this from biography into evidence, all of them unverified now: degree checks through each institution's registrar, because three of the five degrees sit at institutions named nowhere else in the file; patent-inventor records, because eleven university filings and five company filings are checkable and the departed CTO's inventorship is not stated; and reference calls at the four prior employers, most urgently the farm where the chief operating officer worked for seven years. Against the closest comparison available, the company's own history, the fleet went from 12 robots in 2024 to 64 in 2026, a 5.3x in two seasons, while the plan asks for 5.6x in one season and a one-third cost cut. The peer comparison the decision needs — what Harvest CROO Robotics, Agrobot, Advanced Farm Technologies and Tortuga AgTech had built by their third year — could not be sourced and is not asserted. For the lead, the implication is that people risk is priceable and should be priced: a CTO-level hire, a manufacturing leader and a retention grant for the VP Engineering as closing conditions, not intentions [S1].

What would decide between them is checkable: the patent-inventor records for the eleven university and five company filings, the v3 field data behind the 94% pick rate, and reference calls at Corvane Robotics and at the farm supplying the largest 2027 contract. arguments.markdown:
Meridian should pass at the $72M pre-money. Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the field and a real harvest cost pool to sell into, but at the $9,500 a robot-season growers signed and the $48,000 build the company can evidence (company-reported, unverified), every unit loses $8,100 before debt service, and the round prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund: the $12M cheque returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities and 2x only at a $180M exit. [S1, S95]

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pass | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; re-engage at $50-58M with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged | 4.5 | Medium | 12-24 months, to the 2027 season and the licence test | S95 (unverified), S1 (unverified) |
:::

### What is good, and what decides it

The pain is real and independently measured: the UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is cheap against that bill. The picker has the only labelled field dataset in the category — 94% pick rate on 212 rows, 75 paid robot-seasons, 110 robots contracted for 2027 at a $12,700 renewal price — and the two things that usually kill hardware start-ups, no customer and no evidence, are not the problem here. Four facts outweigh that. One robot-season loses $8,100 at the signed price, and the $33,000 build that would fix it is a single quote from a counterparty that is also noteholder, customer, board observer and investor. Bruising at 3.8% has already cost one grower and spends most of the USDA allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. [S119, S1, S95, S86]

The rating is Pass rather than Wait for milestone because the binding objection is the price plus evidence that rests on the company alone, and the re-entry milestones — two independent v4 quotes and 200 robots in paid service — are the conditions for a lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open.

The evidence confidence is medium. The arithmetic is solid and reproducible from the deck; the inputs — build cost, service cost, contract count, preference terms and every executive credential — are management statements with no independent record retrieved. The $36.77M preference stack, at 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, is one sentence in the deck and appears in no document; the 0.94x return and the Pass rating assume it. There is no audit, no registry confirmation of the three entities, no federal award visible against the stated grant, and no patent prosecution record. [S95]

The follow-up diligence is narrow and cheap: two independent manufacturer quotes for the v4, an independent cold-storage bruising trial, the note purchase agreement, the lender's consent, and a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year.

::: one-question

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 风险评估 Risk Assessment (risk, revision 3 by Red Team Analyst, 8,997 characters)
Orrin has a real cost pool and a broken price: every robot-season it has sold loses $8,100 after depreciation at the $9,500 growers signed, the $33,000 v4 that would fix it is quoted by a counterparty that is also customer, noteholder and investor, and the California standard governing the fleet requires a human driver. The mechanism is a lessor whose build cost exceeds the value of its price: equity is consumed on every unit and the preference decides who absorbs it. The risk is that the $12M is subordinated before it is at risk. Company figures are unverified. [S1, S95]

### The 1.0x floor sits at $40M, not $25M

| Exit enterprise value | Equal-rank 1x (deck terms) | Notes senior at 2x | $10M senior 2028 round | Pay-to-play, lead does not follow | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $40M | 0.96x | 0.68x | 0.69x | 0.30x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $25M | 0.59x | 0.21x | 0.31x | 0.05x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $12M | 0.26x | 0.00x | 0.00x | 0.00x | S95 (unverified), calc |

The $36.77M preference is described in the deck, not the documents, and ranks behind $1.6M of secured fleet debt; net of debt and 8% costs the $12M is whole only at a $41.6M enterprise value — $39.4M at the likely $16M close, where the stack is $34.77M — and at $25M it returns 0.59x, which means the bear case must be priced off net proceeds. Down rounds were 11.4% of Carta's Q1 2026 rounds and 12.1% of Cooley's Q2 2026 deals, and new money asks for seniority or pay-to-play; the lead then funds pro rata or converts. With 82 of the plan's own probability points missing the 2027 plan, a 2028 down round is more likely than not at 45-55%, with 30-40% on senior or pay-to-play terms. A $15M purchase of patents, licence and team — the CNH and Oishii structure — pays $13.2M after costs and returns 0.36x; through the lender's collateral, nil. [S95, S123]

### The plan multiplies three numbers the deck does not have

The v4 misses $36,000 with a 55% probability, and FY2027 revenue of $4.6M is 360 robots at $12,778, but 110 are contracted ($1.4M, company-reported) and 250 must be signed in four months by two founders and one vice president hired in June 2025. At 250 robots revenue is $3.18M, and depreciation on 64 v3 and 186 v4 units is $2.30M against $1.78M of gross profit before it: -$0.53M, worse than the plan's -$0.31M, because field service does not shrink with the fleet. The 51.8% FY2027 margin excludes $3.21M of depreciation; with it the year is -5.5%, and the 2026 41% is rental-only. The 2028 plan needs 782 robots and $13.93M of unplanned capex. A close on 2027-02-15 arrives with $1.9M against a $1.5M floor: three weeks of headroom, a January waiver request and the only likely bridge from the counterparty already owed $2.5M — so the position becomes uninvestable at the first waiver request, not the first missed number. The build compounds it: 300 units of an unbuilt design ordered in February cannot reach an April season, so 2027 runs on 64 v3 robots and a partial build, revenue lands at $0.8-1.8M, the licence test fails below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the 2028 raise happens without exclusivity. A six-month delay does not slow this model; it ends the 2027 season. [S1]

### One counterparty, five roles

Tallis Agricultural Machinery holds $2.5M of the $7.77M notes (32.2%), commits $1.0M to this round, buys $1.2M a year of engineering (46% of FY2026E revenue), sits as board observer, and supplies the $33,000 quote behind 300 units and $9.9M of orders (company-reported). One counterparty touches $14.6M of the round and supplies the number that decides viability. A 10% error is $3,300 a unit and $825 a season of depreciation, taking contribution at $12,700 from -$1,150 to -$1,975; at $44,000 the $16,500 list price stops covering depreciation. The chief operating officer's own services company took $310,000 in 2025-2026, about two-thirds of the season's field-service line, on a contract approved by a board he sits on; at a 25% premium the leakage is $62,000. With the independent seat vacant, Meridian cannot carry a related-party resolution alone. The quote is an offer, not evidence: $50-58M with two independent quotes, not $72M. [S1, S95]

### The rule that actually breaks the model

California alone prohibits autonomous agricultural equipment, through Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces; the fix died when AB 187 passed on 2026-08-31, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01, so no rule can change before the 2027 season. Both readings are fatal: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season; if the fleet sits outside it, one citation ends a season that is all of the 2026 revenue. The probability of a material restriction or enforcement action in 2027 is 20% to 25%, with -70% to -90% of equity value. The tariff is likelier and less fatal: the 2026-10-28 proclamation found a threat, imposed nothing and set a Commerce-USTR report within 180 days — 2027-04-26, six days before the season — and a 25% duty is $8,250 a robot, $2.48M on 300 and a 75-robot smaller fleet at 30-35%. Non-USMCA origin at 10% costs $3,300 a robot, 85% of gross profit, with origin undocumented at 40%; Bayh-Dole US manufacture would cost $1,500-3,000 a robot to reshore if a licensed family was federally funded, at 30-40%. The wage floor helps at 60-70% odds but cannot fix bruising. [S126, S124, S88, S89, S85]

### Absence is a finding, not proof

No registry entry, no federal award against the grant the deck describes, no granted patent and no auditor's opinion: the inference is not misrepresentation but that every fact the decision turns on is management representation. Absence proves less than it seems: registries sit behind paywalls, applications stay unpublished for eighteen months, subawards appear on no federal site. It proves enough — the money would be wired on unverified facts, a condition-precedent problem before a price problem.

::: info danger
**The model-breaker is the California equipment prohibition, not the tariff.** California alone bars autonomous agricultural equipment, the fix died on 2026-08-31, and the committee does not sit until 2026-12-01. Both readings end the investment: one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season, and a citation stops the only revenue line. [S126, S124]
:::

AB 187 is expected to be signed by the governor. The bill includes reenactment of Labor Code Section 2695.4, originally passed in 2023, allowing goat herders to be paid a monthly minimum wage—currently $4,938 per month—plus travel and housing. This provision of the labor code had sunset as of July 1, causing a situation in which goat herders would have to be paid nearly $20,000 per month, virtually guaranteeing goats—and probably sheep managed alongside goats—would be unavailable for employment to conduct wildfire fuels control through prescribed grazing.  As reenacted on AB 187, sheep and goat wage parity will be in place until Jan. 1, 2029. Missing from AB 187 was a compromise measure that would have allowed the use of autonomous agricultural equipment by revising outdated Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver to operate self-propelled equipment in agricultural workplaces. As a result, California remains the only state to prohibit the use of such equipment, and it does so only in agricultural workplaces. Language agreed upon by agricultural employers and legislative leaders would have allowed the use of such equipment statewide across the agricultural industry and required reporting on its use, including any injuries or incidents involving the equipment and any resulting employee displacement. The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. The 2024 UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural costs and $112,694 of total cost, on 9,000 trays at $11; UC Davis puts labour at 50-60% of variable production cost, with pickers paid $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour. arguments.markdown:
Meridian should pass at the $72M pre-money. Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the field and a real harvest cost pool to sell into, but at the $9,500 a robot-season growers signed and the $48,000 build the company can evidence (company-reported, unverified), every unit loses $8,100 before debt service, and the round prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund: the $12M cheque returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities and 2x only at a $180M exit. The rating is Pass rather than Wait for milestone because the binding objection is the price plus evidence that rests on the company alone; the re-entry milestones are the conditions for a lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pass | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; re-engage at $50-58M with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged | 4.5 | Medium | 12-24 months, to the 2027 season and the licence test | S95 (unverified), S1 (unverified) |
:::

### What is good, and what decides it

The pain is real and independently measured: the UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is cheap against that bill. The picker has the only labelled field dataset in the category — 94% pick rate on 212 rows, 75 paid robot-seasons, 110 robots contracted for 2027 at a $12,700 renewal price — and the two things that usually kill hardware start-ups, no customer and no evidence, are not the problem here. Four facts outweigh that. One robot-season loses $8,100 at the signed price, and the $33,000 build that would fix it is a single quote from a counterparty that is also noteholder, customer, board observer and investor. Bruising at 3.8% has already cost one grower and spends most of the USDA allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. [S119, S1, S95, S86]

The evidence confidence is medium. The arithmetic is solid and reproducible from the deck; the inputs — build cost, service cost, contract count, preference terms and every executive credential — are management statements, unverified, with no independent record retrieved. The $36.77M preference stack, at 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, is one sentence in the deck and appears in no document; the 0.94x return and the Pass rating assume it. There is no audit, no registry confirmation of the three entities, no federal award visible against the stated grant, and no patent prosecution record. [S95]

The follow-up diligence is narrow and cheap: two independent manufacturer quotes for the v4, an independent cold-storage bruising trial, the note purchase agreement, the lender's consent, and a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year.

::: one-question
What does a fourth-generation robot cost to build at fleet volumes, quoted by a manufacturer that is not also the largest customer?

At the current build cost no price growers have signed makes a robot-season profitable, so the fleet consumes capital on every unit; at a lower cost the list price turns contribution positive and the business becomes financeable. Two competitive quotes settle it in weeks and decide between a capital-consuming lease book and a business that compounds.
:::

::: takeaways

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 4 by Lead Analyst, 8,993 characters)
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, the largest controllable line in the grower's P&L and the one a machine can attack. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, trivial against the harvest bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026, when the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23; the deck's urgency is a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category. The seller measured it on rows the seller chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two core perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus, visible in $4.0M of insider commitments at the mark, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but that we price the lease book on the cash it produces at the price growers signed, $9,500, and on a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. ### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, roughly four times the $87M post-money of its last private round, and it bought a perception platform that fitted an existing sprayer line, not a fleet of leased harvesters. Agtech venture funding fell from $53bn in 2021 to $7bn in 2025; 18 companies shut down that year, and Q2 2026 raised $1bn against $2bn a year earlier. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,944 characters)
Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics, co-founded by Wish Farms owner Gary Wishnatzki, announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester reached performance rates on par with human harvesting in a commercial picking operation at Duette, Florida — a direct open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but it removes the "only player" premise. What disciplines Orrin's price is less the rival robot than the hand crew it must beat, the harvest-aid platform that takes part of the saving at a fraction of the capital, and the 2025 exits that show how hard harvest robotics is to fund [S27, S28].

::: evidence
**The field is thinner than the technology narrative implies, and it is not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in 2025. Source: S27, S28, S34.
:::

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Status (2026) | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest CROO (Tampa, FL) | B8 harvester | Row-following platform, AI vision, LIDAR, RaaS | Commercial trials, Duette FL, 2025-04 | "On par with human harvesting" (company, unverified); no pick rate or bruising data | Not disclosed | Not disclosed; Florida trials only | 13 patents; Wish Farms backing; Florida presence | Florida-only, December-March season; no California service; no independent metrics | S27, S78 |
| Advanced Farm (Davis, CA) | Robotic picker | Vision and arm on mobile platform | Ceased operations 2025 (reported 2025-07-08) | Reached named commercial strawberry growers | Not disclosed | 0% after 2025 exit | Had California commercial relationships | Out of funding; no service network at scale | S28, S79 |
| Tortuga AgTech (US) | Model F/G | Dual-arm picking and direct packing | IP, assets and team acquired by Oishii in 2025 | Commercial fleet before the sale | Not disclosed | 0% open-field after 2025 sale | Commercial deployment and direct packing | Buyer is indoor-focused; open-field business not continued | S34 |
| Agrobot (Spain) | Solar harvest-aid platform | Self-steering solar platform carrying pickers | Commercial platform | 30-40% labour saving (company, unverified) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Low capital cost; no fruit-quality risk; near-zero running cost | Still needs a full crew; no autonomy | S77 |
| Hand crews (status quo) | Piece-rate picking crew | Pickers, carts, conveyors | Universal | 8-12 flats an hour at $1.75-2.25 a flat; 40-50 passes a season | $1.75-2.25 a flat | 99.5% of US acres (author calculation: 100% minus Orrin's 0.5%) | Proven quality, no capex, flexible across varieties | 2025 availability shock; rising wage floor; housing and supervision cost | S12 |
| Tevel; FFRobotics; Metomotion | Orchard and greenhouse harvesters | Flying robots; orchard and greenhouse systems | Commercial in orchards (Tevel: Italy, California, Chile) | Named orchard customers; no strawberry product listed | Not disclosed | 0% of strawberries | Capital and perception engineering | No strawberry end-effector or row system | S30 |

The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm Technologies, which had reached named commercial growers in California, ceased operations in 2025, reported on 2025-07-08; Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and team to vertical-farming company Oishii. No public market shares exist; the best proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre US base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S27, S34].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo said it "was unable to develop the market traction necessary to support its business", and it put its IP and assets up for sale on 2021-06-29. Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, was sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021. The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against a $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30. RaaS shifts capital to Orrin's balance sheet and removes the grower's capex objection, but it concentrates the constraint rather than removing it [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour, and conveyors already raise productivity by cutting walking; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform adds a partial step: it carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost, a company claim that is unverified but captures part of the saving with none of the autonomy risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: the reported transfer of Advanced Farm's IP to CNH Industrial is unverified, but a picking arm on a harvest-aid platform that already sells and services equipment is a cheaper route to the grower than a new autonomous fleet. Orrin must beat a crew costing $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour and charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field row architecture, same RaaS model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim already in the market. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published pick rate or bruising data, and no California service network — where Orrin's 14 pilots and 4 paying growers sit. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct packing into the grower's clamshells so fruit is handled once, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows, and the COO's California grower relationships. It is a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly [S30, S1].

| Product | Orrin's position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest | Challenger: 262 acres, 0.5% share of US base | Harvest CROO (Florida commercial claim, unverified) | Orrin Fieldworks (75 paid robot-seasons) | Agrobot (harvest-aid platform) | Equipment makers integrating picking arms; Tallis as contract manufacturer and noteholder | S27, S1, S77 |

### The price is the tell
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025 and 2026 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase, with renewals averaging $12,700. It is a large increase on a base not yet renewed at list, and the company's own disclosure contains the counter-evidence: Grower E in Plant City ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers. Offsetting it, four growers contracted 110 robots for 2027 (Marisol Ridge 40, Pajaro Bluff 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20), so some buyers accept the quality at the renewal price. If Harvest CROO's parity claim proves true in Florida, Orrin's price converges on displaced labour and the $16,500 list is at risk; if the 3.8% bruising holds across retail specifications, it can keep pricing up. The key diligence question is whether bruising is measured against a retailer specification or only Orrin's test rows, then the Tallis relationship: Tallis is contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, board observer and $1M investor, and could build the competing platform [S1, S28].

| Weaknesses | Florida pilot lost to bruising; 53% of 2026 robot-seasons with two growers; no independent performance data; $48,000 unit cost and 41% gross margin, company-reported and unverified; single product and crop | S1 |
| Opportunities | Advanced Farm closed and Tortuga was absorbed, thinning the direct field; 2025 enforcement shock and 398,258 H-2A certifications keep labour at the top of the grower's agenda; 110 robots contracted for 2027 | S28, S34, S15, S1 |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,908 characters)
At the price Orrin has actually signed, one robot-season does not cover the depreciation on the robot, so the rental business loses money on every unit today; the case rests on an unbuilt v4 and a price increase no grower has signed.

### The revenue is mostly not rental

The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season (company-reported, unaudited): about seven months in California (April-October) and four in Florida (December-March), one season at a time, with Orrin owning, maintaining and insuring the fleet. No multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M divides into robot rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E is little better, with rental at $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%). The engineering customer is also a $2.5M noteholder, a board observer, the quoted manufacturer of the v4 and a $1.0M committed investor in this round, so half of FY2025 revenue is related-party and 80% is one-off, grant-funded or related-party. What the company has proven is that five growers will rent 75 robot-seasons at $9,500; the rest of the revenue line is an engineering contract and a grant, and its own strategy assumes both disappear by 2028 [S1].

### One robot-season loses $8,100 before any overhead

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company, unaudited) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Interest-only debt service ($1.6M x 11.5% / 75 seasons) | (2,453) | 25.8 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Cash contribution after interest-only debt service | 1,447 | 15.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Cash contribution after amortising debt service | (3,051) | (32.1) | S1 (unverified), calc |

The company-reported 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: fleet depreciation sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue. Charging the $48,000 v3 over its four-season life puts $12,000 against each season, more than the $9,500 the grower pays before a single technician is paid. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and should not be added; the economic measure is the negative $8,100 contribution, while the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only and -$3,051 if it amortises over the robot's four-season life. The benchmark: United Rentals earned a gross margin of 38.0% on equipment rentals in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue. Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at the $16,500 list price with the v3, and only reaches +19.1% with both the list price and a $31,000 v4 [S21].

### The 2.1-season payback is the best case of three unproven inputs

The claimed 2.1 seasons is $31,000 divided by ($16,500 list price less $1,750 target service), which drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely. Putting it back gives 2.53 seasons on the company's own target cost and price. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet actually ran in 2026, against a four-season asset life. Even at the $31,000 target build and the signed price the payback is 7.95 seasons; at the list price and the current build it is 4.40 seasons, longer than the asset lasts. Of the four inputs that decide payback, build cost is unbuilt, price unsigned, service cost unreconciled to the technician ratio and transport omitted from the slide. All of these are company-reported, unaudited figures [S1].

### Utilisation cannot repair a per-season capital charge

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two (the California and Florida seasons cover eleven months). At the signed price the fleet needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 seasons, 85% of the maximum; at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles its revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads fixed overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital hurdle. Service cost is no more forgiving. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 loaded field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour, over 213 days, costs $41,611 per technician-season, or $5,201 per robot-season; at the $29.60 machine-operator rate it is $6,305. The deck reports $3,100, which implies a technician costs $24,800 for seven months before a vehicle, tools or travel. At 360 robots the same ratio needs 45 technicians and $1.12M at the reported rate, so the cost is linear in robots, not diluted by scale; on the $6,305 figure, gross profit at the signed price falls to $695, or 7.3%, before depreciation [S1, S10].

### Price is not the constraint; proof and quality are

At one robot per 3.5 acres the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the 2027 list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre - 3.4% to 5.9% of the labour bill the robot targets. At 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray, each percentage point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21% to 36% of the robot fee; the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee and 80% of the list fee. That asymmetry explains why price has not moved to list and why one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising: a grower is buying an option on a harvest, not a proven substitute for a crew. The risk is not that growers cannot afford the robot but that the robot, at 94% of detected ripe fruit and 86% uptime, cannot yet promise the bruising and reliability a retail supply chain requires [S10].

### What would have to be true

The unit turns positive only if both conditions hold at once: a build cost at or below the milestone ceiling and a price at or above the breakeven in the table, with the v4 in service. The investment should therefore be conditioned on signed 2027 contracts at the list price with deposits, a verified v4 bill of materials from a manufacturer independent of the largest revenue customer, an audited service-cost build reconciled to the 1:8 technician ratio, and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on the company's own figures; the service-cost cross-check and the bruise-to-revenue link are medium confidence, and the open questions are the loan amortisation schedule, the Florida season price and the share of bruised fruit actually culled.

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unaudited) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures alone produce the negative contribution, the 12.31-season payback at the signed price and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven [S1].

The full round funds the fleet plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the minimum close the plan is not funded, the cash covenant binds before the season starts, and most of the reported ARR is not recurring rental.

### The statements are unaudited, and incomplete

The company supplies an income statement for FY2023-FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time head of finance. On the company-reported, unaudited numbers revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin falls from 57.7% to 51.8% in FY2027 before reaching 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event, not a trend. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering services or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

### ARR is a forward book, not a run-rate

The company-reported, unaudited $3.2M "ARR" is exactly three numbers: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at the $12,700 renewal average), $1.2M of engineering services that end on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed revenue is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level [S1].

| ARR component, 2026-09-30 | $M | What it is | Treatment | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contracted 2027 robot-seasons | 1.4 | 110 robots x $12,700 | Contracted, not yet earned | S1 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 1.2 | Fixed term to 2027-06-30, related party | Remove: expires mid-2027 | S1 (unverified) |
| Letters of intent | 0.6 | 50 robots, non-binding | Remove: not contracted | S1 (unverified) |
| Like-for-like recurring | 1.4 | 43.8% of the $3.2M headline |  | S1 (unverified), calc |

### The runway claim measures cash to zero, not to the covenant

The nine-month figure is the time to zero cash, but the company must keep a minimum unrestricted balance at all times, so the usable cushion is only the difference; the binding date is the covenant floor, not insolvency, and it falls before the April 2027 season starts. It moves with the closing date: a quarter's delay does not shorten the runway by three months, it lands after the covenant is breached, making the closing date a condition of the investment.

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is 5.4 months to a covenant breach.** Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 (company-reported, unaudited) less the $1.5M minimum leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000 a month: the floor is reached around 2027-03-10, three weeks before the season, and a close that slips from 2026-12-15 to 2027-03-15 lands five days after it. With $12M, 2027 year-end cash is $0.085M, $1.4M below the floor, and the breach comes around November 2027; with $18M it is $6.085M. [S1]
:::

### Capex buys 360 robots, but not the 2028 revenue

On the company-reported, unaudited plan, three hundred new robots at $33,000 is $9.9M, and 360 in service is 64 existing v3 plus 296 new v4, so the 2027 budget is internally consistent. The undrawn $0.9M of the $2.5M facility buys 27 more robots, and the $3.7M of cash is already spoken for by operating burn and the covenant. The revenue lines are not consistent with the contracts: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, $78 above the $12,700 renewal average, but only 110 robots are contracted - at the $16,500 list the same fleet would produce $5.94M and at the $9,500 signed price $3.42M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500, confirmed by the $6.45M of depreciation that reconciles the projected net loss; that is 422 more robots and $13.93M of capex nowhere in the plan. The only capex-free reading is 360 robots each doing two seasons at $17,900, requiring a Florida business that does not exist at scale [S1].

2. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at
peak harvest. Harvest labor is the largest single cost line for most growers.
-  Strawberries are picked by hand every three to four days through a season of up to seven months; a picker covers roughly a quarter of an acre a
day (company estimate).
-  Growers tell us their crews are smaller and older each year, while wages and worker housing keep getting more expensive (grower interviews, 2025).
-  Fruit left unpicked rots on the plant and spreads mold to the next pass, so a short crew costs more than the berries it leaves behind.
-  Harvest aids such as carts and conveyors make pickers faster, but still need a full crew.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 2 of 15

--- p.3 ---
3. Our product: the Orrin Picker
-  An autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives the furrows at night and day, finds ripe berries with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and
picks them with a soft three-finger gripper.
-  Pick rate: 94% of ripe fruit on the rows tested in our 2025 pilots (company measurement; definition on slide 4).
-  Throughput: one robot covers roughly 1.5 acres per 24 hours.
-  Two picking arms place berries straight into the grower's retail clamshells on board, so fruit is handled once.
-  Runs about 20 hours a day on swappable battery packs; one field technician supervises up to 8 robots, on site or remotely.
-  Sold as Robots-as-a-Service: growers pay per robot per season; we own, maintain and insure the fleet.
-  Current model: Orrin Picker v3, released to the field in March 2026. The v4, designed for lower cost, is planned for the 2027 season.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 3 of 15

-  Perception: two stereo camera pairs per arm, with LED lighting for night work. The ripeness model was trained on 1.9 million labelled berry images
from the Calder University lab and our pilots.
-  Gripper: three silicone fingers with slip sensing; the stem is cut, not pulled.
-  Navigation: furrow following without GPS, so robots keep working in coastal fog and at night.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, the largest line a machine can attack. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, trivial against the harvest bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026, when the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23; the deck's urgency is a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is a measured figure with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows and excluded tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus, visible in $4.0M of insider commitments at the mark, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but that we price the lease book on the cash it produces at the price growers signed, $9,500, and on a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, roughly four times its last private post-money, and bought a perception platform that fitted an existing sprayer line, not a fleet of leased harvesters. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. Agtech venture funding fell from $53bn in 2021 to $7bn in 2025 and 18 companies shut down that year. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

### The distribution, not the mean, decides it

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | v4 at or below $33,000 on two quotes; renewals $12,700-16,500; bruising under 2.5%; 360 robots by April 2027; licence test met; USMCA origin certified | Trade sale near $250M: $33.3M, 2.8x, 2.2x after dilution | Two quotes below $33,000 and 200+ robots contracted by 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Base | 40% | v4 at $33,000-36,000 but the build slips; 250-300 robots at $12,700-13,500; revenue $4-6M; 2028 round flat and asking for seniority | Exit near $100M: $12.0M, 1.1x, 1.0x after dilution | Fleet below 300 and ARR below $4M in 2027 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Bear | 42% | v4 above $36,000; renewals at $12,700 or $9,500; a second grower leaves over bruising; close slips past the covenant or prices a senior bridge; licence lapses | Wind-down, foreclosure or $12-40M asset sale: 0.05-0.96x by structure, central 0.35x; 0.21x if the notes are senior, 0.31x behind a $10M senior 2028 round | Waiver request, cash under $2.5M, a second grower exit | S1 (unverified), S95, S89 |
:::

The probability-weighted return is 0.94x on company-reported inputs, unverified: 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x and 42% at 0.35x. The bull case needs the build, price, damage rate, licence and calendar to land together; the bear needs one of five failures, three outside management's control. The $36.77M stack is one deck sentence and no document: the 0.94x and the Pass rating assume the preference is 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, and a $39.27M stack if the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs convert on top would lower the floor further. [S95]

### The five assumptions that carry the value

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | v4 builds at or below $33,000 at 300 units on an arm's-length quote | Low | A second quote above $36,000, or a first article slipping past 2027-01 | Contribution at $12,700 falls to -$1,900 at $36,000 and -$4,900 at $48,000; above $44,000 no price covers depreciation | The only quote is dated 2026-08 and comes from the noteholder and customer | S1 (unverified) |
| 2 | 2027 realisations average $12,700 or more, some at the $16,500 list | Medium | A renewal at $9,500-10,500, or a grower repudiating the rise | Each $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M of revenue and 3 margin points | The first renewal signature and whether it carries a deposit | S1 (unverified) |
| 3 | 360 robots in service by April 2027 against 110 contracted and 64 today | Low | Fewer than 250 delivered by 2027-03, or no build slot reserved | Each 100 robots is $1.27M; a 250-robot fleet is $3.2M against the $4.6M plan | Contracted count below 200 in 2027-02; no deposits on the 50 letters | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| 4 | Bruising at or below 2.5% on a seven-day, 1 degree Celsius test against a named retailer spec | Low | A packer rejecting machine-picked lots, or a second grower exit | One point of cull is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee | Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14; one grower left over bruising in 2026-06 | S1 (unverified) |
| 5 | Close by 2026-12-15 at $12M or more, 1x pari passu preference, 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31 | Low | A close slipping into Q1 2027; senior or 2x note terms; fewer than 100 robots at the test date | A slip breaches the $1.5M covenant near 2027-03-10; senior notes cut the lead at a $25M exit from 0.59x to 0.21x | Cash below $2.5M, a waiver request, no equal-rank warranty | S1 (unverified), S95 |

### Where the price turns

| Terms | Base case, $100M exit | Bear case, $25M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $72M pre-money, 1x pari passu (deck terms) | 1.0x | 0.59x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $72M pre-money, 1.5x on the lead cheque | 1.5x | 0.75x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $50-58M pre-money, 1.5x, half staged | 1.5x | 0.88x | S95 (unverified), calc |

At a $25M exit the lead shares a $36.77M stack after $1.6M of debt and 8% of costs: 0.59x at 1x, 0.75x when its $12M cheque carries a 1.5x preference and the stack becomes $42.77M, and 0.88x at the lower mark where a $12M round leaves the stack at $36.77M. Above the stack the 1x preference and as-converted value meet near a $99M exit, so the base case is 1.0x and a 1.5x preference pays 1.5x. The evidence needs to improve less than the price: the same diligence buys a better base case at the lower mark, and the diligence question is what two manufacturers other than the counterparty quote the v4 at and whether the note agreement warrants equal rank.

### The analogs that teach the rule

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue River to Deere, $305M | Best | 2015-2017 | Four times the last private post-money; the buyer wanted perception for its own sprayer, not a leased fleet, and that is the ceiling a successful platform earned | S128 |
| Bear Flag to Deere, $250M | Best | 2021 | A strategic premium exists for autonomy attached to an OEM line, so the exit plan should target OEMs, not growers | S128 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | Best-funded autonomous tractor entrant; shut down April 2026 after $133M raised and a reported $500M-plus. Capital did not cure unit economics | S131 |
| Tortuga and Advanced Farm | Cautionary | 2024-2025 | Both sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices after real fleets; the fleet was not what buyers paid for | S127 |
:::

This category's exit pays for the perception asset or the team, at a multiple of the last round, not for the lease book. Its most saleable asset is a labelled dataset and two valleys of grower relationships; the least saleable is the fleet it would own.
