Strawberry robotics is often discussed as one broad theme, but Japan’s market is separating into two very different businesses: high-precision harvesting systems aimed at premium fruit growers, and lower-cost pollination robots designed for wider greenhouse deployment. That split matters because it changes how investors, growers, and technology suppliers should judge traction. The key question is no longer whether “strawberry robots” will scale. It is which task can support repeatable economics under Japan’s protected cultivation model.
Japan is a particularly revealing test bed. The country has a large greenhouse fruit market, a labor force that is aging quickly, and a premium retail culture where strawberries are sold not only as food, but as gift products with strict expectations around appearance, ripeness, and handling quality. In that environment, robots are not competing against generic farm labor alone. They are competing against highly specialized cultivation routines where a damaged berry can erase margins on an entire picking cycle.
That is why the economics of harvesting and pollination diverge so sharply. Harvesting robots must identify the right berry, navigate dense foliage, avoid touching neighboring fruit, detach delicately, and place product without bruising it. Pollination robots face a narrower technical problem: visit flowers consistently and at the right time, often in greenhouses where routes and conditions are more controlled. One category sells precision; the other sells coverage.
Why harvesting robots remain technically impressive but commercially narrow
Japan has produced several agricultural robotics efforts over the years, including systems targeting delicate crops grown in structured environments. In strawberries, harvesting remains the showcase application because it is visually compelling and operationally important. But it is also one of the hardest automation tasks in agriculture.
A commercially viable strawberry harvester must solve multiple problems simultaneously:

Ripeness detection under variable lighting and occlusion
End-effector precision for fragile fruit and stems
Mobility through greenhouse layouts that were often not designed for robots
Cycle time fast enough to compete with trained human pickers
Post-pick quality protection to preserve premium selling prices

Those constraints push vendors toward premium growers first. If a farm produces high-value gift-grade strawberries, reducing damage and extending harvest windows can justify a more expensive machine. If the operation sells into lower-price channels, the robot’s capital cost and maintenance burden quickly become harder to defend.
This is the central divide in Japan: harvesting robots are not a mass-market labor replacement product yet. They are closer to a precision tool for selected greenhouse formats and premium economics. That does not make the segment weak; it makes it specialized. The mistake is treating specialized early demand as proof of broad agricultural automation readiness.
From an editorial and market perspective, this resembles surgical robotics more than warehouse automation. Technical performance matters, but workflow integration, crop-specific fit, and operator trust matter just as much. A strawberry harvesting robot may work in demonstrations and still face a very constrained serviceable market because greenhouse geometry, cultivar choice, and pack-out requirements vary too much across farms.
Pollination robots are following a simpler deployment logic
Pollination robotics is gaining attention for a different reason: it fits the operational structure of greenhouse farming more naturally. Companies in this segment are not trying to replicate the most dexterous human task in the field. They are targeting a narrower intervention with more repeatable routes and clearer scheduling logic.
In Japan, where greenhouse management is data-intensive and growers already invest in environmental control systems, pollination robots can be positioned as another layer in a controlled production stack. They may also appeal to growers looking to reduce dependency on biological pollination inputs under specific seasonal or climate conditions.
The commercial case is stronger when vendors can show three things:

Reliable flower visitation consistency
Compatibility with existing greenhouse operations
Lower complexity than full harvesting automation

That lower complexity matters. Pollination robots do not need to manage final product handling. They operate upstream of harvest revenue realization, which changes the tolerance for cycle time and mechanical sophistication. In practical terms, this gives the category a better chance of reaching broader deployment sooner, even if its per-unit pricing is less dramatic than harvesting robots.
It also means the market narrative should not be built around spectacle. Harvesting robots generate headlines because the task looks difficult and futuristic. Pollination robots may generate steadier business because the deployment problem is simpler and the greenhouse adaptation burden is lower.
Japan’s premium fruit economics create a robotics filter few foreign observers appreciate
A common mistake in agricultural robotics coverage is to assume labor scarcity alone creates adoption. In Japanese strawberries, that is incomplete. The bigger issue is that labor scarcity is filtered through premium quality economics. If robotic handling reduces visual quality, shape consistency, or shelf appeal, growers can lose the very price premium that made automation attractive in the first place.
This creates a market filter with three consequences:

Robots that are merely adequate will not be good enough
Structured greenhouse redesign may be required before robots scale
Vendors may need to sell system redesign, not just hardware

That last point is underappreciated. In many Japanese greenhouse deployments, the robot is only one part of the economic equation. A vendor may need to influence bed height, aisle width, plant training methods, sensing infrastructure, and harvest workflow. Once that happens, the sale starts to look less like equipment procurement and more like an integrated cultivation system upgrade.
That can be attractive for specialized growers, but it slows category-wide scaling. A company that must tailor deployment conditions farm by farm is building revenue, but not necessarily building a fast-expanding market. Readers assessing this segment should separate technical credibility from replicable sales motion.
The likely market outcome: two business models, two valuation profiles
If current trajectories hold, strawberry robotics in Japan will not converge into one dominant category. It will likely split into two different business models.
1. Premium harvesting automation
This segment will likely remain smaller in unit volume but higher in average selling price, system integration intensity, and perceived technical moat. Buyers will include premium greenhouse operators willing to redesign workflow for quality-preserving automation. Revenue may be lumpy, with longer sales cycles and deeper deployment support requirements.
2. Scaled pollination assistance
This segment may achieve wider greenhouse penetration because the task is operationally simpler and the robot can fit into controlled-environment routines with less disruption. Pricing may be lower, but deployment counts could scale faster if reliability is proven.
For investors, these are not interchangeable. Then, silicone tentacles on the gripper gently envelop the strawberry like a sea anemone, giving a light tug and twist. A whole, stem-free strawberry is thus neatly picked and gently placed into a collection basket. It takes an average of 20 seconds to pick one strawberry, with a grasping success rate of 84 percent. The harvested strawberries remain in almost perfect condition, similar to those picked by human hands. Many agricultural products are harvested by machines to improve efficiency and reduce costs. However, harvesting soft and easily damaged fruits like strawberries had long remained a challenge. Previous picking robots usually functioned by using scissors to cut the strawberry stems, always leaving a section of stem attached to the fruit. This residual stem easily punctured or scratched adjacent strawberries during transport from farm to processing workshop, causing significant fruit loss. Even more troublesome, workers had to manually trim the stems before boxing the strawberries. Thus, the use of robots had not fully liberated human labor. Wang's team drew inspiration from how sea anemones feed and developed a biomimetic soft gripper powered by pneumatics. Made entirely of flexible silicone material, the gripper is highly elastic and deformable, ensuring it will not crush the strawberries. It can completely wrap around strawberries of various sizes and shapes, grasping with both stability and gentleness. The bottom of the gripper features a pneumatic chamber that enables intelligent extension and retraction of the tentacles via air pressure regulation. The gripper can gently grasp the strawberry inward or spread outward to release the fruit, perfectly adapting to its soft, easily damaged nature. To solve the residual stem problem, the team designed a \"drag-and-rotate\" motion for the robot that mimics human picking. After the gripper seizes the strawberry, the robotic arm first gives a slight upward tug and then completes a small arc rotation, allowing the stem connection point to break naturally. This means the picked strawberry is without any stem, ready to be boxed and sold, with no human processing required. Additionally, the team employed a deep learning model to develop a strategy for handling plant blocking and adjusting the grasping pose. This allows the robot to accurately identify ripe strawberries. Through a comprehensive scoring mechanism, the robot can evaluate the spatial relationships among clustered strawberries, giving higher scores to less blocked ones for priority picking. Relying on visual feedback from the camera, the robot can also dynamically adjust its grasping posture. After picking each strawberry, the system recalculates the next picking target. Data shows that this strategy boosted the robot's grasping success rate from 66 percent to 84 percent. Wang said that in the future, his team will establish a cloud data platform. Standardized picking data from planting bases will be uploaded to the cloud, allowing ordinary farmers to complete picking operations by simple commands without having to train the machine by themselves. {"url":"https://agfundernews.com/driscolls-emerging-tech-robotics-open-innovation","title":"Q&A: Driscoll’s Head of Emerging Technology On Harvesting Robotics and Open Innovation","text":"As head of R&D strategy and emerging technology at Driscoll’s, Nolan Paul has a unique view of the agtech startups in the specialty crop space.
The global berry seller has become known for its technological innovation in breeding and genetics, but the company’s focus on robotics is less well-known. Paul told AgFunderNews that Driscoll’s wants to support the development of automated strawberry harvest and is in contact with many if not all of the startups working in this area of robotics. That interest has led to investments in Harvest CROO and Agrobot and field trials with more.
Strawberry growing is long overdue for a shake-up and stakeholders know it. Robotic harvesting technologies are not quite ready for wide use. Labor is becoming more scarce as immigration uncertainty in the US continues and also because strawberry picking at ground level is a particularly grueling task. Some growers, inside and out, are raising up growing surfaces to waist-height to mitigate these issues and Driscoll’s is in the position to help and encourage its growers to keep up with the times.
We caught up with Paul ahead of the World Agri-Tech Innovation Summit, where he’ll play the shark in several startup pitch presentations, to discuss how Driscoll’s works with startups and lessons learned while trying to determine the future of strawberry growing.
Driscoll’s is constantly testing and verifying technologies, but can growers afford to make major investments in technology right now?
Nolan Paul
It depends on what we’re talking about. The startups are recognizing that this is an issue and moving to a service model where you de-risk the technology for the grower base. They’re not going to have to pay a half a million dollars for a piece of equipment. But at some point, we come in. I think it’s not going to be as simple as just the robotics, let’s say, for harvest. It’s a combination of the robotics and the growing system and actually the genetics too. In that combination of all three is where you’ll really see the success. So Driscoll’s will come in, certainly on the breeding, on the genetics side, we’ll optimize for traits like mechanization. But on the growing system too, we’re supporting our growers with that, we help them out. And of course, we’re dedicated to investing in the development of ag technologies on behalf of our growers.
What is your assessment of the harvesting robotics field? Are outdoor growers transitioning to waist-height tables as well as indoor growers? And does that mean that harvesting machinery could work indoors and outdoors?
The good news is that the last couple years have seen a crop of harvesting startups pop up. Honestly, I doubted that would happen so quickly but I’m glad I was wrong. So today Driscoll’s is currently in active conversations with six automated strawberry harvesting startups. And they’re all taking a unique approach, which is great.
The challenges are certainly different. I think when you look at the visioning systems, that will be the same, but the robustness, the durability, and the scale will be different. And I think that’s what we’re seeing — some startups perhaps don’t appreciate the scale that will be required for outdoor farms in the US. If you’re growing in a greenhouse or a glasshouse, you know that’s one thing. But when you need to be out on a 100-acre ranch, those robots, those harvesters need to cover a lot of space and it’s probably not a reasonable thing to assume that you can just have a bunch of these robots going through a field. It’s hard for a grower to manage that. So I think there is a certain fleet size that can only be so big.
I think that’s something we’ve found that perhaps some of the startups haven’t looked at. And I don’t think you’ll just see one winner, I think you’ll see different solutions going into indoor farming whether that’s greenhouse or glasshouse or vertical farm and solutions for outdoors. I think the ones that are successful have the vision to scale from strawberries to other crops and perhaps indoors that’s easier to do. I think that’s a big deal. I’m still skeptical that harvesting robots are going to be successful if you just focus on one crop. And that’s really where we want to work with the startups, to help them understand that narrative, so they’re able to raise VC money.
That’s fascinating coming from you. It seems like Driscoll’s has done a pretty good job of making a big market for strawberry technology.
Yeah, it’s an interesting space. We’ve certainly recognized in the last three years how we engage with startups has to change because there are a lot of people who give them lip service. But what we’ve realized is you have to really be structured the right way. It’s not even about the money —  there’s plenty of money. You need people who can work alongside these startups and move at the same speed.
It’s easy to go pitch ideas to a CEO, but to actually execute on them is really tough. And certainly we’re learning and getting better at it. Some of these large companies almost want to own what the startup is doing – to have a competitive edge. A lot of times, unless you’re really big, it just doesn’t work and you almost end up killing the startup.
Why doesn’t it work?
Well I think most of the companies aren’t big enough to justify exclusivity — certainly not in the specialty crop space. It’s a very high, high value space, but we’re fragmented. There are a lot of one to five billion dollar crops in the US across grapes, strawberries, nuts, and vegetables. But in and of itself it’s not big enough for a startup to scale. It’s important for folks to focus. But you have to have the vision of how you’re going to scale. The right strategic corporate can be a good partner for startups. But they need to recognize that, if you’re working with a startup it’s great that you’re an anchor customer, but you want the startup to be around in two, four, six, 10 years. And the only way they’re going to be around in six to 10 years is if they’ve been able to scale up and either be acquired or maybe, they have to create that scale themselves. I think people are too short-term when they interact with startups.","truncated":false}

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, the largest line a machine can attack. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, trivial against the harvest bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026, when the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23; the deck's urgency is a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is a measured figure with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus, visible in $4.0M of insider commitments at the mark, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying a perception platform for its sprayer line rather than a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. Agtech venture funding fell from $53bn in 2021 to $7bn in 2025 and 18 companies shut down that year. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

### The distribution, not the mean, decides it

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | v4 at or below $33,000 on two quotes; renewals $12,700-16,500; bruising under 2.5%; 360 robots by April 2027; licence test met; USMCA origin certified | Trade sale near $250M: $33.3M, 2.8x, 2.2x after dilution | Two quotes below $33,000 and 200+ robots contracted by 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Base | 40% | v4 at $33,000-36,000 but the build slips; 250-300 robots at $12,700-13,500; revenue $4-6M; 2028 round flat and asking for seniority | Exit near $100M: $12.0M, 1.1x, 1.0x after dilution | Fleet below 300 and ARR below $4M in 2027 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Bear | 42% | v4 above $36,000; renewals at $12,700 or $9,500; a second grower leaves over bruising; close slips past the covenant or prices a senior bridge; licence lapses | Wind-down, foreclosure or $12-40M asset sale: 0.05-0.96x by structure, central 0.35x; 0.21x if the notes are senior, 0.31x behind a $10M senior 2028 round | Waiver request, cash under $2.5M, a second grower exit | S1 (unverified), S95, S89 |
:::

The probability-weighted return is 0.94x on company-reported inputs, unverified: 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x and 42% at 0.35x. The bull needs the build, price, damage, licence and calendar to land together; the bear needs one of five failures, three outside management's control. The $36.77M stack is one deck sentence and no document: the 0.94x and the Pass rating assume the preference is 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, and a $39.27M stack if the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs convert on top would lower the floor further. [S95]

### The five assumptions that carry the value

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | v4 builds at or below $33,000 at 300 units on an arm's-length quote | Low | A second quote above $36,000, or a first article slipping past 2027-01 | Contribution at $12,700 falls to -$1,900 at $36,000 and -$4,900 at $48,000; above $44,000 no price covers depreciation | The only quote is dated 2026-08 and comes from the noteholder and customer | S1 (unverified) |
| 2 | 2027 realisations average $12,700 or more, some at the $16,500 list | Medium | A renewal at $9,500-10,500, or a grower repudiating the rise | Each $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M of revenue and 3 margin points | The first renewal signature and whether it carries a deposit | S1 (unverified) |
| 3 | 360 robots in service by April 2027 against 110 contracted and 64 today | Low | Fewer than 250 delivered by 2027-03, or no build slot reserved | Each 100 robots is $1.27M; a 250-robot fleet is $3.2M against the $4.6M plan | Contracted count below 200 in 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| 4 | Bruising at or below 2.5% on a seven-day, 1 degree Celsius test against a named retailer spec | Low | A packer rejecting machine-picked lots, or a second grower exit | One point of cull is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee | Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14; one grower left over bruising in 2026-06 | S1 (unverified) |
| 5 | Close by 2026-12-15 at $12M or more, 1x pari passu preference, 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31 | Low | A close slipping into Q1 2027; senior or 2x note terms; fewer than 100 robots at the test date | A slip breaches the $1.5M covenant near 2027-03-10; senior notes cut the $25M recovery from 0.59x to 0.21x | Cash below $2.5M, a waiver request, no equal-rank warranty | S1 (unverified), S95 |

### Where the price turns

| Terms | Base case, $100M exit | Bear case, $25M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $72M pre-money, 1x pari passu (deck terms) | 1.0x | 0.59x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $72M pre-money, 1.5x on the lead cheque | 1.5x | 0.75x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $50-58M pre-money, 1.5x, half staged | 1.5x | 0.88x | S95 (unverified), calc |

At a $25M exit the lead shares a $36.77M stack after $1.6M of debt and 8% of costs: 0.59x at 1x, 0.75x when its $12M cheque carries 1.5x and the stack becomes $42.77M, and 0.88x at the lower mark where a $12M round leaves the stack at $36.77M. The 1x preference and as-converted value meet near a $99M exit, so the base case is 1.0x and 1.5x pays 1.5x. The evidence needs to improve less than the price, and the diligence question is what two independent manufacturers quote the v4 at and whether the note agreement warrants equal rank.

### The analogs that teach the rule

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue River to Deere, $305M | Best | 2015-2017 | Four times the last private post-money; the buyer wanted perception for its own sprayer, not a leased fleet | S128 |
| Bear Flag to Deere, $250M | Best | 2021 | A strategic premium exists for autonomy attached to an OEM line, so the exit plan should target OEMs, not growers | S128 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | Best-funded autonomous tractor entrant; shut down April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus | S131 |
| Tortuga and Advanced Farm | Cautionary | 2024-2025 | Both sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices after real fleets; the fleet was not what buyers paid for | S127 |
:::

This category's exit pays for the perception asset or the team, at a multiple of the last round, not for the lease book. Its most saleable asset is a labelled dataset and two valleys of grower relationships; the least saleable is the fleet it would own.

{"url":"https://strawberry.calpoly.edu/hoop-arch-removal-report","title":"Hoop Arch Removal Report | Strawberry Center","text":"Published: February 28, 2025 | Revised: March 21, 2025

Overview

Hoop houses, also known as high tunnels, are used in fresh fruit production around the world. Hoop houses are temporary structures used to cover an entire field with a thin sheet of white plastic. Hoop houses are used extensively by raspberry growers, where a planting may be harvested sees multiple harvests without disassembling the structure. In the Santa Maria, California area, limited strawberry acreage is also covered with the hoop house system. Both conventional in-ground production as well as the newer tabletop production systems utilize hoop houses. The plants and fruit are protected from direct sunlight, rain and wind (Holmes 2024). Further the hoop houses accelerate transplant growth and fruit production by maintaining higher temperatures inside the houses (Santos et al., (2011). The hoop houses allow growers to continue harvesting fruit throughout the late fall and winter months when prices are typically higher (Carey et al.). Strawberries in hoop houses are often grown organically to capture premium prices and cover the additional costs associated with the hoop house installation process and materials. With the in-ground production, the ground prep, planting and harvesting is done in the same fashion as conventional

strawberry growing for the region. The difference is that after the ground prep is done, the hoops are erected and after harvest is over (perhaps six months later), the hoops are disassembled and placed into storage. This relatively short six-month turnaround contrasts with that of caneberry or tabletop strawberry production, where the same hoop houses may remain in place for multiple years. Thus, in-ground strawberry growers face a unique challenge in the volume of labor required and the high replacement rate of the materials themselves, which are at an increased risk of damage during the installation and removal processes.

Figure 1. Typical hoop house structure covering strawberries in the Santa Maria, California Region.

 The “Hoop House” is an assembly made up of several parts, shown in figure 2. The ’platform,’ is a steel post with two prongs welded on one end and a pointed end with an auger-type feature welded on the other. The platform is driven into the ground with a specialized implement that applies down-pressure on the while also spinning the post like a screw. The platform drives itself into the soil approximately 3 feet deep. The platform can be driven into the bed top or a furrow, based on grower preference. The platforms are spaced approximately 8 feet apart down the row and about 22 feet apart from row to row. Typically, a single hoop house section is centered about and covers three (3) complete strawberry beds, and the platforms are driven into the center of the outside two (2) beds. In the Santa Maria, California area, the beds are spaced 64 inches apart. When all the platforms have been installed, the hoop arches are brought into the field. The ‘hoop arch’ is a long, slender steel pipe which has been formed into an arch shape and had its ends bent such that it has a short straight section at either end where the hoop arch connects to the platform. Both ends of the larger diameter hoop arch pipe slide onto the smaller diameter platform prong and the arch will span about 22 feet across three (3) complete strawberry beds as referenced above.

Figure 2. Hoop arch steel structure dimensions (left) and platform to hoop arch connection (right).

Due to natural variability in the placement of the platforms and dimensions of the arches, each connection between platform and hoop arch is unique. Thus, each hoop arch and platform will have an unknown combination of forces holding the two together. This scenario presents a challenge for hand labor and for future mechanical removal solutions. Once the platforms and arches are connected, bracing is added between the first few arches at either end of a row. A row is typically about 300 feet long and contains forty (40) arches. With the bracing installed, the plastic is draped over the top of the steel structure and tied down with ¼” rope. The plastic is a translucent white polyethylene, 6 mil (0.006 inches) thick and usually comes in 32-foot-wide rolls.

Problem

Strawberries, being an annual crop which require extensive ground prep prior to each planting, provide growers with the unique challenge of installing and removing hoop houses before each planting and after each harvest season. The installation and removal process is labor intensive. Adding to the challenge of removing the hoop houses is that they are often used in areas with high winds and hilly terrain. High winds can cause significant damage to the steel structures which adds to the difficulty in separating the hoop arch from the platform. Damage to the plastic covering leads to increased replacement costs and difficulty removing the plastic from the steel structure. The behavior of each hoop arch as it’s removed is highly unpredictable. When a laborer is removing a hoop arch, they must stand up on the strawberry bed and lift with a great deal of force on the hoop arch. The laborer is frequently lifting at or above chest height, and the hoop arch may spring away from or towards the laborer, depending on condition of the hoop arch to platform connection.

Figure 3. Three workers struggle to remove a hoop arch from platforms in the Santa Maria, California area

Objective

At the request of the California Strawberry Commission and its grower members, The Cal Poly Strawberry Center set out to develop a machine that would reduce labor requirements for the Hoop Arch removal process. Internally, it was determined that the machine should be tractor mounted, relatively low cost, and easy to operate for an average tractor operator employed by a strawberry grower. The initial goal for the machine was that it should be in continuous motion throughout a 300-foot row, completely removing and storing the hoop arches as it traveled. At the end of the row, a forklift should unload approximately 40 hoop arches from the machine and the machine should turn around and drive down the next row.

Summary

A variety of prototypes were built and tested at Cal Poly Strawberry Center facilities. Two different machines were also tested in commercial strawberry fields. The second of the two machines showed potential for commercial adoption but ultimately was not able to economically outperform conventional practices. At project completion, the scope had significantly narrowed from the initial objective. The final version of the machine removed the right side of each hoop arch and left the other side connected. As the machine drove down the row, the hoop arches behind the machine were left hanging from the left side platform. A two (2) person labor crew would follow the machine to complete the removal of the arch and place it on the ground.

Figure 4. Two machines designed and tested by the Cal Poly Strawberry Center in commercial strawberry fields. The Roller Remover, left, was an earlier version of the hoop arch remover which suffered from reliability issues and difficulty in positioning the rollers. The Umbrella Remover, right, was the final product of multiple years of development.

Results

The one-sided Umbrella Remover machine was able to consistently remove the right side of the arch from the platform. The new process utilized two (2) hand laborers, one (1) tractor operator, and one (1) tractor. This process was compared to the conventional practice of two (2) hand laborers. Although the new process with the machine did reduce the difficulty and actual time required to remove the hoop arch compared to the conventional method, it was not fast enough to reduce the total labor hours required when factoring in the additional tractor operator. Additionally, the operating cost of the tractor further reduced the economic viability of the new mechanical removal process. Oper

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, trivial against the harvest bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026, when the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23; the deck's urgency is a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus, visible in $4.0M of insider commitments at the mark, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying a perception platform for its sprayer line rather than a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. Agtech venture funding fell from $53bn in 2021 to $7bn in 2025 and 18 companies shut down that year. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

### The distribution, not the mean, decides it

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | v4 at or below $33,000 on two quotes; renewals $12,700-16,500; bruising under 2.5%; 360 robots by April 2027; licence test met; USMCA origin certified | Trade sale near $250M: $33.3M, 2.8x, 2.2x after dilution | Two quotes below $33,000 and 200+ robots contracted by 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Base | 40% | v4 at $33,000-36,000 but the build slips; 250-300 robots at $12,700-13,500; revenue $4-6M; 2028 round flat and asking for seniority | Exit near $100M: $12.0M, 1.1x, 1.0x after dilution | Fleet below 300 and ARR below $4M in 2027 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Bear | 42% | v4 above $36,000; renewals at $12,700 or $9,500; a second grower leaves over bruising; close slips past the covenant or prices a senior bridge; licence lapses | Wind-down, foreclosure or $12-40M asset sale: 0.05-0.96x by structure, central 0.35x; 0.21x if the notes are senior, 0.31x behind a $10M senior 2028 round | Waiver request, cash under $2.5M, a second grower exit | S1 (unverified), S95, S89 |

The probability-weighted return is 0.94x on company-reported inputs, unverified: 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x and 42% at 0.35x. The bull needs the build, price, damage, licence and calendar to land together; the bear needs one of five failures, three outside management's control. The category's exit pays for the perception asset or the team, not the lease book: a buyer prices the labelled dataset and the grower relationships and treats a leased fleet as a liability it must absorb. The mechanism is that a company owning machines that lose money on each one transfers the loss to whoever holds the equity, and the preference decides whether that is the founder, the noteholder or this fund. For Meridian the implication is to decline at this mark and keep the diligence warm, because the quotes and the note agreement are cheap to obtain and would reprice the same asset at a level where the base case pays.

{"url":"https://foleyhoag.com/news-and-insights/publications/alerts-and-updates/2026/october/robotics-as-a-service-structuring-licensing-agreements-for-robotics-companies/","title":"Robotics as a Service: Structuring Licensing Agreements For Robotics Companies","text":"Robotics companies are rethinking how they bring their machines to market. Under a Robotics-as-a-Service (RaaS) model, a provider deploys robots for a recurring subscription or usage-based fee covering access, maintenance, software updates, and support, while retaining ownership of the hardware and software. For startups, RaaS lowers customers’ upfront costs and lets fleets scale with demand. 

At the heart of every RaaS arrangement is a license. Because RaaS bundles hardware, software, data, and services into one ongoing relationship, its agreements differ in important ways from traditional models. This article outlines the key issues robotics companies should understand. 

RaaS Compared to Traditional Purchase, Lease, and Licensing Models 

In a purchase, the customer owns the robot and bears maintenance, obsolescence, and depreciation risk. In a lease, the lessor retains ownership for a fixed term. Under RaaS, the customer subscribes to a managed service: the provider owns and maintains the robots, supplies the software, and often commits to defined performance levels. 

Characterization of a robotics arrangement matters. A lease may trigger Uniform Commercial Code remedies and implied warranties that cannot be disclaimed, and a provider’s interest treated as a security interest may need to be perfected by filing. Longer leases also generally put a right-of-use asset and liability on the customer’s balance sheet, while service fees do not, comprising a significant distinction for customers with debt covenants. 

RaaS is also inherently hybrid, mixing hardware, software, and services offerings. Because provider-owned equipment operates on the customer’s site, agreements must address risk of loss, insurance, workplace-safety rules, and bodily-injury liability. Maintenance covers both physical repair and software updates, and exit may require decommissioning, equipment removal, and site restoration. 

Key Provisions of a RaaS Agreement 

Scope of Services and Service Levels 

The agreement should define the type and number of robots, their functions, the operating environments, and ancillary services such as installation, training, integration, and support. Sensitive settings, such as hospital patient-care areas, may trigger additional safety, infection-control, and privacy requirements. 

Providers typically commit to measurable service levels, such as uptime (for example, 95% of scheduled operating hours), maintenance response times, task accuracy, and time to repair. Remedies commonly include service credits, fee reductions, and termination rights for chronic underperformance. 

Pricing and Payment 

Pricing may be a flat subscription, per-task fees, volume tiers, or a hybrid. The parties should address annual escalation, minimum commitments, utilization shortfalls, pricing for robots added mid-term, and separate fees for integration, training, or early termination. 

Term, Renewal, and Termination 

Initial terms often run one to five years with automatic renewal, and a pilot phase with clear success criteria can precede full deployment. The agreement should address termination for breach, convenience, performance failures, insolvency, or a change of control, along with surviving licenses, data rights, and transition services. Licensees should also understand the protections of Section 365(n) of the Bankruptcy Code. 

Intellectual Property Ownership and Licensing 

RaaS agreements often combine patent, trade secret, copyright, software, and trademark licenses. The grant should specify the rights licensed; exclusivity; any field-of-use or territorial limits; sublicensing and assignment rights; duration; and permitted users, such as affiliates and subcontractors. 

Typically, the provider retains ownership of the robots, software, and pre-existing IP, and the customer receives only the license needed to receive the services. Harder questions concern improvements created during the relationship. Patent ownership follows inventorship by default, but the parties may reallocate ownership by agreement and should address control of patent prosecution and enforcement. 

Data Rights, Software Licensing, and Security 

Robots generate operational, environmental, and sometimes personal data that can be as valuable as the hardware. The agreement should address who owns that data; whether the provider may use, aggregate, or commercialize it, including to train AI models; and compliance with privacy laws such as the GDPR and CCPA. 

Because deployments depend on continuous updates and connectivity, the agreement should define the platform license, address the provider’s remote-access rights, and allocate cybersecurity responsibility, including encryption, secure authentication, and breach response. 

Liability Allocation, Indemnification, and Risk Management 

Indemnities shift specified third-party claims, such as infringement or bodily-injury claims, between the parties. Limitations of liability, including consequential-damages exclusions and damage caps, guard against catastrophic exposure, typically with negotiated exceptions for confidentiality breaches, indemnification, fraud, willful misconduct, and gross negligence. 

Providers should carry commercial general, product, and professional liability insurance. Generally, the provider ensures the robots meet product-safety standards, while the customer ensures its facility and use comply with OSHA standards, industry-specific rules such as FDA requirements, and local codes. 

Commercial Considerations 

Before drafting, startups should be clear about their business goals, the technology and rights involved, how the technology will be used, the deal economics, exit mechanisms, and the single largest thing that could go wrong. The chosen business model will also shape revenue, IP strategy, financing, and how investors evaluate the company.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, trivial against the harvest bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026: the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, making the deck's urgency a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus, visible in $4.0M of insider commitments, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying perception for its sprayer line, not a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. Agtech venture funding fell from $53bn in 2021 to $7bn in 2025. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

### The distribution, not the mean, decides it

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | v4 at or below $33,000 on two quotes; renewals $12,700-16,500; bruising under 2.5%; 360 robots by April 2027; licence test met; USMCA origin certified | Trade sale near $250M: $33.3M, 2.8x, 2.2x after dilution | Two quotes below $33,000 and 200+ robots contracted by 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Base | 40% | v4 at $33,000-36,000 but the build slips; 250-300 robots at $12,700-13,500; revenue $4-6M; 2028 round flat and asking for seniority | Exit near $100M: $12.0M, 1.1x, 1.0x after dilution | Fleet below 300 and ARR below $4M in 2027 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Bear | 42% | v4 above $36,000; renewals at $12,700 or $9,500; a second grower leaves over bruising; close slips past the covenant or prices a senior bridge; licence lapses | Wind-down, foreclosure or $12-40M asset sale: 0.05-0.96x by structure, central 0.35x; 0.21x if the notes are senior, 0.31x behind a $10M senior 2028 round | Waiver request, cash under $2.5M, a second grower exit | S1 (unverified), S95, S89 |
:::

The probability-weighted return is 0.94x on company-reported inputs, unverified: 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x and 42% at 0.35x. The bull needs the build, price, damage, licence and calendar to land together; the bear needs one of five failures, three outside management's control. The $36.77M stack is one deck sentence and no document: the 0.94x and the Pass rating assume the preference is 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, and a $39.27M stack if the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs convert on top would lower the floor further. [S95]

### The five assumptions that carry the value

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | v4 builds at or below $33,000 at 300 units on an arm's-length quote | Low | A second quote above $36,000, or a first article slipping past 2027-01 | Contribution at $12,700 falls to -$1,900 at $36,000 and -$4,900 at $48,000; above $44,000 no price covers depreciation | The only quote is dated 2026-08 and comes from the noteholder and customer | S1 (unverified) |
| 2 | 2027 realisations average $12,700 or more, some at the $16,500 list | Medium | A renewal at $9,500-10,500, or a grower repudiating the rise | Each $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M of revenue and 3 margin points | The first renewal signature and whether it carries a deposit | S1 (unverified) |
| 3 | 360 robots in service by April 2027 against 110 contracted and 64 today | Low | Fewer than 250 delivered by 2027-03, or no build slot reserved | Each 100 robots is $1.27M; a 250-robot fleet is $3.2M against the $4.6M plan | Contracted count below 200 in 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| 4 | Bruising at or below 2.5% on a seven-day, 1 degree Celsius test against a named retailer spec | Low | A packer rejecting machine-picked lots, or a second grower exit | One point of cull is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee | Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14; one grower left over bruising in 2026-06 | S1 (unverified) |
| 5 | Close by 2026-12-15 at $12M or more, 1x pari passu preference, 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31 | Low | A close slipping into Q1 2027; senior or 2x note terms; fewer than 100 robots at the test date | A slip breaches the $1.5M covenant near 2027-03-10; senior notes cut the $25M recovery from 0.59x to 0.21x | Cash below $2.5M, a waiver request, no equal-rank warranty | S1 (unverified), S95 |

### Where the price turns

| Terms | Base case, $100M exit | Bear case, $25M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $72M pre-money, 1x pari passu (deck terms) | 1.0x | 0.59x | S95 (unverified), calc on a $36.77M stack, net of $1.6M debt and 8% costs |
| $72M pre-money, 1.5x on the lead cheque | 1.5x | 0.75x | S95 (unverified), calc: the cheque holds $18.0M of a $42.77M stack |
| $50-58M pre-money, 1.5x, half staged | 1.5x | 0.88x | S95 (unverified), calc on a $36.77M stack |

Above the stack the 1x preference and as-converted value meet near a $99M exit, so 1x pays 1.0x and 1.5x pays 1.5x. The evidence needs to improve less than the price: two independent quotes for the v4 and a note agreement warranting equal rank would reprice the same asset without waiting for a season.

### The analogs that teach the rule

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue River to Deere, $305M | Best | 2015-2017 | Four times the last private post-money; the buyer wanted perception for its own sprayer, not a leased fleet | S128 |
| Bear Flag to Deere, $250M | Best | 2021 | A strategic premium exists for autonomy attached to an OEM line | S128 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | Best-funded autonomous tractor entrant; shut down April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus | S131 |
| Tortuga and Advanced Farm | Cautionary | 2024-2025 | Both sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices after real fleets; the fleet was not what buyers paid for | S127 |
:::

The category's exit pays for the perception asset or the team, not the lease book: a buyer prices the labelled dataset and the grower relationships and treats a leased fleet as a liability it must absorb. The mechanism is that a company owning machines that lose money on each one transfers the loss to whoever holds the equity, and the preference decides whether that is the founder, the noteholder or this fund. For Meridian the implication is to decline at this mark and keep the diligence warm: the quotes and the note agreement are cheap and would reprice the same asset to where the base case pays.

| Terms | Base case, $100M exit | Bear case, $25M exit | Source |

Above the stack, 1x pays 1.0x and 1.5x pays 1.5x. The evidence needs to improve less than the price: two independent quotes for the v4 and a note agreement warranting equal rank would reprice the same asset.

### The analogs that teach the rule

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue River to Deere, $305M | Best | 2015-2017 | Four times the last private post-money; the buyer wanted perception, not a fleet | S128 |

:::

The category's exit pays for the perception asset or the team, not the lease book: a buyer prices the labelled dataset and the grower relationships and treats a leased fleet as a liability it must absorb. The mechanism is that a company owning machines that lose money on each one transfers the loss to whoever holds the equity, and the preference decides whether that is the founder, the noteholder or this fund. For Meridian the implication is to decline at this mark and keep the diligence warm: the quotes and the note agreement are cheap and would reprice the same asset to where the base case pays.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026: the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, making the deck's urgency a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus, visible in insider commitments at the mark, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying perception for its sprayer line, not a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

### The distribution, not the mean, decides it

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | v4 at or below $33,000 on two quotes; renewals $12,700-16,500; bruising under 2.5%; 360 robots by April 2027; licence test met; USMCA origin certified | Trade sale near $250M: $33.3M, 2.8x, 2.2x after dilution | Two quotes below $33,000 and 200+ robots contracted by 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Base | 40% | v4 at $33,000-36,000 but the build slips; 250-300 robots at $12,700-13,500; revenue $4-6M; 2028 round flat and asking for seniority | Exit near $100M: $12.0M, 1.1x, 1.0x after dilution | Fleet below 300 and ARR below $4M in 2027 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Bear | 42% | v4 above $36,000; renewals at $12,700 or $9,500; a second grower leaves over bruising; close slips past the covenant or prices a senior bridge; licence lapses | Wind-down, foreclosure or $12-40M asset sale: 0.05-0.96x by structure, central 0.35x; 0.21x if the notes are senior, 0.31x behind a $10M senior 2028 round | Waiver request, cash under $2.5M, a second grower exit | S1 (unverified), S95, S89 |
:::

The probability-weighted return is 0.94x on company-reported inputs, unverified: 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x and 42% at 0.35x. The bull needs the build, price, damage, licence and calendar to land together; the bear needs one of five failures. The $36.77M stack is one deck sentence and no document: the 0.94x and the Pass rating assume the preference is 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, and a $39.27M stack if the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs convert on top would lower the floor further. [S95]

### The five assumptions that carry the value

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | v4 builds at or below $33,000 at 300 units on an arm's-length quote | Low | A second quote above $36,000, or a first article slipping past 2027-01 | Contribution at $12,700 falls to -$1,900 at $36,000 and -$4,900 at $48,000; above $44,000 no price covers depreciation | The only quote is dated 2026-08 and comes from the noteholder and customer | S1 (unverified) |
| 2 | 2027 realisations average $12,700 or more, some at the $16,500 list | Medium | A renewal at $9,500-10,500, or a grower repudiating the rise | Each $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M of revenue and 3 margin points | The first renewal signature and whether it carries a deposit | S1 (unverified) |
| 3 | 360 robots in service by April 2027 against 110 contracted and 64 today | Low | Fewer than 250 delivered by 2027-03, or no build slot reserved | Each 100 robots is $1.27M; a 250-robot fleet is $3.2M against the $4.6M plan | Contracted count below 200 in 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| 4 | Bruising at or below 2.5% on a seven-day, 1 degree Celsius test against a named retailer spec | Low | A packer rejecting machine-picked lots, or a second grower exit | One point of cull is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee | Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14; one grower left over bruising in 2026-06 | S1 (unverified) |
| 5 | Close by 2026-12-15 at $12M or more, 1x pari passu preference, 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31 | Low | A close slipping into Q1 2027; senior or 2x note terms; fewer than 100 robots at the test date | A slip breaches the $1.5M covenant near 2027-03-10; senior notes cut the $25M recovery from 0.59x to 0.21x | Cash below $2.5M, a waiver request, no equal-rank warranty | S1 (unverified), S95 |

### Where the price turns

| Terms | Base case, $100M exit | Bear case, $25M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $72M pre-money, 1x pari passu (deck terms) | 1.0x | 0.59x | S95 (unverified), calc on a $36.77M stack, net of $1.6M debt and 8% costs |
| $72M pre-money, 1.5x on the lead cheque | 1.5x | 0.75x | S95 (unverified), calc: the cheque holds $18.0M of a $42.77M stack |
| $50-58M pre-money, 1.5x, half staged | 1.5x | 0.88x | S95 (unverified), calc on a $36.77M stack |

Above the stack the preference and the as-converted share converge, so the premium is worth its face value in the base case. The evidence needs to improve less than the price: independent quotes for the v4 and a note agreement warranting equal rank would reprice the same asset.

### The analogs that teach the rule

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue River to Deere, $305M | Best | 2015-2017 | Four times the last private post-money; the buyer wanted perception, not a fleet | S128 |
| Bear Flag to Deere, $250M | Best | 2021 | A strategic premium exists for autonomy attached to an OEM line | S128 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | Best-funded autonomous tractor entrant; shut down April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus | S131 |
| Tortuga and Advanced Farm | Cautionary | 2024-2025 | Both sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices after real fleets; the fleet was not what buyers paid for | S127 |
:::

The category's exit pays for the perception asset or the team, not the lease book: a buyer prices the labelled dataset and the grower relationships and treats a leased fleet as a liability it must absorb. Because the fee sits below the cost of the asset, each additional robot moves value from equity to the grower, so growth enlarges the loss rather than the return; the preference then decides whether that loss lands on the founder, the noteholder or this fund. For Meridian the implication is to decline at this mark and keep the diligence warm: the quotes and the note agreement are cheap and would reprice the same asset.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin scores 4.5 of 10 on the weighted evidence and the recommendation is to pass at $72M pre-money. The score is not a verdict on the picker: it is a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and a credibly measured machine, set against a lease book that loses $8,100 a robot-season at the price growers signed (company-reported, unverified), a $33,000 build cost quoted only by a counterparty with five roles in the round, and a $90M post-money that returns the lead 1.0x until a $90M exit and 2x only at $180M. Pass rather than Wait for milestone: the binding objection is the price plus company-only evidence, and the milestones are the conditions for the lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

### The weighted score

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market and customer pain | 15% | 7 | The harvest line is large, independently costed and the third-largest noncitrus crop; the crop base is flat (2025 US production -1%), so growth must come from penetration, and the 2026 wage-floor cut lowered the grower's alternative cost by 18-23% | S119, S129, S80 |
| Product and technology | 20% | 6 | 94% pick rate on 212 company-chosen rows is a real measurement, but coverage is 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA allowance, and the core perception families are licensed with an exclusivity cliff at 100 robots | S1 (unverified), S86 |
| Unit economics | 20% | 2 | -$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the $9,500 signed price and $48,000 build; breakeven is $17,600 a season on that build, or a $15,600 build at the signed price; the reported 41% margin precedes $3.21M of FY2027 depreciation and -5.5% follows it, against United Rentals' 35.8-40.3% after depreciation | S1 (unverified), S132 |
| Team and execution | 10% | 5 | The founding pair fits perception and farm access and shipped three hardware generations without a CTO; nobody in the five-person executive group has built hardware at volume, the CTO seat is vacant from 2023-08, and the plan asks for 5.6x fleet growth in one season (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified) |
| Competitive position | 10% | 5 | Not alone: Harvest CROO claims human-parity open-field picking (company-issued, 2025-04-24), while Advanced Farm, Tortuga and Monarch have exited or shut; the licence cliff and ungranted filings leave little enforceable exclusivity | S27, S127, S131 |
| Financial position and funding | 10% | 4 | $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $410,000 monthly burn, a $1.5M covenant reached near 2027-03-10, $4.0M committed of an $18M target, and a $3.2M ARR that is 44% contracted rental, 38% related-party engineering and 19% letters (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Valuation and exit | 15% | 3 | $69.9M enterprise value is 36.8x FY2025 revenue and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median; 2 of 8 ag-robotics companies have exited above $100M and none in harvesting; Blue River, the best case, was a 4x last-round outcome | S95 (unverified), S128, S127 |

Two dimensions carry the largest weight and score lowest: unit economics and valuation. That is deliberate, because the product and market scores are what make the company interesting and they are already paid for in the price. No dimension scores above seven without a named comparator, and the market score is capped there because addressable revenue is bounded by acreage times fee rather than by a growing crop base.

### What the decomposition says

Orrin has an eight-quality insight — strawberry harvest is a large, measurable, labour-dominated cost pool a machine can attack for a fraction of the hand bill — delivered by a six-quality product, financed on four-quality terms and priced at a three-quality mark. Each step down comes from the company's own numbers, not an outside objection: the pick rate is real and the coverage claim is 30-50% too high, the pain is real and the damage rate consumes the saving, the contract book is real and 110 robots is 31% of the plan, the preference is real and pays 1.0x to a $90M exit. [S119, S1]

### The recommendation under the downside structures

| Downside structure | Lead recovery at a $25M exit | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deck terms: 1x, pari passu, $36.77M stack | 0.59x | Pass; the 1.0x floor is a $39.4-41.6M exit, not $25M | S95 (unverified) |
| 2025 notes carry a senior or 2x preference | 0.21x | Pass; require an equal-rank warranty before any cheque | S95 (unverified) |
| A $10M senior 2028 round ahead of the Series A | 0.31x | Pass; the 2028 round is more likely than not to ask for seniority | S95 (unverified) |
| Pay-to-play in a 2028 down round, lead does not follow | 0.05x | Pass; a cheque with no reserve is a one-shot option | S95 (unverified) |

The recommendation does not change across these cases, which is the point: there is no downside structure at this mark in which a lead ticket earns a venture return, and the base case is capital returned over the holding period. The preference stack itself is one deck sentence and no document; the 0.94x and this rating assume it ranks equal and at 1x. It would change on two conditions only: independent quotes at or below the current build cost with a first article built, and a signed next-season contract at or above the renewal price from a grower outside the chief operating officer's circle. Those facts would move the unit-economics score and the composite, supporting a lead at a lower mark.

### Position sizing

Zero at $72M. The Kelly inputs are 2.2x at 18%, 1.0x at 40% and 0.35x at 42%, an expected 0.94x; with a 1.2 net win and a 0.82 chance of not winning, the Kelly fraction is negative and the check size is zero. Re-entry is a $6M first tranche and a $6M second tranche on 200 robots in paid service and two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000, at a $50-58M pre-money, a 1.5x preference and an equal-rank warranty, with the licence covenant and lender consent as conditions precedent. Maximum loss is $6M before the second tranche; the remaining $6M is reserved for the 2028 round only if the licence test is met. [S95, S127]

### The next diligence actions

Before a term sheet: obtain the note purchase agreement and seed certificate of designation and confirm the preference stack ranks equally; commission two manufacturer quotes for the v4 plus a firm first-article date; commission an independent cold-storage bruising trial against a named retailer specification; obtain the lender's consent and identify the entity at which the cash covenant is tested; obtain counsel opinions on the California equipment standard and Bayh-Dole US-manufacture obligations for the licensed families; run a quality-of-earnings review of the last full financial year, separating the related-party engineering contract and the grant; and reference-check the CTO candidates and both founders.

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Lead MOIC at the adverse outcome | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | v4 build cost at 300 units | $33,000, single quote from the noteholder and customer | A second quote above $36,000 | At $44,000 the $16,500 list stops covering depreciation and the base case collapses to a $25M exit | 0.59x | High | A second quote; a first article slipping past 2027-01 | S1 (unverified) |
| 2 | 2027 price realisation | $12,700 average, some at $16,500 | A renewal at $9,500-10,500 | Each $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M of revenue; a reversion to $9,500 takes contribution to -$4,350 and the exit to about $40M | 0.96x | High | The first 2027 renewal signature and deposit | S1 (unverified) |
| 3 | Fleet in service by April 2027 | 360 robots | Fewer than 250 delivered by 2027-03 | Each 100 robots is $1.27M of revenue; a 250-robot fleet is $3.2M against the $4.6M plan, an exit near $60M | 1.0x | High | Contracted count below 200 in 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| 4 | Bruising | 3.8% measured; 2.5% assumed | A packer rejecting machine-picked lots | One point of cull is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee; a second grower exit holds the exit near $70M | 1.0x | Medium | A second grower exit after the 2026-06 loss | S1 (unverified) |
| 5 | Preference structure and closing date | 1x pari passu; close by 2026-12-15 | A senior or 2x note; a close slipping into Q1 2027 | The lead's recovery at a $25M exit falls from 0.59x to 0.21x; a slip breaches the $1.5M covenant near 2027-03-10 | 0.21x | High | Cash below $2.5M; a waiver request | S95 (unverified) |
:::

The distribution explains why the adverse-case column is not monotonic: the 1x preference holds the lead near 1.0x down to a $41.6M exit, so operational misses that leave the company saleable cost little, while the two assumptions that break the structure — a build cost above $44,000 and a preference that does not rank equal — take the recovery to 0.59x and 0.21x.
:::

::: takeaways
1. Pass at $72M pre-money: at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $48,000 build, one robot-season loses $8,100 before any scale benefit, and the $12M ticket returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities (company-reported inputs). [S1, S95]
2. Re-engage at a $50-58M pre-money with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged on two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000 and 200 robots in paid service, which lifts the same $100M exit from 1.0x to about 1.5x on company-reported terms. [S95]
3. Make the closing conditions substantive: an equal-rank warranty on the preference stack, lender consent, a licence covenant that survives the 2027-12-31 test, and an independent bruising result at or below 2.5%. [S95, S120]
:::

Two dimensions carry the largest weight and score lowest: unit economics and valuation. That is deliberate, because the product and market scores are what make the company interesting and they are already paid for in the price. No dimension scores above seven without a named comparator, and the market score is capped there because addressable revenue is bounded by acreage times fee rather than by a growing crop base.

### What the decomposition says

Orrin has an eight-quality insight — harvest is a large, labour-dominated cost pool a machine can attack for a fraction of the hand bill — delivered by a six-quality product, financed on four-quality terms and priced at a three-quality mark. Each step down comes from the company's own numbers: the pick rate is real and the coverage claim 30-50% too high, the pain is real and the damage rate consumes the saving, the contract book is real and 110 robots is 31% of the plan, and the preference pays 1.0x to a $90M exit. [S119, S1]

### The recommendation under the downside structures

| Downside structure | Lead recovery at a $25M exit | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deck terms: 1x, pari passu, $36.77M stack | 0.59x | Pass; the 1.0x floor is a $39.4-41.6M exit, not $25M | S95 (unverified) |
| 2025 notes carry a senior or 2x preference | 0.21x | Pass; require an equal-rank warranty before any cheque | S95 (unverified) |
| A $10M senior 2028 round ahead of the Series A | 0.31x | Pass; the 2028 round is more likely than not to ask for seniority | S95 (unverified) |
| Pay-to-play in a 2028 down round, lead does not follow | 0.05x | Pass; a cheque with no reserve is a one-shot option | S95 (unverified) |

The recommendation does not change across these cases: there is no downside structure at this mark in which a lead ticket earns a venture return, and the base case is capital returned over the holding period. The preference stack is one deck sentence and no document; the 0.94x and this rating assume it ranks equal and at 1x. It would change on two conditions only: independent quotes at or below the current build cost with a first article built, and a signed next-season contract at or above the renewal price from outside the chief operating officer's circle. Those would move the unit-economics score, supporting a lead at a lower mark.

### Position sizing

Zero at $72M. The Kelly inputs are 2.2x at 18%, 1.0x at 40% and 0.35x at 42%, an expected 0.94x; with a 1.2 net win and a 0.82 chance of not winning, the Kelly fraction is negative and the check size is zero. Re-entry is a $6M first tranche and a $6M second tranche on 200 robots in paid service and two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000, at a $50-58M pre-money, a 1.5x preference and an equal-rank warranty, with the licence covenant and lender consent as conditions precedent. Maximum loss is $6M before the second tranche; the remaining $6M is reserved for the 2028 round only if the licence test is met. [S95, S127]

### The next diligence actions

Before a term sheet: obtain the note purchase agreement and seed certificate of designation and confirm the stack ranks equally; commission two manufacturer quotes for the v4 plus a firm first-article date; commission an independent cold-storage bruising trial against a named retailer specification; obtain the lender's consent and identify the entity at which the cash covenant is tested; obtain counsel opinions on the California equipment standard and Bayh-Dole US-manufacture obligations; run a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year, separating the related-party engineering contract and the grant; and reference-check the CTO candidates and both founders.
