| Product and technology | 20% | 6 | 94% pick rate on 212 company-chosen rows is a real measurement, but coverage is 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA allowance, and the core perception families are licensed with an exclusivity cliff at 100 robots | S1 (unverified), S86 |
| Unit economics | 20% | 2 | -$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the $9,500 signed price and $48,000 build; breakeven is $17,600 a season on that build, or a $15,600 build at the signed price; the reported 41% margin precedes $3.21M of FY2027 depreciation and -5.5% follows it, against United Rentals' 35.8-40.3% after depreciation | S1 (unverified), S132 |
| Team and execution | 10% | 5 | The founding pair fits perception and farm access and shipped three hardware generations without a CTO; nobody in the five-person executive group has built hardware at volume, the CTO seat is vacant from 2023-08, and the plan asks for 5.6x fleet growth in one season (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified) |
| Competitive position | 10% | 5 | Not alone: Harvest CROO claims human-parity open-field picking (company-issued, 2025-04-24), while Advanced Farm, Tortuga and Monarch have exited or shut; the licence cliff and ungranted filings leave little enforceable exclusivity | S27, S127, S131 |
| Financial position and funding | 10% | 4 | $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $410,000 monthly burn, a $1.5M covenant reached near 2027-03-10, $4.0M committed of an $18M target, and a $3.2M ARR that is 44% contracted rental, 38% related-party engineering and 19% letters (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified), S95 |

Orrin has an eight-quality insight — strawberry harvest is a large, labour-dominated cost pool — delivered by a six-quality product, financed on four-quality terms and priced at a three-quality mark. | Downside structure | Lead recovery at a $25M exit | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|

| 2025 notes carry a senior or 2x preference | 0.21x | Pass; require an equal-rank warranty before any cheque | S95 (unverified) |
| A $10M senior 2028 round ahead of the Series A | 0.31x | Pass; the 2028 round is more likely than not to ask for seniority | S95 (unverified) |

Zero at $72M. :::

::: takeaways
1. Pass at $72M pre-money: at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $48,000 build, one robot-season loses $8,100 before any scale benefit, and the $12M ticket returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities (company-reported inputs). [S1, S95]

3. Make the closing conditions substantive: an equal-rank warranty on the preference stack, lender consent, a licence covenant that survives the 2027-12-31 test, and an independent bruising result at or below 2.5%. [S95, S120]
:::

Two dimensions carry the largest weight and score lowest: unit economics and valuation. That is deliberate, because the product and market scores are what make the company interesting and they are already paid for in the price. No dimension scores above seven without a named comparator, and the market score is capped there because addressable revenue is bounded by acreage times fee rather than by a growing crop base.

### What the decomposition says

Orrin has an eight-quality insight — strawberry harvest is a large, labour-dominated cost pool — delivered by a six-quality product, financed on four-quality terms and priced at a three-quality mark. The steps down come from the company's own numbers: coverage 30-50% below the claim, a damage rate that consumes the saving, 110 robots at 31% of the plan, and a preference paying 1.0x to a $90M exit. [S119, S1]

### The recommendation under the downside structures

| Downside structure | Lead recovery at a $25M exit | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deck terms: 1x, pari passu, $36.77M stack | 0.59x | Pass; the 1.0x floor is a $39.4-41.6M exit, not $25M | S95 (unverified) |
| 2025 notes carry a senior or 2x preference | 0.21x | Pass; require an equal-rank warranty before any cheque | S95 (unverified) |
| A $10M senior 2028 round ahead of the Series A | 0.31x | Pass; the 2028 round is more likely than not to ask for seniority | S95 (unverified) |
| Pay-to-play in a 2028 down round, lead does not follow | 0.05x | Pass; a cheque with no reserve is a one-shot option | S95 (unverified) |

The recommendation does not change across these cases: there is no downside structure at this mark in which a lead ticket earns a venture return. The preference stack is one deck sentence and no document; the expected return and this rating assume it ranks equal. It would change on two conditions only: independent quotes at or below the current build cost with a first article built, and a signed next-season contract at or above the renewal price from outside the chief operating officer's circle. Those would move the unit-economics score, supporting a lead at a lower mark.

### Position sizing

Zero at $72M. The Kelly inputs are 2.2x at 18%, 1.0x at 40% and 0.35x at 42%, an expected 0.94x; with a 1.2 net win and a 0.82 chance of not winning, the Kelly fraction is negative and the check size is zero. Re-entry is a $6M first tranche and a $6M second tranche on 200 robots in paid service and two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000, at a $50-58M pre-money, a 1.5x preference and an equal-rank warranty, with the licence covenant and lender consent as conditions precedent. Maximum loss is $6M before the second tranche; the remaining $6M is reserved for the 2028 round only if the licence test is met. [S95, S127]

### The next diligence actions

Before a term sheet: obtain the note purchase agreement and seed certificate of designation and confirm the stack ranks equally; commission two manufacturer quotes for the v4 plus a firm first-article date; commission an independent cold-storage bruising trial against a named retailer specification; obtain the lender's consent and identify the entity at which the cash covenant is tested; obtain counsel opinions on the California equipment standard and Bayh-Dole US-manufacture obligations; run a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year, separating the related-party engineering contract and the grant.

arguments.markdown:
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 0.94x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, so it is a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security and grower data; no public robotics M&A record | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga in 2024; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | What the target had | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. The 2025 market recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. The report uses one distribution — 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35 = 0.94x, the same 0.94x carried in sections 10 and 11. The bear's 0.35x is the central recovery across the $12-40M asset-sale range; the deck's pari passu terms give about 0.6x at a $25M exit, senior or 2x note terms about 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round about 0.31x. The counter-case is that Deere or CNH pays $250-305M for the team and perception model, as they did for Blue River and Bear Flag; if Orrin proves 95% pick rates at 360 robots, a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

| Bull | 18% | $250M | $26.7M | 2.2x | 20% Series B dilution; converts | S95, calc |

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Revenue | $5.6M | $13.2M | $13.2M at 7x forward, or $18M at 5x | S95 (unverified) |
| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to US, European and Japanese strategics: Deere and AGCO are US-listed, CNH is Dutch/Italian and Kubota Japanese, and all have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, the Calder license and grower data, and Mexico assembly adds tariff diligence. An IPO is not realistic before 2030 at $1.9M of revenue and a $5.2M FY2025 net loss. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes the exit to 2030-2032. arguments.markdown:
Meridian should pass at the $72M pre-money. Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the field and a real harvest cost pool to sell into, but at the $9,500 a robot-season growers signed and the $48,000 build the company can evidence (company-reported, unverified), every unit loses $8,100 before debt service, and the round prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund: the $12M cheque returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities and 2x only at a $180M exit. The rating is Pass rather than Wait for milestone because the binding objection is the price plus evidence that rests on the company alone; the re-entry milestones are the conditions for a lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pass | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; re-engage at $50-58M with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged | 4.5 | Medium | 12-24 months, to the 2027 season and the licence test | S95 (unverified), S1 (unverified) |
:::

### What is good, and what decides it

The pain is real and independently measured: the UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is cheap against that bill. The picker has the only labelled field dataset in the category — 94% pick rate on 212 rows, 75 paid robot-seasons, 110 robots contracted for 2027 at a $12,700 renewal price — and the two things that usually kill hardware start-ups, no customer and no evidence, are not the problem here. Four facts outweigh that. One robot-season loses $8,100 at the signed price, and the $33,000 build that would fix it is a single quote from a counterparty that is also noteholder, customer, board observer and investor. Bruising at 3.8% has already cost one grower and spends most of the USDA allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. [S119, S1, S95, S86]

::: briefing
| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| The terms | $12M lead cheque at a $72M pre-money and $90M post-money on 15,272,108 fully diluted shares; $69.9M enterprise value after $1.6M of fleet debt and $3.7M of cash | S95 (unverified) |
| What is being bought | 64 robots in service, 110 contracted for 2027 of a 360-robot plan, a labelled field dataset and two valleys of grower relationships; no granted patent | S1 (unverified), S86 |
| Unit economics | -$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the signed price and build cost; breakeven at $17,600 a season on the $48,000 build, and at the signed $9,500 price the breakeven build is $15,600 | S1 (unverified) |
| Key risks | Execution: negative contribution at every signed price, a single build quote, 3.8% bruising, a licence cliff at 100 robots on 2027-12-31, a cash floor near 2027-03-10, and a California standard that still requires a human driver | S1 (unverified), S86, S126 |
| The round | $18M target, $4.0M committed, $12M minimum; at $12M the plan funds about 200 robots and a 2028 down round becomes the base case | S95 (unverified) |
| Cash | $3.7M at 2026-09-30, $410,000 monthly net burn, a $1.5M covenant reached near 2027-03-10 | S1 (unverified) |
| The clock | Licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31; a Section 232 robotics decision falls due 2027-04-26 | S86, S88 |
:::

::: efficiency
| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue, FY2025 | $1.9M, of which $1.2M is related-party engineering and part is grant-funded | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue, FY2026E | $2.6M on 38 employees, about $68,000 per employee | S1 (unverified) |
| Recurring revenue | $1.4M contracted 2027 seasons; $0.71M currently signed | S95 (unverified) |
| Burn | $410,000 monthly net; nine months of stated runway, 5.4 months to the covenant | S1 (unverified) |
| Valuation | $72M pre, $90M post, $69.9M enterprise value | S95 (unverified) |
| Multiples | 36.8x FY2025 revenue, 26.9x FY2026E, 49.9x corrected recurring; peer median 2.3x | S95, S38 |
| Margin | 41% reported before fleet depreciation; -5.5% in FY2027 after it | S1 (unverified) |
:::

The evidence confidence is medium. The arithmetic is solid and reproducible from the deck; the inputs — build cost, service cost, contract count, preference terms and every executive credential — are management statements, unverified, with no independent record retrieved. The $36.77M preference stack, at 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, is one sentence in the deck and appears in no document; the 0.94x return and the Pass rating assume it. There is no audit, no registry confirmation of the three entities, no federal award visible against the stated grant, and no patent prosecution record. [S95]

The follow-up diligence is narrow and cheap: two independent manufacturer quotes for the v4, an independent cold-storage bruising trial, the note purchase agreement, the lender's consent, and a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year.

::: one-question
What does a fourth-generation robot cost to build at fleet volumes, quoted by a manufacturer that is not also the largest customer?

At the current build cost no price growers have signed makes a robot-season profitable, so the fleet consumes capital on every unit; at a lower cost the list price turns contribution positive and the business becomes financeable. Two competitive quotes settle it in weeks and decide between a capital-consuming lease book and a business that compounds.
:::

::: takeaways
1. Pass at $72M pre-money: at the signed $9,500 price and the $48,000 build, one robot-season loses $8,100, and the $12M ticket returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities (company-reported). [S1, S95]
2. The company is worth pursuing at a lower price: at a $50-58M pre-money with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged on two independent quotes at or below $33,000 and 200 robots in paid service, the same $100M exit returns about 1.5x on company-reported terms. [S95]
3. The binding constraints are physical and contractual, not commercial: bruising, coverage of 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, a licence cliff at 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and a California standard that still requires a human driver. [S1, S86, S126]
:::

arguments.markdown:
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 0.94x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security and grower data; no public robotics M&A record | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 (unverified) |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga in 2024; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | What the target had | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River | 2017 | $305M | 3.5x the $87M post-money; revenue n/a | See & Spray, $30M+ raised | S98 |
| Deere / Bear Flag | 2021 | $250M | 31.6x the $7.9M seed; revenue n/a | Autonomous tractor retrofit, 2017 | S96, S118 |
| CNH / Raven | 2021 | $2.1B EV | n/a; 33.6% premium | Public precision-ag company | S99 |
| AGCO / Trimble Ag (85%) | 2023-24 | $2.35B EV | 13.8x 2023E EBITDA | Precision-ag portfolio, $170M EBITDA | S101 |
| Kubota / AgJunction | 2021 | $73M | n/a | Guidance and auto-steer | S104 |
| CNH / Advanced Farm assets | 2025 | Undisclosed | n/a | Strawberry and apple picking IP and team | S97, S28 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2024 | Undisclosed | n/a | $50M deployed, 150 robots | S93 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | n/a | Tomato harvesting robot | S32 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. 2025 recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money the lead owns 13.33%: a $100M exit returns 1.1x before the Series B and 1.0x after 20% dilution, when the $12M preference binds; $250M returns 2.8x and 2.2x. The report uses one distribution — 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35 = 0.94x, the same 0.94x carried in sections 10 and 11. The bear's 0.35x is the central recovery across the $12-40M asset-sale range; the deck's pari passu terms give 0.64x at a $25M exit, senior or 2x note terms 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round 0.31x. Below $90M the preference, not the operating plan, sets the return. The counter-case is a $250-305M Deere or CNH bid for the team and perception model, as for Blue River and Bear Flag; at 95% pick rates and 360 robots a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

| Case | Probability | Exit value | Lead proceeds | MOIC | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | $250M | $26.7M | 2.2x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Base | 40% | $100M | $12.0M | 1.0x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Bear | 42% | $25M (central of $12-40M) | $4.2M | 0.35x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Weighted | 100% | — | — | 0.94x (0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35) | S95 (unverified), calc |

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Metric | 2027 plan | 2028 plan | Test for a Series B above $72M pre | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $5.6M | $13.2M | $13.2M at 7x forward, or $18M at 5x | S95 (unverified) |
| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |
| Renewal | 110 contracted 2027 seasons | n/a | 80% or more of 2026 paying growers renew | S95 (unverified) |
| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to US, European and Japanese strategics: Deere and AGCO are US-listed, CNH Dutch/Italian and Kubota Japanese; all have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, the Calder license and grower data, and Mexico assembly adds tariff diligence. An IPO is not realistic before 2030 at $1.9M of revenue and a $5.2M FY2025 net loss. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes the exit to 2030-2032. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.0x at $90M, 1.1x at $100M (1.0x after dilution), 1.7x at $150M (1.4x) and 2.8x at $250M (2.2x); over five years that is 0% IRR at $100M, 17.1% at $250M and -18.9% at the $25M bear. A 20-30% lower entry price, or a 1.5x preference, would make the same exits work; at $72M the lead is buying an option that needs a $250M+ bid. The 0.94x expected return and the pass recommendation assume the deck's 1x, non-participating, equal-rank preference — one sentence on deck p.14, with no seed charter or note purchase agreement supplied; the seed original issue price is not disclosed and the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs may convert on top, making the stack $39.27M rather than $36.77M. If the notes are senior or 2x the $25M recovery is 0.21x rather than 0.6x, and a $10M senior 2028 round cuts it to 0.31x; the note purchase agreement and seed charter are the open data request that would settle the downside. The implication is to pass at $72M, or invest at a 20-30% lower price with a 1.5x preference and a milestone tranche. Diligence should confirm the Advanced Farm and Tortuga prices, who owns the grower contracts, the Calder license's change-of-control terms and the 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons concentrated in two growers. [S95, S97, S93]

The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool, and hand-pick labour alone is worth $25,000-35,000 an acre, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, 100% of US strawberry acreage is worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** The $310M and $16,500 inputs are company figures, unverified; at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year and 15% adoption is worth $35.4M, while $310M requires 132% of the base. **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is helping growers raise beds to waist height and will breed for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S136, S138.
:::

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces about 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline, while the California Strawberry Commission projects 7-8 million trays a week through August 2026. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### The wage bill sets the price ceiling
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. The 2024 UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural costs and $112,694 of total cost, on 9,000 trays at $11; UC Davis puts labour at 50-60% of variable production cost, with pickers paid $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour. That implies hand-pick labour of $25,000-35,000 an acre. At $16,500 a robot-season and 3.5 acres per robot, Orrin charges $4,714 an acre, 13-19% of the wage bill it targets, and a 10% harvest-cost saving would be worth $7,929 an acre to the grower. Either the robot removes only part of the crew's work, or Orrin is pricing for adoption and has room to raise price later [S10, S12].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%, and at the $12,700 renewal price it implies 7.1%. Density is conservative the other way: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over a 210-day season is 315 acre-passes, which at 40-50 passes serves 6.3-7.9 acres, not 3.5 — one robot per 3.5 acres implies 90 passes. Either throughput is a peak measurement or the fleet count is inflated. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published [S136]. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits [S138]. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove about $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception, and the addressable set is open-field acres with slopes under 4%, no standing water and rows wide enough for a track. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia, where Orrin has no sales or service [S9, S13, S14].

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California | 43,726 acres (2026); $3.47B harvest cost (author calculation) | +2.0% acres 2025-26; terminal price -3.3% CAGR 2024-26 | Entered: 14 pilots since 2024, 4 paying growers | 7-month season; slopes over 4% and standing water excluded; retailer bruising limits | Hand crews, harvest-aid platforms, Harvest CROO | S9, S10, S1 |
| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed | Not disclosed; NASS state series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024, with Florida above 14% of the national total; the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost changed on 2025-10-02, when the Department of Labor replaced the USDA Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate with BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics data; the rule is under litigation and summaries disagree, one showing the average rate falling to $15.96 an hour from $17.74 and another showing entry-level rates up 3.7%. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. A lower OEWS-based wage floor lengthens robot payback; a court overturning the rule restores the higher rate and shortens it. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the pure hand-pick wage line per acre in the 2024 UC budget; the final 2026-27 adverse effect wage rates for California and Florida; and the passes and acres behind the 3.5-acre robot density [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117].

arguments.markdown:
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 0.94x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security and grower data; no public robotics M&A record | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 (unverified) |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga in 2024; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | What the target had | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River | 2017 | $305M | 3.5x the $87M post-money; revenue n/a | See & Spray, $30M+ raised | S98 |
| Deere / Bear Flag | 2021 | $250M | 31.6x the $7.9M seed; revenue n/a | Autonomous tractor retrofit, 2017 | S96, S118 |
| CNH / Raven | 2021 | $2.1B EV | n/a; 33.6% premium | Public precision-ag company | S99 |
| AGCO / Trimble Ag (85%) | 2023-24 | $2.35B EV | 13.8x 2023E EBITDA | Precision-ag portfolio, $170M EBITDA | S101 |
| Kubota / AgJunction | 2021 | $73M | n/a | Guidance and auto-steer | S104 |
| CNH / Advanced Farm assets | 2025 | Undisclosed | n/a | Strawberry and apple picking IP and team | S97, S28 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2024 | Undisclosed | n/a | $50M deployed, 150 robots | S93 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | n/a | Tomato harvesting robot | S32 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. 2025 recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money the lead owns 13.33%: a $100M exit returns 1.1x before the Series B and 1.0x after 20% dilution, when the $12M preference binds; $250M returns 2.8x and 2.2x. The report uses one distribution — 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35 = 0.94x, the same 0.94x carried in sections 10 and 11. The bear's 0.35x is the central recovery across the $12-40M asset-sale range; the deck's pari passu terms give 0.64x at a $25M exit, senior or 2x note terms 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round 0.31x. Below $90M the preference, not the operating plan, sets the return: the first $36.77M of equity goes to the stack, which means a technically good 2027 season still returns only capital. The counter-case is a $250-305M Deere or CNH bid for the team and perception model, as for Blue River and Bear Flag; at 95% pick rates and 360 robots a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

| Case | Probability | Exit value | Lead proceeds | MOIC | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | $250M | $26.7M | 2.2x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Base | 40% | $100M | $12.0M | 1.0x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Bear | 42% | $25M (central of $12-40M) | $4.2M | 0.35x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Weighted | 100% | — | — | 0.94x (0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35) | S95 (unverified), calc |

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Metric | 2027 plan | 2028 plan | Test for a Series B above $72M pre | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $5.6M | $13.2M | $13.2M at 7x forward, or $18M at 5x | S95 (unverified) |
| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |
| Renewal | 110 contracted 2027 seasons | n/a | 80% or more of 2026 paying growers renew | S95 (unverified) |
| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to US, European and Japanese strategics — Deere, AGCO, CNH and Kubota — all of which have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, license and grower data; Mexico assembly adds tariff diligence. An IPO is not realistic before 2030 at $1.9M of revenue and a $5.2M FY2025 net loss. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes exit to 2030-2032. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.0x at $90M, 1.1x at $100M (1.0x after dilution), 1.7x at $150M (1.4x) and 2.8x at $250M (2.2x); over five years that is 0% IRR at $100M, 17.1% at $250M and -18.9% at the $25M bear. A 20-30% lower entry price, or a 1.5x preference, would make the same exits work; at $72M the lead is buying an option that needs a $250M+ bid. The 0.94x expected return and the pass recommendation assume the deck's 1x, non-participating, equal-rank preference — one sentence on deck p.14, with no seed charter or note agreement supplied; the seed issue price is not disclosed and the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs may convert on top, making the stack $39.27M rather than $36.77M. If the notes are senior or 2x the $25M recovery is 0.21x rather than 0.6x, and a $10M senior 2028 round cuts it to 0.31x; the note purchase agreement and seed charter are the open data request that would settle the downside. The implication is to pass at $72M, or invest at a 20-30% lower price with a 1.5x preference and a milestone tranche. Diligence should confirm the Advanced Farm and Tortuga prices, grower-contract ownership, the Calder license's change-of-control terms and the 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons in two growers. [S95, S97, S93]

arguments.markdown:
The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool, and hand-pick labour alone is worth $25,000-35,000 an acre, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, 100% of US strawberry acreage is worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** The $310M and $16,500 inputs are company figures, unverified; at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year and 15% adoption is worth $35.4M, while $310M requires 132% of the base. **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is helping growers raise beds to waist height and will breed for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S136, S138.
:::

| Measure | Top-down | Bottom-up | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global fresh-produce harvest labour | $42B (2025), company estimate, unverified | — | S1 |
| SAM — US strawberry harvest cost | $3.1B company estimate, unverified, vs $3.47B author calculation (43,726 California acres × $79,288 harvest cost/acre) | 50,000 acres × $62,000-79,000 harvest cost/acre = $3.1-3.9B | S1, S9, S10 |
| SOM — company claim, 2031 | $310M, presented as 10% of $3.1B, unverified | 18,788 robots × $16,500 = $310M, requiring 65,758 acres = 132% of the 50,000-acre base | S1 |
| SOM — tested, 2031 at 15% adoption | — | 7,500 acres ÷ 3.5 = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M (author calculation from company assumptions, unverified) | S1 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue, FY2028 | $12.9M RaaS plan, company projection, unverified | 782 robots at $16,500 = 2,737 acres = 5.5% of 50,000 acres | S1 |

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces about 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline, while the California Strawberry Commission projects 7-8 million trays a week through August 2026. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### The wage bill sets the price ceiling
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. The 2024 UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural costs and $112,694 of total cost, on 9,000 trays at $11; UC Davis puts labour at 50-60% of variable production cost, with pickers paid $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour. That implies hand-pick labour of $25,000-35,000 an acre. At $16,500 a robot-season and 3.5 acres per robot, Orrin charges $4,714 an acre, 13-19% of the wage bill it targets, and a 10% harvest-cost saving would be worth $7,929 an acre to the grower. Either the robot removes only part of the crew's work, or Orrin is pricing for adoption and has room to raise price later [S10, S12].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%, and at the $12,700 renewal price it implies 7.1%. Density is conservative the other way: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over a 210-day season is 315 acre-passes, which at 40-50 passes serves 6.3-7.9 acres, not 3.5 — one robot per 3.5 acres implies 90 passes. Either throughput is a peak measurement or the fleet count is inflated. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove about $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception, and the addressable set is open-field acres with slopes under 4%, no standing water and rows wide enough for a track. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia, where Orrin has no sales or service [S9, S13, S14].

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California | 43,726 acres (2026); $3.47B harvest cost (author calculation) | +2.0% acres 2025-26; terminal price -3.3% CAGR 2024-26 | Entered: 14 pilots since 2024, 4 paying growers | 7-month season; slopes over 4% and standing water excluded; retailer bruising limits | Hand crews, harvest-aid platforms, Harvest CROO | S9, S10, S1 |
| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed | Not disclosed; NASS state series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024, with Florida above 14% of the national total; the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost changed on 2025-10-02, when the Department of Labor replaced the USDA Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate with BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics data; the rule is under litigation and summaries disagree, one showing the average rate falling to $15.96 an hour from $17.74 and another showing entry-level rates up 3.7%. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The policy risk cuts both ways: a lower OEWS-based wage floor lengthens robot payback, while a court overturning the rule restores the higher rate and shortens it. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the pure hand-pick wage line per acre in the 2024 UC budget; the final 2026-27 adverse effect wage rates for California and Florida; and the passes and acres behind the 3.5-acre robot density [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117].

rows.benchmark: Recurring-revenue definition: rental only; the engineering contract expires 2027-06-30 and the letters are non-binding.
rows.confidence: high on the components, which the deck lists explicitly; medium on whether the 2027 contracts are cancellable.
rows.finding: The $3.2M ARR is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 at $12,700), $1.2M of related-party engineering services to 2027-06-30 and $0.6M of signed letters of intent; like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M (43.8%) and current signed rental is $0.71M (22.3%).
rows.follow_up: What cancellation and deposit terms sit inside the 110 contracted robot-seasons?
rows.implication: Value the business on $1.4M of 2027 rental, not $3.2M of ARR; the $8M milestone needs list-price contracts and the full engineering rate.
rows.mechanism: Adding an expiring related-party contract and non-binding letters to contracted rental overstates the recurring base by 2.3x.
rows.weakens: The $1.4M is contracted and priced at a 33.7% increase on the signed season, so it is stronger than a pipeline.

rows.benchmark: Covenant floor of $1.5M unrestricted cash; company runway claim of nine months to zero.
rows.confidence: high: arithmetic on deck figures; the principal and working-capital exclusions are stated, not hidden.
rows.finding: The $0.085M 2027 year-end balance is $3.7M opening cash less $1.025M of burn to the 2026-12-15 close plus $12.0M proceeds less $4.69M of 2027 cash operating burn ($7.9M net loss less $3.21M depreciation) less $9.9M capex; it assumes zero working capital and no principal repayment, and the $1.5M covenant is breached around 2027-09-12.
rows.follow_up: What are the grower payment terms and the loan amortisation schedule?
rows.implication: The $12M minimum does not carry the company through 2027 with the covenant intact; the close date and a working-capital facility are conditions.
rows.mechanism: Adding back non-cash depreciation and ignoring working capital makes a plan that consumes the full round look funded to year-end.
rows.weakens: The undrawn $0.9M fleet facility moves year-end to about $0.985M and the breach to November 2027, still inside the plan year.

rows.benchmark: Series B planned for 2028; 2028 revenue $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500.
rows.confidence: high: the $6.085M reconciles exactly on the stated assumptions.
rows.finding: The $18M case follows the same path and ends 2027 at $6.085M; the 2028 plan needs 422 more robots and $13.93M of capex plus about $0.45M of cash operating burn, leaving roughly an $8.3M hole before a Series B.
rows.follow_up: Is the 2028 fleet capex in the Series B plan, and at what assumed price?
rows.implication: $18M buys 2027, not breakeven; the Series B is a financing need, not an option.
rows.mechanism: 2028 revenue growth requires a second fleet that the round does not fund.
rows.weakens: The 2028 fleet could be leased through an enlarged equipment facility rather than equity, though no such commitment is disclosed.

rows.benchmark: Deck use of funds: 55% robots, 25% R&D, 20% sales and field operations; 64 v3 robots already in service.
rows.confidence: high: percentages and prices are in the deck.
rows.finding: At $18M the 55% robot allocation is $9.9M, 300 new v4 at $33,000, which with 64 v3 gives 360 in service; at the $12M minimum the same split is $6.6M, 200 robots and a 264-robot fleet, so the $4.6M 2027 rental line (360 robots at $12,778) is not funded.
rows.follow_up: Will the company scale the 2027 fleet to the money raised, or spend the full $9.9M and underfund R&D and sales?
rows.implication: The minimum close forces a choice between the robot count and the rest of the plan; neither version produces the projected $4.6M.
rows.mechanism: Use-of-funds percentages are fixed to an $18M raise; a smaller raise scales the fleet but not the revenue projection.
rows.weakens: The company could fund the extra 100 robots with the $0.9M undrawn facility and vendor terms, but that covers only 27 robots.

rows.benchmark: 110 robot-seasons contracted for 2027; 2027 renewal average $12,700, list $16,500, signed 2026 price $9,500.
rows.confidence: high: the revenue lines and prices are explicit; the implied fleet is arithmetic.
rows.finding: FY2027 rental revenue of $4.6M equals 360 robots at $12,778, $78 above the renewal average but with only 110 robots contracted; FY2028 rental revenue of $12.9M implies 782 robots at $16,500 and $13.93M of capex, which is 422 more robots than the 2027 plan.
rows.follow_up: Which 250 growers or robot-seasons fill the gap between 110 contracted and 360 planned?
rows.implication: The revenue projections require fleet growth that is neither contracted nor funded; the $8M ARR milestone is a plan, not a book.
rows.mechanism: Revenue is built from robot count times price, but the count and the price are both ahead of the contracted base.
rows.weakens: FY2027 $4.6M could be reached with 360 robots at $12,778 if every planned robot is deployed and priced at the renewal average, which is possible if the fleet is funded.

rows.benchmark: 2026 reported RaaS gross margin of 41%; 2027P 52% and 2028P 61% company-wide.
rows.confidence: high: depreciation is computed from the stated four-season life and fleet counts.
rows.finding: The 52% and 61% gross-margin projections precede $3.21M (2027) and $6.45M (2028) of fleet depreciation; after depreciation, 2027 gross profit of $2.9M becomes -$0.31M (-5.5%) and 2028's $8.0M becomes $1.55M (11.7%). The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while the 52% and 61% are company-wide, so the series changes definition between years.
rows.follow_up: Will the company present gross margin before or after fleet depreciation in the audited accounts?
rows.implication: The margin expansion story is an artefact of depreciation placement; the business is not projected to earn a positive gross profit after fleet capital in 2027.
rows.mechanism: Fleet depreciation sits in operating expense, so gross margin excludes the largest cost of the rental product.
rows.weakens: Depreciation is non-cash, so the cash contribution is better than the accounting contribution; the asset is paid for upfront and the cash is in capex.

rows.benchmark: Deere FY2025 revenue per employee of about $625,000; Orrin $68,421 ($2.6M / 38).
rows.confidence: medium: Orrin revenue is FY2026E and unaudited; Deere is an established manufacturer, not a like-for-like peer.
rows.finding: No balance sheet means ROE, ROIC, asset turnover and working-capital days cannot be computed; interest cover is -29.3x on FY2026E EBIT of -$5.4M and $184,000 of interest; net cash is $2.1M of which $1.5M must stay unrestricted; cumulative losses are $32.0M against $20.5M raised; capital per robot in service is $320,313.
rows.follow_up: Provide the FY2025 and FY2026 balance sheets, cash flow statements and the loan amortisation schedule.
rows.implication: The company is capital-intensive per dollar of revenue and per employee; returns cannot be assessed until a balance sheet is produced.
rows.mechanism: A hardware fleet consumes capital upfront and depreciates over four seasons, so accounting returns depend on utilisation and price, neither of which is yet proven.
rows.weakens: Deere's scale and dealer model make the revenue-per-employee comparison directional only.

rows.benchmark: Audited-account expectations: an auditor, a balance sheet, a cash flow statement, related-party disclosure and revenue recognition.
rows.confidence: high that the documents are absent; the $310,000 related-party figure is from the deck.
rows.finding: There is no auditor, no balance sheet and no cash flow statement; 50% of FY2025 revenue came from a related party that is also a $2.5M noteholder, board observer, v4 contract manufacturer and $1.0M round investor; $310,000 was paid in 2025 and 2026 to the COO's wholly owned haulage and night-shift company, 67% of the 2026 field-service line; a public search on 2026-10-30 found no SBIR, USAspending or press record for the company.
rows.follow_up: Will the company provide audited FY2025 accounts and the data room before the round closes?
rows.implication: Treat all revenue and cash figures as company-reported and unverified; make audited accounts and a related-party schedule a condition of closing.
rows.mechanism: Related-party revenue and a related-party service supplier can move both revenue and cost, so the reported margin and cash burn are not independently confirmed.
rows.weakens: The related-party contracts were board-approved and are disclosed in the deck, which is better than non-disclosure.

P1:
"Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester reached performance rates on par with human harvesting at a commercial operation in Duette, Florida — a direct open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but Driscoll's has invested in Harvest CROO and Agrobot and is talking to six harvesting startups, and Japanese and Chinese university teams are solving the same perception problem in public. What disciplines Orrin's price is the hand crew it must beat, the harvest-aid platform that takes part of the saving at a fraction of the capital, and the 2025 exits that show how hard harvest robotics is to fund [S27, S28, S138]."

Evidence:
"**The field is thinner than the technology narrative implies, and it is not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii; Waseda and Nanjing Agricultural University have working strawberry prototypes; Tallis, Orrin's contract manufacturer, could build the platform. Sources: S27, S28, S34, S139, S135, S1."

Table 9 rows. Then P2 consolidation:
"The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm, which had reached named commercial growers in California, ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii. No public market shares exist; the best proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S27, S34]."

P3:
"### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo said it "was unable to develop the market traction necessary to support its business". Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, was sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021, and Traptic, a strawberry picker, was acquired in 2022 (reported; not independently sourced in this review). The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30 [S29, S32]."

P4:
"### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour, and conveyors already raise productivity by cutting walking; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost, a company claim that is unverified but captures part of the saving with none of the autonomy or bruising risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: a picking arm on a harvest-aid platform that already sells and services equipment is a cheaper route to the grower than a new autonomous fleet. Orrin must beat a crew costing $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour and charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77]."

P5:
"### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field row architecture, same RaaS model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim already in the market. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published pick rate or bruising data, and no California service network — where Orrin's 14 pilots and 4 paying growers sit. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct packing into the grower's clamshells, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows, and the COO's California grower relationships. It is a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly. The international field is earlier but not empty: Waseda University's Sugano Lab, with Maekawa Manufacturing, runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated greenhouse beds with stereo cameras and a stem-clipping arm, a research project with no commercial deployment or price; Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked robot at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success, with no price or commercial deployment; Washington State University researchers have built a robot to pick strawberries hidden under leaves. None is an open-field competitor in 2026 and none has a public price, so none sets a ceiling on the $16,500 list today. What they show is that the perception and gentle-grasp stack is being solved in public — which erodes the licensed families' value if the Calder licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31 [S30, S1, S139, S135, S137, S134]."

P6:
"### The price is the tell
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025 and 2026 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase, with renewals averaging $12,700. The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm, which had reached named commercial growers in California, ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii. No public market shares exist; the best proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S27, S34].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo said it "was unable to develop the market traction necessary to support its business". Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, was sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021, and Traptic, a strawberry picker, was acquired in 2022 (reported; not independently sourced in this review). The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30 [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour, and conveyors already raise productivity by cutting walking; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost, a company claim that is unverified but captures part of the saving with none of the autonomy or bruising risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: a picking arm on a harvest-aid platform that already sells and services equipment is a cheaper route to the grower than a new autonomous fleet. Orrin must beat a crew costing $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour and charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field row architecture, same RaaS model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim already in the market. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct packing into the grower's clamshells, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows, and the COO's California grower relationships; it is a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly. The international field is earlier but not empty: Waseda University's Sugano Lab, with Maekawa Manufacturing, runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated greenhouse beds with stereo cameras and a stem-clipping arm, a research project with no commercial deployment or price; Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked robot at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success, with no price or commercial deployment; Washington State University researchers have built a robot to pick strawberries hidden under leaves. None is an open-field competitor in 2026 and none has a public price, so none sets a ceiling on the $16,500 list today.
