At the signed $9,500 the rental business loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a build cost not yet built.

### Rental is a minority of revenue, and the signed growth is same-store

The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California (April-October) and four in Florida (December-March) — with Orrin owning, maintaining and insuring the fleet; the term is one season at a time and no multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. The 2027 book is 110 robot-seasons at a $12,700 average, $1.4M, and all 110 come from the four growers that paid in 2026. No new grower has signed for 2027; the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters of intent for 50 robots from the eight remaining pilot farms. Same-store robots rise from 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher — real demand evidence from four accounts, and none that the model acquires customers [S1].

### The sales cycle is one season, and the pilot is mostly Orrin's cost

The customer table shows a one-season lag from first field trial to first paid deployment in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 paid seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 paid seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season. That is a 4-12 month cycle, and the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. Who signs is not disclosed: the deck names no signatory, and the executed contracts would show whether the counterparty is the owner, a VP of growing or procurement — a distinction that matters because an owner can buy a strategic pilot while procurement will not accept a 3.8% bruise rate. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost. It owns, maintains and insures the robots, and the grower's contribution appears only in the paid-pilot line of $0.27M in FY2025 and $0.34M in FY2026E. Against nine farms with 2025 test rows that is about $30,000 a pilot farm; at three to four robots a pilot (12 robots at four farms in 2024, four at one 2025 pilot) the direct cost is $53,000-$70,000 a farm-season at $17,600 a robot-season, leaving an estimated $23,000-$40,000 unrecovered per pilot and $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five conversions from 14 pilot farms [S1].

### The contract is an annual option, and one grower has already left

Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. The eight other pilot farms remain pilots and produced the two letters. What the non-renewing accounts chose instead is not disclosed — the deck shows non-conversion, not substitution — and no public evidence shows a lapsed account bought a competing robot, so the hand crew remains the substitute. The contract behind the $9,500 and $12,700 prices is a single season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS agreements run one to five years with pilot success criteria, uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract against a four-season asset gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the 110-robot book is 110 options to renew, not a backlog [S1, S140].

### One robot-season loses $8,100 before any overhead

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company, unaudited) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1, calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1, calc |
| Interest-only debt service ($1.6M x 11.5% / 75 seasons) | (2,453) | 25.8 | S1, calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1, calc |
| Cash contribution after interest-only debt service | 1,447 | 15.2 | S1, calc |
| Cash contribution after amortising debt service | (3,051) | (32.1) | S1, calc |

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation on the $48,000 v3 sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so gross profit of $3,900 becomes a contribution of -$8,100 once the robot is charged to the season it is used. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and must not be added; the economic measure is -$8,100, while the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only and -$3,051 if it amortises over four seasons. The benchmark is United Rentals, which earned a 38.0% gross margin on equipment rentals in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at the $16,500 list price with the v3 and +19.1% only with both the list price and a $31,000 v4 [S21].

The claimed 2.1-season payback uses three inputs no grower has signed at once: a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost. It also drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons on the company's own target inputs. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 service, transport and consumables cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet actually ran in 2026, against a four-season asset life. Even at the $31,000 target build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at the 2027 contracted $12,700 it is 4.37 seasons, longer than the asset lasts. All four inputs are company-reported and unaudited; the build cost is unbuilt, the service cost is unreconciled to the technician ratio and transport is omitted from the payback slide.

### Utilisation cannot repair a per-season capital charge

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026 — 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, because the California and Florida seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price the fleet needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69, 85% of the maximum; at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads fixed overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital hurdle. Service cost is no more forgiving: one technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 loaded field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $41,611 per technician-season, or $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 machine-operator rate), against the $3,100 reported. At 360 robots the same ratio needs 45 technicians and $1.12M at the reported rate, so service cost is linear in robots, not diluted by scale; on the $6,305 figure gross profit at the signed price falls to $695, or 7.3%, before depreciation [S1, S10, S141].

| Offer | $ per robot-season | vs signed | $ per acre (3.5 acres/robot) | % of $79,288/acre harvest cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 3.4% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 contracted average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 4.6% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 5.9% | S1, S10 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 6.3% | S1, calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 4.8% | S1, calc |

At one robot per 3.5 acres the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the 2027 list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre — 3.4% to 5.9% of the labour bill the robot targets. That looks cheap enough to sell, but growers in the Western Growers survey report requiring a one-to-two-year payback and half assign staff to integration; at 1.17 seasons a year, Orrin's 2.84-season payback at the list price and current cost is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5 years. The gap is proof, not affordability: at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray each percentage point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21% to 36% of the robot fee, and the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee. That asymmetry explains why no grower has signed at list and why the Florida grower left over bruising: the grower is buying insurance on a harvest, and 94% pick rate with 86% uptime does not yet underwrite it.

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 3.4-5.9% of the harvest cost it addresses, so a working unit could charge several times more; the answer is that two better-capitalised peers with more robots did not get there. Orrin's $320,313 of capital per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000, so it is running the same capital-intensive model that failed twice.

| Owned-fleet peer | Fleet and capital | Outcome | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tortuga AgTech | 150 harvesting robots; about $50M over eight years | IP, assets and team sold to Oishii, 2025-03 | S93 |
| FarmWise | $45M Series B in 2022; $65M equity in total | Titan run as a service, then Vulcan sold through dealer RDO Equipment; wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms, 2025-04 | S100, S116 |

The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. The investment should be conditioned on executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, a verified v4 bill of materials from a manufacturer independent of the largest revenue customer, an audited service-cost build reconciled to the 1:8 technician ratio and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on the company's own figures; the pilot-cost estimate and the service-cost cross-check are medium, and the open questions are the loan amortisation schedule, the Florida price and the share of bruised fruit culled.

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unaudited) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures alone produce the negative contribution, the 12.31-season payback at the signed price and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven [S1].
:::

The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's figure of a quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14 while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost over 40 passes, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre [S80, S1]." (~830)

### The cut is provisional

"On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing adjustment, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and required the Department of Labor to warn employers of possible back-wage adjustments. A higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, restoring most of that saving and lifting the price ceiling." (~440)

### Who is organised, and against what

"The union that won that case is the group most likely to shape the operating rule. AB 187, the employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the human-driver standard therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. If a technician can satisfy the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure: one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season. If the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. A material restriction or enforcement action in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement, and the one pilot lost is the Florida grower [S82, S115, S1]." (~1,060)

USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper at 50% apply even under USMCA. The Section 232 proclamation of 2026-10-28 on robotics found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days, leaving tariffs, quotas and fees open [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed." (~690)

"The university licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. The 2027 plan clears the threshold, so the cliff needs 72% slippage (conversion risk 20%–25%, analyst estimate). If a licensed family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture products embodying the invention substantially in the United States, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers." (~750)

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

"21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the retail clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and fruit packed in the field reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists to obtain and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed." (~610)

### The social case is a product metric

"Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, contract manufacturer and investor in this round; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no federal award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91]." (~710)

The $72M pre-money buys a $69.9M enterprise — $72M of equity plus $1.6M of drawn fleet debt less $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 — with $1.9M of FY2025 revenue at 36.8x EV/sales and $1.4M of contracted 2027-season revenue at 49.9x; the price already capitalizes the 2028 plan and leaves the $12M lead with a 1.0x return at any exit up to $90M. The deck's figures are company-provided and unverified; no audited statements, 409A or third-party valuation were supplied, though the cap-table arithmetic is consistent. [S95]

### The round reconciles on 15.27M shares, not 12M

The $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money and $90M post-money issues 3,818,008 Series A shares at $4.71449, taking the fully diluted count to 19,090,116 (company-provided, unverified). The $72M reconciles to 15,272,108 pre-money shares: 12,000,000 outstanding today, 2,061,303 shares from the 2025 notes and 1,210,805 new option-pool shares. The 12,000,000 shares today are not the pre-money count: 12,000,000 × $4.7145 is $56.6M, because the note conversion and pool top-up sit inside the $72M. The $7.77M of notes convert at 80% of the round price into shares worth $9.72M at $4.71449, a $1.95M uplift; the cash-equivalent pre-money is $70.05M and the cash-equivalent enterprise value is $67.95M. The last priced round was the March 2023 Series Seed at an implied $3.67/share (the $11.0M round divided by 3,000,000 seed shares), a 28.6% step-up; the February 2025 notes were not a priced round. [S95]

| 2025-06-16 | Kestrel fleet facility | $2.5M ($1.6M drawn) | Debt at 11.5%, secured on fleet | Kestrel Equipment Finance | Fleet build | S95 (unverified) |
| 2026-10 | Series A | $18.0M target ($12M minimum) | $72M pre / $90M post at $4.71449 | Granary $3.0M and Tallis $1.0M committed; Meridian proposed $12M | 300 robots (55%), R&D (25%), sales and field operations (20%) | S95 (unverified) |

### The preference stack is $36.77M on one unverified sentence

The deck's entire preference term is one bullet on p.14 — 1x, non-participating, equal in rank across Series A, Series A-1 and Series Seed (company-provided, unverified). No seed charter, note purchase agreement or closing cap table was supplied, so the ranking and the 1x are company statements, not documents. On them, the full $18M close gives $18.0M Series A + $7.77M notes + $11.0M Series Seed = $36.77M, behind $1.6M of secured fleet debt. The seed issue price is not disclosed; I enter the $11.0M at 1x, and if the $2.5M pre-seed SAFEs converted on top, the seed preference is $13.5M and the stack $39.27M. The price and the pass recommendation assume the deck's terms: a senior or 2x note would cut the lead's $25M-exit recovery to 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round to 0.31x, against 0.64x on the deck's pari passu terms. The option pool rises from 9.0% to 12.0% of post-money, 1,210,805 new shares worth $5.71M at the round price; as a pre-money item it falls on existing holders — founders from 35.57% to 33.32%, seed from 16.78% to 15.71%, noteholders from 11.53% to 10.80% — while the new Series A owns 20.0%. The lead's $12M buys 13.33% of the post-money, $0.90M per percentage point, or $1.02M per point of the operating business excluding the 12% reserve. [S95]

### The price is 9-22x the listed peer median

On the $69.9M enterprise value, Orrin is at 36.8x FY2025 revenue of $1.9M, 26.9x FY2026E revenue of $2.6M, 21.8x the company's $3.2M ARR and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue of $1.4M — 110 contracted 2027 robot-seasons at $12,700, excluding $0.6M of letters of intent and the $1.2M Tallis contract ending 2027-06-30. The revenue and ARR figures are company-provided and unverified; the corrected recurring figure is an analyst construct from the deck's components. The listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.3x EV/sales (AGCO 0.9x, Kubota 1.5x, Toro 2.3x, Deere 3.9x, Trimble 4.4x); at 2.3x FY2026E revenue Orrin's enterprise value would be $6.0M, and at Deere's 3.9x it would be $10.1M. Even on the 2028 plan of $13.2M revenue the current price is 5.3x, still above the peer median. [S95, S38, S103]

### The disclosed private marks sit below $72M

Harvest CROO has raised $10M-$28.5M depending on the aggregator, with no disclosed valuation; Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in September 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M over eight years and 150 robots, then sold its IP and team to Oishii in 2024 for undisclosed terms; Tevel raised $20M in 2021 and carries a reported $63M secondary value. Carbon Robotics raised $70M in October 2024 with no disclosed valuation, and Monarch raised $133M at more than $500M in July 2024 before laying off almost all staff. The only disclosed $100M+ ag-robotics exits are Deere's purchases of Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), both autonomy platforms. Orrin's $90M post is above every disclosed harvesting-robot mark and near Blue River's 2015 $87M post-money, eleven years earlier. [S105, S28, S94]

### A $12M close improves the price and weakens the plan, while the preference delays the upside

The $18M target has only $4.0M committed and a $12M minimum (company-provided, unverified). At $12M the post-money is $84M, the lead owns 14.29% and the preference stack falls to $30.77M; the 2027 plan spends $9.9M of the $18M on 300 robots at a $33,000 average, so $12M funds about 200 robots, the 360-robot and $8M ARR milestones slip and a 2028 down round becomes the base case. At $16M — the lead's $12M plus the $4.0M committed — the post-money is $88M and the lead owns 13.64%. The company has $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly burn, nine months of runway to June 2027, so the close must land in Q1 2027 to order robots for the 2027 season. On the full round the 1x preference returns the $12M in full at $40M, $60M and $90M; only above $90M does the lead participate — $20.0M at $150M (1.7x), $33.3M at $250M (2.8x) — while common and options receive $1.6M at $40M, $21.6M at $60M and $47.1M at $90M after the $1.6M debt. To return 3x in five years the company must be worth $270M at exit, which at a 3-5x revenue multiple requires $54-90M of revenue — four to seven times the 2028 plan. The price is defensible only if the 2027 milestones are met and a strategic buyer pays above the listed peer multiples; the diligence questions are the note schedule and seed charter, the 2027 order book and deposits, the option-pool refresh policy, and the source of the $6M of unfilled Series A. [S95]

That looks cheap, but growers in the Western Growers survey require a one-to-two-year payback and half assign staff to integration; at 1.17 seasons a year, Orrin's 2.84-season payback at list and current cost is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. The gap is proof: at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray each point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21-36% of the fee, and the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee. That is why no grower has signed at list and the Florida grower left over bruising: the grower is buying insurance on a harvest.

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 3.4-5.9% of harvest cost, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers with more robots did not get there. Orrin's $320,313 of capital per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000, the same capital-intensive model that failed twice.

| Owned-fleet peer | Fleet and capital | Outcome | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tortuga AgTech | 150 harvesting robots; about $50M over eight years | IP, assets and team sold to Oishii, 2025-03 | S93 |
| FarmWise | $45M Series B in 2022; $65M equity in total | Titan run as a service, then Vulcan sold through dealer RDO Equipment; wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms, 2025-04 | S100, S116 |

The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. The investment should be conditioned on executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, a verified v4 bill of materials from an independent manufacturer, an audited service-cost build reconciled to the 1:8 ratio and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate and service cross-check are medium, and the open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and the share of bruised fruit culled.

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unaudited) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures alone produce the negative contribution, the 12.31-season payback at the signed price and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven [S1].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The $72M pre-money buys a $69.9M enterprise — $72M of equity plus $1.6M of drawn fleet debt less $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 — with $1.9M of FY2025 revenue at 36.8x EV/sales and $1.4M of contracted 2027-season revenue at 49.9x; the price already capitalizes the 2028 plan and leaves the $12M lead with a 1.0x return at any exit up to $90M. The deck's figures are company-provided and unverified; no audited statements, 409A or third-party valuation were supplied, though the cap-table arithmetic is consistent. [S95]

### The round reconciles on 15.27M shares, not 12M

The $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money and $90M post-money issues 3,818,008 Series A shares at $4.71449, taking the fully diluted count to 19,090,116 (company-provided, unverified). The $72M reconciles to 15,272,108 pre-money shares: 12,000,000 outstanding today, 2,061,303 shares from the 2025 notes and 1,210,805 new option-pool shares. The 12,000,000 shares today are not the pre-money count: 12,000,000 × $4.7145 is $56.6M, because the note conversion and pool top-up sit inside the $72M. The $7.77M of notes convert at 80% of the round price into shares worth $9.72M at $4.71449, a $1.95M uplift; the cash-equivalent pre-money is $70.05M and the cash-equivalent enterprise value is $67.95M. The last priced round was the March 2023 Series Seed at an implied $3.67/share (the $11.0M round divided by 3,000,000 seed shares), a 28.6% step-up; the February 2025 notes were not a priced round. [S95]

| 2025-06-16 | Kestrel fleet facility | $2.5M ($1.6M drawn) | Debt at 11.5%, secured on fleet | Kestrel Equipment Finance | Fleet build | S95 (unverified) |
| 2026-10 | Series A | $18.0M target ($12M minimum) | $72M pre / $90M post at $4.71449 | Granary $3.0M and Tallis $1.0M committed; Meridian proposed $12M | 300 robots (55%), R&D (25%), sales and field operations (20%) | S95 (unverified) |

### The preference stack is $36.77M on one unverified sentence

The deck's entire preference term is one sentence on p.14 — 1x, non-participating, equal in rank across Series A, Series A-1 and Series Seed (company-provided, unverified). No seed charter, note agreement or closing cap table was supplied, so the ranking and the 1x are company statements, not documents. On them, the full $18M close gives $18.0M Series A + $7.77M notes + $11.0M Series Seed = $36.77M, behind $1.6M of secured fleet debt. The seed issue price is not disclosed; I enter the $11.0M at 1x, and if the $2.5M pre-seed SAFEs converted on top, the seed preference is $13.5M and the stack $39.27M. Price and the pass recommendation assume the deck's terms: a senior or 2x note would cut the lead's $25M-exit recovery to 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round to 0.31x, against 0.59-0.64x on the deck's pari passu terms. The option pool rises from 9.0% to 12.0% of post-money, 1,210,805 new shares worth $5.71M at the round price; as a pre-money item it falls on existing holders — founders from 35.57% to 33.32%, seed from 16.78% to 15.71%, noteholders from 11.53% to 10.80% — while the new Series A owns 20.0%. The lead's $12M buys 13.33% of the post-money, $0.90M per percentage point, or $1.02M per point of the operating business excluding the 12% reserve. [S95]

### The price is 9-22x the listed peer median

On the $69.9M enterprise value, Orrin is at 36.8x FY2025 revenue of $1.9M, 26.9x FY2026E revenue of $2.6M, 21.8x the company's $3.2M ARR and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue of $1.4M — 110 contracted 2027 robot-seasons at $12,700, excluding $0.6M of letters of intent and the $1.2M Tallis contract ending 2027-06-30. The revenue and ARR figures are company-provided and unverified; the corrected recurring figure is an analyst construct from the deck's components. The listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.3x EV/sales (AGCO 0.9x, Kubota 1.5x, Toro 2.3x, Deere 3.9x, Trimble 4.4x); at 2.3x FY2026E revenue Orrin's enterprise value would be $6.0M, and at Deere's 3.9x it would be $10.1M. Even on the 2028 plan of $13.2M revenue the current price is 5.3x, still above the peer median. [S95, S38, S103]

### The disclosed private marks sit below $72M

Harvest CROO has raised $10M-$28.5M depending on the aggregator, with no disclosed valuation; Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in September 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M over eight years and 150 robots, then sold its IP and team to Oishii in 2024 for undisclosed terms; Tevel raised $20M in 2021 and carries a reported $63M secondary value. Carbon Robotics raised $70M in October 2024 with no disclosed valuation, and Monarch raised $133M at more than $500M in July 2024 before laying off almost all staff. The only disclosed $100M+ ag-robotics exits are Deere's purchases of Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), both autonomy platforms. Orrin's $90M post is above every disclosed harvesting-robot mark and near Blue River's 2015 $87M post-money, eleven years earlier. [S105, S28, S94]

### A $12M close improves the price and weakens the plan, while the preference delays the upside

The $18M target has only $4.0M committed and a $12M minimum (company-provided, unverified). At $12M the post-money is $84M, the lead owns 14.29% and the preference stack falls to $30.77M; the 2027 plan spends $9.9M of the $18M on 300 robots at a $33,000 average, so $12M funds about 200 robots, the 360-robot and $8M ARR milestones slip and a 2028 down round becomes the base case. At $16M — the lead's $12M plus the $4.0M committed — the post-money is $88M and the lead owns 13.64%. The company has $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly burn, nine months of runway to June 2027, so the close must land in Q1 2027 to order robots for the 2027 season. On the full round the 1x preference returns the $12M in full at $40M, $60M and $90M; only above $90M does the lead participate — $20.0M at $150M (1.7x), $33.3M at $250M (2.8x) — while common and options receive $1.6M at $40M, $21.6M at $60M and $47.1M at $90M after the $1.6M debt. To return 3x in five years the company must be worth $270M at exit, which at a 3-5x revenue multiple requires $54-90M of revenue — four to seven times the 2028 plan. The price is defensible only if the 2027 milestones are met and a strategic buyer pays above the listed peer multiples; the diligence questions are the note schedule and seed charter, the 2027 order book and deposits, the option-pool refresh policy, and the source of the $6M of unfilled Series A. [S95]

arguments.markdown:
Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester matched human picking rates in a commercial operation at Duette, Florida — an open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but Driscoll's has invested in Harvest CROO and Agrobot and is talking to six harvesting startups, and Japanese and Chinese university teams are solving the same perception problem. The hand crew, the harvest-aid platform and the 2025 exits discipline Orrin's price more than any single rival [S27, S28, S138].

::: evidence
**The field is thinner than the technology narrative implies, and it is not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii; Waseda and Nanjing Agricultural University have working prototypes; Tallis, Orrin's contract manufacturer, could build the platform. Sources: S27, S28, S34, S139, S135, S1.
:::

The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm, which had reached named commercial growers in California, ceased operations; Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii. No public market shares exist; the best proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S27, S34].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo said it "was unable to develop the market traction necessary to support its business". Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, was sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021; Traptic, a strawberry picker, was acquired in 2022 (reported; not independently sourced here). The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30 [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost — unverified, but it captures part of the saving with none of the autonomy or bruising risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: a picking arm on an existing harvest-aid platform is cheaper for the grower than a new autonomous fleet. Orrin must beat a crew costing $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour and charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field row architecture, same RaaS model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim already in the market. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published performance data and no California service network — where Orrin's 14 pilots and 4 paying growers sit. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct clamshell packing, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows and the COO's California grower relationships: a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly. The international field is earlier but not empty. Waseda University's Sugano Lab, with Maekawa Manufacturing, runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated greenhouse beds — research, no commercial deployment or price. Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked robot at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success, with no price or commercial deployment, and Washington State University researchers have built a robot to pick hidden strawberries. None is an open-field competitor in 2026 and none has a public price, so none sets a ceiling on the $16,500 list — but the perception stack is being solved in public, which erodes the licensed families' value if the university licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31 [S30, S1, S139, S135, S137, S134].

| Open-field strawberry harvest | Challenger: 262 acres, 0.5% of US base | Harvest CROO (Florida claim, unverified) | Orrin (75 paid robot-seasons) | Agrobot (harvest-aid platform) | Tallis as contract manufacturer; Japanese and Chinese prototypes | S27, S1, S139, S135 |
| Tabletop / high-tunnel harvest | Not addressed: open-field platform only | Manual tabletop crews | Greenhouse robot vendors, not sized here | Waseda/Maekawa rail harvester (research) | Once-over machine-harvest varieties from berry breeders | S136, S138, S139 |

### The price is the tell
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025-26 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase, with renewals averaging $12,700. The company's own disclosure contains the counter-evidence: Grower E in Plant City ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers; four growers nevertheless contracted 110 robots for 2027. If Harvest CROO's parity claim holds, Orrin's price converges on displaced labour and the $16,500 list is at risk; if the 3.8% bruising holds across retail specifications, it can keep pricing up. Two substitutes shrink the acres rather than bid for them: tabletop and high-tunnel production, where Cal Poly calls Santa Maria hoop-house acreage "limited" and Driscoll's is breeding for mechanisation traits, and a once-over variety of the kind that took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% in five years. Tallis is the other exposure: contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, board observer and $1M investor, it has the bill of materials and the unit-cost quote and could build the competing platform. Diligence: is bruising measured against a retailer specification or only Orrin's test rows; what prevents Tallis from competing; and what share of California acreage is tabletop [S1, S28, S136, S138, S33].

arguments.markdown:
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 0.94x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security and grower data; no public robotics M&A record | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 (unverified) |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga in 2024; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | What the target had | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River | 2017 | $305M | 3.5x the $87M post-money; revenue n/a | See & Spray, $30M+ raised | S98 |
| Deere / Bear Flag | 2021 | $250M | 31.6x the $7.9M seed; revenue n/a | Autonomous tractor retrofit, 2017 | S96, S118 |
| CNH / Raven | 2021 | $2.1B EV | n/a; 33.6% premium | Public precision-ag company | S99 |
| AGCO / Trimble Ag (85%) | 2023-24 | $2.35B EV | 13.8x 2023E EBITDA | Precision-ag portfolio, $170M EBITDA | S101 |
| Kubota / AgJunction | 2021 | $73M | n/a | Guidance and auto-steer | S104 |
| CNH / Advanced Farm assets | 2025 | Undisclosed | n/a | Strawberry and apple picking IP and team | S97, S28 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2024 | Undisclosed | n/a | $50M deployed, 150 robots | S93 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | n/a | Tomato harvesting robot | S32 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. 2025 recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money the lead owns 13.33%: a $100M exit returns 1.1x before the Series B and 1.0x after 20% dilution, when the $12M preference binds; $250M returns 2.8x and 2.2x. The report uses one distribution — 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35 = 0.94x, the same 0.94x carried in sections 10 and 11. The bear's 0.35x is the central recovery across the $12-40M asset-sale range; the deck's pari passu terms give 0.64x at a $25M exit, senior or 2x note terms 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round 0.31x. Below $90M the preference, not the operating plan, sets the return: the first $36.77M of equity goes to the stack, which means a technically good 2027 season still returns only capital. The counter-case is a $250-305M Deere or CNH bid for the team and perception model, as for Blue River and Bear Flag; at 95% pick rates and 360 robots a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

| Case | Probability | Exit value | Lead proceeds | MOIC | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | $250M | $26.7M | 2.2x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Base | 40% | $100M | $12.0M | 1.0x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Bear | 42% | $25M (central of $12-40M) | $4.2M | 0.35x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Weighted | 100% | — | — | 0.94x (0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35) | S95 (unverified), calc |

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Metric | 2027 plan | 2028 plan | Test for a Series B above $72M pre | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $5.6M | $13.2M | $13.2M at 7x forward, or $18M at 5x | S95 (unverified) |
| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |
| Renewal | 110 contracted 2027 seasons | n/a | 80% or more of 2026 paying growers renew | S95 (unverified) |
| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to Deere, AGCO, CNH and Kubota, all of which have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, license and grower data; Mexico assembly adds tariff diligence. An IPO is not realistic before 2030 at $1.9M of revenue and a $5.2M FY2025 net loss. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes exit to 2030-2032. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.0x at $90M, 1.1x at $100M (1.0x after dilution), 1.7x at $150M (1.4x) and 2.8x at $250M (2.2x); over five years that is 0% IRR at $100M, 17.1% at $250M and -18.9% at the $25M bear. A 20-30% lower entry price, or a 1.5x preference, would make the same exits work; at $72M the lead is buying an option that needs a $250M+ bid. The 0.94x expected return and the pass recommendation assume the deck's 1x, non-participating, equal-rank preference — one sentence on deck p.14, with no seed charter or note agreement supplied; the seed issue price is not disclosed and the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs may convert on top, making the stack $39.27M rather than $36.77M. If the notes are senior or 2x the $25M recovery is 0.21x rather than 0.59-0.64x, and a $10M senior 2028 round cuts it to 0.31x; the note purchase agreement and seed charter are the open data request that would settle the downside. The implication is to pass at $72M, or invest at a 20-30% lower price with a 1.5x preference and a milestone tranche. Diligence should confirm the Advanced Farm and Tortuga prices, grower-contract ownership, the Calder license's change-of-control terms and the 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons in two growers. [S95, S97, S93]

arguments.markdown:
At the signed $9,500 the rental business loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a build cost not yet built.

### Rental is a minority of revenue, and the signed growth is same-store

The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season at a time and no multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. The 2027 book is 110 robot-seasons at a $12,700 average, all from the four growers that paid in 2026; no new grower has signed, and the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from the eight remaining pilot farms. Same-store robots rise from 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher — real demand evidence from four accounts, none that the model acquires customers [S1].

### The sales cycle is one season, and the pilot is mostly Orrin's cost

First paid deployment follows first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 paid seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 paid seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season. That is a 4-12 month cycle; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. Who signs is not disclosed — the executed contracts would show whether it is the owner, a VP of growing or procurement, which decides whether the 110-robot book is a strategic pilot or a procurement commitment. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost: it owns, maintains and insures the robots, and grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine farms with 2025 test rows that is about $30,000 a pilot farm, versus a direct cost of $53,000-$70,000 for a three-to-four-robot pilot at $17,600 a robot-season; an estimated $23,000-$40,000 is unrecovered per pilot, or $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14 [S1].

### The contract is an annual option, and one grower has already left

Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. What the non-renewing accounts chose instead is not disclosed; no public evidence shows a lapsed account bought a competing robot, so the hand crew remains the substitute. The contract behind the $9,500 and $12,700 prices is a single season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract against a four-season asset gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the 110-robot book is 110 options, not a backlog [S1, S140].

### One robot-season loses $8,100 before any overhead

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company, unaudited) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1, calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1, calc |
| Interest-only debt service ($1.6M x 11.5% / 75 seasons) | (2,453) | 25.8 | S1, calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1, calc |

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation on the $48,000 v3 sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes -$8,100 once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and must not be added; the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only and -$3,051 if it amortises over four seasons. United Rentals earned a 38.0% gross margin on rentals in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at the list price with the v3 and +19.1% only with both the list and a $31,000 v4 [S21].

The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons on the company's own inputs. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026, against a four-season asset life. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts.

### Utilisation cannot repair a per-season capital charge

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against the $3,100 reported; at 360 robots that is 45 technicians and $1.12M, so service cost is linear, not diluted. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation [S1, S10, S141].

| Offer | $ per robot-season | vs signed | $ per acre (3.5 acres/robot) | % of $79,288/acre harvest cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 3.4% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 contracted average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 4.6% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 5.9% | S1, S10 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 6.3% | S1, calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 4.8% | S1, calc |

At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre, 3.4-5.9% of the labour bill. Growers in the Western Growers survey require a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year, Orrin's 2.84-season payback at list and current cost is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. The gap is proof: at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray each point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21-36% of the fee, and the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee. That is why no grower has signed at list and the Florida grower left over bruising.

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 3.4-5.9% of harvest cost, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there, and Orrin's $320,313 of capital per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000.

| Owned-fleet peer | Fleet and capital | Outcome | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tortuga AgTech | 150 harvesting robots; about $50M over eight years | IP, assets and team sold to Oishii, 2025-03 | S93 |
| FarmWise | $45M Series B in 2022; $65M equity in total | Titan run as a service, then Vulcan sold through dealer RDO Equipment; wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms, 2025-04 | S100, S116 |

The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. The investment should be conditioned on executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, a verified v4 bill of materials from an independent manufacturer, an audited service-cost build reconciled to the 1:8 ratio and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate and service cross-check are medium, and the open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and the share of bruised fruit culled.

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unaudited) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures produce the -$8,100 contribution, the 12.31-season payback and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven [S1].

arguments.markdown:
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 0.94x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. 2025 recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money the lead owns 13.33%: a $100M exit returns 1.1x before the Series B and 1.0x after 20% dilution, when the $12M preference binds; $250M returns 2.8x and 2.2x. The report uses one distribution — 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35 = 0.94x, the same 0.94x carried in sections 10 and 11. The bear's 0.35x is the central recovery across the $12-40M asset-sale range; the deck's pari passu terms give 0.59-0.64x at a $25M exit, senior or 2x note terms 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round 0.31x. Below $90M the preference, not the operating plan, sets the return: the first $36.77M of equity goes to the stack, which means a technically good 2027 season still returns only capital. The counter-case is a $250-305M Deere or CNH bid for the team and perception model, as for Blue River and Bear Flag; at 95% pick rates and 360 robots a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. ### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to Deere, AGCO, CNH and Kubota, all of which have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, license and grower data; Mexico assembly adds tariff diligence. An IPO is not realistic before 2030 at $1.9M of revenue and a $5.2M FY2025 net loss. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes exit to 2030-2032. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.0x at $90M, 1.1x at $100M (1.0x after dilution), 1.7x at $150M (1.4x) and 2.8x at $250M (2.2x); over five years that is 0% IRR at $100M, 17.1% at $250M and -18.9% at the $25M bear. A 20-30% lower entry price, or a 1.5x preference, would make the same exits work; at $72M the lead is buying an option that needs a $250M+ bid. The 0.94x expected return and the pass recommendation assume the deck's 1x, non-participating, equal-rank preference — one sentence on deck p.14, with no seed charter or note agreement supplied; the seed issue price is not disclosed and the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs may convert on top, making the stack $39.27M rather than $36.77M. If the notes are senior or 2x the $25M recovery is 0.21x rather than 0.59-0.64x, and a $10M senior 2028 round cuts it to 0.31x; the note purchase agreement and seed charter are the open data request that would settle the downside. The implication is to pass at $72M, or invest at a 20-30% lower price with a 1.5x preference and a milestone tranche. Diligence should confirm the Advanced Farm and Tortuga prices, grower-contract ownership, the Calder license's change-of-control terms and the 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons in two growers. [S95, S97, S93]

arguments.markdown:
Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester matched human picking rates in a commercial operation at Duette, Florida — an open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but Driscoll's has invested in Harvest CROO and Agrobot and is talking to six harvesting startups, and Japanese and Chinese university teams are solving the same perception problem. The hand crew, harvest-aid platform and 2025 exits discipline Orrin's price more than any rival [S27, S28, S138].

::: evidence
**The field is thinner than the narrative implies, and not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii; Waseda and Nanjing Agricultural University have working prototypes; Tallis, Orrin's contract manufacturer, could build the platform. Sources: S27, S28, S34, S139, S135, S1.
:::

| Waseda University / Maekawa (Japan) | Rail-mounted greenhouse harvester | Stereo cameras; stem clipper | Research | Night operation; no published rate | Not disclosed | 0% | Same night-time perception | Elevated beds only; no open field; no price | S139, S134 |
| Nanjing Agricultural University (China) | Tracked strawberry picker | Soft gripper; deep learning | Farm trial, Nanjing | 20 s/berry; 84% grasp success | Not disclosed | 0% | Low-cost hardware | Too slow for commercial crews | S135 |
| Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer / potential platform | Same BOM as Orrin v4 | Quoted v4 manufacturer; noteholder; board observer; $1M investor | Not applicable | Source of unit-cost quote | 0% today | Manufacturing cost; board visibility | Could build the platform; conflict | S1 |

The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm, which had reached named commercial growers in California, ceased operations; Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii. No public shares exist; the best proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S27, S34].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo cited a failure to develop market traction. Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021; Traptic, a strawberry picker, was acquired in 2022 (reported; not independently sourced). The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30 [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost — unverified, but it captures part of the saving with no autonomy or bruising risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: a picking arm on an existing platform is cheaper than a new autonomous fleet. Orrin must beat a crew costing $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour and charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field architecture and RaaS model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published performance data and no California service network — where Orrin has 14 pilots and 4 paying growers. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct clamshell packing, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows and the COO's California grower relationships: a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly. Waseda University's Sugano Lab, with Maekawa Manufacturing, runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated greenhouse beds — research, no commercial deployment or price. Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked robot at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success, with no price or deployment, and Washington State University researchers have built a robot to pick hidden strawberries. None is an open-field competitor in 2026 and none has a public price, so none sets a ceiling on the $16,500 list — but the perception stack is being solved in public, which erodes the licensed families' value if the licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31 [S30, S1, S139, S135, S137, S134].

| Product | Orrin's position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest | Challenger: 262 acres, 0.5% of US base | Harvest CROO (Florida claim, unverified) | Orrin (75 paid robot-seasons) | Agrobot (harvest-aid platform) | Tallis as contract manufacturer; Japanese and Chinese prototypes | S27, S1, S139, S135 |
| Tabletop / high-tunnel harvest | Not addressed: open-field platform only | Manual tabletop crews | Greenhouse robot vendors, not sized here | Waseda/Maekawa rail harvester (research) | Once-over machine-harvest varieties from berry breeders | S136, S138, S139 |

### The price is the tell
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025-26 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase. The deck's own disclosure contains the counter-evidence: Grower E in Plant City ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers; four growers nevertheless contracted 110 robots for 2027. If Harvest CROO's parity claim holds, Orrin's price converges on displaced labour and the $16,500 list is at risk; if the 3.8% bruising holds across retail specifications, it can keep pricing up. arguments.markdown:
At the signed $9,500 the rental business loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a build cost not yet built.

### Rental is a minority of revenue, and the signed growth is same-store

The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. The 2027 book is 110 robot-seasons at a $12,700 average, all from the four growers that paid in 2026; no new grower has signed, and the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from the eight remaining pilot farms. Same-store robots rise from 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher — real demand evidence from four accounts, none that the model acquires customers [S1].

### The sales cycle is one season, and the pilot is mostly Orrin's cost

First paid deployment follows first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 paid seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 paid seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season. The cycle is 4-12 months; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. Who signs is not disclosed — the executed contracts would show whether it is the owner, a VP of growing or procurement, which decides how firm the book is. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost: it owns, maintains and insures the robots, and grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine farms with 2025 test rows that is about $30,000 a pilot farm, versus a direct cost of $53,000-$70,000 for a three-to-four-robot pilot at $17,600 a robot-season; an estimated $23,000-$40,000 is unrecovered per pilot, $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14 [S1].

### The contract is an annual option, and one grower has already left

Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. What the non-renewing accounts chose instead is not disclosed; no public evidence shows a lapsed account bought a competing robot, so the hand crew remains the substitute. The contract behind the $9,500 and $12,700 prices is a single season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract against a four-season asset gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog [S1, S140].

### One robot-season loses $8,100 before any overhead

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company, unaudited) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1, calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1, calc |
| Interest-only debt service ($1.6M x 11.5% / 75 seasons) | (2,453) | 25.8 | S1, calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1, calc |

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation on the $48,000 v3 sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes -$8,100 once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and must not be added; the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only and -$3,051 if it amortises over four seasons. United Rentals earned a 38.0% gross margin on rentals in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at the list price with the v3 and +19.1% only with both the list and a $31,000 v4 [S21].

The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons on the company's own inputs. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026, against a four-season asset life. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts.

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against the $3,100 reported; at 360 robots that is 45 technicians and $1.12M, so service cost is linear, not diluted. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation [S1, S10, S141].

| Offer | $ per robot-season | vs signed | $ per acre (3.5 acres/robot) | % of $79,288/acre harvest cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 3.4% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 contracted average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 4.6% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 5.9% | S1, S10 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 6.3% | S1, calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 4.8% | S1, calc |

At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre, 3.4-5.9% of the labour bill. Growers in the Western Growers survey require a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year, Orrin's 2.84-season payback at list and current cost is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. At 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray each point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21-36% of the fee, and the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee. That is why no grower has signed at list and the Florida grower left over bruising.

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 3.4-5.9% of harvest cost, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there, and Orrin's $320,313 of capital per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000.

| Owned-fleet peer | Fleet and capital | Outcome | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tortuga AgTech | 150 harvesting robots; about $50M over eight years | IP, assets and team sold to Oishii, 2025-03 | S93 |
| FarmWise | $45M Series B in 2022; $65M equity in total | Titan run as a service, then Vulcan sold through dealer RDO Equipment; wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms, 2025-04 | S100, S116 |

The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. The investment should be conditioned on executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, a verified v4 bill of materials from an independent manufacturer, an audited service-cost build at the 1:8 ratio and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate is medium, and the open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and the bruised-fruit share.

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unaudited) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures produce the -$8,100 contribution, the 12.31-season payback and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven [S1].
:::

### The 1.0x floor sits at $40M, not $25M

The v4 misses $36,000 with a 55% probability, and FY2027 revenue of $4.6M is 360 robots at $12,778, but 110 are contracted ($1.4M, company-reported) and 250 must be signed in four months by two founders and one vice president hired in June 2025. The chief operating officer's own services company took $310,000 in 2025-2026, about two-thirds of the season's field-service line, on a contract approved by a board he sits on; at a 25% premium the leakage is $62,000. With the independent seat vacant, Meridian cannot carry a related-party resolution alone. The quote is an offer, not evidence: $50-58M with two independent quotes, not $72M. [S1, S95]

California alone prohibits autonomous agricultural equipment, through Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces; the fix died when AB 187 passed on 2026-08-31, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01, so no rule can change before the 2027 season. ### Absence is a finding, not proof

No registry entry, no federal award against the grant the deck describes, no granted patent and no auditor's opinion: the inference is not misrepresentation but that every fact the decision turns on is management representation. Absence proves less than it seems: registries sit behind paywalls, applications stay unpublished for eighteen months, subawards appear on no federal site. It proves enough — the money would be wired on unverified facts, a condition-precedent problem before a price problem.
