arguments.markdown:
Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester matched human picking rates in a commercial operation at Duette, Florida — an open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but Driscoll's has invested in Harvest CROO and Agrobot and is talking to six harvesting startups, and Japanese and Chinese university teams are solving the same perception problem. The hand crew, harvest-aid platform and 2025 exits discipline Orrin's price more than any rival [S27, S28, S138].

::: evidence
**The field is thinner than the narrative implies, and not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii; Waseda and Nanjing Agricultural University have working prototypes; Tallis, Orrin's contract manufacturer, could build the platform. Sources: S27, S28, S34, S139, S135, S1.
:::

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Status (2026) | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest CROO (FL) | B8 harvester | Row-following, AI vision, LIDAR, RaaS | Trials, Duette FL, 2025-04 | "Human parity" (company, unverified); no data | Not disclosed | Florida only | 13 patents; Wish Farms backing | Florida season only; no California service | S27, S78 |
| Tortuga AgTech (US) | Model F/G | Dual-arm picking, packing | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025 | Commercial fleet before sale | Not disclosed | 0% open-field | Commercial deployment and packing | Buyer indoor-focused | S34 |
| Agrobot (Spain) | E-Series | Self-steering picker platform | Commercial | 30-40% labour saving (company, unverified) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Low capital cost; no fruit-quality risk | Still needs a full crew | S77 |
| Waseda University / Maekawa (Japan) | Rail-mounted greenhouse harvester | Stereo cameras; stem clipper | Research | Night operation; no published rate | Not disclosed | 0% | Same night-time perception | Elevated beds only; no open field; no price | S139, S134 |
| Nanjing Agricultural University (China) | Tracked strawberry picker | Soft gripper; deep learning | Farm trial, Nanjing | 20 s/berry; 84% grasp success | Not disclosed | 0% | Low-cost hardware | Too slow for commercial crews | S135 |
| Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer / potential platform | Same BOM as Orrin v4 | Quoted v4 manufacturer; noteholder; board observer; $1M investor (unverified) | Not applicable | Source of unit-cost quote | 0% today | Manufacturing cost; board visibility | Could build the platform; conflict | S1 |
| Hand crews | Piece-rate crew | Pickers, carts, conveyors | Universal | 8-12 flats/hour at $1.75-2.25/flat | $1.75-2.25 a flat | 99.5% of US acres (author calculation) | Proven quality; no capex | 2025 availability shock; rising wage floor | S12 |

The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm, which had reached named commercial growers in California, ceased operations; Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii. No public shares exist; the proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S27, S34].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo cited a failure to develop market traction. Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021; Traptic, a strawberry picker, was acquired in 2022 (reported; not independently sourced). The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30 [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost — unverified, but it captures part of the saving with no autonomy or bruising risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: a picking arm on an existing platform is cheaper than a new fleet. Orrin must beat a crew costing $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour and charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field architecture and RaaS model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published performance data and no California service network — where Orrin has 14 pilots and 4 paying growers. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct clamshell packing, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows and the COO's California grower relationships: a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly. Waseda University's Sugano Lab, with Maekawa Manufacturing, runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated greenhouse beds — research, no commercial deployment or price. Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked robot at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success, with no price or deployment, and Washington State University researchers have built a robot to pick hidden strawberries. None is an open-field competitor in 2026 and none has a public price, so none sets a ceiling on the $16,500 list — but the perception stack is being solved in public, which erodes the licensed families' value if the licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31 [S30, S1, S139, S135, S137, S134].

| Product | Orrin's position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest | Challenger: 262 acres, 0.5% share of US base | Harvest CROO (Florida claim, unverified) | Orrin (75 paid robot-seasons) | Agrobot (harvest-aid platform) | Tallis as contract manufacturer; Japanese and Chinese prototypes | S27, S1, S139, S135 |
| Tabletop / high-tunnel harvest | Not addressed: open-field platform only | Manual tabletop crews | Greenhouse robot vendors, not sized here | Waseda/Maekawa rail harvester (research) | Once-over machine-harvest varieties from berry breeders | S136, S138, S139 |

### The price is the tell
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025-26 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase. The deck's own disclosure contains the counter-evidence: Grower E in Plant City ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers; four growers nevertheless contracted 110 robots for 2027. If Harvest CROO's parity claim holds, Orrin's price converges on displaced labour and the $16,500 list is at risk; if the 3.8% bruising holds across retail specifications, it can keep pricing up. Two substitutes shrink the acres rather than bid for them: tabletop and high-tunnel production, where Cal Poly calls Santa Maria hoop-house acreage "limited" and Driscoll's is breeding for mechanisation traits, and a once-over variety of the kind that took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% in five years. Tallis is the other exposure: contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, board observer and $1M investor, it has the BOM and cost quote and could build the platform. Diligence: is bruising measured against a retailer spec or only Orrin's test rows; what prevents Tallis competing; and what share of California acreage is tabletop [S1, S28, S136, S138, S33].

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Night operation doubles usable hours; direct clamshell handling; 94% pick rate and 3.8% bruising on 212 rows, company-reported; 75 paid robot-seasons; California relationships | S1 |
| Weaknesses | Florida pilot lost to bruising; 53% of 2026 robot-seasons with two growers; no independent data; $48,000 unit cost and 41% margin, company-reported; open-field only | S1 |
| Opportunities | Advanced Farm closed and Tortuga was absorbed; 398,258 H-2A certifications keep labour on the agenda; 110 robots contracted for 2027 | S28, S34, S15, S1 |
| Threats | Harvest CROO claims human parity; Agrobot's 30-40% labour saving at low capital cost; Tallis could forward-integrate; Japanese and Chinese prototypes; lower OEWS wage floor; tabletop and once-over breeding | S27, S77, S1, S139, S135, S18, S136, S138 |
:::

arguments.markdown:
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 0.94x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security and grower data; no public robotics M&A record | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 (unverified) |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga in 2024; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | n/a | Tomato harvesting robot | S32 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. 2025 recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money the lead owns 13.33%: a $100M exit returns 1.1x before the Series B and 1.0x after 20% dilution, when the $12M preference binds; $250M returns 2.8x and 2.2x. The report uses one distribution — 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35 = 0.94x, matching the 0.94x used across the report. The bear's 0.35x is the central recovery across the $12-40M asset-sale range; the deck's pari passu terms give 0.59-0.64x at a $25M exit, senior or 2x note terms 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round 0.31x. Below $90M the preference, not the operating plan, sets the return: the first $36.77M of equity goes to the stack, which means a technically good 2027 season still returns only capital. The counter-case is a $250-305M Deere or CNH bid for the team and perception model, as for Blue River and Bear Flag; at 95% pick rates and 360 robots a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. ### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

The trade-sale route is open to Deere, AGCO, CNH and Kubota, all of which have completed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection. A Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, license and grower data; Mexico assembly adds tariff diligence. An IPO is not realistic before 2030 at $1.9M of revenue and a $5.2M FY2025 net loss. The holding period is three to five years; a 2028 Series B pushes exit to 2030-2032. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.0x at $90M, 1.1x at $100M (1.0x after dilution), 1.7x at $150M (1.4x) and 2.8x at $250M (2.2x); over five years that is 0% IRR at $100M, 17.1% at $250M and -18.9% at the $25M bear. arguments.markdown:
Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester matched human picking rates in a commercial operation at Duette, Florida — an open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but Driscoll's has invested in Harvest CROO and Agrobot and is talking to six harvesting startups, and Japanese and Chinese university teams are solving the same perception problem. The hand crew, harvest-aid platform and 2025 exits discipline Orrin's price more than any rival [S27, S28, S138].

::: evidence
**The field is thinner than the narrative implies, and not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii; Waseda and Nanjing Agricultural University have working prototypes; Tallis, Orrin's contract manufacturer, could build the platform. Sources: S27, S28, S34, S139, S135, S1.
:::

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Status (2026) | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest CROO (FL) | B8 harvester | Row-following, AI vision, LIDAR, RaaS | Trials, Duette FL, 2025-04 | "Human parity" (company, unverified); no data | Not disclosed | Florida only | 13 patents; Wish Farms backing | Florida season only; no California service | S27, S78 |
| Tortuga AgTech (US) | Model F/G | Dual-arm picking, packing | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025 | Commercial fleet before sale | Not disclosed | 0% open-field | Commercial deployment and packing | Buyer indoor-focused | S34 |
| Agrobot (Spain) | E-Series | Self-steering picker platform | Commercial | 30-40% labour saving (company, unverified) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Low capital cost; no fruit-quality risk | Still needs a full crew | S77 |
| Waseda University / Maekawa (Japan) | Rail-mounted greenhouse harvester | Stereo cameras; stem clipper | Research | Night operation; no published rate | Not disclosed | 0% | Same night-time perception | Elevated beds only; no open field; no price | S139, S134 |
| Nanjing Agricultural University (China) | Tracked strawberry picker | Soft gripper; deep learning | Farm trial, Nanjing | 20 s/berry; 84% grasp success | Not disclosed | 0% | Low-cost hardware | Too slow for commercial crews | S135 |
| Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer / potential platform | Same BOM as Orrin v4 | Quoted v4 manufacturer; noteholder; board observer; $1M investor (unverified) | Not applicable | Source of unit-cost quote | 0% today | Manufacturing cost; board visibility | Could build the platform; conflict | S1 |
| Hand crews | Piece-rate crew | Pickers, carts, conveyors | Universal | 8-12 flats/hour at $1.75-2.25/flat | $1.75-2.25 a flat | 99.5% of US acres (author calculation) | Proven quality; no capex | 2025 availability shock; rising wage floor | S12 |

The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm, which had reached named commercial growers in California, ceased operations; Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii. No public shares exist; the proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S28, S34, S1].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo cited a failure to develop market traction. Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021; Traptic, a strawberry picker, was acquired in 2022 (reported; not independently sourced). The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30 [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost — unverified, but it captures part of the saving with no autonomy or bruising risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: a picking arm on an existing platform is cheaper than a new fleet. Orrin must beat a crew costing $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour and charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field architecture and RaaS model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published performance data and no California service network — where Orrin has 14 pilots and 4 paying growers. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct clamshell packing, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows and the COO's California grower relationships: a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly. Waseda University's Sugano Lab, with Maekawa Manufacturing, runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated greenhouse beds — research, no commercial deployment or price. Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked robot at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success, with no price or deployment, and Washington State University researchers have built a robot to pick hidden strawberries. None is a commercial open-field competitor in 2026 and none has a public price, so none sets a ceiling on the $16,500 list — but the perception stack is being solved in public, which erodes the licensed families' value if the licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31 [S30, S1, S139, S135, S137, S134].

| Product | Orrin's position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest | Challenger: 262 acres, 0.5% share of US base | Harvest CROO (Florida claim, unverified) | Orrin (75 paid robot-seasons) | Agrobot (harvest-aid platform) | Tallis as contract manufacturer; Japanese and Chinese prototypes | S27, S1, S139, S135 |
| Tabletop / high-tunnel harvest | Not addressed: open-field platform only | Manual tabletop crews | Greenhouse robot vendors, not sized here | Waseda/Maekawa rail harvester (research) | Once-over machine-harvest varieties from berry breeders | S136, S138, S139 |

### The price is the tell
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025-26 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase. The deck's own disclosure contains the counter-evidence: Grower E in Plant City ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers; four growers nevertheless contracted 110 robots for 2027. If Harvest CROO's parity claim holds, Orrin's price converges on displaced labour and the $16,500 list is at risk; if the 3.8% bruising holds across retail specifications, it can keep pricing up. Two substitutes shrink the acres rather than bid for them: tabletop and high-tunnel production, where Cal Poly calls Santa Maria hoop-house acreage "limited" and Driscoll's is breeding for mechanisation traits, and a once-over variety of the kind that took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% in five years. Tallis is the other exposure: contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, board observer and $1M investor, it has the BOM and cost quote and could build the platform. Diligence: is bruising measured against a retailer spec or only Orrin's test rows; what prevents Tallis competing; and what share of California acreage is tabletop [S1, S28, S136, S138, S33].

| Strengths | Night operation doubles usable hours; direct clamshell handling; 94% pick rate and 3.8% bruising on 212 rows, company-reported; 75 paid robot-seasons; California relationships | S1 |
| Weaknesses | Florida pilot lost to bruising; 53% of 2026 robot-seasons with two growers; no independent data; $48,000 unit cost and 41% margin, company-reported; open-field only | S1 |
| Opportunities | Advanced Farm closed and Tortuga was absorbed; 398,258 H-2A certifications keep labour on the agenda; 110 robots contracted for 2027 | S28, S34, S15, S1 |
| Threats | Harvest CROO claims human parity; Agrobot's 30-40% labour saving at low capital cost; Tallis could forward-integrate; Japanese and Chinese prototypes; lower OEWS wage floor; tabletop and once-over breeding | S27, S77, S1, S139, S135, S18, S136, S138 |

arguments.markdown:
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case sit outside its control before the 2027 season: a wage floor a California court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff due by 2027-04-26, a licence test on 2027-12-31 and a California driver requirement AB 187 leaves in force. The balance is negative for 2027 and positive after: tranche the round rather than decline it.

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14 while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre. On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and warned of possible back wages. A higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, restoring most of that saving and lifting the price ceiling [S80, S81, S1].

### The rule that stands, and who is organised

The United Farm Workers, which won that case, will shape the rule. AB 187, the session's employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142, S82, S115, S1]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. If a technician can satisfy the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure: one technician a machine puts field service above the season price. If the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. A material restriction or enforcement action in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement, and the one pilot lost is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its own capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. The Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed, and metals duties of 50% apply even when it does.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The university licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A binary test with no cure is harsher than standard practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones and cure periods. The plan clears the threshold; the cliff needs 72% slippage (conversion risk 20%–25%). If either family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture substantially in the US, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the retail clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and field-packed fruit reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, contract manufacturer and investor; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no federal award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91, S1].

Four records are requested — the H-2A disclosure files and wage table (the department's page returned an error on 2026-10-30), the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the chaptered AB 187 text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. The four factors change what a season is worth, not whether Orrin can sell one: price against the wage-floor outcome and make the USMCA certificate and licence warranty conditions of closing.

arguments.markdown:
On the company's reported, unaudited figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a build cost not yet built [S1].

The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. On company-reported, unaudited figures, FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. The 2027 book is 110 robot-seasons at a $12,700 average, all from the four 2026 payers; no new grower has signed, and the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from the eight remaining pilot farms. Same-store robots rise from 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher — real demand evidence from four accounts, none that the model acquires customers [S1].

### The sales cycle is one season, and the pilot is mostly Orrin's cost

First paid deployment follows first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 paid seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 paid seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season (company-reported, unaudited). The cycle is 4-12 months; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. Who signs is not disclosed — the executed contracts would show whether it is the owner, a VP of growing or procurement, which decides how firm the book is. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost: it owns, maintains and insures the robots, and grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine farms with 2025 test rows that is about $30,000 a pilot farm, versus $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost for a three-to-four-robot pilot at $17,600 a robot-season; an estimated $23,000-$40,000 is unrecovered per pilot, $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14 [S1].

Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. What the non-renewing accounts chose instead is not disclosed; no public evidence shows a lapsed account bought a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is a single season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract against a four-season asset gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog [S1, S140].

### One robot-season loses $8,100 before any overhead

arguments.markdown:
On the company's reported, unaudited figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a build cost not yet built [S1].

The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. On company-reported, unaudited figures, FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. The 2027 book is 110 robot-seasons at a $12,700 average, all from the four 2026 payers; no new grower has signed, and the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise from 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher — real demand evidence from four accounts, none that the model acquires customers [S1].

### The sales cycle is one season, and the pilot is mostly Orrin's cost

First paid deployment follows first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 paid seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 paid seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season (company-reported, unaudited). The cycle is 4-12 months; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. Who signs is not disclosed — the executed contracts would show whether it is the owner, a VP of growing or procurement, which decides how firm the book is. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost: it owns, maintains and insures the robots, and grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine farms with 2025 test rows that is about $30,000 a pilot farm, versus $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost for a three-to-four-robot pilot at $17,600 a robot-season; an estimated $23,000-$40,000 is unrecovered per pilot, $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14 [S1].

Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. What the non-renewing accounts chose instead is not disclosed; no public evidence shows a lapsed account bought a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog [S1, S140].

### One robot-season loses $8,100 before any overhead

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company-reported, unaudited) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation on the $48,000 v3 sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes a contribution margin of -85.3%, or -$8,100, once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and must not be added; the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only (11.5%, $2,453 a season over 75 seasons) and -$3,051 if it amortises over four seasons ($521,246 a year, $6,951 a season). United Rentals earned a 38.0% rental gross margin in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at list with the v3 and +19.1% only with both list and a $31,000 v4 [S21]. The economics are inverted: gross margin rises as capital moves into opex, while the cash to build each robot leaves before the season.

The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons on the company's own inputs. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts (company-reported, unaudited) [S1].

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against $3,100 reported; at 360 robots that is 45 technicians and $1.12M, so service cost is linear. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation (company-reported, unaudited) [S1, S10, S141].

| Offer | $ per robot-season | vs signed | $ per acre (3.5 acres/robot) | % of $79,288/acre harvest cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 3.4% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 contracted average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 4.6% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 5.9% | S1, S10 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 6.3% | S1, calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 4.8% | S1, calc |

At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre, 3.4-5.9% of the labour bill. Growers in the Western Growers survey require a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year, Orrin's 2.84-season payback at list and current cost is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. At 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray each point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21-36% of the fee, and the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee [S1, S10, S141].

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 3.4-5.9% of harvest cost, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there. Tortuga deployed 150 harvesting robots and about $50M over eight years before selling to Oishii in 2025-03; FarmWise raised $65M, ran Titan as a service, moved Vulcan to dealer sales and wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms in 2025-04. Orrin's $320,313 per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000 [S93, S100, S116].

The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. For an investor, the signed book is $1.4M of 2027 rental; the $16,500 list and $31,000 v4 must be proven before paying for fleet capex. Conditions should be executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, a verified v4 bill of materials from an independent manufacturer, an audited service-cost build at the 1:8 ratio and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate is medium, and the open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and the bruised-fruit share [S1].

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unaudited) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures produce the -$8,100 contribution, the 12.31-season payback and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven [S1].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case sit outside its control before the 2027 season: a wage floor a California court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff due by 2027-04-26, a licence test on 2027-12-31 and a California driver requirement AB 187 leaves in force. The balance is negative for 2027 and positive after: tranche, do not decline. (S1, S126)

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14 while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre. On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and warned of possible back wages. A higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, restoring most of that saving and lifting the ceiling [S80, S81, S1].

### The rule that stands, and who is organised

The United Farm Workers, which won that case, will shape the rule. AB 187, the session's employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142, S82, S115, S1]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. The effect is asymmetric: the technical reading costs the service margin, the compliance reading costs the season. If a technician can satisfy the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure: one technician a machine puts field service above the season price. If the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. Material restriction or enforcement in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement, and the one pilot lost is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. The Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed; metals duties of 50% apply even when it does.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A binary test with no cure is harsher than standard practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones and cure periods. The plan clears the threshold; the cliff needs 72% slippage (conversion risk 20%–25%). If either family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture substantially in the US, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and field-packed fruit reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, contract manufacturer and investor; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no federal award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91, S1].

Four records are requested — the H-2A files and wage table (the department's page returned an error on 2026-10-30), the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the chaptered AB 187 text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. The factors change what a season is worth, not whether Orrin can sell one: price against the wage-floor outcome and make the USMCA certificate and licence warranty closing conditions. (S80, S91, S85, S126)

arguments.markdown:
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case sit outside its control before the 2027 season: a wage floor a California court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff due by 2027-04-26, a licence test on 2027-12-31 and a California driver requirement AB 187 leaves in force. My judgement is that the balance is negative for 2027 and positive after: tranche, do not decline. (S1, S126)

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 to 14 robots while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre. On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and warned of possible back wages. A higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, restoring most of that saving and lifting the ceiling [S80, S81, S1].

### The rule that stands, and who is organised

The United Farm Workers, which won that case, will shape the rule. AB 187, the session's employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142, S82, S115, S1]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. The effect is asymmetric: the technical reading costs the service margin, the compliance reading costs the season. If a technician can satisfy the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure: a 1:1 technician puts field service above the season price. If the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. Material restriction or enforcement in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement, and the lost pilot is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. The Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed; metals duties of 50% apply even when it does.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A binary test with no cure is harsher than practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones and cure periods. The plan clears the threshold; the cliff needs 72% slippage (conversion risk 20%–25%). If either family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture substantially in the US, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and field-packed fruit reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. arguments.markdown:
On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a build cost not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. The 2027 book is 110 robot-seasons at a $12,700 average, all from the four 2026 payers; no new grower has signed, and the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise from 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher — real demand evidence from four accounts, none that the model acquires customers [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 paid seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 paid seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. Who signs is not disclosed — the executed contracts would show whether it is the owner, a VP of growing or procurement, which decides how firm the book is. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost: it owns, maintains and insures the robots, and grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine farms with 2025 test rows that is about $30,000 a pilot farm, versus $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost for a three-to-four-robot pilot at $17,600 a robot-season; an estimated $23,000-$40,000 is unrecovered per pilot, $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. What the non-renewing accounts chose instead is not disclosed; no public evidence shows a lapsed account bought a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation on the $48,000 v3 sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes a contribution margin of -85.3%, or -$8,100, once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and must not be added; the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only (11.5%, $2,453 a season over 75 seasons) and -$3,051 if it amortises over four seasons ($521,246 a year, $6,951 a season). United Rentals earned a 38.0% rental gross margin in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at list with the v3 and +19.1% only with both list and a $31,000 v4 [S21]. The economics are inverted: gross margin rises as capital moves into opex, while the cash to build each robot leaves before the season. The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S21].

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against $3,100 reported; at 360 robots that is 45 technicians and $1.12M, so service cost is linear. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation. At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre, 3.4-5.9% of the labour bill. Growers in the Western Growers survey require a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year, Orrin's 2.84-season payback at list and current cost is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. At 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray each point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21-36% of the fee, and the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee (company-reported, unverified deck figures; external benchmarks) [S1, S10, S141].

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 3.4-5.9% of harvest cost, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there. Tortuga deployed 150 harvesting robots and about $50M over eight years before selling to Oishii in 2025-03; FarmWise raised $65M, ran Titan as a service, moved Vulcan to dealer sales and wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms in 2025-04. Orrin's $320,313 per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000. The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. For an investor, the signed book is $1.4M of 2027 rental; the $16,500 list and $31,000 v4 must be proven before paying for fleet capex. Conditions should be executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, a verified v4 bill of materials from an independent manufacturer, an audited service-cost build at the 1:8 ratio and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate is medium, and the open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and the bruised-fruit share (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S93, S100, S116].

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unverified) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures produce the -$8,100 contribution, the 12.31-season payback and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven [S1].
:::

arguments.markdown:
On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a build cost not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. The 2027 book is 110 robot-seasons at a $12,700 average, all from the four 2026 payers; no new grower has signed, and the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise from 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher — real demand evidence from four accounts, none that the model acquires customers [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 paid seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 paid seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. Who signs is not disclosed — the executed contracts would show whether it is the owner, a VP of growing or procurement, which decides how firm the book is. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost: it owns, maintains and insures the robots, and grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine farms with 2025 test rows that is about $30,000 a pilot farm, versus $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost for a three-to-four-robot pilot at $17,600 a robot-season; an estimated $23,000-$40,000 is unrecovered per pilot, $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. What the non-renewing accounts chose instead is not disclosed; no public evidence shows a lapsed account bought a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company-reported, unverified) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation on the $48,000 v3 sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes a contribution margin of -85.3%, or -$8,100, once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and must not be added; the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only (11.5%, $2,453 a season over 75 seasons) and -$3,051 if it amortises over four seasons ($521,246 a year, $6,951 a season). United Rentals earned a 38.0% rental gross margin in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at list with the v3 and +19.1% only with both list and a $31,000 v4 [S21]. The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S21].

The economics are inverted: gross margin rises as capital moves into opex, while the cash to build each robot leaves before the season.

| Offer | $ per robot-season | vs signed | $ per acre (3.5 acres/robot) | % of $79,288/acre harvest cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 3.4% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 contracted average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 4.6% | S1, S10 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 5.9% | S1, S10 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 6.3% | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 4.8% | S1 (unverified), calc |

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against $3,100 reported; at 360 robots that is 45 technicians and $1.12M, so service cost is linear. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation. At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre, 3.4-5.9% of the labour bill. Growers in the Western Growers survey require a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year, Orrin's 2.84-season payback at list and current cost is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. At 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray each point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21-36% of the fee, and the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee (company-reported, unverified deck figures; external benchmarks) [S1, S10, S141].

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 3.4-5.9% of harvest cost, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there. Tortuga deployed 150 harvesting robots and about $50M over eight years before selling to Oishii in 2025-03; FarmWise raised $65M, ran Titan as a service, moved Vulcan to dealer sales and wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms in 2025-04. Orrin's $320,313 per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000. The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. For an investor, the signed book is $1.4M of 2027 rental; the $16,500 list and $31,000 v4 must be proven before paying for fleet capex. Conditions should be executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, a verified v4 bill of materials from an independent manufacturer, an audited service-cost build at the 1:8 ratio and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate is medium, and the open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and the bruised-fruit share (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S93, S100, S116].

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unverified) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures produce the -$8,100 contribution, the 12.31-season payback and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven. Source S1.
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case sit outside its control before 2027: a wage floor a California court reopened, a robotics tariff due by 2027-04-26, a licence test on 2027-12-31 and a California driver requirement AB 187 leaves in force. My judgement: the balance is negative for 2027 and positive after, which argues for tranching the round rather than declining it. (S1, S126)

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 to 14 robots while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre. On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and warned of possible back wages. A higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, restoring most of that saving and lifting the ceiling [S80, S81, S1].

### The rule that stands, and who is organised

The United Farm Workers, which won that case, will shape the rule. AB 187, the session's employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142, S82, S115, S1]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. The effect is asymmetric: the technical reading costs the service margin, the compliance reading costs the season. If a technician can satisfy the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure: a 1:1 technician puts field service above the season price. If the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. Material restriction or enforcement in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement, and the lost pilot is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. The Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed; metals duties of 50% apply even when it does.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A binary test with no cure is harsher than practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones and cure periods. The plan clears the threshold; the cliff needs 72% slippage (20%–25% conversion risk). If either family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture substantially in the US, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and field-packed fruit reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, contract manufacturer and investor; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91, S1].

Four records are requested — the H-2A files and wage table (the department's page failed), the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the chaptered AB 187 text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. The factors change what a season is worth, not whether Orrin can sell one: the cheapest protection is to price against the wage-floor outcome and make the USMCA certificate and licence warranty closing conditions. (S80, S91, S85, S126)
