arguments.markdown:
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case sit outside its control before 2027: a wage floor a California court reopened, a robotics tariff due by 2027-04-26, a licence test on 2027-12-31 and a California driver requirement AB 187 leaves in force. My judgement: the balance is negative for 2027 and positive after, which argues for tranching the round rather than declining it. (S1, S126)

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 to 14 robots while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre. On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and warned of possible back wages. A higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, restoring most of that saving and lifting the ceiling [S80, S81, S1].

### The rule that stands, and who is organised

The United Farm Workers, which won that case, will shape the rule. AB 187, the session's employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142, S82, S115, S1]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. The mechanism is asymmetric: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and a 1:1 technician puts field service above the season price — which means the service margin fails; if the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. Material restriction or enforcement in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement, and the lost pilot is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. The Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed; metals duties of 50% apply even when it does.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A binary test with no cure is harsher than practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones and cure periods. The plan clears the threshold; the cliff needs 72% slippage (20%–25% conversion risk). If either family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture substantially in the US, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and field-packed fruit reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, contract manufacturer and investor; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91, S1].

Four records are requested — the H-2A files and wage table (the department's page failed), the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the chaptered AB 187 text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. For the investor, the factors change what a season is worth, not whether Orrin can sell one: the cheapest protection is to price against the wage-floor outcome and make the USMCA certificate and licence warranty closing conditions. (S80, S91, S85, S126)

arguments.markdown:
On the company's unverified figures, the $18M is sized to the 2027 robot budget but not to 2028, and the minimum $12M funds only about 200 robots; on the plan the $12M case breaches the $1.5M cash covenant in September 2027, and most reported ARR is not recurring rental. The company supplies an income statement for FY2023-FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor, with a part-time finance head. Revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin is 51.8% in FY2027 before 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

| Net loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S1 (unverified) |
| Total gross margin | 0% | 75.0% | 52.6% | 57.7% | 51.8% | 60.6% | S1 (unverified), calc |

The $3.2M ARR is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 at $12,700), $1.2M of related-party engineering services that end on 2027-06-30 and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed rental is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level [S1].

The $0.085M 2027 year-end balance reconciles exactly, but only because $3.21M of 2027 depreciation is added back to the $7.9M net loss. Opening cash of $3.7M less 2.5 months of $410,000 burn to the 2026-12-15 close gives $2.675M; adding $12M, deducting $4.69M of cash operating burn and $9.9M of capex gives $0.085M. The path assumes zero working capital, no principal repayment and interest inside the net loss; it breaches the $1.5M covenant around 2027-09-12, before the season ends, not at year-end, and a $4.6M season-end receivable would pull the breach into the first half. The $18M case follows the same path to $6.085M, before working capital and principal, and leaves 2028's $13.93M fleet capex unfunded. A quarter's slip to 2027-03-15 leaves opening cash of $1.445M, below the floor before the money arrives [S1].

*$12M case below the $1.5M floor from about 2027-09-12. The closing balances use $7.9M net loss less $3.21M depreciation, $9.9M capex in January-June and no working-capital or principal repayment.

Use of funds is 55% robots. At $18M that is $9.9M, 300 new v4 at $33,000 on top of 64 v3, which matches 360 in service. At the $12M minimum the same 55% is $6.6M, 200 robots and a 264-robot fleet, so the $4.6M 2027 rental line — 360 robots at $12,778 — is not funded; at the $12,700 renewal average a 264-robot fleet earns $3.35M, a $1.25M revenue hole. If the company instead spends the full $9.9M on robots from a $12M round, it has $2.1M left against the $8.1M of R&D and sales budget on the same slide. The undrawn $0.9M facility buys 27 robots, not 100 [S1].

| Undrawn facility | $2.5M - $1.6M | $0.9M = 27 robots | S1 (unverified), calc |

The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into -$0.31M, or -5.5%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% reported for 2026 is RaaS-only, while 52% and 61% equal the company-wide margin, so the series changes definition between years. Returns cannot be computed without a balance sheet: ROE, ROIC and working-capital days are not disclosed, interest cover is -29.3x on FY2026E EBIT of -$5.4M, net cash of $2.1M includes $1.5M the company must keep, cumulative losses of $32.0M compare with $20.5M raised, capital per robot in service is $320,313, near Tortuga's $333,000, and revenue per employee is $68,421 against Deere's $625,000 [S1, S21, S37, S93].

None of this is audited: no auditor, no balance sheet, no cash flow, 50% of FY2025 revenue from a related party that is also the largest creditor, board observer, v4 manufacturer and new investor, and $310,000 paid to the COO's wholly owned haulage and night-shift company, 67% of the 2026 field-service line. A search on 2026-10-30 found no SBIR, USAspending or press record. The data room would settle revenue recognition on the engineering contract, whether grower payments are in arrears, the loan's amortisation and covenant test, and whether the v3 fleet is impaired by the v4 launch; until then the figures are company-reported and unverified. The matrix is the decision: only the top-right corner — list price with a build at or below the milestone ceiling — produces positive contribution; price realisation is the bigger swing between $12,700 and $16,500, but build cost is the gate because no price makes the v3 work. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 5分钟速读 Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, 6,561 characters)
Meridian should pass at the $72M pre-money. Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the field and a real harvest cost pool to sell into, but at the $9,500 a robot-season growers signed and the $48,000 build the company can evidence (company-reported, unverified), every unit loses $8,100 before debt service, and the round prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund: the $12M cheque returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities and 2x only at a $180M exit. The rating is Pass rather than Wait for milestone because the binding objection is the price plus evidence that rests on the company alone; the re-entry milestones are the conditions for a lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pass | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; re-engage at $50-58M with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged | 4.5 | Medium | 12-24 months, to the 2027 season and the licence test | S95 (unverified), S1 (unverified) |
:::

### What is good, and what decides it

The pain is real and independently measured: the UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is cheap against that bill. The picker has the only labelled field dataset in the category — 94% pick rate on 212 rows, 75 paid robot-seasons, 110 robots contracted for 2027 at a $12,700 renewal price — and the two things that usually kill hardware start-ups, no customer and no evidence, are not the problem here. Four facts outweigh that. One robot-season loses $8,100 at the signed price, and the $33,000 build that would fix it is a single quote from a counterparty that is also noteholder, customer, board observer and investor. Bruising at 3.8% has already cost one grower and spends most of the USDA allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. [S119, S1, S95, S86]

::: briefing
| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| The terms | $12M lead cheque at a $72M pre-money and $90M post-money on 15,272,108 fully diluted shares; $69.9M enterprise value after $1.6M of fleet debt and $3.7M of cash | S95 (unverified) |
| What is being bought | 64 robots in service, 110 contracted for 2027 of a 360-robot plan, a labelled field dataset and two valleys of grower relationships; no granted patent | S1 (unverified), S86 |
| Unit economics | -$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the signed price and build cost; breakeven at $17,600 a season on the $48,000 build, and at the signed $9,500 price the breakeven build is $15,600 | S1 (unverified) |
| Key risks | Execution: negative contribution at every signed price, a single build quote, 3.8% bruising, a licence cliff at 100 robots on 2027-12-31, a cash floor near 2027-03-10, and a California standard that still requires a human driver | S1 (unverified), S86, S126 |
| The round | $18M target, $4.0M committed, $12M minimum; at $12M the plan funds about 200 robots and a 2028 down round becomes the base case | S95 (unverified) |
| Cash | $3.7M at 2026-09-30, $410,000 monthly net burn, a $1.5M covenant reached near 2027-03-10 | S1 (unverified) |
| The clock | Licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31; a Section 232 robotics decision falls due 2027-04-26 | S86, S88 |
:::

::: efficiency
| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue, FY2025 | $1.9M, of which $1.2M is related-party engineering and part is grant-funded | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue, FY2026E | $2.6M on 38 employees, about $68,000 per employee | S1 (unverified) |
| Recurring revenue | $1.4M contracted 2027 seasons; $0.71M currently signed | S95 (unverified) |
| Burn | $410,000 monthly net; nine months of stated runway, 5.4 months to the covenant | S1 (unverified) |
| Valuation | $72M pre, $90M post, $69.9M enterprise value | S95 (unverified) |
| Multiples | 36.8x FY2025 revenue, 26.9x FY2026E, 49.9x corrected recurring; peer median 2.3x | S95, S38 |
| Margin | 41% reported before fleet depreciation; -5.5% in FY2027 after it | S1 (unverified) |
:::

The evidence confidence is medium. The arithmetic is solid and reproducible from the deck; the inputs — build cost, service cost, contract count, preference terms and every executive credential — are management statements, unverified, with no independent record retrieved. The $36.77M preference stack, at 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, is one sentence in the deck and appears in no document; the 0.94x return and the Pass rating assume it. There is no audit, no registry confirmation of the three entities, no federal award visible against the stated grant, and no patent prosecution record. [S95]

The follow-up diligence is narrow and cheap: two independent manufacturer quotes for the v4, an independent cold-storage bruising trial, the note purchase agreement, the lender's consent, and a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year.

::: one-question
What does a fourth-generation robot cost to build at fleet volumes, quoted by a manufacturer that is not also the largest customer?

At the current build cost no price growers have signed makes a robot-season profitable, so the fleet consumes capital on every unit; at a lower cost the list price turns contribution positive and the business becomes financeable. Two competitive quotes settle it in weeks and decide between a capital-consuming lease book and a business that compounds.
:::

::: takeaways
1. Pass at $72M pre-money: at the signed $9,500 price and the $48,000 build, one robot-season loses $8,100, and the $12M ticket returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities (company-reported). [S1, S95]
2. The company is worth pursuing at a lower price: at a $50-58M pre-money with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged on two independent quotes at or below $33,000 and 200 robots in paid service, the same $100M exit returns about 1.5x on company-reported terms. [S95]
3. The binding constraints are physical and contractual, not commercial: bruising, coverage of 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, a licence cliff at 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and a California standard that still requires a human driver. [S1, S86, S126]
:::"}],"isError":false}

plan.counter_evidence: Three hardware generations and two paid pilot conversions were achieved after the CTO left, which shows the remaining team can ship; the long grower relationships are a genuine commercial moat; and the vacancy may reflect a deliberate cost choice rather than an inability to hire.
plan.decision_question: Does this team have the specific capability to take a hand-built pilot fleet to 360 robots in one season?
plan.mechanism: Scaling from 64 to 360 robots is a manufacturing-engineering and supply-chain problem, while the founders' depth is perception science and grower access; the binding constraint is therefore the missing CTO and manufacturing leader, not the robot's agronomic fit.
plan.prohibited: 'Strong team'; 'experienced team'; unverified credentials presented as fact; 'world-class'; vague counts of patents or years.
plan.thesis_sentence: The founding pair is credible for perception and farm access but unproven at volume manufacturing, and the executive who owned the technical roadmap left 26 months ago, so people risk is critical until a CTO and a manufacturing leader are hired.
plan.visual: Team assessment matrix with the education and career tables labelled by verification status.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that tests the people: the product and technology sections cover what the robot does, while this section covers who can build 360 of them and who can sell them.

queries: Orrin Fieldworks deck pp.1-15 (founders, executives, dates, patents)
"Orrin Fieldworks"
Orrin Fieldworks patent agricultural robot
"Orrin Fieldworks" Salinas California robotics
"Orrin Fieldworks" patents.justia.com OR patent assignee
"Orrin Fieldworks, Inc." Delaware OR California corporation
Shared source register: Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm Technologies, Tortuga AgTech

rows.benchmark: Peer robotics founders typically pair a technical founder with a manufacturing or operations founder; Orrin pairs perception science with harvest operations.
rows.confidence: low — all credentials company-reported, no registrar or employer record retrieved
rows.finding: Dr. Imani Castellano is a perception researcher with a robotics PhD and five years in a university field-robotics lab, credited with eleven patent filings; Teodor Vashti ran harvest operations for two large berry growers over twenty years; neither has founded or sold a company and neither has built hardware at volume.
rows.follow_up: Will the founders authorise degree verification and reference calls at their prior institutions and employers?
rows.implication: The pairing covers seeing ripe fruit and getting onto the farm, not making 360 robots; a CTO and manufacturing leader are conditions, not intentions.
rows.mechanism: The founding pair's comparative advantage is perception science and grower access, which solves technical feasibility and land access but not the manufacturing engineering and supply chain needed for a 5.6x fleet increase.
rows.weakens: The deck's account is the only source; no degree, employer or publication record was retrievable, so the credentials could be overstated or understated.

rows.benchmark: A seed-stage company normally has a CTO or equivalent technical owner; Orrin has had none for 26 months.
rows.confidence: low — company-reported, no public footprint found
rows.finding: Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy left on 2023-08-31 and the role is still open; he keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% pre-round, 3.8% post) and the deck does not state whether he is a named inventor on the two licensed university families or the five company filings.
rows.follow_up: What assignment, non-disparagement and invention-assignment agreements bind the former CTO, and does he retain access to the licensed IP?
rows.implication: A 3.8% holder with unrestricted shares and the core perception work in his head is a hireable asset for a competitor; retention and IP assignment need to be settled before closing.
rows.mechanism: Vested equity without a continuing role creates a shareholder with upside but no retention incentive, while the technical roadmap he owned is now split between a VP Engineering and an unfilled CTO seat.
rows.weakens: He may have left amicably with a clean invention assignment; the deck's silence is not evidence of a dispute.

rows.benchmark: Unpublished US applications are not public for 18 months, so absence from the register is expected for recent filings but not for anything filed before 2025.
rows.confidence: medium — search executed and returned no assignee record; inherent lag caveat
rows.finding: A patent-register and assignee-index search under the company's name returned no record of Orrin Fieldworks as an assignee and no inventor list for the two licensed families or the five company filings; a name search also returned no Delaware or California entity record.
rows.follow_up: Will the company produce the five application numbers, the two licensed patent numbers and the inventors named on each?
rows.implication: The patent estate cannot be moved off company-only support; people risk stays critical until the application numbers and inventor declarations are produced.
rows.mechanism: Without a public assignee or inventor record, the report cannot test whether the founders' and former CTO's claimed inventorship is real, which is the one credential that could be verified at a register.
rows.weakens: Provisional and unpublished applications legitimately do not appear; the licensed patents may be assigned to the university, not to Orrin, so an assignee search under Orrin would miss them.

rows.benchmark: The company's own history: 12 robots in 2024 to 64 in 2026, a 5.3x over two seasons, versus a plan of 5.6x in one season with a one-third unit-cost cut.
rows.confidence: medium — outcome facts sourced, first-three-year team detail not retrieved
rows.finding: The peer set shows how hard the transition is: Harvest CROO Robotics was still demonstrating commercial viability in 2025-04, Advanced Farm Technologies ceased operations in 2025-07, and Tortuga AgTech was acquired by Oishii in 2025.
rows.follow_up: What were the founding teams, headcount and fleet sizes of Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm and Tortuga at the equivalent stage?
rows.implication: The category's base rate is failure or acquisition, not independent scale; the team should be priced for a higher execution discount than the deck assumes.
rows.mechanism: Ag-robotics companies have repeatedly reached demonstration but not volume, so the scarce capability is manufacturing and field service, exactly where Orrin's executive group is thinnest.
rows.weakens: None of the three peer outcomes is a like-for-like comparison on crop, business model or funding; the comparison is directional only.

rows.benchmark: At the same point in 2026 the company had 64 robots in the field and five paying growers; the 2027 plan requires 360.
rows.confidence: low — deck figures only, no pipeline by stage
rows.finding: The 2027 book is 110 contracted robots plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, 31% of the 360-robot plan five months before the season; Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales in 2025-06 after twenty years in crop inputs, sixteen months in robotics.
rows.follow_up: What is the pipeline by stage and deposit status, and who closes the 250-robot gap?
rows.implication: Add a senior manufacturing leader and a second enterprise seller, or reduce the 2027 build to the contracted book.
rows.mechanism: A seasonal rental business must commit the build before orders exist; with one new sales leader and two founder-sellers, the order book is the binding constraint on the 360-robot plan.
rows.weakens: The letters of intent and the 2027 season may convert late, as the industry buys late; the deck may also omit a pipeline that exists.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, 8,973 characters)
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026: the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, making the deck's urgency a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus, visible in insider commitments at the mark, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying perception for its sprayer line, not a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

### The distribution, not the mean, decides it

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | v4 at or below $33,000 on two quotes; renewals $12,700-16,500; bruising under 2.5%; 360 robots by April 2027; licence test met; USMCA origin certified | Trade sale near $250M: $33.3M, 2.8x, 2.2x after dilution | Two quotes below $33,000 and 200+ robots contracted by 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Base | 40% | v4 at $33,000-36,000 but the build slips; 250-300 robots at $12,700-13,500; revenue $4-6M; 2028 round flat and asking for seniority | Exit near $100M: $12.0M, 1.1x, 1.0x after dilution | Fleet below 300 and ARR below $4M in 2027 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Bear | 42% | v4 above $36,000; renewals at $12,700 or $9,500; a second grower leaves over bruising; close slips past the covenant or prices a senior bridge; licence lapses | Wind-down, foreclosure or $12-40M asset sale: 0.05-0.96x by structure, central 0.35x; 0.21x if the notes are senior, 0.31x behind a $10M senior 2028 round | Waiver request, cash under $2.5M, a second grower exit | S1 (unverified), S95, S89 |
:::

The probability-weighted return is 0.94x on company-reported inputs, unverified: 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x and 42% at 0.35x. The bull needs the build, price, damage, licence and calendar to land together; the bear needs one of five failures. The $36.77M stack is one deck sentence and no document: the 0.94x and the Pass rating assume the preference is 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, and a $39.27M stack if the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs convert on top would lower the floor further. [S95]

### The five assumptions that carry the value

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | v4 builds at or below $33,000 at 300 units on an arm's-length quote | Low | A second quote above $36,000, or a first article slipping past 2027-01 | Contribution at $12,700 falls to -$1,900 at $36,000 and -$4,900 at $48,000; above $44,000 no price covers depreciation | The only quote is dated 2026-08 and comes from the noteholder and customer | S1 (unverified) |
| 2 | 2027 realisations average $12,700 or more, some at the $16,500 list | Medium | A renewal at $9,500-10,500, or a grower repudiating the rise | Each $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M of revenue and 3 margin points | The first renewal signature and whether it carries a deposit | S1 (unverified) |
| 3 | 360 robots in service by April 2027 against 110 contracted and 64 today | Low | Fewer than 250 delivered by 2027-03, or no build slot reserved | Each 100 robots is $1.27M; a 250-robot fleet is $3.2M against the $4.6M plan | Contracted count below 200 in 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| 4 | Bruising at or below 2.5% on a seven-day, 1 degree Celsius test against a named retailer spec | Low | A packer rejecting machine-picked lots, or a second grower exit | One point of cull is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee | Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14; one grower left over bruising in 2026-06 | S1 (unverified) |
| 5 | Close by 2026-12-15 at $12M or more, 1x pari passu preference, 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31 | Low | A close slipping into Q1 2027; senior or 2x note terms; fewer than 100 robots at the test date | A slip breaches the $1.5M covenant near 2027-03-10; senior notes cut the $25M recovery from 0.59x to 0.21x | Cash below $2.5M, a waiver request, no equal-rank warranty | S1 (unverified), S95 |

### Where the price turns

| Terms | Base case, $100M exit | Bear case, $25M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $72M pre-money, 1x pari passu (deck terms) | 1.0x | 0.59x | S95 (unverified), calc on a $36.77M stack, net of $1.6M debt and 8% costs |
| $72M pre-money, 1.5x on the lead cheque | 1.5x | 0.75x | S95 (unverified), calc: the cheque holds $18.0M of a $42.77M stack |
| $50-58M pre-money, 1.5x, half staged | 1.5x | 0.88x | S95 (unverified), calc on a $36.77M stack |

Above the stack the preference and the as-converted share converge, so the premium is worth its face value in the base case. The evidence needs to improve less than the price: independent quotes for the v4 and a note agreement warranting equal rank would reprice the same asset.

### The analogs that teach the rule

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue River to Deere, $305M | Best | 2015-2017 | Four times the last private post-money; the buyer wanted perception, not a fleet | S128 |
| Bear Flag to Deere, $250M | Best | 2021 | A strategic premium exists for autonomy attached to an OEM line | S128 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | Best-funded autonomous tractor entrant; shut down April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus | S131 |
| Tortuga and Advanced Farm | Cautionary | 2024-2025 | Both sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices after real fleets; the fleet was not what buyers paid for | S127 |
:::

The category's exit pays for the perception asset or the team, not the lease book: a buyer prices the labelled dataset and the grower relationships and treats a leased fleet as a liability it must absorb. Because the fee sits below the cost of the asset, each additional robot moves value from equity to the grower, so growth enlarges the loss rather than the return; the preference then decides whether that loss lands on the founder, the noteholder or this fund. For Meridian the implication is to decline at this mark and keep the diligence warm: the quotes and the note agreement are cheap and would reprice the same asset."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 综合评分与投资建议 Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 5 by Lead Analyst, 8,980 characters)
Orrin scores 4.5 of 10 on the weighted evidence and the recommendation is to pass at $72M pre-money. The score is not a verdict on the picker: it is a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and a credibly measured machine, set against a lease book that loses $8,100 a robot-season at the price growers signed (company-reported, unverified), a $33,000 build cost quoted only by a counterparty with five roles in the round, and a $90M post-money that returns the lead 1.0x until a $90M exit and 2x only at $180M. Pass rather than Wait for milestone: the binding objection is the price plus company-only evidence, and the milestones are the conditions for the lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

### The weighted score

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market and customer pain | 15% | 7 | The harvest line is large, independently costed and the third-largest noncitrus crop; the crop base is flat (2025 US production -1%), so growth must come from penetration, and the 2026 wage-floor cut lowered the grower's alternative cost by 18-23% | S119, S129, S80 |
| Product and technology | 20% | 6 | 94% pick rate on 212 company-chosen rows is a real measurement, but coverage is 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA allowance, and the core perception families are licensed with an exclusivity cliff at 100 robots | S1 (unverified), S86 |
| Unit economics | 20% | 2 | -$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the $9,500 signed price and $48,000 build; breakeven is $17,600 a season on that build, or a $15,600 build at the signed price; the reported 41% margin precedes $3.21M of FY2027 depreciation and -5.5% follows it, against United Rentals' 35.8-40.3% after depreciation | S1 (unverified), S132 |
| Team and execution | 10% | 5 | The founding pair fits perception and farm access and shipped three hardware generations without a CTO; nobody in the five-person executive group has built hardware at volume, the CTO seat is vacant from 2023-08, and the plan asks for 5.6x fleet growth in one season (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified) |
| Competitive position | 10% | 5 | Not alone: Harvest CROO claims human-parity open-field picking (company-issued, 2025-04-24), while Advanced Farm, Tortuga and Monarch have exited or shut; the licence cliff and ungranted filings leave little enforceable exclusivity | S27, S127, S131 |
| Financial position and funding | 10% | 4 | $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $410,000 monthly burn, a $1.5M covenant reached near 2027-03-10, $4.0M committed of an $18M target, and a $3.2M ARR that is 44% contracted rental, 38% related-party engineering and 19% letters (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Valuation and exit | 15% | 3 | $69.9M enterprise value is 36.8x FY2025 revenue and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median; 2 of 8 ag-robotics companies have exited above $100M and none in harvesting; Blue River, the best case, was a 4x last-round outcome | S95 (unverified), S128, S127 |

Two dimensions carry the largest weight and score lowest: unit economics and valuation. That is deliberate, because the product and market scores are what make the company interesting and they are already paid for in the price. No dimension scores above seven without a named comparator, and the market score is capped there because addressable revenue is bounded by acreage times fee rather than by a growing crop base.

### What the decomposition says

Orrin has an eight-quality insight — strawberry harvest is a large, labour-dominated cost pool — delivered by a six-quality product, financed on four-quality terms and priced at a three-quality mark. The steps down come from the company's own numbers: coverage 30-50% below the claim, a damage rate that consumes the saving, 110 robots at 31% of the plan, and a preference paying 1.0x to a $90M exit. [S119, S1]

### The recommendation under the downside structures

| Downside structure | Lead recovery at a $25M exit | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deck terms: 1x, pari passu, $36.77M stack | 0.59x | Pass; the 1.0x floor is a $39.4-41.6M exit, not $25M | S95 (unverified) |

On the company's unverified figures, the $18M is sized to the 2027 robot budget but not to 2028, and the minimum $12M funds only 200 robots; on the plan the $12M case breaches the $1.5M cash covenant in September 2027, and most reported ARR is not recurring rental. The company supplies an income statement for FY2023-FY2028P but no balance sheet, no cash flow statement and no auditor. Revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin is 51.8% in FY2027 before 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

The $3.2M ARR is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 at $12,700), $1.2M of related-party engineering services that end on 2027-06-30 and $0.6M of signed letters of intent. The engineering contract is with the related party that is also a noteholder, board observer, contract manufacturer and round investor; the letters are non-binding; and the contracted season has not started. Strip the two non-recurring components and like-for-like recurring rental is $1.4M, 43.8% of the headline; the current season's signed rental is $0.71M, 22.3%. The $8M 2027 milestone needs 360 robots at the full $16,500 list plus the full $1.2M engineering rate, the $0.6M of letters and $0.4M of pilots; three of the four are not signed at that level (unverified) [S1].

The $0.085M 2027 year-end balance reconciles exactly, but only because $3.21M of 2027 depreciation is added back to the $7.9M net loss. The path assumes zero working capital, no principal repayment and interest inside the net loss; it breaches the $1.5M covenant on 2027-09-12, before the season ends, not at year-end, and a $4.6M season-end receivable would pull the breach into the first half. The $18M case follows the same path to $6.085M, before working capital and principal, and leaves 2028's $13.93M fleet capex unfunded. A quarter's slip to 2027-03-15 leaves opening cash of $1.445M, below the floor before the money arrives (unverified) [S1].

Use of funds is 55% robots. At $18M that is $9.9M, 300 new v4 at $33,000 on top of 64 v3, which matches 360 in service. At the $12M minimum the same 55% is $6.6M, 200 robots and a 264-robot fleet, so the $4.6M 2027 rental line — 360 robots at $12,778 — is not funded; at the $12,700 renewal average a 264-robot fleet earns $3.35M, a $1.25M revenue hole. If the company instead spends the full $9.9M on robots from a $12M round, it has $2.1M left against the $8.1M of R&D and sales budget on the same slide. The 52% and 61% projections are blended gross margins before fleet depreciation: adding the 2027 charge of $3.21M (64 v3 at $12,000 plus 296 v4 at $8,250) to $2.7M of cost of revenue turns $2.9M of gross profit into -$0.31M, or -5.5%; 2028 turns $8.0M into $1.55M, 11.7%, after $6.45M. The 41% is RaaS-only; 52% and 61% are company-wide, so the series changes definition. Orrin Fieldworks's $72.0M pre-money is arithmetically coherent, but the issuer is not the entity that holds the grower contracts, the fleet and the equipment lien, and no charter, registry or UCC record has been retrieved; the $12M should be committed only on verified entity, lien and licence conditions. The company is a Delaware corporation formed 2021-09-14 with 38 staff, three hardware generations shipped by 2026-03, $1.9M FY2025 revenue and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 — all company-reported and unverified. The price works only on a share count the deck does not print: $72.0M ÷ 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares = $4.7145, and $18.0M buys 3,818,008 shares, 20.0% of a $90.0M post. But 15,272,108 is not the "12,000,000 fully diluted total" beside it, which at $4.7145 is $56.6M. The count absorbs the $7.77M note conversion and a 12% post-money pool; every derived figure needs rebuilding before a term sheet [S1].

No Delaware charter, California foreign-qualification record, UCC-1, Mexico Registro Público de Comercio entry or registrar confirmation was retrieved: the Delaware and California registry endpoints were blocked, and the only public entity the name returns is an unrelated Massachusetts LLC filed 2025-12-01 [S143]. In every table below, "Unverified — company-reported" means the deck is the sole support [S1]; no structural, ownership or lien statement is diligence-grade, and confidence is capped at company-reported. The peer base rate belongs in the price: Advanced Farm Technologies ceased operations in 2025-07 and Harvest CROO Robotics was still demonstrating viability in 2025-04 [S27, S28].

### Three entities, and the investor buys the one without the contracts

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Salinas, CA | Corporation | Series A issuer; US staff; five filings; Calder licence | Shareholders, below; no voting agreement disclosed | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Orrin Fleet Services LLC | California, formed 2023-11-02 | LLC | Fleet; grower contracts; Kestrel borrower | 100% parent; manager not disclosed | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. | Jalisco, 2024-07-19 | S. de R.L. de C.V. | Gripper and harness assembly; seven staff | 99% parent / 1% fleet LLC; not checked in RPC | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |

The parent holds five US patent filings and an exclusive Calder University licence dated 2022-01-20 for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum. The California LLC holds the fleet, the grower contracts and the Kestrel facility: $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 2025-06-16, 11.5%, secured on the fleet, with a $1.5M minimum cash covenant. The Mexican company assembles grippers and harnesses. Three questions are unanswered: whether the licence permits affiliate operation or sublicensing; whether Kestrel has consented to new equity and where the covenant is tested; and whether the 99/1 split is in a registered deed [S1].

| Shareholder | Class | % post-round | % votes | Status | Source |

| Dr. Imani Castellano | Common | 18.23% | 18.23% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |

| Dr. Soren Abernathy, former CTO | Common, vested | 3.77% | 3.77% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Granary Ventures | Series Seed | 9.43% | 9.43% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Furrowline Angels and other seed | Series Seed | 6.29% | 6.29% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| 2025 noteholders, converted | Series A-1 | 10.80% | 10.80% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| New Series A money, $18.0M | Series A | 20.00% | 20.00% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Options granted | Common | 8.17% | 8.17% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Unallocated pool | Common, reserved | 12.00% | 0.00% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |

On the company's cap table the unallocated pool rises from 1,080,000 to 2,290,805 shares, up 112%, costing existing holders $5.71M at the round price, 7.9% of the pre-money. Founders fall from 47.0% to 29.5%; 2.0 points is the pool, and the former CTO keeps 3.3% of the combined founder block. The 80% note conversion yields 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares against 1,648,000 at full price, moving $1.95M to noteholders and an estimated $0.6M from the founders. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit. At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at $79M and needs $180M for 2x, so the pre-money is best underwritten as an option struck at $79M, not a mark on the common. The structure is founder-friendly; the stack decides whether a modest success reaches the common [S1].

Orrin sells a robot-season, not a robot. The customer is a strawberry grower, the user is the crew the robot displaces, and the budget owner holds the harvest-labour line. Growth comes from converting pilots into paid seasonal rentals: 14 pilot farms since 2024, two conversions in 2025, five paying growers in 2026, 110 robots contracted for 2027 plus 50 letters of intent. Revenue quality is thinner than the $3.2M ARR headline: $1.4M is contracted robot-seasons at the $12,700 renewal price, $1.2M is engineering services ending 2027-06-30, $0.6M is non-binding letters. The $8M ARR milestone is unreachable on the funded fleet: 360 robots at $12,700 is $4.6M, at the $16,500 list price $5.9M [S1].

### Governance: five roles in one counterparty and an empty chair

After closing the board is five seats — two common, one seed, one Series A, one independent agreed by both — but the independent seat is vacant, so the tie-breaker is unfilled and the chair is the chief executive. Tallis Agricultural Machinery is at once a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer at 37.5% of stated ARR, the quoted manufacturer whose $33,000 unit cost underpins the $9.9M robot budget, a board observer and a $1.0M investor; it also employed the chief executive in 2010-2011. The chief operating officer's wholly owned services company took $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date under a contract approved by a board he sits on, and his 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer [S1]. Conditions before closing:

- An independent director at signing, agreed by the lead, chairing audit and compensation.
- Observer rights limited to non-confidential sessions.
- A second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials.
- Kestrel consent, a covenant waiver through the 2027 build, and Calder consent to affiliate operation and sublicensing.
- Founder reverse-vesting and a full-time chief financial officer by closing.

arguments.markdown:
The team is built for the problem Orrin had in 2021, not the one it has in 2027. Dr. Imani Castellano, chief executive and chair, is a perception researcher with a robotics PhD, five years in a university field-robotics lab and eleven claimed patent filings; Teodor Vashti, chief operating officer, ran harvest operations for two large berry growers over twenty years. Neither has founded or sold a company, none of the five executives has built hardware at volume, and the co-founder who owned the technical roadmap left on 2023-08-31. Every degree, date, employer and patent count here is company-reported and unverified: no registrar, employer or patent-inventor record was retrievable, so the people-risk score is critical on unverified credentials, not medium [S1].

### The pairing fits two problems and misses the third

The combination matches the first two problems a picking robot has to solve — seeing ripe fruit, and being allowed onto a farm — and not the third, making 360 of them. Castellano invents and raises: the licensed families come out of her lab, the company holds five filings, and she is the face of the raise. Vashti sells and operates: five paying growers in 2026, the two named ones taking 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons, and the largest is the farm where he was harvest operations director from 2014 to 2021, contracted for 40 robots in 2027. That is commercial proof and its limit: the funnel is one man's twenty-year network, and the plan needs 250 more in a four-month window. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### A CTO seat empty for 26 months

The co-founder and CTO, Dr. Soren Abernathy, left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. He keeps 720,000 vested common shares — 6.0% before the round, 3.8% after — a permanent cap-table party without a reason to protect it. A patent-register search under the company's name on 2026-10-30 returned no Orrin assignee record and no inventor list for the two licensed families or five company filings; unpublished applications are not public for 18 months, so this is a gap, not a contradiction, but the deck's claim that he is a named inventor cannot be verified. The licensed families sit in the university's name, so an Orrin assignee search would miss them. No public footprint or new venture found. A 3.8% holder with unrestricted shares and the core perception work in his head is hireable by any competitor; California does not let the company restrain where he works. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The technical bet sits one level below the executive team

Dr. Mei Hollander joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at one robotics company, moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — company-reported, unverified. That matches the bruising problem — 3.8% of berries damaged in the 2025 pilots, one Florida grower gone in 2026-06 — and not the problem that decides 2027: cutting the build from $48,000 to a $33,000 average while multiplying the fleet by 5.6. With no CTO above her, the hardest programme sits with one vice president hired 32 months ago, on an undisclosed equity package. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### Selling 360 robots with one new sales leader

Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales in 2025-06 after twenty years at a crop-inputs company, ending as regional sales director for the West: sixteen months in robotics, unverified. The 2027 book is 110 robots contracted plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, 31% of the 360-robot plan five months before the season, with two founder-sellers and one VP to close the gap. The risk is not product rejection; this industry buys late, the season opens in April in California and December in Florida, and a 360-unit build must be committed before the orders exist. No stage pipeline is shown. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### What would settle it

Three records would turn biography into evidence; none was retrievable: degree checks through each registrar, patent-inventor records for the eleven claimed filings and the five company filings, and reference calls at the four prior employers. The peer record shows why the hires matter. Their first-three-year metrics could not be retrieved, so the comparison is one of outcomes, not like-for-like execution. Against the company's own history, the fleet went from 12 robots in 2024 to 64 in 2026, a 5.3x over two seasons, while the plan asks for 5.6x in one season and a one-third cost cut. People risk should therefore be priced: a CTO, a manufacturing leader and a retention grant for the VP Engineering are closing conditions, not intentions. For the $12M decision, the implication is that people risk is a condition precedent, not a diligence note. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks's $72.0M pre-money is arithmetically coherent, but the issuer is not the entity that holds the grower contracts, the fleet and the equipment lien, and no charter, registry or UCC record has been retrieved; the $12M should be committed only on verified entity, lien and licence conditions. The company is a Delaware corporation with 38 staff, three hardware generations shipped by 2026-03, $1.9M FY2025 revenue and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 — all unverified — company-reported. The price works only on a share count the deck does not print: $72.0M ÷ 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares = $4.7145, and $18.0M buys 3,818,008 shares, 20.0% of a $90.0M post. But 15,272,108 is not the "12,000,000 fully diluted total" beside it, which at $4.7145 is $56.6M. The count absorbs the $7.77M note conversion and a 12% post-money pool; every derived figure needs rebuilding before a term sheet. No Delaware charter, California foreign-qualification record, UCC-1, Mexico Registro Público de Comercio entry or registrar confirmation was retrieved: both registry endpoints were blocked. In every table below, "Unverified — company-reported" means the deck is the sole support; no structural, ownership or lien statement is diligence-grade, and confidence is capped at company-reported [S1].

### Three entities, and the investor buys the one without the contracts

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Salinas, CA | Corporation | Series A issuer; US staff; five filings; Calder licence | Shareholders, below; no voting agreement disclosed | Unverified — company-reported; no registry trace | S1, S143 |
| Orrin Fleet Services LLC | California, formed 2023-11-02 | LLC | Fleet; grower contracts; Kestrel borrower | 100% parent; manager not disclosed | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. | Jalisco, 2024-07-19 | S. de R.L. de C.V. | Gripper and harness assembly; seven staff | 99% parent / 1% fleet LLC; not checked in RPC | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |

The parent holds five US patent filings and an exclusive Calder University licence, at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum. The California LLC holds the fleet, the grower contracts and the Kestrel facility: $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 2025-06-16, 11.5%, secured on the fleet, with a $1.5M minimum cash covenant. Three questions are unanswered: whether the licence permits affiliate operation or sublicensing; whether Kestrel has consented to new equity and where the covenant is tested; and whether the 99/1 split is in a registered deed. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The cap table clears; the headline does not

| Shareholder | Class | % post-round | % votes | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dr. Imani Castellano | Common | 18.23% | 18.23% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Teodor Vashti | Common | 11.31% | 11.31% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Dr. Soren Abernathy, former CTO | Common, vested | 3.77% | 3.77% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Granary Ventures | Series Seed | 9.43% | 9.43% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Furrowline Angels and other seed | Series Seed | 6.29% | 6.29% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| 2025 noteholders, converted | Series A-1 | 10.80% | 10.80% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| New Series A money, $18.0M | Series A | 20.00% | 20.00% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Options granted | Common | 8.17% | 8.17% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Unallocated pool | Common, reserved | 12.00% | 0.00% | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |

On the company's cap table the unallocated pool rises from 1,080,000 to 2,290,805 shares, up 112%, costing existing holders $5.71M, 7.9% of the pre-money. Founders fall from 47.0% to 29.5%; 2.0 points is the pool, and the former CTO keeps 3.3% of the combined founder block. The 80% note conversion yields 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares against 1,648,000 at full price, moving $1.95M to noteholders. Voting assumes one vote per share, no voting agreement, undisclosed; material, because two common seats of five is all that keeps the founders off a board they do not control. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The $72M sits below its own preference stack

The 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M assumed from the 2023 round size, not stated in the deck): a $36.8M stack, 40.9% of the $90.0M post. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit. At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at $79M and needs $180M for 2x, so the pre-money is best underwritten as an option struck at $79M, not a mark on the common. The structure is founder-friendly; the stack decides if a modest success reaches common. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### What it sells, and to whom

Orrin sells a robot-season, not a robot. The customer is a strawberry grower and the budget owner holds the harvest-labour line. Growth comes from converting pilots into paid seasonal rentals: 14 pilot farms since 2024, two conversions in 2025, five paying growers in 2026, 110 robots contracted for 2027 plus 50 letters of intent. Revenue quality is thinner than the $3.2M ARR headline: $1.4M is contracted robot-seasons at the $12,700 renewal price, $1.2M is engineering services ending 2027-06-30, $0.6M is non-binding letters. The $8M ARR milestone is unreachable on the funded fleet: 360 robots at $12,700 is $4.6M, at the $16,500 list price $5.9M. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### Governance: five roles in one counterparty and an empty chair

The board is five seats — two common, one seed, one Series A, one independent agreed by both — but the independent seat is vacant, so the tie-breaker is unfilled and the chair is the chief executive. Tallis Agricultural Machinery is at once a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the quoted manufacturer whose $33,000 unit cost underpins the $9.9M robot budget, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The chief operating officer's wholly owned services company took $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date under a contract approved by a board he sits on, and his 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer. Company-reported, unverified [S1]. Conditions before closing:

- An independent director at signing, agreed by the lead, chairing audit and compensation.
- Observer rights limited to non-confidential sessions.
- A second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials.
- Kestrel consent, a covenant waiver through the 2027 build, and Calder consent to affiliate operation and sublicensing.
- Founder reverse-vesting and a full-time chief financial officer by closing.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, 8,973 characters)
Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026: the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, making the deck's urgency a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus, visible in insider commitments at the mark, is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying perception for its sprayer line, not a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. The score is not a verdict on the picker: it is a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and a credibly measured machine, set against a lease book that loses $8,100 a robot-season at the price growers signed (company-reported, unverified), a $33,000 build cost quoted only by a counterparty with five roles in the round, and a $90M post-money that returns the lead 1.0x until a $90M exit and 2x only at $180M. Pass rather than Wait for milestone: the binding objection is the price plus company-only evidence, and the milestones are the conditions for the lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

### The weighted score

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market and customer pain | 15% | 7 | The harvest line is large, independently costed and the third-largest noncitrus crop; the crop base is flat (2025 US production -1%), so growth must come from penetration, and the 2026 wage-floor cut lowered the grower's alternative cost by 18-23% | S119, S129, S80 |
| Product and technology | 20% | 6 | 94% pick rate on 212 company-chosen rows is a real measurement, but coverage is 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA allowance, and the core perception families are licensed with an exclusivity cliff at 100 robots | S1 (unverified), S86 |
| Unit economics | 20% | 2 | -$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the $9,500 signed price and $48,000 build; breakeven is $17,600 a season on that build, or a $15,600 build at the signed price; the reported 41% margin precedes $3.21M of FY2027 depreciation and -5.5% follows it, against United Rentals' 35.8-40.3% after depreciation | S1 (unverified), S132 |
| Team and execution | 10% | 5 | The founding pair fits perception and farm access and shipped three hardware generations without a CTO; nobody in the five-person executive group has built hardware at volume, the CTO seat is vacant from 2023-08, and the plan asks for 5.6x fleet growth in one season (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified) |
| Competitive position | 10% | 5 | Not alone: Harvest CROO claims human-parity open-field picking (company-issued, 2025-04-24), while Advanced Farm, Tortuga and Monarch have exited or shut; the licence cliff and ungranted filings leave little enforceable exclusivity | S27, S127, S131 |
| Financial position and funding | 10% | 4 | $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $410,000 monthly burn, a $1.5M covenant reached near 2027-03-10, $4.0M committed of an $18M target, and a $3.2M ARR that is 44% contracted rental, 38% related-party engineering and 19% letters (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Valuation and exit | 15% | 3 | $69.9M enterprise value is 36.8x FY2025 revenue and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median; 2 of 8 ag-robotics companies have exited above $100M and none in harvesting; Blue River, the best case, was a 4x last-round outcome | S95 (unverified), S128, S127 |

Two dimensions carry the largest weight and score lowest: unit economics and valuation. That is deliberate, because the product and market scores are what make the company interesting and they are already paid for in the price. No dimension scores above seven without a named comparator, and the market score is capped there because addressable revenue is bounded by acreage times fee rather than by a growing crop base.

### What the decomposition says

Orrin has an eight-quality insight — strawberry harvest is a large, labour-dominated cost pool — delivered by a six-quality product, financed on four-quality terms and priced at a three-quality mark. The steps down come from the company's own numbers: coverage 30-50% below the claim, a damage rate that consumes the saving, 110 robots at 31% of the plan, and a preference paying 1.0x to a $90M exit. [S119, S1]

### The recommendation under the downside structures

| Downside structure | Lead recovery at a $25M exit | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deck terms: 1x, pari passu, $36.77M stack | 0.59x | Pass; the 1.0x floor is a $39.4-41.6M exit, not $25M | S95 (unverified) |
| 2025 notes carry a senior or 2x preference | 0.21x | Pass; require an equal-rank warranty before any cheque | S95 (unverified) |
| A $10M senior 2028 round ahead of the Series A | 0.31x | Pass; the 2028 round is more likely than not to ask for seniority | S95 (unverified) |
| Pay-to-play in a 2028 down round, lead does not follow | 0.05x | Pass; a cheque with no reserve is a one-shot option | S95 (unverified) |

The recommendation does not change across these cases: there is no downside structure at this mark in which a lead ticket earns a venture return. The preference stack is one deck sentence and no document; the expected return and this rating assume it ranks equal. It would change on two conditions only: independent quotes at or below the current build cost with a first article built, and a signed next-season contract at or above the renewal price from outside the chief operating officer's circle. Those would move the unit-economics score, supporting a lead at a lower mark.

### Position sizing

Zero at $72M. The Kelly inputs are 2.2x at 18%, 1.0x at 40% and 0.35x at 42%, an expected 0.94x; with a 1.2 net win and a 0.82 chance of not winning, the Kelly fraction is negative and the check size is zero. Re-entry is a $6M first tranche and a $6M second tranche on 200 robots in paid service and two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000, at a $50-58M pre-money, a 1.5x preference and an equal-rank warranty, with the licence covenant and lender consent as conditions precedent. Maximum loss is $6M before the second tranche; the remaining $6M is reserved for the 2028 round only if the licence test is met. [S95, S127]

### The next diligence actions

Before a term sheet: obtain the note purchase agreement and seed certificate of designation and confirm the stack ranks equally; commission two manufacturer quotes for the v4 plus a firm first-article date; commission an independent cold-storage bruising trial against a named retailer specification; obtain the lender's consent and identify the entity at which the cash covenant is tested; obtain counsel opinions on the California equipment standard and Bayh-Dole US-manufacture obligations; run a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year, separating the related-party engineering contract and the grant.

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Lead MOIC at the adverse outcome | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | v4 build cost at 300 units | $33,000, single quote from the noteholder and customer | A second quote above $36,000 | At $44,000 the $16,500 list stops covering depreciation and the base case collapses to a $25M exit | 0.59x | High | A second quote; a first article slipping past 2027-01 | S1 (unverified) |
| 2 | 2027 price realisation | $12,700 average, some at $16,500 | A renewal at $9,500-10,500 | Each $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M of revenue; a reversion to $9,500 takes contribution to -$4,350 and the exit to about $40M | 0.96x | High | The first 2027 renewal signature and deposit | S1 (unverified) |
| 3 | Fleet in service by April 2027 | 360 robots | Fewer than 250 delivered by 2027-03 | Each 100 robots is $1.27M of revenue; a 250-robot fleet is $3.2M against the $4.6M plan, an exit near $60M | 1.0x | High | Contracted count below 200 in 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| 4 | Bruising | 3.8% measured; 2.5% assumed | A packer rejecting machine-picked lots | One point of cull is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee; a second grower exit holds the exit near $70M | 1.0x | Medium | A second grower exit after the 2026-06 loss | S1 (unverified) |
| 5 | Preference structure and closing date | 1x pari passu; close by 2026-12-15 | A senior or 2x note; a close slipping into Q1 2027 | The lead's recovery at a $25M exit falls from 0.59x to 0.21x; a slip breaches the $1.5M covenant near 2027-03-10 | 0.21x | High | Cash below $2.5M; a waiver request | S95 (unverified) |
:::

::: takeaways
1. Pass at $72M pre-money: at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $48,000 build, one robot-season loses $8,100, and the $12M ticket returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities (company-reported inputs). [S1, S95]
2. Re-engage at a $50-58M pre-money with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged on two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000 and 200 robots in paid service, which lifts the same $100M exit from 1.0x to about 1.5x on company-reported terms. [S95]
3. Make the closing conditions substantive: an equal-rank warranty on the preference stack, lender consent, a licence covenant that survives the 2027-12-31 test, and an independent bruising result at or below 2.5%. [S95, S120]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 5分钟速读 Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, 6,561 characters)
Meridian should pass at the $72M pre-money. Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the field and a real harvest cost pool to sell into, but at the $9,500 a robot-season growers signed and the $48,000 build the company can evidence (company-reported, unverified), every unit loses $8,100 before debt service, and the round prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund: the $12M cheque returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities and 2x only at a $180M exit. The rating is Pass rather than Wait for milestone because the binding objection is the price plus evidence that rests on the company alone; the re-entry milestones are the conditions for a lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pass | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; re-engage at $50-58M with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged | 4.5 | Medium | 12-24 months, to the 2027 season and the licence test | S95 (unverified), S1 (unverified) |
:::

### What is good, and what decides it

The pain is real and independently measured: the UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is cheap against that bill. The picker has the only labelled field dataset in the category — 94% pick rate on 212 rows, 75 paid robot-seasons, 110 robots contracted for 2027 at a $12,700 renewal price — and the two things that usually kill hardware start-ups, no customer and no evidence, are not the problem here. Four facts outweigh that. One robot-season loses $8,100 at the signed price, and the $33,000 build that would fix it is a single quote from a counterparty that is also noteholder, customer, board observer and investor. Bruising at 3.8% has already cost one grower and spends most of the USDA allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. [S119, S1, S95, S86]

| What is being bought | 64 robots in service, 110 contracted for 2027 of a 360-robot plan, a labelled field dataset and two valleys of grower relationships; no granted patent | S1 (unverified), S86 |

The evidence confidence is medium. The arithmetic is solid and reproducible from the deck; the inputs — build cost, service cost, contract count, preference terms and every executive credential — are management statements, unverified, with no independent record retrieved. The $36.77M preference stack, at 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, is one sentence in the deck and appears in no document; the 0.94x return and the Pass rating assume it. There is no audit, no registry confirmation of the three entities, no federal award visible against the stated grant, and no patent prosecution record. [S95]

The follow-up diligence is narrow and cheap: two independent manufacturer quotes for the v4, an independent cold-storage bruising trial, the note purchase agreement, the lender's consent, and a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year.

::: one-question
What does a fourth-generation robot cost to build at fleet volumes, quoted by a manufacturer that is not also the largest customer?

At the current build cost no price growers have signed makes a robot-season profitable, so the fleet consumes capital on every unit; at a lower cost the list price turns contribution positive and the business becomes financeable. Two competitive quotes settle it in weeks and decide between a capital-consuming lease book and a business that compounds.
:::

::: takeaways
1. Pass at $72M pre-money: at the signed $9,500 price and the $48,000 build, one robot-season loses $8,100, and the $12M ticket returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities (company-reported). [S1, S95]
2. The company is worth pursuing at a lower price: at a $50-58M pre-money with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged on two independent quotes at or below $33,000 and 200 robots in paid service, the same $100M exit returns about 1.5x on company-reported terms. [S95]
3. The binding constraints are physical and contractual, not commercial: bruising, coverage of 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, a licence cliff at 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and a California standard that still requires a human driver. [S1, S86, S126]
:::"}],"isError":false}
