{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 风险评估 Risk Assessment (risk, revision 3 by Red Team Analyst, 8,997 characters)
Orrin has a real cost pool and a broken price: every robot-season it has sold loses $8,100 after depreciation at the $9,500 growers signed, the $33,000 v4 that would fix it is quoted by a counterparty that is also customer, noteholder and investor, and the California standard governing the fleet requires a human driver. The mechanism is a lessor whose build cost exceeds the value of its price: equity is consumed on every unit and the preference decides who absorbs it. The risk is that the $12M is subordinated before it is at risk. Company figures are unverified. [S1, S95]

### The 1.0x floor sits at $40M, not $25M

| Exit enterprise value | Equal-rank 1x (deck terms) | Notes senior at 2x | $10M senior 2028 round | Pay-to-play, lead does not follow | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $40M | 0.96x | 0.68x | 0.69x | 0.30x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $25M | 0.59x | 0.21x | 0.31x | 0.05x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| $12M | 0.26x | 0.00x | 0.00x | 0.00x | S95 (unverified), calc |

The $36.77M preference is described in the deck, not the documents, and ranks behind $1.6M of secured fleet debt; net of debt and 8% costs the $12M is whole only at a $41.6M enterprise value — $39.4M at the likely $16M close, where the stack is $34.77M — and at $25M it returns 0.59x, which means the bear case must be priced off net proceeds. Down rounds were 11.4% of Carta's Q1 2026 rounds and 12.1% of Cooley's Q2 2026 deals, and new money asks for seniority or pay-to-play; the lead then funds pro rata or converts. With 82 of the plan's own probability points missing the 2027 plan, a 2028 down round is more likely than not at 45-55%, with 30-40% on senior or pay-to-play terms. A $15M purchase of patents, licence and team — the CNH and Oishii structure — pays $13.2M after costs and returns 0.36x; through the lender's collateral, nil. [S95, S123]

### The plan multiplies three numbers the deck does not have

The v4 misses $36,000 with a 55% probability, and FY2027 revenue of $4.6M is 360 robots at $12,778, but 110 are contracted ($1.4M, company-reported) and 250 must be signed in four months by two founders and one vice president hired in June 2025. At 250 robots revenue is $3.18M, and depreciation on 64 v3 and 186 v4 units is $2.30M against $1.78M of gross profit before it: -$0.53M, worse than the plan's -$0.31M, because field service does not shrink with the fleet. The 51.8% FY2027 margin excludes $3.21M of depreciation; with it the year is -5.5%, and the 2026 41% is rental-only. The 2028 plan needs 782 robots and $13.93M of unplanned capex. A close on 2027-02-15 arrives with $1.9M against a $1.5M floor: three weeks of headroom, a January waiver request and the only likely bridge from the counterparty already owed $2.5M — so the position becomes uninvestable at the first waiver request, not the first missed number. The build compounds it: 300 units of an unbuilt design ordered in February cannot reach an April season, so 2027 runs on 64 v3 robots and a partial build, revenue lands at $0.8-1.8M, the licence test fails below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the 2028 raise happens without exclusivity. A six-month delay does not slow this model; it ends the 2027 season. [S1]

### One counterparty, five roles

Tallis Agricultural Machinery holds $2.5M of the $7.77M notes (32.2%), commits $1.0M to this round, buys $1.2M a year of engineering (46% of FY2026E revenue), sits as board observer, and supplies the $33,000 quote behind 300 units and $9.9M of orders (company-reported). One counterparty touches $14.6M of the round and supplies the number that decides viability. A 10% error is $3,300 a unit and $825 a season of depreciation, taking contribution at $12,700 from -$1,150 to -$1,975; at $44,000 the $16,500 list price stops covering depreciation. The chief operating officer's own services company took $310,000 in 2025-2026, about two-thirds of the season's field-service line, on a contract approved by a board he sits on; at a 25% premium the leakage is $62,000. With the independent seat vacant, Meridian cannot carry a related-party resolution alone. The quote is an offer, not evidence: $50-58M with two independent quotes, not $72M. [S1, S95]

### The rule that actually breaks the model

California alone prohibits autonomous agricultural equipment, through Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces; the fix died when AB 187 passed on 2026-08-31, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01, so no rule can change before the 2027 season. Both readings are fatal: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season; if the fleet sits outside it, one citation ends a season that is all of the 2026 revenue. The probability of a material restriction or enforcement action in 2027 is 20% to 25%, with -70% to -90% of equity value. The tariff is likelier and less fatal: the 2026-10-28 proclamation found a threat, imposed nothing and set a Commerce-USTR report within 180 days — 2027-04-26, six days before the season — and a 25% duty is $8,250 a robot, $2.48M on 300 and a 75-robot smaller fleet at 30-35%. Non-USMCA origin at 10% costs $3,300 a robot, 85% of gross profit, with origin undocumented at 40%; Bayh-Dole US manufacture would cost $1,500-3,000 a robot to reshore if a licensed family was federally funded, at 30-40%. The wage floor helps at 60-70% odds but cannot fix bruising. [S126, S124, S88, S89, S85]

### Absence is a finding, not proof

No registry entry, no federal award against the grant the deck describes, no granted patent and no auditor's opinion: the inference is not misrepresentation but that every fact the decision turns on is management representation. Absence proves less than it seems: registries sit behind paywalls, applications stay unpublished for eighteen months, subawards appear on no federal site. It proves enough — the money would be wired on unverified facts, a condition-precedent problem before a price problem.

::: info danger
**The model-breaker is the California equipment prohibition, not the tariff.** California alone bars autonomous agricultural equipment, the fix died on 2026-08-31, and the committee does not sit until 2026-12-01. Both readings end the investment: one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season, and a citation stops the only revenue line. [S126, S124]
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin scores 4.5 of 10 on the weighted evidence and the recommendation is to pass at $72M pre-money. The score is not a verdict on the picker: it is a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and a credibly measured machine, set against a lease book that loses $8,100 a robot-season at the price growers signed (management figures, no independent check), a $33,000 build cost quoted only by a counterparty with five roles in the round, and a $90M post-money that returns the lead 1.0x until a $90M exit and 2x only at $180M. Pass rather than Wait for milestone: the binding objection is the price plus company-only evidence, and the milestones are the conditions for the lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

### The weighted score

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market and customer pain | 15% | 7 | The harvest line is large, independently costed and the third-largest noncitrus crop; the crop base is flat (2025 US production -1%), so growth must come from penetration, and the 2026 wage-floor cut lowered the grower's alternative cost by 18-23% | S119, S129, S80 |
| Product and technology | 20% | 6 | 94% pick rate on 212 company-chosen rows is a real measurement, but coverage is 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA allowance, and the core perception families are licensed with an exclusivity cliff at 100 robots | S1 (unverified), S86 |
| Unit economics | 20% | 2 | -$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the $9,500 signed price and $48,000 build; breakeven is $17,600 a season on that build, or a $15,600 build at the signed price; the reported 41% margin precedes $3.21M of FY2027 depreciation and -5.5% follows it, against United Rentals' 35.8-40.3% after depreciation | S1 (unverified), S132 |
| Team and execution | 10% | 5 | The founding pair fits perception and farm access and shipped three hardware generations without a CTO; nobody in the five-person executive group has built hardware at volume, the CTO seat is vacant from 2023-08, and the plan asks for 5.6x fleet growth in one season (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified) |
| Competitive position | 10% | 5 | Not alone: Harvest CROO claims human-parity open-field picking (company-issued, 2025-04-24), while Advanced Farm, Tortuga and Monarch have exited or shut; the licence cliff and ungranted filings leave little enforceable exclusivity | S27, S127, S131 |
| Financial position and funding | 10% | 4 | $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $410,000 monthly burn, a $1.5M covenant reached near 2027-03-10, $4.0M committed of an $18M target, and a $3.2M ARR that is 44% contracted rental, 38% related-party engineering and 19% letters (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Valuation and exit | 15% | 3 | $69.9M enterprise value is 36.8x FY2025 revenue and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median; 2 of 8 ag-robotics companies have exited above $100M and none in harvesting; Blue River, the best case, was a 4x last-round outcome | S95 (unverified), S128, S127 |

Two dimensions carry the largest weight and score lowest: unit economics and valuation. That is deliberate, because the product and market scores are what make the company interesting and they are already paid for in the price. No dimension scores above seven without a named comparator, and the market score is capped there because addressable revenue is bounded by acreage times fee rather than by a growing crop base.

### What the decomposition says

Orrin has an eight-quality insight — strawberry harvest is a large, labour-dominated cost pool — delivered by a six-quality product, financed on four-quality terms and priced at a three-quality mark. The steps down come from the company's own numbers: coverage 30-50% below the claim, a damage rate that consumes the saving, 110 robots at 31% of the plan, and a preference paying 1.0x to a $90M exit. [S119, S1]

### The recommendation under the downside structures

| Downside structure | Lead recovery at a $25M exit | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deck terms: 1x, pari passu, $36.77M stack | 0.59x | Pass; the 1.0x floor is a $39.4-41.6M exit, not $25M | S95 (unverified) |
| 2025 notes carry a senior or 2x preference | 0.21x | Pass; require an equal-rank warranty before any cheque | S95 (unverified) |
| A $10M senior 2028 round ahead of the Series A | 0.31x | Pass; the 2028 round is more likely than not to ask for seniority | S95 (unverified) |
| Pay-to-play in a 2028 down round, lead does not follow | 0.05x | Pass; a cheque with no reserve is a one-shot option | S95 (unverified) |

The recommendation does not change across these cases: there is no downside structure at this mark in which a lead ticket earns a venture return. The preference stack is one deck sentence and no document; the expected return and this rating assume it ranks equal. It would change on two conditions only: independent quotes at or below the current build cost with a first article built, and a signed next-season contract at or above the renewal price from outside the chief operating officer's circle. Those would move the unit-economics score, supporting a lead at a lower mark.

### Position sizing

Zero at $72M. The Kelly inputs are 2.2x at 18%, 1.0x at 40% and 0.35x at 42%, an expected 0.94x; with a 1.2 net win and a 0.82 chance of not winning, the Kelly fraction is negative and the check size is zero. Re-entry is a $6M first tranche and a $6M second tranche on 200 robots in paid service and two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000, at a $50-58M pre-money, a 1.5x preference and an equal-rank warranty, with the licence covenant and lender consent as conditions precedent. Maximum loss is $6M before the second tranche; the remaining $6M is reserved for the 2028 round only if the licence test is met. [S95, S127]

### The next diligence actions

Before a term sheet: obtain the note purchase agreement and seed certificate of designation and confirm the stack ranks equally; commission two manufacturer quotes for the v4 plus a firm first-article date; commission an independent cold-storage bruising trial against a named retailer specification; obtain the lender's consent and identify the entity at which the cash covenant is tested; obtain counsel opinions on the California equipment standard and Bayh-Dole US-manufacture obligations; run a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year, separating the related-party engineering contract and the grant.

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Lead MOIC at the adverse outcome | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | v4 build cost at 300 units | $33,000, single quote from the noteholder and customer | A second quote above $36,000 | -45% to -60% of equity value: at $44,000 the $16,500 list stops covering depreciation and the base case falls to a $25M exit | 0.59x | High | A second quote; a first article slipping past 2027-01 | S1 (unverified) |
| 2 | 2027 price realisation | $12,700 average, some at $16,500 | A renewal at $9,500-10,500 | -25% to -35% of equity value: each $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M of revenue, and a reversion to $9,500 puts the exit near $40M | 0.96x | High | The first 2027 renewal signature and deposit | S1 (unverified) |
| 3 | Fleet in service by April 2027 | 360 robots | Fewer than 250 delivered by 2027-03 | -20% to -30% of equity value: each 100 robots is $1.27M of revenue and a 250-robot fleet is $3.2M against the $4.6M plan | 1.0x | High | Contracted count below 200 in 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| 4 | Bruising | 3.8% measured; 2.5% assumed | A packer rejecting machine-picked lots | -15% to -20% of equity value: one point of cull is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee, and a second grower exit holds the exit near $70M | 1.0x | Medium | A second grower exit after the 2026-06 loss | S1 (unverified) |
| 5 | Preference structure and closing date | 1x pari passu; close by 2026-12-15 | A senior or 2x note; a close slipping into Q1 2027 | -45% of the lead's recovery: at a $25M exit the return falls from 0.59x to 0.21x, and a slip breaches the $1.5M covenant near 2027-03-10 | 0.21x | High | Cash below $2.5M; a waiver request | S95 (unverified) |
:::

::: takeaways
1. Pass at $72M pre-money: at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $48,000 build, one robot-season loses $8,100, and the $12M ticket returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities (company-reported inputs). [S1, S95]
2. Re-engage at a $50-58M pre-money with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged on two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000 and 200 robots in paid service, which lifts the same $100M exit from 1.0x to about 1.5x on company-reported terms. [S95]
3. Make the closing conditions substantive: an equal-rank warranty on the preference stack, lender consent, a licence covenant that survives the 2027-12-31 test, and an independent bruising result at or below 2.5%. [S95, S120]
:::

At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026: the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, making the deck's urgency a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying perception for its sprayer line, not a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

### The distribution, not the mean, decides it

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | v4 at or below $33,000 on two quotes; renewals $12,700-16,500; bruising under 2.5%; 360 robots by April 2027; licence test met; USMCA origin certified | Trade sale near $250M: $33.3M, 2.8x, 2.2x after dilution | Two quotes below $33,000 and 200+ robots contracted by 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Base | 40% | v4 at $33,000-36,000 but the build slips; 250-300 robots at $12,700-13,500; revenue $4-6M; 2028 round flat and asking for seniority | Exit near $100M: $12.0M, 1.1x, 1.0x after dilution | Fleet below 300 and ARR below $4M in 2027 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Bear | 42% | v4 above $36,000; renewals at $12,700 or $9,500; a second grower leaves over bruising; close slips past the covenant or prices a senior bridge; licence lapses | Wind-down, foreclosure or $12-40M asset sale: 0.05-0.96x by structure, central 0.35x; 0.21x if the notes are senior, 0.31x behind a $10M senior 2028 round | Waiver request, cash under $2.5M, a second grower exit | S1 (unverified), S95, S89 |
:::

The probability-weighted return is 0.94x on company-reported inputs, unverified: 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x and 42% at 0.35x. The bull needs the build, price, damage, licence and calendar to land together; the bear needs one of five failures. The $36.77M stack is one deck sentence and no document: the 0.94x and the Pass rating assume the preference is 1x, non-participating and equal in rank, and a $39.27M stack if the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs convert on top would lower the floor further. [S95]

### Key assumptions, ranked

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | v4 builds at or below $33,000 at 300 units on an arm's-length quote | Low | A second quote above $36,000, or a first article slipping past 2027-01 | -45% to -60% of equity value: contribution at $12,700 falls to -$1,900 at $36,000 and -$4,900 at $48,000 | The only quote is dated 2026-08 and comes from the noteholder and customer | S1 (unverified) |
| 2 | 2027 realisations average $12,700 or more, some at the $16,500 list | Medium | A renewal at $9,500-10,500, or a grower repudiating the rise | -25% to -35% of equity value: each $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M of revenue and 3 margin points | The first renewal signature and whether it carries a deposit | S1 (unverified) |
| 3 | 360 robots in service by April 2027 against 110 contracted and 64 today | Low | Fewer than 250 delivered by 2027-03, or no build slot reserved | -20% to -30% of equity value: each 100 robots is $1.27M and a 250-robot fleet is $3.2M against the $4.6M plan | Contracted count below 200 in 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| 4 | Bruising at or below 2.5% on a seven-day, 1 degree Celsius test against a named retailer spec | Low | A packer rejecting machine-picked lots, or a second grower exit | -15% to -20% of equity value: one point of cull is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee | Grower B cut from 22 robots to 14; one grower left over bruising in 2026-06 | S1 (unverified) |
| 5 | Close by 2026-12-15 at $12M or more, 1x pari passu preference, 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31 | Low | A close slipping into Q1 2027; senior or 2x note terms; fewer than 100 robots at the test date | -45% of the lead's recovery: a slip breaches the $1.5M covenant near 2027-03-10; senior notes cut the $25M recovery from 0.59x to 0.21x | Cash below $2.5M, a waiver request, no equal-rank warranty | S1 (unverified), S95 |

### Where the price turns

| Terms | Base case, $100M exit | Bear case, $25M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $72M pre-money, 1x pari passu (deck terms) | 1.0x | 0.59x | S95 (unverified), calc on a $36.77M stack, net of $1.6M debt and 8% costs |
| $72M pre-money, 1.5x on the lead cheque | 1.5x | 0.75x | S95 (unverified), calc: the cheque holds $18.0M of a $42.77M stack |
| $50-58M pre-money, 1.5x, half staged | 1.5x | 0.88x | S95 (unverified), calc on a $36.77M stack |

Above the stack the preference and the as-converted share converge, so the premium is worth its face value in the base case. The evidence needs to improve less than the price: independent quotes for the v4 and a note agreement warranting equal rank would reprice the same asset.

### The analogs that teach the rule

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue River to Deere, $305M | Best | 2015-2017 | Four times the last private post-money; the buyer wanted perception, not a fleet | S128 |
| Bear Flag to Deere, $250M | Best | 2021 | A strategic premium exists for autonomy attached to an OEM line | S128 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | Best-funded autonomous tractor entrant; shut down April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus | S131 |
| Tortuga and Advanced Farm | Cautionary | 2024-2025 | Both sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices after real fleets; the fleet was not what buyers paid for | S127 |
:::

The category's exit pays for the perception asset or the team, not the lease book: a buyer prices the labelled dataset and the grower relationships and treats a leased fleet as a liability it must absorb. Because the fee sits below the cost of the asset, each additional robot moves value from equity to the grower, so growth enlarges the loss rather than the return; the preference then decides whether that loss lands on the founder, the noteholder or this fund. For Meridian the implication is to decline at this mark and keep the diligence warm: the quotes and the note agreement are cheap and would reprice the same asset.

The team is built for the problem Orrin had in 2021, not the one it has in 2027. Dr. Imani Castellano, chief executive and chair, is a perception researcher with a robotics PhD, five years in a university field-robotics lab and eleven claimed patent filings; Teodor Vashti, chief operating officer, ran harvest operations for two large berry growers over twenty years. Neither has founded or sold a company, none of the five executives has built hardware at volume, and the co-founder who owned the technical roadmap left on 2023-08-31. Every degree, date, employer and patent count here is company-reported and unverified: no registrar, employer or patent-inventor record was retrievable, so the people-risk score is critical on unverified credentials, not medium [S1].

### The pairing fits two problems and misses the third

The combination matches the first two problems a picking robot has to solve — seeing ripe fruit, and being allowed onto a farm — and not the third, making 360 of them. Castellano invents and raises: the licensed families come out of her lab, the company holds five filings, and she is the face of the raise. Vashti sells and operates: five paying growers in 2026, the two named ones taking 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons, and the largest is the farm where he was harvest operations director from 2014 to 2021, contracted for 40 robots in 2027. That is commercial proof and its limit: the funnel is one man's twenty-year network, and the plan needs 250 more in a four-month window. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### A CTO seat empty for 26 months

The co-founder and CTO, Dr. Soren Abernathy, left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. He keeps 720,000 vested common shares — 6.0% before the round, 3.8% after — a permanent cap-table party without a reason to protect it. A patent-register search under the company's name on 2026-10-30 returned no Orrin assignee record and no inventor list for the two licensed families or five company filings; unpublished applications are not public for 18 months, so this is a gap, not a contradiction, but the deck's claim that he is a named inventor cannot be verified. The licensed families sit in the university's name, so an Orrin assignee search would miss them. No public footprint or new venture found. A 3.8% holder with unrestricted shares and the core perception work in his head is hireable by any competitor; California does not let the company restrain where he works. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The technical bet sits one level below the executive team

Dr. Mei Hollander joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at one robotics company, moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — company-reported, unverified. That matches the bruising problem — 3.8% of berries damaged in the 2025 pilots, one Florida grower gone in 2026-06 — and not the problem that decides 2027: cutting the build from $48,000 to a $33,000 average while multiplying the fleet by 5.6. With no CTO above her, the hardest programme sits with one vice president hired 32 months ago, on an undisclosed equity package. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### Selling 360 robots with one new sales leader

Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales in 2025-06 after twenty years at a crop-inputs company, ending as regional sales director for the West: sixteen months in robotics, unverified. The 2027 book is 110 robots contracted plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, 31% of the 360-robot plan five months before the season, with two founder-sellers and one VP to close the gap. The risk is not product rejection; this industry buys late, the season opens in April in California and December in Florida, and a 360-unit build must be committed before the orders exist. No stage pipeline is shown. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### What would settle it

Three records would turn biography into evidence; none was retrievable: degree checks through each registrar, patent-inventor records for the eleven claimed filings and the five company filings, and reference calls at the four prior employers. The peer record shows why the hires matter. Their first-three-year metrics could not be retrieved, so the comparison is one of outcomes, not like-for-like execution. Against the company's own history, the fleet went from 12 robots in 2024 to 64 in 2026, a 5.3x over two seasons, while the plan asks for 5.6x in one season and a one-third cost cut. People risk should therefore be priced: a CTO, a manufacturing leader and a retention grant for the VP Engineering are closing conditions, not intentions. For the $12M decision, the implication is that people risk is a condition precedent, not a diligence note. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG评估 ESG Assessment (esg, revision 8 by Regulatory Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,949 characters)
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case sit outside its control before 2027: a wage floor a California court reopened, a robotics tariff due by 2027-04-26, a licence test on 2027-12-31 and a California driver requirement AB 187 leaves in force. My judgement: the balance is negative for 2027 and positive after, which argues for tranching the round rather than declining it. (S1, S126)

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 to 14 robots while Grower E left over bruising. The repricing removed $4,506 an acre of hand cost, 1.7 times the robot's annual price per acre. On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four challenged grounds — skill tiers, housing, the wage survey, the primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and warned of possible back wages. A higher California entry-level rate is more likely than not to apply to the 2027 season, restoring most of that saving and lifting the ceiling [S80, S81, S1].

### The rule that stands, and who is organised

The United Farm Workers, which won that case, will shape the rule. AB 187, the session's employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142, S82, S115, S1]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. The mechanism is asymmetric: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and a 1:1 technician puts field service above the season price — which means the service margin fails; if the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. Material restriction or enforcement in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement, and the lost pilot is the Florida grower.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. The Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed; metals duties of 50% apply even when it does.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A binary test with no cure is harsher than practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones and cure periods. The plan clears the threshold; the cliff needs 72% slippage (20%–25% conversion risk). If either family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture substantially in the US, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and field-packed fruit reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, contract manufacturer and investor; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91, S1].

Four records are requested — the H-2A files and wage table (the department's page failed), the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the chaptered AB 187 text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. For the investor, the factors change what a season is worth, not whether Orrin can sell one: the cheapest protection is to price against the wage-floor outcome and make the USMCA certificate and licence warranty closing conditions. (S80, S91, S85, S126)

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 退出策略分析 Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 10 by Valuation Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,984 characters)
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 0.94x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not an equipment platform. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, a liability in a sale unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security and grower data; no public robotics M&A record | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 (unverified) |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga in 2024; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93]

| Deere / Bear Flag | 2021 | $250M | 31.6x the $7.9M seed; revenue n/a | Autonomous tractor retrofit, 2017 | S96, S118 |
| CNH / Raven | 2021 | $2.1B EV | n/a; 33.6% premium | Public precision-ag company | S99 |
| AGCO / Trimble Ag (85%) | 2023-24 | $2.35B EV | 13.8x 2023E EBITDA | Precision-ag portfolio, $170M EBITDA | S101 |
| Kubota / AgJunction | 2021 | $73M | n/a | Guidance and auto-steer | S104 |
| CNH / Advanced Farm assets | 2025 | Undisclosed | n/a | Strawberry and apple picking IP and team | S97, S28 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2024 | Undisclosed | n/a | $50M deployed, 150 robots | S93 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | n/a | Tomato harvesting robot | S32 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Count the exits rather than impression: of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. 2025 recorded 14 ag-robotics acquisitions and $668M of funding. At the $90M post-money the lead owns 13.33%: a $100M exit returns 1.1x before the Series B and 1.0x after 20% dilution, when the $12M preference binds; $250M returns 2.8x and 2.2x. The report uses one distribution — 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35 = 0.94x, matching the 0.94x used across the report. The bear's 0.35x is the central recovery across the $12-40M asset-sale range; the deck's pari passu terms give 0.59-0.64x at a $25M exit, senior or 2x note terms 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round 0.31x. Below $90M the preference, not the operating plan, sets the return: the first $36.77M of equity goes to the stack, which means a technically good 2027 season still returns only capital. The counter-case is a $250-305M Deere or CNH bid for the team and perception model, as for Blue River and Bear Flag; at 95% pick rates and 360 robots a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

The UC Central Coast strawberry budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026: the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, making the deck's urgency a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying perception for its sprayer line, not a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised at a reported $500M-plus. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 5分钟速读 Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 6,561 characters)
Meridian should pass at the $72M pre-money. Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the field and a real harvest cost pool to sell into, but at the $9,500 a robot-season growers signed and the $48,000 build the company can evidence (company-reported, unverified), every unit loses $8,100 before debt service, and the round prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund: the $12M cheque returns 0.94x on the plan's own probabilities and 2x only at a $180M exit. The rating is Pass rather than Wait for milestone because the binding objection is the price plus evidence that rests on the company alone; the re-entry milestones are the conditions for a lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pass | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; re-engage at $50-58M with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged | 4.5 | Medium | 12-24 months, to the 2027 season and the licence test | S95 (unverified), S1 (unverified) |
:::

### What is good, and what decides it

The pain is real and independently measured: the UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural cost, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is cheap against that bill. The picker has the only labelled field dataset in the category — 94% pick rate on 212 rows, 75 paid robot-seasons, 110 robots contracted for 2027 at a $12,700 renewal price — and the two things that usually kill hardware start-ups, no customer and no evidence, are not the problem here. Four facts outweigh that. One robot-season loses $8,100 at the signed price, and the $33,000 build that would fix it is a single quote from a counterparty that is also noteholder, customer, board observer and investor. Bruising at 3.8% has already cost one grower and spends most of the USDA allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. [S119, S1, S95, S86]

The evidence confidence is medium. The arithmetic is solid and reproducible from the deck; the inputs — build cost, service cost, contract count, preference terms and every executive credential — are management statements, unverified, with no independent record retrieved. There is no audit, no registry confirmation of the three entities, no federal award visible against the stated grant, and no patent prosecution record. [S95]

The follow-up diligence is narrow and cheap: two independent manufacturer quotes for the v4, an independent cold-storage bruising trial, the note purchase agreement, the lender's consent, and a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year.

::: one-question
What does a fourth-generation robot cost to build at fleet volumes, quoted by a manufacturer that is not also the largest customer?

At the current build cost no price growers have signed makes a robot-season profitable, so the fleet consumes capital on every unit; at a lower cost the list price turns contribution positive and the business becomes financeable. Orrin scores 4.5 of 10 on the weighted evidence and the recommendation is to pass at $72M pre-money. The score is not a verdict on the picker: it is a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and a credibly measured machine, set against a lease book that loses $8,100 a robot-season at the price growers signed (unverified management figures), a $33,000 build cost quoted only by a counterparty with five roles in the round, and a $90M post-money that returns the lead 1.0x until a $90M exit and 2x only at $180M. Pass rather than Wait for milestone: the binding objection is the price plus company-only evidence, and the milestones are the conditions for the lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

### The weighted score

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market and customer pain | 15% | 7 | The harvest line is large, independently costed and the third-largest noncitrus crop; the crop base is flat (2025 US production -1%), so growth must come from penetration, and the 2026 wage-floor cut lowered the grower's alternative cost by 18-23% | S119, S129, S80 |
| Product and technology | 20% | 6 | 94% pick rate on 212 company-chosen rows is a real measurement, but coverage is 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA allowance, and the core perception families are licensed with an exclusivity cliff at 100 robots | S1 (unverified), S86 |
| Unit economics | 20% | 2 | -$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the $9,500 signed price and $48,000 build; breakeven is $17,600 a season on that build, or a $15,600 build at the signed price; the reported 41% margin precedes $3.21M of FY2027 depreciation and -5.5% follows it, against United Rentals' 35.8-40.3% after depreciation | S1 (unverified), S132 |
| Team and execution | 10% | 5 | The founding pair fits perception and farm access and shipped three hardware generations without a CTO; nobody in the five-person executive group has built hardware at volume, the CTO seat is vacant from 2023-08, and the plan asks for 5.6x fleet growth in one season (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified) |
| Competitive position | 10% | 5 | Not alone: Harvest CROO claims human-parity open-field picking (company-issued, 2025-04-24), while Advanced Farm, Tortuga and Monarch have exited or shut; the licence cliff and ungranted filings leave little enforceable exclusivity | S27, S127, S131 |
| Financial position and funding | 10% | 4 | $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 against $410,000 monthly burn, a $1.5M covenant reached near 2027-03-10, $4.0M committed of an $18M target, and a $3.2M ARR that is 44% contracted rental, 38% related-party engineering and 19% letters (company-reported, unverified) | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Valuation and exit | 15% | 3 | $69.9M enterprise value is 36.8x FY2025 revenue and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median; 2 of 8 ag-robotics companies have exited above $100M and none in harvesting; Blue River, the best case, was a 4x last-round outcome | S95 (unverified), S128, S127 |

Two dimensions carry the largest weight and score lowest: unit economics and valuation. That is deliberate: the product and market scores are what make the company interesting and the price already pays for them. No dimension scores above seven without a named comparator, and the market score is capped there because addressable revenue is bounded by acreage times fee rather than by a growing crop base.

### What the decomposition says

Orrin has an eight-quality insight — strawberry harvest is a large, labour-dominated cost pool — delivered by a six-quality product, financed on four-quality terms and priced at a three-quality mark. The steps down come from the company's own numbers: coverage 30-50% below the claim, a damage rate that consumes the saving, 110 robots at 31% of the plan, and a preference paying 1.0x to $90M. [S119, S1]

### The recommendation under the downside structures

| Downside structure | Lead recovery at a $25M exit | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deck terms: 1x, pari passu, $36.77M stack | 0.59x | Pass; the 1.0x floor is a $39.4-41.6M exit, not $25M | S95 (unverified) |
| 2025 notes carry a senior or 2x preference | 0.21x | Pass; require an equal-rank warranty before any cheque | S95 (unverified) |
| A $10M senior 2028 round ahead of the Series A | 0.31x | Pass; the 2028 round is more likely than not to ask for seniority | S95 (unverified) |
| Pay-to-play in a 2028 down round, lead does not follow | 0.05x | Pass; a cheque with no reserve is a one-shot option | S95 (unverified) |

The recommendation does not change: no downside structure at this mark gives a lead ticket a venture return. The preference stack is one deck sentence and no document; the expected return and this rating assume it ranks equal. It would change on two conditions only: independent quotes at or below the current build cost with a first article built, and a signed renewal at or above the renewal price from outside the chief operating officer's circle. Those would move the unit-economics score, supporting a lead at a lower mark.

### Position sizing

Zero at $72M. The Kelly inputs are 2.2x at 18%, 1.0x at 40% and 0.35x at 42%, an expected 0.94x; with a 1.2 net win and 0.82 odds of losing, the Kelly fraction is negative and the check size is zero. Re-entry is a $6M first tranche and a $6M second tranche on 200 robots in paid service and two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000, at a $50-58M pre-money, a 1.5x preference and an equal-rank warranty, with the licence covenant and lender consent as conditions precedent. Maximum loss is $6M before the second tranche; the remaining $6M is reserved for the 2028 round only if the licence test is met. [S95, S127]

### The next diligence actions

Before a term sheet: obtain the note purchase agreement and seed certificate of designation to confirm the stack ranks equally; commission two manufacturer quotes for the v4 and a firm first-article date; commission an independent cold-storage bruising trial against a named retailer specification; obtain the lender's consent and identify where the cash covenant is tested; obtain counsel opinions on the California equipment standard and Bayh-Dole US-manufacture obligations; run a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year, separating the related-party contract and the grant.

On them, the full $18M close gives $18.0M Series A + $7.77M notes + $11.0M Series Seed = $36.77M, behind $1.6M of secured fleet debt. The seed issue price is not disclosed; I enter the $11.0M at 1x, and if the $2.5M pre-seed SAFEs converted on top, the seed preference is $13.5M and the stack $39.27M. Price and the pass recommendation assume the deck's terms: a senior or 2x note would cut the lead's $25M-exit recovery to 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round to 0.31x, against 0.59-0.64x on the deck's pari passu terms. The option pool rises from 9.0% to 12.0% of post-money, 1,210,805 new shares worth $5.71M at the round price; as a pre-money item it falls on existing holders — founders from 35.57% to 33.32%, seed from 16.78% to 15.71%, noteholders from 11.53% to 10.80% — while the new Series A owns 20.0%. The lead's $12M buys 13.33% of the post-money, $0.90M per percentage point, or $1.02M per point of the operating business excluding the 12% reserve. [S95]

### The price is 9-22x the listed peer median

On the $69.9M enterprise value, Orrin is at 36.8x FY2025 revenue of $1.9M, 26.9x FY2026E revenue of $2.6M, 21.8x the company's $3.2M ARR and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue of $1.4M — 110 contracted 2027 robot-seasons at $12,700, excluding $0.6M of letters of intent and the $1.2M Tallis contract ending 2027-06-30. ### The disclosed private marks sit below $72M

Harvest CROO has raised $10M-$28.5M depending on the aggregator, with no disclosed valuation; Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in September 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M over eight years and 150 robots, then sold its IP and team to Oishii in 2024 for undisclosed terms; Tevel raised $20M in 2021 and carries a reported $63M secondary value. Carbon Robotics raised $70M in October 2024 with no disclosed valuation, and Monarch raised $133M at more than $500M in July 2024 before laying off almost all staff. The only disclosed $100M+ ag-robotics exits are Deere's purchases of Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), both autonomy platforms. Orrin's $90M post is above every disclosed harvesting-robot mark and near Blue River's 2015 $87M post-money, eleven years earlier. [S105, S28, S94]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 7 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,996 characters)
Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester matched human picking rates in a commercial operation at Duette, Florida — an open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but Driscoll's has invested in Harvest CROO and Agrobot and is talking to six harvesting startups, and Japanese and Chinese university teams are solving the same perception problem. The hand crew, harvest-aid platform and 2025 exits discipline Orrin's price more than any rival [S27, S28, S138].

::: evidence
**The field is thinner than the narrative implies, and not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii; Waseda and Nanjing Agricultural University have working prototypes; Tallis, Orrin's contract manufacturer, could build the platform. Sources: S27, S28, S34, S139, S135, S1.
:::

The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm, which had reached named commercial growers in California, ceased operations; Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii. No public shares exist; the proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S28, S34, S1].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; its liquidation memo cited a failure to develop market traction. Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021; Traptic, a strawberry picker, was acquired in 2022 (reported; not independently sourced). The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: its v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30 [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour; labour is 50-60% of variable cost and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost — unverified, but it captures part of the saving with no autonomy or bruising risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: a picking arm on an existing platform is cheaper than a new fleet. Orrin must beat a crew costing $25,000-35,000 an acre of hand-pick labour and charges $4,714 an acre; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field architecture and RaaS model, a grower-backed founder, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published performance data and no California service network — where Orrin has 14 pilots and 4 paying growers. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct clamshell packing, a 3.8% bruising rate on its own test rows and the COO's California grower relationships: a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly. Waseda University's Sugano Lab, with Maekawa Manufacturing, runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated greenhouse beds — research, no commercial deployment or price. Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked robot at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success, with no price or deployment, and Washington State University researchers have built a robot to pick hidden strawberries. None is a commercial open-field competitor in 2026 and none has a public price, so none sets a ceiling on the $16,500 list — but the perception stack is being solved in public, which erodes the licensed families' value if the licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31 [S30, S1, S139, S135, S137, S134].

### The price is the tell
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025-26 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase. The deck's own disclosure contains the counter-evidence: Grower E in Plant City ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers; four growers nevertheless contracted 110 robots for 2027. If Harvest CROO's parity claim holds, Orrin's price converges on displaced labour and the $16,500 list is at risk; if the 3.8% bruising holds across retail specifications, it can keep pricing up. Two substitutes shrink the acres rather than bid for them: tabletop and high-tunnel production, where Cal Poly calls Santa Maria hoop-house acreage "limited" and Driscoll's is breeding for mechanisation traits, and a once-over variety of the kind that took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% in five years. Tallis is the other exposure: contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, board observer and $1M investor, it has the BOM and cost quote and could build the platform. Diligence: is bruising measured against a retailer spec or only Orrin's test rows; what prevents Tallis competing; and what share of California acreage is tabletop [S1, S28, S136, S138, S33].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 7 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,878 characters)
The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool, and hand-pick labour alone is worth $25,000-35,000 an acre, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, 100% of US strawberry acreage is worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** The $310M and $16,500 inputs are company figures, unverified; at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year and 15% adoption is worth $35.4M, while $310M requires 132% of the base. **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is helping growers raise beds to waist height and will breed for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S136, S138.
:::

| Measure | Top-down | Bottom-up | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global fresh-produce harvest labour | $42B (2025), company estimate, unverified | — | S1 |
| SAM — US strawberry harvest cost | $3.1B company estimate, unverified, vs $3.47B author calculation (43,726 California acres × $79,288 harvest cost/acre) | 50,000 acres × $62,000-79,000 harvest cost/acre = $3.1-3.9B | S1, S9, S10 |
| SOM — company claim, 2031 | $310M, presented as 10% of $3.1B, unverified | 18,788 robots × $16,500 = $310M, requiring 65,758 acres = 132% of the 50,000-acre base | S1 |
| SOM — tested, 2031 at 15% adoption | — | 7,500 acres ÷ 3.5 = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M (author calculation from company assumptions, unverified) | S1 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue, FY2028 | $12.9M RaaS plan, company projection, unverified | 782 robots at $16,500 = 2,737 acres = 5.5% of 50,000 acres | S1 |

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces about 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline, while the California Strawberry Commission projects 7-8 million trays a week through August 2026. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### The wage bill sets the price ceiling
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. The 2024 UC Central Coast budget puts harvest at $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural costs and $112,694 of total cost, on 9,000 trays at $11; UC Davis puts labour at 50-60% of variable production cost, with pickers paid $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour. That implies hand-pick labour of $25,000-35,000 an acre. At $16,500 a robot-season and 3.5 acres per robot, Orrin charges $4,714 an acre, 13-19% of the wage bill it targets, and a 10% harvest-cost saving would be worth $7,929 an acre to the grower. Either the robot removes only part of the crew's work, or Orrin is pricing for adoption and has room to raise price later [S10, S12].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%, and at the $12,700 renewal price it implies 7.1%. Density is conservative the other way: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over a 210-day season is 315 acre-passes, which at 40-50 passes serves 6.3-7.9 acres, not 3.5 — one robot per 3.5 acres implies 90 passes. Either throughput is a peak measurement or the fleet count is inflated. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove about $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception, and the addressable set is open-field acres with slopes under 4%, no standing water and rows wide enough for a track. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia, where Orrin has no sales or service [S9, S13, S14].

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California | 43,726 acres (2026); $3.47B harvest cost (author calculation) | +2.0% acres 2025-26; terminal price -3.3% CAGR 2024-26 | Entered: 14 pilots since 2024, 4 paying growers | 7-month season; slopes over 4% and standing water excluded; retailer bruising limits | Hand crews, harvest-aid platforms, Harvest CROO | S9, S10, S1 |
| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed | Not disclosed; NASS state series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024, with Florida above 14% of the national total; the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost changed on 2025-10-02, when the Department of Labor replaced the USDA Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate with BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics data; the rule is under litigation and summaries disagree, one showing the average rate falling to $15.96 an hour from $17.74 and another showing entry-level rates up 3.7%. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The policy risk cuts both ways: a lower OEWS-based wage floor lengthens robot payback, while a court overturning the rule restores the higher rate and shortens it. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the pure hand-pick wage line per acre in the 2024 UC budget; the final 2026-27 adverse effect wage rates for California and Florida; and the passes and acres behind the 3.5-acre robot density [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 9 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,887 characters)
On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a build cost not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. The 2027 book is 110 robot-seasons at a $12,700 average, all from the four 2026 payers; no new grower has signed, and the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise from 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher — real demand evidence from four accounts, none that the model acquires customers [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 paid seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 paid seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. Who signs is not disclosed — the executed contracts would show whether it is the owner, a VP of growing or procurement, which decides how firm the book is. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost: it owns, maintains and insures the robots, and grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine farms with 2025 test rows that is about $30,000 a pilot farm, versus $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost for a three-to-four-robot pilot at $17,600 a robot-season; an estimated $23,000-$40,000 is unrecovered per pilot, $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. What the non-renewing accounts chose instead is not disclosed; no public evidence shows a lapsed account bought a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation on the $48,000 v3 sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes a contribution margin of -85.3%, or -$8,100, once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and must not be added; the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only (11.5%, $2,453 a season over 75 seasons) and -$3,051 if it amortises over four seasons ($521,246 a year, $6,951 a season). United Rentals earned a 38.0% rental gross margin in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at list with the v3 and +19.1% only with both list and a $31,000 v4 [S21]. The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S21].

The economics are inverted: gross margin rises as capital moves into opex, while the cash to build each robot leaves before the season.

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against $3,100 reported; at 360 robots that is 45 technicians and $1.12M, so service cost is linear. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation. At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, against a UC Davis 2024 harvest cost of $79,288 an acre, 3.4-5.9% of the labour bill. Growers in the Western Growers survey require a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year, Orrin's 2.84-season payback at list and current cost is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. At 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray each point of fruit lost is $990 an acre, 21-36% of the fee, and the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 an acre, more than the entire signed fee (company-reported, unverified deck figures; external benchmarks) [S1, S10, S141].

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 3.4-5.9% of harvest cost, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there. Tortuga deployed 150 harvesting robots and about $50M over eight years before selling to Oishii in 2025-03; FarmWise raised $65M, ran Titan as a service, moved Vulcan to dealer sales and wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms in 2025-04. Orrin's $320,313 per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000. The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. For an investor, the signed book is $1.4M of 2027 rental; the $16,500 list and $31,000 v4 must be proven before paying for fleet capex. Conditions should be executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, a verified v4 bill of materials from an independent manufacturer, an audited service-cost build at the 1:8 ratio and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate is medium, and the open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and the bruised-fruit share (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S93, S100, S116].
