arguments.markdown:
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 1.04x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not equipment. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, a liability unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security and grower data; no public robotics M&A record | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 (unverified) |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga 2025-03; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93, S144 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93, S144]

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | What the target had | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River | 2017 | $305M | 3.5x the $87M post-money; revenue n/a | See & Spray, $30M+ raised | S98 |
| Deere / Bear Flag | 2021 | $250M | 31.6x the $7.9M seed; revenue n/a | Autonomous tractor retrofit, 2017 | S96, S118 |
| CNH / Raven | 2021 | $2.1B EV | n/a; 33.6% premium | Public precision-ag company | S99 |
| AGCO / Trimble Ag (85%) | 2023-24 | $2.35B EV | 13.8x 2023E EBITDA | Precision-ag portfolio, $170M EBITDA | S101 |
| Kubota / AgJunction | 2021 | $73M | n/a | Guidance and auto-steer | S104 |
| CNH / Advanced Farm assets | 2025 | Undisclosed | n/a | Strawberry and apple picking IP and team | S97, S28 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2025-03 | Undisclosed | n/a | $50M deployed, 150 robots | S93, S144 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | n/a | Tomato harvesting robot | S32 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. At the $90M post-money the lead owns 13.33%: a $100M exit returns 1.1x before the Series B and 1.0x after 20% dilution, when the preference binds; $250M returns 2.8x and 2.2x. The distribution is 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.59 = 1.04x. The $25M bear is an equity exit on the deck's pari passu terms, not a blended asset-sale recovery: the lead takes 32.6% of the $36.77M stack, about $7.1M, after fleet debt and costs. A $12-40M asset sale returns less; senior or 2x notes would cut the $25M recovery to 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round to 0.31x — structure cases, not the base distribution. Below $90M the preference, not the operating plan, sets the return: the first $36.77M goes to the stack, so a technically good 2027 season still returns only capital. The counter-case is a $250-305M Deere or CNH bid for the team and perception model, as at Blue River and Bear Flag; at 95% pick rates and 360 robots a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

| Case | Probability | Exit value | Lead proceeds | MOIC | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | $250M | $26.7M | 2.2x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Base | 40% | $100M | $12.0M | 1.0x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Bear | 42% | $25M | $7.1M | 0.59x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Weighted | 100% | — | — | 1.04x (0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.59) | S95 (unverified), calc |

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Metric | 2027 plan | 2028 plan | Test for a Series B above $72M pre | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $5.6M | $13.2M | $13.2M at 7x forward, or $18M at 5x | S95 (unverified) |
| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |
| Renewal | 110 contracted 2027 seasons | n/a | 80% or more of 2026 paying growers renew | S95 (unverified) |
| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

Deere, AGCO, CNH and Kubota have closed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection; a Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, license and grower data, and Mexico assembly adds tariff diligence. An IPO is not realistic before 2030 at $1.9M of revenue and a $5.2M FY2025 net loss. The holding period is three to five years, 2030-2032 after a Series B. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.1x at $100M (1.0x after dilution), 1.7x at $150M (1.4x) and 2.8x at $250M (2.2x); over five years that is 0% IRR at $100M, 17.1% at $250M and -10.0% at the $25M bear. A 20-30% lower price or 1.5x preference would make the same exits work; at $72M the lead is buying an option that needs a $250M+ bid. The 1.04x expected return and the pass assume the deck's 1x, non-participating, equal-rank preference — one sentence on deck p.14, with no seed charter or note agreement supplied; the seed issue price is not disclosed and the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs may convert on top, making the stack $39.27M rather than $36.77M. The Pass rests on the 1.0x floor holding at a $39.4-41.6M exit — $36.77M of stack plus debt and costs — not on a sub-1x mean. If the notes are senior or 2x the $25M recovery is 0.21x rather than 0.59x, and a $10M senior 2028 round cuts it to 0.31x; the note purchase agreement and seed charter are the open data request that would settle the downside. The implication is to pass at $72M, or invest at a 20-30% lower price with a 1.5x preference and a milestone tranche. Diligence should confirm the Advanced Farm and Tortuga prices, grower-contract ownership, the Calder license's change-of-control terms and the 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons in two growers. [S95, S97, S93]

arguments.markdown:
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case sit outside its control before 2027: a wage floor a California court reopened, a robotics tariff due by 2027-04-26, a licence test on 2027-12-31 and a California driver requirement AB 187 leaves in force. My judgement: the balance is negative for 2027 and positive after, and the inputs that decide it are conditions the company would have to meet, not risks a valuation absorbs. (S1, S126)

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 to 14 robots while Grower E left over bruising. On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on all four grounds — skill tiers, housing, wage survey, primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and warned of back wages. A higher California rate is more likely than not to apply in 2027, restoring most of the 17.6% cut and lifting the ceiling [S80, S81, S1].

### The rule that stands, and who is organised

The United Farm Workers, which won that case, will shape the rule. AB 187, the session's employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142, S82, S115, S1]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. The mechanism is asymmetric: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and a 1:1 technician puts field service above the season price, which means the service margin fails; if the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. Material restriction or enforcement in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. The restriction becomes acceptable only on three conditions, none met today: a counsel opinion that a technician satisfies the human-driver standard; a Cal/OSHA interpretation or an advisory-committee outcome confirming that reading; and field service at 1:8 or better. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. The Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed; metals duties of 50% apply even when it does.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A binary test with no cure is harsher than practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones and cure periods. The plan clears the threshold; the cliff needs 72% slippage (20%–25% conversion risk). If either family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture substantially in the US, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and field-packed fruit reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, contract manufacturer and investor; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91, S1].

Four records are requested — the H-2A files and wage table, the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the AB 187 text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. For the investor, the factors change what a season is worth, not whether Orrin can sell one; the test they set is whether the three California conditions hold before the 2027 season. (S80, S91, S85, S126)

arguments.markdown:
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case sit outside its control before 2027: a wage floor a California court reopened, a robotics tariff due by 2027-04-26, a licence test on 2027-12-31 and a California driver requirement AB 187 leaves in force. My judgement: the balance is negative for 2027 and positive after, and the inputs that decide it are conditions the company would have to meet, not risks a valuation absorbs. (S1, S126)

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 to 14 robots while Grower E left over bruising. On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on four grounds — skill tiers, housing, wage survey, primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and warned of back wages. A higher California rate is more likely than not to apply in 2027, restoring most of the 17.6% cut and lifting the ceiling [S80, S81, S1].

### The rule that stands, and who is organised

The United Farm Workers, which won that case, will shape the rule. AB 187, the session's employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142, S82, S115, S1]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. The mechanism is asymmetric: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and a 1:1 technician puts field service above the season price, which means the service margin fails; if the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. Material restriction or enforcement in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. The restriction becomes acceptable only on three conditions, none met today: a counsel opinion that a technician satisfies the human-driver standard; a Cal/OSHA interpretation or an advisory-committee outcome confirming that reading; and field service at 1:8 or better. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. The Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed; metals duties of 50% apply even when it does.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A binary test with no cure is harsher than practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones and cure periods. The plan clears the threshold; the cliff needs 72% slippage (20%–25% conversion risk). If either family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture substantially in the US, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and field-packed fruit reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, contract manufacturer and investor; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91, S1].

Four records are requested — the H-2A files and wage table, the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the AB 187 text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. For the investor, the factors change what a season is worth, not whether Orrin can sell one; the test they set is whether the three California conditions hold before the 2027 season. (S80, S91, S85, S126)

The team is built for the problem Orrin had in 2021, not the one it has in 2027. Every degree, date, employer and patent count here is company-reported and unverified: no registrar, employer or patent-inventor record was retrievable, so the people-risk score is critical on unverified credentials, not medium [S1].

### The pairing fits two problems and misses the third

The combination matches the first two problems a picking robot has to solve — seeing ripe fruit, and being allowed onto a farm — and not the third, making 360 of them. Castellano invents and raises: the licensed families come out of her lab, the company holds five filings, and she is the face of the raise. Vashti sells and operates: five paying growers in 2026, four contracted for 2027, the two named ones taking 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons, and the largest is the farm where he was harvest operations director from 2014 to 2021, contracted for 40 robots in 2027. That is commercial proof and its limit: the funnel is one man's twenty-year network, and the plan needs 250 more in a four-month window. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### A CTO seat empty for 26 months

The co-founder and CTO, Dr. Soren Abernathy, left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. He keeps 720,000 vested common shares — 6.0% before the round, 3.8% after — a permanent cap-table party without a reason to protect it. A patent-register search under the company's name on 2026-10-30 returned no Orrin assignee record and no inventor list for the two licensed families or five company filings; unpublished applications are not public for 18 months, so this is a gap, not a contradiction, but the deck's claim that he is a named inventor cannot be verified. The licensed families sit in the university's name, so an Orrin assignee search would miss them. No public footprint or new venture found. A 3.8% holder with unrestricted shares and the core perception work in his head is hireable by any competitor; California does not let the company restrain where he works. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The technical bet sits one level below the executive team

Dr. Mei Hollander joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at one robotics company, moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — company-reported, unverified. That matches the bruising problem — 3.8% of berries damaged in the 2025 pilots, one Florida grower gone in 2026-06 — and not the problem that decides 2027: cutting the build from $48,000 to a $33,000 average while multiplying the fleet by 5.6. Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales in 2025-06 after twenty years at a crop-inputs company, ending as regional sales director for the West: sixteen months in robotics, unverified. The 2027 book is 110 robots contracted plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, 31% of the 360-robot plan five months before the season, with two founder-sellers and one VP to close the gap. Three records would turn biography into evidence; none was retrievable: degree checks through each registrar, patent-inventor records for the eleven claimed filings and the five company filings, and reference calls at the four prior employers. 2. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at
peak harvest. Harvest labor is the largest single cost line for most growers.
-  Strawberries are picked by hand every three to four days through a season of up to seven months; a picker covers roughly a quarter of an acre a
day (company estimate).
-  Growers tell us their crews are smaller and older each year, while wages and worker housing keep getting more expensive (grower interviews, 2025).
-  Fruit left unpicked rots on the plant and spreads mold to the next pass, so a short crew costs more than the berries it leaves behind.
-  Harvest aids such as carts and conveyors make pickers faster, but still need a full crew.

-  An autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives the furrows at night and day, finds ripe berries with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and

-  Runs about 20 hours a day on swappable battery packs; one field technician supervises up to 8 robots, on site or remotely.
-  Sold as Robots-as-a-Service: growers pay per robot per season; we own, maintain and insure the fleet.
-  Current model: Orrin Picker v3, released to the field in March 2026. The v4, designed for lower cost, is planned for the 2027 season.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG评估 ESG Assessment (esg, revision 10 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,998 characters)
Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case sit outside its control before 2027: a wage floor a California court reopened, a robotics tariff due by 2027-04-26, a licence test on 2027-12-31 and a California driver requirement AB 187 leaves in force. My judgement: the balance is negative for 2027 and positive after, and the inputs that decide it are conditions the company would have to meet, not risks a valuation absorbs. (S1, S126)

### The wage floor, not the robot, sets the price

The grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin in 2026. The skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 puts California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate at $16.45 an hour against the $19.97 Farm Labor Survey rate that governed to 2025-10-01 — a 17.6% cut — with the experienced level at $18.71; Florida fell from $16.23 to $12.47 and $15.06. On the deck's quarter-acre per picker-day, one pass over an acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II: $21,056–$23,949 an acre over a 40-pass season. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres the robot is $2,714 an acre, 11%–13% of that, and $4,714 at the 2027 list price, so price is not what stops adoption: Grower B cut from 22 to 14 robots while Grower E left over bruising. On 2026-08-26 a California district court held the October 2025 methodology unlawful on four grounds — skill tiers, housing, wage survey, primary-duty rule — ordered a replacement and warned of back wages. A higher California rate is more likely than not to apply in 2027, restoring most of the 17.6% cut and lifting the ceiling [S80, S81, S1].

### The rule that stands, and who is organised

The United Farm Workers, which won that case, will shape the rule. AB 187, the session's employment trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256 without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have let unpiloted machines work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01 [S126, S124, S142, S82, S115, S1]. Both readings of that rule end the investment. The mechanism is asymmetric: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and a 1:1 technician puts field service above the season price, which means the service margin fails; if the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line. Material restriction or enforcement in 2027: 20%–25% probability, -70% to -90% of equity value — probability times impact, not probability alone. The restriction becomes acceptable only on three conditions, none met today: a counsel opinion that a technician satisfies the human-driver standard; a Cal/OSHA interpretation or an advisory-committee outcome confirming that reading; and field service at 1:8 or better. California overtime adds to the hand cost displaced; Florida's exposure is immigration enforcement.

### The robot crosses a border being re-priced

Orrin owns the fleet, so duty lands on its capital cost. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, non-qualifying robots at 10%: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 26% of the $12,700 renewal price and 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit. The Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a Commerce–USTR update within 180 days [S88, S89]. At 25% that is $8,250 a robot, or $2.48M against a $9.9M 2027 build budget. Whether the robot meets USMCA origin is not disclosed; metals duties of 50% apply even when it does.

### A licence with a cliff, and a statute nobody has checked

The licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum — the floor binds in FY2026 at 5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue — and falls to non-exclusive below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet [S1, S85, S86]. A binary test with no cure is harsher than practice, where exclusive licences carry diligence milestones and cure periods. The plan clears the threshold; the cliff needs 72% slippage (20%–25% conversion risk). If either family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to manufacture substantially in the US, and Guadalajara assembles the grippers.

### Food safety is an equipment problem now

21 CFR Part 112 names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable and cleaned and sanitised as necessary [S83, S92]. Picking into the clamshell makes the machine's interior a packing surface, and field-packed fruit reaches the consumer unwashed. No federal certificate exists and no FDA action on machine-harvested berries was found; the gate is a retailer audit and the penalty a delisting. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, is voluntary, and no assessment against it is disclosed.

### The social case is a product metric

Labour substitution is an asset only where labour supply binds, not where quality binds: the numbers that move a purchase are the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime, on rows excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%. No retailer standard or campaign aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was identified. Governance carries more weight: Tallis is noteholder, board observer, customer, contract manufacturer and investor; the COO's own company is paid for robot moves and night supervision; the independent board seat is vacant; and ARR includes letters of intent and a contract ending 2027-06-30. USAspending returns no award under the company's name against the Phase II award the deck describes [S91, S1].

Four records are requested — the H-2A files and wage table, the SBIR award, the USPTO assignment chain and licence, and the AB 187 text — so confidence is medium on tariff and licence exposure and low on food-safety compliance. For the investor, the factors change what a season is worth, not whether Orrin can sell one; the test they set is whether the three California conditions hold before the 2027 season. (S80, S91, S85, S126)

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 10 by Lead Analyst, 8,986 characters)
Orrin has found a real harvest bill — $21,056-23,949 an acre-season of hand-pick labour — and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season on 9,000 trays at a $1.75-2.25 piece rate plus burden. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026: the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, making the deck's urgency a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at realistic fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying perception for its sprayer line, not a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

### The distribution, not the mean, decides it

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 18% | v4 at or below $33,000 on two quotes; renewals $12,700-16,500; bruising under 2.5%; 360 robots by April 2027; licence test met; USMCA origin certified | Trade sale near $250M: $33.3M, 2.8x, 2.2x after dilution | Two quotes below $33,000 and 200+ robots contracted by 2027-02 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Base | 40% | v4 at $33,000-36,000 but the build slips; 250-300 robots at $12,700-13,500; revenue $4-6M; 2028 round flat and asking for seniority | Exit near $100M: $12.0M, 1.1x, 1.0x after dilution | Fleet below 300 and ARR below $4M in 2027 | S1 (unverified), S95 |
| Bear | 42% | v4 above $36,000; renewals at $12,700 or $9,500; a second grower leaves over bruising; close slips past the covenant or prices a senior bridge; licence lapses | Wind-down, foreclosure or $25M equity exit: 0.59x on deck terms; 0.21x with senior or 2x notes, 0.31x behind a $10M senior 2028 round | Waiver request, cash under $2.5M, a second grower exit | S1 (unverified), S95, S89 |
:::

The probability-weighted return is 1.04x on company-reported inputs, unverified — 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x, 42% at 0.59x — capital preservation over five years, not a venture return; the Pass rests on the 1.0x floor at a $39.4-41.6M exit, not on the mean. The bull needs build, price, damage, licence and calendar together; the bear needs one of five failures. The $36.77M stack is one deck sentence and no document: the 1.04x and the rating assume it ranks 1x, non-participating and equal, and a $39.27M stack if the $2.5M of SAFEs convert would lower the floor further. Orrin scores 4.5 of 10 on the weighted evidence and the recommendation is to pass at $72M pre-money. The score is not a verdict on the picker: it is a real harvest bill — $21,056-23,949 an acre-season of hand-pick labour — and a credibly measured machine, set against a lease book that loses $8,100 a robot-season at the signed price (unverified management figures), a $33,000 build cost quoted only by a counterparty with five roles in the round, and a $90M post-money that returns the lead 1.0x until a $90M exit and 2x only at $180M. ### What the decomposition says

Orrin has an eight-quality insight — strawberry harvest is a large, labour-dominated cost pool — delivered by a six-quality product, financed on four-quality terms and priced at a three-quality mark. The steps down come from the company's own numbers: coverage 30-50% below the claim, a damage rate that consumes the saving, 110 robots at 31% of the plan, and a preference paying 1.0x to $90M. The pain is real and independently measured: hand-pick labour runs $21,056-23,949 an acre-season on the report's own yield and piece rate, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is 11-13% of that bill. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 退出策略分析 Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 12 by Valuation Analyst, 8,992 characters)
A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 1.04x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not equipment. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, a liability unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Route | Named buyer or venue | What they buy | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategic OEM | Deere & Co. | Perception model, gripper IP, grower relationships | 2029-2031 | Medium | S96, S98 |
| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security and grower data; no public robotics M&A record | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 (unverified) |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga 2025-03; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93, S144 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93, S144]

| Deere / Bear Flag | 2021 | $250M | 31.6x the $7.9M seed; revenue n/a | Autonomous tractor retrofit, 2017 | S96, S118 |
| CNH / Raven | 2021 | $2.1B EV | n/a; 33.6% premium | Public precision-ag company | S99 |
| AGCO / Trimble Ag (85%) | 2023-24 | $2.35B EV | 13.8x 2023E EBITDA | Precision-ag portfolio, $170M EBITDA | S101 |
| Kubota / AgJunction | 2021 | $73M | n/a | Guidance and auto-steer | S104 |
| CNH / Advanced Farm assets | 2025 | Undisclosed | n/a | Strawberry and apple picking IP and team | S97, S28 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2025-03 | Undisclosed | n/a | $50M deployed, 150 robots | S93, S144 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | n/a | Tomato harvesting robot | S32 |

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. At the $90M post-money the lead owns 13.33%: a $100M exit returns 1.1x before the Series B and 1.0x after 20% dilution, when the preference binds; $250M returns 2.8x and 2.2x. The distribution is 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.59 = 1.04x. The $25M bear is an equity exit on the deck's pari passu terms, not a blended asset-sale recovery: the lead takes 32.6% of the $36.77M stack, about $7.1M, after fleet debt and costs. A $12-40M asset sale returns less; senior or 2x notes would cut the $25M recovery to 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round to 0.31x — structure cases, not the base distribution. Below $90M the preference, not the operating plan, sets the return: the first $36.77M of equity goes to the stack, which means a technically good 2027 season still returns only capital. The counter-case is a $250-305M Deere or CNH bid for the team and perception model, as at Blue River and Bear Flag; at 95% pick rates and 360 robots a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

| Base | 40% | $100M | $12.0M | 1.0x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Bear | 42% | $25M | $7.1M | 0.59x | S95 (unverified), calc |
| Weighted | 100% | — | — | 1.04x (0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.59) | S95 (unverified), calc |

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]

| Metric | 2027 plan | 2028 plan | Test for a Series B above $72M pre | Source |

| Revenue | $5.6M | $13.2M | $13.2M at 7x forward, or $18M at 5x | S95 (unverified) |
| RaaS gross margin | 52% | 61% | 60% or higher | S95 (unverified) |
| Robots in service | 360 | n/a | 360 or more, 95% pick rate at 3 farms | S95 (unverified) |
| Renewal | 110 contracted 2027 seasons | n/a | 80% or more of 2026 paying growers renew | S95 (unverified) |
| Unit cost | Below $36,000 | $31,000 target at 500 units | Below $36,000 | S95 (unverified) |

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

Deere, AGCO, CNH and Kubota have closed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection; a Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, license and grower data, and Mexico assembly adds tariff diligence. An IPO is not realistic before 2030 at $1.9M of revenue and a $5.2M FY2025 net loss. The holding period is three to five years, 2030-2032 after a Series B. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.1x at $100M (1.0x after dilution), 1.7x at $150M (1.4x) and 2.8x at $250M (2.2x); over five years that is 0% IRR at $100M, 17.1% at $250M and -10.0% at the $25M bear. A 20-30% lower price or 1.5x preference would make the same exits work; at $72M the lead is buying an option that needs a $250M+ bid. The 1.04x expected return and the pass assume the deck's 1x, non-participating, equal-rank preference — one sentence on deck p.14, with no seed charter or note agreement supplied; the seed issue price is not disclosed and the $2.5M of pre-seed SAFEs may convert on top, making the stack $39.27M rather than $36.77M. The Pass therefore rests on the 1.0x floor holding at a $39.4-41.6M exit — $36.77M of stack plus debt and costs — not on a sub-1x mean. If the notes are senior or 2x the $25M recovery is 0.21x rather than 0.59x, and a $10M senior 2028 round cuts it to 0.31x; the note purchase agreement and seed charter are the open data request that would settle the downside. The implication is to pass at $72M, or invest at a 20-30% lower price with a 1.5x preference and a milestone tranche. Diligence should confirm the Advanced Farm and Tortuga prices, grower-contract ownership, the Calder license's change-of-control terms and the 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons in two growers. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 公司概览 Company Overview (company_overview, revision 7 by Company Analyst, 8,944 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks's $72.0M pre-money is arithmetically coherent, but the issuer is not the entity that holds the grower contracts, the fleet and the equipment lien; the $12M should be committed only on verified entity, lien and licence conditions. The company is a Delaware corporation with 38 staff, three hardware generations shipped by 2026-03, $1.9M FY2025 revenue and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 — all company-reported, unverified. The price works only on a share count the deck does not print: $72.0M ÷ 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares = $4.7145, and $18.0M buys 3,818,008 shares, 20.0% of a $90.0M post. No Delaware charter, California foreign-qualification record, UCC-1, Mexico Registro Público de Comercio entry or registrar confirmation was retrieved; the section rests on three source IDs — S1, S27 and S28 — and "Unverified — company-reported" in every table means the deck is the sole support; no structural, ownership or lien statement is diligence-grade, and confidence is capped at company-reported [S1].

### Three entities, and the investor buys the one without the contracts

| Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Salinas, CA | Corporation | Series A issuer; US staff; five filings; Calder licence | Shareholders, below; no voting agreement disclosed | Unverified — company-reported; no registry trace | S1 |
| Orrin Fleet Services LLC | California, formed 2023-11-02 | LLC | Fleet; grower contracts; Kestrel borrower | 100% parent; manager not disclosed | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |
| Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. | Jalisco, 2024-07-19 | S. de R.L. de C.V. | Gripper and harness assembly; seven staff | 99% parent / 1% fleet LLC; not checked in RPC | Unverified — company-reported | S1 |

The parent holds five US patent filings and an exclusive Calder University licence, at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum. The California LLC holds the fleet, the grower contracts and the Kestrel facility: $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 2025-06-16, 11.5%, secured on the fleet, with a $1.5M minimum cash covenant. Three questions are unanswered: whether the licence permits affiliate operation or sublicensing; whether Kestrel has consented to new equity and where the covenant is tested; and whether the 99/1 split is in a registered deed. ### The cap table clears; the headline does not

On the company's cap table the unallocated pool rises from 1,080,000 to 2,290,805 shares, costing existing holders $5.71M, 7.9% of the pre-money. Founders fall from 47.0% to 29.5%; 2.0 points is the pool, and the former CTO keeps 3.3% of the combined founder block. The 80% note conversion yields 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares against 1,648,000 at full price, moving $1.95M to noteholders. Voting assumes one vote per share, no voting agreement disclosed; material, because two common seats of five is all that keeps the founders off a board they do not control. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The $72M sits below its own preference stack

The 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M assumed from the 2023 round size, not stated in the deck): a $36.8M stack, 40.9% of the $90.0M post. The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces about 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline, while the California Strawberry Commission projects 7-8 million trays a week through August 2026. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### One acre-season, three figures that reconcile
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces, stated once and in one unit. Yield is 9,000 trays an acre — the 8-lb flat of the UC budget, about 72,000 lb. Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season. Total harvest cost is $79,288 an acre, of which hand-pick labour is 27-30%; the rest is packing materials, supervision, hauling and cooling, and none of it is what the robot displaces. The labour figure has two independent supports that agree: 1,280 picker-hours an acre-season (four picker-days a pass over 40 passes at eight hours) at the 2026 California adverse effect wage rates of $16.45 and $18.71 an hour is $21,056-23,949, and 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 a tray is $15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% payroll burden, the same range. There are 9,000 trays, not 1,125: reading a tray as eight flats understates the wage bill eight-fold, to $2,000-2,500. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill; at the $16,500 list, $4,714, or 20-22%. A 10% harvest-cost saving is worth $7,929 an acre, so the grower's payback survives the list price; what binds is quality and capital, not the size of the wage bill [S10, S12, S80, S1].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%, and at the $12,700 renewal price it implies 7.1%. Density is conservative the other way: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over a 210-day season is 315 acre-passes, 6.3-7.9 acres at 40-50 passes rather than 3.5. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove about $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception, and the addressable set is open-field acres with slopes under 4%, no standing water and rows wide enough for a track. California holds four of Orrin's five paying growers in 2026 and Florida one; four of the five have contracted 110 robots for 2027. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia, where Orrin has no sales or service [S9, S13, S14].

The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool and hand-pick labour alone is worth $21,056-23,949 an acre-season, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** At $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US acres are worth $236M and 15% adoption $35.4M; $310M needs 132% of the base. **One acre-season, three figures:** 9,000 trays (about 72,000 lb), hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 and total harvest cost of $79,288; the robot fee is $2,714 an acre at $9,500 (11-13% of the wage bill) and $4,714 at $16,500 (20-22%). **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is raising beds and breeding for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S80, S10, S136, S138.
:::

| Measure | Top-down | Bottom-up | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global fresh-produce harvest labour | $42B (2025), company estimate, unverified | — | S1 |
| SAM — US strawberry harvest cost | $3.1B company estimate, unverified, against $3.47B from 43,726 California acres at $79,288 an acre | 50,000 acres × $62,000-79,000 = $3.1-4.0B | S1, S9, S10 |
| SOM — company claim, 2031 | $310M, presented as 10% of $3.1B, unverified | 18,788 robots × $16,500 = $310M, requiring 65,758 acres = 132% of the 50,000-acre base | S1 |
| SOM — tested, 2031 at 15% adoption | — | 7,500 acres ÷ 3.5 = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M (author calculation from company assumptions, unverified) | S1 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue, FY2028 | $12.9M RaaS plan, company projection, unverified | 782 robots at $16,500 = 2,737 acres = 5.5% of 50,000 acres | S1 |

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces about 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline, while the California Strawberry Commission projects 7-8 million trays a week through August 2026. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### One acre-season, three figures that reconcile
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. Yield is 9,000 trays an acre — the 8-lb flat of the UC budget, about 72,000 lb. Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season. Total harvest cost is $79,288 an acre, of which hand-pick labour is 27-30%; the rest is packing materials, supervision, hauling and cooling, and none of it is what the robot displaces. The labour figure has two independent supports that agree: 1,280 picker-hours an acre-season (four picker-days a pass over 40 passes at eight hours) at the 2026 California adverse effect wage rates of $16.45 and $18.71 an hour is $21,056-23,949, and 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 a tray is $15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% payroll burden, the same range. There are 9,000 trays, not 1,125: reading a tray as eight flats understates the wage bill eight-fold, to $2,000-2,500. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill; at the $16,500 list, $4,714, or 20-22%. A 10% harvest-cost saving is worth $7,929 an acre, so the grower's payback survives the list price; what binds is quality and capital, not the size of the wage bill [S10, S12, S80, S1].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%, and at the $12,700 renewal price it implies 7.1%. Density is conservative the other way: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over a 210-day season is 315 acre-passes, 6.3-7.9 acres at 40-50 passes rather than 3.5. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove about $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception, and the addressable set is open-field acres with slopes under 4%, no standing water and rows wide enough for a track. California holds four of Orrin's five paying growers in 2026 and Florida one; four of the five have contracted 110 robots for 2027. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia [S9, S13, S14].

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California | 43,726 acres (2026); $3.47B harvest cost (author calculation) | +2.0% acres 2025-26; terminal price -3.3% CAGR 2024-26 | Entered: 14 pilots since 2024; 4 of the 5 paying growers | 7-month season; slopes over 4% and standing water excluded; retailer bruising limits | Hand crews, harvest-aid platforms, Harvest CROO | S9, S10, S1 |
| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed | Not disclosed; NASS state series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin before it moved for it. The 2026 notice set California's entry-level and experienced adverse effect wage rates at $16.45 and $18.71 an hour and Florida's at $12.47 and $15.06, below the Farm Labor Survey rates they replaced; on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the methodology unlawful and ordered a replacement, so a higher California rate is more likely than not in 2027. H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024, with Florida above 14% of the national total: the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the 40 passes and 3.5-acre density behind the robot count; the final 2027 California and Florida rates after the court order; and the share of California acreage in tabletop [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117].

arguments.markdown:
On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a $31,000 build not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. Five growers paid in 2026; four of them contracted 110 robot-seasons for 2027 at a $12,700 average, and the fifth, Grower D, is in discussion. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. No new grower has signed for 2027; the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise from 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher — real demand evidence from four accounts, none that the model acquires customers [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows the first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 paid seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 paid seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. The buying unit includes the marketer or packer, not only the grower: the robot packs straight into retail clamshells, so whoever sells or packs the fruit must accept machine-picked berries, and the 3.8% bruising that ended Grower E's pilot shows acceptance can be lost after a field trial. Whether a marketer's acceptance is a contract condition, and who signs — owner, VP of growing or procurement — is not disclosed; the executed 2027 contracts and the packer's fruit specification would settle both. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost: it owns, maintains and insures the robots, and grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine 2025 test farms, about $30,000 paid a pilot farm against $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost leaves $23,000-$40,000 unrecovered per pilot and $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. No lapsed account is disclosed as buying a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company-reported, unverified) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation on the $48,000 v3 sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes a contribution margin of -85.3%, or -$8,100, once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and amortising debt service are two views of the same asset and must not be added; the cash view is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only (11.5%, $2,453 a season over 75 seasons) and -$3,051 if it amortises over four seasons ($521,246 a year, $6,951 a season). United Rentals earned a 38.0% rental gross margin in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at list with the v3 and +19.1% only with both list and a $31,000 v4 [S21]. The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S21].

The economics are inverted: gross margin rises as capital moves into opex, while the cash to build each robot leaves before the season.

| Offer | $ per robot-season | vs signed | $ per acre (3.5 acres/robot) | % of $21,056-23,949 hand-pick labour | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 11.3-12.9% | S1, S80 |
| 2027 contracted average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 15.2-17.2% | S1, S80 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 19.7-22.4% | S1, S80 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 21.0-23.9% | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 15.9-18.1% | S1 (unverified), calc |

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against $3,100 reported; at 360 robots that is 45 technicians and $1.12M, so service cost is linear. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation. At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, 11.3-12.9% and 19.7-22.4% of hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 an acre-season: one pass over an acre costs $526-599 (8 hours at the $16.45-18.71 Level I-II adverse effect wage rate over a quarter acre) and a season is 40 passes, which on 9,000 trays is $2.34-2.66 a tray all-in against a $1.75-2.25 piece rate plus burden. Growers in the Western Growers survey require a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year, the 2.84-season payback with the $31,000 build is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. At 3.8% bruising, $3,762 an acre of fruit is lost, more than the signed fee (company-reported, unverified deck figures; external benchmarks) [S1, S10, S80, S141].

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 11-13% of hand-pick labour at the signed price and 20-22% at list, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there. Tortuga deployed 150 harvesting robots and about $50M over eight years before selling its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03; FarmWise raised $65M, ran Titan as a service, moved Vulcan to dealer sales and wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms in 2025-04. Orrin's $320,313 per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000. The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. For an investor, the signed book is $1.4M of 2027 rental; the $16,500 list and $31,000 v4 must be proven before paying for fleet capex. Conditions should be executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, an independent v4 bill of materials, an audited service-cost build at 1:8 and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate is medium, and the open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price, the marketer's acceptance and the bruised-fruit share (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S93, S100, S116].

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unverified) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. Those figures produce the -$8,100 contribution, the 12.31-season payback and the 3.08-season depreciation breakeven. Source S1.
:::
