arguments.markdown:
The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool and hand-pick labour alone is worth $21,056-23,949 an acre-season, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** All 50,000 US acres at $16,500 and one robot per 3.5 acres are worth $236M; 15% adoption is $35.4M and $310M needs 132% of the base. **One acre-season, three figures:** 9,000 trays (about 72,000 lb), hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 and total harvest cost of $79,288; the robot fee is $2,714 an acre at $9,500 (11-13% of the wage bill) and $4,714 at $16,500 (20-22%). **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is raising beds and breeding for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S80, S10, S136, S138.
:::

| Measure | Top-down | Bottom-up | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global fresh-produce harvest labour | $42B (2025), company estimate, unverified | — | S1 |
| SAM — US strawberry harvest cost | $3.1B company estimate, unverified, against $3.47B from 43,726 California acres at $79,288 an acre | 50,000 acres × $62,000-79,000 = $3.1-4.0B | S1, S9, S10 |
| SOM — company claim, 2031 | $310M, presented as 10% of $3.1B, unverified | 18,788 robots × $16,500 = $310M, requiring 65,758 acres = 132% of the 50,000-acre base | S1 |
| SOM — tested, 2031 at 15% adoption | — | 7,500 acres ÷ 3.5 = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M (author calculation from company assumptions, unverified) | S1 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue, FY2028 | $12.9M RaaS plan, company projection, unverified | 782 robots at $16,500 = 2,737 acres = 5.5% of 50,000 acres | S1 |

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces about 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### One acre-season, three figures that reconcile
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. Yield is 9,000 trays an acre — the 8-lb flat of the UC budget, about 72,000 lb. Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season. Total harvest cost is $79,288 an acre, of which hand-pick labour is 27-30%; the rest is packing materials, supervision, hauling and cooling, and none of it is what the robot displaces. The labour figure has two independent supports that agree: 1,280 picker-hours an acre-season (four picker-days a pass over 40 passes at eight hours) at the 2026 California adverse effect wage rates of $16.45 and $18.71 an hour is $21,056-23,949, and 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 a tray is $15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% payroll burden, the same range. There are 9,000 trays, not 1,125: reading a tray as eight flats understates the wage bill eight-fold, to $2,000-2,500. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill; at the $16,500 list, $4,714, or 20-22%. A 10% harvest-cost saving is worth $7,929 an acre, so the grower's payback survives the list price; what binds is quality and capital, not the size of the wage bill [S10, S12, S80, S1].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%. Density is the other way: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days is 315 acre-passes, 6.3-7.9 acres at 40-50 passes, so 3.5 acres implies 90 passes. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove about $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception. California holds four of Orrin's five paying growers in 2026 and Florida one; four of the five have contracted 110 robots for 2027. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia [S9, S13, S14].

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California | 43,726 acres (2026); $3.47B harvest cost (author calculation) | +2.0% acres 2025-26; terminal price -3.3% CAGR 2024-26 | Entered: 14 pilots since 2024; 4 of the 5 paying growers | 7-month season; slopes over 4% and standing water excluded; retailer bruising limits | Hand crews, harvest-aid platforms, Harvest CROO | S9, S10, S1 |
| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed | Not disclosed; NASS state series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin before it moved for it. The 2026 notice set California's entry-level and experienced adverse effect wage rates at $16.45 and $18.71 an hour and Florida's at $12.47 and $15.06, below the Farm Labor Survey rates they replaced; on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the methodology unlawful and ordered a replacement, so a higher California rate is more likely than not in 2027. H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024: the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the 40 passes and 3.5-acre density behind the robot count; the final 2027 California and Florida rates after the court order; and the share of California acreage in tabletop [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117].

arguments.markdown:
On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a $31,000 build not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. Five growers paid in 2026; four of them contracted 110 robot-seasons for 2027 at a $12,700 average, and the fifth, Grower D, is in discussion. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. No new grower has signed for 2027; the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher: real demand from four accounts, none a new logo [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows the first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. The buying unit includes the marketer or packer, not only the grower: the robot packs straight into retail clamshells, so whoever sells or packs the fruit must accept machine-picked berries, and the 3.8% bruising that ended Grower E's pilot shows acceptance can be lost after a field trial. Whether a marketer's acceptance is a contract condition, and who signs — owner, VP of growing or procurement — is not disclosed; the executed contracts and the packer's fruit specification would settle both. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost; grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine 2025 test farms, about $30,000 paid a pilot farm against $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost leaves $23,000-$40,000 unrecovered per pilot and $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. No lapsed account is disclosed as buying a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes -$8,100, or -85.3%, once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and debt service are two views of one asset and must not be added: cash is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only (11.5%, $2,453 a season) and -$3,051 if it amortises over four years ($6,951 a season). United Rentals earned a 38.0% rental gross margin in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at list with the v3 and +19.1% only with both list and a $31,000 v4 [S21]. The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S21].

The economics are inverted: gross margin rises as capital moves into opex, while the cash to build each robot leaves before the season.

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against $3,100 reported; at 360 robots that is 45 technicians and $1.12M, so service cost is linear. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation. At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, 11.3-12.9% and 19.7-22.4% of hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 an acre-season: one pass over an acre costs $526-599 (8 hours at the $16.45-18.71 Level I-II adverse effect wage rate over a quarter acre) and a season is 40 passes, which on 9,000 trays is $2.34-2.66 a tray all-in against a $1.75-2.25 piece rate plus burden. Growers surveyed by Western Growers require a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year the 2.84-season payback is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. At 3.8% bruising, $3,762 an acre of fruit is lost, more than the signed fee (company-reported, unverified deck figures; external benchmarks) [S1, S10, S80, S141].

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 11-13% of hand-pick labour at the signed price and 20-22% at list, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there. Tortuga deployed 150 harvesting robots and about $50M over eight years before selling its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03; FarmWise raised $65M, ran Titan as a service, moved Vulcan to dealer sales and wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms in 2025-04. Orrin's $320,313 per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000. The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. For an investor, the signed book is $1.4M of 2027 rental; the $16,500 list and $31,000 v4 must be proven before paying for fleet capex. Conditions should be executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, an independent v4 bill of materials, a service-cost build at 1:8 and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate is medium; open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price, marketer acceptance and the bruised-fruit share (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S93, S100, S116].

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unverified) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. These produce the -$8,100 contribution, 12.31-season payback and 3.08-season breakeven. Source S1.
:::

arguments.markdown:
The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool and hand-pick labour alone is worth $21,056-23,949 an acre-season, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** All 50,000 US acres at $16,500 and one robot per 3.5 acres are worth $236M; $310M needs 132% of the base. **One acre-season, three figures:** 9,000 trays (72,000 lb at 8 lb a tray), hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 and total harvest cost of $79,288; the robot fee is $2,714 an acre at $9,500 (11-13% of the wage bill) and $4,714 at $16,500 (20-22%). **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is raising beds and breeding for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S80, S10, S136, S138.
:::

| Measure | Top-down | Bottom-up | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global fresh-produce harvest labour | $42B (2025), company estimate, unverified | — | S1 |
| SAM — US strawberry harvest cost | $3.1B company estimate, unverified, against $3.47B from 43,726 California acres at $79,288 an acre | 50,000 acres × $62,000-79,000 = $3.1-4.0B | S1, S9, S10 |
| SOM — company claim, 2031 | $310M, presented as 10% of $3.1B, unverified | 18,788 robots × $16,500 = $310M, requiring 65,758 acres = 132% of the 50,000-acre base | S1 |
| SOM — tested, 2031 at 15% adoption | — | 7,500 acres ÷ 3.5 = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M (author calculation from company assumptions, unverified) | S1 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue, FY2028 | $12.9M RaaS plan, company projection, unverified | 782 robots at $16,500 = 2,737 acres = 5.5% of 50,000 acres | S1 |

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### One acre-season, three figures that reconcile
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. Yield is 9,000 trays an acre — the 8-lb flat of the UC budget, 72,000 lb. Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season. Total harvest cost is $79,288 an acre, of which hand-pick labour is 27-30%; the rest is packing materials, supervision, hauling and cooling, and none of it is what the robot displaces. The labour figure has two independent supports that agree: 1,280 picker-hours an acre-season (four picker-days a pass over 40 passes at eight hours) at the 2026 California adverse effect wage rates of $16.45 and $18.71 an hour is $21,056-23,949, and 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 a tray is $15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% payroll burden, the same range. There are 9,000 trays, not 1,125: reading a tray as eight flats understates the wage bill eight-fold, to $2,000-2,500. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill; at the $16,500 list, $4,714, or 20-22%. A 10% harvest-cost saving is worth $7,929 an acre, so the grower's payback survives the list price; what binds is quality and capital, not the size of the wage bill [S10, S12, S80, S1].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception. California holds four of Orrin's five paying growers in 2026 and Florida one; four of the five have contracted 110 robots for 2027. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia [S9, S13, S14].

| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed | Not disclosed; NASS state series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin before it moved for it. The 2026 wage-floor policy set California's entry-level and experienced adverse effect wage rates at $16.45 and $18.71 an hour and Florida's at $12.47 and $15.06, below the Farm Labor Survey rates they replaced; on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the methodology unlawful and ordered a replacement, so a higher California rate is more likely than not in 2027. The risk cuts both ways: a lower Florida floor lengthens payback, a California reversal shortens it. H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024: the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the 40 passes and 3.5-acre density behind the robot count; the final 2027 California and Florida rates after the court order; and the share of California acreage in tabletop [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117].

arguments.markdown:
On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a $31,000 build not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. Five growers paid in 2026; four of them contracted 110 robot-seasons for 2027 at a $12,700 average, and the fifth, Grower D, is in discussion. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. No new grower has signed for 2027; the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher: real demand from four accounts, none a new logo [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows the first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. The buying unit includes the marketer or packer, not only the grower: the robot packs straight into retail clamshells, so whoever sells or packs the fruit must accept machine-picked berries, and the 3.8% bruising that ended Grower E's pilot shows acceptance can be lost after a field trial. Whether a marketer's acceptance is a contract condition, and who signs — owner, VP of growing or procurement — is not disclosed; the executed contracts and the packer's fruit specification would settle both. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost; grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine 2025 test farms, about $30,000 paid a pilot farm against $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost leaves $23,000-$40,000 unrecovered per pilot and $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. No lapsed account is disclosed as buying a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company-reported, unverified) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Contribution after depreciation | (8,100) | (85.3) | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Four-year amortising debt service ($521,246 / 75) | (6,951) | 73.2 | S1 (unverified), calc |

The 41.1% gross margin is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes -$8,100, or -85.3%, once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and debt service are two views of one asset and must not be added: cash is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only (11.5%, $2,453 a season) and -$3,051 if it amortises over four years ($6,951 a season). United Rentals earned a 38.0% rental gross margin in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at list with the v3 and +19.1% only with both list and a $31,000 v4 [S21]. The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S21].

The economics are inverted: gross margin rises as capital moves into opex, while the cash to build each robot leaves before the season.

| Offer | $ per robot-season | vs signed | $ per acre (3.5 acres/robot) | % of $21,056-23,949 hand-pick labour | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-26 signed contracts | 9,500 | - | 2,714 | 11.3-12.9% | S1, S80 |
| 2027 contracted average | 12,700 | +33.7% | 3,629 | 15.2-17.2% | S1, S80 |
| 2027 list, new contracts | 16,500 | +73.7% | 4,714 | 19.7-22.4% | S1, S80 |
| Breakeven at $48,000 v3 | 17,600 | +85.3% | 5,029 | 21.0-23.9% | S1 (unverified), calc |
| Breakeven at $31,000 v4 | 13,350 | +40.5% | 3,814 | 15.9-18.1% | S1 (unverified), calc |

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against $3,100 reported; at 360 robots that is 45 technicians and $1.12M, so service cost is linear. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation. At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, 11.3-12.9% and 19.7-22.4% of hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 an acre-season: one pass over an acre costs $526-599 (8 hours at the $16.45-18.71 Level I-II adverse effect wage rate over a quarter acre) and a season is 40 passes, which on 9,000 trays is $2.34-2.66 a tray all-in against a $1.75-2.25 piece rate plus burden. Growers surveyed by Western Growers require a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year the 2.84-season payback is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5. At 3.8% bruising, $3,762 an acre of fruit is lost, more than the signed fee (company-reported, unverified deck figures; external benchmarks) [S1, S10, S80, S141].

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 11-13% of hand-pick labour at the signed price and 20-22% at list, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there. Tortuga deployed 150 harvesting robots and about $50M over eight years before selling its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03; FarmWise raised $65M, ran Titan as a service, moved Vulcan to dealer sales and wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms in 2025-04. Orrin's $320,313 per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000. The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. For an investor, the signed book is $1.4M of 2027 rental; the $16,500 list and $31,000 v4 must be proven before paying for fleet capex. Conditions should be executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, an independent v4 bill of materials, a service-cost build at 1:8 and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate is medium; open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and marketer acceptance (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S93, S100, S116].

::: evidence
**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unverified) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. These produce the -$8,100 contribution, 12.31-season payback and 3.08-season breakeven. Source S1.
:::

On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a $31,000 build not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. Five growers paid in 2026; four of them contracted 110 robot-seasons for 2027 at a $12,700 average, and the fifth, Grower D, is in discussion. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. No new grower has signed for 2027; the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher: real demand from four accounts, none a new logo [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows the first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. The buying unit includes the marketer or packer, not only the grower: the robot packs straight into retail clamshells, so whoever sells or packs the fruit must accept machine-picked berries, and the 3.8% bruising that ended Grower E's pilot shows acceptance can be lost after a field trial. Whether a marketer's acceptance is a contract condition, and who signs — owner, VP of growing or procurement — is not disclosed; the executed contracts and the packer's fruit specification would settle both. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost; grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine 2025 test farms, about $30,000 paid a pilot farm against $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost leaves $23,000-$40,000 unrecovered per pilot and $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. No lapsed account is disclosed as buying a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

Conditions should be executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, an independent v4 bill of materials, a service-cost build at 1:8 and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence on company figures; the pilot-cost estimate is medium; open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and marketer acceptance (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S93, S100, S116].

arguments.markdown:
The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool and hand-pick labour alone is worth $21,056-23,949 an acre-season, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** All 50,000 US acres at $16,500 and one robot per 3.5 acres are worth $236M; $310M needs 132% of the base. **One acre-season, three figures:** 9,000 trays (72,000 lb at 8 lb a tray), hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 and total harvest cost of $79,288; the robot fee is $2,714 an acre at $9,500 (11-13% of the wage bill) and $4,714 at $16,500 (20-22%). **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is raising beds and breeding for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S80, S10, S136, S138.
:::

| Measure | Top-down | Bottom-up | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global fresh-produce harvest labour | $42B (2025), company estimate, unverified | — | S1 |
| SAM — US strawberry harvest cost | $3.1B company estimate, unverified, against $3.47B from 43,726 California acres at $79,288 an acre | 50,000 acres × $62,000-79,000 = $3.1-4.0B | S1, S9, S10 |
| SOM — company claim, 2031 | $310M, presented as 10% of $3.1B, unverified | 18,788 robots × $16,500 = $310M, requiring 65,758 acres = 132% of the 50,000-acre base | S1 |
| SOM — tested, 2031 at 15% adoption | — | 7,500 acres ÷ 3.5 = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M (author calculation from company assumptions, unverified) | S1 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue, FY2028 | $12.9M RaaS plan, company projection, unverified | 782 robots at $16,500 = 2,737 acres = 5.5% of 50,000 acres | S1 |

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### One acre-season, three figures that reconcile
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. Yield is 9,000 trays an acre — the 8-lb flat of the UC budget, 72,000 lb. Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season. Total harvest cost is $79,288 an acre, of which hand-pick labour is 27-30%; the rest is packing materials, supervision, hauling and cooling, and none of it is what the robot displaces. The labour figure has two independent supports that agree: 1,280 picker-hours an acre-season (four picker-days a pass over 40 passes at eight hours) at the 2026 California adverse effect wage rates of $16.45 and $18.71 an hour is $21,056-23,949, and 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 a tray is $15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% payroll burden, the same range. There are 9,000 trays, not 1,125: reading a tray as eight flats understates the wage bill eight-fold, to $2,000-2,500. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill; at the $16,500 list, $4,714, or 20-22%. A 10% harvest-cost saving is worth $7,929 an acre, so the grower's payback survives the list price; what binds is quality and capital, not the size of the wage bill [S10, S12, S80, S1].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception. California holds four of Orrin's five paying growers in 2026 and Florida one; four of the five have contracted 110 robots for 2027. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia [S9, S13, S14].

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California | 43,726 acres (2026); $3.47B harvest cost (author calculation) | +2.0% acres 2025-26; terminal price -3.3% CAGR 2024-26 | Entered: 14 pilots since 2024; 4 of the 5 paying growers | 7-month season; slopes over 4% and standing water excluded; retailer bruising limits | Hand crews, harvest-aid platforms, Harvest CROO | S9, S10, S1 |
| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed | Not disclosed; NASS state series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin before it moved for it. The Department of Labor's 2025-10-02 interim final rule replaced the Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate; its 2026 rates were $16.45 and $18.71 an hour in California and $12.47 and $15.06 in Florida, below the rates they replaced, and on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the methodology unlawful and ordered a replacement, so a higher California rate is more likely than not in 2027. The risk cuts both ways: a lower Florida floor lengthens payback, a California reversal shortens it. H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024: the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the 40 passes and 3.5-acre density behind the robot count; the final 2027 California and Florida rates after the court order; and the share of California acreage in tabletop [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117].

On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a $31,000 build not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. Five growers paid in 2026; four of them contracted 110 robot-seasons for 2027 at a $12,700 average, and the fifth, Grower D, is in discussion. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. No new grower has signed for 2027; the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher: real demand from four accounts, none a new logo [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows the first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. The buying unit includes the marketer or packer, not only the grower: the robot packs straight into retail clamshells, so whoever sells or packs the fruit must accept machine-picked berries, and the 3.8% bruising that ended Grower E's pilot shows acceptance can be lost after a field trial. Whether a marketer's acceptance is a contract condition, and who signs — owner, VP of growing or procurement — is not disclosed; the executed contracts and the packer's fruit specification would settle both. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost; grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine 2025 test farms, about $30,000 paid a pilot farm against $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost leaves $23,000-$40,000 unrecovered per pilot and $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. No lapsed account is disclosed as buying a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. arguments.markdown:
The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool and hand-pick labour alone is worth $21,056-23,949 an acre-season, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** All 50,000 US acres at $16,500 and one robot per 3.5 acres are worth $236M; $310M needs 132% of the base. **One acre-season, three figures:** 9,000 trays (72,000 lb at 8 lb a tray), hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 and total harvest cost of $79,288; the robot fee is $2,714 an acre at $9,500 (11-13% of the wage bill) and $4,714 at $16,500 (20-22%). **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is raising beds and breeding for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S80, S10, S136, S138.
:::

| Measure | Top-down | Bottom-up | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global fresh-produce harvest labour | $42B (2025), company estimate, unverified | — | S1 |
| SAM — US strawberry harvest cost | $3.1B company estimate, unverified, against $3.47B from 43,726 California acres at $79,288 an acre | 50,000 acres × $62,000-79,000 = $3.1-4.0B | S1, S9, S10 |
| SOM — company claim, 2031 | $310M, presented as 10% of $3.1B, unverified | 18,788 robots × $16,500 = $310M, requiring 65,758 acres = 132% of the 50,000-acre base | S1 |
| SOM — tested, 2031 at 15% adoption | — | 7,500 acres ÷ 3.5 = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M (author calculation from company assumptions, unverified) | S1 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue, FY2028 | $12.9M RaaS plan, company projection, unverified | 782 robots at $16,500 = 2,737 acres = 5.5% of 50,000 acres | S1 |

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### One acre-season, three figures that reconcile
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. Yield is 9,000 trays an acre — the 8-lb flat of the UC budget, 72,000 lb. Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season. Total harvest cost is $79,288 an acre, of which hand-pick labour is 27-30%; the rest is packing materials, supervision, hauling and cooling, and none of it is what the robot displaces. The labour figure has two independent supports that agree: 1,280 picker-hours an acre-season (four picker-days a pass over 40 passes at eight hours) at the 2026 California adverse effect wage rates of $16.45 and $18.71 an hour is $21,056-23,949, and 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 a tray is $15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% payroll burden, the same range. There are 9,000 trays, not 1,125: reading a tray as eight flats understates the wage bill eight-fold, to $2,000-2,500. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill; at the $16,500 list, $4,714, or 20-22%. A 10% harvest-cost saving is worth $7,929 an acre, so the grower's payback survives the list price; what binds is quality and capital, not the size of the wage bill [S10, S12, S80, S1].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception. California holds four of Orrin's five paying growers in 2026 and Florida one; four of the five have contracted 110 robots for 2027. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia [S9, S13, S14].

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California | 43,726 acres (2026); $3.47B harvest cost (author calculation) | +2.0% acres 2025-26; terminal price -3.3% CAGR 2024-26 | Entered: 14 pilots since 2024; 4 of the 5 paying growers | 7-month season; slopes over 4% and standing water excluded; retailer bruising limits | Hand crews, harvest-aid platforms, Harvest CROO | S9, S10, S1 |
| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed | Not disclosed; NASS state series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin before it moved for it. The Department of Labor's 2025-10-02 interim final rule — the wage-floor policy — replaced the Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate; its 2026 rates were $16.45 and $18.71 an hour in California and $12.47 and $15.06 in Florida, below the rates they replaced, and on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the methodology unlawful and ordered a replacement, so a higher California rate is more likely than not in 2027. The risk cuts both ways: a lower Florida floor lengthens payback, a California reversal shortens it. H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024: the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the 40 passes and 3.5-acre density behind the robot count; the final 2027 California and Florida rates after the court order; and the share of California acreage in tabletop [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117].

The 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M assumed from the 2023 round size, not stated in the deck): a $36.8M stack, 40.9% of the $90.0M post. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit. At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at $79M and needs $180M for 2x, so the pre-money is best underwritten as an option struck at $79M, not a mark on the common. The structure is founder-friendly; the stack decides if a modest success reaches common. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### What it sells, and to whom

Orrin sells a robot-season, not a robot. The customer is a strawberry grower and the budget owner holds the harvest-labour line: in the 2024 UC Davis Central Coast cost study, harvest costs $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural costs, 70.4% of the $112,694 total cost per acre, so the machine targets most of the grower's cost base [S1, S10]. Growth comes from converting pilots into paid seasonal rentals: 14 pilot farms since 2024, two conversions in 2025, five paying growers in 2026, four of them contracted for 2027 (110 robots), plus 50 letters of intent. Revenue quality is thinner than the $3.2M ARR headline: $1.4M is contracted robot-seasons at the $12,700 renewal price, $1.2M is engineering services ending 2027-06-30, $0.6M is non-binding letters. The $8M ARR milestone is unreachable on the funded fleet: 360 robots at $12,700 is $4.6M, at the $16,500 list price $5.9M. Company-reported, unverified.

### Governance: five roles in one counterparty and an empty chair

The board is five seats — two common, one seed, one Series A, one independent agreed by both — but the independent seat is vacant, so the tie-breaker is unfilled and the chief executive chairs. Tallis Agricultural Machinery is at once a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the quoted manufacturer whose $33,000 unit cost underpins the $9.9M robot budget, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The chief operating officer's wholly owned services company took $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date under a contract approved by a board he sits on, and his 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer. Company-reported, unverified [S1]. Conditions before closing:

- An independent director at signing, agreed by the lead, chairing audit and compensation.
- Observer rights limited to non-confidential sessions.
- A second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials.
- Kestrel consent, a covenant waiver through the 2027 build, and Calder consent to affiliate operation and sublicensing.
- Founder reverse-vesting and a full-time chief financial officer by closing.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester matched human picking rates in a commercial operation at Duette, Florida — an open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but Driscoll's has invested in Harvest CROO and Agrobot and is talking to six harvesting startups. The hand crew, harvest-aid platform and 2025 exits discipline Orrin's price more than any rival [S27, S28, S138].

::: evidence
**The field is thinner than the narrative implies, and not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii; Tallis could build the platform. **Commercial proof is concentrated:** five paying growers in 2026, four of which contracted 110 robots for 2027. Sources: S27, S28, S34, S1.
:::

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Status (2026) | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest CROO (FL) | B8 harvester | Row-following, AI vision, LIDAR, RaaS | Trials, Duette FL, 2025-04 | "Human parity" (company, unverified); no data | Not disclosed | Florida only | 13 patents; Wish Farms backing | Florida season only; no California service | S27, S78 |
| Tortuga AgTech (US) | Model F/G | Dual-arm picking, packing | IP and team bought by Oishii, 2025 | Commercial fleet before sale | Not disclosed | 0% open-field | Commercial deployment and packing | Buyer indoor-focused | S34 |
| Agrobot (Spain) | E-Series | Self-steering picker platform | Commercial | 30-40% labour saving (company, unverified) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Low capital cost; no fruit-quality risk | Still needs a full crew | S77 |
| Waseda University / Maekawa (Japan) | Greenhouse rail harvester | Stereo cameras; stem clipper | Research | Night operation; no published rate | Not disclosed | 0% | Same night-time perception | Elevated beds only; no open field; no price | S139, S134 |
| Nanjing Agricultural University (China) | Tracked strawberry picker | Soft gripper; deep learning | Farm trial, Nanjing | 20 s/berry; 84% grasp success | Not disclosed | 0% | Low-cost hardware | Too slow for commercial crews | S135 |
| Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer / potential platform | Same BOM as Orrin v4 | Quoted v4 manufacturer; noteholder; board observer | Not applicable | Source of unit-cost quote | 0% today | Manufacturing cost; board visibility | Could build the platform; conflict | S1 |
| Hand crews | Piece-rate crew | Pickers, carts, conveyors | Universal | 8-12 trays/hour at $1.75-2.25 a tray | $1.75-2.25 a tray | 99.5% of US acres (author calculation) | Proven quality; no capex | 2025 availability shock; rising wage floor | S12 |

The direct field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm, which had reached named California growers, ceased operations; Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii. No public shares exist; the proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S28, S34, S1].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking

The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 11 by Market Analyst, 8,955 characters)
The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool and hand-pick labour alone is worth $21,056-23,949 an acre-season, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** All 50,000 US acres at $16,500 and one robot per 3.5 acres are worth $236M; $310M needs 132% of the base. **One acre-season, three figures:** 9,000 trays (72,000 lb at 8 lb a tray), hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 and total harvest cost of $79,288; the robot fee is $2,714 an acre at $9,500 (11-13% of the wage bill) and $4,714 at $16,500 (20-22%). **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is raising beds and breeding for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S80, S10, S136, S138.
:::

| Measure | Top-down | Bottom-up | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM — global fresh-produce harvest labour | $42B (2025), company estimate, unverified | — | S1 |
| SAM — US strawberry harvest cost | $3.1B company estimate, unverified, against $3.47B from 43,726 California acres at $79,288 an acre | 50,000 acres × $62,000-79,000 = $3.1-4.0B | S1, S9, S10 |
| SOM — company claim, 2031 | $310M, presented as 10% of $3.1B, unverified | 18,788 robots × $16,500 = $310M, requiring 65,758 acres = 132% of the 50,000-acre base | S1 |
| SOM — tested, 2031 at 15% adoption | — | 7,500 acres ÷ 3.5 = 2,143 robots × $16,500 = $35.4M (author calculation from company assumptions, unverified) | S1 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue, FY2028 | $12.9M RaaS plan, company projection, unverified | 782 robots at $16,500 = 2,737 acres = 5.5% of 50,000 acres | S1 |

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### One acre-season, three figures that reconcile
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces. Yield is 9,000 trays an acre — the 8-lb flat of the UC budget, 72,000 lb. Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season. Total harvest cost is $79,288 an acre, of which hand-pick labour is 27-30%; the rest is packing materials, supervision, hauling and cooling, and none of it is what the robot displaces. The labour figure has two independent supports that agree: 1,280 picker-hours an acre-season (four picker-days a pass over 40 passes at eight hours) at the 2026 California adverse effect wage rates of $16.45 and $18.71 an hour is $21,056-23,949, and 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 a tray is $15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% payroll burden, the same range. There are 9,000 trays, not 1,125: reading a tray as eight flats understates the wage bill eight-fold, to $2,000-2,500. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill; at the $16,500 list, $4,714, or 20-22%. A 10% harvest-cost saving is worth $7,929 an acre, so the grower's payback survives the list price; what binds is quality and capital, not the size of the wage bill [S10, S12, S80, S1].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception. California holds four of Orrin's five paying growers in 2026 and Florida one; four of the five have contracted 110 robots for 2027. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia [S9, S13, S14].

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California | 43,726 acres (2026); $3.47B harvest cost (author calculation) | +2.0% acres 2025-26; terminal price -3.3% CAGR 2024-26 | Entered: 14 pilots since 2024; 4 of the 5 paying growers | 7-month season; slopes over 4% and standing water excluded; retailer bruising limits | Hand crews, harvest-aid platforms, Harvest CROO | S9, S10, S1 |
| Florida | 10% of US production; acreage not disclosed | Not disclosed; NASS state series would settle it | Entered: 1 paying grower; 1 pilot ended over bruising | December-March season; rain and hurricanes; low annual utilisation | Harvest CROO (Duette, FL), hand crews | S14, S1 |
| Mexico | 20% of US terminal quotes | Not disclosed; USDA AMS movement data would settle it | Not a customer market; Guadalajara assembly only | No sales or service; different field systems | Mexican growers using hand crews | S9, S1 |

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin before it moved for it. The Department of Labor's 2025-10-02 interim final rule — the wage-floor policy — replaced the Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate; its 2026 rates were $16.45 and $18.71 an hour in California and $12.47 and $15.06 in Florida, below the rates they replaced, and on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the methodology unlawful and ordered a replacement, so a higher California rate is more likely than not in 2027. The risk cuts both ways: a lower Florida floor lengthens payback, a California reversal shortens it. H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024: the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the 40 passes and 3.5-acre density behind the robot count; the final 2027 California and Florida rates after the court order; and the share of California acreage in tabletop [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 11 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,993 characters)
On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a $31,000 build not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. Five growers paid in 2026; four contracted 110 robot-seasons for 2027 at a $12,700 average, and the fifth is in discussion. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. No new grower has signed for 2027; the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher: real demand from four accounts, none a new logo [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows the first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. The buying unit includes the marketer or packer, not only the grower: the robot packs straight into retail clamshells, so whoever sells or packs the fruit must accept machine-picked berries, and the 3.8% bruising that ended Grower E's pilot shows acceptance can be lost after a field trial. Whether a marketer's acceptance is a contract condition, and who signs — owner, VP of growing or procurement — is not disclosed; the executed contracts and the packer's fruit specification would settle both. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost; grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine 2025 test farms, about $30,000 paid a pilot farm against $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost leaves $23,000-$40,000 unrecovered per pilot and $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. No lapsed account is disclosed as buying a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

| Per unit (robot-season, 2026; company-reported, unverified) | $ | % of price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |

The gross margin of 41.1% is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes a contribution margin of -85.3%, or -$8,100, once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and debt service are two views of one asset and must not be added: cash is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only (11.5%, $2,453 a season) and -$3,051 if it amortises over four years ($6,951 a season). United Rentals earned a 38.0% rental gross margin in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at list with the v3 and +19.1% only with both list and a $31,000 v4 [S21]. The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S21].

The economics are inverted: gross margin rises as capital moves into opex, while the cash to build each robot leaves before the season.
