consensus.consensus: The company and the $4.0M of insiders committing at the mark price Orrin as the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90% pick rate, on a 2.1-season payback, 52-61% gross margins at scale and $8M of ARR in 2027, in an agtech market that will fund the 2028 round.
consensus.our_view: The thesis is consensus on the pain and non-consensus on everything that pays for it. The pain is real and independently measured; the price is not: one robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation at the signed price, 44% of the $3.2M ARR is contracted rental, the company is not alone in the field, and $69.9M of enterprise value is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x peer median. We pass at $72M pre-money.
consensus.evidence: The 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none of them signed, and omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line [S1]. The 'only above 90%' premise is contradicted by Harvest CROO's 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity open-field picking at Duette, Florida [S27]. The 52-61% margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of fleet depreciation that sits below the gross line; after it 2027 is -5.5% [S1]. Agtech venture funding fell from $53bn in 2021 to $7bn in 2025 and Q2 2026 raised $1bn against $2bn a year earlier, so the 2028 round is not a given [S127, S130]. The sector's best exit, Deere's $305M for Blue River, was four times that company's last private post-money [S128].
consensus.proof_event: A grower outside the chief operating officer's network signing a 2027 contract at or above $12,700, together with a second independent manufacturer's quote for the v4 at or below $33,000, both by 2027-03.

one_question.question: What does the v4 cost to build at 300 units, quoted by a manufacturer that is not also the largest customer?
one_question.why: At the $48,000 v3 cost no price in the range growers have signed makes a robot-season profitable - contribution is negative even at the $16,500 list - so the fleet consumes capital on every unit. At $31,000-33,000 the list price turns contribution positive ($2,650-3,150 a season) and the business becomes financeable. The answer is not a projection: two competitive quotes settle it in weeks, and it decides between a capital-consuming lease book and a business that compounds.

modules.position_sizing: "Zero at $72M pre-money. Kelly inputs: bull 2.2x at 18%, base 1.0x at 40%, bear 0.35x at 42%, expected return 0.94x; with a 1.2 net win and 0.82 probability of not winning, f* = (0.18 x 1.2 - 0.82) / 1.2 < 0, so the Kelly fraction is zero and the check size is zero. Re-entry terms: $6M at closing and $6M on two conditions (200 robots in paid service, and two independent v4 quotes at or below $33,000), at a $50-58M pre-money, a 1.5x preference and 1x pari passu warranty on the notes; total exposure $12M against a $36.8M+ preference, with the licence warranty and lender consent as conditions precedent and a $6M reserve held for the 2028 round only if the licence test is met."

rows.belief: The pain is real and countable: $79,288 an acre of harvest cost on California's Central Coast against $22,264 of cultural cost, with labour at 50-60% of variable production cost. But the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026 — the skill-based wage floor effective 2026-08-03 cut California's entry-level adverse effect wage rate to $16.45 an hour from $19.97 (-17.6%) and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23 (-23.2%) — so urgency is weaker than the deck assumes.
rows.evidence: Harvest cost per acre and labour share from the UC Central Coast budget and UC Davis cost study [S10, S12]; 2026 adverse effect wage rates from the Federal Register notice [S80]; the 10-15% crop-loss claim is company-only [S1].
rows.counter_evidence: H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024, so the guest-worker programme is relieving the shortage rather than the shortage worsening [S15]; independent crop-loss evidence is episodic (Ventura County, June 2025) rather than annual.
rows.confidence: high on the size of the cost pool; medium on the urgency
rows.change: A California court restoring the Farm Labor Survey wage basis (the OEWS basis was held unlawful on 2026-08-26, replacement pending) or falling H-2A certifications in California strawberry counties would sharpen the pain again.

rows.belief: The picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its deck: 94% pick rate on 212 company-chosen rows across 9 of 14 farms is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator, but 5.6 seconds a berry x 2 arms x 20 hours x 86% uptime is 22,114 berries, about 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours at a realistic ripe-fruit density, not 1.5. The durable advantage is 75 paid robot-seasons of labelled fleet data and service density in two California valleys; the patents are not the moat.
rows.evidence: Pick rate, bruising 3.8%, unripe 2.1%, uptime 86% and the 1.5-acre claim [S1]; the coverage arithmetic against 9,000 trays an acre and a 3-5 day pick interval [S119, S1]; Harvest CROO's identical per-arm arithmetic at 8 times the acreage shows coverage follows capital per machine [S27].
rows.counter_evidence: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, one Florida pilot ended over bruising in 2026-06, and all five own filings are ungranted — the lead gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed 2026-05, and the two core perception families are licensed from a university, lapsing to non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 [S1, S120, S86].
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: An independent field trial measuring pick rate and damage after seven days at 1 degree Celsius, or a granted claim on the gripper, would raise it; a second grower loss to bruising would lower it.

rows.belief: The crop is stable, not growing — California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0%, and terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat against $24.75 in 2025 — and the addressable revenue is far smaller than the deck: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year, so the $310M obtainable market requires 132% of the US acreage base and 15% adoption in 2031 is worth $35.4M.
rows.evidence: Acreage and price series [S9]; harvest cost per acre and 9,000 trays [S10]; the $310M, $3.1B and $42B figures are company estimates [S1].
rows.counter_evidence: Penetration can still compound quickly when the crop is redesigned for the machine: processing tomatoes went from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966 after a machine-harvestable variety — the one precedent for a fast curve, and it required a system change fresh-market berries have not made [S33].
rows.confidence: high that the plan's adoption curve is too steep
rows.change: A published adoption base rate for fresh-market berry harvesting, or a retailer programme requiring machine-harvested fruit, would move the curve.

rows.belief: The funnel is one man's twenty-year network: 5 paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026, 110 robots contracted for 2027 (31% of the 360-robot plan) plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, with 53% of 2026 seasons in two growers, the larger being the chief operating officer's former employer.
rows.evidence: Grower count, contracted robots and concentration [S1]; contract values at the $12,700 renewal average [S95].
rows.counter_evidence: Four growers did contract 110 robots for 2027 at the renewal price, so some buyers accept the quality — the objection is price and scale, not rejection; but two founder-sellers and one vice president hired 2025-06 must close 250 more robots in a four-month window [S1].
rows.confidence: medium-high on concentration; low on how the 250-robot gap closes
rows.change: A 2027 contract signed at or near list by a grower outside the COO's network, with a deposit, would raise it; a fifth consecutive quarter of founder-only selling would lower it.

rows.belief: One robot-season loses money at the price Orrin has actually signed: $3,900 of reported gross profit on $9,500 less $12,000 of depreciation on a $48,000 build is -$8,100, and contribution stays negative at every price up to a $17,600 breakeven. The reported 41% gross margin is a policy artefact of charging fleet depreciation in operating expense rather than cost of revenue.
rows.evidence: Per-season price, service and transport cost [S1]; depreciation at $48,000 over four seasons and the breakeven at $17,600 [S1, S21]; United Rentals' 38.0% rental gross margin after $2,670M of fleet depreciation is the benchmark a working lessor reaches [S21].
rows.counter_evidence: At the $16,500 list price with a $31,000 v4, contribution turns positive at $3,150 a season, so the model is not broken in principle — it is broken at today's build cost and today's price [S1].
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the service-cost line
rows.change: An audited service-cost build reconciled to the one-technician-to-eight-robots ratio ($5,201-6,305 a season against the $3,100 reported), or an independent v4 quote at or below $33,000.

rows.belief: The founding pair fits the first two problems a picking robot has — perception and farm access — and has shipped three hardware generations without a CTO; it does not fit the third. Nobody in the five-person executive group has built hardware at volume or founded and sold a company, the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, and the plan asks for 5.6x fleet growth in one season after 5.3x in two.
rows.evidence: Roles, dates and the CTO vacancy [S1]; 12 robots in 2024 to 64 in 2026 against 360 planned for 2027 [S1].
rows.counter_evidence: The VP Engineering hired 2024-02 spent eleven years in grippers, a direct match for the bruising problem, and the COO's grower relationships produced the contracted book — company-reported and unverified, as is every credential here [S1].
rows.confidence: low; every credential is company-reported and unverified
rows.change: A CTO and a manufacturing leader hired before closing, with reference checks at the four prior employers, would raise it; a second senior departure would lower it.

rows.belief: $69.9M of enterprise value is 36.8x FY2025 revenue and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue of $1.4M, against a 2.3x median for listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers; the $36.77M equal-rank 1x preference returns the $12M lead 1.0x at any exit up to $90M and needs a $180M exit for 2x. The $72M pre-money reconciles only on 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares, not the 12,000,000 printed beside it.
rows.evidence: Cap table, preference stack and multiples [S95]; peer multiples [S38, S103]; cash-equivalent pre-money of $70.05M after the $1.95M note discount [S95].
rows.counter_evidence: The mark is only a 28.6% step-up on the implied 2023 seed price of $3.67 a share over three years, and $4.0M of existing holders are committing at it — an insider signal, though one from parties with preference and related-party exposure [S95].
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the comparability of the peer set
rows.change: A third-party 409A or a priced round led by an unrelated investor at the same mark would defend it; signed 2027 contracts at list would begin to justify it.

rows.belief: No harvesting-robot company in the comparison set has sold for $100M+: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits, Deere/Blue River at $305M and Deere/Bear Flag at $250M, were autonomy platforms, while Advanced Farm and Tortuga sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts and Abundant Robotics shut down. The realistic route is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns this entry 1.1-2.8x.
rows.evidence: Precedent transactions and what each target had [S98, S96, S99, S93, S97]; base rate of 2 of 8 ag-robotics companies above $100M and 0 of 5 in harvesting [S95, S98, S96].
rows.counter_evidence: Deere and CNH have both paid up for pre-revenue autonomy, and CNH bought Advanced Farm's harvesting IP in 2025, so a strategic bid above the harvesting base rate is possible [S97, S96].
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: A strategic term sheet, or a 2028 Series B priced above $72M pre-money.

answers.most_damaging_fact: The v4 unit cost. It is the only variable that turns a loss-making lease book into a viable one, and the one input with no independent evidence: $33,000 appears once, in an August 2026 bill-of-materials quote from a counterparty that is also the $2.5M noteholder, the $1.2M-a-year customer, the board observer and a $1.0M investor. At $44,000 the $16,500 list price stops covering depreciation and no price in the deck works; at $31,000-33,000 on two independent quotes contribution turns positive at list (+$2,650-3,150 a season). Second: the $3.7M of cash and the $1.5M covenant, both unaudited, put the floor at 2027-03-10 and make the closing date an investment condition rather than a timing preference [S1, S95].
answers.company_only_claims: All of the positive claims that carry value: the $33,000 v4 cost and $48,000 v3 cost; the $3.2M ARR and its $1.4M contracted component; 110 robots contracted for 2027 and 50 letters of intent; 75 paid robot-seasons and 5 paying growers; the 94% pick rate on 212 company-chosen rows, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime; the $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II; the Calder licence terms including the 100-robot test; the preference terms; and every executive credential in section 2. The 41% gross margin is a definitional choice, not just an estimate: fleet depreciation sits in operating expense. None of these is corroborated by an independent record retrieved in this run.
answers.generic_section: Section 1 (company_overview) is the weakest: 19 claims resting only on company material, with no verification status, and one distinct source ID. It asserts the three-entity structure, the Kestrel lien, the $11.0M seed and the board composition, all unverified, while the decision turns on whether the Series A buys the parent that holds the patents and licence or the LLC that holds the grower contracts, the fleet and the debt. Section 2 (team) is next: one source ID, every credential company-reported. Both need record-level evidence, not more wording.
answers.unpriced_risk: Three. First, the California equipment prohibition: section 13 (esg) treats the rule as a pending trailer bill with a 30-40% spotter risk [S84]; AB 187 passed on 2026-08-31 without the Cal/OSHA fix, so California still requires a human driver in agricultural workplaces, the advisory committee does not meet until 2026-12-01, and the binary is a 20-25% probability of -70% to -90% of equity value [S126, S124]. Second, bridge seniority: at the 2027-03-10 covenant floor the only likely lender is the conflicted counterparty, and bridge paper prices ahead of the Series A — a 35% risk the scenario analysis folds into a generic 'round slips'. Third, preference non-equality: a 30% chance the stack is senior or 2x, worth -$3.8M of recovery at a $25M exit, which no scenario carries [S95].
answers.first_challenge: Show me the note purchase agreement and the seed certificate of designation. The entire downside in section 8 (funding_valuation) and in the scenario analysis rests on one deck sentence — that the $36.77M preference is 1x, non-participating and equal in rank across Series A, Series A-1 and Series Seed [S95]. If the 2025 notes carry a 2x or senior preference, the lead's recovery at a $25M exit falls from 0.59x to 0.21x, and at $40M from 0.96x to 0.68x. The second challenge is the build cost: a single quote from a counterparty that is also the customer, noteholder and investor is an offer, not evidence.
answers.downside_survival: The conclusion (pass) survives and strengthens; the downside model does not. A market 50% smaller caps 2031 revenue near $17.7M and a 3-5x exit at $53-88M, or 1.3-2.2x — capital returned, no venture multiple at a $72M pre-money. Revenue 30% lower takes the 2028 plan to $9.2M and the exit to $28-46M, or 0.7-1.1x. But the 0.6-1.0x bear is too generous: at a $25M exit the lead recovers 0.59x on deck terms, 0.21x if the notes are 2x senior, 0.31x behind a $10M senior 2028 round and 0.05x if a pay-to-play converts the Series A; the 1.0x floor is a $39.4-41.6M exit, not $25M. With financing six months late the covenant is breached on 2027-03-10, the 300-unit build misses the April season, the licence test fails below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 and the 2028 round is down: the position returns about its capital on the plan's own probabilities and less once structure risk is priced [S95, S123].
answers.ocr_claims: None. No OCR-derived claims are used: the deck was read as text, and every figure cited from it is labelled company-provided and unverified. The absence of registry, grant, patent-prosecution and audit records is reported as a confidence ceiling, not as evidence of misrepresentation.

rows.finding: California strawberry acreage is 43,726 in the 2026 Commission projection (32,412 fall-planted + 11,314 summer-planted) after 42,885 in 2025, and California supplies about 90% of US production; Florida is the only other significant state at about 10%.
rows.mechanism: Acreage is the denominator of every bottom-up robot count; if the US base is larger than the company's 50,000 acres, the 14,300-robot figure is understated, not overstated.
rows.benchmark: Company plan assumes about 50,000 US strawberry acres; California alone is 43,726, i.e. 87% of that base before Florida and other states.
rows.weakens: Florida acreage and the 2019-2023 NASS series were not retrieved in this run, so the 50,000-acre total cannot be reconciled exactly; the California Commission figure is a projection, not a harvested-acre census.
rows.implication: Use 50,000 acres as a floor. The market is big enough to matter, but its ceiling is set by acreage, not by the $42B global figure.
rows.confidence: high on California; medium on the national total
rows.follow_up: What are Florida planted and harvested strawberry acres for 2019-2025 in USDA NASS Quick Stats, and does the state total exceed 50,000?

rows.finding: The 2024 UC Central Coast sample budget puts harvest cost at $79,288 per acre against $22,264 of cultural costs and $112,694 of total cost per acre on 9,000 trays at $11; UC Davis puts labour at 50-60% of variable production cost and piece rates at $1.75-2.25 per flat with 8-12 flats picked per hour.
rows.mechanism: The robot competes for the harvest line, not the whole farm budget. Hand-pick labour is roughly $25,000-35,000 per acre (author calculation from the 50-60% labour share), so a robot priced at $4,714 per acre (one per 3.5 acres at $16,500) costs 13-19% of the wage bill it targets.
rows.benchmark: Robot rental of $4,714 per acre per season versus $79,288 of harvest cost and $25,000-35,000 of hand-pick labour per acre.
rows.weakens: The $79,288 harvest line bundles packing, cooling and supervision, so it overstates displaceable wages; the UC budget is one Central Coast scenario with a 48% labour overhead, and Florida costs are lower.
rows.implication: The value proposition is real on paper: even a 10% harvest-cost saving is worth about $7,929 per acre. The open question is what share of the wage bill the robot actually removes.
rows.confidence: medium: strong university source, but a sample budget summarised by trade press
rows.follow_up: What is the pure hand-pick wage line per acre (excluding trays, cooling and hauling) in the 2024 UC study, and what is the equivalent Florida budget?

rows.finding: The company's obtainable-market figure does not survive its own unit economics: $310M at $16,500 per robot-season requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, which is 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M.
rows.mechanism: Revenue = acres / 3.5 x price. At the list price the entire US strawberry acreage is worth $236M a year, so a $310M obtainable market cannot come from US strawberries at the stated density and price.
rows.benchmark: Company's own $236M full-penetration figure and its 15% 2031 adoption assumption.
rows.weakens: The $310M could include other soft fruit or higher value-based pricing, but the deck presents it as 10% of a $3.1B serviceable market and separately values strawberries alone at $236M.
rows.implication: Treat $310M as a harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast. The 2031 revenue case is closer to $35M at 15% adoption, which changes what the $72M pre-money is paying for.
rows.confidence: high: arithmetic from company figures
rows.follow_up: Which crops and what price per robot-season are inside the $310M, and what revenue does the company actually underwrite for 2031?

rows.finding: The financial plan is ahead of the adoption statement: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of 50,000 acres, not the 2% the market slide assumes; at the $12,700 renewal price it implies 7.1%.
rows.mechanism: Either the adoption curve on the market slide understates the plan the company is actually selling, or the revenue plan has no acreage basis.
rows.benchmark: Company's 2% by 2028 assumption versus its FY2028P revenue of $12.9M.
rows.weakens: Mixed pricing ($9,500 legacy, $12,700 renewal, $16,500 list) and pilot revenue make the implied robot count a range, not a point.
rows.implication: Ask management to reconcile the market slide with the financial plan before accepting either the adoption curve or the revenue build.
rows.confidence: medium: relies on company projections and a price mix
rows.follow_up: Provide the 2028 robot count and average price behind the $12.9M RaaS line.

rows.finding: The robot-density assumption is internally conservative: at 1.5 acres per 24 hours over a 210-day California season a robot covers 315 acre-passes, which at the 40-50 picks per season documented by UC Davis serves 6.3-7.9 acres, not 3.5; one robot per 3.5 acres implies about 90 passes a season.
rows.mechanism: Utilisation sets revenue per robot. If throughput is real, the fleet needed for a given acreage is smaller (about 6,300-7,900 robots for 50,000 acres), which lowers the TAM in robot units or implies the 3.5-acre figure already discounts uptime, weather and partial-row work.
rows.benchmark: Company's 1.5 acres/24h, 86% uptime and one robot per 3.5 acres versus UC Davis' 40-50 harvest passes.
rows.weakens: The 1.5 acres per 24 hours is a company measurement on selected rows; field uptime, fog, mud and row ends will lower it.
rows.implication: The robot count is not the constraint; the constraint is how many passes a robot can do at commercial quality. Underwrite revenue per robot, not acres per robot.
rows.confidence: medium: company throughput against university harvest frequency
rows.follow_up: What is the measured acres-per-24-hours on unselected commercial rows, and how many passes per season does Orrin actually contract for?

rows.finding: The labour shortage is acute but the policy tailwind is turning: H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025 (+13,358, +3.5%) with Florida above 14% of the national total, while the October 2025 interim final rule replaced the USDA Farm Labor Survey basis for the AEWR with BLS OEWS data and is under litigation; trade summaries conflict, one showing the average AEWR falling to $15.96 from $17.74 and another showing entry-level rates up about 3.7% with declines in 13 states.
rows.mechanism: The AEWR sets the grower's legal alternative wage, so a lower wage floor lengthens robot payback exactly when the technology is trying to scale; a higher floor shortens it.
rows.benchmark: FY2019 berries were 10% of 258,000 certified H-2A jobs; FY2025 total is 398,258. June 2025 Ventura County enforcement left up to 70% of workers absent.
rows.weakens: The structural-shortage story is supported by the 2025 enforcement shock but not by the guest-worker programme, which has kept expanding; the direction of the 2026-27 wage floor is unresolved and the DOL rate table returned HTTP 503 on 2026-10-30.
rows.implication: Policy is the biggest single swing factor in willingness to pay. Model both a 4% wage increase and a 10% cut; do not underwrite the deck's 10-15% crop-loss premise as permanent.
rows.confidence: high on H-2A counts and the rule change; low on the 2026-27 rate level
rows.follow_up: What are the final 2026-27 AEWRs for California and Florida, and what hourly rate do Santa Maria and Plant City growers actually pay hand pickers?

rows.finding: The only comparable mechanisation succeeded through crop redesign, not a drop-in machine: California processing tomatoes went from 25 machines and 0.5% of the crop in 1961 to 512 machines and 70% in 1966, after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers switched to once-over harvest.
rows.mechanism: Mechanisation is a system change: uniform ripening, one pass and an industrial end use. Fresh-market strawberries are picked 40-50 times and graded on appearance, so the tomato curve is an upper bound on speed.
rows.benchmark: 0.5% to 70% in five years for processing tomatoes versus 0% of US fresh strawberry acres harvested commercially by robot in 2025 and the plan's 2% by 2028 / 15% by 2031.
rows.weakens: The tomato case proves adoption can be fast when genetics, agronomy and the buyer all change together, which is the scenario Orrin would need; it also shows a machine alone was not enough.
rows.implication: Use 2-5% specialty-crop robotic harvest penetration as the base case for 2028 and treat 15% by 2031 as the upside case that requires a variety and buyer reset.
rows.confidence: high on the history; medium on the analogy
rows.follow_up: Has any US retailer or shipper committed to a robot-picked fresh strawberry programme, and do the varieties in Orrin's pilot farms ripen uniformly enough for night-only passes?

plan.decision_question: Is the US strawberry harvest-labour pool large and urgent enough to support 2% acreage adoption by 2028 and 15% by 2031, and is the $310M obtainable market arithmetically reachable at the company's own price and robot density?
plan.thesis_sentence: The harvest-labour pool is real — roughly $3.1-3.5B a year of US strawberry harvest cost, with hand-pick labour around $25,000-35,000 an acre — but at the company's own $16,500 price and one-robot-per-3.5-acres density, 100% of US strawberry acreage is worth only about $236M a year, so the $310M obtainable market is the size of the cost pool rather than a revenue forecast, and the investment case depends on adoption speed and pricing power, not on market size.
plan.why_different: This section sizes the prize and tests the adoption arithmetic; the competition section tests who else can take the same harvest budget, and the financial section tests whether Orrin can deliver at its cost structure.
plan.mechanism: Revenue = strawberry acres x penetration / acres per robot x price per robot-season. The grower's willingness to pay is bounded by the hand-pick wage bill the robot displaces (roughly $25,000-35,000 an acre), which the AEWR sets at the margin; the plan's $310M requires 132% of US strawberry acreage at the stated density and price.
plan.comparison_set: Processing-tomato mechanisation (0.5% to 70% in five years after a varietal and system redesign), current robotic harvest of fresh strawberries (no commercial scale identified in 2025), and H-2A growth (398,258 certified positions in FY2025, +3.5%).
plan.counter_evidence: The 2025 immigration enforcement shock (up to 70% of workers absent in Ventura County) makes the shortage urgent, and a lower 2026-27 AEWR would weaken the grower's willingness to pay; a Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising; tabletop and tunnel acres are excluded from the addressable set; and hand crews remain the default for small growers.
plan.visual: A market-size table with TAM, SAM and SOM built top-down and bottom-up, plus a regional table separating California, Florida, Mexico and the non-US competitor geographies.
plan.prohibited: huge market, large and growing, strong demand, clear runway, tailwinds, well positioned, fierce competition, risks are manageable, about 5

rows.finding: One acre-season reconciles to 9,000 trays (8-lb flats, about 72,000 lb), hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 and total harvest cost of $79,288. Hand-pick labour is 27-30% of harvest cost. The wage bill is independently supported by 1,280 picker-hours at the 2026 California AEWR of $16.45-18.71 ($21,056-23,949) and by 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 ($15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% burden). Reading a tray as eight flats gives $2,000-2,500, an eight-fold unit error.
rows.mechanism: The robot displaces the picking wage line only, not packing materials, supervision, hauling or cooling, so the comparable figure is $21,056-23,949 and the fee is $2,714 an acre at $9,500 (11-13%) or $4,714 at $16,500 (20-22%).
rows.benchmark: The $25,000-35,000 figure derived from a 50-60% labour share of variable cost, and the $2,000-2,500 figure implied by 1,125 flats an acre
rows.weakens: All hand-cost figures in the report that are not the $21,056-23,949 wage line; the $79,288 budget line is total harvest cost, not labour.
rows.implication: Replace every hand-pick figure with $21,056-23,949 an acre-season and the $236M full-adoption ceiling; the grower payback survives the $16,500 list, so quality and capital, not price, bind adoption.
rows.confidence: high: two independent constructions agree within the range, and the AEWR build is exact (1,280 hours x $16.45/18.71)
rows.follow_up: Confirm the 40-pass season and the 8-lb tray weight with the grower contracts and the UC budget's harvest line.

rows.finding: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports 'limited strawberry acreage' under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and newer tabletop systems using them; no US tabletop acreage figure is published. Driscoll's says it helps growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits.
rows.mechanism: Tabletop and tunnel production moves acreage to a different robot format, and a mechanisation-bred variety can move acreage to a once-over machine; both shrink the open-field selective-picking base rather than compete for it.
rows.benchmark: The 50,000-acre US base and 43,726 California acres in 2026
rows.weakens: The implicit assumption that all 50,000 acres are open-field and available to a furrow-running robot.
rows.implication: Apply a haircut to the base and demand evidence that Orrin can serve tabletop, or cap the addressable market at open-field acreage.
rows.confidence: medium: direction is documented, acreage is not
rows.follow_up: What share of California and Florida strawberry acreage is tabletop or high tunnel, and what is the planting trend?

rows.finding: Processing tomatoes went from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966, but only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass; Driscoll's is now optimising berry genetics for mechanisation.
rows.mechanism: Genetic change, not robot dexterity, drove the fastest specialty-crop mechanisation on record; a berry variety bred for once-over harvest would change the machine the grower buys.
rows.benchmark: Processing tomato mechanisation 1961-1966
rows.weakens: The adoption curve's implicit assumption that selective robots are the only mechanisation path for strawberries.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a selective-picking monopoly; the breeding route is a substitute that could bypass Orrin.
rows.confidence: high on the tomato history, low on berry timing
rows.follow_up: Which berry marketers have active machine-harvest breeding trials, and for processing or fresh use?

rows.finding: H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024; the AEWR basis changed to OEWS on 2025-10-02, and the 2026 notice set California entry-level and experienced rates at $16.45 and $18.71 an hour, Florida $12.47 and $15.06, before the 2026-08-26 court order reopened the methodology.
rows.mechanism: The guest-worker programme expands the grower's alternative labour supply and the wage floor sets the robot's payback; a lower AEWR lengthens payback, a court reversal shortens it.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 H-2A certifications and the prior Farm Labor Survey AEWR
rows.weakens: The deck's 10-15% crop-loss claim and the assumption of an ever-worsening shortage.
rows.implication: The labour shortage is real but policy-relieved; underwrite adoption on wage trends, not on a permanent shortage.
rows.confidence: high on certifications, medium on the 2027 rate after litigation
rows.follow_up: What are the final 2027 California and Florida rates after the replacement rule?

rows.finding: California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces about 90% of the US crop; USDA AMS terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline.
rows.mechanism: A flat-to-shrinking crop value limits how much growers can pay per acre, so robot revenue must come from penetration and price, not crop growth.
rows.benchmark: 2024-2026 California acreage and terminal prices
rows.weakens: Any market-growth case for the robot.
rows.implication: Model Orrin as a share-gainer in a mature crop; do not rely on strawberry market growth.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are Florida acreage and value for 2024-2026, which NASS state series would settle?

plan.decision_question: Is the harvest-labour need large and urgent enough to support 2% of US strawberry acreage by 2028, 15% by 2031 and 10% of a $3.1B serviceable market by 2031?
plan.thesis_sentence: The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool and hand-pick labour is worth $21,056-23,949 an acre-season, but Orrin's $310M obtainable market is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year and 15% adoption is worth $35.4M, and the base shrinks further once tabletop production and mechanisation breeding are counted.
plan.why_different: This section sizes and tests the demand; the competition section maps who else bids for the same harvest budget and the technology section covers the product.
plan.mechanism: One unit, the acre-season: 9,000 trays (about 72,000 lb), hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 and total harvest cost of $79,288. The robot fee is 11-13% of the wage bill at $9,500 and 20-22% at $16,500, so adoption depends on quality, capital and the wage floor, not on the headline labour market.
plan.comparison_set: Processing tomatoes 1961-1966; California acreage and terminal prices 2024-2026; H-2A certifications FY2024-FY2025; the $236M full-adoption revenue ceiling.
plan.counter_evidence: H-2A expansion and a lower OEWS-based wage floor relieve the shortage; tabletop and once-over breeding shrink the addressable acres; strawberry prices are falling; the $310M obtainable market is 132% of the base.
plan.visual: Market size table (TAM/SAM/SOM top-down and bottom-up) and the regional market table.
plan.prohibited: huge market; strong team; high barriers to entry; clear business model; fierce competition; risks are manageable; well positioned; recently; about 5; many patents

Read Harvest CROO April 2025 press release, Tevel product site, Sacramento Business Journal Advanced Farm closure, Future Farming Oishii-Tortuga acquisition, The Robot Report Abundant shutdown, HortiDaily Root AI acquisition
SEC EDGAR full-text search for Advanced Farm Technologies

rows.finding: Harvest CROO Robotics reported on 2025-04-24 that its B8 autonomous harvester reached performance rates on par with human harvesting in a commercial picking operation at Duette, Florida, with 13 patents, an NVIDIA-based vision upgrade and a robotics-as-a-service model.
rows.mechanism: A direct open-field competitor with a working machine and a grower-backed founder (Wish Farms) turns Orrin's differentiating claim into a comparison the buyer can test, and gives the buyer a second bid.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's 94% pick rate and 3.8% bruising on 212 selected rows versus Harvest CROO's undefined 'on par with human harvesting'.
rows.weakens: Harvest CROO publishes no pick rate, bruising rate, throughput per acre, price or count of paying growers; the claim is company-issued and unverified, and the Florida season is only December-March, which limits asset utilisation.
rows.implication: The deck's 'only above 90% in open field' claim is contradicted by a public claim from a named competitor. Price the risk of a Florida price contest and ask for Harvest CROO's independent trial data.
rows.confidence: medium: near-primary company release, no third-party measurement
rows.follow_up: Has any independent agronomist or grower measured Harvest CROO's pick rate, bruising and cost per flat against a hand crew?

rows.finding: The two most credible US strawberry-robot peers left the market in 2025: Advanced Farm Technologies, which had reached named commercial strawberry growers, ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and engineering team to vertical-farming company Oishii.
rows.mechanism: Exit removes near-term price competition but also shows that field reliability, service cost and the next financing round, not picking demos, decide survival; Orrin's RaaS model shifts capex to its own balance sheet, which makes it more exposed to the same financing risk.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's $48,000 v3 unit cost, 2.1-season payback target and $3.7M cash against a $410,000 monthly net burn.
rows.weakens: Both exits have company-specific causes that are not fully disclosed; Tortuga's buyer was an indoor-farming company, which may reflect a protected-environment route rather than a verdict on open-field demand.
rows.implication: The competitive field is thinner than the technology narrative implies, but the base rate of failure is high. Underwrite Orrin's service cost and uptime, not its demo.
rows.confidence: high on the exits; low on their causes
rows.follow_up: Why did Advanced Farm fail to raise, and what were its gross margins and uptime at exit? What did Oishii pay for Tortuga and what fleet did Tortuga have in service?

rows.finding: The status quo is a piece-rate hand crew: $1.75-2.25 per flat, 8-12 flats per hour, 40-50 passes a season, labour at 50-60% of variable cost, with conveyors already raising picker productivity.
rows.mechanism: The grower compares the robot with a crew that costs $16-27 per hour per picker and is paid by output; a robot that runs slower than the crew or bruises fruit has to beat the crew on cost per saleable flat, not on cost per hour.
rows.benchmark: Robot at $4,714 per acre per season versus a hand-pick wage bill of roughly $25,000-35,000 per acre.
rows.weakens: The 2025 enforcement shock left up to 70% of workers absent in Ventura County, so the crew is not always available at any price, which is the strongest argument for automation.
rows.implication: The addressable buyer is a large grower with a labour-availability problem and a packing line that can absorb robot-picked fruit, not every strawberry farm.
rows.confidence: high on the wage structure; medium on current availability
rows.follow_up: What share of Orrin's contracted acres would have gone unpicked without the robots, and what did those growers pay in overtime or H-2A costs in 2026?

rows.finding: Agrobot markets a solar-propelled, self-steering strawberry harvest-aid platform that carries pickers and claims 30-40% labour savings at near-zero running cost; it assists rather than replaces the crew.
rows.mechanism: Partial automation can capture much of the harvest-cost saving with a fraction of the capital and no fruit-quality risk, which caps what a grower will pay for full autonomy.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's full autonomy at $16,500 per robot-season versus a harvest-aid platform sold or leased at an undisclosed price.
rows.weakens: Company promotional claim with no independent trial data, price, units sold or named growers.
rows.implication: Harvest aids are the most under-priced competitor in the deck. Orrin must show that full autonomy beats a 30-40% labour saving enough to justify its fee.
rows.confidence: low: company video only
rows.follow_up: What does an Agrobot platform cost, and has any California or Florida grower measured its labour saving against a conveyor-equipped crew?

rows.finding: The 2021 harvest-robotics cohort failed on traction and financing, not on picking: Abundant Robotics shut down with its liquidation memo citing an inability to develop market traction, and Root AI was sold to AppHarvest for $60M after building an indoor tomato picker.
rows.mechanism: Harvest robotics is a capital-intensive hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume, while growers buy on a one-season payback; the gap between the two killed the first cohort and applies directly to Orrin's $48,000 unit cost and 2.1-season payback.
rows.benchmark: Abundant raised capital and ran commercial apple trials for years before liquidation in 2021; Orrin is raising $18M after 75 paid robot-seasons.
rows.weakens: Abundant targeted apples with a vacuum picker and Root AI targeted indoor farms, so neither is a direct strawberry comparable; 2021 capital markets were also unusually tight for hardware.
rows.implication: The failure mode to underwrite is not 'the robot cannot pick' but 'the robot cannot be built and serviced cheaply enough before the money runs out'.
rows.confidence: high on the facts; medium on the analogy
rows.follow_up: What is Orrin's service cost per robot-season at 360 robots, and how much of the $48,000 unit cost is labour that Tallis can remove at 500 units?

rows.finding: Orrin's own commercial record contains the counter-evidence: a Plant City grower ended its pilot over fruit bruising, 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers, and the price rises from $9,500 in 2025-26 to a $16,500 2027 list (+74%) with renewals averaging $12,700.
rows.mechanism: Concentration and churn reveal willingness to pay: a 3.8% bruising rate is enough to lose a Florida buyer, and a 74% price increase is being tested on a customer base that has not yet renewed at that level.
rows.benchmark: Hand-pick bruising is the quality benchmark; Orrin's own 3.8% puncture/bruise rate and one lost pilot.
rows.weakens: Four other growers contracted 2027 robots (110 units across three named contracts), so some buyers accept the quality at the renewal price.
rows.implication: Quality, not pick rate, is the commercial gate. Ask for bruise rates by variety, season and retailer specification before assuming the 2027 price holds.
rows.confidence: high: company disclosure against itself
rows.follow_up: What bruising rate do Marisol Ridge and Pajaro Bluff accept in their retail contracts, and what happened to the 11 robots Grower E returned?

rows.finding: Non-strawberry harvest robots are not direct competitors: Tevel's flying robots pick apples, peaches, apricots, nectarines, plums and pears for named orchard customers in Italy, California and Chile, and no strawberry product or customer is listed.
rows.mechanism: An orchard robot cannot pick a strawberry without a new end-effector, perception model and row system, so its capital and learning do not transfer directly; it is a valuation and technology comparable, not a bidder for the same harvest budget.
rows.benchmark: Tevel's named commercial customers versus Orrin's five paying growers.
rows.weakens: Tevel or an orchard player could enter strawberries with a purpose-built arm, and the deck itself flags well-funded greenhouse robot companies moving into open fields.
rows.implication: Do not count orchard robotics as current competition; do count it as the source of the next well-capitalised entrant.
rows.confidence: high on scope; medium on intent
rows.follow_up: Which orchard-robot company has the shortest technical path to a strawberry end-effector, and has any filed strawberry patents since 2024?

plan.decision_question: Is Orrin really alone in open-field strawberry picking above a 90% pick rate, and what happens to its $12,700-16,500 price per robot-season if it is not?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin is not alone — Harvest CROO publicly claimed human-parity open-field strawberry harvesting in Florida in April 2025 — but the discipline on its price comes less from rival robots than from the hand crew it must beat and from harvest-aid platforms that take part of the saving at a fraction of the capital, and the 2025 exit of Advanced Farm and the absorption of Tortuga by Oishii show that reliability and unit economics, not a shortage of entrants, are what break harvest-robotics companies.
plan.why_different: This section identifies who else can take the grower's harvest budget and what that does to price and share; the technology section tests whether Orrin's robot works, and the market section tests whether the pool is large enough.
plan.mechanism: Every contender competes for the same harvest budget, which is anchored to the hand-pick piece rate ($1.75-2.25 per flat) and the AEWR. A competitor that reaches human parity converts the market from a technology race into a price contest on displaced labour; a competitor that fails the way Advanced Farm and Abundant Robotics failed removes capacity but also proves the unit-economics constraint.
plan.comparison_set: Harvest CROO (direct, Florida), Advanced Farm (direct, closed 2025), Tortuga (direct, absorbed by Oishii in 2025), Agrobot (harvest-aid substitute), Tevel and FFRobotics (orchard non-comparables), hand crews (status quo) and the 2021 harvest-robotics exit cohort (Abundant Robotics, Root AI).
plan.counter_evidence: Harvest CROO's parity claim is unverified and Florida-only; Orrin's 94% pick rate and 3.8% bruising are company measurements on selected rows; a Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising; the $9,500 to $16,500 price increase is untested at scale and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers; equipment makers and Tallis could integrate picking arms onto platforms that already sell.
plan.visual: A per-product competitor table (direct, substitute, non-comparable, future entrant) with technology, status, performance, price, share and source, plus a positioning table and a SWOT quad.
plan.prohibited: no competition, first-mover advantage, moat, best-in-class, strong team, high barriers to entry, fierce competition, well positioned

rows.finding: Waseda University's Sugano Lab, with Maekawa Manufacturing, runs a rail-mounted strawberry harvester under elevated greenhouse beds, using stereo cameras at night and a stem-clipping end effector; it is a research project with no commercial deployment or price. Japan's harvesting robotics segment is characterised as premium greenhouse, not mass-market.
rows.mechanism: Japanese development targets elevated protected culture, the format that tabletop production uses, so it competes for the tabletop acreage rather than setting an open-field price ceiling.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's open-field furrow-running platform at $16,500 per season
rows.weakens: The claim that the perception and night-picking stack cannot be bought or replicated.
rows.implication: Japan is not a near-term price threat to the $16,500 list, but it confirms the perception stack is being solved in public and the tabletop format has a robot supply.
rows.confidence: high on the project, low on Japan's commercial status
rows.follow_up: Which Japanese supplier has a commercial strawberry harvester in service, at what price and on how many farms?

rows.finding: Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked strawberry-picking robot with a soft pneumatic gripper and drag-and-rotate stem detachment: about 20 seconds per berry and an 84% grasp success rate at a farm in Jiangning, Nanjing; no price or commercial deployment is reported.
rows.mechanism: Chinese academic work is solving gentle, stem-free picking with low-cost hardware; at 20 seconds a berry it is far slower than Orrin's 5.6 seconds per arm, so it is a capability signal, not a 2026 competitor.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's 5.6 seconds a berry per arm and 94% pick rate
rows.weakens: Any claim that gentle robotic picking is a durable Western monopoly.
rows.implication: The low-end price ceiling is not yet set; watch Chinese commercialisation for a machine priced below $16,500 per season.
rows.confidence: medium: single state-media report, no independent metrics
rows.follow_up: Is the Nanjing robot a prototype or a product, and what does it cost per season?

rows.finding: Driscoll's has invested in Harvest CROO and Agrobot, is in active conversations with six automated strawberry harvesting startups, will optimise its breeding programme for mechanisation traits and is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height.
rows.mechanism: The largest berry marketer is a gatekeeper to grower adoption and is hedging across rivals; its breeding and tabletop push can route acreage away from selective open-field picking.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026
rows.weakens: The deck's 'only player' premise and the assumption that adoption is a direct grower sale.
rows.implication: Orrin needs a marketer relationship or a defensible quality niche; a marketer-backed rival can scale faster.
rows.confidence: high on Driscoll's statements, medium on the competitive effect
rows.follow_up: Which of the six startups has a paid commercial deployment with Driscoll's growers in 2026?

rows.finding: Tallis Agricultural Machinery is Orrin's quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in the round; it is the source of the unit-cost quote and could build a competing platform from the same bill of materials.
rows.mechanism: A manufacturing partner with the BOM, the cost data and board visibility can forward-integrate; the relationship is both a cost advantage and a conflict.
rows.benchmark: Contract-manufacturer forward integration in agricultural equipment
rows.weakens: The assumption that Orrin controls its manufacturing cost curve and its IP.
rows.implication: Price the Tallis relationship as a strategic risk and diligence the exclusivity, IP assignment and non-compete terms.
rows.confidence: high that the relationship exists, medium that Tallis would compete
rows.follow_up: What contract terms prevent Tallis from building a competing strawberry platform, and who owns the v4 tooling?

rows.finding: A hand crew costs $1.75-2.25 a flat at 8-12 flats an hour and is paid by output; Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost.
rows.mechanism: The robot competes with the grower's harvest budget, and a harvest-aid platform captures part of the saving with none of the autonomy or fruit-quality risk.
rows.benchmark: Orrin at $4,714 an acre against $25,000-35,000 of hand-pick labour an acre
rows.weakens: The framing that Orrin competes only with other autonomous harvesters.
rows.implication: The cheapest competitor is not another robot; Orrin must beat a crew plus a platform on cost per tray and bruising.
rows.confidence: high on crew economics, low on Agrobot's claim
rows.follow_up: What is the measured labour saving of a conveyor or platform per acre in California strawberries?

rows.follow_up: Which marketer or packer accepts machine-picked fruit, on what bruising spec, and by what date does each pilot convert?

rows.finding: Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025 after named California commercial growers; Tortuga's IP, assets and team went to Oishii; Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 on a failure to develop market traction; Root AI sold to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021.
rows.mechanism: The failures were unit economics, field reliability and the next financing round, not picking: hardware cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback.
rows.benchmark: The 2021 robotic-harvest cohort and the 2025 consolidation
rows.weakens: The idea that a thinning field is a durable moat; the same causes apply to Orrin's $48,000 unit cost and 2.1-season payback.
rows.implication: Underwrite the financing runway and unit-cost curve as hard as the picking performance.
rows.confidence: high on the exits, medium on the causes
rows.follow_up: What did Advanced Farm's last unit cost and price per season look like before it closed?

rows.finding: Agrobot's self-steering platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving at near-zero running cost; hand crews pick 8-12 flats an hour at $1.75-2.25 a tray; a picking arm on an existing platform is cheaper than a new fleet.
rows.mechanism: The robot competes for the harvest budget with capital-light substitutes that capture part of the saving without autonomy or bruising risk, so Orrin's price is capped below the full wage bill.
rows.benchmark: Orrin at $2,714-4,714 an acre against hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949
rows.weakens: The assumption that the only alternative is a hand crew at the full wage bill.
rows.implication: Expect price pressure from picker-assist platforms before robot-to-robot pressure.
rows.confidence: medium: the labour-saving claim is company-issued
rows.follow_up: What does an Agrobot platform cost per acre-season, and how many are in commercial use?

rows.finding: Waseda University's Sugano Lab with Maekawa Manufacturing runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated greenhouse beds; Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked picker at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success; Washington State University has built a robot to pick hidden strawberries. All are research, with no commercial open-field deployment and no published price.
rows.mechanism: The perception stack is being solved in public, which erodes the licensed families' value when the Calder licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31, but none is a commercial open-field rival in 2026.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's 94% pick rate and 5.6 seconds a berry per arm
rows.weakens: The technology moat, not the current market position; Nanjing's 20 seconds a berry is slower than Orrin's two-arm rate.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a perception monopoly; price the licence cliff and the low-cost hardware route.
rows.confidence: high on the research, low on the price point because none is published
rows.follow_up: What would a Chinese or Japanese protected-culture unit cost at volume, and would either enter open field?

plan.decision_question: Is Orrin really alone in open-field strawberry picking above 90%, and what happens to pricing if it is not?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin is not alone: Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025, the 2025 consolidation removed two rivals but left the field thin, and the grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a $16,500 robot while the marketer, not only the grower, must accept machine-picked fruit.
plan.why_different: This section maps who bids for the same harvest budget and what the competition does to price; the market section sizes the pool and the technology section covers the product.
plan.mechanism: The robot bids for the grower's harvest budget against hand crews, harvest-aid platforms and picking arms on existing platforms; the grower's buying unit also includes the marketer/packer who must accept machine-picked fruit, and the price converges on the displaced wage line of $21,056-23,949 an acre.
plan.comparison_set: Harvest CROO, Agrobot, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, FFRobotics, Waseda/Maekawa, Nanjing, Tallis, hand crews and harvest-aid platforms; the 2021 cohort (Abundant, Root AI, Traptic); the 2025 consolidation.
plan.counter_evidence: Harvest CROO's April 2025 open-field parity claim; Agrobot's low-capital picker-assist; Tallis forward-integration; Japanese and Chinese prototypes; tabletop and once-over breeding shrinking the base; marketer acceptance of machine-picked fruit; one Florida pilot lost to bruising.
plan.visual: Competitor table and positioning table, with the SWOT quad.
plan.prohibited: huge market; strong team; high barriers to entry; clear business model; fierce competition; risks are manageable; well positioned; recently; about 5; many patents

rows.source_type: primary (DOL notice 91 FR 48946) as reported by independent trade press; the DOL state table itself returned HTTP 503
rows.finding: The 2026 H-2A wage floor for California fell from $19.97/hr (the last Farm Labor Survey rate, in force to 2025-10-01) to $16.45/hr at Skill Level I and $18.71/hr at Skill Level II, a 17.6% cut at Level I; Florida fell from $16.23/hr to $12.47/hr and $15.06/hr, a 23.2% cut at Level I. Rates took effect 2026-08-03, and 2026-08-17 in the 17 states covered by Kansas v. DOL, which include Florida.
rows.mechanism: The AEWR is a legal floor paid both to H-2A workers and to US workers in corresponding employment, so it sets the marginal cost of an hour of hand picking and therefore the maximum a grower will pay to avoid that hour. A 17.6% cut in the floor cuts hand-harvest cost per acre by 17.6% with no change in the robot's price or cost.
rows.benchmark: Prior Farm Labor Survey basis: California $19.97, Florida $16.23. National average AEWR used for H-2A labour contractor surety bonds fell to $15.96 from $17.74, about -10%.
rows.weakens: Provisional: on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the interim final rule unlawful on all four challenged components, ordered a new methodology and required DOL to warn employers of possible back wage adjustments.
rows.implication: The grower's alternative cost fell faster than the robot's price in 2026. Do not underwrite 2027 renewals at $12,700 as if the labour shortage had deepened; model the wage floor as a litigated variable.
rows.confidence: high on the rates (two independent reports of the same notice); medium on durability, because the rule is in litigation
rows.follow_up: What will DOL's replacement methodology set for California Skill Level I before the 2027 season, and does a back-wage order reach 2026-season growers?

rows.source_type: company-provided (deck) combined with primary wage data; the arithmetic is mine
rows.finding: On the deck's own productivity figure (one picker covers about 0.25 acre a day) and the 2026 California floor, a single pass over one acre costs $526 of hand labour at Level I and $599 at Level II, at 8 paid hours. A 40-pass season is $21,053-$23,948 an acre; a 60-pass season is $31,580-$35,922. The robot at $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres is $2,714 an acre, 7.5%-13% of that; at the 2027 list price of $16,500 it is $4,714 an acre, 13%-22%.
rows.mechanism: A grower buys the robot out of the hand-labour budget, so the ceiling on price is hand cost avoided less quality losses and overtime premiums avoided. The robot is priced an order of magnitude below the labour it displaces, so price is not the constraint on adoption and the 74% price increase from $9,500 to $16,500 is not the risk it looks like in the financials.
rows.benchmark: No company disclosure of grower payback or of a hand-harvest cost per acre. The UC Davis 2024 Central Coast strawberry cost study is the reference benchmark and its harvest-labour figures were not obtained.
rows.weakens: Depends on a company estimate of picker productivity and on an assumed number of passes; a robot that completes fewer passes earns less of that avoided cost than the comparison implies.
rows.implication: The adoption constraint is quality and uptime, not price. A valuation case that leans on the 2027 list price increase should be discounted until bruising is below the hand-picked benchmark.
rows.confidence: medium; the wage figures are solid, the pass count is assumed
rows.follow_up: How many harvest passes does a California strawberry field take in a season, and what does the UC 2024 study put harvest labour at per acre and per tray?

rows.source_type: primary wage data plus company-provided pricing; the arithmetic is mine
rows.finding: The $3.52 an hour cut in the California Level I rate removes about $4,224 of hand-harvest cost per acre over a 40-pass season (160 picker-days at $131.60 falling to $105.20). That is 1.6 times the robot's $2,714 an acre-season price, so one court ruling is worth more to the grower per acre than a season of Orrin's service.
rows.mechanism: When the policy input is larger than the product's price, the value proposition is partly a function of litigation the company does not control. It cuts both ways: reinstating a higher floor would add value equal to 1.6 robot-seasons an acre.
rows.benchmark: Against a 17.6% cut in the wage floor and a $2,714 an acre robot price.
rows.weakens: Assumes the robot covers the acres and passes it is priced for; if it works a fraction of the season the comparison overstates the stake.
rows.implication: The 2027 pricing environment is set by a docket, not by sales execution, which argues for a milestone-linked tranche rather than a single close.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Will growers build their 2027 labour budget on the OEWS rate, the old Farm Labor Survey rate, or wait for the new methodology?

rows.source_type: primary (Federal Register notice) plus independent advisers
rows.finding: USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter at 0%, but a non-qualifying robot pays about 10% on customs value: $3,300 on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, equal to 26% of the $12,700 2027 renewal price and 85% of the 2026 gross profit of $3,900 a robot-season. Section 232 duties on steel, aluminium and copper (50%) apply even to USMCA goods. On 2026-10-28 a Section 232 robotics proclamation found imports threaten national security, imposed no tariff, and set a first joint Commerce-USTR update within 180 days, about 2027-04-26, with tariffs, quotas and fees left open.
rows.mechanism: Orrin owns the fleet, so an import duty is levied on its own capital cost rather than passed to the grower. It lands on the $9.9M robot budget and on the Kestrel facility secured on those robots, which requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times.
rows.benchmark: MFN duty on agricultural machinery is effectively zero and national USMCA utilization reached 85% in January 2026, so the entire exposure is policy-created rather than tariff-schedule-created.
rows.weakens: Whether the robot meets USMCA rules of origin is not disclosed; 10% is the non-qualifying case, and the metals exposure depends on undisclosed material content. The 180-day clock may end in a negotiated outcome with no duty.
rows.implication: Stress the 2027 build at +10% landed cost ($990,000 on $9.9M) and at a 25% Section 232 outcome ($2.48M, which would consume the round). Make a USMCA certificate of origin a condition precedent.
rows.confidence: high on the architecture of the rules; medium on the exposure size
rows.follow_up: Does Orrin hold a USMCA certificate of origin for v3 and v4, and what share of the bill of materials is steel, aluminium or copper?

rows.source_type: company-provided (deck) plus primary statute and independent practice guidance
rows.finding: The university licence pays 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 a year minimum; the minimum binds in FY2026 (2.5% of $0.71M is $17,750, so the floor is 5.6% of RaaS revenue), and the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet in 2026. If the licensed inventions were federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires the exclusive US licensee to agree that products embodying the invention are manufactured substantially in the United States, while grippers and wiring harnesses are assembled in Guadalajara.
rows.mechanism: Exclusivity on the two families is the legal bar to a better-funded entrant buying the same rights from the university. Conversion to non-exclusive removes that bar at a fixed date, and the licensor holds no equity, so it has no upside to trade away for an extension. Section 204 separately conditions the exclusive US right on domestic manufacture.
rows.benchmark: University practice is a schedule of escalating diligence milestones with cure periods and step-in rights; a single binary test at a fixed date with no cure is harsher than the norm.
rows.weakens: The 360-robot 2027 plan clears the threshold comfortably, so conversion requires a slippage of about 72% rather than a miss of a stretch target. Whether the two families were federally funded is not disclosed, so Section 204 may not bind.
rows.implication: Treat exclusivity as conditional until 2028-01-01 and reprice the moat; require a representation that the licence is in good standing and that the robot count is measured on the company's own definition.
rows.confidence: high on the licence terms; medium on the Section 204 conclusion
rows.follow_up: Is the 100-robot test measured on robots in service on 2027-12-31 or cumulatively, is there a cure period, and were the two university families federally funded?

rows.finding: Strawberries are covered produce under 21 CFR Part 112; the rule names mechanical harvesters as equipment, and 21 CFR 112.123 requires food-contact surfaces to be smooth, cleanable, inspected and cleaned and sanitised as necessary to protect against contamination. Picking directly into the retail clamshell makes the interior of the machine a food-contact and food-packing surface. No harvester-specific federal certification exists and none is disclosed.
rows.mechanism: The legal duty sits on the grower as the farm, but the equipment design sets the contamination risk, and a clamshell packed in the field reaches the consumer without a further wash step. Retailer audit standards rather than the FDA are the practical gate, and a recall traced to machine contact is a delisting rather than a fine.
rows.benchmark: Hand crews meet the same rule through worker hygiene and container sanitation; machine surfaces can be validated and documented in a way hand labour cannot, which is an unexploited advantage.
rows.weakens: No FDA warning letter, recall or enforcement action against machine-harvested berries was found; the risk is prospective.
rows.implication: A sanitary-design and cleaning validation for the v4 is a cheap condition that removes a retailer objection and a diligence discount.
rows.confidence: high on the rule; low on current compliance, which is undisclosed
rows.follow_up: Does the company hold a cleaning and sanitation protocol or validation for the clamshell path, and has a retailer or third-party auditor reviewed it?

rows.source_type: primary (ISO) plus independent press, article body blocked
rows.finding: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles, verification and information-for-use requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery. In August 2026 California was considering a trailer bill to allow unpiloted machines to work alongside farmworkers, which labour groups opposed. No US federal approval or certification requirement for autonomous field machinery was identified, and the company discloses no ISO 18497 assessment.
rows.mechanism: The unit economics assume one technician supervises up to eight robots and a $3,100 a robot-season field-service line. A rule requiring a human spotter within sight of each machine converts 1:8 into 1:1 and multiplies that line by roughly eight.
rows.benchmark: Road-vehicle autonomy is regulated through exemptions and permits; agricultural autonomy has no equivalent US regime, so the rule is being written now and the standard is voluntary.
rows.weakens: The bill number, text and status could not be read because the article body returned HTTP 403, so neither the timing nor the content of any rule is established.
rows.implication: Model the field-service line at a 1:4 supervision ratio as a downside case; at 1:1 gross margin on the $9,500 price turns negative.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What supervision ratio would the California proposals require, and what ratio does the fleet insurer require?

rows.source_type: independent litigation reporting plus company-provided deck
rows.finding: The United Farm Workers is the plaintiff that overturned the AEWR methodology in district court on 2026-08-26, and labour groups opposed the California trailer bill on unpiloted machines. On quality, 3.8% of berries were bruised or punctured in the 2025 pilots, Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026.
rows.mechanism: Labour substitution sells a robot only where labour supply is the binding constraint. Where quality is the constraint it does not, and a union with a recent court win has both the motive and the standing to shape the operating rule that decides whether a machine can run beside a crew.
rows.benchmark: The company's own targets are a pick rate above 95% and, by implication, bruising below the 3.8% pilot level; no retailer standard specific to machine-harvested berries was identified.
rows.weakens: No boycott, campaign, shareholder resolution or retailer sourcing policy aimed at machine-harvested strawberries was found, so the social liability is potential rather than actual.
rows.implication: Credit neither an ESG premium nor an ESG discount: the material social metric here is bruising and pick rate, which belongs in the product and risk sections.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Has any retailer or buyer requested a labour-impact or food-safety statement, and what are the bruising rates at the two largest customers?

rows.finding: USAspending returns zero federal awards to a recipient named Orrin Fieldworks, against a deck claim of a $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award over 2024-2026 and grant revenue of $0.80M across FY2023-FY2026E, which is more than the stated award.
rows.mechanism: A grant line that cannot be traced to an award is either a subaward, a different legal entity or not federal money. It is non-recurring and vanishes from the FY2027 plan, so it does not change enterprise value, but a checkable fact that does not check bears on disclosure quality, which is a governance input to the valuation.
rows.benchmark: A federal prime award to a named small business is normally visible in USAspending within the reporting lag.
rows.weakens: A zero result does not prove absence: awards can be recorded under another legal name or as subawards, and part of the $0.80M may be state money.
rows.implication: Treat the grant line as zero in the model and ask for the award notice before the round closes.
rows.confidence: high on the search result; medium on the conclusion
rows.follow_up: What is the award number, agency and period, and is any of the $0.80M state rather than federal?

plan.decision_question: Which policy and regulatory facts change the grower's alternative cost of hand labour, the company's cost of goods, or its right to operate - and do they raise or lower what Meridian should pay for a $12M Series A at $72M pre-money?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin holds no licence it can lose, but four inputs to its value case are being decided by other people before the 2027 season - a wage floor a court reopened on 2026-08-26, a robotics tariff decision due by about 2027-04-26, a university exclusivity test on 2027-12-31 and a California rule on unpiloted machines - and on the evidence available the balance of them is mildly negative for the 2027 season and positive thereafter, which is a reason to price and stage the round rather than a reason to pass.
plan.why_different: The other sections treat policy as background or as a risk category. This one converts each policy into a dollar per acre, per robot or per season so the market, financials and risk sections can carry a number instead of an adjective. It is also the only section that owns the registries where these decisions land.
plan.mechanism: The AEWR is a legal wage floor paid to H-2A and corresponding US workers, so it sets the grower's hand-labour cost per acre and therefore the ceiling on what a robot-season can be sold for. USMCA rules of origin and Section 232 duties set the landed cost of a Mexico-assembled robot, which Orrin bears because it owns the fleet rather than selling equipment. The licence's 100-robot test decides whether a competitor can buy the same two patent families from the same university. A California operating rule would set the technician-to-robot ratio behind the $3,100 field-service line, and 21 CFR 112 makes the robot a piece of food-contact equipment whose cleaning regime the grower must be able to document.
plan.comparison_set: Hand crews at the 2026 AEWR against the pre-October-2025 Farm Labor Survey rate; the robot's $2,714 an acre-season against a derived $21,000-$36,000 an acre of hand harvest; $12,700 renewal against $16,500 list; a US-manufactured build against the Guadalajara build for the Bayh-Dole question; and university-licence practice - a milestone schedule with cure and step-in - against a single binary test with no cure.
plan.counter_evidence: The strongest case against the judgement is that the wage-floor cut is the least durable of the four factors: a district court has already held the rule unlawful, ordered a replacement methodology and required a back-wage notice, so the grower's alternative cost is more likely to rise than fall before the 2027 season, which restores the robot's value case. Second, the company may already satisfy USMCA origin and may never be caught by a robotics tariff, in which case the cost-of-goods exposure is zero. Third, no regulator, retailer or union has yet acted against machine-harvested berries, so the food-safety and social liabilities are potential rather than actual, and an ESG discount would be as unearned as an ESG premium.
plan.visual: Three tables: the ESG issues table (issue, why material, evidence, rating impact), the regulatory record table (regulator, record, date, status) and the policy impact matrix (factor, exposure, probability, impact, mitigant). The matrix carries the section's judgement because it puts a date and a dollar figure on each policy.
plan.prohibited: No 'ESG premium', 'regulatory moat', 'tailwind', 'headwind', 'responsible AI', 'sustainable agriculture' or 'well positioned' as unearned labels; no 'recently', 'soon' or 'going forward' without an absolute date; no claim that a policy is supportive or adverse without a dollar figure attached; no reference to how the section was researched, to review items, or to internal records.
