rows.finding: AB 187, the 2026 employment policy trailer bill, passed both houses on 2026-08-31 and was chaptered on 2026-09-18 as Chapter 256, Statutes of 2026, without the Cal/OSHA amendment that would have allowed unpiloted machines to work beside crews; the standard requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces therefore stands through the 2027 season.
rows.mechanism: The only legislative route to legalise unattended operation in California closed for the session; the operating model must carry a technician or not run in California until the Standards Board revises Title 8.
rows.benchmark: California is the only state that bars autonomous agricultural equipment in workplaces where workers are present; other states permit operation under manufacturer instructions.
rows.weakens: The human-driver requirement is a general safety order, not an outright ban; a technician aboard may satisfy it, which is why the probability is 20%-25% rather than certain.
rows.implication: The restriction is a live 2027 risk, not a 2028 option: price it at 20%-25% probability and -70% to -90% of equity value, matching the risk section.
rows.confidence: high on the legislative record; medium on how the standing standard is enforced through 2027
rows.follow_up: Does a technician riding the machine satisfy Title 8 section 3441(b), or must the operator drive it? Counsel's opinion is needed.

rows.finding: The Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board directed staff on 2026-09-17 to convene a new advisory committee on autonomous agricultural tractors and equipment; the committee first meets on 2026-12-01, so no revised standard can be adopted before the 2027 season.
rows.mechanism: The rulemaking sequence - advisory committee, proposed rule, comment period, board vote - has not started, and the Board's 2024-2025 committee took about nine months to reach a staff recommendation.
rows.benchmark: The earlier advisory committee first met on 2025-03-26 and staff recommended a manufacturer-approval system in November 2025, a nine-month cycle; the 2026 committee starts from zero in December.
rows.weakens: The Board could act faster in an emergency, and the committee could recommend a narrow exemption; no evidence of either.
rows.implication: Underwrite the 2027 season on the current standard; no regulatory relief is available inside the investment horizon.
rows.confidence: medium-high: primary agency page plus trade-press account
rows.follow_up: What is the new committee's scope and timetable, and does it cover strawberry harvesters or only tractors?

rows.finding: A material California restriction or enforcement action in 2027 carries a 20%-25% probability and -70% to -90% of equity value. Both readings are fatal: if a technician can satisfy the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and field service rises above the price of a season; if the fleet cannot satisfy it, one citation stops the only revenue line.
rows.mechanism: A citation or insurer refusal removes the California revenue line; a 1:1 technician requirement multiplies the $3,100 field-service cost to $24,800 per robot-season, above the $9,500 season price.
rows.benchmark: The risk section carries the same 20%-25% probability and -70% to -90% impact; the 1:8 ratio is management's assumption, not a regulatory allowance.
rows.weakens: If California is a small share of revenue or the fleet runs only with drivers, the exposure is smaller; the deck does not disclose the California revenue share.
rows.implication: Probability times impact, not probability alone, drives the expected loss; the California tail alone consumes a large share of the equity.
rows.confidence: medium: analyst estimate anchored to the risk section
rows.follow_up: What share of 2026 and 2027 revenue is California? Does the insurance policy exclude unpermitted autonomous operation?

rows.finding: The 2026 AEWR notice (91 FR 48946) cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 an hour from $19.97 (-17.6%), with the experienced level at $18.71, and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23 (-23.2%), $15.06 experienced, effective 2026-08-03 (Florida 2026-08-17).
rows.mechanism: The wage floor sets the grower's alternative hand-harvest cost and therefore the robot's price ceiling; a 17.6% cut lowers the ceiling by $4,506 an acre over a 40-pass season.
rows.benchmark: Hand harvest costs $21,056-$23,949 an acre against $2,714 an acre for the robot at $9,500 a season ($4,714 at the 2027 list), 11%-13%.
rows.weakens: The 2026-08-26 district court order held the methodology unlawful and may restore higher rates for 2027, which would raise the ceiling again.
rows.implication: Price is not the adoption constraint; bruising and pick quality are. The wage cut weakens the labour-shortage sales case for 2027.
rows.confidence: high on the published rates; medium on the 2027 outcome
rows.follow_up: Will DOL's replacement rule raise the 2027 California rate, and are back-wage adjustments likely?

rows.finding: Non-USMCA Mexico origin at 10% costs $3,300 a robot on the $33,000 v4 bill of materials, 85% of a robot-season's $3,900 gross profit; the Section 232 robotics proclamation of 2026-10-28 found a threat, imposed no duty and set a 180-day Commerce-USTR update to 2027-04-26, and a 25% duty would be $8,250 a robot or $2.48M on the $9.9M 2027 build.
rows.mechanism: Orrin owns the fleet, so duty is a capital cost, not a pass-through to growers; origin rules decide whether the cost is 0% or 10% before any new action.
rows.benchmark: USMCA-qualifying goods enter at 0%; Section 232 metals duties of 50% apply even under USMCA; the tariffs are due six days before the 2027 season.
rows.weakens: The robot may qualify under USMCA, and no duty has been imposed yet; origin is not disclosed.
rows.implication: A 25% duty consumes a quarter of the build budget and 75 robots of a 300-unit plan; the USMCA certificate is a condition of closing.
rows.confidence: medium: independent tax summaries plus the proclamation
rows.follow_up: Provide the bill of materials by tariff shift and the USMCA certificate of origin; model a 25% duty case.

rows.finding: The university licence costs 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 annual minimum (5.6% of robots-as-a-service revenue in FY2026) and falls to non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 75 paid robot-seasons and a 64-robot fleet; if a licensed family was federally funded, 35 U.S.C. 204 requires substantially US manufacture while Guadalajara assembles the grippers.
rows.mechanism: A binary exclusivity test with no cure removes the moat; the US-manufacture preference conflicts with the Mexico assembly route.
rows.benchmark: Standard university exclusive licences carry diligence milestones, cure periods and step-in rights rather than a single robot-count cliff.
rows.weakens: The licence may have a cure period or a different threshold in the executed text, which the company has not provided.

rows.finding: The two $100M+ ag-robotics exits are Blue River ($305M to Deere in 2017, ~3.5x its $87M post-money) and Bear Flag ($250M to Deere in 2021, after a $7.9M seed); both were autonomy/perception platform deals. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven (precision ag) and AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA. Harvesting-robot outcomes are smaller: Kubota/AgJunction $73M, Root AI/AppHarvest $60M, CNH/Advanced Farm assets undisclosed, Oishii/Tortuga undisclosed.
rows.mechanism: Strategic buyers pay for technology and team fit with their equipment platforms; the harvesting-robot assets have been bought as IP/team tuck-ins, not as $250M+ platform deals. That caps the likely bid for a service-heavy harvesting business.
rows.benchmark: Orrin at $90M post needs $100M+ for a 1.1x return and $250M+ for 2.8x; the precedent range for ag-robotics platform exits is $250-305M, and for harvesting assets $60M or undisclosed.
rows.weakens: Blue River and Bear Flag were autonomy platforms with clear OEM fit, not harvesting service companies; CNH/Raven and AGCO/Trimble are precision-ag portfolio deals, not robot deals. The comparison is directional, not exact.
rows.implication: Underwrite a $100-250M trade sale, not a $500M outcome; at $90M post the lead returns 1.0-2.8x.

business_model.author: Fundamentals Analyst
queries: Orrin Fieldworks SBIR USDA strawberry harvesting robot award (public-record check on the grant claim)
Tortuga AgTech strawberry harvesting robots funding business model / Oishii acquires Tortuga AgTech 2025
Harvest CROO Robotics strawberry harvester service model
FarmWise weeding robots service model pivot equipment sales Vulcan
2024 strawberry cost study Central Coast harvest labor cost per acre dollars
United Rentals 10-K equipment rental revenue and depreciation of rental equipment; Deere 10-K employees

rows.finding: At the signed $9,500 per robot-season, price less $3,100 field service and $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables leaves $3,900 (41.1%); straight-line depreciation of the $48,000 v3 over four seasons is $12,000 per season, so contribution after depreciation is -$8,100 (-85.3% of price). Interest-only debt service on $1.6M at 11.5% adds $2,453 per robot-season (75 seasons) and a four-year amortising loan adds $6,951.
rows.mechanism: The reported gross margin excludes the consumption of the rented asset, so the per-season price ($9,500) is below one season's depreciation ($12,000) before any service cost: the unit cannot recover capital at any utilisation.
rows.benchmark: United Rentals FY2025 equipment rental gross margin is 38.0% after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of $13,806M rental revenue [S21].
rows.weakens: The deck reports 41% and projects 60%+ at scale; the company may argue the v4 at $31,000 changes the depreciation charge to $7,750.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite growth: every additional signed 2026-priced robot-season consumes about $8,100 of capital, so scaling the current contract price destroys cash faster.
rows.confidence: high - arithmetic on the deck's own figures
rows.follow_up: What is the Kestrel facility amortisation schedule and is the parent a guarantor? What residual value, if any, is assumed on the v3 fleet?

rows.finding: The 2.1-season payback equals $31,000 / ($16,500 list price - $1,750 target service), which omits the $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables entirely. Including it gives 2.53 seasons; at the $9,500 signed price and $5,600 actual cost the payback is 12.31 seasons ($48,000 / $3,900), or 7.95 seasons even at the $31,000 target build. At 1.17 seasons per robot per year (75 seasons / 64 robots) that is 10.5 years against a four-season asset life.
rows.mechanism: The payback claim stacks three unproven inputs - target build cost, list rather than signed price, and a service cost 55% below the reported line - and drops a real cash cost; each alone doubles or worse the payback.
rows.benchmark: Four-season straight-line life; 2026 actual mix of 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots.
rows.weakens: If v4 hits $31,000, the price reaches $16,500 and transport is bundled into the grower contract, payback is 2.53 seasons, still 20% worse than claimed.
rows.implication: The payback slide should be rejected as an underwriting input; the investor should require verified v4 cost and signed $16,500 contracts before crediting any payback.
rows.confidence: high - arithmetic
rows.follow_up: Are the 2027 renewals signed at $12,700 or is that a list average? Who bears transport in the 2027 contract?

rows.finding: FY2025 revenue of $1.9M was 20.0% robot rental ($0.38M), 14.2% paid pilots ($0.27M), 50.0% engineering services to Tallis ($0.95M) and 15.8% grants ($0.30M). The engineering customer is also a $2.5M noteholder, a board observer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M committed investor in this round. On a like-for-like basis, no more than 20% of FY2025 revenue was recurring robot rental.
rows.mechanism: The company is currently an engineering contractor and grant recipient with a pilot rental business attached; the related party sets the BOM quote that underpins the cost case while buying the engineering service that keeps revenue up.
rows.benchmark: A hardware-as-a-service underwriter would treat recurring rental as the only product-market-fit evidence; 80% of FY2025 revenue is one-off, grant-funded or related-party.
rows.weakens: Engineering services may be genuine third-party demand for Orrin's perception work and could seed a licensing business; grants are non-dilutive.
rows.implication: Value the company on the $0.38M FY2025 rental line and the 110 contracted 2027 robot-seasons, not on $1.9M or $2.6M of reported revenue.
rows.confidence: high - disclosed segments, relationship disclosed by the company
rows.follow_up: What are the pricing, scope and termination terms of the engineering contract, and is any of it a pass-through of v4 development cost?

rows.finding: One technician per eight robots at California loaded field-labour rates ($24.42/hour including 48% overhead, 8-hour days over a 213-day season) costs $41,611 per technician-season, or $5,201 per robot-season; at the machine-operator rate of $29.60/hour it is $6,305. The deck reports $3,100, which implies a technician costs $24,800 per seven-month season before vehicles, tools and travel.
rows.mechanism: Service cost is linear in robot count because the technician ratio is fixed at 1:8, so fleet scale does not dilute it; at 360 robots the same $3,100 line funds 45 technicians at $24,800 each, below the loaded wage.
rows.benchmark: UC Davis 2024 Central Coast strawberry cost study loaded labour rates and harvest cost of $79,288 per acre [S10].
rows.weakens: Technicians may supervise remotely across more than eight robots off-peak, and the deck's line may exclude only some field costs; the point is that the reported $3,100 is not reconcilable to the 1:8 ratio.
rows.implication: Gross profit at the signed price falls from $3,900 to $1,800-$550 per robot-season on this cross-check, before depreciation; the 60% margin claim needs a service cost the plan does not show.
rows.confidence: medium - assumes 8-hour days, a 213-day season and no vehicle/tool cost
rows.follow_up: Provide the field-service cost build: technicians, overtime, vehicles, battery packs, silicone fingers and remote-supervision software per robot-season.

rows.finding: The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 seasons per robot against a physical maximum of 2 (11 months of the 7-month California and 4-month Florida seasons). At the signed price the fleet needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation (154% of the maximum); at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85% of maximum); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10.
rows.mechanism: Depreciation is charged per season of use, so running a robot twice a year doubles annual revenue and doubles asset consumption: utilisation cannot lower the per-season capital hurdle, it only spreads fixed overhead.
rows.benchmark: Two-season physical maximum; 2026 actual utilisation 58.5% of maximum.
rows.weakens: If the same robot is billed for a California and a Florida season at a full price, annual revenue per robot doubles to $19,000-$25,400, covering depreciation in cash terms but not in economic terms.
rows.implication: The plan's scale argument cannot repair a unit that loses $8,100 per season; only price or build cost can, so the investment case is a repricing case, not a growth case.
rows.confidence: high - arithmetic
rows.follow_up: What price is charged for a Florida season, and does the 2027 plan assume Florida seasons for the same 360 robots?

rows.finding: At one robot per 3.5 acres the signed price is $2,714 per acre and the 2027 list is $4,714 per acre, against UC Davis's $79,288 per acre harvest cost (3.4%-5.9%). At 9,000 trays per acre and $11 a tray, each 1 percentage point of fruit lost is $990 per acre, 21%-36% of the robot fee; the reported 3.8% bruising is $3,762 per acre, more than the entire signed price per acre and 80% of the list price.
rows.mechanism: The robot is priced at a small fraction of the harvest labour it targets, so price is not the grower's binding constraint; quality loss and reliability are, which is why one Florida pilot ended over bruising and why the price has not moved to list.
rows.benchmark: UC Davis 2024 harvest cost $79,288 per acre and 9,000 trays at $11 [S10].
rows.weakens: Not all bruised fruit is unsaleable and a 94% pick rate may still replace most of a crew; a working robot could be priced several times higher.
rows.implication: Treat the signed $9,500 as an option price, not a market price; the 2027 $16,500 is still only 5.9% of harvest cost, so the risk is proof and quality, not affordability.
rows.confidence: medium - the bruise-to-revenue link is an assumption
rows.follow_up: What share of bruised fruit was culled or discounted at the pilot farms, and what did the lost Florida grower quantify as its loss?

rows.finding: The closest owned-fleet peers did not scale independently: Tortuga AgTech built a 150-robot strawberry/grape harvesting fleet, deployed about $50M over eight years and sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii in March 2025; FarmWise raised a $45M Series B, moved from its Titan weeding service to selling the Vulcan through dealer RDO Equipment, wound down and was bought by Taylor Farms in April 2025.
rows.mechanism: Owning and renting harvest robots ties up capital in a seasonal asset while the technology and service cost are still improving; when venture funding tightens, the asset-heavy operator is sold to a customer or a strategic rather than scaling.
rows.benchmark: Tortuga $50M deployed for 150 robots ($333,000 per robot) [S93]; FarmWise $45M Series B then wind-down [S100, S116]; Harvest CROO still offers harvesting-as-a-service but discloses no fleet or revenue.
rows.weakens: Both peers operated in a venture downturn and with different crops/quality tolerances; Orrin's 94% pick rate and 86% uptime are better than research robots, and the strawberry harvest window is a genuine pain point.
rows.implication: The base rate for this model is an asset sale, not a scale-up; the investor should structure entry around a verified 2027 season and a price that covers depreciation.
rows.confidence: medium-high - trade press and company profiles, financial terms undisclosed
rows.follow_up: Did either peer ever reach positive contribution per robot-season? At what price and fleet size? What did Oishii and Taylor Farms pay?

rows.finding: Orrin has raised $20.5M before this round ($2.5M SAFEs, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes) and has 64 robots in service whose gross build cost is $3.07M at $48,000, so capital deployed per robot in service is $320,313 and only 15.0% of capital raised sits in the fleet at gross cost.
rows.mechanism: Most of the capital has gone into R&D and operating losses rather than revenue-generating assets, so each additional robot is funded by new equity, not by the cash the fleet throws off.
rows.benchmark: Tortuga deployed about $50M for 150 robots, $333,000 per robot [S93] - Orrin's capital intensity per deployed robot is essentially the same.
rows.weakens: Early fleets are expected to be capital-inefficient, and Orrin's v4 is designed to cut build cost 35%; R&D spend creates the IP that the next fleet uses.
rows.implication: At $72M pre-money the investor is paying for the v4 and the 2027 fleet, not for the current one; require a per-robot capital-efficiency commitment in the milestones.
rows.confidence: high - arithmetic on disclosed funding and fleet

plan.decision_question: Does one robot-season make money today, at the $9,500 signed price, before any scale benefit?
plan.thesis_sentence: At the price Orrin has actually signed, one robot-season returns $3,900 before its $12,000 share of the build cost and loses $8,100 after depreciation, so the rental model is a bet on an unbuilt $31,000 v4 and an unsigned 74% price increase, not a working business.
plan.why_different: This section tests the per-unit cash engine - price, direct cost, depreciation, debt service, utilisation and lifetime value. Section 7 tests company-level cash, funding and accounting quality. Only this section recomputes the deck's per-robot waterfall with the asset's depreciation and the actual signed price.
plan.mechanism: Depreciation is charged per season of use, so utilisation cannot lower the per-season capital hurdle; only price and build cost can. Reporting depreciation in operating expense rather than cost of revenue makes a 41% gross margin out of a unit that consumes 126% of its price in capital each season.
plan.comparison_set: United Rentals equipment rental gross margin 38.0% after fleet depreciation; Tortuga AgTech (150 robots, $50M, asset sale) and FarmWise ($45M Series B, service to dealer sales, wind-down); UC Davis 2024 Central Coast harvest cost of $79,288 per acre; Deere revenue per employee as a hardware-productivity benchmark.
plan.counter_evidence: If the v4 hits $31,000 and growers accept $16,500, contribution turns positive at $3,150 per robot-season (19.1% after depreciation) and a grower still pays only 5.9% of its harvest cost. The unit is not structurally doomed if both conditions are met; the counter-evidence is that neither is signed or built.
plan.visual: Unit-economics table with depreciation and debt service, plus a pricing table with per-acre equivalents.
plan.prohibited: clear business model, strong team, huge market, well positioned, scalable, flying wheel, unit economics are improving

rows.weakens: A one-season lag from trial to revenue is fast for agricultural capital equipment, and signing six months ahead is reasonable notice.

rows.weakens: The pilot fee may cover more than the average implies; pilot robots may be older v2 units at a lower cost; the 14 farms span three years, so dividing FY2025 revenue by nine farms is approximate.

rows.mechanism: Bruising is a quality veto that ends a relationship regardless of price, and a grower can shrink robot count between seasons, so the revenue base is not sticky.
rows.benchmark: 3.8% of berries bruised or punctured in the 2025 pilots; each percentage point of fruit lost is $990 an acre at 9,000 trays and $11 a tray.

rows.finding: The contract behind the $9,500 and $12,700 prices is a single season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit, uptime or renewal terms; standard RaaS agreements run one to five years with pilot success criteria, service levels and early-termination fees.

rows.benchmark: RaaS contract norm of one-to-five-year initial terms, automatic renewal, uptime remedies and early-termination fees (S140).
rows.weakens: A one-season term suits growers' seasonal cash flow and the company says growers rent by the season; a short term may be a selling point, not only a risk.

rows.finding: One robot-season at the signed $9,500 returns $3,900 of reported gross profit but loses $8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation; the 2.1-season payback relies on a $31,000 build, $16,500 list price and $1,750 service cost, and becomes 12.31 seasons at the signed price and reported $5,600 service, transport and consumables cost.
rows.mechanism: Depreciation in operating expense flatters gross margin; charging the robot to the season it is used turns a 41.1% gross margin into a -85.3% contribution, and payback lengthens beyond the four-season asset life.
rows.benchmark: United Rentals FY2025 equipment-rental gross margin of 38.0% after $2,670M of fleet depreciation (19.3% of rental revenue).
rows.weakens: The v3 is a first-generation build; a $31,000 v4 at the $16,500 list price would return +$3,150 a season and pay back in 2.84 seasons at the reported service cost.
rows.implication: Every season sold at the signed price consumes capital; the investment depends on a price increase and a cost reduction that are both unproven.

rows.finding: Utilisation cannot cover the per-season capital charge: the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots (1.17 of a physical maximum of two) and needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year at the signed price (154% of the maximum), 1.69 at $12,700 (85%) or 1.10 at $16,500 with the v3; one technician per eight robots at $24.42 an hour costs $5,201 a robot-season, not the $3,100 reported.
rows.mechanism: Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue but consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but does not lower the capital cost per season; service cost scales with robots.
rows.benchmark: UC Davis 2024 loaded field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days; machine-operator rate $29.60, giving $6,305 per robot-season.
rows.weakens: Remote supervision and night operations may let one technician cover more than eight robots; the $3,100 may be a cash cost that excludes loaded labour.
rows.implication: At 360 robots the 1:8 ratio needs 45 technicians and $1.12M, so gross margin does not improve with scale on service alone.
rows.confidence: medium: the technician ratio is the company's, the wage rate is an external benchmark.
rows.follow_up: Provide the field-service cost build: headcount, loaded wage, vehicles, tools and remote-supervision ratio.

rows.mechanism: Owned-fleet harvesting burns capital per robot before the unit economics work; both peers retreated to asset sales or exit rather than scaling rental.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's $320,313 of capital per robot in service ($20.5M raised / 64) versus Tortuga's roughly $333,000 ($50M / 150).

rows.follow_up: What did Tortuga and FarmWise charge per robot-season, and why did the rental model fail?

plan.decision_question: Does $18M actually fund 360 robots and $8M ARR, and does the ARR definition survive scrutiny?
plan.thesis_sentence: $18M funds the 360-robot plan on the company's own projections only if every assumption lands and no working capital is needed; at the $12M minimum the plan is about a third short, the $1.5M cash covenant binds during 2027, and $1.8M of the $3.2M ARR is an expiring related-party contract and unsigned letters of intent.
plan.why_different: This section tests the company-level cash path, funding adequacy, revenue and ARR definitions, margin quality and what an audit would change. Section 6 tests the per-robot engine; this section tests whether the balance sheet and the plan can carry 360 robots.
plan.mechanism: Cash is consumed by capex before the first 2027 harvest cheque, so the round size and close date set the runway; ARR is a forward contracted book plus an expiring related-party contract and unsigned letters, so it overstates the recurring base; depreciation held outside gross margin flatters the margin trajectory.
plan.comparison_set: Orrin's own plan versus its cash; Deere revenue per employee $625,000; United Rentals depreciation at 19.3% of rental revenue; venture burn-multiple norms; Tortuga $50M deployed for 150 robots.
plan.counter_evidence: If the 250 uncontracted robots are signed at $16,500 and the v4 lands at $31,000, 2027 revenue reaches $5.5M and contribution $1.1M, and the $18M case ends 2027 with about $6.1M, enough to reach a Series B. The minimum $12M case still breaches the covenant.
plan.visual: Financial-statements table with derived margins and cash, plus a returns-and-working-capital table and an ARR decomposition table.
plan.prohibited: nine months of runway, ARR of $3.2M without definition, strong pipeline, fully funded, derisked

rows.finding: Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86 percent uptime pick 22,114 berries in 24 hours (25,714 at full uptime); at 9,000 trays of 8 one-pound clamshells an acre and 23-28 g a berry there are about 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre a season, so at a 3.5-day interval about 21,800 berries stand ripe per acre-pass and one robot clears 1.0-1.2 acres a day, not 1.5.
rows.mechanism: Throughput is fixed by cycle time and arm count; acres a day is only meaningful once a ripe-fruit density and a pick interval are assumed, and the company's 1.5 acres implies either a 2.4-day interval or picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop.
rows.benchmark: UC Davis 2024 Central Coast study: 7,000-12,000 trays an acre, 9,000 assumed, and a 3-4 day pick interval stated in the deck itself.
rows.weakens: Berry weight is my assumption from a 16-20 berry one-pound clamshell; a 20 g berry cuts coverage to about 0.85 acres, a 30 g berry raises it to about 1.25.
rows.implication: Value the fleet at 1.0-1.2 acres a day and about 3 acres served per robot, not 3.5; the 2027 robot count needed for a given acreage rises by a third.
rows.confidence: medium-high: the arithmetic is exact, the density assumption moves the answer by about 20 percent.
rows.follow_up: What ripe-fruit density per row and what pick interval did the 212 test rows actually see?

rows.finding: Harvest CROO states 16 independently working picking units and up to 8 acres a day; at Orrin's 5.6 seconds a berry, 16 arms yield about 205,000 berries a day, or 9.4 acres at the same density, so the two vendors' claims are consistent and Orrin's 1.5 acres is explained by having two arms rather than by a different technology.
rows.mechanism: Coverage scales with arm count and capital per machine, so a two-arm platform needs roughly eight times the machines per acre of a 16-arm gantry and carries eight times the fleet capital per acre of coverage.
rows.benchmark: Harvest CROO B8: 16 units, 8 acres a day (vendor-stated, via a registry listing).
rows.weakens: Registry data is vendor-stated and unverified; CROO's commercial deployment is small and it has not published an audited acreage figure.
rows.implication: Coverage is not a differentiator and the RaaS balance sheet, not the pick rate, is where the model is stressed: at $48,000 a robot and 3.5 acres served, fleet capital is $13,700 an acre.
rows.confidence: medium: two vendor sources agree arithmetically, neither is independently audited.
rows.follow_up: Has CROO delivered 8 acres a day in a paying grower block, and at what damage rate?

rows.finding: 3.8 percent of picked berries are bruised or punctured and 2.1 percent are picked unripe; against the U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance of 10 percent total defects, 5 percent serious damage and 2 percent decay, picking alone consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the total.
rows.mechanism: The USDA tolerance is a lot-level budget shared with field defects, decay and later handling, so a machine that spends most of it at the point of picking leaves no room for the cold chain and forces packers to divert fruit to processing or reject the lot. Bruising that expresses two to five days later is measured by the packer, not the grower.
rows.benchmark: USDA AMS U.S. No. 1 tolerances: 10 percent defects, 5 percent serious damage, 2 percent decay.
rows.weakens: The company does not define 'bruised or punctured' or say whether it is measured at pick or after cooling; the grade tolerance is a lot-level inspection standard, not a contractual rejection threshold.
rows.implication: Price the bruising risk as a per-lot revenue risk, not a quality nicety: it is the mechanism that already lost Grower E, and one lost block costs more than a season of gross profit on that block.
rows.confidence: high on the tolerance figures, medium on the comparison because the definitions differ.
rows.follow_up: What is the damage rate after 7 days at 1 degree C, and what did the packer pay for the last three robot-picked lots?

rows.finding: Uptime of 86 percent in scheduled hours and an operator intervention every 3.4 hours means 5.9 interventions per robot-day; at the stated one technician per 8 robots that is 47 interventions per technician per 20-hour day, one every 26 minutes.
rows.mechanism: Intervention frequency, not mean time between failures, sets the labour cost of a fleet; the service cost of $3,100 a robot-season assumes a supervision ratio the intervention rate does not support, and the COO's related-party company is paid $310,000 to cover night shifts.
rows.benchmark: The company's own 8-robot-per-technician supervision claim on the same page as the 3.4-hour intervention figure.
rows.weakens: Some interventions may be remote and take seconds, and the 3.4 hours may be an average over good weeks; neither is disclosed.
rows.implication: The 41 percent gross margin is the number at risk: if the ratio has to fall from 8 to 4 robots a technician, field service doubles and gross profit per robot-season falls by about $3,100.
rows.confidence: medium: derived from two company metrics that may not describe the same crews.
rows.follow_up: How many of the 3.4-hourly interventions need a person in the field, and how long does each take?

rows.finding: Of five own filings none is granted: the lead gripper application US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action with a response filed 2026-05, US 18/655,430 awaits examination, PCT/US2025/027761 reaches its 30-month national-phase date today (2026-10-30) with the decision recorded as not made, and one filing is a provisional that must convert by 2027-04-17.
rows.mechanism: A rejected first office action on the only gripper filing leaves the mechanical design unprotected while the licence that matters expires on a usage test; pending filings protect nothing until granted and a PCT that misses national phase secures nothing outside the US.
rows.benchmark: No record of US 17/902,118 returned by public patent indexes on 2026-10-30; EPO and Australia allow 31 months from priority against Mexico's 30, so two of the three named entries may have a month left.
rows.weakens: First office action rejections are common and often overcome by amendment; absence from public indexes may reflect publication timing rather than a dead filing.
rows.implication: Treat the IP as one licensed perception stack plus trade secrets; do not pay a patent premium, and make national-phase entry a closing condition.
rows.confidence: medium: the status is company-stated and could not be checked against a registry in this run.
rows.follow_up: Was the PCT national phase entered on 2026-10-30, and what did the 2026-05 response give up?

rows.finding: The two perception families are licensed, not owned: exclusive for agricultural harvesting since 2022-01-20 at a 2.5 percent royalty with a $40,000 minimum, but the exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31.
rows.mechanism: The licence is a usage-linked option: the company must convert capital into deployed robots before the cliff or the technology becomes available to Harvest CROO, Deere or CNH at the same terms. University licences also carry diligence and termination-for-failure-to-commercialise clauses that survive the cliff.
rows.benchmark: Standard university exclusive-licence practice: milestone and termination-for-failure clauses, and the Bayh-Dole US-industry preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 if the underlying work was federally funded.
rows.weakens: 100 robots is well below the 360 planned, so on the current plan the cliff is passed comfortably; the risk is a slipped season, not the test itself.
rows.implication: The licence cliff is a schedule risk disguised as an IP risk: a 2027 season that lands 90 robots hands the same patent families to a better-capitalised competitor.
rows.confidence: high on the licence terms, medium on the Bayh-Dole applicability, which is not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Is the Calder licence agreement assignable on a change of control, and does it name the 100-robot count as deployed or revenue-generating?

rows.finding: The only quantitative asset the company can call its own is 1.9 million labelled berry images and a fleet that has run 75 paid robot-seasons across 5 growers; the gripper, its most mechanical and copyable component, is the filing with every claim rejected.
rows.mechanism: Perception data compounds with deployed robot-hours and is hard to buy; a silicone three-finger gripper with slip sensing is a design a funded team reproduces in a season, and the published literature is already dense on strawberry detection and pose estimation.
rows.benchmark: Peer-reviewed work in the register (SLFCNet 2025, HAV-Pose 2026) shows mature public methods for strawberry classification and obstacle-aware pose; no paper in my searches reports an open-field pick rate above 95 percent for any gripper.
rows.weakens: Image count is not data advantage: 1.9 million labels from one university lab and 9 farms may under-represent the 86 percent of acreage the test rows excluded.
rows.implication: Underwrite the fleet data and the service density as the moat and the replication time as about two to three years, not as a patent wall.
rows.confidence: medium: the data claim is unaudited and the literature search was narrow.
rows.follow_up: What share of the 1.9 million images came from Orrin's own fields rather than the university lab?

plan.decision_question: What has actually been proven about the Orrin Picker, and under what field conditions does it fail in a commercial block?
plan.thesis_sentence: The Picker's 94 percent pick rate is a real but narrow result: the company's own arm speed and the UC Davis yield standard imply about 1.0-1.2 acres of clean picking per 24 hours rather than the 1.5 acres claimed, a 3.8 percent damage rate already consumes three quarters of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and with the core perception families licensed rather than owned and the gripper claims rejected, the durable asset is the fleet data and service network, not the patents.
plan.why_different: Section 3 tests the physics and the measurement definitions; other sections price the business or size the market. Only here is the 5.6-second cycle time converted into berries, acres and a damage budget.
plan.mechanism: Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry fix a hard ceiling of about 22,100 berries per 20-hour day at 86 percent uptime; against roughly 21,800 ripe berries standing on an acre at a 3.5-day pick interval, that is about one acre of clean picking a day. Any deficit is made up either by picking less of the ripe crop or by stretching the pick interval, both of which show up as grower value, not as a headline pick rate. Damage and unripe picks are counted per berry picked, so they compound the same way.
plan.comparison_set: Harvest CROO (16 picking units, vendor-stated 8 acres a day), Tortuga AgTech (dual-arm, per-kilogram RaaS, IP bought by Oishii 2025), Advanced Farm (ceased operations 2025-07, IP to CNH), Agrobot and Tevel (harvest-aid and flying platforms); benchmarks are the UC Davis 9,000-tray yield, the California Strawberry Commission $87,000 an acre cost and the USDA No. 1 defect tolerances.
plan.counter_evidence: If detection recall on dense canopies is materially below 100 percent, the true field pick rate is 94 percent times recall, so the headline overstates; the 212 rows were company-chosen at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4 percent, and one of six named growers left over bruising. Conversely, Harvest CROO's 8 acres a day at 16 units is arithmetically consistent with Orrin's per-arm speed, which supports the arm-speed figure and undermines the idea that coverage is a differentiator.
plan.visual: Performance metrics table with derived columns (Metric | Company claim | Independent benchmark | Method | Source) plus the technology comparison table and the patent table.
plan.prohibited: Do not write 'world-class', 'moat' without the replication test, 'proven at scale', 'patent-protected', or any pick rate without its denominator; do not call the licensed families owned; do not describe the 1.5 acres as a picked figure.

rows.finding: At the $12,700 average renewal price and the reported $5,600 a season of field service, transport, insurance and consumables, a robot must cost no more than $28,400 to pay for itself over the four-season depreciation life; the v4 is budgeted at $33,000, so the season the plan depends on does not break even on renewals.
rows.mechanism: A leased asset is a fixed cost the lessor carries; the price only covers depreciation if price minus service cost times seasons exceeds build cost, and at $12,700 the allowed build is $28,400.
rows.benchmark: Current v3 build $48,000; company target $31,000 at 500 units; the 2027 v4 budget assumes $33,000.
rows.weakens: Service cost is expected to fall to $1,750 at scale; if that happens the allowed build at $12,700 rises to $43,800 and the conclusion softens.
rows.implication: Underwrite the round on the 2027 list price of $16,500, not the renewal average, and treat the v4 cost target as a condition: at $33,000 the fleet is a cash consumer at the price most growers will actually pay.
rows.confidence: high: all three numbers are in the deck and the arithmetic is exact.
rows.follow_up: What is the v4 bill of materials at 50, 150 and 300 units, and which line items carry the cost-down?

rows.finding: The 2.1-season payback claim uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, omitting $3,850 of current per-robot-season cost; on the reported $5,600 service cost the payback is 2.8 seasons at $31,000 and 4.4 seasons at today's $48,000 build, longer than the four-season life the same page assumes.
rows.mechanism: Payback is build cost divided by price minus the cost of keeping the robot running; leaving out two thirds of the running cost cuts the payback in half.
rows.benchmark: Reported 2026 year-to-date cost of $3,100 field service plus $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables, against a target service cost of $1,750 and a 4-season life.
rows.weakens: Transport and insurance are partly distance-driven and may fall with denser grower clusters; the deck gives no cluster economics.
rows.implication: Treat payback as roughly double the company figure and require a per-robot-season cost bridge before the next round.
rows.confidence: high: the omission is visible by comparing two lines of the same slide.
rows.follow_up: Which cost lines are inside the $1,750 target and what evidence supports the 69 percent reduction?

rows.finding: Five of the six comparable capital-heavy ag-robot companies ended in an asset sale, a shutdown or a pivot from service to selling machines; the one that scaled, Carbon Robotics, sells equipment and reached nine-figure revenue, while the four that carried the asset or the service model did not survive independently.
rows.mechanism: RaaS converts working capital into a fleet the company must finance, insure and service through a seven-month season with no revenue in the other five months, while a machine sale converts the grower's balance sheet into the company's cash.
rows.benchmark: Carbon Robotics (machines sold, $70M Series D 2024); Advanced Farm ($25M Series B 2021, ceased operations 2025-07, IP to CNH); Tortuga (IP and team to Oishii 2025-03); Monarch ($133M Series C 2024, layoffs, assets to Caterpillar 2026-04); Abundant Robotics (shut 2021); FarmWise (Titan service to Vulcan dealer sales).
rows.weakens: Survivorship cuts both ways: the failures were orchard and apple harvesters and a tractor, not strawberry pickers, and Orrin's per-season rental matches the crop calendar better than a year-round tractor subscription.
rows.implication: A $72M pre-money on a RaaS model prices the option that five of six peers failed to hold; the credible exit is an incumbent buying the fleet data and grower contracts, at a price set by the buyer.
rows.confidence: high on the events, medium on the inference from five cases.
rows.follow_up: What did CNH and Caterpillar pay per dollar raised, and what did the RaaS contracts convert to in the asset sale?

rows.finding: Tallis Agricultural Machinery is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, the $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer (50 percent of FY2025 revenue), the quoted contract manufacturer for the v4, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round; the services contract ends 2027-06-30, so 46 percent of FY2026 estimated revenue disappears within two quarters of the season the round funds.
rows.mechanism: When one counterparty sets the build cost, buys the engineering hours and holds debt, the bill of materials is not a market price and the cost-down the plan needs cannot be tested.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 revenue $1.9M of which $0.95M engineering services and $0.30M grants; FY2026E $2.6M with $1.20M services and $0.35M grants.
rows.weakens: A single supplier with a board seat may genuinely be the fastest route to a 2027 season, and the deck discloses every role.
rows.implication: Require a second and third build quote and a related-party committee sign-off before any capital is released against the 300-robot order; the supplier is also the customer and a creditor.
rows.confidence: high: the concentration is disclosed and the contract end date is dated.
rows.follow_up: What is the arm's-length evidence for the v4 bill of materials quote, and who else priced it?

rows.finding: The 2027 season needs 360 robots by April 2027, of which 300 are to be built with $9.9M of this round; the round is $14M short of its lead as of 2026-10-30 with a 2026-12-15 target close, leaving about three and a half months from cash to a build that must be finished before the California season opens.
rows.mechanism: Hardware ramps are set by supplier slot bookings and deposits months before revenue; a five-times fleet increase inside one season leaves no slack for a late close or a re-quote.
rows.benchmark: Cash $3.7M at 2026-09-30, monthly net burn $410,000, 9 months of runway; the equipment facility requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, so usable cash is about $2.2M, or five months.
rows.weakens: The $1.5M minimum is a covenant test, not a spend restriction, and the company could raise a bridge.
rows.implication: The round is not growth capital, it is the season's working capital: a close after January 2027 makes 360 robots arithmetically impossible, which in turn puts the 100-robot licence test at risk.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, high on the dates.
rows.follow_up: What is the build slot lead time with the contract manufacturer, and what deposits are due before the season?

rows.finding: The v4 is to be assembled in Guadalajara by a supplier that is also an investor, into a market where the US opened a Section 232 investigation into imported robotics and industrial machinery in 2025-09-26 and issued a related proclamation on 2026-10-28; the deck's $33,000 unit cost carries no tariff line.
rows.mechanism: An outsourced build moves cost risk to a border; a duty applies to the landed value and cannot be designed out in one season, and the cost-down roadmap assumed a stable landed cost.
rows.benchmark: USMCA-qualifying goods enter the US at 0 percent; non-qualifying Mexican goods face 10 percent; a Section 232 investigation into robotics and industrial machinery was opened in 2025-09 with a proclamation on 2026-10-28.
rows.weakens: USMCA qualification at 0 percent is plausible if regional value content is met, and the Section 232 outcome is not yet a duty.
rows.implication: Model a 10 percent tariff on the build as a base case: it adds $3,300 a robot, which alone exceeds the $28,400 break-even headroom on renewals.
rows.confidence: medium: the tariff regime is moving and the bill of materials content is not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: What share of the v4 bill of materials is US content, and does it qualify under USMCA rules of origin?

plan.decision_question: Can 64 robots become 360 in one season on an outsourced build and a price 74 percent above signed contracts?
plan.thesis_sentence: The plan does not add up on its own numbers: at the current $48,000 build even the 2027 list price leaves each robot-season about $1,100 short over a four-season life, the v4 must come in below $28,400 to earn its keep on a $12,700 renewal, and a 5.6-times fleet increase by April 2027 depends on a single outsourced build quote and a $14M gap in a round that has not closed.
plan.why_different: Section 9 tests whether the resources match the plan and what must be true in twelve months; the business model section prices the unit economics as reported, the technology section tests the picker. Only here is the sequence of capital, season calendar and supplier dependence judged against the peer base rate.
plan.mechanism: RaaS puts the asset on Orrin's balance sheet: each robot-season sold at $16,500 against a $48,000 build over four seasons and $5,600 of current service cost loses about $1,100, so growth consumes cash precisely where the plan assumes it generates gross profit; and a $33,000 v4 build only breaks even on the $12,700 renewal price if the build comes in under $28,400.
plan.comparison_set: Capital-heavy ag robotics peers and their exits: Monarch (133M Series C, layoffs, Caterpillar asset purchase 2026-04), Advanced Farm (25M Series B, ceased operations 2025-07, IP to CNH), Tortuga (IP and team to Oishii 2025-03), Abundant Robotics (shut down 2021), FarmWise (service to dealer-sale pivot), Carbon Robotics (machines sold outright, 70M Series D). Base rate: of six, one is still selling machines; four ended in asset sales or shutdowns; one pivoted from service to dealer sales.
plan.counter_evidence: If the 360-robot season lands, the 2027 list price and the v4 cost-down turn gross margin from 41 to 52 percent, and 100+ robots in service preserves the licence, the plan looks self-funding and a Series B at a higher price is credible. The outsourced build also keeps fixed costs low, which is exactly what the peer failures lacked.
plan.visual: Milestone table with target date, status and what it proves, then the partner table showing Tallis's five simultaneous roles.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong pipeline', no 'well positioned', no market-size restatement, no adopting the company's ARR definition as revenue, no describing LOIs as contracted.

rows.finding: The $4.7145 price is $72.0M divided by 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares, a count that already includes the $7.77M note conversion and the option pool at 12% of post-money. The line printed as 'fully diluted total' is 12,000,000, and 12,000,000 x $4.7145 = $56.6M, not $72.0M.
rows.mechanism: Pre-money is set on the share count after the note conversion and the pool shuffle, so the headline share count understates the priced count by 27.3% and the price per share falls from an implied $6.00 to $4.7145.
rows.benchmark: Standard Series A convention: price = pre-money / pre-money fully diluted shares including pool increase and converting notes. At $72.0M on 12,000,000 shares the price would be $6.00 and $18.0M would buy 3,000,000 shares, not 3,818,008.
rows.weakens: If the 12,000,000 line is only a label applied to the pre-conversion count, the economics are unchanged and this is a presentation defect rather than a pricing defect.
rows.implication: The round is arithmetically coherent at a $90.0M post-money, so the deal is not mispriced by accident; but the presentation conflates two share counts, which means every other derived figure in the deck needs rebuilding before it is used in a term sheet.
rows.confidence: High: pure arithmetic on the deck's own figures, self-consistent to the share.
rows.follow_up: Which share count does the term sheet use for the pre-money, and does the note conversion sit inside or outside it?

rows.finding: The unallocated pool rises from 1,080,000 shares (9.0% of today's count) to 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money), an increase of 1,210,805 shares or 112%. At $4.7145 that transfers $5.71M, 7.9% of the $72.0M pre-money, from the eight existing holders to the pool. Founder ownership falls from 47.0% to 29.5% in the round; the pool widening alone accounts for about 2.0 percentage points of that.
rows.mechanism: A pool increase placed inside the pre-money is paid for by existing holders, not by the new investor; the larger the post-money pool percentage, the more of the pre-money the founders finance.
rows.benchmark: Total option pool after the round is 20.2% of post-money (8.2% granted plus 12.0% unallocated) against the 10-15% post-money pool that is usual at Series A; the pool more than doubles in one step before a single new hire is named.
rows.weakens: A 12% pool is defensible if the 2027 plan genuinely needs 40+ hires; the deck names no hiring plan to justify it.
rows.implication: Negotiate the pool as a term: at 9.0% retained, existing holders keep 72.6% of the post instead of 68.0%. The $5.71M is real money and it is being asked of founders and seed investors, not of the lead.
rows.confidence: High on the arithmetic; medium on whether 12% is the negotiated number or a placeholder.
rows.follow_up: What hiring plan supports 12% post-money, and how much of it is for the missing CTO and manufacturing roles?

rows.finding: The 2025 notes convert at 80% of the Series A price ($3.7716), giving 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares or 10.8% of the post-money, against 1,648,000 shares at the full price. The 20% discount is worth about $1.95M, of which the founders bear roughly $0.6M and the seed investors about $0.3M.
rows.mechanism: A conversion discount inside the pre-money moves value from earlier holders to noteholders and raises the effective price the new investor pays per unit of ownership.
rows.benchmark: Note discounts typically run 15-25%; 20% is market. What is not market is that $2.5M of the $7.77M converting is held by a counterparty that is simultaneously a customer, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round.
rows.weakens: The noteholders took real risk in 2025-02 when the company had $0.4M of FY2024 revenue, so the discount is earned rather than extracted.
rows.implication: The discount itself is acceptable; the counterparty mix is not. Require the note conversion mechanics and any side letters to be disclosed, and confirm no noteholder holds a most-favoured-nation or additional discount.
rows.confidence: High on the arithmetic; medium on the allocation between Granary ($3.5M), Tallis ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M), which is inferred from the 2025-02-10 principal amounts plus accrued interest.
rows.follow_up: What is the accrued interest and the exact conversion formula, and are there side letters?

rows.finding: The 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed (about $11.0M on the 2023 round size, which the deck does not state), a stack of about $36.8M or 40.9% of the $90.0M post-money. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit, where 46.5% as-converted equals the preference.
rows.mechanism: A preference stack sets a floor below which common is worthless and a crossover above which the preferred converts; between the two the new investor is effectively a 1x lender with equity upside.
rows.benchmark: 1x non-participating and broad-based weighted average are the founder-friendly end of market terms; the risk here is size, not structure, because the stack equals 41% of the post-money.
rows.weakens: If the seed preference is materially below $11.0M (for example if the SAFEs converted at a cap inside the seed), the stack is smaller and the crossover moves down.
rows.implication: At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at a $79M sale and needs about a $180M exit for 2x. The $72.0M pre-money should be underwritten as an option struck at $79M, not as a mark on the common.
rows.confidence: Medium-high: the maths is exact but the seed preference amount is assumed from the round size, not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: What is the Series Seed liquidation preference and price per share, and do the SAFEs carry a separate preference?

rows.finding: Revenue-generating assets sit below the issuer. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (Delaware) holds the five US patent filings and the Calder University licence; Orrin Fleet Services LLC (California, 2023-11-02) owns the fleet, signs the grower contracts and is the Kestrel borrower; Orrin Fieldworks Mexico S. de R.L. de C.V. (Jalisco, 2024-07-19) does gripper and harness assembly with 7 staff and is 1% owned by the California fleet LLC.
rows.mechanism: A holdco/opco split lets the lender take a security interest in the revenue contracts while the equity investor buys the parent; the investor's claim on the cash flow is therefore indirect and conditional on intercompany funding and lender consent.
rows.benchmark: Standard for asset-backed equipment finance; unusual only in that a pre-revenue-hardware company has put its entire commercial contracting layer into the borrower.
rows.weakens: There is no evidence in the deck of an actual lien conflict or consent failure; the structure works perfectly well if the intercompany arrangements are documented.
rows.implication: Conditions before closing: Calder's consent to operation and sublicense by the fleet subsidiary; Kestrel's consent to the round and confirmation of which entity and which balance the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant is tested against; a parent-level guarantee or a restriction on moving assets out of the borrower.
rows.confidence: Medium: entity roles are stated in the deck, but the licence's sublicense terms, the loan agreement and the intercompany agreements are not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Does the Calder licence permit sublicensing or operation by an affiliate, and is the Kestrel covenant tested at parent or borrower level?

rows.finding: The $1.5M minimum unrestricted cash covenant is met with $2.2M of headroom at 2026-09-30 cash of $3.7M against $410,000 monthly net burn, which runs out around 2027-03. Runway to zero is about 2027-06, three months before the 2027 season ships, while $9.9M of hardware must be spent before April 2027.
rows.mechanism: A covenant struck on a cash balance falls before the equity does; it converts a slow fundraising process into an event of default at the worst point in the season calendar.
rows.benchmark: An 18-24 month post-Series-A runway is the norm; this round buys about 9 months of the current burn even at the full $18M, so the Series B is a 2027 event, not a 2028 option.
rows.weakens: If the $12M lead is only the first tranche of a larger close and the $2.0M gap is filled, the arithmetic improves by $2M but does not change the 2027 funding requirement.
rows.implication: The round must close by 2026-12-15 to build the 2027 fleet at all. A $12M lead plus the $4.0M committed leaves about $7.3M at season start against a planned FY2027 net loss of $7.9M, so the minimum close is under-funded before the first robot ships.
rows.confidence: High: arithmetic from stated cash, burn, covenant and use of funds.
rows.follow_up: At which entity is the covenant tested, and will Kestrel waive it through the 2027 build?

rows.finding: Five roles sit in one counterparty: Tallis Agricultural Machinery is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer (37.5% of stated $3.2M ARR, ending 2027-06-30), the quoted manufacturer whose $33,000 v4 unit cost underpins the $9.9M robot budget, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round. The COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services LLC was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date, and the COO's 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer.
rows.mechanism: Related-party revenue and related-party cost estimates are not arm's length, so both the revenue multiple and the unit-cost path in the plan are set by parties with an interest in the outcome.
rows.benchmark: Two of the deck's own five paying 2026 growers are named, and they are 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons; neither is labelled a related party although one is the COO's former employer.
rows.weakens: Tallis funding its own customer and manufacturing its product may be genuine strategic alignment, and the deck does disclose the roles, which is more than most decks do.
rows.implication: Conditions: a second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials, a fairness review of the Vashti contract, the Tallis observer seat limited to non-confidential sessions, and the valuation tested on revenue excluding related parties.
rows.confidence: High on the roles (deck p.12); medium on how much of Tallis's revenue is at non-market prices, which the deck does not say.
rows.follow_up: What are the Vashti contract's rates against local market, and what does an independent quote put the v4 robot at?

gate: 2+ numeric facts/proxies or explicit missing-data note

plan.decision_question: Is the legal and ownership structure clean enough to wire $12M into, and does the $72M pre-money survive its own cap table?
plan.thesis_sentence: The structure is wire-ready only with conditions: the $72.0M pre-money is arithmetically coherent at a $90.0M post-money but is struck on a share count 27% larger than the deck's headline, it sits $7M below the level at which the preference stack stops absorbing all common proceeds, and the grower contracts, the fleet and the equipment debt all sit in a subsidiary the Series A does not buy.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that can disqualify the wire rather than the business: it tests who the issuer is, what it actually owns, who else holds claims on the cash flow, and how the round's own arithmetic moves value between holders. Technology, market and unit economics are tested elsewhere and are irrelevant if the entity is wrong.
plan.mechanism: Value transfer through share-count and preference conventions: the pool shuffle, the 80% note conversion and a $36.8M equal-rank preference determine how much of any given exit reaches the founders and the new investor, independently of the operating story.
plan.comparison_set: Standard Series A conventions (pre-money fully diluted including pool and note conversion; 1x non-participating; 10-15% post-money pool) and the company's own prior rounds: $2.5M pre-seed SAFEs 2022-04, $11.0M Series Seed 2023-03, $7.0M convertible notes 2025-02, $2.5M equipment facility 2025-06.
plan.counter_evidence: The terms the deck does state are founder-friendly: 1x non-participating rather than participating preferred, broad-based weighted average rather than full ratchet, equal ranking rather than a senior stack, and a 20% note discount that is market. Disclosed related parties can be a strength when a manufacturer funds its own customer. No lien conflict, entity lapse or litigation is evidenced anywhere in the deck.
plan.visual: kpi table of six decision metrics, plus the rebuilt post-round cap table and the legal entity map
plan.prohibited: clean structure, solid structure, huge market, strong team, well positioned, about five, many

rows.finding: The $4.7145 price is $72.0M divided by 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares, a count that already includes the $7.77M note conversion and the option pool at 12% of post-money. The line printed as fully diluted total is 12,000,000, and twelve million shares at $4.7145 come to $56.6M, not $72.0M.
rows.mechanism: Pre-money is set on the share count after the note conversion and the pool shuffle, so the headline count understates the priced count by 27.3% and the implied price per share falls from $6.00 to $4.7145.
rows.benchmark: Standard Series A convention: price = pre-money divided by pre-money fully diluted shares including pool increase and converting notes. At $72.0M on 12,000,000 shares the price would be $6.00 and $18.0M would buy 3,000,000 shares rather than 3,818,008.
rows.weakens: If the 12,000,000 line is only a label applied to the pre-conversion count, the economics are unchanged and this is a presentation defect rather than a pricing defect.
rows.implication: The round is arithmetically coherent at a $90.0M post-money, so the deal is not mispriced by accident; but the presentation conflates two share counts, which means every other derived figure in the deck needs rebuilding before it reaches a term sheet.
rows.confidence: High: arithmetic on the deck's own figures, self-consistent to the share.
rows.follow_up: Which share count does the term sheet use for the pre-money, and does the note conversion sit inside or outside it?

rows.finding: The unallocated pool rises from 1,080,000 shares (9.0% of today's count) to 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money), an increase of 1,210,805 shares or 112%. At $4.7145 that transfers $5.71M, 7.9% of the $72.0M pre-money, from the eight existing holders to the pool. Founder ownership falls from 47.0% to 29.5% in the round, and the pool widening alone accounts for about 2.0 percentage points of that.
rows.mechanism: A pool increase placed inside the pre-money is paid for by existing holders, not by the new investor; the larger the post-money pool percentage, the more of the pre-money the founders finance.
rows.benchmark: Total option pool after the round is 20.2% of post-money (8.2% granted plus 12.0% unallocated) against the 10-15% post-money pool usual at Series A; the pool more than doubles in one step before a single new hire is named.
rows.weakens: A 12% pool is defensible if the 2027 plan genuinely needs forty or more hires; the deck names no hiring plan to justify it.
rows.implication: Negotiate the pool as a term: at 9.0% retained, existing holders keep 72.6% of the post rather than 68.0%. The $5.71M is real money asked of founders and seed investors, not of the lead.
rows.confidence: High on the arithmetic; medium on whether 12% is the negotiated number or a working assumption.
rows.follow_up: What hiring plan supports 12% post-money, and how much of it is for the missing CTO and manufacturing roles?

rows.finding: The 2025 notes convert at 80% of the Series A price ($3.7716), giving 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares or 10.8% of the post-money, against 1,648,000 shares at the full price. The discount is worth about $1.95M, of which the founders bear roughly $0.6M and the seed investors about $0.3M.
rows.mechanism: A conversion discount inside the pre-money moves value from earlier holders to noteholders and raises the effective price the new investor pays per unit of ownership.
rows.benchmark: Note discounts typically run 15-25%, so 20% is market. What is not market is that $2.5M of the $7.77M converting is held by a counterparty that is simultaneously a customer, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round.
rows.weakens: The noteholders took real risk in 2025-02 when FY2024 revenue was $0.4M, so the discount is earned rather than extracted.
rows.implication: The discount is acceptable; the counterparty mix is not. Require the conversion mechanics and any side letters to be disclosed, and confirm no noteholder holds a most-favoured-nation clause or an additional discount.
rows.confidence: High on the arithmetic; medium on the allocation between Granary ($3.5M), Tallis ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M), inferred from the 2025-02-10 principal amounts plus accrued interest.
rows.follow_up: What is the accrued interest and the exact conversion formula, and are there side letters?

rows.finding: The 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed (about $11.0M on the 2023 round size, which the deck does not state): a stack of about $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90.0M post-money. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit, where 46.5% as-converted equals the preference.
rows.mechanism: A preference stack sets a floor below which common is worthless and a crossover above which the preferred converts; between the two the new investor is effectively a 1x lender with equity upside.
rows.benchmark: 1x non-participating with broad-based weighted average is the founder-friendly end of market terms; the risk here is the size of the stack, which equals 41% of the post-money.
rows.weakens: If the seed preference is materially below $11.0M, for example where the SAFEs converted at a cap inside the seed, the stack is smaller and the crossover moves down.
rows.implication: At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at a $79M sale and needs about a $180M exit for 2x. Underwrite the $72.0M pre-money as an option struck at $79M, not as a mark on the common.
rows.confidence: Medium-high: the arithmetic is exact but the seed preference is assumed from the round size, not stated.
rows.follow_up: What is the Series Seed liquidation preference and price per share, and do the SAFEs carry a separate preference?

rows.finding: Revenue-generating assets sit below the issuer. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (Delaware) holds the five US patent filings and the Calder University licence; Orrin Fleet Services LLC (California, 2023-11-02) owns the fleet, signs the grower contracts and is the Kestrel borrower; Orrin Fieldworks Mexico S. de R.L. de C.V. (Jalisco, 2024-07-19) does gripper and harness assembly with 7 staff and is 1% owned by the California fleet LLC.
rows.mechanism: A holdco and opco split lets the lender take a security interest in the revenue contracts while the equity investor buys the parent, so the investor's claim on cash flow is indirect and conditional on intercompany funding and lender consent.
rows.benchmark: Standard for asset-backed equipment finance; unusual only in that a company this young has put its entire commercial contracting layer inside the borrower.
rows.weakens: The deck shows no actual lien conflict or consent failure; the structure works if the intercompany arrangements are documented.
rows.implication: Conditions before closing: Calder's consent to operation and sublicensing by the fleet subsidiary; Kestrel's consent to the round and confirmation of which entity and which balance the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant is tested against; a parent-level guarantee or a restriction on moving assets out of the borrower.
rows.confidence: Medium: entity roles are stated in the deck, but the licence's sublicense terms, the loan agreement and the intercompany agreements are not.
rows.follow_up: Does the Calder licence permit sublicensing or operation by an affiliate, and is the Kestrel covenant tested at parent or borrower level?

rows.finding: The $1.5M minimum unrestricted cash covenant is met with $2.2M of headroom at 2026-09-30 cash of $3.7M against $410,000 monthly net burn, which runs out around 2027-03. Runway to zero is about 2027-06, three months before the 2027 season ships, while $9.9M of hardware must be spent before April 2027.
rows.mechanism: A covenant struck on a cash balance falls before the equity does, turning a slow fundraising process into an event of default at the worst point in the season calendar.
rows.benchmark: An 18-24 month post-Series-A runway is the norm; this round buys about nine months of the current burn even at the full $18M, so the Series B is a 2027 event rather than a 2028 option.
rows.weakens: If the $12M lead is the first tranche of a larger close and the $2.0M gap is filled, the arithmetic improves by $2M but the 2027 funding requirement does not change.
rows.implication: The round must close by 2026-12-15 to build the 2027 fleet at all. A $12M lead plus the $4.0M committed leaves roughly $7.3M at season start against a planned FY2027 net loss of $7.9M, so the minimum close is under-funded before the first robot ships.
rows.confidence: High: arithmetic from stated cash, burn, covenant and use of funds.
rows.follow_up: At which entity is the covenant tested, and will Kestrel waive it through the 2027 build?

rows.finding: Five roles sit in one counterparty: Tallis Agricultural Machinery is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer (37.5% of stated $3.2M ARR, ending 2027-06-30), the quoted manufacturer whose $33,000 v4 unit cost underpins the $9.9M robot budget, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round. The COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services LLC was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date, and the COO's 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer.
rows.mechanism: Related-party revenue and related-party cost estimates are not arm's length, so both the revenue multiple and the unit-cost path in the plan are set by parties with an interest in the outcome.
rows.benchmark: Two of the deck's own five paying 2026 growers are named, and they are 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons; neither is labelled a related party although one is the COO's former employer.
rows.weakens: Tallis funding its own customer and manufacturing its product may be genuine strategic alignment, and the deck does disclose the roles, which is more than most decks do.
rows.implication: Conditions: a second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials, a fairness review of the Vashti contract, the Tallis observer seat limited to non-confidential sessions, and the valuation tested on revenue excluding related parties.
rows.confidence: High on the roles, from the deck's own entity page; medium on how much of Tallis revenue is at non-market prices, which the deck does not say.
rows.follow_up: What are the Vashti contract's rates against the local market, and what does an independent quote put the v4 robot at?

gate: 2+ numeric facts/proxies or explicit missing-data note

rows.mechanism: Concentrated counterparties and an unfilled independent seat leave related-party pricing and conflict approval with the founders and the lead, with no disinterested director.
rows.benchmark: Standard venture governance expects an independent director or a disinterested committee for related-party contracts above a threshold.

rows.implication: Make an independent director, observer confidentiality limits and a second v4 quote conditions before closing.
rows.confidence: low — company-reported, no contracts seen
rows.follow_up: Who negotiated the Tallis manufacturing quote and the COO services contract, and what are the termination rights?

rows.weakens: The company may hold all of these documents and simply not have provided data-room access.
rows.implication: Cap confidence at company-reported and require the records as closing conditions.

plan.decision_question: Is the legal and ownership structure clean enough to wire $12M into, and does the $72M pre-money survive its own cap table?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin's $72M pre-money is arithmetically coherent, but the issuer is not the entity that holds the contracts, fleet and lien, and no charter, registry or UCC record has been retrieved, so the $12M should be committed only on verified entity, lien and licence conditions.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that maps the legal entities, rebuilds the cap table and prices the governance conflicts; the other sections take the issuer and its ownership as given.
plan.mechanism: Contracts, fleet and the Kestrel lien sit in the California LLC while the Calder licence and the equity sit in the Delaware parent; the Series A buys the parent's cap table, and the 1x preference stack sets the exit threshold at which that equity participates.
plan.comparison_set: US ag-robotics peers, including Advanced Farm Technologies' 2025-07 shutdown and Harvest CROO Robotics' 2025-04 commercial demonstration; standard venture cap-table mechanics for pool widening and note conversion; a 1x non-participating preference as the base case.
plan.counter_evidence: The price arithmetic is internally consistent and the entity split may be cured by intercompany agreements the deck does not show; a deliberately low public profile explains the missing press and registry trace without implying a defect.
