rows.finding: Of the four executives plus the departed co-founder, none has manufacturing, supply chain or quality experience. The chief financial role is part-time and fractional (since 2024-09), the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, and 22 of 38 employees are engineers who report through a VP Engineering hired in 2024-02.
rows.mechanism: A company's binding constraint shifts as it scales, and the organisation has to shift with it. Orrin's moved from perception research to manufacturing engineering, and the executive bench did not follow: no one on the team has taken a hardware product past a few dozen units.
rows.benchmark: A 300-unit hardware build with a 35% unit-cost reduction normally has a VP Operations or manufacturing leader and a full-time CFO in place before the Series A, not after it.
rows.weakens: A small team can rent manufacturing capability from a contract manufacturer, which is exactly what the Tallis quote implies; the absence of a manufacturing executive matters less if the contract manufacturer owns the process.
rows.implication: Treat the two missing executive hires as conditions or accept that the $9.9M hardware budget is being spent by people doing the job for the first time. The hiring plan behind the pool increase should be published before the pool is agreed.
rows.confidence: High on the role structure; medium on whether an unstated hire is already in progress.
rows.follow_up: Who signs the 300-unit purchase orders and the quality plan, and will the lead require a VP Manufacturing and a full-time CFO as closing conditions?

rows.finding: Sales run through the co-founder's own grower relationships. Five paying growers in 2026, two of them named, and those two are 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons. One of the two is the company where the COO was director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021.
rows.mechanism: Founder network sales convert fast up to the size of the network and stop. With about 15 remaining large California growers named as the addressable top tier, the network exhausts around the point the plan needs to quadruple the fleet.
rows.benchmark: Enterprise hardware companies typically enter a Series A with a sales leader who has carried a quota at scale in the category; here the vice president has twenty years in crop inputs and sixteen months in robotics.
rows.weakens: Founder-led selling is normal at this stage and the relationships are the company's single biggest commercial asset; a 40-robot contract from a former employer is a real endorsement, not a favour.
rows.implication: Value the book as founder-led revenue, not as a repeatable sales motion, and test whether the two named accounts pay the same price as the three unsigned ones. The 2027 plan needs roughly 250 more robots sold in a four-month window.
rows.confidence: High on the concentration; medium on whether the two named customers were introduced by the COO, which the deck implies but does not state.
rows.follow_up: How many of the five 2026 customers came through the COO, and what is the pipeline outside his network?

rows.finding: The co-founder and CTO left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. He retains 720,000 vested common shares, 6.0% today and 3.8% after the round, and whether he is a named inventor on the two licensed university families is not stated in the deck and could not be checked at the patent office. No public footprint or new venture could be retrieved for him.
rows.mechanism: A departed technical founder is a permanent option held by third parties: his shares are vested so there is no forfeiture leverage, his knowledge sits in the licensed families, and California does not let the company restrain where he works.
rows.benchmark: A 26-month vacancy in the role that owns the technical roadmap is unusual at any stage; the plan it leaves behind (a 35% unit-cost cut and a 5.6x fleet increase) is the hardest technical programme the company has attempted.
rows.weakens: The company shipped three hardware generations after he left, so the organisation clearly no longer depends on him day to day; the vacancy may reflect a deliberate decision to run engineering through the VP rather than a failure to hire.
rows.implication: Before closing: confirm every invention assignment from him to the company and to the university, confirm the company holds no repurchase right it has failed to exercise, and check whether he now works for a competitor or a customer; a 3.8% holder with unrestricted vested shares and the core technology in his head is a hireable asset for anyone else.
rows.confidence: High on the vacancy and the dates; low on the circumstances, which only a reference check can settle.
rows.follow_up: What did the departure agreement say about IP assignment, non-solicit and share repurchase, and where is he now?

rows.finding: The VP Engineering joined in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at a single robotics company, progressing from manipulation engineer to engineering manager for grippers. That is a direct match for the bruising and pick-rate problem, and no match at all for the cost-down and fleet-reliability problem that decides 2027.
rows.mechanism: The engineering leader's prior scale becomes the company's ceiling. A gripper programme inside a larger robotics company is a subsystem budget; a 360-robot build with a 35% cost target is a full product and supply-chain programme.
rows.benchmark: Eleven years at one robotics company is a strong retention signal and a narrow one: it means one employer's processes, not a range of builds.
rows.weakens: She has now shipped the v3 into the field in 2026-03 within two years of joining, which is evidence of delivery beyond her prior job title.
rows.implication: The person carrying the 2027 milestone is one level below the executive team with no CTO above her, which concentrates retention risk in an untested equity package: budget a CTO-level hire and a retention grant for her before the round closes.
rows.confidence: Medium-high: dates and employer are from the deck; the scope of her role there is not.
rows.follow_up: What did her gripper programme ship, at what unit cost and volume, and why did she leave after eleven years?

rows.finding: 110 robots are contracted for the 2027 season plus 50 under letters of intent, against a 360-robot plan: 31% of the target is signed or nearly signed five months before the season, and the letters of intent are not binding and are excluded from revenue.
rows.mechanism: Unit cost and volume are the same variable: the v4 cost target is quoted at 500 units, the plan builds 300, and the contracted book supports 110, so the cost curve depends on selling ahead of building.
rows.benchmark: A 360-robot season needs roughly three times the contracted book signed within about four months, sold by one vice president and two founder-sellers.
rows.weakens: Seasonal orders in this industry land late, and the two named growers have already increased their commitment every year since 2024.
rows.implication: Size the 2027 build to the contracted book rather than the plan. At 110 robots the unit cost stays near the $48,000 v3 build, the $31,000 target is not reached at that volume, and the payback case does not close without the 500-unit pricing.
rows.confidence: High: share counts and contract quantities are stated; the sales capacity judgement is mine.
rows.follow_up: What is the conversion rate on letters of intent to date, and what happens to the 2027 plan if only the contracted 110 robots are built?

rows.finding: Every credential in the team table (three degrees for the chief executive, four other degrees, five prior employers and eleven patent filings) rests on the deck alone. No education record, employer page, patent record or press mention could be retrieved for any named executive, and no prior company, exit or board seat outside this company is claimed for anyone.
rows.mechanism: In a private deal the deck is the only evidence the company controls, so every credential is simultaneously the claim and the proof; independent records are the only way to separate them.
rows.benchmark: A Series A team normally shows at least one prior build, exit or scale event across the executive bench; this one shows none, and none of the five degree claims could be verified.
rows.weakens: Nothing in the deck contradicts itself on education or dates, and the career chronology is internally consistent from degree year to employer to founding date.
rows.implication: Treat the team section as unverified until the registries and the patent office confirm it. That is not a reason to decline, but it is a reason not to let the biographies into an investment committee memo as established fact.
rows.confidence: High that nothing was verifiable from this environment; the underlying credentials may well be genuine.
rows.follow_up: Run degree verification through the institutions' registrars and a patent-inventor check before the reference calls.

plan.decision_question: Does this team have the specific capability to take a hand-built pilot fleet to 360 robots in one season?
plan.thesis_sentence: Castellano and Vashti are a credible perception researcher and a credible harvest operator, but the specific capability the 2027 plan needs, building and servicing 360 robots at a 35% lower unit cost, is held by nobody on the executive team: the co-founder CTO who owned it left on 2023-08-31, the seat is still open, and the two people now carrying it have never run a volume build.
plan.why_different: Every other section prices what the company has, this one prices who can build what it does not yet have. The product claims and the market map are only as good as the organisation's ability to ship 360 units and service them in a seven-month season.

plan.comparison_set: What the first three years of the closest harvesting-robotics founding teams produced could not be sourced in this review, so the comparison is stated as an open test rather than a finding; the firm comparison used instead is the company's own progression (14 pilots, 2 paying conversions in 2025, 5 paying growers in 2026, 1 pilot lost) against the 2027 plan and against a 360-unit build capability.

plan.prohibited: strong team, experienced team, world-class, about five, many patents, seasoned

rows.finding: The $12M returns 1.0x only at a $39.4M-41.6M enterprise value once $1.6M of secured fleet debt and 8% transaction costs are deducted; at $25M it is 0.59x and at $12M 0.26x.
rows.mechanism: The $36.77M preference stack ranks behind the Kestrel lien and is reduced by sale costs, so the headline 1x multiple is a gross number.
rows.benchmark: The deck's own statement that the lead is whole at any exit up to $90M, which ignores debt and costs (S95).
rows.weakens: The bear case of 0.6-1.0x, which assumes gross exit proceeds reach the stack intact.
rows.implication: Price the downside off net proceeds and a $40M breakeven, not a $25M one; at $72M pre-money the option is struck about 40% above the level at which capital is returned.
rows.confidence: high; arithmetic on company-provided cap table
rows.follow_up: Obtain the note purchase agreement, seed certificate of designation and Kestrel facility agreement to confirm ranking and any multiple.

rows.finding: Under a 2x senior note the $12M recovers 0.68x at a $40M exit and 0.21x at $25M; under a $10M senior 2028 Series B, 0.69x and 0.31x; if a pay-to-play converts the Series A to common, 0.30x and 0.05x.
rows.mechanism: Ranking and conversion, not the multiple, decide recovery in a modest exit; new money in a down round takes seniority and existing holders either fund pro rata or lose the preference.
rows.benchmark: Down rounds were 11.4% of Carta Q1 2026 rounds and 12.1% of Cooley Q2 2026 deals; pay-to-play appeared in 8.4% (S123).
rows.weakens: The assumption that the deck's equal-rank 1x survives to the exit; a 2028 raise at a $72M+ pre-money is needed to avoid it and 82% of the plan's probability mass misses the plan.
rows.implication: A 45-55% unconditional chance of a down round by 2028, and a 30-40% chance that its terms are senior or pay-to-play, is enough to cut expected value below 1.0x even on the plan's own probabilities.
rows.confidence: medium; structure probabilities are analyst estimates, base rates are sourced
rows.follow_up: Which existing holders have pro-rata rights and will they fund a 2028 round; does the seed charter allow senior ranking.

rows.finding: California is the only state that prohibits autonomous agricultural equipment through Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces; the compromise that would have revised them was dropped from AB 187, passed 2026-08-31, and the Standards Board advisory committee first meets 2026-12-01.
rows.mechanism: A licensing condition, not a cost: without a permissive standard the fleet cannot operate unpiloted; with a per-technician reading, the 1:8 supervision ratio is the exposure and 1:1 takes field service to $24,800 a season against a $16,500 list price.
rows.benchmark: The ESG section treated the rule as a pending trailer bill with a 30-40% spotter risk; the bill is now dead and the prohibition stands (S84 vs S126).
rows.weakens: The 2027 revenue plan, which is 100% California, and the 1:8 field-service assumption inside the 41% gross margin.
rows.implication: This is the one regulatory item that can end the business; 20-25% probability of a material restriction or citation in 2027, impact -70% to -90% of equity value.
rows.confidence: high on the legal position; medium on enforcement probability
rows.follow_up: On what legal basis did 64 robots operate in California in 2026: a variance, an interpretation, or supervision; produce counsel's written opinion.

rows.finding: One counterparty is a $2.5M noteholder (32.2% of $7.77M), a $1.0M investor, the $1.2M-a-year engineering customer (46% of FY2026E revenue), the board observer and the quoted manufacturer of the v4 at 300 x $33,000 = $9.9M.
rows.mechanism: The single input that decides viability is supplied by the party that gains $9.9M of purchase orders and needs the round to close; a 10% error is $3,300 a robot and $825 a season of depreciation, taking contribution at $12,700 from -$1,150 to -$1,975.
rows.benchmark: Related-party revenue is 50% of FY2025 revenue and 46% of FY2026E; no independent director sits on the board that approved $310,000 of payments to the COO's own company.
rows.weakens: Any treatment of the $33,000 build cost as an arm's-length estimate, and therefore the $9.9M capex line and the valuation.
rows.implication: The quote must be replaced by two independent quotes as a condition precedent, and the mark cut for a conflicted single source; a 10-15% price haircut or a staged close, not $72M pre-money.
rows.confidence: high on the facts, which are company-disclosed; medium on the size of any overstatement
rows.follow_up: What is the second and third quote for the v4 bill of materials, and is the manufacturer paid on a cost-plus or fixed-price basis.

rows.finding: A close on 2027-02-15 leaves about $1.9M of cash against a $1.5M covenant floor, three weeks of headroom; a six-month delay puts the floor breach at 2027-03-10, before the April season.
rows.mechanism: The covenant, not insolvency, is the binding constraint; a waiver or bridge follows, and a bridge prices senior or converts at a discount, subordinating the Series A before it is invested.
rows.benchmark: $3.7M at 2026-09-30 less $1.5M leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410,000; the plan needs 300 units ordered before April.
rows.weakens: The base case in which a late close merely shortens the runway; it changes the capital structure and the season.
rows.implication: The closing date is a condition of the investment; the position becomes uninvestable at the first Kestrel waiver request, not at the first missed number.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; medium on build lead time, which the deck does not disclose
rows.follow_up: Kestrel's covenant test date and waiver terms; whether Tallis or Granary has offered a bridge and on what terms.

rows.finding: No registry record was retrievable for any of the three entities, USAspending shows no award against the claimed $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II, no granted patent appears in any retrieved record, and no auditor has seen the accounts.
rows.mechanism: Every figure the decision rests on is management representation: $3.7M cash, the covenant, 110 contracted robots, the licence's affiliate rights, and whether the patents are owned or licensed.
rows.benchmark: A $650,000 prime SBIR Phase II is above the reporting threshold and should appear in USAspending (S91); 80% of FY2025 revenue was pilots, related-party services or grants.
rows.weakens: The reliability of company-provided figures rather than their truth; absence is a confidence ceiling, not proof of misrepresentation.
rows.implication: Close only on a quality-of-earnings review, good-standing certificates, an SBIR award letter and the IP chain of title; without them the $12M is wired on unverified facts.
rows.confidence: high that records were not retrieved; low on what that implies about the company
rows.follow_up: SBIR award number and contracting agency; USPTO assignee and assignment chain; audited or reviewed accounts for FY2025.

rows.finding: The revenue-leading ag-robotics company reached $100M of revenue at about a $548M valuation (roughly 5.5x) and still cut about 49 of 275 roles in October 2026.
rows.mechanism: Later-stage capital is priced off revenue and is rationing even for the category leader, so a 2028 Series B for a company with $4-6M of revenue and a down-round structure is the realistic funding path.
rows.benchmark: Orrin at 36.8x FY2025 revenue and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median (S38, S103).
rows.weakens: The bull case's assumption of a flat-to-up 2028 Series B and a 2029-2031 strategic exit at $100-250M.
rows.implication: Assume the 2028 round is down and structure the preference accordingly; do not rely on a 2028 markup to avoid dilution.
rows.confidence: medium; layoff count from trade press citing GeekWire and Inc
rows.follow_up: What multiple would a 2028 lead pay for $5M of contracted rental revenue with negative contribution.

rows.finding: A 50% smaller market caps 2031 revenue at about $17.7M and a 3-5x exit at $53-88M, or 1.3-2.2x; 30% lower revenue takes the 2028 plan to $9.2M and the exit to $28-46M, or 0.7-1.1x.
rows.mechanism: At the price paid, even a halved market returns capital but not a venture multiple, because the entry multiple already capitalises the full plan.
rows.benchmark: The stated $310M obtainable market requires 132% of US strawberry acreage; 15% adoption in 2031 is $35.4M (S9, S10, S1).
rows.weakens: The bull case's $250M exit, which needs the plan to land and a strategic to pay above listed peers.
rows.implication: There is no market-size scenario in which $72M pre-money produces a 3x without the 2028 plan being exceeded; the price, not the market, is the problem.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; medium on the multiple range
rows.follow_up: What acreage and price does the plan assume per robot-season in 2029-2031.

plan.decision_question: At what exit value and under which preference structure does the $12M come back whole, and what single event makes the position uninvestable regardless of price?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin's cost pool is real but its price is broken: every robot-season it has sold loses money after depreciation, and the three inputs that would fix it are unproven — one of them quoted by a counterparty that profits from it — so Meridian's $12M is more likely to be subordinated than to be multiplied.
plan.why_different: The other sections establish what the company is, sells and is worth; this one prices the ways the $12M is lost, including the structures in which the stated 1x preference does not return capital, and identifies the single binary trigger that ends the business.
plan.mechanism: A capital-intensive lessor whose build cost exceeds the capitalised value of its rental price consumes equity on every unit; the fix (a cheaper build, a higher price, a lower damage rate) is unproven, and the entity that supplies the build-cost number also buys the robots, holds the notes and sells services to the company, so the number is an offer rather than evidence. Preference recovery is then a function of ranking, not of the headline multiple.
plan.comparison_set: United Rentals' 38.0% rental margin after fleet depreciation (S21); Carbon Robotics at about 5.5x revenue on $100M sales and still cutting staff (S125); Down rounds 11.4-12.1% of 2026 rounds and pay-to-play 8.4% of deals (S123); the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were autonomy platforms, harvesting assets sold as IP and team (S96-S99, S93); the Cal/OSHA prohibition and AB 187 failure (S126, S124).
plan.counter_evidence: Four growers did contract 110 robots for 2027 at the renewal price, so the product is not rejected; a v4 at $31,000-33,000 makes contribution positive at list (S1); an AEWR reinstatement would raise growers' hand cost by $4,506 an acre and help pricing (S80); the states outside California may permit autonomous equipment (S126).
plan.visual: A waterfall table of the lead's recovery at $40M, $25M and $12M under four structures, plus a ten-row risk matrix ranked by probability and impact.
plan.prohibited: risks are manageable, well positioned, strong team, high barriers to entry, fierce competition, clear business model, huge market, about 5/many patents/experienced team, any sentence about how the section is written, bot or tool names.

rows.finding: Global agtech venture investment fell from a 2021 peak of $53bn to $7bn in 2025 (-87%), and 18 agtech startups shut down in 2025 across four continents, including firms with field-validated technology and more than $650M raised.
rows.mechanism: Capital-intensive hardware adoption outruns the funding market that must carry it; when the next round is not available, a negative-contribution lease book converts a technology success into a shutdown.
rows.benchmark: 2021 agtech peak of $53bn; 18 shutdowns in one year.
rows.weakens: The premise that field validation or a large prior raise protects an entrant; Orrin's own $1.9M revenue and nine-month runway sit inside this distribution.
rows.implication: The round must be priced so that a 2028 raise is optional, not required; at $72M pre-money it is required.
rows.confidence: medium - single aggregator, consistent with PitchBook and CropLife counts.
rows.follow_up: How many of the 18 were hardware and how many had raised a Series A or later?

rows.finding: Agtech venture funding fell to $1bn across 143 deals in Q2 2026, from $1.5bn in Q1 2026 and $2bn a year earlier, while robotics M&A heated up as funding cooled.
rows.mechanism: A shrinking check market pushes hardware companies toward trade sales earlier and at lower prices than the venture plan assumes.
rows.benchmark: $2bn a year earlier; $1.5bn in Q1 2026.
rows.weakens: Any assumption that a 2028 Series B clears at or above the 2026 mark.
rows.implication: Plan the exit as a 2029-2031 trade sale, not a 2028 up-round; that caps the multiple the $90M post-money can earn.
rows.confidence: medium - PitchBook report summary, not the underlying data.
rows.follow_up: What is the median late-stage agtech round size and step-up in 2026?

rows.finding: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, roughly four times the $87M post-money valuation of its last private round; Blue River was a perception and see-and-spray company with about 60 staff, not a harvesting-robot company.
rows.mechanism: Strategic buyers pay for a perception platform that fits an existing machine line, not for a fleet of leased harvesters; the multiple is earned by the last private round, not by the acquirer's revenue.
rows.benchmark: ~4x the last private post-money; $87M post-money in 2015 against Orrin's $90M post in 2026.
rows.weakens: The bull case's 2.8x on a $250M trade sale: the best ag-robotics outcome on record produced about 4x for its last private holders, and Orrin starts eleven years later at the same post-money.
rows.implication: A $250M exit at a $90M post is a good outcome, not a base case; the price should assume a ~4x ceiling for a successful platform sale.
rows.confidence: high - investor announcement of the deal and the prior round.
rows.follow_up: What revenue and fleet did Bear Flag have at its $250M Deere sale in 2021?

rows.finding: A scaled equipment lessor earns 35.8% rental gross margin in general rentals and 40.3% in specialty rentals after fleet depreciation, and its margin moves inversely with depreciation as a share of revenue.
rows.mechanism: Rental economics are set by depreciation and utilisation, so a lessor that reports gross margin before fleet depreciation reports a number that cannot be compared with the industry.
rows.benchmark: 35.8-40.3% after depreciation for United Rentals, 2025.
rows.weakens: Orrin's reported 41% gross margin, which charges fleet depreciation in operating expense; after it, FY2027 plan margin is -5.5%.
rows.implication: Score unit economics on contribution after depreciation and debt service, not on the reported gross margin.
rows.confidence: high - company results release.
rows.follow_up: What utilisation and rental rate does United Rentals need to hold 35-40% through a downturn?

rows.finding: US utilized production of the 21 estimated noncitrus fruit crops was 15.8 million tons in 2025, down 1% on 2024, with strawberries the third-largest by utilized production.
rows.mechanism: The addressable crop base is flat, so the service market grows only through penetration and price, not through a growing orchard of demand.
rows.benchmark: 2024 utilized production; strawberries third of 21 crops.
rows.weakens: The deck's adoption curve, which needs 15% of US acreage by 2031 to reach $310M of obtainable market.
rows.implication: Value the company on penetration of a fixed cost pool, not on market growth.
rows.confidence: high - USDA NASS annual summary.
rows.follow_up: What were California and Florida strawberry acreage and value for 2025 in the state-level tables?

plan.decision_question: Is a $12M lead ticket at a $72M pre-money an attractive risk-adjusted investment in Orrin Fieldworks, and what price or structure would make it one?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin has found a real $79,288-an-acre harvest cost pool and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that assigns probabilities, states the price at which the case turns, and makes the decision rule; the other sections supply the facts it prices.
plan.mechanism: Lessor economics: contribution per robot-season is price minus service cost minus depreciation on build cost. At $9,500 signed and $48,000 v3 build, contribution is -$8,100; the price must rise to $17,600 or the build must fall to $28,400 at the $12,700 renewal to break even. Because depreciation is per season of use, utilisation cannot fix it, and because the preference stack is 1x pari passu at $36.77M behind $1.6M of fleet debt, the lead is whole only above a ~$40M exit.
plan.comparison_set: Blue River (Deere, 2017, $305M = ~4x its $87M last-round post-money), Bear Flag (Deere, 2021, $250M), Tortuga and Advanced Farm (IP-and-team sales, undisclosed), 18 agtech shutdowns in 2025, agtech VC down 87% from $53bn (2021) to $7bn (2025), United Rentals 35.8-40.3% rental gross margin after depreciation.
plan.counter_evidence: Harvest CROO publicly claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida on 2025-04-24, so the 'only above 90%' premise is contested; four growers contracted 110 robots for 2027 at the renewal price, so buyers do accept the quality; at a $31,000-33,000 build contribution turns positive at the $16,500 list ($2,650-3,150 a season); $4.0M of insiders are committing at the mark.
plan.visual: scenarios component (Bull/Base/Bear with probabilities and returns) and analogs component (Blue River, Bear Flag, Tortuga/Advanced Farm, Monarch, Abundant).
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, about 5, many patents, experienced team; no labels such as 'Investor implication:' or 'Economic mechanism:'.

plan.decision_question: What score, rating and position size does the evidence support for Meridian at $72M pre-money, and what would change them?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin scores in the bottom third of the venture scale on every dimension that is priced by cash: a defensible product in a real cost pool, against a unit economics, funding and structure profile that at $72M pre-money offers capital preservation at best, so the recommendation is pass at the mark and re-engage at $50-58M with a 1.5x preference and a staged close.

user_data_requests.database: SBIR.gov award database (and the USDA NIFA SBIR Phase II award record)
user_data_requests.query: Award(s) to Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (Salinas, California; also check Orrin Fleet Services LLC): award number, agency and programme (USDA SBIR Phase II), obligation and total amount, period of performance, and the project title. The deck cites a $650,000 Phase II award over 2024-2026 and grant revenue of $0.80M cumulatively across FY2023-FY2026E.
user_data_requests.why: A USAspending recipient-name search returned zero federal awards on 2026-10-30, so either the award sits under another legal name, is a subaward, or the grant revenue line is not federal money. Grant revenue is 13% of FY2026E revenue and disappears from FY2027P onward, and any federal funding also triggers Bayh-Dole obligations on the licensed university patents, including the US manufacturing preference. Verification changes both the revenue quality and the IP risk.
user_data_requests.how: Search awards at sbir.gov/awards by firm name and by state; cross-check the USDA NIFA SBIR Phase II award list. A screenshot or export of the award record is sufficient.

user_data_requests.database: US DOL Office of Foreign Labor Certification — H-2A disclosure data and AEWR state table (flag.dol.gov)
user_data_requests.query: Certified H-2A positions and employers by state (California, Florida) and SOC code 45-2092 (farmworkers and labourers, crops) for programme years 2019-2026, plus the official AEWR state table published with 91 FR 48946 (California and Florida, Skill Level I and II, before and after the housing adjustment).
user_data_requests.why: This is the size and price of the labour pool the robot competes against. The certified-position count tells us whether H-2A is a binding constraint for California and Florida berry growers (which supports adoption) or whether growers can simply certify more workers (which caps the robot's price). The official wage table is the single input to the grower's hand-harvest cost per acre; the DOL wage page returned HTTP 503 on 2026-10-30 and the rates used in the report are taken from a secondary report of the notice.
user_data_requests.how: Download the quarterly H-2A disclosure files at flag.dol.gov/performance-data/performance-data-downloads (no login, but the site was unreachable from here) and the AEWR spreadsheet linked from flag.dol.gov/wage-data/adverse-effect-wage-rates. A CSV export of the two states and SOC code is enough.

user_data_requests.database: USPTO Patent Assignment Search and Patent Center; the university licence agreement in the data room
user_data_requests.query: Chain of title for the two licensed patent families (stereo ripeness model, docket CU-2017-031, US patent granted 2020; berry-stem localisation, docket CU-2019-114, US patent granted 2022): patent numbers, recorded assignments from the university to Orrin Fieldworks, Inc., and whether the underlying inventions were made with federal funding. Also the executed licence: exclusivity field, the 100-robot test wording, cure rights, the royalty and minimum, and any federal-agency waiver under 35 U.S.C. 204.
user_data_requests.why: Three things turn on these documents. First, whether the licence's US rights are exclusive at all, which is the moat the $72M pre-money is priced on. Second, whether 35 U.S.C. 204's US manufacturing preference binds, because the company assembles grippers and harnesses in Guadalajara. Third, whether the 2027-12-31 robot-count test has a cure period; on the deck's own plan the company is at 75 paid robot-seasons against a 100-robot threshold. The licensor cannot be searched by name, so only the data room or the patent record settles this.
user_data_requests.how: USPTO Patent Assignment Search (assignment.uspto.gov) by assignee and by patent number; Patent Center for the two patents' prosecution and government-interest statements (the "Government Support" clause on the face of the patent). From the company: the licence agreement and any agency waiver letter.

user_data_requests.database: California Legislative Information (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) — 2026 trailer bill on autonomous farm equipment
user_data_requests.query: The bill number, author, committee and status of the 2026 draft trailer bill reported on 2026-08-25 as allowing unpiloted farm machines to work alongside farmworkers, and the text of any labour-relations or safety conditions it would impose (spacing, human oversight, notification, liability).
user_data_requests.why: This is the only identified state-level rule that would govern whether the robot may run unattended beside a crew, which is the operating model the unit economics assume (one technician per eight robots, remote supervision). If the bill fails or is amended to require a human spotter per machine, the field-service line of $3,100 a robot-season roughly doubles and the 41% gross margin goes with it. The news article body was blocked, so the bill itself must be read.
user_data_requests.how: Search leginfo.legislature.ca.gov for 2026 bills by subject (food and agriculture, labour) or by keyword "autonomous" or "unpiloted"; the Assembly and Senate agriculture and labour committee agendas for August 2026 will name it.

user_data_requests.query: Federal awards to Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (Salinas, California; Delaware corporation formed 2021-09-14): the USDA SBIR Phase II award of $650,000 said to run 2024-2026, its award number, obligation dates and whether the recipient is the parent or Orrin Fleet Services LLC; any other federal grant or contract since 2021.
user_data_requests.why: Grant revenue is $0.30M of FY2025 revenue (15.8%) and $0.35M of FY2026E; cumulative disclosed grant revenue of $0.80M exceeds the single $650,000 award, and a public search on 2026-10-30 found no federal record for the company. If the grant cannot be verified, 16% of FY2025 revenue and 13% of FY2026E revenue rest on an unaudited company claim, which lowers confidence in the revenue base and in the non-dilutive funding assumption in the plan.
user_data_requests.how: Search SBIR.gov's award database by firm name and by the USDA agency, and USAspending.gov's recipient search by legal name and UEI; export the award summary page with award number, amount, period of performance and recipient address. A screenshot or PDF of the award record is enough.

user_data_requests.database: California Secretary of State UCC filings; Delaware Division of Corporations; California Secretary of State business search
user_data_requests.query: UCC-1 financing statements naming Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. or Orrin Fleet Services LLC as debtor (secured party Kestrel Equipment Finance), including collateral description, filing date and continuation; the Delaware corporate record for Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (file number, status, officers) and the California LLC record for Orrin Fleet Services LLC (entity number, status, manager, statement of information).

top_three: Sections 1 and 2: label every company-only statement (entity structure, Kestrel lien, cap table, board, every credential) as unverified in the tables as well as the prose, add the public patent-inventor record, and state the confidence ceiling where no registry or registrar record exists.

1.name: Completeness sweep
1.notes: Completeness sweep against the lens checklist. Strong across 3-14: legal entities with dates and roles, cap table by class, preference stack, dated timeline, per-product tables, patent table with numbers and status, regional market table, competitor table with hand crews and Agrobot, unit-economics matrix, funding history, exit routes and precedents, red-team risk matrix with probabilities. Sections 3-14 sit at 8,400-9,000 characters with source columns throughout, which is the right depth. Answer to the Lead's question on the report-level "no key assumptions or sensitivity analysis" finding: the substance exists (section 11 ranked assumptions table, section 14 sensitivity component) but the impact column in both is expressed as contribution per robot-season, revenue or a single MOIC delta, not as equity value or lead MOIC across the whole table, so the checker cannot read a sensitivity in the units of the recommendation. Treat the finding as a presentation defect, not a missing analysis: add a MOIC/value column to the section 14 sensitivity table and name the component explicitly. Also: S1 and S7 in the register are the same 15-page deck, so the second ID cannot be used to reach the 4-source floor in sections 1 and 2.

2.name: Claim verification
2.notes: Claim-by-claim. Compliant: the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising, 86% uptime, $48,000/$33,000 build costs, $3.2M ARR and 110 contracted robots are all labelled company-reported and unverified with the status named; the derived figures (1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours, -$8,100 contribution, 12.31-season payback, 36.8x revenue, 132% of US acreage for the $310M SOM) are reproducible arithmetic from stated inputs and are marked as calculations. Independent anchors are real and well chosen: UC Central Coast 2024 budget, USDA AMS terminal prices, California acreage (43,726 in 2026), United Rentals' 38.0% rental margin after fleet depreciation, five listed ag-equipment peers at a 2.3x median, Blue River and Bear Flag, Advanced Farm and Tortuga, Carta and Cooley down-round rates. Stale but disclosed: Harvest CROO's April 2025 parity claim is company-issued and 18 months old; the 2024 UC cost study is the latest available. Single-source and unstated: the June 2025 Ventura enforcement figure (up to 70% of workers absent) rests on one news report; the $79,288-an-acre harvest cost is read from a secondary summary of the UC study (S10, medium confidence) rather than the study itself. Not verifiable in-run and properly filed as user data requests: SBIR award (U1, U5), H-2A and AEWR tables (U2), USPTO chain of title (U3), California bill text (U4), UCC and entity records (U6, U10), data room (U7, U8), 2027 order book (U9). Register hygiene: S1 and S7 are the same 15-page deck under two IDs and must not be counted as two sources.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: Present and adequate: hand crews as the real competitor with the piece-rate economics; Agrobot's harvest-aid platform as the cheap half-measure; the 2021-2025 cohort failures (Abundant, Root AI, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Monarch, FarmWise) with dated outcomes; CNH, Kubota, Deere and AGCO as acquirers rather than competitors; Tallis as the conflicted counterparty. Candidly absent rather than glossed: no public market shares exist and the section says so, using paid robot-seasons as the proxy. The open-source question does not apply to a mechanical harvester in the way it does to software, but the academic-spin-out question does, because the reading model is the licensed asset.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: The five questions answered as the report stands. Hardest thing about selling: not price - the fee is 3.4-5.9% of a $79,288-an-acre harvest cost - but fruit quality and reliability, which is the mechanism behind the single documented loss (Grower E, Plant City, 2026-06, bruising) and behind Grower B cutting 22 robots to 14. Budget owner: the grower's harvest-labour line; the report asserts it and does not evidence it, and the buyer-versus-user split (the crew the robot displaces) is drawn well. Sales cycle: undocumented; the only data points are 14 pilots since 2024, 2 conversions in 2025, 5 paying growers in 2026, and a 2027 book of 110 contracted plus 50 letters of intent against a 360-robot plan, 31% five months before the season. Why adoption is not faster: well answered at the product level (3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA serious-damage allowance; 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5) and at the market level (the OEWS wage-floor cut lowered the grower's alternative cost by 17.6-23% in 2026). Lost deals: one loss documented, the alternative chosen not stated - this is the gap the item addresses. Strongest PMF evidence in the report: five growers paying, a renewal average of $12,700 (+33.7%) and four growers contracting 110 robots for 2027, one of them 40 robots at the COO's former employer. Weakest: 53% of 2026 paid seasons in two named growers, one of them an insider relationship, which the report states plainly.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Stress arithmetic checked. (1) The section 10 waterfall is internally consistent: lead's share of net proceeds is 12/36.77 = 32.6% (two thirds of an A class taking its pro rata of a 36.77 stack), so $40M gives (40 - 1.6) × 0.92 × 0.326 = 0.96x, $25M gives 0.59x, $12M gives 0.26x, and the 1.0x floor sits at 41.6/39.4 - all reproduced. (2) Expected return reproduced: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.35 = 0.94x, and Kelly is negative on b = 1.2/0.65 with p = 0.18. (3) 30%-worse tests: build at $62,400 takes contribution at the signed price from -$8,100 to -$11,700 and makes the licence test irrelevant; a 30% throughput miss (0.7 rather than 1.0 acres per 24 hours) needs 107 robots where 75 are sold and 882 acres for the $8M ARR the 360-robot plan claims, which is the most damaging single miss because it hits revenue per capital unit and the licence test together; a 30% lower exit takes $100M to 0.77x and $25M to 0.41x. None of these reverses Pass, which is why the rating survives. (4) Other figures spot-checked and correct: 36.8x on $69.9M/$1.9M, 49.9x on $1.4M, 132% of US acreage for the $310M SOM, 21,800 ripe berries an acre at 60 passes, 12.31-season payback, 3.08 seasons needed to cover depreciation at the signed price, 9,000 trays × $11 = $990 an acre per point of cull, 2-of-8 base rate, and the $5.71M pool cost. (5) Figures given as single-source and accepted because the section labels them: the $33,000 v4 quote, the $3,100 field-service line, the 86% uptime and the 2.5%-of-revenue licence royalty. (6) Not tested for lack of a public data point: whether the Kestrel interest is 11.5% fixed and whether the amortisation is straight-line over four seasons; both are stated as company figures with the alternative cash view given.

## 5分钟速读 Executive Briefing

Meridian should pass at the $72M pre-money. Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the field and a real harvest cost pool to sell into, but at the $9,500 a robot-season growers signed and the $48,000 build the company can evidence (company-reported, unverified), every unit loses $8,100 before debt service, and the round prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund: the $12M cheque returns 1.04x on the plan's own probabilities — capital preservation over a five-year hold, with the 1.0x floor holding down to a $39.4-41.6M exit — and 2x only at a $180M exit. ### What is good, and what decides it

The pain is real and independently measured: hand-pick labour runs $21,056-23,949 an acre-season on the report's own yield and piece rate, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is 11-13% of that bill. Four facts outweigh that. One robot-season loses $8,100 at the signed price, and the $33,000 build that would fix it is a single quote from a counterparty that is also noteholder, customer, board observer and investor. Bruising at 3.8% has already cost one grower and spends most of the USDA allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. The team is built for the problem Orrin had in 2021, not the one it has in 2027. Every degree, date, employer and patent count here is company-reported and unverified: no registrar, employer or patent-inventor record was retrievable, so the people-risk score is critical on unverified credentials, not medium [S1].

### The pairing fits two problems and misses the third

The combination matches the first two problems a picking robot has to solve — seeing ripe fruit, and being allowed onto a farm — and not the third, making 360 of them. Castellano invents and raises: the licensed families come out of her lab, the company holds five filings, and she is the face of the raise. Vashti sells and operates: five paying growers in 2026, four contracted for 2027, the two named ones taking 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons, and the largest is the farm where he was harvest operations director from 2014 to 2021, contracted for 40 robots in 2027. That is commercial proof and its limit: the funnel is one man's twenty-year network, and the plan needs 250 more in a four-month window. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### A CTO seat empty for 26 months

The co-founder and CTO, Dr. Soren Abernathy, left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. He keeps 720,000 vested common shares — 6.0% before the round, 3.8% after — a permanent cap-table party without a reason to protect it. A patent-register search under the company's name on 2026-10-30 returned no Orrin assignee record and no inventor list for the two licensed families or five company filings; unpublished applications are not public for 18 months, so this is a gap, not a contradiction, but the deck's claim that he is a named inventor cannot be verified. The licensed families sit in the university's name, so an Orrin assignee search would miss them. No public footprint or new venture found. A 3.8% holder with unrestricted shares and the core perception work in his head is hireable by any competitor; California does not let the company restrain where he works. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The technical bet sits one level below the executive team

Dr. Mei Hollander joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at one robotics company, moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — company-reported, unverified. That matches the bruising problem — 3.8% of berries damaged in the 2025 pilots, one Florida grower gone in 2026-06 — and not the problem that decides 2027: cutting the build from $48,000 to a $33,000 average while multiplying the fleet by 5.6. With no CTO above her, the hardest programme sits with one vice president hired 32 months ago, on an undisclosed equity package. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### Selling 360 robots with one new sales leader

Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales in 2025-06 after twenty years at a crop-inputs company, ending as regional sales director for the West: sixteen months in robotics, unverified. The 2027 book is 110 robots contracted plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, 31% of the 360-robot plan five months before the season, with two founder-sellers and one VP to close the gap. The risk is not product rejection; this industry buys late, the season opens in April in California and December in Florida, and a 360-unit build must be committed before the orders exist. No stage pipeline is shown. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### What would settle it

Three records would turn biography into evidence; none was retrievable: degree checks through each registrar, patent-inventor records for the eleven claimed filings and the five company filings, and reference calls at the four prior employers. The peer record shows why the hires matter. Their first-three-year metrics could not be retrieved, so the comparison is one of outcomes, not like-for-like execution. Against the company's own history, the fleet went from 12 robots in 2024 to 64 in 2026, a 5.3x over two seasons, while the plan asks for 5.6x in one season and a one-third cost cut. People risk should therefore be priced: a CTO, a manufacturing leader and a retention grant for the VP Engineering are closing conditions, not intentions. The implication is that people risk is a condition precedent, not a diligence note. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

## 技术与产品 Technology & Product

The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position is a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure, not a picked-acre figure. Compared with Harvest CROO, the unit arithmetic is identical and the acreage eight times higher, so coverage follows capital per machine, not a better algorithm [S1, S27].

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the week in which a bruise expresses itself. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling. [S1, S120]**

Packers work to a lot-level allowance for total defects, serious damage and decay rather than a per-machine one, and a bruise that appears after a week in the cooler is still the grower's loss.

## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis

The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

### One acre-season, three figures that reconcile
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces: one acre-season is 9,000 trays (72,000 lb, the 8-lb flat of the UC budget), $21,056-23,949 of hand-pick labour and $79,288 of total harvest cost; hand-pick labour is 27-30% of that, and the rest — packing materials, supervision, hauling and cooling — is not what the robot displaces. The labour figure has two independent supports that agree: 1,280 picker-hours an acre-season (four picker-days a pass, company estimate, over 40 passes at eight hours) at the 2026 California adverse effect wage rates of $16.45 and $18.71 an hour is $21,056-23,949, and 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 a tray is $15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% payroll burden, the same range. There are 9,000 trays, not 1,125: reading a tray as eight flats understates the wage bill eight-fold, to $2,000-2,500. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill; at the $16,500 list, $4,714, or 20-22%. A 10% harvest-cost saving is worth $7,929 an acre, so the grower's payback survives the list price; what binds is quality and capital, not the size of the wage bill [S10, S12, S80, S1].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception. California holds four of Orrin's five paying growers in 2026 and Florida one; four of the five have contracted 110 robots for 2027. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia [S9, S13, S14].

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin before it moved for it. The Department of Labor's 2025-10-02 interim final rule — the wage-floor policy — replaced the Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate; its 2026 rates were $16.45 and $18.71 an hour in California and $12.47 and $15.06 in Florida, below the rates they replaced, and on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the methodology unlawful and ordered a replacement, so a higher California rate is more likely than not in 2027. The risk cuts both ways: a lower Florida floor lengthens payback, a California reversal shortens it. H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024: the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the 40 passes and 3.5-acre density behind the robot count; the final 2027 California and Florida rates after the court order; and the share of California acreage in tabletop [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021; Traptic, a strawberry picker, was acquired in 2022 (reported). The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: the v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30 [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a tray at 8-12 trays an hour; hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving — unverified, but it captures part of the saving with no autonomy or bruising risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: a picking arm on an existing platform is cheaper than a fleet. Orrin charges $2,714 an acre at $9,500 and $4,714 at the $16,500 list, 11-22% of the hand-pick bill; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field architecture and RaaS model, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published performance data and no California service network, where Orrin has five paying growers in 2026, four of which contracted 110 robots for 2027. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct clamshell packing, a 3.8% bruising rate on its test rows and the COO's California grower relationships: a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly. Waseda University's Sugano Lab with Maekawa runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated beds; Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked robot at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success; Washington State University has built a hidden-fruit picker — all research, no commercial open-field deployment and no published price, so none sets a ceiling on the $16,500 list today, though the perception stack is being solved in public and erodes the licensed families' value when the Calder licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31 [S30, S1, S139, S135, S137, S134].

## 商业模式 Business Model

On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a $31,000 build not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. Five growers paid in 2026; four contracted 110 robot-seasons for 2027 at a $12,700 average, and the fifth is in discussion. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. No new grower has signed for 2027; the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher: real demand from four accounts, none a new logo [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows the first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. The buying unit includes the marketer or packer, not only the grower: the robot packs straight into retail clamshells, so whoever sells or packs the fruit must accept machine-picked berries, and the 3.8% bruising that ended Grower E's pilot shows acceptance can be lost after a field trial. Whether a marketer's acceptance is a contract condition, and who signs — owner, VP of growing or procurement — is not disclosed; executed contracts and the packer's fruit specification would settle both. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost; grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine 2025 test farms, about $30,000 paid a pilot farm against $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost leaves $23,000-$40,000 unrecovered per pilot and $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. No lapsed account is disclosed buying a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 11-13% of hand-pick labour at the signed price and 20-22% at list, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there. Tortuga deployed 150 harvesting robots and about $50M over eight years before selling its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03; FarmWise raised $65M, ran Titan as a service, moved Vulcan to dealer sales and wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms in 2025-04. Orrin's $320,313 per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000. The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. For an investor, the signed book is $1.4M of 2027 rental; the $16,500 list and $31,000 v4 must be proven before paying for fleet capex. Conditions: executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, an independent v4 bill of materials, a service-cost build at 1:8 and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence; the pilot-cost estimate is medium; open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and marketer acceptance (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S93, S100, S116].

**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The only disclosed $100M+ ag-robotics exits are Deere's purchases of Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), both autonomy platforms. Orrin's $90M post is above every disclosed harvesting-robot mark and near Blue River's 2015 $87M post-money, eleven years earlier. [S105, S28, S94, S144]

### A $12M close improves the price and weakens the plan, while the preference delays the upside

The $18M target has only $4.0M committed and a $12M minimum (company-provided, unverified). At $12M the post-money is $84M, the lead owns 14.29% and the preference stack falls to $30.77M; the 2027 plan spends $9.9M of the $18M on 300 robots at a $33,000 average, so $12M funds about 200 robots, the 360-robot and $8M ARR milestones slip and a 2028 down round becomes the base case. At $16M — the lead's $12M plus the $4.0M committed — the post-money is $88M and the lead owns 13.64%. The company has $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly burn, nine months of runway to June 2027, so the close must land in Q1 2027 to order robots for the 2027 season. On the full round the 1x preference returns the $12M in full at $40M, $60M and $90M; only above $90M does the lead participate — $20.0M at $150M (1.7x), $33.3M at $250M (2.8x) — while common and options receive $1.6M at $40M, $21.6M at $60M and $47.1M at $90M after the $1.6M debt. To return 3x in five years the company must be worth $270M at exit, which at a 3-5x revenue multiple requires $54-90M of revenue — four to seven times the 2028 plan. The price is defensible only if the 2027 milestones are met and a strategic buyer pays above the listed peer multiples; the diligence questions are the note schedule and seed charter, the 2027 order book and deposits, the option-pool refresh policy, and the source of the $6M of unfilled Series A. ## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy

The plan does not add up on its own numbers, which are company-stated and unverified. At the current $48,000 build even the 2027 list price leaves each robot-season $1,100 short over a four-season life, the v4 must land below $28,400 to earn its keep at the $12,700 renewal price, the company's own FY2027 revenue projection implies an average price of $12,778 rather than the $16,500 list, and a 5.6-times fleet increase by April 2027 rests on one outsourced build quote and a $14M gap in a round that has not closed [S1].

### The price rise is a solvency requirement, not a margin story

At $5,600 a season of reported, unverified field service, transport, insurance and consumables, a robot priced at the $12,700 renewal average can cost at most $28,400 and still repay itself over four seasons; the v4 budget is $33,000. Priced at the $16,500 list it can cost $43,600 and still repay, which the $48,000 v3 does not. The gap is not theoretical: on the reported costs each robot-season at the renewal price loses $4,900, so a 360-robot fleet at the 2027 revenue line of $4.6M loses $1.76M a season before a dollar of overhead, and even the $33,000 v4 turns positive only if service cost also falls to the $1,750 target. Depreciation sits in operating expenses rather than cost of revenue, so the reported 52 percent gross margin for 2027 excludes $3.24M of hardware consumption on a $4.6M revenue line, alongside $2.02M of service cost, against total gross profit of $2.9M. The payback figure that carries the story uses the best case at every input: at a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, 2.1 seasons is right, but at the $5,600 the company reports, unverified, for 2026, payback stretches to 2.8 seasons at that build and 4.4 seasons at today's $48,000, longer than the four-season life the same page assumes. The gap between $1,750 and $5,600 is $3,850 a robot-season, $1.386M across 360 robots, and no cost bridge is disclosed for it [S1].

### A price that is too low to be replacing a hand crew

The pricing question runs the other way from the usual one. At $9,500 for the 3.5 acres a robot serves, a grower pays $2,714 an acre a season; the 2027 list is $4,714 an acre. The California Strawberry Commission puts the cost to cultivate and harvest strawberries at an average $87,000 an acre, $15.34 a tray, rising to $17.73 a tray in 2023, so Orrin's asking price is between 3 and 5 percent of the total cost of the crop [S1, S121]. A machine that replaced the hand crew over 3.5 acres would be worth several times that, and five growers buying 75 robot-seasons would not have left it on the table. Either the robot harvests a small fraction of the fruit on the acres it drives, or the price was set to buy pilots and the 2027 increase is the first real test of willingness to pay. Grower B cutting from 22 robots to 14 and Grower E exiting over bruising say the test is live; the two letters of intent for 50 robots are not contracts.

### Peers that carried the asset did not survive it

RaaS makes Orrin the lessor: at 64 robots it carries $3.07M of fleet on its balance sheet, at 360 $17.28M at the v3 build or $11.88M at the v4 budget, funded by $18M of equity and a $2.5M secured facility. Five of six comparable companies did not hold that position. Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP to CNH; Tortuga moved to a per-kilogram service and sold its IP and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025; Monarch raised a $133M Series C at a reported valuation above $500M in 2024, cut staff, and had its assets bought by Caterpillar in April 2026 after failing to pivot to software services; Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021; FarmWise moved from a per-acre Titan service to selling through Vulcan dealers. Carbon Robotics, which sells machines and raised a $70M Series D, is the exception. The same arithmetic that makes RaaS hard for Orrin is why growers like it, and the base rate says the model is financeable only if the fleet turns fast: 75 paid robot-seasons from 5 growers in 2026 against 360 planned in 2027, with 53 percent of 2026 seasons in two named customers, one of them the chief operating officer's former employer [S1, S28, S93, S97, S109, S116, S122].

### What must be true in twelve months

Three things. The round closes by 2026-12-15 so that build slots and deposits are in place for an April 2027 season; the v4 reaches $33,000 or less on a second and third quote, because at $48,000 the fleet consumes its own gross profit; and at least one grower renews at or near the $16,500 list after a season with an independently measured pick rate and damage rate. The signposts are dated and checkable: a signed 2027 contract at list price, a second contract-manufacturing quote, the v4 first-article build date, and whether the 100-robot licence test is met by robots in commercial service rather than robots built. Against $3.7M of cash, $410,000 of monthly net burn and a $1.5M cash covenant, usable runway is 5.4 months; a close in January 2027 makes 360 robots impossible and puts the licence cliff at risk [S1, S91].

Two limitations bound this judgement. The v4 unit cost is a single unverified quote and the service-cost target has no disclosed bridge from the reported figure, so the margin case cannot be tested from outside; and the public record returns no federal award to the company, which contradicts the SBIR revenue line in the plan.

The mechanism is a lessor whose build cost exceeds the value of its price: equity is consumed on every unit and the preference decides who absorbs it. ### One counterparty, five roles

Tallis Agricultural Machinery holds $2.5M of the $7.77M notes (32.2%), commits $1.0M to this round, buys $1.2M a year of engineering (46% of FY2026E revenue), sits as board observer, and supplies the $33,000 quote behind 300 units and $9.9M of orders (company-reported). One counterparty touches $14.6M of the round and supplies the number that decides viability. A 10% error is $3,300 a unit and $825 a season of depreciation, taking contribution at $12,700 from -$1,150 to -$1,975; at $44,000 the $16,500 list price stops covering depreciation. The chief operating officer's own services company took $310,000 in 2025-2026, about two-thirds of the season's field-service line, on a contract approved by a board he sits on; at a 25% premium the leakage is $62,000. With the independent seat vacant, Meridian cannot carry a related-party resolution alone. The quote is an offer, not evidence: $50-58M with two independent quotes, not $72M. [S1, S95]

### The rule that actually breaks the model

California alone prohibits autonomous agricultural equipment, through Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces; the fix died when AB 187 passed on 2026-08-31, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01, so no rule can change before the 2027 season. Both readings are fatal: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season; if the fleet sits outside it, one citation ends a season that is all of the 2026 revenue. The probability of a material restriction or enforcement action in 2027 is 20% to 25%, with -70% to -90% of equity value. The tariff is likelier and less fatal: the 2026-10-28 proclamation found a threat, imposed nothing and set a Commerce-USTR report within 180 days — 2027-04-26, six days before the season — and a 25% duty is $8,250 a robot, $2.48M on 300 and a 75-robot smaller fleet at 30-35%. Non-USMCA origin at 10% costs $3,300 a robot, 85% of gross profit, with origin undocumented at 40%; Bayh-Dole US manufacture would cost $1,500-3,000 a robot to reshore if a licensed family was federally funded, at 30-40%. The wage floor helps at 60-70% odds but cannot fix bruising. [S126, S124, S88, S89, S85]

### Absence is a finding, not proof

No registry entry, no federal award against the grant the deck describes, no granted patent and no auditor's opinion: the inference is not misrepresentation but that every fact the decision turns on is management representation. Absence proves less than it seems: registries sit behind paywalls, applications stay unpublished for eighteen months, subawards appear on no federal site. It proves enough — the money would be wired on unverified facts, a condition-precedent problem before a price problem.

**The model-breaker is the California equipment prohibition, not the tariff.** California alone bars autonomous agricultural equipment, the fix died on 2026-08-31, and the committee does not sit until 2026-12-01. Both readings end the investment: one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season, and a citation stops the only revenue line. [S126, S124]

## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis

Orrin has found a real harvest bill — $21,056-23,949 an acre-season of hand-pick labour — and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season on 9,000 trays at a $1.75-2.25 piece rate plus burden. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026: the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, making the deck's urgency a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at realistic fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying perception for its sprayer line, not a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

The exit pays for the perception asset or the team, not the lease book: a buyer prices the dataset and the grower relationships and treats a leased fleet as a liability. Because the fee sits below the cost of the asset, each additional robot moves value from equity to the grower, so growth enlarges the loss; the preference then decides whether that loss lands on the founder, the noteholder or this fund. For Meridian the implication is to decline at this mark and keep the diligence warm: both documents are cheap and would reprice the same asset.

### Policy, holding period and what would change the answer

Deere, AGCO, CNH and Kubota have closed ag-tech deals without a public CFIUS objection; a Chinese buyer would face CFIUS review of the perception model, license and grower data, and Mexico assembly adds tariff diligence. At the $90M post-money the lead gets 1.1x at $100M (1.0x after dilution), 1.7x at $150M (1.4x) and 2.8x at $250M (2.2x); over five years that is 0% IRR at $100M, 17.1% at $250M and -10.0% at the $25M bear.
